title: Educación, clave para la justicia social: ministra de Igualdad Racial de Brasil
content:
Rachel Barros de Oliveira resaltó en conferencia magistral el papel central de las acciones afirmativas
Miércoles 2 de septiembre de 2026, p. 12
La ministra de Igualdad Racial de Brasil, Rachel Barros de Oliveira, enfatizó el papel primordial de las acciones afirmativas para alcanzar la igualdad y la justicia social. Al dictar una conferencia magistral, en el contexto de su participación en la convención internacional A 25 años de Durban, destacó que brindar oportunidades educativas a las juventudes negras, indígenas y afrodescendientes es central para consolidar la democracia, la justicia y la igualdad en nuestras sociedades.
Ante la presencia de estudiantes de licenciatura y posgrado, especialistas, docentes y activistas reunidos en el auditorio Benito Juárez de la Facultad de Derecho de la Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM), recordó que Brasil fue el último país en América Latina en abolir la esclavitud, el 13 de mayo de 1888. Sin embargo, pasarían 100 años más antes de que se incluyera en su Constitución el reconocimiento a la dignidad y plenos derechos de la población negra y afrodescendiente.
Destacó que fue en los años 90 del siglo pasado cuando los movimientos por la defensa de los derechos de los pueblos negros en Brasil elaboraron un pliego de demandas centrales que entregaron al Estado, las cuales se verán reflejadas en la propia agenda del encuentro mundial de Naciones Unidas para combatir el racismo, la discriminación racial, la xenofobia y toda forma de intolerancia, celebrado en Durban, Sudáfrica, en 2001, que daría como resultado la Declaración y el Programa de Acción de Durban.
Reconocimiento
Barros de Oliveira recibió un reconocimiento por el programa Caminos Amefricanos, que promueve la formación e intercambio de conocimientos entre Brasil y los países de África, América Latina y el Caribe.
Con este esfuerzo, señaló, son seleccionados profesores de enseñanza básica, estudiantes y otros profesionales de la educación para participar en experiencias de formación e intercambio internacional mediante estancias cortas, y que el año próximo incluirá a México.
Destacó las acciones afirmativas en pro de los grupos más vulnerables, como el programa de cuotas para el ingreso de jóvenes negros y afrodescendientes a las universidades públicas, con las que se logró matricular a más de 4 millones de estudiantes; el Plan Juventud Negra Viva para el derecho a una vida digna; el programa de impulso a las mujeres negras en la ciencia, y la aprobación de una ley que indica la enseñanza de la historia y la cultura afrobrasileñas y africanas en los niveles de educación básica y media superior.
La ministra de Igualdad Racial de Brasil subrayó el papel central de la educación como vía para fortalecer la justicia social, pero también el ejercicio pleno de otros derechos para la población negra, afrodescendiente e indígena de nuestra región, así como para reconocer su aportación cultural, social y de conocimientos en América Latina y el mundo.

title: Vietnã completa 81 anos: o que o país socialista conquistou após triunfar na resistência contra os EUA
content:
Há 81 anos, em 2 de setembro de 1945, na Praça Ba Đình, em Hanói, o revolucionário vietnamita Ho Chi Minh lia a Declaração de Independência do Vietnã. As forças comunistas resistiram primeiro à França e, em seguida, a uma das maiores e mais brutais agressões militares estadunidenses da história, que terminou com a derrota dos invasores, em 1975.
Hoje o Vietnã registra um dos processos de desenvolvimento social mais acelerados do mundo, tendo conseguido em apenas cinco décadas reduzir a pobreza de 58% para 4% da população, eliminando a fome crônica e se tornando um dos maiores exportadores de arroz do planeta, segundo dados do governo vietnamita e do Programa das Nações Unidas para o Desenvolvimento (PNUD).
A estabilidade atual, no entanto, tem raízes em um passado marcado por guerras e pela resistência vietnamita às potências do Norte Global.
A França ocupava a região, incluindo Laos, Camboja e a cidade chinesa de Zhanjiang, desde o final do século XIX, sob o nome de Indochina. Durante a Segunda Guerra Mundial, a partir de 1940, o Império do Japão passou a co-ocupar a Indochina mediante acordo com a França. Em agosto de 1945, com a derrocada japonesa, o movimento Liga pela Independência do Vietnã, comandado por Ho Chi Minh, assumiu o poder na Revolução de Agosto.
O país europeu não reconheceu a declaração de independência vietnamita em 1945 e no ano seguinte passou a combater as forças comunistas lideradas por Ho Chi Minh. A chamada “Guerra da Indochina” foi de 1946 a 1954, quando as forças vietnamitas derrotaram o exército francês em Dien Bien Phu.
A presença militar francesa começou a se enfraquecer só em 1954, quando Paris decidiu negociar uma saída da região. A partir de então, os Estados Unidos, que já vinham financiando a França militarmente de forma significativa, decidiram se envolver mais diretamente na ocupação do Vietnã.
Em 1955, os Estados Unidos boicotaram as eleições previstas nos Acordos de Genebra do ano anterior para decidir sobre a reunificação, já que acordos anteriores haviam definido a divisão do país ao longo do paralelo 17, que cortava o país praticamente “pela metade”, como medida temporária.
O governo dos EUA, sob a presidência de Dwight D. Eisenhower, determinou que o Grupo Consultivo de Assistência Militar (MAAG, na sigla em inglês), que antes apoiava as tropas francesas na região, passasse a treinar o Exército da República do Vietnã, aliado dos EUA. Isso se efetivou em 1º de novembro de 1955, o que é tido como a data oficial do início da chamada “Guerra do Vietnã”.
Apenas três décadas depois, em 30 de abril de 1975, o Exército de Libertação do Vietnã, comandado pelo governo de Ho Chi Mihn, tomaria Saigon, no sul do país.
A destruição pelos Estados Unidos
A guerra de invasão promovida pelos estadunidenses contra o governo socialista deixou um saldo nefasto. Segundo dados oficiais citados pela agência de Notícias do Vietnã, no total, as ações dos Estados Unidos causaram a morte de quase 3 milhões de pessoas. Cerca de 175 mil soldados continuam desaparecidos e quase 300 mil túmulos seguem não identificados.
Entre os crimes de guerra mais destacados, está o “Massacre de My Lai”, cometido em 16 de março de 1968. Soldados estadunidenses massacraram 504 civis na comuna de Tinh Khe, província de Quang Ngai: 182 mulheres, 173 crianças e 60 idosos com mais de 60 anos, conforme documentos preservados no Museu de Vestígios de Guerra, em Cidade Ho Chi Minh, no sul do país. O caso é um dos mais documentados entre, pelo menos, 320 crimes contra civis registrados num relatório de 9 mil páginas do exército dos Estados Unidos, desclassificado em 1994 e citado por múltiplas fontes vietnamitas.
Além disso, as sequelas são sentidas até hoje. O Corpo Químico das Forças Armadas do Vietnã estima que o exército estadunidense pulverizou cerca de 80 milhões de litros de produtos químicos tóxicos sobre territórios no sul do Vietnã, dos quais 61% eram formados pelo material extremamente tóxico chamado “Agente Laranja”, contendo 366 kg de dioxina, segundo o general Ha Van Cu, comandante do Corpo Químico.
Cerca de 4,8 milhões de pessoas foram expostas à dioxina presente nesses produtos. Entre 3 e 3,2 milhões são consideradas vítimas diretas, sofrendo cânceres, malformações congênitas ou doenças neurológicas.
Os efeitos continuam sendo observados até a terceira e quarta gerações de famílias afetadas. Só na província de Nghệ An, mais de 600 pessoas da terceira geração de ex-combatentes expostos apresentam sequelas. O número de mortes desde 1975 atribuíveis ao Agente Laranja chega a quase 1 milhão, segundo a Previdência Social do Vietnã.
Os militares dos Estados Unidos também lançaram cerca de 15 milhões de toneladas de bombas, minas e projéteis sobre o território vietnamita, segundo a rádio estatal Voz do Vietnã. O país calcula que ainda há 800 mil toneladas de artefatos não detonados que cobrem 20% do território do país; desde o fim do conflito, esses resíduos causaram mais de 40 mil mortes e 60 mil feridos. No ritmo atual de desarmamento de minas, serão necessários 300 anos para eliminá-las completamente, segundo a emissora estatal.
A reconstrução
Em 1975, o Vietnã era uma economia completamente destruída, com campos envenenados e infraestrutura em ruínas. Em 1986, o VI Congresso Nacional do Partido Comunista do Vietnã aprovou as reformas do Đổi Mới (“renovação”), que combinaram planejamento estatal com abertura econômica controlada. De 1990 a 2004, o PIB quase triplicou, com crescimento médio de 7,5% ao ano, segundo dados oficiais. A participação da agricultura no PIB caiu de 38% para 21,7% em duas décadas de reformas, enquanto a indústria e a construção subiram de 28,9% para 40,1%.
Em 1993, 58,1% da população vivia na pobreza. Em 1998, a cifra caiu para 37,4%, e em 2004, para 24,1%, segundo o Escritório Geral de Estatísticas do Vietnã.
Em 2024, a pobreza multidimensional atingiu 4,06%, com a pobreza extrema em 1,3%, segundo o Diário do Povo, jornal oficial do Partido Comunista do Vietnã.
A redução da pobreza foi mais lenta entre as minorias étnicas. Em 1993, a taxa de pobreza entre os grupos minoritários era de 84,6%; em 1998, recuou para 75,2%, enquanto a população de etnia Kinh reduzia a pobreza em ritmo mais acelerado, segundo o Escritório Nacional de Estatísticas do Vietnã. A desigualdade entre as planícies e as províncias montanhosas ainda é o principal desafio distributivo do modelo vietnamita.
Em dezembro do ano passado, a 15ª Assembleia Nacional aprovou 423 trilhões de VND (mais de R$ 83,7 bilhões) do Programa Nacional de Metas para Áreas Rurais de Novo Estilo, Redução Sustentável da Pobreza e Desenvolvimento Socioeconômico em Regiões Étnicas Minoritárias e Montanhosas para o período de 2026 a 2035.
Já o Índice de Desenvolvimento Humano (IDH) passou de 0,499 em 1990 para 0,766 em 2023, alta de 53,5% em 33 anos, conforme o Programa das Nações Unidas para o Desenvolvimento (PNUD). O Vietnã ocupa hoje a 93ª posição entre 193 países no grupo de desenvolvimento humano.
A taxa de alfabetização entre pessoas de 15 a 60 anos é de 99,1%, e a cobertura de seguro-saúde ultrapassa 95% da população, segundo o Partido. A expectativa de vida média chegou a 74,7 anos, segundo o Escritório Geral de Estatísticas do Vietnã, com base na Pesquisa Intermediária de População e Habitação de 2024.
Em 2025, o Vietnã exportou mais de 8,06 milhões de toneladas de arroz para cerca de 80 países e territórios, faturando cerca de 4,1 bilhões de dólares (mais de R$ 21,1 bilhões), segundo o Departamento de Alfândega.
Vietnã e Cuba: internacionalismo
Cuba foi o primeiro país do hemisfério ocidental a estabelecer relações diplomáticas com o Vietnã e enviou conselheiros e especialistas militares para auxiliar as forças vietnamitas na resistência a agressão estadunidense. Seis deles inclusive morreram por um ataque aéreo dos EUA em Hanoi em 1966.
Fidel Castro é lembrado no Vietnã como um grande amigo do país. Em 1973, Fidel visitou o país e declarou: “Por Vietnam, Cuba está disposta a dar o seu próprio sangue”.
Nessa visita, Cuba entregou ao Vietnã cinco obras socioeconômicas avaliadas em cerca de US$ 80 milhões: o Hotel Thang Loi em Hanói, o Hospital Vietnã-Cuba em Dong Hoi, a estrada que liga Son Tay a Xuan Mai, uma fazenda de criação de gado em Moc Chau e uma fábrica de frangos em Luong My.
Cuba também doou mais de 1.000 vacas leiteiras para o desenvolvimento da pecuária vietnamita e forneceu mais de 6 milhões de dólares para a aquisição de equipamentos destinados a ampliar a rodovia Ho Chi Minh.
Os laços históricos se mantém e hoje, quando Cuba atravessa uma das piores crises de sua história, o Vietnã tenta retribuir.
Nas comemorações dos 65 anos de relações diplomáticas, em 2025, a Cruz Vermelha do Vietnã lançou uma campanha com meta inicial de 65 bilhões de dongs vietnamitas ( cerca de R$ 12,8 milhões), atingida em 20 dias. A campanha encerrou com 657,5 bilhões de dongs (mais de R$ 130 milhões) entregues a Cuba em duas parcelas, segundo a Cruz Vermelha do Vietnã.
Em 2026, uma nova campanha mobilizou quase 590 mil pessoas e arrecadou mais 537 bilhões de dongs (mais R$ 106 milhões), em homenagem ao centenário de Fidel Castro. O país também doou, em fevereiro de 2026, 250 toneladas de arroz, segundo a Agência de Notícias do Vietnã.
Além disso, o país estreitou suas relações comerciais com Havana e implementou neste ano um projeto conjunto entre a empresa estatal de arroz de Granma, em Cuba, e a companhia vietnamita Thai Binh — presente há anos no setor comercial da ilha —, que recentemente realizou sua primeira colheita no município de Yara.
A iniciativa conjunta, denominada TBAgri, ainda está em fase inicial e atualmente abrange cerca de 160 hectares nos terraços planos da comunidade José Martí. No entanto, o plano prevê uma expansão gradual até alcançar 25 mil hectares destinados ao cultivo de arroz.
O projeto opera sob um modelo de capital 100% estrangeiro e utiliza terras concedidas em usufruto pelo Estado cubano, com duração estimada de 25 anos. Em uma primeira etapa, a produção será destinada principalmente ao consumo interno, tendo como principal objetivo o autoabastecimento territorial.

title: La gerontolescencia
content:
La revolución de la longevidad ha comenzado en el mundo. La gerontolescencia significa -no un programa privado de envejecimiento activo y autónomo-, sino el descubrimiento de una nueva etapa de la vida de hombres y mujeres, entre los 65 y 80 años de edad, reconocida por la Organización Mundial de la Salud (OMS).
Su creador es el investigador Alexandre Karachi, quien, junto a otros estudiosos del envejecimiento, como Pere Estupinyá en la obra “Qué quieres ser de mayor”, proporcionan las claves para afrontar el paso de los años con ilusión, mediante una base psicológica y social, física y médica.
La propuesta es clara: promover un envejecimiento activo para lograr una buena salud con autonomía. Según la OMS, la gerontolescencia corresponde a un nuevo período vital, entre la adultez y la vejez (65-80 años), que implica el ejercicio de un derecho humano a disfrutar de un envejecimiento activo y pleno, sentirse jóvenes de cuerpo y espíritu, y contribuir a la sociedad con experiencias y conocimientos.
La edad biológica es importante para los gerontolescentólogos, pero más aún la edad psicológica cuya impronta es la plenitud, entendida como el proceso vital que conjuga la totalidad del ser humano: encontrar sentido para vivir y seguir viviendo, en relación con otras personas, el movimiento, la alimentación sana y la naturaleza. Así, la plenitud vital se articula con la plenitud ocupacional.
Los gerontolescentes son abuelos y jubilados. Esta condición les permite aprovechar al máximo la esperanza de vida vigente y fortalecerla, mediante estrategias que combinen, de manera equilibrada, la salud física, mental y emocional.
La OMS ha reconocido que el mapa de la población mundial está cambiando, por el control de las enfermedades globales, y las políticas públicas en salud que aplican los gobiernos. En el Ecuador, la esperanza de vida al nacer (2024) se cifra en 77.58 años promedio. Las mujeres en 80.31 años, y los hombres en 74.88 años. El país ocupa el número 66, que corresponde a la parte media entre las naciones del orbe.
Las Naciones Unidas han comenzado a debatir este tema. El Estado ecuatoriano tiene una deuda con los adultos mayores, especialmente con aquellos que no están afiliados al seguro social. De ahí que es necesario que se diseñen políticas públicas para este sector de población, que sufre carencias y exclusiones. ¡El reconocimiento de la gerontolescencia es un gran paso!

title: Africa: Global Initiative Launched to Improve Access to Mpox Vaccines
content:
A global initiative to establish a stockpile of mpox vaccines was launched on 27 August, creating a long-term mechanism to ensure countries have access to vaccines when responding to mpox outbreaks.
Set to begin operations later this month, this new global mpox vaccine stockpile that all countries can access is a resource that was approved by the Board of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance (Gavi) in 2025, and is funded by Gavi and coordinated by the International Coordinating Group (ICG) on Vaccine Provision. The ICG partners are the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) and the World Health Organization (WHO).
The initiative builds on the Access and Allocation Mechanism established in 2024 during the last mpox Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC), and will ensure that countries have timely and equitable access to vaccines for outbreak response.
Mpox continues to cause outbreaks globally, with two-thirds of reported cases occurring in the African Region. From 1 January 2022 to 31 July 2026, 145 countries and territories reported 190 683 confirmed cases and 529 deaths. Mpox is a viral disease that spreads primarily through close physical contact between people, while animal-to-human transmission continues to occur in parts of Africa, contributing to the ongoing risk of new outbreaks. Mpox can cause severe disease, especially in children and people with suppressed immune systems. By protecting people at risk of infection and severe disease, vaccines help contain mpox outbreaks more quickly, prevent severe illness and save lives.
Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn
Quotes from partners:
Dr Sania Nishtar, CEO of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, said: "During the 2022 mpox outbreak, lower-income countries were left behind when it came to access to vaccines and it was clear that a mechanism was needed to ensure this global public good could be accessed by those who need it most. Core to the Gavi Leap approach is increasing our responsiveness to country needs, and the bottom line is that any country in the world - not just those with the ability to pay the most - should be able to use this tool to save lives. That is why Gavi supported the international response to the 2024 global mpox emergency by securing rapid access to doses through our First Response Fund, and why our Board agreed to establish and finance a global stockpile managed by our ICG partners. Our hope is that this stockpile will keep the world safer from the threat of this deadly disease."
Jagan Chapagain, Secretary General and CEO of the IFRC, said: "Mpox is a horrible illness so I'm pleased that we've got to this important step in the battle to control it. Access to vaccines - for all who need them - is absolutely vital. That's why this global coordination mechanism and vaccine stockpile matters. Both will help ensure vaccines reach the people and communities at greatest risk - when and where they are needed most. This is rare good news."
Dr Daniela Garone, International Medical Coordinator, MSF, said: "MSF welcomes the establishment of a global mpox vaccine stockpile under the International Coordinating Group (ICG) on Vaccine Provision, a mechanism that allows for the equal allocation of vaccines as based on demand and impact in controlling disease outbreaks. The distinctive nature of mpox, with the coexistence of different variants that affect different populations, now demands a close collaboration between country, regional and global mechanisms as well as between disease programmes, health managers, communities and public health partners to reach more people with mpox vaccines."
Catherine Russell, UNICEF Executive Director, said: "Mpox can be devastating for children - not just its physical effects, but also the stigma, interrupted learning, and fear that can come with being isolated from family and friends. This vital initiative will help us quickly get vaccines to the children, families, and communities most at risk of the disease."
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, said: "The launch of a stockpile of mpox vaccines is an important step towards a more sustainable and equitable approach to mpox outbreak response. By establishing a dedicated global stockpile, using an approach that has proven successful for managing other emergency vaccines, we are ensuring that countries can access them more quickly when they need them, saving lives and containing outbreaks before they spread further."
Note to editors
Mpox
Mpox is a viral illness that spreads mainly through close physical contact, including sexual contact. The disease can be debilitating and disfiguring, affecting men, women and children in different contexts, and can, in some cases, lead to severe complications and death. WHO Mpox factsheet
International Coordinating Group (ICG) on Vaccine Provision
The ICG was established in 1997, following major outbreaks of meningitis in Africa, as a mechanism to manage and coordinate the provision of emergency vaccine supplies and antibiotics to countries during major outbreaks. Although the occurrence of outbreaks is often unpredictable, further disease spread can be controlled by timely vaccination.
The core mandate of the ICG is to make available and ensure equitable access to licensed vaccines for cholera, meningitis, yellow fever, and Ebola virus disease during outbreaks.
The ICG mechanism seeks to ensure timely and targeted deployment of vaccines so that they can be used effectively in emergency settings where they are most needed.
The ICG manages the global emergency vaccine stockpiles and, working with partners, donors, and manufacturers, determines their size and composition with the goal of ensuring that adequate stocks of emergency supplies are accessible for emergency response.
In 2024, WHO and partners created the ad hoc Access and Allocation Mechanism for mpox vaccines. The longer term ICG will continue the work initiated under the AAM.
In 2025, the Gavi Board formally approved the establishment and financing of the global mpox vaccine stockpile. under the long-standing ICG mechanism to include mpox.

title: Public money needs new job in Africa agriculture
content:
Africa's agricultural sector accounts for roughly a fifth of the continent's GDP yet receives less than 5.0 per cent of commercial bank lending. For two decades, guarantee funds, blended finance facilities, and donor-backed risk-sharing mechanisms have worked to close that gap, with real but uneven progress. Now the risk landscape they were built for is shifting, and the tools need to shift too.
Three lessons stand out from years of engagement with banks and value chain financing. Guarantees alone don't move money; capacity does: a $6.9 million guarantee facility in Kenya unlocked a $32 million loan portfolio only because it was paired with technical assistance for banks and borrowers.
Partner selection matters as much as guarantee size: risk-sharing with well-capacitated banks achieved roughly 10 times leverage, more than double the Kenya ratio. And some of the most valuable work isn't the money at all: absorbing the risk of untested approaches early, then sharing what worked, is a public good in itself.
This experience was mostly built handling idiosyncratic risk, meaning one farmer's bad season or one client's default, which banks can increasingly manage with better data.
But a different risk is growing faster: systemic, covariate risk (variable not of primary interest) that hits an entire region at once, as seen this year in fertiliser price shocks from the Iran conflict's disruption of trade routes, and a super El Niño building for late 2026 into 2027.
No bank can diversify away a risk that hits its whole loan book at once. That isn't a confidence problem private capital will eventually solve; it's structural, and public capital is specifically suited to absorb it.
African governments have already committed to this. The Kampala CAADP Declaration calls for at least 10 percent of public expenditure to go toward agrifood systems, with $100 billion mobilised by 2035, and names resilience to climate, health, and economic shocks as a core pillar.
The complication: this is the third time the target has been set, after Maputo in 2003 and Malabo in 2014, and tracking already shows some regions falling short again. What needs to change is what the money is spent on.
Much of today's agricultural support, in Africa and among OECD countries alike, isn't idle; it's actively working against resilience.
Globally, governments spend more than $840 billion a year supporting agriculture, and roughly two-thirds of producer-level support comes in the most market-distorting forms: payments tied to specific commodities or inputs rather than outcomes.
Coupled support like this discourages the diversification that builds climate resilience and locks farmers into patterns that make sense only as long as the subsidy lasts.
In Africa, input subsidy programs remain politically popular and fiscally significant, but they're structured around maintaining current yields rather than building the buffers, such as soil health, water management, and diversified income, that let farmers absorb a bad season without a full-blown crisis.
This is why the case isn't simply "find money to redirect toward guarantees." It's "recognize that some of what we're already spending is making the problem worse."
The lessons from guarantee work don't need to be discarded; they need redirecting. Three shifts would move guarantee mechanisms from covering generic default risk to managing climate risk specifically.
Trigger design tied to climate events, not just loan performance. Guarantees can use parametric or index-based triggers, such as rainfall thresholds, satellite-observed drought indices, and temperature anomalies, that release coverage automatically when a covariate climate event hits a region, rather than waiting for it to show up loan by loan.
Regional parametric insurance schemes have already shown payouts reaching governments within weeks of a confirmed drought or cyclone.
Layered capital stacks that separate ordinary risk from tail risk.
A guarantee facility can carry a first-loss tranche for ordinary credit risk, and a second, climate-specific tranche, potentially reinsured regionally or globally, that activates only for systemic, weather-driven losses. Donors absorbing the first-loss layer can catalyse several times that amount in commercial lending banks would otherwise consider too risky, so scarce public capital concentrates on the risk private markets can't diversify away.
Conditioning guarantee eligibility on resilience-building practices. Coverage, or preferential pricing on it, can be tied to farmers adopting practices that measurably reduce climate exposure: drought-tolerant varieties, soil and water conservation, diversified cropping. This turns the guarantee from a purely financial tool into one that actively drives the resilience it's meant to protect.
Each of these mechanisms depends on observing, at scale and low cost, what farmers are actually doing, something that used to require expensive field verification.
AI tools combining satellite imagery, weather models, and yield analysis can now verify farming conditions for millions of smallholders far more cheaply and extend to guarantee design: confirming whether a farmer planted a drought-resilient variety, setting more accurate localized triggers, and scoring producers without formal credit histories.
None of this requires new money nobody can find. It requires applying what guarantee work has already taught us, about leverage, partner selection, and paired capacity-building, to the risk that's actually growing, using tools only now becoming affordable. Ordinary risk is a job for banks and better data. Climate shocks are a job for public capital, structured to unlock private capital. The Kampala Declaration already gives us the vehicle. The question is whether we finally use it.
Martien Van Nieuwkoop is a member of the AGRA Board of Directors

title: Gov't prioritizes human-centered AI principle for inclusivity
content:
"AI is a tool. Who operates it? Humans do. So we need to look at it from the human-centered AI perspective, with humans serving as the operators who use it," Triyanto said during a discussion held by OpenAI here on Thursday.
To uphold this principle, the ministry pursues an approach of "AI for all, for many, and for few", especially in AI-specific digital talent literacy activities.
Through this approach, the ministry expressed hopes that every AI digital talent in Indonesia can produce innovations and solutions that remain human-centered.
According to him, the AI development principle is also reflected in every step taken by the ministry and other ministries responsible for AI development.
He cited the ministry's initiative in issuing a joint decree with seven ministries focused on ensuring young people can use AI responsibly without losing their critical thinking skills as the nation's future generation.
The joint decree refers to guidelines on the use of digital technology and AI in education.
Under the guidelines, students from primary to secondary school levels are not allowed to use instant AI services to directly answer school assignments.
However, AI use remains permitted if the technology is specifically designed for educational needs and guided learning purposes.
Another example is Government Regulation Number 17 of 2025 on Electronic System Governance for Child Protection in Digital Spaces (PP TUNAS).
The regulation prioritizes children's safety, including when accessing AI services provided by electronic system operators.
The government is also translating this principle into concrete programs so AI can be introduced even to regions with limited digital infrastructure access.
"Now there is integrated Sekolah Rakyat, as well as Sekolah Unggul Garuda, and others. At the education level, social facilities (for AI access) have been provided," Triyanto said.

title: La ONCE recuerda que la inclusión no debe quedarse en las aulas: "Tiene que estar en el recreo, el comedor..."
content:
La ONCE recuerda que la inclusión no debe quedarse en las aulas: "Tiene que estar en el recreo, el comedor, las extraescolares..."
Basado en hechos observados y verificados directamente por nuestros periodistas o por fuentes informadas.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
Más de 7.000 estudiantes con ceguera o con deficiencia visual grave inician estos días el nuevo curso escolar.
Más de 7.000 estudiantes con ceguera o con deficiencia visual grave inician estos días el nuevo curso escolar. El 99% de ellos lo hace en centros ordinarios, dentro de un modelo de educación inclusiva respaldado por equipos de atención educativa de la ONCE, que proporcionan los apoyos necesarios para seguir el currículo en igualdad de oportunidades.
Sin embargo, volver al colegio no significa únicamente regresar a las aulas. La experiencia educativa también se construye en otros espacios y momentos que forman parte de la vida diaria de los centros y que son fundamentales para el desarrollo personal y social del alumnado. “La jornada escolar incluye otros tiempos y actividades. El recreo, el comedor, horarios ampliados o actividades complementarias y extraescolares son esenciales para el aprendizaje y tienen una influencia decisiva en el desarrollo de la autonomía personal y de las competencias sociales”, explica Ana Llauradó, responsable de Atención Educativa de la ONCE.
Por ello, la ONCE recuerda que el alumnado con discapacidad visual tiene tanto el derecho como la necesidad de participar plenamente en todas estas actividades en igualdad de condiciones que el resto de sus compañeros.
Recreos para todos
El recreo constituye un espacio clave de convivencia y socialización. Para que sea realmente inclusivo, debe ofrecer oportunidades de juego y participación para todo el alumnado. La ONCE impulsa patios accesibles, organizados en diferentes zonas, con propuestas variadas que favorezcan la interacción y el juego compartido. Asimismo, resulta fundamental disponer de un repertorio de juegos inclusivos que puedan elegir y disfrutarse de forma autónoma, siempre con la adecuada supervisión adulta.
El comedor como espacio de autonomía
Del mismo modo, el comedor escolar representa una oportunidad privilegiada para fomentar habilidades esenciales para la vida diaria. “Espacios como el comedor permiten reforzar la autonomía del alumnado con discapacidad visual en tareas cotidianas como la alimentación o el aseo”, señala Llauradó.
Los técnicos de rehabilitación de la ONCE enseñan a estos estudiantes a desenvolverse de forma independiente según su edad y desarrollo, realizando acciones como cortar los alimentos, servirse agua o mantener hábitos de higiene personal. Además, forman a los profesionales que trabajan en estos entornos para que puedan reforzar dichas habilidades en el día a día.
Aprender también fuera del aula
Las actividades complementarias, desarrolladas dentro del horario lectivo, enriquecen el aprendizaje a través de experiencias prácticas y vivenciales. Para garantizar la participación de todo el alumnado, es importante que incorporen enfoques multisensoriales y que los materiales se preparen y adapten previamente cuando sea necesario. Las actividades extraescolares también desempeñan un papel fundamental. Son un entorno idóneo para descubrir intereses, desarrollar habilidades artísticas o deportivas y fortalecer las relaciones sociales, aspectos especialmente relevantes para el desarrollo integral del alumnado.
“Todos los espacios, tiempos y actividades que conforman la vida escolar son enormemente enriquecedores para el alumnado y, especialmente, para los estudiantes con discapacidad visual, siempre que se planifiquen teniendo en cuenta la diversidad y se incorporen estrategias y recursos que hagan efectiva la inclusión”, concluye la responsable de Atención Educativa de la ONCE.
Más de 400 profesionales al servicio de la inclusión
La ONCE cuenta con equipos específicos de atención educativa integrados por maestros y maestras, tanto de la ONCE como de las administraciones educativas, que prestan apoyo directo en los centros escolares. Su labor incluye la atención al alumnado en aspectos relacionados con la discapacidad visual o la sordoceguera, el acompañamiento a las familias y el asesoramiento al profesorado mediante herramientas, recursos y estrategias que favorecen el acceso al currículo ordinario en igualdad de oportunidades. Actualmente, más de 400 profesionales desarrollan esta tarea en todas las comunidades autónomas.
Junto al personal docente, estos equipos están formados por psicólogos, trabajadores sociales, técnicos de rehabilitación, instructores de tiflotecnología y braille, especialistas en animación sociocultural y mediadores para alumnado con sordoceguera. Todos ellos contribuyen, desde una perspectiva multidisciplinar, al desarrollo integral y la plena inclusión educativa.
Durante el curso 2025/2026 se atendió a más de 7.000 estudiantes con ceguera o con deficiencia visual, incluidos aquellos con sordoceguera o discapacidades asociadas: 1.103 en Educación infantil, 1.421 en Primaria, 1.128 en Secundaria, 298 en Bachillerato, 526 en Formación Profesional, 803 en la universidad, 1.306 en Educación Básica Obligatoria y 549 en otras enseñanzas.

title: Descentraliza tu conocimiento
content:
Descentraliza tu conocimiento
Basado en interpretaciones y juicios del autor sobre hechos, datos y eventos.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
La innovación social cobra sentido cuando el conocimiento y la tecnología se comparten para mejorar vidas y garantizar un desarrollo más inclusivo.
Durante años se ha asumido una visión paternalista de la innovación: la idea de que la tecnología debe diseñarse en despachos, protegerse tras patentes y entregarse en forma de "ayuda" puntual donde haga falta. Sin embargo, tras años de aprendizaje en el terreno diseñando innovaciones sanitarias en más de 70 países, me he convencido de algo fundamental: la tecnología que no se comparte pierde su verdadero sentido, y la innovación que no se descentraliza acaba perpetuando las mismas brechas de siempre.
Cuando viajé por primera vez a Kenia en 2017 para entregar las primeras prótesis, el objetivo era llevar una respuesta física a quien jamás podría permitirse una prótesis. Aquella experiencia me sirvió, sobre todo, para comprender una lección vital: el valor real de la tecnología radica en democratizar la herramienta que la hace posible. Entendí que la tecnología no debe concebirse como una aportación puntual, sino como una capacidad instalada en el propio entorno. La verdadera innovación social consiste en sembrar la autonomía técnica para que sea la propia comunidad quien lidere sus soluciones.
Ahí es donde cobra sentido la descentralización tecnológica. Viajé con varias impresoras 3D en maletas y creamos laboratorios de impresoras 3D en Kenia o Tanzania para transferir el conocimiento y ceder el control. Esto implica enseñar a crear prótesis a la vez que se desarrollan modelos de negocio sostenibles para que la propia comunidad genere empleo, mantenga los equipos y entregue los dispositivos de forma gratuita. Cuando ves a estudiantes locales llegar horas antes para imprimir, tomar medidas a sus vecinos y adaptar cada diseño a las necesidades de su entorno, entiendes que la tecnología ha dejado de ser un objeto ajeno para convertirse en una herramienta de desarrollo propio.
Hoy la tecnología nos permite "teletransportar" con un clic archivos digitales validados por ingenieros biomédicos a cualquier rincón del mundo. Descentralizar no es solo repartir máquinas; es democratizar el derecho a crear. El conocimiento debe ser universal. Si disponemos de soluciones capaces de cambiar vidas a un coste mínimo, guardarnos esa capacidad por recelo comercial o burocrático es un error ético.
No tiene sentido innovar si no es socialmente. Tan facil como pensar que cuando descubres algo nuevo quieres compartirlo con los tuyos ¿por qué no ayudar con ese descubrimiento a quien lo necesita? Ayudar es demasiado fácil como para no hacerlo.

title: Como a Turquia transformou resíduos em riqueza
content:
Como a Turquia transformou resíduos em riqueza
Projeto Lixo Zero combina reciclagem, conservação de recursos e educação ambiental e já movimentou US$ 3,48 bilhões
Projeto Lixo Zero combina reciclagem, conservação de recursos e educação ambiental e já movimentou US$ 3,48 bilhões
Desde que foi lançado, em 2017, o Projeto Lixo Zero (Zero Waste) da Turquia vem mostrando que políticas de gestão de resíduos podem produzir efeitos que vão além da redução do lixo enviado aos aterros. A iniciativa combina reciclagem, economia de recursos naturais, redução de emissões e conscientização da população, com impactos também sobre a economia do país.
Idealizado por Emine Erdoğan, primeira-dama da Turquia, e implementado pelo Ministério do Meio Ambiente, Urbanização e Mudanças Climáticas, o programa tem como objetivo incentivar o gerenciamento dos resíduos de acordo com princípios de desenvolvimento sustentável e reduzir a poluição.
De acordo com dados do ministério, o projeto já evitou a emissão de 3,9 milhões de toneladas de gases de efeito estufa. A iniciativa também resultou na economia de mais de 530 milhões de quilowatts-hora de energia e 572 milhões de metros cúbicos de água. Os resultados se estendem à conservação de recursos naturais, o programa evitou o abate de 347 milhões de árvores, impediu a queima de 87 milhões de barris de petróleo e reduziu o consumo de 650 milhões de toneladas de matérias-primas
Desde o início da iniciativa, 33,8 milhões de toneladas de resíduos deixaram de ser encaminhadas para aterros e foram direcionadas à reciclagem. O volume inclui 20,4 milhões de toneladas de papel, 5,4 milhões de toneladas de plástico, 2,3 milhões de toneladas de vidro, 500 mil toneladas de metal e 5,2 milhões de toneladas de resíduos orgânicos. Além de reduzir a pressão sobre os recursos naturais, a reciclagem também gerou retorno financeiro. Segundo o governo turco, os materiais recuperados movimentaram o equivalente a US$ 3,48 bilhões na economia do país.
Outra frente do programa é a mobilização da população. A iniciativa busca ampliar o conhecimento sobre a geração de resíduos e estimular hábitos de consumo e descarte mais sustentáveis. Até o momento, cerca de 16 milhões de cidadãos turcos foram informados sobre os benefícios das práticas de lixo zero, segundo dados do Ministério do Meio Ambiente, Urbanização e Mudanças Climáticas.
Os resultados fizeram o projeto ganhar visibilidade fora da Turquia. A iniciativa recebeu reconhecimento do Programa das Nações Unidas para o Desenvolvimento (PNUD) e do ONU-Habitat, além de ter sido apontada como uma experiência promissora em um relatório da Organização para a Cooperação e Desenvolvimento Econômico (OCDE) publicado em 2019. Mais recentemente, Emine Erdoğan recebeu do Banco Mundial o prêmio de Liderança em Clima e Desenvolvimento, em reconhecimento ao trabalho desenvolvido por meio do Projeto Lixo Zero.

title: Cherokee youth win legal rights for waterway in first all-female U.S. effort
content:
- On Jan. 8, 2026, the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Council unanimously passed a resolution recognizing the inherent legal rights of the Longperson (Ganvhidv Asgaya), an interconnected waterway system whose headwaters rise in the Great Smoky Mountains and end in the sea.
- The resolution was brought forward by the NAIWA Daughters, a group of Indigenous girls aged 10 to 17, making it the first all-female-led rights-of-nature effort in the U.S., and only the second such youth-led resolution passed by a Tribal nation.
- The effort followed 18 months of grassroots organizing and built on the foundations of the rights-of-nature movement, which holds that ecosystems and natural entities should have legal standing to exist and flourish.
- The Longperson resolution grants the waterway five inherent rights and has already spurred related action, including a separate tribal resolution to raise funds for removing the Ela Dam.
Before the proceedings began, the young women carried Longperson into the room with them, water gathered from the mountain headwaters and held in traditional pottery. The chamber filled beyond capacity, supporters spilling into the lobby. When the vote came, the council passed the resolution unanimously. The crowd and the council rose in standing ovation.
On Jan. 8, 2026, the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians (EBCI) Tribal Council convened in Cherokee, in what is today the U.S. state of North Carolina, to consider a resolution brought forward by the NAIWA Daughters, the youth arm of the North American Indian Women’s Association, made up of a group of Indigenous girls between the ages of 10 and 17.
The resolution recognizes the inherent legal rights of the Longperson, or vwi Ganvhida, the interconnected waterway system whose headwaters rise in the Great Smoky Mountains and travel more than 1,270 kilometers (790 miles), branching through multiple states before its “feet,” as the Cherokee describe it, reach the Gulf of Mexico.
To the Tribe, Longperson (formerly Long Man) is a living entity of great cultural and spiritual significance.
“The room was heavy with the presence of Ancestors and community alike,” said Jasmine Smith, NAIWA Daughters chair and co-founder, describing the moment in a keynote speech at the Bioneers Conference in Berkeley, California. She delivered her speech wearing the moccasins of her Ancestor Ruth Littlejohn.
“That day crystallized in my memories,” she said. “The honor to bring Longperson into the chamber to speak for it, beside it.”
This marks the first all-female-led rights-of-nature effort in the U.S., according to the Earth Law Center, and only the second youth-led rights-of-nature resolution passed by a tribal nation.
“We look to [Longperson] for a lot of strength,” Juanita Wilson, an enrolled EBCI member who has led the Tribe’s annual Honoring Longperson cleanup efforts since 2021 but was not involved with the resolution, told Mongabay. “There are a number of rituals that people do for medicine, physical and emotional health.”
“Whatever’s on land is going to end up in the water,” Wilson added. “It’s literally the lifeblood of everything.”
After the vote, the NAIWA Daughters returned the vessel of water to the Oconaluftee River in a water ceremony.
Rights of Nature movement
The Rights of Nature movement holds that ecosystems and natural entities should have legal standing to exist and flourish, the same way an individual being is endowed with those rights. This framework has been recognized in laws across more than 40 countries. Ecuador added the rights of nature to its Constitution in 2008.
While Indigenous peoples are not universally advocates for the legal rights framework, some have been part of the movement globally, drawing on worldviews that have long considered the natural world as a web of relatives rather than a collection of resources.
In the U.S., many Tribal nations have adopted rights-of-nature legislation. The Ho-Chunk Nation became the first tribal sovereign entity to propose adding the Rights of Nature to its Constitution in 2016, followed by a cascade of resolutions across Indian Country: the Ponca Nation of Oklahoma recognized nature’s right to exist in 2017; the White Earth Band of Ojibwe affirmed the rights of manoomin, or wild rice, to flourish in 2018. The Yurok Tribe established the rights of the Klamath River in 2019. In 2020, the Nez Perce recognized the Snake River as a living entity, and the Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin asserted the Menominee River’s right to remain unpolluted.
Tribes have carried the framework into the courts as well. In 2022, the Sauk-Suiattle Indian Tribe sued the city of Seattle with salmon named as the plaintiff, a case that ended with the city agreeing to build fish passages at its hydroelectric dams.
These efforts — constitutional proposals, resolutions, and lawsuits brought on behalf of rivers, fish, and food sources — form the lineage the NAIWA Daughters have now brought eastward to the Longperson.
“Do we see nature as something we own, or do we view it as something we have the responsibility to protect?” Kyndra Postoak, the group’s Rights of Nature project lead, said in a statement to the EBCI council.
The resolution grants the Longperson five inherent rights: to exist, persist, and regenerate its vital cycles free from harmful human disturbance; to maintain and restore its natural integrity, including freedom from pollution and invasive species; to serve as habitat for nonhuman relatives; to maintain free-flowing conditions; and to be protected under EBCI law and tradition.
“This historic resolution holds a mirror to the Cherokee understanding that the Longperson is a sacred, living relative — not mere property — and translates this relationship into a powerful legal framework,” Grant Wilson, executive director of the Earth Law Center, which supported the effort, told Mongabay in an email. “Those with the deepest cultural and spiritual connections to the land are often the ones best equipped to give Nature a voice in law.”
Old-fashioned organizing
The journey began when the girls were tubing down the river. They noticed tourists staking rocks, which disturbs the habitat for the eastern hellbender salamander (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis alleganiensis, known to the Cherokee as tsuwa). “We were frustrated,” Smith said. “We thought, what if we made a resolution that says you can’t do this?”
Then at the 2024 Indigenous Environmental Network Conference, the NAIWA Daughters met Britt Gondolfi, a lawyer who serves as the Rights of Nature project coordinator for the Bioneers Indigeneity program.
Gondolfi invited them to participate in Bioneers’ six-week rights-of-nature training, introducing the young women to the legal framework that could support their idea. They also connected with other Indigenous communities pursuing similar efforts, including the Mashpee Wampanoag youth, whose 2023 Rights of the Herring resolution had passed their tribal council unanimously.
The NAIWA Daughters initially set out to advocate for protections for the salamanders before elders guided them toward the foundational issue: the waterway itself.
With Bioneers’ support over the following 18 months, Smith said, the NAIWA Daughters were able to focus their efforts on advocating for Longperson. They spent a year and a half hosting community dinners, conducting input surveys, tabling at Cherokee events, and meeting one-on-one with council members to build support.
Smith said the efforts demanded real sacrifice from the young women. “I have watched them give everything to this, showing up tired, overwhelmed, emotional, sacrificing school breaks, weekends, and still fighting for our sovereign rights to be Cherokee,” she said.
“The young women behind this law didn’t AI themselves into this historic moment,” Gondolfi told Mongabay. “They consulted with elders, lawyers, experts in the field, and culture keepers. They put in 18 months of community organizing and created a grassroots movement to honor this ecosystem in law and deed. They revived a traditional customary Indigenous moral philosophy into law.”
“To have feedback from the community say we are 100% behind you,” Smith said, “that’s a win in and of itself, even if the resolution didn’t make it to the floor.”
What comes next
The NAIWA Daughters say their work is far from over. The first Rights of Nature task force meeting took place in May. The task force plans to monitor Longperson’s health, guide further policy implementation, and educate the community as well as other tribal youth.
Within weeks of the passage of the rights-of-nature legislation, the Tribe’s natural resources department and the NAIWA Daughters submitted a resolution committing the EBCI to lead a fundraising campaign to remove the now decommissioned Ela Dam. The resolution passed in March.
For more than a century, the Ela Dam has divided the watershed, blocking the migration path of the critically imperiled sicklefin redhorse (Moxostoma ugidatli). This culturally important fish has been called “the salmon of the south” and its scientific name comes from its Cherokee name meaning “it wears a feather.”
“Just removing the dam will provide safe passage for an aquatic relative,” Kimberly Smith, NAIWA Daughters mentor, told Mongabay.
Smith said removing the dam would also allow sediment buildup at the dam site to be used to create a new Cherokee mound, continuing a cultural practice that stretches back thousands of years.
The NAIWA Daughters plan to present their story at the next national NAIWA convergence in hopes of “inspiring Indigenous women across the country to pursue similar efforts,” Kimberly Smith said.
In the meantime, the annual event Honoring Longperson will take place Sept. 25, during which volunteers and community members clean up the river and NAIWA Daughters plan to hold workshops to teach their younger community members. This year, they also celebrate the success of their rights-of-nature journey.
“Success lives in the groundswell of community and collaboration,” Jasmine Smith said. “We are blessed to live in the oasis of our homelands … we hold the responsibility of stewarding the headwaters, so every living being downstream has water for life.”
New guidebook supports U.S. tribal nations in adopting rights-of-nature laws
Liz Kimbrough is a staff writer for Mongabay and holds a Ph.D. in ecology and evolutionary biology from Tulane University, where she studied the microbiomes of trees. View more of her reporting here.

title: Deutscher Umweltpreis für Klimajuristin und Membranforscher
content:
Deutscher Umweltpreis Klimajuristin und Membranforscher ausgezeichnet
Klares Wasser aus Klärschlamm und klare Regeln für den Klimaschutz: Für ihr Engagement zu diesen Themen erhalten ein Membranfilter-Ingenieur und eine Juristin den Deutschen Umweltpreis.
Die Deutsche Bundesstiftung Umwelt (DBU) zeichnet Membranfilter-Ingenieur Klaus Vossenkaul und Umweltjuristin Roda Verheyen mit dem Deutschen Umweltpreis aus.
Vossenkaul erhält den Preis für innovative Entwicklungen in der Abwasserreinigung in Kläranlagen. Die von ihm entwickelten Hohlfasermembranfilter filtrieren aus Klärschlamm klares Wasser.
Die Membranen haben so feine Poren, dass sie problematische Stoffe wie Mikroplastik, Krankheitserreger und multiresistente Keime sowie mittels Aktivkohle auch Arznei- und Kosmetikrückstände aus dem Abwasser herausfiltern. Vossenkaul sei "Wegbereiter einer Technologie, die bereits heute die Standards von morgen erfüllt - für eine neue Ära der Abwasserreinigung in Kläranlagen", betonte DBU-Generalsekretär Alexander Bonde.
Membranfilter-Ingenieur Klaus Vossenkaul steht an einer Maschine.
Abstrakte Vorgaben auf konkrete Fälle anwenden
Verheyen verschafft Menschen Gehör, die von Klimafolgen betroffen sind. Die Rechtsanwältin ist Mitglied des Hamburgischen Verfassungsgerichts und setzt sich für klare rechtliche Vorgaben zum Schutz von Klima und Umwelt ein.
"Roda Verheyen wendet abstrakte Vorgaben aus dem nationalen und internationalen Recht auf konkrete Fälle an und macht sie so wirksam", lobte Bonde. Als Kommunikatorin vermittle Verheyen komplexe Sachverhalte einer breiten Öffentlichkeit und sei ein Vorbild für eine neue Generation von Juristinnen und Juristen.
Roda Verheyen setzt sich als Mitglied des Hamburgischen Verfassungsgerichts für rechtliche Vorgaben zum Umwelt- und Klimaschutz ein.
Verleihung durch Bundespräsident Steinmeier
Verheyen und Vossenkaul teilen sich den mit insgesamt 500.000 Euro dotierten Preis, der am 25. Oktober in Aachen von Bundespräsident Frank-Walter Steinmeier überreicht werden soll. Der Deutsche Umweltpreis wird jährlich von der DBU vergeben.

title: Accessible Technology for Hope: Bridging Gaps with Innovative Tools
content:
Accessible technology for hope is transforming lives by removing barriers that have long kept people with disabilities from full participation in society. At Global Positive News Network, we believe that innovation in digital tools isn’t just about convenience-it’s about fundamental human dignity and equal opportunity.
The solutions emerging today are real, practical, and already making measurable differences in employment, education, and independence. This blog post explores how these innovations work and what comes next in building a truly inclusive digital world.
How Accessible Technology Creates Real Opportunity
Removing Barriers That Block Daily Life
Accessible technology works because it removes specific, concrete barriers that people with disabilities face every day. A person who is blind can navigate websites and applications through screen readers that convert text to speech, allowing them to apply for jobs, manage finances, and access educational content independently. According to the American Foundation for the Blind, screen reader users have access to properly configured digital tools that support workplace inclusion. Voice recognition technology has advanced significantly, with tools like Google Assistant and Apple’s Siri achieving 95% accuracy rates in understanding speech commands, enabling people with mobility limitations to control computers, smartphones, and smart home devices without touching a keyboard or mouse. These aren’t theoretical improvements-they translate directly into people working, learning, and living without constant dependence on others.
Employment Gains Through Accessible Design
The employment impact is measurable and substantial. The World Health Organization reports that people with disabilities experience unemployment rates nearly double those of people without disabilities, yet accessible technology supports an estimated 1.3 billion people who experience significant disability globally. When employers implement proper accessibility features like adjustable font sizes, customizable color schemes, and keyboard navigation options, they tap into this talent pool. Companies like Microsoft and IBM have reported that accessible hiring practices increased their qualified applicant pools by 30% or more, while simultaneously improving retention rates.
Education and Independence Through Technology
Educational access has expanded equally-online learning platforms with captions, transcripts, and adjustable playback speeds enable deaf and hard-of-hearing students to participate fully in courses. Research from the National Association of the Deaf shows that captioned videos improve comprehension for all learners by an average of 15%. Independence grows when technology adapts to individual needs rather than forcing people to adapt to rigid systems. This shift from one-size-fits-all design to personalized, flexible interfaces represents a fundamental change in how we build digital tools.
The real power of accessible technology lies not in its complexity but in its practical results. People with disabilities gain control over their own lives, employers access wider talent pools, and educational institutions reach more students effectively. These outcomes depend on continued innovation and widespread adoption of accessibility standards across industries. Understanding what innovations currently exist sets the stage for examining the tools and technologies that are already reshaping possibilities for millions of people worldwide.
What Technology Powers Accessibility Today
Voice Assistants Transform Daily Control
AI-powered voice assistants have become the most practical entry point for accessibility because they work across devices and require minimal setup. Google Assistant, Apple’s Siri, and Amazon’s Alexa now handle complex commands with 95% accuracy rates, allowing people with mobility or visual impairments to control computers, phones, and smart home systems without keyboards or touchscreens. These tools work in real homes and workplaces right now, not in laboratories. A person with severe arthritis can dictate emails, schedule appointments, and navigate applications entirely through speech, eliminating the physical strain that previously forced many out of the workforce. The National Federation of the Blind reports that voice-controlled devices have become an increasingly adopted accessibility solution by people with disabilities.
Screen Readers Enable Workplace Productivity
Screen readers remain the backbone of web and application accessibility, converting digital text into audio output that blind users can navigate at their own pace. NVDA, a free open-source screen reader, has become standard in education and many workplaces because it costs nothing and works reliably across Windows systems. JAWS, a commercial alternative, costs around $1,200 but offers advanced features for complex professional software. The difference between these tools and older solutions matters significantly-speed and accuracy directly impact productivity. A 2024 WebAIM study found that screen readers enable blind employees to work effectively in professional environments, with adoption of tools like VoiceOver growing significantly among users with disabilities.
Natural-Sounding Speech Technology
Text-to-speech technology has improved dramatically beyond robotic-sounding voices, with natural-sounding options now available through tools like Natural Reader and Read&Write. These solutions integrate directly into Microsoft Office and Google Workspace, making them workplace standards that employers must provide to comply with accessibility regulations in most developed countries. The shift from specialized software to integrated tools means organizations can support accessibility without expensive separate purchases.
Adaptive Hardware and Built-In System Features
Physical accessibility requires both hardware adaptation and software flexibility working together. Customizable keyboards with programmable keys, eye-tracking devices that translate eye movement into cursor control, and switch-activated systems that respond to single button presses have all become more affordable and powerful. Tobii’s eye-tracking technology, once limited to research settings, now costs under $400 for consumer versions and integrates with Windows 10 and 11 natively.
The real innovation lies in how operating systems now support these devices. Windows Accessibility Settings and macOS Accessibility features allow users to adjust font sizes, increase color contrast, enable high-contrast modes, and remap keyboard functions without purchasing specialized software.
This shift toward built-in accessibility means a person with low vision can make a computer usable within minutes instead of spending hundreds on dedicated adaptive technology. Organizations worldwide have recognized this trend, making accessibility a standard feature rather than an afterthought.
These technological advances have created the foundation for broader change. Yet technology alone cannot sustain progress-the organizations, policies, and communities that champion accessibility standards determine whether these innovations reach the people who need them most.
Who’s Making Accessibility Happen Right Now
Tech Giants Embed Accessibility Into Core Products
Microsoft and Apple have embedded accessibility into their core product development rather than treating it as an afterthought, which fundamentally changes what gets built. Microsoft’s Accessibility Insights tool works publicly and free, allowing developers to test websites and applications for accessibility compliance without expensive audits. Apple’s commitment shows in concrete numbers: iOS supports over 20 accessibility features built directly into the operating system, from VoiceOver to Switch Control, meaning users don’t need to purchase separate adaptive technology. These represent actual engineering resources and product roadmap decisions that prioritize disabled users from the beginning of development.
Regulations Transform Accessibility Into Business Requirements
The European Union’s Web Accessibility Directive, which took effect in 2020, requires all public sector websites and applications to meet WCAG 2.1 AA standards or face legal consequences. This regulatory pressure has forced organizations across Europe to invest in accessibility compliance, creating demand for accessible design expertise and pushing vendors to build accessible products as standard features. The Americans with Disabilities Act’s digital accessibility requirements produce similar effects in the United States, though enforcement remains inconsistent. Countries like Canada and Australia have followed with their own standards, meaning multinational organizations now find it simpler to build accessible products globally than to maintain separate accessible and inaccessible versions.
This regulatory shift matters because it transforms accessibility from a nice-to-have feature into a business requirement with financial consequences for non-compliance. Organizations ignoring these standards face lawsuits-Target paid $6 million in 2008 for website accessibility violations, and similar cases continue today, making accessibility a liability issue that finance departments finally understand.
Disability Advocates Hold Companies Accountable
Grassroots momentum comes from disability advocacy organizations that test products, publish accessibility ratings, and hold companies accountable. The National Federation of the Blind publishes accessibility scorecards for major technology companies, directly influencing purchasing decisions by government agencies and large employers. Disabled people themselves have become accessibility auditors and consultants, moving beyond passive users to active participants in product design. Companies like Deque Systems now employ disabled professionals specifically to audit accessibility, recognizing that disabled people understand accessibility barriers better than non-disabled designers ever will. This shift from consultation to employment of disabled people in accessibility roles has accelerated progress because it embeds lived experience into product decisions rather than relying on theoretical guidelines.
Final Thoughts
Accessible technology for hope has moved from concept to reality, with screen readers, voice assistants, and adaptive devices now serving as working tools that people depend on daily for employment, education, and independence. Employers who implement accessibility features report 30% increases in qualified applicants, while educational platforms with captions improve comprehension for all learners by 15%. Regulatory standards like the EU’s Web Accessibility Directive have transformed accessibility from optional to mandatory, forcing meaningful change across industries and proving that progress happens when organizations prioritize disabled people in product design.
Technology companies must continue embedding accessibility into core products rather than treating it as an afterthought, and governments need consistent enforcement of existing standards alongside stronger regulations. Organizations that hire disabled people as accessibility consultants and product designers gain competitive advantages because lived experience drives better solutions than external expertise alone. Companies that build accessible products access wider talent pools and customer bases while societies that prioritize accessibility benefit from fuller participation of disabled people in economic and civic life.
This isn’t charity-it’s recognizing that accessibility benefits everyone while creating fundamental fairness. title: How a Secret Orangutan Breeding Program Is Creating a Baby Boom
content:
“It’s a girl!” Melissa Peterson exclaims.
Just outside the operating room, the hallway erupts in cheers. Joseph Dewane, an ob-gyn, has just delivered a healthy baby via C-section; Autumn Joi Goodwin-Samson, a neonatalist, tends to the newborn still slick with a waxy film.
It’s a successful delivery just like any other except for one, minor, difference: The patient is an orangutan.
Ruhana—or just “Ru” for short—is one of eight orangutan babies born in a collection of US zoos since the beginning of 2025. For these critically endangered primates, that’s a staggering figure. It’s also not random: The baby boom is the result of a meticulous breeding plan and decades of research to weave a conservation safety net, one birth at a time.
“It might seem like it was all a coincidence that everyone was born at the same time, but it was very carefully planned,” says Angie Selzer, a senior animal care specialist with the Fort Wayne Zoo in Indiana and the Orangutan Species Survival Plan (SSP) program coordinator.
The SSP has been coordinating breeding recommendations since 1985; every two years, the program creates a breeding and transfer plan for animals at zoos accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA). Geneticists from the SSP consult a “studbook,” which contains the pedigree of all the animals in their system.
“We want to maintain a healthy and sustainable population that mimics the natural history of wild orangutans while ensuring successful mother-rearing of offspring,” Seltzer tells WIRED. Their recommendation accounts for a number of breeding factors, including underrepresented genetic lines, each animal’s unique personality, and group dynamics—always aiming for the lowest relation between breeding pairs.
“We’ve had a very good, happy outcome,” she says. It all started in February 2025 when the Indianapolis Zoo welcomed Edi, a healthy baby boy. After that, Weila was delivered at the Hogle Zoo in Utah in June; Bintang arrived at the Los Angeles Zoo, and in December, the Memphis Zoo welcomed Ruhana. Peterson, the associate primates curator at the Memphis Zoo says being present for that moment was a “remarkable experience.” The run of babies has continued this year, with baby girls born at the Cameron Park Zoo in Waco, Texas, Sedgwick County Zoo in Wichita, Kansas, and Fort Wayne Zoo in Indiana. Just a few months ago, the Denver Zoo welcomed a baby boy named Rambutan.
Humans share over 90 percent of their DNA with orangutans, a figure well-evidenced in how they breed and give birth. Orangutans in the program are routinely given human birth control and human prenatal vitamins; they’re taught to pee on human pregnancy tests; they gestate for nearly nine months; and after humans, their offspring have the longest childhood of any mammal. While C-sections like Jahe’s are rare, some zoos keep ob-gyns on call for their orangutans and other primates.
“Looking at their eyes and their hands, it’s like a mirror,” says Matthew Lenyo, assistant curator of predators at Denver Zoo. “It’s humbling.”
As with humans, maternal behaviors are learned; training is a critical part of ensuring the health of orangutan babies. For first-time mom Hesty, the Sumatran orangutan at the Denver Zoo, training involved teaching her to pass the baby to and from keepers for essential health checks and nursing since Hesty’s mother had struggled with it.
For many zoos, prebirth training involves other orangutans in their care too. To be successful, this training requires a deep and hard-earned trust between keepers and these animals, and can prove invaluable if an orangutan cannot be cared for by their biological mother.
That happened at the Hogle Zoo, when Weila’s biological mom failed to bond with her. She was hand-reared by keepers while they prepared Acara—a proven foster who raised her younger brother—to take over as mom using a stuffed animal as a proxy. They slowly introduced the two to each other, rewarding Acara for properly handling Weila. “She also has a gentle behavior” and uses a very gentle touch, says Hannah Comstock, the animal care supervisor of primates at Hogle Zoo. The pair live together full-time now. Acara is a model parent, and Weila is thriving; she has even started adopting some of Acara’s mannerisms.
Still, zookeepers aim to be as hands-off as possible. “We do all this work, but then at the same time, the best outcome is when you’re not needed,” says Lenyo.
It’s estimated that there are around 100,000 Bornean orangutans and 11,000 Sumatran orangutans left in the wild. The population of Tapanuli orangutans is even more dire, with estimates indicating a few more than 700 are left in the wild. The rainforest habitat they rely on in their native Borneo and Sumatra is being razed to create palm oil plantations, and the great apes are also targeted by traffickers who kill orangutan mothers, kidnap their babies, and sell them on the black market as pets. Some estimates indicate that orangutans could go extinct in the wild within 50 years; some experts caution it could be even sooner, in the next 10 to 20 years.
While these new orangutan babies will not be released into the wild, they are a critical part of species conservation. Zookeepers call them ambassadors; when visitors can see the apes, abstract ideas like climate change and deforestation become more real.
But the captive population also has a direct impact on the well-being of wild and rehabilitated populations: Research conducted at AZA zoos on everything from disease management to quality of life is then relayed back to teams in Southeast Asia. Felicity Oram is a conservation practitioner and co-director of OrangJUGA, a Borneo-based conservation organization. Her research on orangutan’s teeth has been critical in the care of young orangutans rescued from the pet trade who live in rehabilitation and rescue centers. She quips that “captive orangutans can help their cousins in the wild and in rehabilitation centers just by opening their mouths.”
Before Oram’s research, estimating age was an imperfect science at best. “It’s very difficult with size,” Oram says. “It’s just like with human children—you go, ‘Isn’t that a cute 4-year-old!’ And then they tell you it’s 2.” She partnered with zoos, using data collected from captive orangutans to link tooth stages to behavioral and developmental stages. In turn, this research allowed rescuers to more accurately make critical decisions about nutrition, medical care, and socialization, giving these orangutans the best shot at having a successful life—and maybe one day having offspring of their own.

title: How Gloria Steinem helped change the way women’s health is researched
content:
5 min readUpdated: Sep 4, 2026 01:49 PM IST

For much of the 20th century, medical research was conducted largely through a male lens. Women were often excluded from clinical studies, reproductive health was treated as a private matter, and illnesses disproportionately affecting women received comparatively little scientific attention.
Gloria Steinem did not create the women’s health movement, nor did she single-handedly transform medical research. But as one of feminism’s most influential public voices, she helped make women’s health a political issue and helped create the pressure for medicine and research institutions to change.
Reproductive rights: Health as a matter of autonomy
Steinem’s campaign for reproductive rights placed control over women’s bodies at the heart of the feminist movement. She argued that access to contraception and abortion was not simply a social or moral question but fundamental to women’s equality.
That argument helped shift reproductive health from the private sphere into public policy. The growing political movement around reproductive autonomy also encouraged greater attention to contraception, pregnancy, fertility and the health consequences of reproductive decisions. For Steinem, the underlying principle was straightforward: women could not have genuine equality without control over their own bodies.
Menstruation: Breaking the silence
Steinem brought another neglected subject into public conversation: menstruation. Her celebrated 1978 essay, “If Men Could Menstruate,” used satire to expose the stigma surrounding periods and the cultural tendency to regard women’s biology as embarrassing or inconvenient.
The essay was more than a feminist joke. By making menstruation discussable, Steinem challenged the silence surrounding menstrual symptoms and disorders. That mattered because conditions associated with menstruation had often been normalised rather than investigated.
Her broader message was that women’s everyday physical experiences deserved to be taken seriously—and, ultimately, scientifically understood.
Story continues below this ad
Women’s pain: From dismissal to investigation
The women’s health movement gave political force to a common complaint: women were not always believed when they described pain.
It helped shift the lens to conditions such as endometriosis, a chronic condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus, often causing severe menstrual and pelvic pain, inflammation, and sometimes infertility. Endometriosis can cause severe pelvic pain, infertility and other complications, yet diagnosis has historically been delayed and the disease remains incompletely understood. In fact, earlier this year, Steinem spearheaded conversations around it.
By challenging the dismissal of women’s bodily experiences, she helped establish the principle that women’s pain should be investigated rather than simply endured. That cultural shift helped create an environment in which neglected conditions could become legitimate research priorities.
Challenging the male model of medicine
Perhaps Steinem’s most important contribution was challenging the assumption that medical knowledge derived from men could simply be applied to women.
Story continues below this ad
By the 1970s and 1980s, women’s health advocates were exposing the consequences of women’s underrepresentation in research. The issue was not merely fairness: biological differences could affect symptoms, disease progression, drug responses and treatment outcomes.
In 1986, the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the US agency for biomedical and public-health research, introduced a policy encouraging the inclusion of women in clinical research. In 1990, it established the Office of Research on Women’s Health, giving women’s health a permanent institutional presence within the nation’s leading biomedical research agency.
The Women’s Health Initiative
The new emphasis on women’s health produced large-scale research. In 1991, the NIH launched the Women’s Health Initiative, ultimately enrolling more than 150,000 postmenopausal women.
The programme investigated major causes of illness and death among women, including cardiovascular disease, cancer and osteoporosis, while also examining the effects of hormone therapy and dietary interventions. Its scale was significant not simply because of the findings it produced, but because it demonstrated that women’s health questions warranted major, long-term scientific investment.
Story continues below this ad
Changing the rules of clinical research
The movement’s influence eventually became embedded in federal policy. The 1993 NIH Revitalization Act required women and minorities to be included in NIH-supported clinical research and required researchers to examine whether treatments affected different populations differently. This represented a fundamental change. Women’s participation in research was no longer merely encouraged as a matter of representation; it became part of the structure of federally funded clinical science.
Steinem’s most important contribution to women’s health research was, therefore, indirect but profound. She helped turn women’s experiences — from reproductive choices to menstruation and bodily pain— into subjects of public debate and demands for institutional accountability. Her enduring message was ultimately a scientific one as much as a political one: Women’s experiences are evidence, women’s health questions deserve investigation, and women’s bodies cannot be understood adequately by treating men as the default patient.

title: [아프리카인물열전](36) '두 나라 퍼스트레이디' 그라사 마셸
content:
