title: Rescued bears begin new lives after years of captivity in Vietnam
content:
One of these centers is the Vietnam Bear Rescue Center in Bach Ma National Park in the central city of Hue, supported by Animals Asia. It covers 12 hectares.
The bears at the center have been rescued from captivity farms in Thai Nguyen, Hanoi, Nghe An and other localities.
For years, many were confined to cramped, suffocating metal cages.
At the rescue center, they are given individual indoor spaces of about 10 square meters, along with proper care, hygiene and nutrition.
A safe and happy final chapter for bears once kept captive. Photo: Animals Asia
Every morning, the center's young men and women rise early to begin caring for and monitoring the bears.
When they first arrive, the animals are often emaciated and in poor condition.
With time, proper food and attentive care, many regain their health and develop glossy black coats.
Whether a bear is allowed into the semi-wild enclosure each day depends on factors including the weather and its health.
The semi-wild habitat is surrounded by large mesh-covered structures.
Inside are swings, pools of water and climbing structures designed to encourage the bears to play and explore.
Tree trunks are secured at their bases to prevent the animals from climbing or damaging them.
In the semi-natural enclosure, the bears take part in activities designed to restore their natural instincts and improve their physical condition.
Rather than placing food in a single feeding trough, staff scatter it throughout the enclosure, putting treats on elevated poles or hiding them in hollows and bamboo stems.
The bears must move around and use their senses to find their meals.
“This helps bears recover their natural foraging instincts,” said Phan Thi Thuy Trinh, a manager at the center.
“Their environment and food are also varied as much as possible to stimulate them and partly recreate the vast and diverse conditions of a natural habitat.”
The center primarily cares for Asiatic black bears and sun bears.
Both are omnivores, although plants make up between 70 percent and 90 percent of a bear's natural diet.
Their food includes forest fruits, seeds, bamboo shoots, leaves, young shoots, roots and tubers.
Their diets change regularly with the seasons and are supplemented with other foods, including dry feed providing protein, calcium and minerals.
Menus are rotated so that it takes roughly two weeks before a particular meal is repeated.
In addition to their main meals, essential oils and honey are hidden in tree hollows throughout the semi-wild enclosure, encouraging the bears to use their senses and search for food.
Health monitoring is another essential part of their care.
Every bear receives a routine health examination at least once every two years.
Emergency examinations are conducted whenever caregivers notice signs of illness or other abnormal behavior.
Bears that have spent many years in captivity commonly suffer from dental problems, musculoskeletal disorders, high blood pressure and liver or gallbladder diseases.
Veterinarians are able to treat most of these conditions, while particularly complex cases may require assistance from leading specialists in Vietnam or abroad.
Two decades of efforts to end bear bile farming
According to Vietnam's Department of Forestry and Forest Protection, the country recorded 4,239 captive bears in 2005.
After more than two decades of coordinated management, rescue and public-awareness efforts, the number had fallen to 206 animals as of July this year, a reduction of nearly 95 percent from its peak.
Over the past two years alone, the captive population has fallen from 384 to 206, demonstrating the impact of cooperation among government agencies, forest rangers and conservation organizations.
Nevertheless, 129 bears remain in the hands of 46 households and private facilities.
These animals are considered a priority for continued efforts to persuade their owners to voluntarily transfer them to rescue centers.
The localities with the largest remaining populations include Hanoi, Nghe An, Hai Phong and Dong Nai, along with several northern provinces.
“The biggest challenge now is no longer rescue capacity, but shortening the time between reaching an agreement with an owner and safely bringing the bear to a rescue center,” said Nguyen Vu Linh, director of Bach Ma National Park.
For years, rumors about the supposed medicinal value of bear bile, bear paws, claws and gallbladder products as well as the practice of keeping bears as pets, have helped drive the species toward decline.
Although people involved in the illegal trade in bear bile continue to face penalties, demand among consumers has proved difficult to eliminate.
In mid-March, a court in Ho Chi Minh City sentenced D.M.H., born in 1997, to 18 months in prison for illegally possessing and trading 39 bear claws and teeth.
Education for Nature Vietnam (ENV) has warned that efforts to end bear bile farming cannot be completed as long as a market for bear bile remains.
Of particular concern is the growing availability of jewelry made from bear teeth and claws on online marketplaces.
The department has set 2026 as the target year for completely ending the bear bile farming industry.
Animals Asia began rescuing bears in Vietnam in 2007.
The organization has rescued 300 bears, including Asiatic black bears and sun bears.
Of these, 183 are currently living in lush semi-natural environments at two bear rescue centers, located in the buffer zone of Tam Dao National Park in Phu Tho Province, northern Vietnam and Bach Ma National Park in Hue City, central Vietnam.

title: JEP resolvió la situación jurídica de más de mil comparecientes
content:
La Jurisdicción Especial para la Paz (JEP) ya ha resuelto unas 1.030 renuncias a la persecución penal. En términos más simples, son casos de comparecientes que no fueron considerados máximos responsables de crímenes durante el conflicto y cuya situación jurídica ya quedó definida.
La medida hace parte de la Ruta No Sancionatoria, que está a cargo de la Sala de Definición de Situaciones Jurídicas. Esa ruta se ocupa de los comparecientes que estuvieron involucrados en crímenes, pero no tuvieron un papel determinante en su planeación o ejecución.
“Es por esta vía entonces que los familiares de las víctimas del conflicto armado pueden acceder a respuestas sobre el cómo, cuándo y dónde ocurrieron los hechos”, dijo el presidente del tribunal de paz, Alejandro Ramelli.
En su intervención el presidente de la JEP, magistrado Alejandro Ramelli Arteaga, habló sobre el significado que tiene para las víctimas encontrarse con los comparecientes que no son máximos responsables en la Ruta No Sancionatoria:
— Jurisdicción Especial para la Paz (@JEP_Colombia) September 9, 2026
“Para las víctimas, este proceso ha… pic.twitter.com/Lls4jpG5Ex
El 95% de los beneficiarios son de la Fuerza Pública. De las 1.030 decisiones, 979 fueron para sus integrantes. Otras 46 fueron para comparecientes de las extintas Farc y las cinco restantes, para agentes del Estado, civiles colaboradores y un tercero civil.
La medida se concretó en 43 resoluciones entre 2024 y 2026. Son decisiones definitivas que cierran la situación jurídica de los comparecientes.
- En la práctica, borran sus antecedentes penales y extinguen las sanciones disciplinarias, administrativas o fiscales relacionadas con los hechos.
- Los comparecientes cobijados estuvieron involucrados en 377 hechos que dejaron 643 víctimas directas en distintos departamentos.
- Entre ellos están Antioquia, Boyacá, Casanare, Caquetá, Cesar, Córdoba, Cundinamarca, Huila, Meta, Norte de Santander y Santander.
¿Por qué importa? Porque para las víctimas y sus familias, que un caso termine por esta vía no significa simplemente que el compareciente quede libre de responsabilidad. La renuncia a la persecución penal viene con compromisos como contar la verdad, ayudar a buscar y entregar dignamente a las víctimas y hacer actos de reparación simbólica.
Además, como varios de ellos estuvieron involucrados directamente en los crímenes, pueden aportar detalles importantes sobre lo que pasó.
Un ejemplo es el famoso abrazo que ocurrió en esta Sala entre el compareciente Andrés Rosero y la mamá y la hija de John Darío Giraldo Quintero, asesinado y presentado como guerrillero muerto en combate por integrantes del Batallón de Artillería No. 4 “Jorge Eduardo Sánchez”.
“Este es un momento que necesitábamos para poder sanar”, aseguraron en su momento.

title: Child cancer groups call for concerted action
content:
It's one of the cruelest ironies in health and medicine. Pediatric sarcomas are among the rarest yet most aggressive forms of childhood cancer and some of the hardest to cure. Whereas many adult cancers are now treatable with new therapeutic strategies, such as immunotherapies, pediatric sarcomas have not seen nearly as many advances. Survival rates have remained largely unchanged for decades.
In 2014, parents from advocacy groups across Long Island, New York, who'd lost children to rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) banded together to form a coalition supporting a new research initiative aimed at better understanding this deadly disease so that one day a cure could be found.
The group met at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory's Banbury Center. This world-renowned think tank was built to bring together scientists, clinicians and patient advocates to launch initiatives like this one, focused on a particular area of research or public health.
Since that fateful first meeting, scientists have made progress not only in RMS but also in other sarcomas and childhood diseases. Likewise, what began as a small but dedicated coalition of RMS groups has grown into a full-fledged pediatric sarcoma movement. After more than a decade of progress, the movement returned to Banbury Center.
In 2025, the think tank hosted Pediatric Sarcomas: Targets for Therapeutic Development. The meeting was organized by CSHL Adjunct Professor Christopher Vakoc, now at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, and Kimberly Stegmaier, chair of the Department of Pediatric Oncology at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.
"It was an intense and inspiring three days," recalls Phil Renna, founder of the Christina Renna Foundation, one of the advocacy groups that supported both Banbury meetings.
"So many ideas were proposed and discussed. Most importantly, we came away with a roadmap to help bring today's cutting-edge research from bench to bedside."
That roadmap recently appeared in an article in Genes & Development, published by CSHL Press. In the article, meeting attendees called for more collaboration in the spirit of the Banbury sessions.
The authors wrote that for today's pediatric cancer discoveries to eventually benefit patients, it would be crucial to "foster interdisciplinary partnerships among medical chemists, scientists, clinicians, advocates, and industry partners."
After outlining obstacles to progress, the group laid out three top priorities for the future: 1) creating an open-access platform for data and model sharing; 2) bridging pediatric and adult oncology through unified clinical infrastructure; and 3) fostering multidisciplinary collaboration.
"Together, these priorities underscore the need for a more interconnected research ecosystem that matches the complexity of the disease itself," the authors wrote.
"As emerging tools continue to reveal new vulnerabilities in pediatric sarcomas, the challenge ahead lies in translating this knowledge into durable therapies, guided by collaboration, shared infrastructure, and a sustained commitment to bridging discovery and treatment."

title: An activist writes how the Chipko Movement inspired him to conserve forests in South India
content:
Parvatiya Navjeevan Ashram is situated on a small hillock overlooking the Bhilangana Valley along the Bhilangana River, one of the tributaries of the Bhagirathi, in Tehri Garhwal district, Uttarakhand (formerly Uttaranchal). This was the epicentre of the Chipko Andolan led by Sunderlal and Vimla Bahuguna. Unlike other Gandhian ashrams or communities, it had simple cottages and a small office from where Chipko activists worked, evolving strategies and creating hand-printed pamphlets to be distributed in the villages. There was a primary school on the campus run by the ashram and it had a small patch of agricultural land. As part of the ashram rules, those living on the campus had to participate in common activities like prayer and cleaning, but they also contributed towards the labour, working on the farm to produce food, or assisting in agricultural activities. The concept behind establishing the ashram was to prepare the younger generation of activists to fight for the cause of social and economic justice, based on Gandhian ideology. Thus, equal opportunity was given for both intellectual and physical work.
When I arrived at the ashram to learn from the Chipko movement, Sunderlal Bahuguna said to me, “If you are visiting the ashram to build a career for yourself then you have arrived in the wrong place. But if you want to become an activist to protect Nature and natural resources, to work with the hill people, then it is the right place for you”. Later I learnt that Vimla agreed to marry him only after he quit his career in politics to dedicate himself to the cause of the hill people and set up this ashram in a remote region. Thus, I was fortunate enough to be trained as an activist in the legacy of Gandhi.
I was an idealistic youth, fresh from my post-graduation training from Delhi School of Social Work, University of Delhi. The theories of social work and community development that I had learnt in the books were tested against the realities of Himalayan village life. I was enrolled on grassroots work with senior Chipko activists like Dhoom Singh Negi, a longtime colleague of Sunderlal Bahuguna, who had quit his secure profession as a high school teacher to join Chipko. Pratap Shikhar was another youth from Chhatra Yuva Sangharsh Vahini, the youth organisation motivated by the ideals of the late Jayaprakash Narayan. Thus it was a mix of young and old activists who had already put in their hard labour to organise the Chipko struggle in the remote hill regions, motivating people, especially the women, to save the forests from being cut down by contractors.
Often, we had to walk long distances in the hills to organise the villagers, most of the time establishing contacts and trying to convince them about the need to form a strong organised group to fight the government to stop the felling of trees. Many times we had to spend the nights in the villages and the rule was to not ask for food and accommodation. However, we never faced any problem as the farming communities in these villages were so warm and hospitable that they fed us and also provided us a place to sleep, sharing whatever they had. This helped us to understand the ground level reality of the socio-economic factors, and how village life was deeply linked to the surrounding forests from where they brought fodder, fuel, and water. In fact, instead of creating awareness, we were learning from the villagers how their lifestyle evolved through the interaction with surrounding natural resources like forests and streams which was the lifeline for their everyday living.
Having learnt the basic lessons of organising grassroots movements to protect forests, I was keen to launch a movement similar to Chipko in order to conserve the tropical forests in South India. The Trans-Himalayan Kashmir to Kohima foot march inspired me to start a similar foot march along the banks of the Kali River in Uttara Kannada district, Karnataka. I started walking alone from Karwar, the coastal town and district headquarters on the banks of Kali. I walked with the message of Chipko to Diggi, the origin of the Kali River on the border of Goa and Karnataka. Though local people joined me on the walk and provided accommodation and food, it was a challenging task to convey the message of forest conservation. The Kali valley was witnessing massive tree-cutting for building the Supa Dam that would help to harness the water of the Kali for generating power. However, the sight of the clearfelling of old-growth forests strengthened my determination to fight those policies that caused this destruction. By sheer coincidence, about a hundred kilometres from Kali, in the Sirsi region, there were spontaneous sparks of protest against the forest destruction as the village youth were keen to stop the felling of natural forests in order to establish teak plantations in the guise of “scientific forestry”.
Initially, the demand of the Appiko movement was to halt the clear-felling of natural forests and their conversion to monoculture plantations. The launching of the movement was a threat to the government policy. They tried every means to stop the spread of the movement. However, the hidden hardships of the people and the conflict over the natural resources led to the spread of the movement in numerous districts of Karnataka from Kodagu in the south to South Kanara and Shimoga districts.
Realising there was widespread people’s support to the movement, the government agreed to stop the clear-felling of the old-growth forests for teak plantations. However, the activists realised that the timber concessions given to wood-based industries and even the removal of two trees per hectare was causing large-scale damage to the existing forest resources. In order to halt the further process of deforestation and the threat to the existing forests, the movement put forth the demand for a moratorium on the felling of green trees in the natural forests of the Western Ghats.
Well-organised grassroots actions occurring over a decade and pressure from numerous groups forced the state government to change its forest policy. In 1989, the state government imposed a ban on the felling of green trees in natural forests. This ban continues till today thanks to the Appiko movement and the positive response of the state government, which has taken action to conserve the forests.
Excerpted with permission from ‘From the Himalaya to the Western Ghats: Relevance of Chipko’, Pandurang Hegde in 50 Years of Chipko: The Movement and Its Afterlives’, edited by Murali Sivaramakrishnan, Orient Black Swan.

title: Zorgcentra na Seksueel Geweld hielpen vorig jaar meer dan 5.000 slachtoffers, vooral vrouwen en meisjes
content:
De Zorgcentra na Seksueel Geweld (ZSG) in ons land hebben in het afgelopen jaar meer dan 5.000 slachtoffers opgevangen. Dat blijkt uit nieuwe cijfers van de centra. 9 op de 10 slachtoffers zijn meisjes en vrouwen. Vaak is de pleger een bekende, zoals een (ex)-partner, vriend of kennis.
Zorgcentra na Seksueel Geweld hielpen vorig jaar meer dan 5.000 slachtoffers, vooral vrouwen en meisjes
Heb je een vraag over seksueel geweld? Dan kan je terecht bij de hulplijn 1712. Voor een gesprek kan je ook 24/7 terecht bij Tele-Onthaal op het nummer 106. Je kan ook chatten via www.tele-onthaal.be . Jongeren kunnen terecht bij Awel op het telefoonnummer 102, via chat op awel.be , of bij chathulplijn Nupraatikerover.be .
Wil je medische, psychologische en/of juridische hulp, kan je terecht bij 1 van de (voorlopig) 10 Zorgcentra na Seksueel Geweld , ook via e-mail of telefoon.
Tussen de oprichting in 2017 en 2025 zijn al meer dan 22.500 slachtoffers opgevangen in een van de Zorgcentra na Seksueel Geweld in ons land. Daar kan je als slachtoffer van seksueel geweld gratis en de klok rond terecht voor medische, forensische en psychologische hulp. Je kan er ook sporen laten verzamelen en aangifte doen bij de politie.
In het grootste deel van de gevallen waren de slachtoffers meisjes en vrouwen (90 procent). Voor het merendeel van de slachtoffers (62 procent) is de pleger een bekende, zoals een huisgenoot, (ex-)partner, vriend of kennis. De gemiddelde leeftijd van de slachtoffers is 24 jaar.
Vorig jaar lag het aantal slachtoffers dat zich meldde op meer dan 5.000. Het aantal stijgt al enkele jaren, al is die stijging grotendeels te verklaren doordat het aantal centra en de bekendheid ervan toenemen. Niet omdat het fenomeen steeds toeneemt, klinkt het.
België telt in totaal 10 Zorgcentra na Seksueel Geweld. Dit jaar nog worden 3 bijkomende centra geopend: in het UZ Jette, in het ziekenhuis van Doornik en in Ottignies, in Waals-Brabant. Het Instituut voor de Gelijkheid van Vrouwen en Mannen (IGVM) coördineert en ondersteunt mee de zorgcentra.
Documentaire
De voorstelling van de cijfers in Cinema Palace in Brussel ging gepaard met de vertoning van een nieuwe documentaire, 'The sessions', genaamd. Die geeft een inkijk in het verwerkingsproces van een jonge vrouw die het slachtoffer werd van seksueel geweld.
Vanaf 30 september loopt de documentaire in bioscopen en culturele centra. Vanaf januari 2027 is de docu ook te zien op VRT Canvas en VRT MAX.

title: Alice Kang’ethe: The economist fighting for a healthier Africa
content:
Early in Alice Kang'ethe's public-health career, on a trip to Mbita, a scorpion stung her. The pain was ferocious. She was far from a proper hospital, and her international health insurance was useless there. The immediate help at her disposal was a modest clinic, where health workers gave her an antidote and got her the care she needed.
"Those people saved my life," Alice says. It is, in a way, the whole argument she has built a career on: Fix the small clinic, and the rest of the country survives with it. Ignore it, and geography decides who lives.
Alice has spent 20 years chasing that idea across borders, first as a volunteer in Dar es Salaam. She had just returned from the London School of Economics (LSE), hoping to work in a think tank, using economics to influence policy.
"I came back to Kenya from LSE and reality hit. Unemployment. A friend asked if I would consider volunteering for a foundation just starting out in HIV care and treatment. My parents were frustrated," she says.
She now runs the Beginnings Fund, built with a coalition that includes the Gates Foundation and the Children's Investment Fund Foundation, to attack what she calls the "core drivers of death" in maternal and newborn health. It has raised $493 million (Sh63 billion) and pushed $199 million Sh25 billion) into 30 grants across six African countries.
"I could do something here that will touch millions of lives on my continent."
TIME magazine put her on its inaugural TIME100 Philanthropy list this year. Her mother called it, simply, the fulfilment of her dream, the same mother who told a young girl decades ago that she would have to work twice as hard to be taken half as seriously.
What frustrates her now is the pace of change. “My struggle is, it’s not moving fast enough.”
You've had such a good run, haven't you?
I would say so. I'm not done yet. But I'm proud of what we have achieved. I say "we" because I've had a team.
Do you remember how you stood out, as a young woman getting into this career?
I'm actually an economist by training. After high school I went to Catholic University of Eastern Africa and majored in Economics, then to the London School of Economics (LSE). My dream was to be in a think tank, using economics to influence policy. Somehow I ended up in public health instead, I'd say by accident.
I came back to Kenya from LSE and reality hit. Unemployment. A friend asked if I would consider volunteering for a foundation just starting out in HIV care and treatment as I waited for a full-time job. My parents were frustrated, they had funded my postgraduate studies in London, no small feat, and now I needed money to go and volunteer. Reluctantly, they supported me.
My first stop was Dar es Salaam, thrown straight into the deep end. The more senior volunteers had to fly back to the US, and left me
to convene stakeholders from across Tanzania, government, development agencies, experts, to develop the country's first national HIV care and treatment plan. I had no office, I was working out of a hotel room, and most people were essentially asking, 'who are you, what mandate do you even have?' I did not give up.
Every time I go back today and see people sitting calmly in those clinics, no stigma, getting their treatment, it is so fulfilling.
From there I went to South Africa, a different scale altogether, a government not yet convinced it should support care at scale. Our first attempt failed. I left, joined KPMG for a year, and no sooner had I settled in than my former team lead called to say they were setting up an office in Kenya. I went right back.
Why did you go back, and why economics in the first place?
Because I cherished the experience. The people, the patients, the doctors, former President Bill Clinton himself. But also I realised I could do something that would impact millions of people.
I hear doctors who've moved from clinical practice to public health use this analogy: I could see one patient at a time in my clinic, or influence millions at a time. I got drawn into that. At the Clinton Foundation it was, here's a problem, go solve it, how you get there is up to you. I enjoyed that.
And economics, because I have a problem with the way Africa is described. I strongly believe there's a place for economic policy to lift people out of poverty.
What's been the most difficult thing you've ever had to do?
As a volunteer in South Africa, convincing the government that it was a moral imperative to provide care and treatment to everyone infected with HIV. Getting people with decision-making power to do the right thing, when you think it's obvious, but it isn't.
I see the same today in maternal and newborn health. No woman should die from preventable causes bringing life into the world, but we've almost normalised these deaths.
On a more practical level, fundraising. The world has waves and fads. There's a time HIV was very well funded. We see that too in maternal and child health, these peaks and troughs, when it needs to stay on the priority list for the long haul.
Go back to childhood a little. What do you remember, and what did you want then?
I was born in Nairobi, then my parents moved to Tigoni. My father was a banker with Barclays. Later we moved to Nakuru, to a farm. It was difficult for me because I'd lived in the city. I used to admire air hostesses, wanted to be one, but my father shut that down immediately, said that was no career.
Growing up, what I remember most is struggling with inequities. My parents weren't rich, but we didn't lack, we went to public schools, we had meals, the basics. In high school it was in the dormitory, seeing a girl with nothing in her box.
I still remember, from a very young age, struggling with why some children didn't have shoes, why they looked so ragged.
I believe everything I've done since has been toward social justice. I still struggle with it today. You go to some hospitals, find four premature babies sharing one incubator and ask, are these children of a lesser God?
In this season, are there habits you're trying to unlearn?
I'm trying to stop and smell the roses more. In academics, in my career, I invested everything into the work. Some of my friends say I take life too seriously, that I should stop, celebrate what I've done. So I'm doing more of that now.
You've a stellar career. What's one thing you failed at, and what did it teach you?
At the Clinton Health Access Initiative, I was given a programme on prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV. We succeeded in preventing transmission at delivery. But mothers still needed to breastfeed, and still carried the virus, and the science for that wasn't advanced yet. So, in essence, we failed.
Babies born HIV-negative eventually turned positive through breastfeeding. There was the option of infant formula, but that brought complications around clean water, and you could save a child from HIV only to lose them to dehydration and diarrhoea.
That taught me that much as we were the crazy ones who thought we could change the world, and for the most part we did, we needed to bring everyone along. We jumped ahead of the science, assuming the rest would catch up. Ambition must be matched with reality.
Is there anything you've always wanted to do but haven't gotten around to?
I keep saying I want to retire in Nanyuki, on a farm. I think I'm a rural girl now. I haven't gotten around to finding that place, that solace, and I realise I don't have so much time left, so I'd better do it. I think of retirement more now, in part because I believe in empowering others to carry the baton. I don't want to hold it for too long before I hand over.
Are there things you struggle with as a female leader that male leaders of your cadre don't?
Certainly, we haven't moved past that. Early in my career, we were supporting the Kenyan government to hire additional nurses and doctors, the money had been put in Treasury but staff hadn't been paid.
I kept urging the leads to honour that commitment, and one of them told me, 'young girl, don't get emotional, it's normal for doctors and nurses to wait six months for their first salary.' I said, but the money is already there, we're failing them by not moving it.
I don't think if the person raising that concern had been a man, the response would have been the same. As women, especially African women, you have to work twice as hard to earn that level of respect. I've sat in a waiting room while someone said, 'we're still waiting for your boss', only for my colleague to correct them, 'this is the boss.'
What personal fears keep you up at night?
I'm a mum to a 10-year-old girl, and I think about what happens if I'm not there, who takes care of her. And whether she'll turn out well, whether I'm teaching her the real strokes of life, or sheltering her too much.
Where do you get your affirmation from now?
My family, especially my husband. Even on tough days he's good at telling me I'm doing a great job. And my mother, a core pillar of my strength. In May, when I got the TIME100 Philanthropy recognition, she told me I had fulfilled her dream. She's one of my biggest cheerleaders.
What's your struggle in this season of your life?
Speed. The rate at which I want to see change. I feel it every time I sit in rooms where Africa is described negatively, especially on maternal and newborn mortality. I know the approach of working with governments is the right one, but I want to inject more pace into it.
What's your love language?
Service. I do gifting too, but acts of service is the predominant one. I believe in showing up.
Is there anything you'd like to share that you thought I'd ask?
Early in my career, leading the Kenya programme, I was on a trip to Beta Point, today's Homa Bay County, when I felt something creep up my trousers. I'd been stung by a scorpion.
What stuck with me is that health workers at the local health centre treated me quickly, crushed the scorpion, gave me the antidote. My international health insurance didn't matter in that moment. Those were the people who saved my life.
I tell that story because it's why I'm such a strong believer in building systems for everyone. That experience grounded me, and it's part of why I keep chasing equity for all.
If the Level Five hospital is functioning, it's for all of us. Getting anywhere else for treatment at the time was far-fetched. That grounded me, and it's part of why I keep chasing equity for all.
If you were reincarnated, what profession would you choose? And what do you do now to unwind?
I think I'd get into large-scale farming, combining another inequity I care about, food security, with the peace and serene life I look forward to in retirement. To unwind I love to travel to peaceful, serene places. Water calms me a lot. I also read, and I take time with friends, and with my daughter.

title: ‘Não podemos aceitar retrocessos’, diz ministra do MDA sobre reforma agrária no Brasil
content:
Em meio a uma jornada de mobilização por soberania popular, democracia, reforma agrária e direitos para o povo do campo e da cidade, organizada pelo Movimentos dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra (MST), o governo de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) faz entregas emblemáticas para Minas Gerais, nesta sexta-feira (11).
Com a presença de Fernanda Machiaveli, ministra do Ministério do Desenvolvimento Agrário e Agricultura Familiar (MDA), o encontro, que será realizado na Serraria Souza Pinto, no Centro de Belo Horizonte, promete consolidar a criação do assentamento Terra Prometida, local onde aconteceu o Massacre de Felisburgo, no Vale do Jequitinhonha.
“Além disso, nós também vamos celebrar a entrega dos primeiros CCUs, que são esses documentos titulatórios para os assentados da reforma agrária lá na área de Campo do Meio. A área de Ariadnópolis, essa fazenda foi também desapropriada em 2025 e, a partir desse processo, nós já fizemos a obtenção da área e já estamos na fase de entrega dos títulos”, conta Machiaveli.
Antes de chegar à cidade, a ministra concedeu entrevista ao Brasil de Fato MG, na qual, além de abordar as entregas que o governo federal faz nesta sexta, explicou os números da reforma agrária e as expectativas para o futuro.
Confira a entrevista completa:
Brasil de Fato MG – A senhora entrega, nesta sexta-feira (11), uma área destinada à reforma agrária em Minas Gerais e deve anunciar novas ações do MDA para o estado. Em síntese, o que será anunciado na sexta-feira e quais são os planos para Minas Gerais?
Fernanda Machiaveli – Nesta semana, nós vamos fazer duas entregas muito importantes para a reforma agrária. A primeira se refere à criação do assentamento Terra Prometida, ali na Fazenda Santa Lúcia, o local onde aconteceu o Massacre de Felisburgo, que culminou no assassinato de cinco trabalhadores rurais, em 2004. O presidente Lula, em 2026, fez o decreto que desapropriou essa área para interesse social e, com isso, nós já conseguimos avançar para criar esse assentamento. Então, é uma entrega em um tempo bastante célere entre o processo de desapropriação e a criação do assentamento.
Além da assinatura da portaria com a criação do assentamento, nós também vamos celebrar a entrega dos primeiros CCUs, que são esses documentos titulatórios para os assentados da reforma agrária lá na área de Campo do Meio, da fazenda Ariadnópolis desapropriada em 2025. Estamos na fase de entrega dos títulos.
Os CCUs serão entregues neste momento para 42 famílias, cinco lotes. O Quilombo Campo Grande, 1, 2, 3, 4 e 5. E nós vamos entregar, além disso, até 10 de outubro, para 457 famílias de quatro projetos de assentamento desses quatro quilombos Campo Grande, que estão só aguardando a finalização do edital de seleção.
Hoje em dia, a gente tem essa etapa, que é uma etapa relevante e demorada, que é publicar um edital. As famílias se apresentam, a gente seleciona aquelas que têm o perfil da reforma agrária e, aí sim, destinamos para o processo de recebimento do CCU e, na sequência, ao aguardo do crédito instalação, apoio inicial e depois o crédito habitação e os demais créditos aos quais fazem jus os beneficiários do Programa Nacional de Reforma Agrária.
A reforma agrária tem em seu bojo a expectativa de plantio de árvores, produção de alimentos saudáveis e a possibilidade de um desenvolvimento rural sustentável e justo. Mas, para isso de fato se consolidar, é preciso de terra e de recursos. Até julho de 2026, segundo o Portal O Joio e o Trigo, o atual governo havia assentado 58,6 mil novas famílias, segundo dados do painel do Incra, número insuficiente para zerar a fila de espera. Atualmente, 113.232 famílias estão acampadas em todo o Brasil, destas, 55 mil estão no Cadastro Único para Programas Sociais (CadÚnico) e são o público prioritário da reforma agrária. O governo destaca um número bem maior: 266 mil famílias incluídas no Programa Nacional de Reforma Agrária desde 2023. Qual é a avaliação do Ministério sobre esse cenário e há alguma expectativa para que isso mude?
Esses dados estão corretos. Então, sim, são 266.000 famílias incluídas no Programa Nacional de Reforma Agrária. Dessas, 58.000 são em projetos de assentamento e assentamentos ambientalmente diferenciados. 117.000 são famílias reconhecidas. O que isso quer dizer? São famílias quilombolas, são famílias de assentamentos estaduais, são famílias que são beneficiárias do processo de reforma agrária, mas não necessariamente em assentamentos criados pelo Incra, mas que devem ser reconhecidas como famílias que foram assentadas naquele período.
Além disso, há as famílias regularizadas, porque durante a vida de um assentado também há novas conformações de núcleos familiares. Então, famílias que se separam, viúvas, filhos que não ficam no assentamento e vão embora, ou outros que se casam e acabam ficando lá, e os irmãos vão embora; enfim, outros desenhos. Nesse momento, o Incra vai lá, verifica se a família que está no lote tem o perfil da reforma agrária e regulariza a situação daquela família. Então, são novas famílias em lotes existentes. Essa é a diferença: os regularizados são novas famílias em lotes existentes. E os novos, esses que nós contabilizamos como novas famílias assentadas, são famílias novas em lotes novos. Para unificarmos e compreendermos também.
O governo do presidente Lula 1, só para termos uma dimensão de comparação, assentou 89.000 famílias, nesse critério de lotes novos com famílias novas. No total, foram 384.000 famílias, somando reconhecimento, regularização e novos assentamentos. No Lula 2, foram 38.000 famílias assentadas, 19.000 reconhecidas e 174.000 regularizadas, em um total de 232.000. O que isso quer dizer? Que nós, neste momento, depois de todo o processo de desmantelamento do Incra, de paralisação da reforma agrária e de interrupção de todos os processos que orientavam as ações na ponta executadas pelo Incra, já conseguimos ultrapassar a marca do segundo mandato do presidente Lula. Nós já conseguimos reconstruir a nossa capacidade de assentar famílias.
Se você comparar com o governo Dilma 1, teremos números menores. Foram 22.000 nos novos assentamentos e 107.000 no total. Mas quando olhamos o total do governo Temer, foram 8.000 famílias naquele total, e nenhuma nova família assentada. No governo Bolsonaro, 2.000 famílias foram assentadas em um total de 21.000 famílias que foram incluídas no Programa Nacional de Reforma Agrária.
Então, nós saímos desse patamar de 2.000 famílias para um patamar de 58.000; saímos de um patamar total de inclusão no Programa Nacional de Reforma Agrária de 21.000 famílias e fomos para 266.000 famílias. Tudo isso em um cenário em que os servidores do Incra estão em número muito menor, o orçamento do Incra estava completamente reduzido e os servidores enfrentavam a desvalorização da carreira. Foi todo um esforço de valorizar a carreira, aumentar os salários, contratar pessoas, refazer as estruturas do Incra e voltar a ter normas que permitissem fazer a reforma agrária, porque desmantelaram todo o arcabouço institucional e criaram várias dificuldades para conseguirmos assentar as famílias e recuperar o orçamento do Incra. E nós chegamos agora com esse resultado.
É suficiente para um país que tem a concentração fundiária que o Brasil tem? Certamente não. Precisamos avançar muito mais. É por isso que precisamos de mais tempo e não podemos aceitar nenhum tipo de retrocesso. Agora é o momento de acelerar. O orçamento do Incra começou com 300 milhões, em 2022. Agora, o orçamento que foi enviado para o Congresso está em 2 bilhões para o Incra, mais 1 bilhão e 700 milhões apenas para os vários créditos: o crédito de instalação e os aportes que fazemos no Fundo de Terras e da Reforma Agrária. Então, eu estou falando de um aumento muito impressionante do percentual e do volume de recursos destinados agora para as políticas públicas executadas pelo Incra, que envolvem a reforma agrária, a regularização fundiária e a titulação de terras quilombolas.
É realmente uma aposta que mostra o compromisso que o nosso presidente tem: todo o esforço que foi feito, ano a ano, ampliando o orçamento. As famílias que hoje estão acampadas são a nossa prioridade, e nós vamos continuar trabalhando para elas, para que todas possam trabalhar, ter acesso à terra e ter as condições dos créditos para a produção de alimentos. Esse é o nosso grande objetivo. Só que, infelizmente, não é possível fazer toda a revolução agrária que o país demanda há tantos séculos em um único mandato. Nós precisamos percorrer um caminho e agir de forma cada vez mais célere, acumulando conquistas que permitam que, de fato, saiamos dessa situação.
O Plano Safra trouxe avanços muito importantes à agricultura familiar. E nós temos também alguns dados de que, no Plano Safra de 2025/2026, os recursos destinados aos pequenos agricultores chegaram a R$ 89 bilhões, com crescimento também no número de contratos de crédito rural. Trazendo um pouco aqui para Minas Gerais, dados de 2024 mostram que foram aplicados só aqui R$ 4,8 bilhões no Plano Safra, com a realização de 143.000 contratos, um número mais de 40% superior aos 115.000 do plano anterior. Como tem sido a destinação desses recursos no estado de Minas Gerais atualmente e quais são as mudanças que vocês já observaram com o aumento desse recurso?
Minas Gerais tem performado muito bem. É um estado que tem uma agricultura familiar forte e que tem cada vez mais acessado o crédito. Fico contente em dizer que, só para essa safra, estão previstas as execuções de recursos no montante de 8,5 bilhões para o Plano Safra de Minas Gerais, recursos que estão sendo disponibilizados para financiar a produção no estado.
Se você for comparar, de fato, nós saímos de uma base no governo anterior em que foram financiados R$ 11 bilhões no total dos quatro anos para a agricultura familiar mineira. Agora, estamos chegando em 2026 já com R$ 22 bilhões executados, ou seja, já dobramos o volume de crédito que chega para os agricultores familiares do estado de Minas Gerais.
Nós aumentamos, no caso do crédito para os assentados da reforma agrária, que é o Pronaf A, 233% no volume destinado e 70% no número de operações. Ou seja, quase dobramos o número de operações, mas ampliamos de forma muito significativa o volume que está sendo acessado pelos assentados. Isso permitiu, então, que acessássemos um volume de crédito bem maior para essa política no Brasil como um todo. Saímos de um patamar em que, no primeiro ano, colocamos R$ 500 milhões e não foi executado nem a metade. No outro ano, colocamos R$ 500 milhões de novo.
Agora, na última safra, já fechamos com R$ 2,7 bilhões executados e, por conta desse total acumulado, já estão previstos mais R$ 2 bilhões no ano que vem, só para o crédito dos assentados da reforma agrária. O presidente Lula assinou ontem um crédito extraordinário que já colocou mais R$ 375 milhões para disponibilizar para o Pronaf A no Brasil todo, porque já tinha acabado o recurso. Então, nós temos hoje não só os agricultores familiares estruturados acessando o crédito, não só o microcrédito chegando nas regiões que têm fundos constitucionais como Norte e Nordeste, mas temos agora os assentados da reforma agrária no Brasil inteiro acessando o Pronaf.
Vocês têm um planejamento específico por parte do Ministério para melhorar processos, ampliar os sistemas agroecológicos e recuperar as áreas degradadas? Como está essa visão do Ministério em relação a esse enfrentamento da crise climática atualmente?
O Brasil propôs uma meta bastante ousada de redução de emissões de gases que têm o potencial de provocar o aquecimento global. Para alcançarmos essas metas, foi construído o Plano Clima. Dentro do Plano Clima, há a parte de adaptação e a parte de mitigação.
Na adaptação, pela primeira vez, temos o setorial da agricultura familiar, que prevê um conjunto de ações para permitir que os agricultores familiares, nas suas várias características — desde os camponeses aos povos e comunidades tradicionais, passando por indígenas, assentados da reforma agrária e agricultores como um todo —, consigam fazer esse percurso de se adaptar a uma realidade que está cada vez menos estável. Temos eventos climáticos mais frequentes que impactam as lavouras, a capacidade produtiva e também os nossos próprios recursos naturais, começando pelo próprio solo.
A partir disso, nós fizemos neste plano algumas ações estratégicas. Sem dúvida, impulsionar a transição agroecológica é um grande objetivo do processo de adaptação. Estamos falando de manter os solos cobertos a maior parte do ano para justamente reter menos calor e também emitir menos gás carbônico. Estamos falando de adotar as melhores práticas de acesso à água, com programas como o de cisternas e o de irrigação para permitir a adaptação. Programas de ajuste das próprias áreas de serra e encosta para evitar que chuvas muito fortes levem todo o material orgânico para os lagos e rios, adaptando técnicas de produção a essa característica para evitar a perda da riqueza dos nossos solos. E também estamos visualizando um processo de adaptação para áreas mais áridas, como é o caso da nossa Caatinga.
Agora, temos na praça um edital que destina R$ 400 milhões só para a área do semiárido, que inclui uma parte importante de Minas Gerais, para fazer a adaptação das famílias ao contexto de mudança climática. Isso é a adaptação. Aí temos a mitigação.
A mitigação envolve frentes que são, principalmente, a redução do desmatamento e a recuperação das áreas. A redução do desmatamento tem sido feita com bastante conscientização e também valorizando os produtos que vêm da floresta em pé. E a restauração tem sido feita por meio de um programa chamado Florestas Produtivas, que apoia, com a construção de viveiros e assistência técnica, o processo de restauro. Um restauro que não tem apenas a finalidade de recuperar a mata nativa, mas também de ser feito com variedades produtivas que gerem renda para as famílias e, assim, criem incentivos para manter aquelas áreas restauradas preservadas.
Então, temos feito essas duas frentes de trabalho, além de investir em insumos e outras tecnologias que vão permitir que a nossa agricultura se torne mais resiliente e menos impactante para o conjunto do meio ambiente.

title: Health Leaders Talk Expanding Access to Specialty Care
content:
When there are breakthrough technologies like xenotransplants, or novel cancer therapies, they’re transformative for diseases and conditions once thought incurable—but they can only save lives if the people that need them can access them. On September 10, TIME hosted the third annual TIME100 Health Leadership Forum in New York City, bringing together the TIME and TIME100 Health communities to discuss equity, longevity, and solution-driven care. The evening featured five expert panels, including The Access Gap: Expanding Pathways to Life-Saving Care. Moderated by TIME senior health correspondent Alice Park, the panel invited faculty physicians specializing in cell therapies from Oregon Health & Science University and Penn Medicine to take part in conversation with Amy Ronneberg, chief executive officer of NMDP, a global nonprofit connecting patients with lifesaving cell therapies and transplants. NMDP is a sponsor of the 2026 TIME100 Health Leadership Forum.
While modern science has solved some access issues, others still remain. “If we go back six years, the biggest barrier was the fact that there were not donors to match,” says Ronneberg. “As more patients have a donor, we now are facing issues around referral. Thousands of patients are not getting referred to transplant centers in a timely manner, those that are oftentimes are facing major barriers from a financial perspective.”
Dr. Eneida R. Nemecek, director of Pediatric Cell Therapy and Transplant & Cancer Clinical Research at Oregon Health & Science University, agreed that geography is a big problem for patients who need care. She said it’s a symptom of a bigger problem with the way our health systems have been designed. “When we're designing systems for healthcare, we forget that we're designing the systems for the patient. The system designs the system for itself, and then we try to adjust it to the patient,” Nemecek says.
Because of how specialized CAR-T therapies were designed and tested, there can be natural bottlenecks when it comes to scaling up and disseminating it to a wider audience. Dr. David L. Porter, director of the Center for Cell Therapy and Transplant at Penn Medicine, says that advanced therapies like bone marrow transplants or cellular immunotherapies are developed and largely performed at major academic institutions in big cities, usually as a proof of concept. However, swaths of the population in the country do not live near one of these institutions or have to drive hours to one that has both the technology and the expertise. Now, there are seven FDA-approved commercial CAR-T cells, and the manufacturers have no problem receiving cells from collection centers, manufacturing them, and returning them. “The barrier is actually collecting the cells,” Porter says. “It's a very specialized process.”
Additionally, undergoing collection and treatment causes huge displacement in patients and their caregivers’ lives. The entire process of treatment and testing can take weeks. “We have those discussions all the time that people would accept suboptimal therapy and give up the potential for curative therapy because they can’t do that,” Porter says. “There are an enormous number of initiatives trying to improve, and they move the needle a little bit.” One of these methods is to try to give these therapies in community health centers closer to where the patients are. Porter and his colleagues recently conducted a pilot study at the University of Pennsylvania with two of their community partners to implement high-end CAR-T cell therapy in a community setting. Over the course of about a year, they’ve been able to treat over 60 patients who otherwise largely would not have had access because they would not have traveled to a big city for it.
With science changing fast and treatment outcomes improving, Ronneberg says that it’s more important than ever to “get the education and awareness out to the community,” and provide them with “funds to travel.” As a cancer survivor herself, Ronneberg recalled having a hard time navigating the process even when she had everything at her fingertips—a husband who’s a doctor, resources from her job at the NMDP. The organization’s focus has moved beyond simply finding donors to now getting patients to the right treatment they need at the right locations, whether that’s an academic center or a community center.
To this end, Nemecek and her colleagues have been working on projects like ACCESS Initiative, in partnership with NMDP, in order to start training community centers and equip them with accreditation needed to collect cells. “With valuable telehealth, with use of technology,” Nemecek says, “that’s really where the future of our field is.”
The TIME100 Health Leadership Forum was presented by the American Cancer Society, Kite—a Gilead Sciences company, Insulet, Musely, and NMDP.

title: The ‘National Park’ That Stretches From Coast to Coast
content:
On Doug Tallamy’s 10-acre property in rural Pennsylvania, the evidence arrives on wings. Wood thrushes now nest in shrubs that were once cut for hay. Luna moths — emerald-green giants that had become increasingly rare — have reached record numbers. Tallamy recounts enthusiastically that he has documented more than 1,380 species of moths on the land, along with 62 breeding bird species. “We hear the birds in the morning. I see the gray tree frog sitting on my window sill,” he raves. “That is a real reward for me.”
When he and his wife Cindy bought the 300-year-old farm in 2000, its surroundings looked green. But when Tallamy walked the property he noticed it was overrun by invasive plants — like the Japanese stiltgrass and the aptly named mile-a-minute-weed, a smothering vine — that supported few pollinators. “There were no caterpillars!” he recalls. That recognition turned him from a researcher with a passion for insects into a passionate advocate for native plants. The transformation of his land didn’t require expensive engineering or high-tech equipment. Tallamy simply weeded out invasives and put native plants back. “I think in the last 26 years we spent about $100,” he says. “Because I simply go get seeds and put them in the ground.”
For more than two decades, the bestselling author and entomologist at the University of Delaware has argued that the biodiversity crisis won’t be solved only in national parks or on other protected lands. It will be solved — or lost — in millions of ordinary backyards and schoolyards, on corporate campuses and apartment balconies. “Nearly 80 percent of land east of the Mississippi is privately owned, and 135 million acres are now in residential landscapes,” he says. “That puts the private property owner in charge of conservation. If 10 to 20 percent of landowners planted native plants, this would add up to a habitat larger than 10 Yellowstones.”
National parks are much needed and beloved, but Tallamy points out that many species migrate beyond their borders and won’t survive if they don’t find sustenance and habitat along the way. “In between protected areas is no man’s land for most creatures and plants,” he says. “All of the parks and preserves, including Yellowstone, are too small and too isolated.” Connecting those islands with habitat on private land, he argues, “is going to be the solution.”
This premise led to his creation of Homegrown National Park, a nonprofit that encourages people to replace conventional lawns with native habitat and register their efforts on a nationwide biodiversity map. The initiative has now grown to over 52,000 registered participants who tend to more than 187,000 acres, figures Tallamy says are rapidly rising. “The real argument is that natural systems are generating your life support,” he urges. “They make your oxygen, they manage your watershed, they minimize extreme weather conditions, sequester carbon to help [mitigate] climate change. They’re doing all kinds of things to keep you alive on this planet.”
While the current administration guts the Endangered Species Act, reduces national monuments, defunds national parks and opens millions of acres of public lands to drilling and grazing, Tallamy is urging every American to give nature a boost where they can. “Everything we plant, don’t plant, or apply to our yard impacts the greater ecosystem in which our yard exists, and thus everything that depends on that ecosystem,” he writes in his most recent book, How Can I Help? Saving Nature with Your Yard. He argues that we don’t have the luxury to ignore that simple truth. “Everybody requires healthy ecosystems whether they know it or not,” he says. “That means it’s everybody’s responsibility to contribute to taking care of these systems.”
Tallamy emphasizes the urgency: “When you read that we’ve lost three billion breeding birds and have 22 percent fewer butterflies just since the year 2000, global insect decline, two-thirds of wildlife gone — that’s upsetting to a lot of people,” he says. “Even if they don’t know anything about biology, they don’t want to hear that everything on the planet is dying.”
Weighed down by negative news?

Rather than stopping there, Tallamy pivots toward agency. “Our simple message is: There are things you can do. You can see the results. It empowers you to be part of the solution instead of part of the problem.” He argues that the reward of taking action is immediate: “If you plant an oak tree in your yard, you can see the difference tomorrow.”
Homegrown National Park’s website and Tallamy’s books give detailed practical advice on what anybody can do, from planting keystone species to shrinking one’s lawn and leaving the leaves as shelter for pollinators. But even people without a yard can find plenty of useful information. “If everybody did container gardening on their balcony, it [would become] a resource for native bee species in cities,” he says. “Migrating monarchs will use these plants.” And if someone really does not want to handle plants, Tallamy has hands-on advice for them, too: “Then change the light bulb outside from a white bulb to an amber bulb to stop killing moths all night long. You don’t need a PhD to do that, but it would make a huge difference.”
Whether this grassroots movement can scale fast enough to make a measurable ecological difference remains an open question. But as governments struggle to halt biodiversity loss, Tallamy is betting on changing culture.
Referring to the U.N.’s initiative of conserving 30 percent of land and water by 2030, commonly referred to as 30 x 30, he says, “You’ve got to count what’s happening on private property. And nobody’s doing that. Nobody’s recording it. That’s what that biodiversity map is all about.”
In his books, which have sold over half a million copies, Tallamy propagates a stubbornly upbeat view. “The cultural change from an adversarial relationship with nature to a collaborative one is starting to happen,” he writes in his latest book, “and it gives me hope about the future of biodiversity and thus our own future.”
Tallamy’s initiative is especially trying to reach people not usually interested in ecosystem health. “That is of course most people,” he acknowledges. “We try to create a social network to motivate people who don’t have a clue, who don’t know they are responsible for good earth stewardship right where they live.” He tours the country relentlessly giving speeches “and there is usually someone who has been dragged in by their neighbor.”
In parts of the Deep South, Tallamy says, traditional landscaping culture remains resistant to rewilding. Many homeowners associate tidy lawns with safety and social acceptance.
Tallamy is refreshingly candid about the limitations of his approach. Even converting every targeted lawn would represent less than one percent of U.S. land, he acknowledges. Critics argue that such a change cannot solve biodiversity loss on its own. “I never said Homegrown National Park is going to solve the biodiversity crisis,” he says. “Getting everybody involved and changing the culture is going to help. It’s going to help a lot.”
A recent feature in the New York Times questioned whether his insistence on native plants is out of date because some species adapt to a changing habitat. But Tallamy has shown in dozens of studies that native plants are crucial for many species’ survival.
The real metric, he argues, isn’t simply acreage restored but whether ecological thinking becomes mainstream. Evidence of that cultural shift, he believes, is already emerging. Demand for native plants now exceeds supply in many regions. Conservation landscaping is beginning to increase property values rather than diminish them. Native plant professionals are increasingly booked months in advance.
Still, Tallamy admits the movement remains tiny relative to the challenge. Even counting the two million people who visit Homegrown National Park’s website annually, “That’s nothing compared to 340 million people in the U.S. we need to reach.”
Mostly, he wants people to stop thinking of conservation as something professionals do somewhere else. “The object is to get people to realize that they have agency over what happens on their little piece of the Earth,” he emphasizes. “And that it matters.”

title: Good News in History, September 11
content:
65 years ago today, the World Wildlife Fund was formed to save diverse species across the planet. With 35 million supporters and offices in nearly 100 countries, WWF has helped establish protected areas like the Galapagos National Park and worked to conserve iconic species including pandas, tigers, rhinos, and elephants—giving these animals and many more a brighter future. SEE the dozens of WWF headlines on GNN… (1961)
They also launched the world’s first eco-labels for food and consumer products, engineered debt swaps for nature in Africa, and advocated for the adoption of global agreements on wetlands, wildlife trade, biodiversity, and climate.
From its beginnings as a small group of committed naturalists, WWF has expanded from protecting species to a systemic approach to conservation and sustainable development, tackling the main drivers of nature loss including energy and food production, as well as improving the governance of natural resources. Its familiar panda logo has become a symbol of hope that people and nature can live in harmony.
MORE Good News on this Day:
- Mahatma Gandhi coined the term ‘Satyagraha’ (Truth-Force) to characterize Non-Violent movements (1906)
- The Beatles recorded their first single, “Love Me Do” at EMI studios in London (1962)
- At Camp David, President Jimmy Carter, Egyptian President Sadat, and Israeli Prime Minister Begin agreed on a framework for peace in the Middle East (1978)
- Pete Rose of the Cincinnati Reds recorded his 4,192nd hit, breaking Ty Cobb’s career record (1985)
- Scots voted to create their own Parliament after a 291-year union with England (1997)
133 years ago today, Roshi Soyen Shaku arrived to teach the doctrine of Zen to the United States. Shaku’s arrival was not on a lark, but rather coincided with the World Conference of Religions, at which he delivered a speech titled “The Law of Cause and Effect as Taught by Lord Buddha”. Though unable to speak English, he encountered an American publisher named Paul Carus, who asked Shaku to send a Zen practitioner knowledgeable in English to the US to write an introductory volume for American audiences.
In response to Carus’ request, Roshi Shaku sent Daisetsu Suzuki to work with Carus at Open Court Publishing. Suzuki, a student of Shaku, would far exceed in fame his master, and become the first and one of the greatest authority of Zen Buddhism in the West, one anchored by his prolific skills and output as a translator.
In 1905, Shaku returned to America as a guest of Ida Russell and her husband, businessman Alexander Russell. He spent 9 months at their isolated oceanside house on the Great Highway in San Francisco teaching the entire household Zen.
Mrs. Russell was the first American to study the Zen form of poetry known as koan. During this time he also gave lectures, some to Japanese immigrants and some translated by Suzuki for English-speaking audiences, around California. (1893)
On this day across history, imperial aggression was resisted or rolled back by indigenous peoples in both the Battle of the Teutoberg Forest (9) and the Battle of Stirling Bridge (1297). In the first case, it was one of the greatest defeats in the history of the Roman Empire, and dissuaded them, even commanded as they were by the great Emperor Augustus, from further conquests in Germany. In the second case, William Wallace and Andrew Moray turned back the English forces at the bridge near Stirling, and while details of the battle remain disputed, it’s clear it gave the Scottish nobles and forces belief that they could hold their own in future battles.
At Teutoberg, the battle took place near the modern village of Kalkriese, in Lower Saxony. Several Roman legions (5,000 men or thereabouts) were led in a long column by Publius Quinctilius Varus, whose general, Arminius, was preparing to betray him. Arminius was a German who had acquired Roman citizenship and joined the army. He had sent advanced word to a coalition of Germanic tribes that the Romans would be passing down a road flanked on one side by a wooded hill and the other with a marsh.
While the army was spread out across this hill, German tribes attacked them on the morning of September 8th, and harried them for days. A downpour began, and the Romans undertook a night march to escape, however Arminius had constructed a wooden palisade on the road which the Romans were forced to try and storm—failing, and afterwards disintegrating as another German tribe attacked them from side.
While Romans are often looked at as a civilizing force, their conquests of a very similar people to the Germans—the Gauls—has been described as the ‘Celtic Holocaust,’ and Arminius and the Germans likely saved their whole people and posterity from a similar fate by banding together.
The Battle of Stirling, where the Scottish beat back attempts by the English to enter Scotland, also features a clever tactician making use of the terrain—in this case a wooden bridge which the English foolishly attempted to cross even though only two men abreast could do so. Once William Wallace, a commoner and commander of the Scots, saw that enough of the English had crossed the bridge, he ordered his men to storm down the lip of a nearby hill with their spears.
They pushed back the charge of the English heavy cavalry, and with more and more of the English army still on the bridge, there was nowhere for those who had already crossed to flee to, allowing the Scots to inflict tremendous casualties on the invading army. (9) – (1297)
197 years ago today, American landscape painter Thomas Hill was born in Warwickshire, England. Loosely affiliated with the Hudson River School, he joined the burgeoning movement of American landscape painters in awe of North American natural beauty, and his time in the Sierra Nevada mountains of California, and the White Mountains of New Hampshire contributed their splendor to the majority of his canvasses.
Moving to the United States from Birmingham with his family at the age of 15, he would marry a local of Massachusetts and sire 9 children. One of his daughters, Anne Mary Hill, had a son whose paintings captivated America like few others could—Norman Rockwell. (1829)
Today is Grandparents Day in America, a day to honor the elderly population and express gratitude and love for your grandparents. 45 years ago, the day was officially proclaimed by President Carter, after decades of lobbying from two distinct people, Jacob Reingold and Marian McQuade, the West Virginia woman who persuaded her state to become the first one to celebrate elders with a special day. (1979)
25 years ago today, while waiting for a train in New York City to commute to work as a comic book illustrator, Gerard Way witnessed the World Trade Center collapse after the 9/11 attack.
The experience prompted him to start a new band, My Chemical Romance, for which he became the lead singer. He realized, “I need to do something that means something or my life will mean nothing… You don’t have to save the world, but make some kind of difference or say something that has some kind of value to it.” In March 2013, at the height of their success, the band broke up and Way became a successful solo artist for Warner Bros. Records. (2001)
On this day 29 years ago, the Mars Global Surveyor reached its destination—a stable orbit around the red planet.
NASA’s robotic spacecraft traveled nearly 466 million miles in 300 days (750 Million km) on a quest to map and examine the entire planet, from the ionosphere down through the atmosphere to photographing the surface—including images that appeared to prove the presence of water.
Powered by solar panels, it made 88 orbits, and continued its expedition for ten years, even taking pictures of two other NASA spacecraft that had arrived. After its launch in 1996, the mission was extended twice, outlasting expectations, before the robot in 2006 finally quit transmitting a signal. The MGS remains in a stable near-polar circular orbit at about 450 km altitude, and will crash onto the surface of the planet in about 2047. (1997)
Happy 86th Birthday to Brian De Palma, the film director and screenwriter of such films as The Untouchables and the 1996 Tom Cruise debut in Mission: Impossible.
Born in New Jersey, he was a computer enthusiast enrolled at Columbia as a physics student, but became enraptured with the filmmaking process after viewing Citizen Kane, and the films of Alfred Hitchcock, to whom he has often been compared.
With a career spanning over 50 years, he is best known for his work in the suspense, crime, and psychological thriller genres, with such box office hits as Carrie, Dressed to Kill, Scarface, and Carlito’s Way. Ironically, he says he doesn’t like “scary movies” and would never go to see his own films. (1940)
And, on this day in 1945, the Dutch Physician Willem J Kolff performed the first successful kidney dialysis using his artificial hemodialysis machine.
After becoming a doctor in the Netherlands, one of his first patients was a 22-year-old man who was slowly dying of renal failure. This prompted Kolff to perform research on an artificial dialyzer. His first prototype, built from orange juice cans, used auto parts, and sausage casings, lead to the successful treatment two years later that has saved the lives of millions ever since. (During his residency as a youth in 1940, Kolff also organized the first blood bank in Europe.)
Also on this day in 1967, the Carol Burnett Show premiered on CBS. The influential variety show ran for 11 seasons and featured the unforgettable ensemble of Carol Burnett, Vicki Lawrence, Harvey Korman, Lyle Waggoner, and Tim Conway.
The show won 25 Emmy Awards and was ranked number 16 on TV Guide’s 50 Greatest TV Shows of All Time. WATCH a few classic scenes below, from The Carol Burnett Show.
And, finally, on this day in 1893, the World’s Parliament of Religions conference opened—the very first organized interfaith gathering.
7,000 people met in Chicago from at least 11 religions at the inaugural event that brought together both Eastern and Western spiritual traditions. Organized by the Swedenborgian layman and judge Charles Carroll Bonney, the vision of the Parliament was for a just, peaceful, and sustainable world.
Their idealistic values adopted included…
- Religious and spiritual communities live in harmony and contribute to a better world from their riches of wisdom and compassion.
- Religious and cultural fears and hatreds are replaced with understanding and respect.
- People everywhere come to know and care for their neighbors.
- The richness of human and religious diversity is woven into the fabric of communal, civil, societal, and global life.
- The world’s most powerful and influential institutions move beyond narrow self-interest to realize the common good.
- The Earth and all life are cherished, protected, healed, and restored.
- All people commit to living out their highest values and aspirations.
SHARE the Milestones, Memories, and Movies…

title: Bộ Y tế phát động Chương trình quốc gia về bảo vệ trẻ em
content:
Nhiều nguy cơ mới trên môi trường mạng
Phát biểu tại lễ phát động, Thứ trưởng Bộ Y tế Lê Đức Luận cho biết công tác bảo vệ trẻ em thời gian qua đã đạt được nhiều kết quả đáng ghi nhận.
Tỉ lệ trẻ em lao động trái quy định của pháp luật đã giảm từ 5,4% còn 1,31%. 100% trẻ em bị xâm hại được áp dụng các biện pháp hỗ trợ, can thiệp phù hợp. Hệ thống dịch vụ bảo vệ trẻ em được tổ chức theo ba cấp độ gồm phòng ngừa, hỗ trợ và can thiệp.
Tổng đài điện thoại quốc gia bảo vệ trẻ em 111 tiếp tục là địa chỉ tiếp nhận thông tin, tư vấn và phối hợp xử lý các vụ việc liên quan đến quyền trẻ em. Việt Nam cũng đã chính thức khai trương Tổng đài phòng, chống bạo lực gia đình 117.
Tuy nhiên theo ông Luận, công tác bảo vệ trẻ em vẫn đứng trước nhiều khó khăn, thách thức. Tình trạng bạo lực trẻ em có xu hướng gia tăng trên phạm vi toàn cầu trong bối cảnh suy thoái kinh tế, lạm phát và những cú sốc từ thiên tai, xã hội. Đây là những yếu tố khiến trẻ em yếu thế có nguy cơ bỏ học và tham gia lao động sớm.
Lao động trẻ em vẫn tồn tại tại khu vực nông, lâm, thủy sản, trong các hộ gia đình và cơ sở sản xuất, kinh doanh nhỏ lẻ - những nơi khó kiểm tra, giám sát.
Trong khi đó mạng lưới cung cấp dịch vụ bảo vệ trẻ em tại một số địa phương còn mỏng, việc kết nối, liên thông và chuyển tuyến dịch vụ chưa đồng bộ.
Đặc biệt, các nguy cơ đối với trẻ em không chỉ diễn ra trong đời sống thực, mà ngày càng mở rộng sang môi trường mạng.
Bà Michaela Bauer, Phó trưởng đại diện UNICEF tại Việt Nam, cho biết trẻ em tại Việt Nam vẫn phải đối mặt với nhiều nguy cơ như bạo lực, bóc lột, xâm hại tình dục, trong đó có xâm hại và bóc lột trên môi trường mạng, cùng nguy cơ phải làm những công việc nặng nhọc, độc hại.
Theo bà Michaela Bauer, để giải quyết những thách thức này, chỉ hoàn thiện luật pháp và chính sách là chưa đủ. Việt Nam cần một hệ thống bảo vệ trẻ em vững mạnh, tích hợp và được bảo đảm nguồn lực tài chính.
Hệ thống này cần đội ngũ nhân viên công tác xã hội có năng lực, dữ liệu tin cậy, cơ chế phối hợp hiệu quả và các dịch vụ bảo vệ trẻ em có thể tiếp cận tại mọi cộng đồng.
"Các bằng chứng quốc tế cho thấy trẻ em được bảo vệ tốt nhất khi công tác phòng ngừa và ứng phó được triển khai như một hệ thống thống nhất, xuyên suốt từ cấp quốc gia đến gia đình, nhà trường và cộng đồng", bà Michaela Bauer nhấn mạnh.
Phấn đấu giảm 5% trẻ em bị bạo lực, xâm hại mỗi năm
Chương trình quốc gia về bảo vệ trẻ em và phòng ngừa, giảm thiểu trẻ em lao động trái quy định của pháp luật giai đoạn 2026 - 2030 đặt ra nhiều mục tiêu đến năm 2030.
Theo đó tỉ lệ trẻ em bị bạo lực và xâm hại tình dục sẽ giảm ít nhất 5% mỗi năm. Tỉ lệ lao động trẻ em trong độ tuổi từ 5 đến 17 tuổi được đặt mục tiêu giảm xuống dưới 1,1%.
Đặc biệt, chương trình hướng đến tăng cường quản lý, kết nối dữ liệu để kịp thời nhận diện và hỗ trợ trẻ em có nguy cơ.
Theo mục tiêu đề ra, 100% trẻ em thuộc đối tượng bảo vệ và trẻ em có nguy cơ sẽ được quản lý trên hệ thống cơ sở dữ liệu trẻ em, kết nối dùng chung với các cơ sở dữ liệu liên quan.
Việc xây dựng hệ thống dữ liệu và tăng cường kết nối giữa các cơ quan, đơn vị được kỳ vọng giúp công tác bảo vệ trẻ em chuyển mạnh từ xử lý khi vụ việc xảy ra sang chủ động phòng ngừa, phát hiện sớm và can thiệp kịp thời.

title: 19 Years of the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
content: 19 Years of the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Country Global agnes Sun, 09/13/2026 - 13:49 Issues Human Rights Program 5 Main Image September 13, 2026, marks 19 years since the United Nations General Assembly adopted the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP). In a historic vote on September 13, 2007, 144 countries voted for the Declaration, 11 abstained, and only four (Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and the United States) voted against it. Since 2007, all four countries, including the United States, have reversed their positions and now officially endorse the Declaration. The Declaration is the outcome of 25 years of hard negotiations. The rights spelled out in the document "constitute the minimum standards for the survival, dignity, and well-being of the Indigenous Peoples of the world." The Declaration protects the collective rights and individual rights of Indigenous Peoples in relation to self-government, land, education, employment, health, and other areas. The Declaration also requires countries to consult with Indigenous Peoples with the goal of obtaining their consent on matters that concern them. As explained by former UN Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, James Anaya (Apache and Purépecha), the right of self-determination is "to be full and equal participants in the creation of the institutions of government under which they live and, further, to live within a governing institutional order in which they are perpetually in control of their own destinies." While several countries have made steps towards aligning their policies with the standards enshrined in the Declaration, an implementation gap remains. "Governments around the world must honor their responsibilities to move from Declaration endorsement to adoption and align their domestic laws and policies with the rights, self-governance, and self-determination of Indigenous Peoples," says Cultural Survival Executive Director Aimee Roberson (Choctaw and Chickasaw). Cultural Survival has put together this interactive timeline to display the history of the Declaration and progress towards its implementation since 2007. The History of the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and Its Implementation Read "16th Anniversary of the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples: Seeding the Generational Legacy of the International Indigenous Rights Movement," by Wakinyan LaPointe (Sicangu Lakota). ...This international Indigenous rights movement was not solely a political movement, it was a spiritual and cultural movement that ultimately disrupted the global status quo and colonial norms of States that had for too long ignored the existence of Indigenous Peoples.... Read more. Read our anniversary issue of the Cultural Survival Quarterly on the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. A Modern Declaration Woven into an Ancient Art Hartman Deetz (Mashpee Wampanoag) and human rights lawyer Michelle Cook (Diné), founder of Divest Invest Protect speak about the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples wampum belt. Listen to our Indigenous Rights Radio Podcasts on the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples A Modern Declaration Weaved into an Ancient Custom - The UNDRIP Wampum Belt In this podcast, we share with you the incredible work of Hartman Deetz (Mashpee Wampanoag) and human rights lawyer Michelle Cook (Diné), founder of Divest Invest Protect (DIP), on the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples wampum belt. Indigenous artist and advocate Hartman Deetz looks to his ancestors, to his past, to wampum-- the ancient tool of art, law, ritual, and diplomacy to find guidance and ways forward for his people. The UNDRIP wampum belt is a means of teaching Indigenous human rights using and centering Indigenous Peoples' technology and pedagogical legal practices with wampum as both the medium and the message of accountability, healing, and change. Les Malezer on Commemorating UNDRIP Listen to Les Malezer (Gubbi Gubbi), former Expert Member on the Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues, on commemorating 13 years of the Declaration. Malezer with the Global Indigenous Peoples Caucus worked to advance the Declaration through the final stages to the UN General Assembly in 2007. Escuche y descargue los 46 articulos de la Declaración de las Naciones Unidas sobre los Derechos de los Pueblos Indigenas, junto con una explicación simple de que significa para usted y su comunidad.
