title: Circular Bharat: Turning waste into value
content:
By Sanjiv Kumar, President – Strategy, Renvion Solutions Private Limited
Twenty-five years ago, when India notified the Municipal Solid Wastes (MSW) Rules, 2000, waste management was a very different world. It was largely viewed as a municipal responsibility to collect the waste, transport it and find a place to dispose of it. However, what began primarily as an environmental compliance requirement has gradually developed into an ecosystem of infrastructure, technology, investment, entrepreneurship, resource recovery and employment. That change captures India’s journey from Swachh Bharat towards Circular Bharat.
Swachh Bharat changed the scale
The MSW Rules, 2000 created an important national regulatory foundation. But the launch of the Swachh Bharat Mission in 2014 transformed sanitation and cleanliness from primarily municipal subjects into a national movement. The progress is visible. Door-to-door waste collection, negligible in 2014–15, now covers about 98 per cent of urban wards. More than 250,000 collection vehicles support the system, while MSW processing has increased from about 16 per cent in 2014–15 to around 80 per cent in 2025–26.
Behind these sanitation statistics lies another story the creation of an environmental economy. Collection vehicles need drivers, operators, maintenance and digital tracking. Material recovery facilities (MRFs) need sorters, supervisors and logistics. Composting, biomethanation, recycling, refuse-derived fuel (RDF) and waste-to-energy (WtE) facilities need engineers, technicians and plant operators. Every tonne moved away from dumping towards organised collection, processing and recovery potentially creates environmental as well as economic value.
From disposal to resource recovery
The Solid Waste Management (SWM) Rules, 2016 accelerated this transition by strengthening segregation, processing, recycling, MRFs, composting, biomethanation, RDF and energy recovery. The philosophy gradually changed: landfill should no longer be the first destination of waste; it should increasingly become the last resort. Once waste is segregated, its identity changes. Wet waste can produce compost, biogas or compressed biogas. Dry waste can yield paper, plastics, metals and other secondary raw materials. Combustible fractions can substitute conventional fuels. Construction waste can return to the economy as recycled building material. Waste becomes feedstock. Disposal becomes recovery. Cost can become value. That is circular economy in practice.
Compliance can create markets
Good environmental regulation can do more than enforce compliance: it can create conditions for markets. When segregation is mandatory, collection and sorting solutions are required. When processing is required, infrastructure must be created. When bulk waste generators (BWGs) are given responsibility, a professional B2B waste-management market emerges. When recovered materials are required by industry, investment in recovery becomes more viable. The SWM Rules, 2026 take this evolution further through four-stream segregation, greater BWG responsibility, digital tracking, stronger restrictions on landfilling, environmental compensation and progressive RDF substitution requirements.
Rise of the wastepreneur
Perhaps the most encouraging change is the profile of people entering waste management. A new entrepreneur is emerging: the “wastepreneur” – someone who sees economic value where society previously saw something to throw away. Today, startups are working on automated sorting, plastics recovery, recycling, digital traceability, biomining, decentralised processing, IoT-enabled collection, secondary materials and circular economy technologies. Government initiatives are encouraging this ecosystem. The first cohort of 30 startups under the Swachhata Startup Challenge reportedly managed more than 63,000 tonnes of waste and generated more than 2,000 employment opportunities.
The employment opportunity is equally significant. Waste management remains labour-intensive, and frontline sanitation workers will always be essential. But they are increasingly being joined by engineers, plant operators, recycling specialists, equipment technicians, environmental scientists, logistics professionals, GIS and data specialists, sustainability professionals and compliance experts.
India also had a circular economy long before we started using the term. Waste pickers, kabadiwalas, aggregators and scrap dealers have recovered materials for decades. They are, in many respects, India’s original circular-economy entrepreneurs. The objective of modernisation should not be to displace them, but to integrate and strengthen them through recognition, personal protective equipment, training, technology, social protection and opportunities to become organised aggregators, service providers and entrepreneurs.
From Clean India to Circular India
Waste should no longer be viewed merely as garbage. India’s wider circular economy has been estimated to have the potential to reach around $2 trillion by 2050 and create approximately 10 million jobs. The opportunity extends well beyond municipal waste.
Swachh Bharat gave India a cleanliness movement. Circular Bharat can turn that movement into a resource revolution. We should no longer measure success only by asking, “How much waste did we collect?” We must also ask: How much did we recover? How much material is returned to productive use? How many enterprises did we enable? And how many green careers did we create?

title: Cuatro pioneras ginecólogas catalanas
content:
Cuatro pioneras ginecólogas catalanas
Lectores Expertos
Dolors Aleu i Riera se convirtió en el año 1882 en la primera mujer licenciada en Medicina en España
* El autor forma parte de la comunidad de lectores de La Vanguardia
El siglo XIX marcó el acceso de las primeras mujeres a los estudios universitarios en España. Las pioneras de la medicina catalana encontraron en la ginecología y la pediatría sus espacios naturales de ejercicio profesional.
El nacimiento de la Pediatría como especialidad surge en España a finales del siglo XIX. Hasta entonces se englobaba dentro de la especialidad de Obstetricia, enfermedades de los niños y mujeres.
1. Dolors Aleu i Riera
Nacida en Barcelona (7 de abril de 1857 - 18 de febrero de 1913), se convirtió en 1882 en la primera mujer licenciada en Medicina en España. Se matriculó en la Universitat de Barcelona en 1874. Terminó sus estudios con una calificación excelente en 1879, pero las trabas burocráticas del gobierno retrasaron su examen de grado oficial hasta 1882.
Se convirtió en la segunda mujer del país en obtener el título de doctora, defendiendo en Madrid su tesis “De la necesidad de encaminar por una nueva senda la educación higiénico-moral de la mujer (1883). El texto original, que fue publicado formalmente en Barcelona en 1883, constituyó una defensa pionera de los derechos de las mujeres.
Ejerció de forma muy activa durante más de 25 años en su propia consulta en Barcelona, especializándose en ginecología y pediatría. Fue profesora de Higiene Doméstica en la Academia de Ciencias, Artes y Oficios para la mujer, fundada el 2 de mayo de 1885 en el número 10 de la Rambla de Canaletes por la artista y concertista Clotilde Cerdà y Bosch (conocida como Esmeralda Cervantes), con el propósito de promover la emancipación y la educación superior y profesional de las mujeres. Fue un centro pionero en España para dar acceso a la formación técnica, científica y artística a la mujer en el siglo XIX.
Fue una firme defensora de los derechos de la mujer y de la salud femenina, llegando a criticar públicamente el uso del corsé de la época por los problemas médicos que causaba.
Dolors Aleu es recordada con el nombre Centre Sociosanitari Putget Dolors Aleu, actualmente denominado Hospital d'Atenció Intermèdia Colisée Barcelona Dolors Aleu.
La Universidad de Barcelona dio el nombre de Dolors Aleu a un aula de la Facultad de Medicina y Ciencias de la Salud.
2. Trinitat Sais i Plaja
Fue una de las médicas pioneras de España, nacida a finales del siglo XIX y con una destacada trayectoria en ginecología y pediatría.
Nació el 22 de julio de 1878 en La Bisbal de l'Empordà (Girona). Falleció el 17 de octubre de 1933 en Barcelona. Era hija de una comadrona y un sastre, lo que muy probablemente despertó su temprana vocación por la salud de las mujeres y los nacimientos.
Fue la octaba mujer en estudiar Medicina en Catalunya y la primera mujer médica de la provincia de Girona.
Estudió magisterio y obtuvo el título en Barcelona en 1893. Posteriormente estudió el bachillerato en el Instituto de Figueras y obtuvo el premio extraordinario en 1896. Siguió despues estudios de Medicina en la universidad de Barcelona donde se licenció en 1903
Tras graduarse en 1903, la Dra. Sais desarrolló una intensa labor profesional enfocada principalmente en la salud materno-infantil, un campo donde las mujeres médicas de la época encontraron un espacio fundamental para ejercer.
Participó en la organización de diversos congresos como el primer congreso Español de la Tuberculosis en la que fue vicepresidenta del Comité de Damas.
Tuvo sus principales consultas médicas en la calle de Pelayo y posteriormente en la calle de Bergara, anunciando sus servicios para la atención de “mujeres y niños”. Más tarde también ejerció como pediatra y tocóloga (obstetra) en el barrio de Sant Gervasi.
Divulgó sus conocimientos científicos mediante conferencias y cursos en los que también defendía los derechos de la mujer en revistas como como La mujer moderna en Manresa y Feminal .
En 1914 fue la primera mujer en impartir la conferencia de apertura de curso en el Colegio Oficial de Médicos de Barcelona, donde cuestionó la falta de formación de las mujeres en puericultura, y la falta de higiene como primera causa de mortalidad infantil. Sus hijas, Teresa y Edelmira, también fueron médicas.
3. Francesca Fontova i Rosell
Francesca Fontova i Rosell (Lleida, 31 d'octubre de 1877 – Avilés, Astúries, 25 d'agost de 1961). Fue la primera mujer licenciada en Medicina en la provincia de Lleida y una de las pioneras de la Medicina en la Cataluña de finales del siglo XIX y principios del XX.
Estudió Magisterio y obtuvo el título de bachiller en Artes por el Instituto de Lleida el 1895. Intentó ingresar en la Facultad de Medicina de la Universidad de Barcelona. Sin embargo, una circular oficial de 1893 prohibía el acceso de las mujeres a la educación superior.
Solicitó una autorización directamente al Ministerio de Instrucción Pública, el cual le concedió el permiso definitivo en 1898, cinco años después.
Se licenció en Medicina en 1903. Formó parte de una promoción histórica de pioneras junto a Trinitat Sais y Miracle Andreu (quienes sí se volcaron más directamente en la Ginecología y la Tocología).
Inicialmente ejerció en Lleida y en varios municipios de la comarca del Segrià. En 1906, tras contraer matrimonio con el también médico Miquel Real, se trasladó al barrio de Gràcia en Barcelona. Allí colaboró activamente en la clínica de su esposo, asumiendo tareas médicas generales, quirúrgicas y de anestesia.
En Barcelona, ejercieron dos hijas farmacéuticas, Paquita y Teresa Real Fontova y también un hijo médico Miquel Real Fontova.
4. Maria Lluïsa Quadras Bordes
Maria Lluïsa Quadras Bordes nació el 28 de junio de 1898 en Barcelona. Era hija de Joan Quadras Vidal, un comerciante, y de Agnès Bordes Casal. Maria Lluïsa estudió Medicina. Empezó la carrera en Barcelona, más adelante se mudó a Zaragoza y, finalmente, realizó el último curso en Valencia.
Obtuvo su licenciatura en 1920 y se especializó en Ginecología. Un año después de finalizar la carrera abrió su propia consulta. Fue una Ginecóloga con gran implicación en la actividad benéfica.
Abrió su primera consulta especializada en Barcelona en octubre de 1921 en la calle de Santa Anna, y meses más tarde trasladó y amplió su centro médico al número 127 de la calle Mallorca. La prensa de Barcelona la dio a conocer como la primera mujer radióloga y abrió el Instituto de Electrología, Radiología y Ginecología, un centro que también atendía a las mujeres sin recursos económicos.
Realizó numerosos viajes de formación profesional , principalmente a Francia, en los que visitaba centros médicos para completar su formación .
En 1931, su hermana Maria Victòria terminó la carrera de Medicina y empezó a trabajar con ella en la consulta y tuvieron su consulta abierta hasta 1984.
La doctora Quadras trabajó también en el Hospital Sant Pau y en el Hospital Clínic. Fue socia de la Academia y Laboratorio de Ciencias Médicas, de la Academia de Higiene de Catalunya, socia honorífica de la Sociedad Francesa de Gi necología y miembro de la Catalana de Ginecología y Obstetricia.
Tuvo un papel esencial en la fundaciónde la Asociación contra la Toxicomanía, que se constituyó en el Colegio de Médicos de Barcelona en 1926.
Fundó una entidad llamada El abrigo de los pobres, cuya finalidad era ofrecer ropa y elementos para el hogar a las personas más necesitadas y a los hospitales. Maria Lluïsa Quadras Bordes falleció el 10 de septiembre de 1989 en Barcelona.
¡Participa!
¿Quieres compartir tus conocimientos?
Si tienen interés en participar en Lectores Expertos pueden escribir un email a la dirección de correo de nuestra sección de Participación (participacion@lavanguardia.es) adjuntando sus datos biográficos y el texto que proponen para su publicación.

title: Clean seas, safe coasts: How India is transforming its 11,000 km coastline through citizen power
content:
Opinion Clean seas, safe coasts: How India is transforming its 11,000 km coastline through citizen power
Somewhere between the India that once measured its wealth in coral and catch, and the India of today, the ocean began sending us a message written in litter. This is the story of how we began writing back
There is a memory the sea keeps that no monsoon can wash away. Walk along any of India’s 11,098 kilometres of coastline at first light, and you will find it in the same tide that once carried spice ships to Malabar and pearl divers to the Gulf of Mannar: A restless, ancient rhythm that has shaped how Indians live, trade, worship and dream. But walk that same shore today, and increasingly the tide brings back something else too — a torn fishing net tangled with a shampoo sachet, a turtle hatchling nosing past a bottle cap mistaken for food, a fisherman’s morning catch thinner than his father’s, and heavier with plastic than with fish. Somewhere between the India that once measured its wealth in coral, cowrie and catch, and the India of today, the ocean began sending us a message written in litter. This is the story of how, over the last decade, we finally began writing back.
For too long, the coast lived at the edge of our imagination the way it lived at the edge of our map — visited, admired, occasionally mourned after a cyclone, but rarely defended as a shared inheritance. Ocean governance earlier was, in the main, an administrative afterthought scattered across departments, driven by disaster response rather than daily stewardship, with no national platform that asked the ordinary citizen to see the sea as theirs to protect. Meanwhile, the threat was quietly compounding. Plastic waste, much of it single-use, was finding its way through our rivers and drains into estuaries and open water, breaking down not into harmlessness but into microplastics — fragments smaller than five millimetres that fish mistake for food, that enter the catch on our plates, and that we now know travel silently up the food chain into our own bodies. Marine animals were dying entangled in abandoned nets. Coral reefs, mangroves and fish stocks that sustain the livelihoods of millions of coastal families were absorbing a slow, invisible injury. It was, by any honest reckoning, one of the most under-addressed environmental challenges of our time, hiding in plain sight along a coastline that touches nine states and four Union Territories.
What changed was not merely a policy. It was a decision, taken consciously by the Modi government, that cleanliness could no longer be treated as somebody else’s job. It had to become, as the Prime Minister put it when he launched the Swachh Bharat Mission in 2014, a Jan Andolan, a movement of the people. That civilisational instinct — Mission LiFE, a Lifestyle for Environment that asks each citizen to make sustainability a daily habit rather than an occasional virtue — has since travelled from our streets to our shores. As the Ministry entrusted with the science of our oceans, atmosphere and Earth systems, we asked ourselves a simple question: If India could mobilise a nation to clean its cities, could it not do the same for its seas? The answer arrived in 2022, in the form of Swachh Sagar Surakshit Sagar — Clean Seas, Safe Coasts — a campaign conceived not as a one-day photo opportunity but as a sustained, science-backed, citizen-powered movement, timed each year to converge with International Coastal Cleanup Day, the third Saturday of September, a global tradition that began in 1986 and today draws volunteers in more than a hundred countries to their nearest coastline with nothing but gloves, bags and resolve.
The comparison, even within this campaign’s own short life, tells its own story of scale. In its first year, Swachh Sagar Surakshit Sagar ran for 75 days and reached 75 locations, largely through the efforts of our own ocean research institutes. But as other ministries joined hands, as voluntary organisations such as Seema Jagran Manch and Paryavaran Sanrakshan Gatividhi lent their networks, and as the idea began to travel by word of mouth along the coast, that same campaign, within the same year, had grown to touch 836 coastal locations and mobilise more than a lakh volunteers. That is not incremental growth; that is a movement finding its feet and then finding its stride. Four editions later, as we launch Swachh Sagar Surakshit Sagar 5.0 this September, the coalition has widened further still — the Indian Coast Guard and Navy, the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, the NCC and NSS, Scouts and Guides, schools, universities, corporates and, crucially, fisherfolk associations and women’s groups who know these waters as intimately as their own courtyards. Our own institutes — the National Institute of Ocean Technology in Chennai, the National Centre for Coastal Research, INCOIS in Hyderabad, and sister institutions along both coasts — are coordinating clean-up drives across more than a hundred beaches this year alone, with partners like Bisleri independently bringing another 50 locations under the same banner. This is what a Jan Andolan looks like when it matures.
What makes this year’s edition distinctive is not only its reach but its rhythm. From September 12 to September 19, the coastline will host, in effect, a week-long festival of stewardship rather than a single ceremonial gesture. There will be a cyclothon along both the eastern and western seaboards, young people pedalling from town to town in a living relay of intent. There will be a Fit India morning on the sands, a marathon, and on World Ozone Day, a clean-up drive that quietly reminds us that the health of the atmosphere above and the ocean below are two chapters of the same story. There will be a human chain along our beaches, hands linked from Gujarat to the Sundarbans, from Kanyakumari to the Andamans, and an Ocean Olympiad that turns marine science into a contest young minds will remember long after the trophies are handed out. Students will compete in drawing and essay competitions that ask them to imagine the sea their children will inherit. Young volunteers will ride to the beach in the Bike-to-Beach campaign and post their clean-up as an Eco-Selfie, because a movement that wants to last must also learn to speak the language of the generation that will carry it forward. And on September 19, International Coastal Cleanup Day itself, it will all converge in the campaign’s largest single-day clean-up, geo-tagged and digitally logged so that every bag of waste collected becomes data, not just diligence — a record we can measure, publish and improve upon next year.
That last detail matters more than it seems. Technology has quietly become this movement’s backbone. Volunteers register digitally, drives are mapped and geo-tagged in real time, and participants receive digital certificates that turn a morning of hard, sweaty work into a recognised act of citizenship. This is governance choosing to trust its citizens with data and, in turn, being held accountable by them.
But behind every statistic in this campaign is a face I keep returning to when I think about why this work matters. It is the fisherman off the Odisha coast who tells you his net now needs an extra hour of sorting before the catch is clean enough to sell. It is the mother in a Keralam fishing hamlet who worries less about polio these days and more about what her children’s food carries invisibly within it. It is the small hotel owner in Goa or Puducherry whose livelihood depends entirely on a beach staying beautiful enough for a family to want to return to it next year. Clean seas are not an abstraction for these citizens; they are grocery money, school fees, and the health of a child. When we speak of the Blue Economy — of oceans as engines of trade, tourism, fisheries and energy that can power a Viksit Bharat — we are also speaking, in the most literal sense, about their kitchen tables.
I have often said that India’s relationship with nature was never meant to be transactional; it was meant to be filial. Swachh Sagar Surakshit Sagar is, at its heart, an attempt to recover that relationship at scale. We are not asking India to fall in love with its coastline. That love was always there, written into our festivals, our fishing songs, our pilgrimages to the sea. We are simply asking India to act on it, one beach, one bag of plastic, one Saturday in September at a time — until safe seas are no longer a season’s campaign, but simply how we live.
The writer is Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences; Minister of State, PMO, Department of Atomic Energy, Department of Space, and Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions

title: Justice Minister: Jordan advancing comprehensive legislative, judicial modernization
content:
Ammon News - Minister of Justice Bassam Talhouni emphasized that Jordan is advancing a comprehensive pathway to modernize its legislative and judicial infrastructure, encompassing laws, digital services, facilities, and human capital to keep pace with national development goals and rapid technological shifts.
In an interview marking World Law Day, Talhouni stated that law is a dynamic framework that organizes societal life, protects rights and freedoms, and secures the environment necessary for stability and investment. He explained that the essence of legal modernization lies in shifting from a reactive tool for problem-solving after a crisis occurs to a proactive instrument capable of anticipating transformations.
Talhouni stressed that citizens remain the focal point of the legislative and reform process, noting that a law's quality is measured by its capacity to achieve its intended objective and reflect positively on people's lives. The ministry carefully evaluates proposed legislation against specific criteria, including responsiveness, constitutional harmony, and socio-economic impact.
Rapid advancements require rethinking how laws are drafted to anticipate future transformations in business, commerce, and social interactions. Talhouni asserted that forward-looking legislation requires early reading of emerging shifts, stakeholder engagement, and rigorous legislative impact assessments throughout a law's lifecycle.
Turning to digital transformation, Talhouni affirmed that technology has become central to modernizing justice. The ministry is leveraging tech to re-engineer workflows, simplify services, and minimize time and financial costs. Milestones in this digital pivot include expanding e-services, remote court trials, electronic archiving, and digital signatures.
Regarding artificial intelligence, Talhouni noted that emerging technologies present complex questions regarding liability, privacy, data protection, and digital rights, requiring a balance between encouraging innovation and safeguarding the rule of law.
On the economic front, Talhouni stressed that stable, transparent laws and swift dispute resolution mechanisms serve as cornerstone determinants of national competitiveness. He pointed to the development of alternative dispute resolution frameworks, highlighting that the draft Arbitration Law for 2026 and the establishment of the Jordanian International Arbitration Center represent decisive steps toward providing flexible tools to safeguard business and investment.
Addressing access to justice, Talhouni underscored that financial capacity should never act as a barrier to litigation, affirming the importance of legal aid and streamlined digital outreach to bring justice closer to everyday citizens.
Reaffirming the principle of the rule of law, Talhouni concluded that public trust is forged through fair, transparent, and effective application, ensuring that Jordanian law remains clear, fair, and adaptable to future change.

title: First Permit to Clean Up Old Mine Waste Issued for WA State Under 2024 ‘Good Samaritan Act’
content:
The US Environmental Protection Agency has approved the first permit under the its new “Good Samaritan” law to remediate abandoned mine workings.
The permit has been issued to Trout Unlimited, a fishing and sportsmen focused nonprofit that engages in riverine conservation all over the West.
The Good Samaritan act passed in 2024 with broad bipartisan support after 20 years of campaigning by groups including Trout Unlimited.
The legislation was championed by US Senators Martin Heinrich (D-NM) and Jim Risch (R-ID) and US House Reps Celeste Maloy (R-UT), Mary Peltola (D-AK), and Susie Lee (D-NV).
It facilitates state agencies and other third parties to clean up abandoned mines more quickly and effectively, tens of thousands of which are known to pollute rivers and streams across the country.
As historic sites often a century old or more whose owners are long gone or deceased, it’s rare that any party can be held responsible for cleaning them up. At the same time, federal laws treat organizations that volunteer to clean up these mines, including state agencies and private groups like Trout Unlimited, as if they are the very polluters who left behind the mine waste.
This complicates permitting and long-term legal and financial liability for any mine pollution remaining after cleanup, disincentivizing the same. The Good Samaritan law created a pilot program to provide limited liability protections for up to 15 low-risk projects conducted by state agencies or other third parties.
“Hardrock abandoned mines are a scourge on the landscape. No one is required to clean them up, so every day they release their toxic brew of zinc, cadmium, lead, and arsenic into our drinking water and trout streams,” said Chris Wood, president and CEO of Trout Unlimited in a statement.
The permit thusly issued to Trout Unlimited will address ongoing contamination of Toroda Creek in Okanogan County, Washington state, about 140 miles northwest of Spokane.
At the site, known as the Bodie Mine, historic mine tailings will be removed and streambanks restored to reduce contamination of the stream by arsenic, cadmium, lead, mercury and other toxins. The project will improve the health of the broader watershed, part of the Columbia River Basin.
“Bully for the EPA [for] authorizing the first abandoned mine cleanup under the Good Samaritan Remediation of Abandoned Hardrock Mines Act of 2024,” Wood added. “May their efforts lead many more states and communities, non-profits, and yes, even mining companies, to lend a hand and make our waters more fishable and swimmable.”
MORE GOOD NEWS FOR RIVERS: Toronto River Once So Polluted it Caught on Fire Now Is Flush with Fish
While many Americans have never picked up any mining jargon, it’s likely they’ve seen mine tailings before. If you’ve driven by a mining site and seen the long metal chute depositing gravel and dirt into a large conical pile—those are tailings, and they are either stored in landfill type installations or as a slurry in a pond or dam.
Back in the day, however, they were often just stored on site wherever there was space. Many ore bodies that contain useful and valuable metals like zinc, gold, or silver, may also contain—as Wood mentioned—arsenic, lead, and other toxic heavy metals. The process of grinding and separation that allows for the extraction of the former also liberates the latter. Left in piles of derelict tailings, they present a much greater risk of toxicity than when they were underground.
CLEANER, MODERN MINING: Quebec Firm Pioneers Cyanide-Free Gold Extraction and Arsenic-Capture to Clean up Mining Industry
GNN recently reported on Trout Unlimited’s activities contributing to the truly hair-raising numbers of central California coho salmon running up rivers along the Mendocino coast. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration had been contracting Trout Unlimited to remove barriers in the Navarro, Big, Garcia, and Noyo River watersheds for years leading up to the salmons’ return.
SHARE This Great Start Towards A Cleaner West With This New Law…

title: Episode 183: The Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing – Beth Pratt on Reaching the Finish Line
content:
Episode 183: The Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing – Beth Pratt on Reaching the Finish Line
September 11, 2026
Podcast: Play in new window | Download | Embed
Subscribe to Rewilding Earth Podcast: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | Amazon Music | iHeartRadio | Email | Youtube Music | RSS | More
Summary
Fourteen years in the making, the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing over Southern California’s ten-lane Highway 101 is finally nearing completion. In this episode of the Rewilding Earth Podcast, Beth Pratt, California regional executive director with the National Wildlife Federation and founder of the The Wildlife Crossing Fund, sits down with host Jack Humphrey to talk about what it really takes to pull off a monumental conservation feat in the modern-day United States.
A tireless champion, Beth shares the emotional reality of reaching the finish line, the enduring legacy of mountain lion P-22, and why this wildlife bridge is far more than simple conveyance. From engineering sound and light baffles with more than 300,000 daily vehicles passing below to cultivating a million hyper-local seeds, the details of bringing this crossing to life sets a new global benchmark for habitat fidelity. The project proves that with stubborn persistence and scientific rigor, we can successfully rewild our most fractured landscapes.
Talking Points
- Reality of the Home Stretch: What it feels like to reach the end of a grueling 14-year campaign marked by personal sacrifice, skeletal staffing, and navigating everything from high-level politics to ground-level project management.
- Living Legacy of P-22: How one solitary mountain lion trapped in Griffith Park took the abstract concept of genetic fragmentation and turned it into an urgent, global movement for connectivity.
- Beyond Simple Conveyance: Why modern rewilding demands true fidelity to habitat, building living ecosystems with native soils, micro-drainage, and hyper-local flora rather than bare concrete bridges just meant to funnel large game.
- Engineering Silence and Darkness: The intricate science of soundproofing, specialized low-reflective concrete stains, and vegetated barriers designed to trick wildlife into feeling safe over one of the busiest freeways in the world.
- Signs of Life Before the Ribbon Cutting: Early proof of concept on the bridge deck, including barn owls utilizing newly created dark corridors, native lizards, and migrating monarchs and painted lady butterflies laying eggs on site.
- Hidden Crisis of Habitat Fragmentation: Moving beyond direct vehicle collisions to confront the deeper ecological toll of roads, including severe inbreeding among mountain lions, blocked wildfire escape routes, and broken evolutionary pathways.
- Institutional Culture Shifts: How large transportation agencies like Caltrans evolved from skepticism to building dedicated wildlife connectivity divisions, setting precedents for retrofitting global infrastructure.
- Rigorous Post-Construction Monitoring: The scientific framework ahead, including dozens of motion-triggered cameras, collar data, and adaptive management to assess how animals interact with the crossing in the coming years.

title: Asia’s Economic Integration: A Roadmap for Peacebuilding in the Middle East
content:
When the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, ASEAN, was formed in 1967, the five founding states intended to produce a front against the spread of communism. The venture has since grown to include a total of 11 countries, producing a remarkable set of unforeseen consequences, from becoming the fifth-largest economy in the world to reinforcing peace across a swath of diverse and developing countries.
Instead of pursuing Cold War initiatives, the bloc has become increasingly integrated, tied together through manufacturing supply chains, trade infrastructure, and shared financial institutions like the Chiang Mai Initiative. ASEAN now produces over $4 trillion in GDP and has a population of 678 million people. The collaboration’s biggest success, however, has not simply been increased commerce. With economic integration comes regional stabilization and peace, a consequence further fostered by the signing of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) in 2020, which includes Australia, China, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea. Economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific has been the key driver of peace in the region ever since 1952 with the Treaty of San Francisco, and it serves today as a key example of how market mechanics can drive peacebuilding. In fact, it was ASEAN that eroded tensions from the Konfrontasi war in the early 1960s, and has solidified the climate of peace between the Southeast Asian members ever since.
Economists and politicians have often considered the question of whether trade contributes to peaceful relations between states. The affirmative answer is not novel; however, in the case of ASEAN and the Asia-Pacific, the specifics begin to clarify the theory. Peacebuilding through economic means is more a matter of building economic capacity and trade interdependence than of simply trading goods between nations. This crucial specification turns the Asia-Pacific from a successful case study into a model for peacebuilding elsewhere, and it is one that has been imitated by the Gulf Cooperation Council or, more recently, by the C5 in Central Asia.
Economic interdependence is a consequence of cooperation, occurring over time by building trust and relying on companies that diversify operations across countries. Daron Acemoglu, a Nobel Prize winner in Economic Sciences, has regularly argued for this by pointing out that both prosperity and stability mutually flow from systems or institutions that offer a broad stake in the economic growth of a nation. Thus, when firms create cross-border commerce, war becomes economically unviable and politically undesirable. The principle is not exclusive to the Asia-Pacific, and despite ASEAN’s success, it is clear that outliers perpetuate risks by building up economic barriers instead of interdependence. Examples include relations between North and South Korea or China and Taiwan. The question, therefore, remains: how can peace be built today through economic interdependence, or in other words, how can rivals begin working together in an economic capacity?
Answers learned in the Asia-Pacific could resound further away. In the Middle East, for example, diplomatic efforts for peace in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, and Israel and the Palestinian Territories have worked through a long campaign of advocacy; however, it is only with the additional incentives that economic cooperation brings that peace efforts actually remain sustainable and enduring. For Israel and the Palestinian Territories, economic interdependence and a shared aspiration could enhance the ongoing international effort to ameliorate decades-long tensions. Syria offers an immediate test case as well. When the Assad regime fell in 2025 and the United States and the European Union both lifted sanctions, organizations began to move in, building relationships and supporting the fragile new state’s desire for peace. American companies have established power generation projects, the Gulf states and Turkey have signed dozens of economic memoranda of understanding with the new state, and startups like Behti Betak or nonprofit organizations like the Words of Isa are building grassroots relationships aimed at creating a newly integrated Syria, driving peace across the Middle East. Integration leads to interdependence. Interdependence self-reinforces peace.
Peacebuilding of this sort may be especially critical for Israel and the Palestinian Territories, where conflict and violence have persisted for decades before the Gaza War. Reconstruction and reconciliation efforts require that businesses spread their operations across the divide. Organizations like the Portland Trust, based in the United Kingdom, have focused on the region on the basis that economic co-operation and dialogue between the parties is inseparable from diplomatic peacebuilding efforts. And such economic development (alongside political will) can create hope, ambition, and opportunities for Palestinians. The founding Chief Executive of The Portland Trust, Lord Jonathan Kestenbaum, brings a personal history to the work of reconciliation. His family’s own flight from Nazi persecution ultimately led them to the UK, where he grew up, and whilst a student in London, he was General Secretary (mazkir) of Bnei Akiva UK, a branch of the global youth movement. He then studied at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem in the 1980s completing an MA in education, and thereafter helped to build an international training program for young educators. As a dual national at the time, Kestenbaum was conscripted to military service, with this experience influencing his life-long commitment to reconciliation between Palestinians and Israelis with a particular focus on building bridges through economic co-operation.
Lord Kestenbaum returned home to the U.K. after a few years in Jerusalem and gave up his dual nationality, retaining only British citizenship. He helped found the Portland Trust, and spent many years fostering peace efforts between Israelis and Palestinians. This history gave him a grounding in the region, a commitment to co-existence and a familiarity that exemplifies how peacebuilding through commerce is not abstract policy but is instead built through relationships and real-life experiences. The Portland Trust has to date worked extensively to support Palestinians and Israelis through projects like the Palestinian Agriculture Impact Fund and the building of the city of Rawabi.
Personal experiences bring markets together, and when they come together, they accelerate growth and integration among an increasing number of actors. Each of these actors learns to empathize with their business partners, regardless of historical or political differences. The process reinforces peace, builds harmony, and creates trust. In the case of Israel and the Palestinian Territories, the process is needed alongside reconstruction efforts like Trump’s Board of Peace, which aims to produce lasting peace but has yet to break ground.
Peace is not guaranteed through economics; however, throughout the last century, and in the case of the Asia-Pacific, it has become the most reliable mechanism of sustaining peace, cultivating the types of relationships that grow closer instead of farther apart. Private investment adds a financial tie to the process; however, intentional relationships with an empathetic desire for peace fundamentally secure the process. Southeast Asia’s history, compared to Syria’s cautious reopening or Gaza’s Board of Peace, shows that commerce can lay groundwork that politics otherwise cannot. The region will need institutional support, perhaps even at the level of an ASEAN, but the foundation is growing. More inter-state commerce will bring stronger relationships, paving the way forward to a future of peace, stability, and economic growth.

title: 25 Years After September 11th, New York City Changed the Way We Prepare for Disasters
content:
This post was originally published by the National Center for Disaster Preparedness.
Twenty-five years after September 11th, 2001, it is still difficult to contemplate what happened without first thinking about the people. The firefighters and police officers who ran toward the World Trade Center, the emergency managers and health professionals trying to make sense of an unconceivable situation, the transit workers helping people evacuate Lower Manhattan, and the countless New Yorkers who simply tried to help one another are part of the city’s history. For those of us who work in the disaster risk management sector, September 11th is also a marker in the history of how we prepare, respond, and recover. The attacks exposed serious weaknesses in information sharing and coordination, but they also demonstrated an aspect of equal importance: when a disaster overwhelms an entire system, disaster survivors and organizations need to find ways to collaborate that may not have existed before the disaster began.
One of the most distinct ways to understand how dramatically the field has changed is to consider the technical tools emergency managers had available to them in 2001. New York City was already using geographic information systems (GIS), and these digital maps became enormously valuable during the response and recovery. However, transferring large digital files across networked systems was constrained by limited bandwidth, slower network speeds, and substantially less mature data infrastructure than emergency responders have access to today. Internet capacity was so limited that critical GIS disk drives had to be delivered daily by state troopers from offices in Albany to New York City so they could be used in the response. There were no smartphones, no social media, and no cloud-based systems through which responders could immediately share information or communicate with the public. Today, satellite imagery, digital maps, mobile communications, real-time data and increasingly sophisticated analytical tools are so commonplace that it can be easy to forget how innovative and useful they would have seemed on September 11th.
The communications problems that morning were not simply a matter of having cumbersome technology tools. The destruction of infrastructure in Lower Manhattan, combined with the extraordinary volume of people trying to communicate, overwhelmed telephone, cellular, and radio systems. Responders lost contact with colleagues and leadership and, critically, did not always have the information they needed about what was happening inside the towers. In the middle of an emergency, information can be as critical as any physical resource, yet it only becomes useful when it can move between people and organizations. This lesson helped change emergency management for the better. Since September 11th, New York City and other jurisdictions have invested heavily in interoperable communications, emergency operations centers, GIS, mass notification, mutual aid, regional planning, and training programs that bring agencies together to practice before a disaster occurs. We have become much more aware that a major disaster in New York is never the responsibility of a single agency.
Perhaps the most important change, however, has been cultural. Emergency management has become much more focused on relationships among organizations and on the ability to adapt to emergent events. The people responding to September 11th were not unprepared; many were among the most highly trained public safety professionals in the U.S. Instead, they were confronting something for which there was no precedent. The lesson was not that planning had failed, but that no plan can anticipate every scenario. Good preparedness therefore means creating organizations that can recognize when their assumptions are wrong, share information quickly, request assistance, and adapt. Contemporary training exercises are most valuable when they expose those unnerving moments when a plan breaks down, and responders have to figure out together what to do next.
A new generation of leaders has also developed professionally in the years since September 11th. Many of today’s emergency managers, public safety officials, hospital managers and disaster researchers began their careers around that time or were shaped by its aftermath. They have subsequently dealt with hurricanes, floods, wildfires, pandemics, infrastructure failures and other emergencies that have reinforced the same primary lesson: disasters cross boundaries. A hospital may depend on the electric grid; a transit system may determine whether people can reach safety; a private company may control infrastructure essential to public response; and community organizations may know things that government agencies cannot fathom from an emergency operations center. The strongest response is therefore rarely about one institution having all the answers. It is about people knowing whom to call, trusting one another, and being willing to share what they know.
We should be proud of how far this evolution has taken us, but we should also be cautious to assume that progress means we are prepared for everything. That’s far from true. The U.S. remains vulnerable to unprecedented disasters that could overwhelm the systems we have built, and preparedness requires sustained attention even when the immediate crisis has passed. Changes in federal priorities, programs and policies can also create uncertainty for state, local, Tribal, and territorial emergency managers who are trying to plan years ahead. At the same time, technology is moving faster than many of our public institutions. Artificial intelligence, remote sensing, automated damage assessments and predictive modeling may dramatically improve our ability to understand a disaster as it unfolds, but such digital tools cannot replace leadership or trust. A sophisticated system is of limited value if the people who need to use it do not adequately communicate with one another.
Twenty-five years later, I think that is one of the most important lessons we should carry forward. We cannot know what the next catastrophic event will look like, and the technologies available to us in another 25 years may be difficult to imagine today. What we can do is continue learning from experience, investing in systems that let credible information flow freely, and developing leaders who know how to collaborate and build relationships before they are needed. The greatest homage to the people who responded on September 11th is not to just remember what they did that day. It is to use what we learned from their experience to make the next response more effective. New York City has spent 25 years doing exactly that, and the work is not finished.
Thomas Chandler is a senior research scientist and the director of the National Center for Disaster Preparedness.

title: Anganwadis shape the future. They are our responsibility
content:
Opinion Anganwadis shape the future. They are our responsibility
When every community takes responsibility for its anganwadi, Bharat takes responsibility for every child’s future
The Bharat of 2047 will be built by children who have not yet entered school. Their journey towards a healthy, confident and capable adulthood begins much earlier, most decisively in the first 1,000 days of life. For millions of Indian children and their mothers, that journey is supported by a familiar neighbourhood institution: The anganwadi.
Long before entering the classroom, children are weighed and measured at an anganwadi, get a warm meal and hear rhymes outside the home. Expectant parents also receive counselling. Today, 14 lakh anganwadi centres serve as the first point of contact between the citizens and the state, reaching over 8.9 crore children, women and adolescent girls. The 25.2 lakh anganwadi workers and helpers are drawn from the communities they serve. The anganwadi has always belonged to the neighbourhood.
This institution became the foundation of a national movement when Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched POSHAN Abhiyaan in March 2018. The ninth Rashtriya Poshan Maah began on September 9 with the theme “Hamari Anganwadi, Hamari Jimmedari”. The government’s commitment to providing quality services is unwavering. But an anganwadi centre truly flourishes when the community embraces it as its own. A Viksit Bharat can be built only through sabka prayas (everyone’s effort). Nutrition cannot be seen only as a government service.
Community ownership has too often remained an appeal. This year, it becomes an institution. Anganwadi management committees bring parents, panchayat representatives and self-help groups into the centre to ensure every eligible child is reached. Social audits enable communities to review services, verify entitlements and record findings. Accountability becomes verification from within by the families served.
Mothers are at the heart of this process. The menu board of the Supplementary Nutrition Programme (SNP) displays daily entitlements for the hot meals and take-home rations. When a mother knows what her child is entitled to, transparency becomes a habit. The community becomes an informed partner in ensuring quality. During Poshan Maah 2026, committees, social audits and menu boards are being activated, alongside Tithi Bhoj, tasting sessions and recipe demonstrations.
A Suposhit Bharat requires balanced meals — cereals and millets, pulses, nuts and seeds, milk and milk products, eggs, fruits and green vegetables. The Comprehensive Guidelines for SNP 2026, released in July, define hot cooked meals and reinforce micronutrient norms under the National Food Security Act, 2013.
The second is early learning. What a child eats and learns are deeply connected. Anganwadi workers track 34 developmental milestones in a child’s first three years. The Navchetna and Aadharshila curricula carry nutrition and care into school readiness.
The third begins before the child arrives. A mother’s nutrition in pregnancy shapes her child’s start in life. This Poshan Maah marks 10 years of the Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana, reflecting the Prime Minister’s conviction that no woman should have to choose between earnings and health. A decade on, 4.65 crore beneficiaries have received Rs 21,511 crore directly into their accounts. Strengthened under Mission Shakti, it provides an additional benefit for a second girl child. The Economic Survey 2025-26 makes clear that such a transfer achieves its full purpose when it travels with counselling that enables informed decisions within the household. Reviewing Rajasthan’s Cash Plus model, which paired these transfers with sustained behaviour change communication, it records that the share of women spending the benefit on food rose from 30 per cent to 89 per cent, and that myths surrounding maternal nutrition receded as husbands and families were drawn into the conversation. Partnership grows around anganwadis because a mother’s nutrition was never hers to secure alone.
Community ownership cannot mean placing the entire burden of nutrition and early childhood care on the anganwadi worker. It must mean respecting, supporting and strengthening her. This September, I call upon every citizen to visit at least one anganwadi centre in their locality. Speak to the worker, read the menu board and ask how you can support them. Fathers, grandparents, panchayats and self-help groups all have a role. The children being weighed at anganwadis this September will be in their twenties when India completes a century of Independence. The health and confidence they carry into that year are being shaped today. When every community takes responsibility for its anganwadi, Bharat takes responsibility for every child’s future.
The writer is Union Minister for Women and Child Development

title: American doctor visited Kainchi Dham; Neem Karoli Baba changed his life
content:
In the early 1970s, American physician Dr. Larry Brilliant travelled to India and spent time at Neem Karoli Baba’s ashram at Kainchi Dham, seeking spiritual guidance during a period of personal uncertainty. Baba reportedly began calling him “Doctor America”. In an interview with Tricycle: The Buddhist Review, he said the spiritual guru later urged him to go to Delhi and work for the United Nations to help eradicate smallpox.
Brilliant eventually joined the World Health Organization’s smallpox eradication programme in India. His journey to the ashram and his work against the disease became closely connected in his later recollections. For Brilliant, the journey was deeply connected to his encounter with Neem Karoli Baba, whom he credited with giving his life a new direction.
When he recalled his conversation with Neem Karoli Baba
Brilliant recalled that the spiritual teacher had called him “Dr. America”.
In an interview published by Tricycle: The Buddhist Review in 2023, Dr. Larry Brilliant spoke about his time with Neem Karoli Baba and the teacher’s instruction to help eradicate smallpox. He said, “One day in July 1973, Neem Karoli Baba told me to go to Delhi immediately to work for the United Nations and help eradicate smallpox.”
Brilliant recalled that the spiritual teacher had called him “Dr. America”.
In the interview, he also spoke about the money he had with him and in America. “He (Neem Karoli Baba) said to me, Dr. America, because that was the name he had given me, Dr. America, how much money do you have? And that, you know, there's a whole other channel down which that goes. And I said, I have $500. He said, $500. You're lying. How much money do you have back in America?”
Brilliant then thought about the time he had worked as an emergency room doctor. “And I said, I have $500 in America too.” The conversation soon turned into a joke, as Brilliant remembered it. “And then he started to chant. You have to understand that everything was funny. Everything was a comedian. Everything was a joke. He turned every single moment into something funnier than you ever thought anything could ever be.”
Brilliant recalled Baba chanting about the money he had in India and the money he had in America. “And he started to chant $500 here, $500 there. You are no doctor, which is exactly what my mother had said to me. You can't make any money. You're not a real doctor.”
He recalled that Baba continued repeating the words, first in Hindi and then in English. “$500 here, $500 there. You are no doctor. U-N-O doctor.” It was then that the conversation took a turn Brilliant would remember for the rest of his life.
“United Nations organization. Dr. America is going to become a United Nations doctor. And you're going to work to help eradicate smallpox.” According to Brilliant’s recollection, Baba then spoke about the disease and its future. “Because this horrible disease is going to be lifted off of the back of humanity by God, who has a gift to humanity, will conquer this one form of suffering.”
From Kainchi Dham to the fight against smallpox
Brilliant’s account of his encounter with Neem Karoli Baba is closely connected to his later work in public health. He eventually joined the World Health Organization’s smallpox eradication programme in India. The WHO campaign became one of the most significant achievements in global public health.
In 1980, the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated worldwide. It was the first human disease to be officially declared eradicated. For Brilliant, the memory of Kainchi Dham remained connected to his professional journey. In his recollections, Neem Karoli Baba’s words gave him a new direction and encouraged him to use his medical skills in the fight against smallpox.

title: Wildfire strategy doesn't need a winner—with 3 camps fighting for dominance, the system can't keep up with the risk
content:
One of the problems with how America deals with wildfires is the belief that there is one primary strategy that can end the nation's wildfire crisis. Whether that's detecting and putting out every fire fast, increasing logging and forest thinning, or allowing fires to burn under safe conditions, the default choice today is to pour more money and effort into the star approach of the moment.
But an effective wildfire strategy in the face of worsening fire seasons demands a system of actions—interconnected pieces that reinforce one another.
Right now, those pieces mostly are not connected. Research groups, governments and organizations tend to separate into distinct camps, each promoting its own specific strategy. The result is a system that can't keep up with the rising fire risk.
Our team of researchers, along with fire ecologist Jim Menakis, who recently retired from the U.S. Forest Service, has been looking at wildfires from social, ecological and risk-science perspectives to help forest and fire managers and communities in fire-prone areas turn research into practices that can reduce fire-related risks.
We have seen the pitfalls of current fire management approaches and also examples of what actually works.
Three separate camps
Wildfire strategy tends to break into three distinct camps today, each focusing heavily on one approach over the others.
One camp wants to double down on suppressing every ignition quickly and aggressively, contending that it's the surest way to prevent immediate loss. The direction to put out every fire quickly has been a foundation of the U.S. government response to wildfires since the early 1900s and persists despite attempts over the years to change it.
A second camp says the real problem is fuel: flammable vegetation that has been piling up for decades in forests and rangelands because of too much fire suppression.
This group's solution is to scale up forest and brush thinning through logging and controlled burning. Calls for these actions span political administrations, from the U.S. Forest Service's Wildfire Crisis Strategy during the Biden administration to the Trump administration's 2025 executive order calling for the expansion of American timber production and rescinding protections for roadless areas of national forests. But while excessive fuel is a problem, particularly during dry periods, it isn't the only issue.
A third camp says fire is coming regardless, and people have to live with it by accepting and promoting more fire, but allowing it to burn on our terms, when and where it's safe. This is often called managed wildfire. It sometimes includes creating landscapes and communities that can survive and recover from fire.
Each camp tends to operate in isolation from the others, often with its own budget, workforce, practices and culture. These silos can inhibit communication and coordination, which can make fire management less effective.
Success stories at the intersections
The question for fire management shouldn't be "which of the three is right?" It should be "where do they reinforce each other?"
Successful fire strategies combine many approaches to lower risk. If you look closely, you can see some of the ways these methods intersect.
Fuel treatments, such as prescribed burning of vegetation and forest thinning, used in the right locations, don't stop fires on their own, but they can make suppression safer and more effective by lowering a fire's intensity.
Using prescribed burns and forest thinning strategically can also make it safer for managers to allow lower-intensity fire to expand under favorable weather conditions, thereby dampening future fire risk and letting fire play its ecological role in renewing natural systems. A fire meant to spread still needs a safe edge to stop at, and fuel treatments serve this purpose.
And while suppression and the idea of living with fire appear to oppose each other, the same detection and real-time decision tools that let crews hit a fire hard and fast are exactly the tools needed to allow a fire to burn under safe conditions. Living with fire becomes credible only after fuel treatments have lowered risk to communities.
A place where everyone is working together
Wildfire activity has increased markedly across many parts of the U.S. in recent decades, resulting in destruction in communities, harm to water supplies and tragic fatalities. We believe that changing this trajectory requires a shift in thinking, from promoting a single "best" wildfire strategy to designing stronger connections between strategic options.
Building these connections has to begin long before a fire starts, continue while the fire burns and endure long after the fire has ended. It includes how fire research and fire-risk-reduction projects are designed and funded, how communities are brought into planning to build trust and support, and how communities can lessen their vulnerability to wildfires, such as home hardening, developing escape routes and updating land-use codes.
Reducing fire risk isn't solely the responsibility of a single government agency or private entity; all sectors of society must contribute.
This is already happening where people are willing to do the hard work.
For example, the Northern Colorado Fireshed Collaborative brings together federal and state agencies, local governments, water utilities and residents. It coordinates reducing flammable vegetation across land ownership boundaries, prepares homeowners and communities through education and financial assistance for wildfire prevention measures, and organizes response and recovery efforts as one connected system rather than separate ones.
Everyone has a role
The wildfire problem exceeds what any single entity can effectively tackle on its own.
Fire scientists, government agencies and local communities all play a role, which means you do, too. Check whether your area has a fire collaborative or community wildfire protection plan. Show up to public meetings to stay informed, and start making an impact at home by clearing dry brush around your property and helping neighbors do the same.
The path to better strategies is built by people working together, not by policy on a page.
