쿠메 대법원장은 케냐 최초의 여성 대법원장으로, 여성과 아동 등 사회적 약자의 권리를 보호하고 국민의 사법 접근성을 확대하는 데 힘써 왔다. 취임 후에는 젠더 폭력 사건을 신속히 해결하기 위한 전문법원을 구축하고 사법 제도 현대화와 사법부에 대한 국민 신뢰 회복을 위한 개혁을 추진했다.
한국가정법률상담소는 1956년 설립된 한국 최초의 법률구조기관으로, 가정폭력 피해자와 한부모·다문화가정 및 저소득층 등 취약계층을 위한 법률 구조 활동으로 높은 평가를 받는다. 과거 여성과 가족의 법률문제가 개인의 고통으로 여겨지던 시절부터 무료 상담·구조를 했다.
데이비드 설리번 세계은행 부총괄 법률고문 등도 자리를 함께했다. 그는 "공정한 사법 실현은 인간의 존엄과 발전을 증진하는 강력한 수단"이라며 "굳건한 법률제도와 법치주의는 경제적 기회와 사회적 포용, 공공의 신뢰를 뒷받침하는 중요한 토대"라고 강조했다.
강경주 기자 qurasoha@hankyung.com

title: Florida confirma el aumento del salario mínimo a US$15: entra en vigor este 30 de septiembre y estos trabajadores recibirán más
content:
El calendario aprobado por los votantes de Florida en 2020 llegará a su último tramo el miércoles 30 de septiembre de 2026, cuando el salario mínimo estatal pase a ser de US$15 por hora. El cambio se sentirá en empleos de restaurantes, hoteles, supermercados, comercios, limpieza, mantenimiento y atención al cliente, actividades con amplia presencia de trabajadores hispanos en Miami, Hialeah, Orlando, Tampa, Fort Lauderdale, West Palm Beach y Jacksonville. Para muchas familias, el ingreso adicional llegará en medio de gastos que siguen marcando el presupuesto del hogar, como el alquiler, la comida, la gasolina, el seguro del vehículo y los servicios básicos. No se trata de una norma reciente ni de una medida anunciada a última hora, sino del cierre de una ruta de incrementos que fue incorporada a la Constitución estatal tras las elecciones de 2020.
Desde esa fecha, quienes no reciben propinas deberán percibir al menos US$15 por cada hora trabajada. Para meseros, bartenders y otros empleados de hospitalidad que cumplan las condiciones legales, el pago directo mínimo del empleador será de US$11.98 por hora, más las propinas aplicables. Con este incremento termina la etapa de alzas automáticas de US$1 y comienza una transición hacia un mecanismo vinculado a la inflación.
¿CUÁNDO SUBIRÁ EL SALARIO MÍNIMO EN FLORIDA?
La fecha clave es el miércoles 30 de septiembre de 2026. Ese día comenzará a regir el último incremento de US$1 por hora previsto en la enmienda constitucional conocida como Raising Florida’s Minimum Wage. Los votantes aprobaron esa iniciativa el 3 de noviembre de 2020.
La disposición estableció una ruta progresiva para pasar de US$10 por hora en 2021 a US$15 en 2026. Por esa razón, la actualización no requiere una nueva votación de la Legislatura de Florida ni la aprobación de una norma adicional.
La reforma constitucional ordenó aumentos de US$1 cada 30 de septiembre hasta alcanzar la tarifa de US$15 por hora en 2026.
¿CUÁL SERÁ EL NUEVO SALARIO MÍNIMO?
Las personas que no reciben propinas pasarán de US$14 a US$15 por hora.
En la práctica, esto significa US$1 adicional por cada hora registrada. Quien mantenga una jornada de 40 horas semanales durante 52 semanas podría obtener cerca de US$2,080 más al año antes de impuestos, si conserva la misma cantidad de horas durante ese período.
Los cálculos reflejan únicamente la diferencia de US$1 por hora. No incluyen horas extra, bonificaciones, comisiones, propinas, cambios de turno ni descuentos aplicados a la nómina.
Para alguien que trabaja en retail, cocina, limpieza, cuidado de adultos mayores, almacenes o servicios turísticos, la modificación puede notarse en cada paycheck. En el sur de Florida, donde muchas familias combinan más de un empleo o dependen de ingresos por hora, será importante revisar la tarifa aplicada desde finales de septiembre.
¿CUÁNTO COBRARÁN LOS TRABAJADORES CON PROPINAS?
Los empleados que reciben propinas también estarán cubiertos por la actualización, aunque su esquema de pago funciona de otra manera.
Florida permite que los empleadores elegibles apliquen un crédito de hasta US$3.02 por hora en propinas para cumplir con el mínimo establecido por el estado. Desde el 30 de septiembre de 2026, el negocio podrá pagar una tarifa directa de US$11.98 por hora, siempre que los ingresos por propinas permitan alcanzar al menos US$15 por hora.
El empleador puede contabilizar hasta US$3.02 por hora en propinas para completar el mínimo exigido, siempre que se cumplan los requisitos legales.
La regla puede ser especialmente relevante para meseros, bartenders, personal de cafeterías, hoteles, bares y negocios turísticos de Miami Beach, Brickell, Wynwood, Key West, Orlando, Kissimmee, Fort Lauderdale o Clearwater.
Las propinas no eliminan el derecho a recibir la tarifa mínima. Si el pago directo y los ingresos por servicio no llegan al monto legal, la empresa debe cubrir la diferencia.
¿QUIÉNES SE BENEFICIARÁN DEL AUMENTO?
La actualización cubre a los empleados protegidos por la normativa estatal de salario mínimo. No se limita a una industria específica ni depende del tamaño de la compañía.
Entre quienes podrían recibir el ajuste se encuentran:
- Personas que actualmente cobran US$14 por hora.
- Empleados de tiendas, supermercados y comercios minoristas.
- Personal de restaurantes, cafeterías, bares y hoteles.
- Trabajadores de limpieza, mantenimiento y servicios.
- Jóvenes que ingresan al mercado laboral con la tarifa base.
- Empleados de negocios turísticos y de hospitalidad.
- Personas que reciben propinas y están sujetas a las reglas estatales.
- Trabajadores por hora en compañías que pagan el monto mínimo permitido.
Los empleadores deben aplicar la tarifa correspondiente a todas las horas trabajadas dentro de Florida, siempre que la persona esté cubierta por las normas federales y estatales aplicables.
¿QUÉ REVISAR EN EL PAYCHECK?
La medida empieza a regir el 30 de septiembre. Por ello, conviene revisar el próximo comprobante de pago, sobre todo si el período de nómina abarca días laborados antes y después de la actualización.
Estos son algunos puntos que pueden verificarse:
- La tarifa por hora que aparece en el recibo.
- El total de horas registradas durante el período.
- El pago de las horas trabajadas desde el 30 de septiembre.
- El cálculo del pago directo y las propinas en empleos de hospitalidad.
- Los descuentos aplicados a la nómina.
- Los horarios, recibos, mensajes y registros personales de trabajo.
No todos verán el depósito actualizado el mismo día, porque cada compañía tiene su propio calendario de pago. Aun así, las horas laboradas desde el 30 de septiembre deben calcularse con la nueva tarifa que corresponda.
¿QUÉ PASARÁ DESPUÉS DE LLEGAR A US$15?
La actualización de septiembre de 2026 será el último aumento fijo de US$1 incluido en la enmienda aprobada en 2020. Después cambiará la fórmula. El primer cálculo basado en la inflación se realizará el 30 de septiembre de 2027, tomando como referencia la variación de precios registrada durante los 12 meses anteriores al 1 de septiembre de ese año. El monto resultante comenzará a regir el 1 de enero de 2028.
La fórmula utiliza el Índice de Precios al Consumidor para trabajadores urbanos y empleados administrativos, conocido como CPI-W. Por ello, las futuras alzas dependerán de la inflación y ya no estarán definidas previamente en incrementos de un dólar.
¿POR QUÉ FLORIDA LLEGÓ A LOS US$15 POR HORA?
El origen de este proceso se encuentra en las elecciones de 2020. Ese año, los votantes aprobaron la Enmienda 2, que modificó la Constitución estatal para establecer un incremento gradual del mínimo salarial.
La iniciativa fijó el siguiente calendario:
- US$10 por hora desde el 30 de septiembre de 2021.
- Incrementos de US$1 por hora cada 30 de septiembre.
- Llegada a US$15 por hora el 30 de septiembre de 2026.
- Ajustes posteriores según la inflación, a partir del cálculo de septiembre de 2027.
El plan generó respaldo y cuestionamientos desde su aprobación. Sus defensores sostienen que una tarifa más alta ayuda a trabajadores con ingresos bajos a afrontar el costo de vida. Sus críticos advierten que el encarecimiento de la nómina puede afectar a pequeños negocios, restaurantes independientes y comercios con márgenes reducidos.
Para los hogares del estado, especialmente en zonas donde la vivienda se ha encarecido, la discusión seguirá centrada en el alcance real de ese ingreso frente a gastos como renta, comida, transporte, electricidad, cuidado infantil y seguros.
LOS TRABAJADORES TIENEN PROTECCIÓN ANTE INCUMPLIMIENTOS
La nueva cifra no solo modifica los avisos de empleo o los recibos de pago. La normativa de Florida prohíbe que un empleador tome represalias contra una persona por exigir el mínimo correspondiente, presentar una queja, informar sobre una posible infracción o ayudar a otro trabajador a ejercer sus derechos.
Si alguien considera que recibió un pago inferior al requerido, existe un procedimiento previo antes de presentar una demanda.
- Debe enviar una notificación escrita al empleador.
- El documento debe indicar la tarifa aplicable, las fechas, las horas trabajadas y el monto que considera adeudado.
- La empresa tendrá 15 días calendario desde la recepción del aviso para pagar o resolver el reclamo.
- Si no existe una solución, el trabajador puede iniciar una acción civil para reclamar salarios pendientes, daños y honorarios legales, según corresponda.
Además, los empleadores deben colocar en un lugar visible un aviso sobre el salario mínimo de Florida en inglés y español.
FLORIDA TENDRÁ UN MÍNIMO SUPERIOR AL FEDERAL
Con la subida de septiembre, la diferencia entre la tarifa estatal y la federal será todavía más marcada.
El mínimo federal sigue establecido en US$7.25 por hora. Florida, en cambio, llegará a US$15 por hora para quienes no reciben propinas, por lo que su piso salarial será más del doble de la referencia nacional.
En síntesis, Florida completará el 30 de septiembre de 2026 el plan de incrementos avalado por los votantes seis años antes. La nueva tarifa será de US$15 por hora para empleados sin propinas y de US$11.98 por hora más propinas para trabajadores elegibles bajo ese sistema.
La siguiente etapa comenzará en 2027, cuando el estado calcule el futuro ajuste conforme a la inflación. La cantidad que resulte de ese proceso entrará en vigor el 1 de enero de 2028.

title: New assessment finds five EU Missions are driving systemic change
content:
All five EU Missions are making steady progress towards their objectives – with the Climate Adaptation Mission having already met and surpassed its 2030 targets.
The five EU Missions were launched in 2021 under Horizon Europe 2021-2027. They are designed to translate scientific and technological innovation into practical solutions that can be tested and deployed in real-life settings across Europe, addressing pressing societal challenges – climate change, soil and waters health, and cancer – by going beyond traditional instruments and giving research and innovation a new role. Their time-bound objectives help mobilise coordinated action and support long-term societal transformation.
According to the assessment, all five EU Missions are making good progress towards their 2030 goals:
Climate Adaptation:
The goal of this mission is to support at least 150 European regions, local authorities and communities to become climate resilient. The target has already been largely surpassed, with 292 regional and local authorities having already implemented climate adaptation measures.
Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities:
Its objective is to support at least 100 cities in achieving climate neutrality, and to inspire other cities across Europe. Currently, already 107 cities have Climate City Contracts. They are projected to cut emissions by 76% by 2030, backed by more than €13 billion in supported or developing investment.
Cancer:
Its aim is to improve the lives of more than 3 million people through prevention, early detection, treatment and care for not only those affected by cancer, but also their families. The current actions show that it will be able to improve the lives of 2.3 million people by 2030. Upcoming projects expected to raise this figure beyond the target of 3 million.
Restore our Ocean and Waters:
The goal is to restore the health of our ocean and waters by protecting and restoring aquatic ecosystems, reducing pollution and making the blue economy carbon-neutral and circular. It has delivered 121 innovative solutions tested in 349 real-world demonstration sites, engaged 86 regions in replication efforts and secured over 1,000 Charter Actions from stakeholders. Under the Mission, the design of the core infrastructure of the European Digital Twin Ocean – expected to be fully operational by 2030 – was completed and is now accessible to all.
A Soil Deal for Europe:
The Mission is progressing towards its goal of 100 Living Labs, with 45 already established. It involves over 500 real sites (such as farms) across Europe, and 60 to 70 additional ones are expected to become operational by 2028.
According to a mid-term assessment published by the European Commission, the five EU Missions in Horizon Europe are delivering tangible positive results in addressing some of Europe’s most pressing societal challenges through scientific and technological innovation.

title: Cambodia is closing scam centers but needs help tracking the money
content:
Closing an online scam center stops criminal activity, but it does not dismantle the network behind it.
The people directing the operation may be in another country, while the money can move across borders through bank accounts or digital payment systems. If we want to eliminate online scams rather than simply force them to move elsewhere, we have to follow the money. That is the next phase of Cambodia’s campaign.
Combating online scams is a national priority for Cambodia. Our goal is not just to close sites but to pursue the criminal masterminds and financial networks behind them.
Our campaign is delivering tangible results. Over the last 12 months, Cambodian authorities investigated 832 suspected locations and carried out crackdowns at 663. Eighty-six scam compounds have been dismantled and brought under control pending legal seizure.
Authorities have forwarded 446 cases to court involving 3,927 accused from 29 nationalities, including ringleaders and accomplices. Regulators have also taken action against 27 casinos linked to online scams, revoking 18 licenses and suspending nine.
Recent arrests of high-profile businesspeople and senior officials show that the campaign is reaching beyond low-level offenders. Cambodia’s Anti-Corruption Unit has also acted in four cases involving 15 senior officials and law-enforcement officers suspected of involvement. No one is above the law.
The next step is to make these gains permanent by ensuring that closed operations remain closed and criminal networks cannot simply reappear elsewhere. We are already seeing those networks change tactics, moving away from large compounds toward smaller, decentralized operations. That makes it even more important to pursue the people and financial networks behind them rather than focusing only on physical sites.
In April, Cambodia strengthened its legal framework with the Law on Combating Online Scams. The law gives authorities stronger tools to pursue those who organize or support these crimes and to trace and seize criminal proceeds.
Financial institutions and other regulated businesses must report suspicious transactions to the Cambodia Financial Intelligence Unit, which shares relevant intelligence with investigators. This helps authorities trace criminal proceeds and identify the people behind scam operations.
Cambodian authorities have already frozen more than $300 million in bank accounts linked to online scams, with additional assets undergoing freezing procedures and assessment. But once the money crosses a border, international cooperation becomes essential.
A victim of an online scam may be in London or Los Angeles while the people running the scam are thousands of miles away. Criminal proceeds can pass through several jurisdictions before reaching those who ultimately control the operation. No police force can follow that chain alone.
In July, the United Kingdom assumed the presidency of the Financial Action Task Force, which sets global standards against money laundering and terrorist financing. Under the UK’s leadership, FATF has made combating fraud a priority, including the financial flows linked to scam compounds. It is focused on strengthening financial intelligence and international information sharing.
Cambodia supports that approach. We continue to work with international law-enforcement partners and through the Asia/Pacific Group on Money Laundering. In July, FBI Director Kash Patel visited Cambodia to discuss scam operations targeting Americans and to strengthen cooperation between US and Cambodian law enforcement.
Cooperation against transnational crime should cut across geopolitical divisions. The same networks target people in the United States and China, among many other countries.
International cooperation will be a focus of the International Conference on Combating Online Scams (ICCOS 2026), which Cambodia is hosting in Phnom Penh on September 23 and 24. Participants include representatives from China, the UK, and the United States, including the FBI, alongside governments from across Asia and international organizations such as Interpol.
The theme is “Acting Together towards Breaking the Chain and Eradication of Online Scams.” The challenge is to turn international cooperation into operational cooperation. Financial intelligence must move quickly across borders to identify criminal proceeds before they are moved beyond investigators’ reach. Countries also need to be able to freeze and recover criminal proceeds more effectively.
There is also a human cost to consider. Many people found inside scam operations have themselves been trafficked or coerced, while victims around the world have lost their savings to these crimes. Protecting those who have been exploited also requires cross-border cooperation. Following the money helps us pursue those who profit from both trafficking and fraud.
Cambodia will continue to disrupt scam operations and prosecute those responsible. We will work to ensure that closed operations cannot simply reopen elsewhere. But these are transnational criminal networks, and lasting success requires international action.
Cambodia is doing its part. In Phnom Penh later this September, we will work with our international partners to dismantle the financial networks behind these scams and cut off the profits that keep this global criminal industry alive.
Chhay Sinarith is a Senior Minister in the Cambodian Government and the Vice-Chairman of the Commission for Combating Online Scams. He is leading Cambodia’s nationwide campaign to dismantle online scam networks and implement the country’s new Law on Combating Online Scams.

title: Mary Goretti Kariaga: The Kenyan scientist who pioneered mushroom farming in Kenya
content:
Mary Goretti Kariaga: The Kenyan scientist who pioneered mushroom farming in Kenya
What you need to know:
- From plant pathology and sugarcane research to pioneering commercial mushroom production, Mary Goretti Kariaga built a remarkable career in Kenyan science and agriculture.
- Her journey took her from the University of Nairobi to Zimbabwe and back to Kenya, where she pioneered mushroom farming and trained aspiring growers.
On August 1, 1982, Mary Goretti Kariaga was in her third trimester of pregnancy with her first child when intense anxiety took hold of her. She was in her rented house in Arina, Kisumu, listening to KBC news of an emerging coup. She grew more worried as she wondered whether hospitals would be operational in time for her delivery.
Mary's father, John Joseph Odera, a successful entrepreneur, valued academic advancement. He funded her O-Levels at Loreto Girls in Limuru and her A-Levels at Kenya High School, instilling in her a strong drive for intellectual achievement. She enrolled at the University of Nairobi in 1975 and graduated four years later with a Bachelor of Education (Science).
She was recruited as an Agricultural Research Officer at the Kenya Agricultural Research Institute in Kibos, Kisumu. After the attempted coup, Mary safely delivered her first child, Patricia, on the night of August 17, 1982, at Kisumu's Victoria Hospital. She later travelled to Port Louis to spend three months at the Mauritius Sugar Industry Institute, studying the agronomy of sugarcane cultivation.
In 1986, she began her master's degree in plant pathology at the University of Nairobi, focusing on fungal, bacterial and nematode diseases. Her thesis centred on parasitic nematodes of sugar cane, and she later authored an academic manual titled Plant Parasitic Nematodes Associated with Sugar Cane at the Nyanza Sugar Belt. She also looked into the challenges of communal sugarcane farming and completed her studies in 1988, a year before giving birth to her son, Stephen.
She became a member of African Women in Science and Engineering, an associate of the International Network of Women Engineers and Scientists, and a founding scholar of the Kenya Professional Association of Women in Agriculture and Environment. Her expertise led to her appointment at the Lake Basin Development Authority's Fibre Research Station in Kibos.
In 1995, she began lecturing at Maseno University before moving with her family to Harare, Zimbabwe, on January 5, 1999, after her husband, Billy, was employed by the University of Zimbabwe. Her deep interest in fungi led her to start a botanical programme to study mushroom cultivation. She began culturing and bulking spawn (mushroom seeds), and in 2000, she started producing Agaricus bisporus (button mushrooms) at the secondary entrance to her home, at the back of the University of Zimbabwe campus.
Also read: Kabete's queen of mushroom farming
Mary held weekend mushroom training sessions for interested participants at her house and went on to study the production of other edible mushrooms, including Ganoderma lucidum, shiitake and Pleurotus ostreatus (oyster mushrooms).
In September 2001, she walked into Standard Chartered Bank on Bond Street at the Mount Pleasant Shopping Centre, within walking distance of the university. Suddenly, five armed men carrying AK-47 rifles rushed into the bank and ordered the crowd in Shona, "Vese rarai pasi! (Everybody lie down!).”
Because of the similarities between Shona and Swahili, both Bantu languages, Mary understood the order and lay face-down along with the other clients. An overweight white client appeared stunned and confused by the Shona commands until a rifle was pointed directly at his face. Because of his large belly, he ended up lying on his back instead of his stomach, while a terrified woman lying next to Mary began sobbing as the robbers collected money from the tellers.
In her book, The Woman Who Pioneered Mushroom Production in Kenya, Mary writes that minutes after the gunmen left with their loot, everyone remained frozen on the floor in fear. When a person walked in and whispered, “They've gone,” Mary was the first to get up and run out of the bank.
In 2002, she relocated to Kisumu, applied for a position at Maseno's Faculty of Botany, and began pursuing her long-term goal of fighting protein deficiency and raising income levels through mushroom production.
At the time, there were no individual commercial mushroom producers in Kenya. Mary set out to introduce mushroom farming to empower smallholder farmers using oyster mushrooms, which were highly resistant to infection, in high demand and had significant medicinal value.
Because of the uniqueness of her work in mushroom cultivation, Maseno called on her on July 29, 2004, to deliver the keynote presentation to President Mwai Kibaki at the annual Kisumu Agricultural Show. That morning, Kibaki, First Lady Lucy and their security detail listened in astonishment as Mary gave a compelling address on the potential of mushroom production.
Her passion caught the attention of KTN reporter David Ohito, who arranged an interview with Mary and filed a story with his colleague, sparking demand for mushrooms across Kenya. Mary began receiving calls from entrepreneurs requesting mushroom training, as interest in mushroom cultivation grew. She registered her company, Mount Pleasant Mushroom Consultants, named after her former residential suburb in Zimbabwe, and used it to partner different organisations.
She was later elected treasurer of the Universities' Academic Staff Union and negotiated a 50 per cent salary increment for lecturers during the 2007 nationwide strike, the highest lecturers' salary increment in Kenya's history.
In late 2007, Mary's research in sugarcane diseases caught the interest of the Faculty of Agriculture, Veterinary Science and Technology at Masinde Muliro University in Kakamega. She joined the institution and completed her PhD dissertation on Rice Blast, identifying a sequence of four races of the same pathogen, which were later registered at the National Centre for Biotechnology Information. Shortly after being promoted to senior lecturer at Masinde Muliro, she narrowly survived a harrowing carjacking at gunpoint at the entrance of her home.
The writer is a novelist, Big Brother Africa 2 Kenyan representative and founder of Jeff's Fitness Centre (@jeffbigbrother).

title: North Carolina county gets $23 million as PFAS polluters pay for cleaner water
content:
Robeson County, North Carolina, is expected to receive nearly $23 million for clean-water work under a major PFAS settlement. The funding follows decades of contamination tied to chemical manufacturers throughout the state.
Here's what to know
North Carolina says it has reached a $590 million agreement with DuPont, Chemours, and Corteva. The deal, announced by North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson and North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality Secretary Reid Wilson, is intended to address the contamination of state waters by per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS.
According to local outlet WMBF News, Robeson County is projected to get close to $23 million over time, including roughly $2.3 million in the first year. The overall package includes a $455 million settlement payout and a $135 million reserve fund, making it the largest environmental-damages recovery in state history.
County officials told the station the money is planned for public-water treatment upgrades, including advanced filtration, and for continued landfill analysis and monitoring. They also said a pilot program is already underway at the Rocco Water Treatment Plant as broader infrastructure improvements continue.
Jackson described the settlement as a way to make the companies answer for harm done in North Carolina.
"It is a massive step forward in giving our state more dollars to help fund clean water programs," Jackson said in the announcement. "This settlement puts even more teeth behind the consent order with NCDEQ. Chemours made this mess, and we're making sure Chemours cleans it up."
PFAS are a class of human-made chemicals that can persist in habitats and human bodies for long periods.
More background
The North Carolina case centers on contamination associated with the Fayetteville Works facility. The settlement announcement noted DuPont began operating the site in the early 1970s and used southeastern North Carolina as a PFAS dumping ground.
More than 500,000 people in the area rely on the Cape Fear River for drinking water, according to WMBF News, and the watershed is also important for farming and recreation. State researchers found very high PFAS concentrations there in a late-2016 study.
State efforts to curb the pollution began almost 10 years ago. Then, in 2019, the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality secured an order to mandate that Chemours stop wastewater discharges, reduce air pollution from GenX and other PFAS, provide filtration for people with contaminated drinking water wells, cut PFAS pollution in the Cape Fear River, and address contamination sources at the facility.
What's being done?
The settlement provides funding for a range of local governments and utilities. WMBF reported that the money will help pay for filtration and other cleanup work intended to make household water safer.
According to the local outlet, the agreement is separate from a federal lawsuit filed in June that alleges groundwater feeding the Rocco plant was contaminated by Robeson County's landfill, not Chemours' Fayetteville Works. Still, the county said it will keep moving ahead with efforts to improve water quality.
"This settlement provides our county with the critical, dedicated resources needed to ensure that our residents have the safest drinking and household use water possible," officials said, per WMBF.
Where can I learn more?
This settlement is part of a wider push for cleaner water and more accountability from both polluters and public officials:
• In Colorado, regulators now direct payments from pollution violators toward environmental justice needs.
• In Arizona, residents can report local businesses wasting water as drought pressure persists.
• In Alberta, Canada, critics blasted use of tax dollars for a fossil-fuel ad campaign.
• Inditex, Zara's parent company, faced backlash after a concerning operational change increased emissions.
Fights over pollution, water protection, and corporate accountability rarely stay confined to one place. That broader picture helps explain why this PFAS settlement matters beyond a single cleanup effort.

title: Colorado's Mesa Verde will return more than 4,000 sacred objects and remains of 85 Indigenous people
content:
Mesa Verde National Park is preparing to return more than 4,000 sacred objects and the remains of 85 Indigenous people in a major repatriation effort tied to Tribal history in the Southwest.
Here's what to know
In its largest repatriation effort in history, UNESCO site Mesa Verde National Park is taking a long-overdue step in returning 4,304 culturally significant objects along with the remains of 85 individuals to their rightful Tribes in Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado, according to local officials, via The Denver Post.
In 1990, the federal Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA) required federal agencies and institutions, like museums and universities, that receive federal funds to return Native American human remains and other cultural items to Tribal nations.
However, many of the country's most prestigious museums and universities still hold onto Indigenous objects and remains.
After conducting an inventory, Mesa Verde National Park identified ceramic bowls and jars, sandals, matting, ropes made of human hair, animal bones, feather boxes, crystals, turquoise, and buckskin bags. Tribe members can now submit repatriation requests now that the inventory is complete.
For descendant communities, repatriation is far more than a symbolic paperwork exercise. It can mean regaining stewardship of ancestors, burial items, and ceremonial objects removed from their original context—more often than not, without consent.
That makes the decision especially significant at well-known Native archaeological sites that have become tourist destinations, because it shows these areas are still part of a living cultural story for Native communities.
Tribal nations have long been trying to recover the remains of their ancestors and their sacred belongings from federal agencies, universities, and museums that acquired and kept them during eras when Native communities were shut out of the process. For these communities, the returns can support cultural preservation, spiritual practice, and healing from historical trauma.
What's being done?
Federal officials and Tribal representatives are moving through the legal and cultural steps needed to identify items, determine affiliation, and arrange their return. That work is often slow, but it is essential to getting repatriation right.
Support for cultural and environmental stewardship often goes hand in hand. If you want to back efforts that protect communities and the places they care for, it may be worth learning more about donating money to climate causes, especially those that center frontline and Indigenous leadership.
While the harm of the past and how these items fell into the wrong hands to begin with cannot be undone, returning ancestors and sacred belongings marks an important shift that recognizes respect and accountability.
"It feels amazing to know that these ancestors and different objects are going to go home and be buried, that they get to finish their journey finally," said David Hyde, Western Colorado's museum volunteer curator and collections manager. "There's no reason for Native American ancestral remains to be in museums, cabinets, or campuses. This is a long time coming."
Where can I learn more?
The articles below cover Indigenous stewardship, land, and the long legacy of displacement. They aren't specifically about repatriation, but they do show how Tribal leadership and conservation efforts across the country are rebuilding ties.
• In Arizona, the Cocopah Tribe is sparking a revival of once-pristine land with native plants.
• Across Indigenous homelands, leaders are bringing iconic native animals back to strengthen culture and grasslands.

title: Earthshot and the science of positive tipping points: How environmental progress can become unstoppable
content:
It must be tough being a judge for the world's most prestigious environmental prize: Imagine having to choose between an ingenious machine that removes microplastics from a river in Europe or a company in East Africa that sells clean cookstoves through affordable weekly installments.
Over the last six months, we have been working with colleagues at Green Futures Solutions at the University of Exeter to make that job a little easier. We have found a way to distinguish between solutions that carry on working as long as people keep putting money into them and those with "tipping potential" that get better, cheaper and easier to adopt the more successful they are.
Our new report applies the science of positive tipping points to the five Earthshot categories—nature, air, oceans, waste and climate—for the first time.
After a northern summer of record-breaking heat, wildfires, floods and a deadly glacier collapse in the Nepal–Tibet border region, it would be easy to conclude the planet is only headed toward collapse. But tipping points science says otherwise. The same dynamic principle that leaves coral reefs and rainforests vulnerable to a relatively abrupt breakdown can also work in our favor—if we know the right levers to pull.
What is a positive tipping point?
Most environmental interventions assume change is incremental and proportionate: Bigger problems require bigger budgets and lead to slower progress. But many complex systems we rely on (technologies, markets, societal norms, ecosystems) can shift abruptly once a critical threshold is crossed.
Solar power is a great example. Its cost fell around 90% in a decade because every panel sold stimulated innovation that made the next one cheaper. This attracted more investment, which cut costs again and improved performance. The tipping point happened when self-propelling feedback took over. Clean electricity, our report finds, is now a "master cascade": As solar and wind have tipped in many markets, clean power can accelerate further progress in electric mobility, residential heating, industrial emissions and air quality.
Our report identifies the potential for such self-propelling feedback across 51 solution areas. Specifically, we identify whether the innovative solution is, or could quickly become, more affordable, accessible and attractive than the polluting incumbent system it seeks to replace. We have also assigned measurable 2030 targets to each solution area so progress can be tracked.
Three that could soon tip
Around 2.1 billion people still cook on wood, charcoal or dung, and the smoke kills nearly 3 million people a year, including more than 300,000 children under five. Pay-as-you-go finance (borrowed from off-grid solar) turns an unaffordable stove into a small weekly payment. Clean cooking is now close to tipping in several African markets. People switch primarily because it saves them time and money.
Methane is responsible for about 30% of global heating so far, but lasts only around 12 years in the atmosphere. Cutting methane emissions therefore helps cool the climate within a decade, rather than a century. A new generation of satellites can now pinpoint methane leaks from individual oil and gas facilities from space, and they are cheap to fix. The gas saved is worth more than the repair.
Inside a well-enforced marine protected area, where commercial fishing is banned, fish biomass typically reaches 4–7 times that of the surrounding waters within 5–10 years. Fish spill out across the boundary, nearby fish catches rise, and the fishers who initially opposed the marine protected area become the constituency demanding more of them.
Only around 3% of the ocean is fully protected, but the landmark high seas treaty (itself an Earthshot Prize winner) entered into force this year and aims to protect 30% of the world's oceans by 2030. Satellites can now monitor some industrial fishing fleets, so enforcement of marine protected areas is getting easier. The science, the technology and the politics are coming together.
Not everything is about to tip. The biggest brake is investment: Africa receives only 3% of clean energy finance despite holding 60% of the world's best solar resources. Our report shows where innovative financing could create the conditions to address these barriers and highlights how the current investment gaps in adaptation financing can be closed.
By using our research to shape how the prize searches for, selects and supports solutions, Earthshot can help trigger positive tipping points to accelerate out of trouble.

title: Lower fees, more places in facilities for PWDs among first moves by disability task force
content:
Lower fees, more places in facilities for PWDs among first moves by disability task force
- By 2028, the Singapore government will lower fees and increase subsidies for disability services, benefiting around 5,000 people with disabilities and making care more affordable for families.
- The government will add 1,300 more spaces to day activity centres and sheltered workshops by 2030, easing long waiting lists and helping PWDs build skills and community ties.
- Subsidy eligibility will expand to more middle-income households, with fee caps introduced and costs for families with higher support needs dropping by up to 80%, easing financial stress on caregivers.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – By 2028, families will pay less for disability services, as the Government lowers fees and increases means-tested subsidies.
More spaces will also be added to day activity centres and sheltered workshops by 2030.
Around 5,000 people with disabilities (PWDs) accessing community and residential disability services are expected to benefit from these changes by 2030.
Fee caps for all government-funded disability services will be introduced, with the amounts varying for different facilities.
For most families, subsidy rates will rise by at least 10 percentage points. These subsidies are means-tested, and apply to a wide range of disability services, including day activity centres, adult disability hostels and homes.
The income ceiling for households to qualify for these subsidies will also be raised. The maximum per capita monthly household income will increase from $4,800 to $6,000.
This will extend financial support to more middle-income households, and covers about 80 per cent of households with PWDs, said the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF).
These moves to make disability services more affordable are among the first set of recommendations by the Taskforce on Assurance for Families with Persons with Disabilities released on Sept 17.
The task force was formed in December 2025 to review how support for the PWD community can be strengthened across life stages, and has held several engagement sessions with groups including families and service providers.
Senior Minister of State for Social and Family Development Goh Pei Ming, who leads the task force with four other political office-holders, announced the moves on the sidelines of a visit to the TOUCH Centre for Independent Living at the Enabling Village in Lengkok Bahru.
Goh said affordability was one of the biggest concerns for caregivers, and some had expressed uncertainty about meeting their loved ones’ care needs over their lifetime.
“Over time, care costs can add up. Families hope to get assurances that support will continue to be affordable,” he said.
Another key move tackles a growing waiting list for day activity centres and sheltered workshops – facilities where adults with disabilities can be engaged in daily activities.
MSF will add another 1,300 day activity centre and sheltered workshop spaces by 2030, on top of the 1,000 additional places previously announced in 2024.
Goh said this “significant expansion” would bring the total number to about 5,800 places.
Families had told the task force that long wait times for such services can be stressful, he added.
Day activity centres are community-based facilities for those with disabilities who are aged 18 and above and cannot work, while sheltered workshops provide work skills training and job support for those with disabilities who can work, but are unable to or not yet ready to take up open employment.
Full recommendations to come in October
Costs for disability services were last adjusted in July 2026, when the Government increased subsidies for residential and community disability services by up to 15 per cent and 10 per cent respectively, and raised the household per capita income ceiling for subsidies from $3,600 to $4,800.
With the newest announcements, families of those with higher support needs will see their monthly fees after government subsidies for selected services drop by about 25 per cent to 80 per cent.
Lower-income households will pay no more than $10 per month for community-based services such as the day activity centres and Enabling Skills for Life Programme (ESLP), down from between $20 and $60 today.
The ESLP equips adult PWDs with independent living, communication, social-emotional functioning and vocational skills.
The Government will work with social service agencies over the next few years to expand capacity and carry out the adjustments to fees and subsidies, said MSF.
The inter-agency task force, which has looked into areas such as employment and lifelong learning for PWDs, will announce its full set of recommendations in early October.
Health product distributor Wu Ping’s son Sherman Jian, 24, has multiple disabilities and has attended the TOUCH Centre for Independent Living since 2021. Any additional savings will give the middle-income family more room to plan for his future, said the 56-year-old.
They currently pay $660 monthly for him to attend the day activity centre after government subsidies, down from $1,135 previously before the July adjustments.
Their out-of-pocket costs are likely to fall further with the latest changes.
She said in Mandarin: “These subsidies make me feel that it’s not only the family and parents caring for the child... There are people walking with us on this journey.”

title: “Centering Community” Starts with the Mission and Ends with the Work
content:
Amidst a backlash against diversity, equity, and inclusion work, it is critical to recall the intention behind the work in the first place—which is to advance progress for communities being left behind.
The long-established practice of “centering” communities can help us ground again the intention behind equity work. When an organization’s core constituents are prioritized and centered in its programming, resources, and decision-making, concepts like equity and inclusion are expressed through action and impact. That is, they become part of routine choices instead of statements. Solutions and approaches can be asset-based rather than deficit-based. It reframes community members from being “beneficiaries” to stakeholders with their own values, culture, voice, and agency.
“Centering” is not new—James Charlton’s Nothing About Us Without Us: Disability Oppression and Empowerment made the case in 2000—but it can be hard to implement in practice. As Tulaine Montgomery wrote, proximity to community “may be the most powerful untapped force for change we have,” yet philanthropy has too often looked at communities through a paternalistic lens. More recently, Lori Bartczak and Sandra Moore observed that while many nonprofit organizations understand solutions work better when affected people shape them, “when it comes to including that voice…the work often stalls before it starts.”
For an organization looking to “center” the community, the starting point is often hiding in plain sight: the words the organization uses to describe itself. Do the organization’s core statements, such as its mission, vision, and values, reflect language and lenses of external professionals and/or funders – or the language of the community it serves? A mission statement is more than a communication device. It signals whose knowledge counts, whose aspirations are centered, and who the organization ultimately answers to. Can anyone in the community read it and say, “That’s us”?
Two Feathers Native American Family Services offers one example of what this shift can look like in practice. Public Equity Group was honored to collaborate with Two Feathers between January and December 2023 as part of its strategic evolution.
Two Feathers Native American Family Services
Two Feathers Native American Family Services was established in 1998 to respond to the acute mental health needs of Native Americans in low-income and geographically isolated coastal and mountain communities in rural Humboldt County, CA. Overall, Humboldt County is one of just two California counties with the highest proportion of residents reporting four or more Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs). With respect to Humboldt County Native youth in particular, 50 percent of youth experience struggles with substance abuse and 60 percent report some degree of involvement with special or alternative education schools, foster care, mental health systems, and/or justice systems.
“It took 150 years to colonize our people, it’s going to take that much time to heal.”
With the appointment of Virgil Moorehead Jr. (Yurok/Tolowa and member of the Big Lagoon Rancheria), as Two Feathers’ director of behavioral health in 2017, and later, its executive director, Two Feathers began investing in increasingly robust clinical programming, growing the organization’s ranks of formally trained clinical staff, and contributing to the organization’s reputation as a highly effective, culturally affirming mental health and wellness program. Under Moorehead, who holds a doctorate in Psychology from the Wright Institute and completed his post-doctoral fellowship at Stanford University, the organization expanded from a small clinical provider to a multi-site organization partnering with all local tribes and 14 school districts, providing clinical therapy to more than 800 unique youth over five years.
As a result of its successful investments in robust, culturally competent clinical services, “Two Feathers has become [regarded as] the premier Native youth mental health program in California,” noted a leading California mental health expert, a distinction recognized most recently by the 2026 James Irvine Leadership Award.
Per one Two Feathers’ community partner we spoke with during our consulting work, “The vision is that you break these intergenerational cycles of substance abuse, domestic violence, social determinants of health, foster care. You start with some kids, and [help] them have a different experience, opportunities, and environment. And perhaps their children won’t experience the same. It’s a long-term life process…It took 150 years to colonize our people, it’s going to take that much time to heal.”
Alongside its clinical programs, around the year 2018, Two Feathers also began offering increasingly intensive cultural programs, especially during summer months, to reinforce connection, identity, and belonging as core components of Native youth mental health. Two Feathers, for example, played a leading role in expanding youth participation in the Stick Game, “an inter-Tribal competition played regionally on Tribal Lands,” and the Flower Dance, “a young woman’s coming-of-age ceremony,” according to the California Reducing Disparities Project.
During an interview with Two Feathers program staff, one program participant reflected: “Culture is important to me…it’s made me more mature, and it’s helped me with a lot of things in life and will help me in the future. It’s important for more youth to grow up with their culture; they can carry on that knowledge to future generations…. Culture can help people in our struggling communities.”
Although Two Feathers’ cultural programs were highly praised and deeply valued by participants and community members, they ebbed and flowed over the course of a given year, in part because of limited resources and staff capacity. In the beginning, the connections between Two Feathers’ clinical and cultural programs were unclear to many within the organization and in the community. While participants were referred from the clinical program to cultural programs and vice versa, the two programs felt siloed to participants, staff, and partners—related and very important, yet somewhat separate, efforts.
To address these challenges, in 2022 Two Feathers launched a new strategy that clarified the central role of community, culture, and lived experiences in its approach to mental health and wellbeing. The organization reframed its work beyond crisis response, articulating a holistic model that integrates clinical care, cultural programming, youth leadership, and pathways to economic stability as mutually reinforcing supports for long-term healing.
“We have gone from crisis intervention to approaching mental health more holistically.”
Sign up for our free newsletters
Subscribe to NPQ's newsletters to have our top stories delivered directly to your inbox.
By signing up, you agree to our privacy policy and terms of use, and to receive messages from NPQ and our partners.
As part of this shift, Two Feathers updated its formerly “deficit-based” mission (“to reduce unnecessary suffering among Native American Children and Families living in Humboldt County”) to an asset-based one that more clearly reflects the communities’ strengths, values, and aspirations: “To empower Native American youth and their families to achieve their full potential by offering culturally affirming mental health and wellness programs in Humboldt County.” This view is paired with a long-term vision that reflects a holistic and intergenerational worldview: “Two Feathers envisions a world filled with love and in balance within ourselves and with all of creation for generations to come.”
Cultural practice, community knowledge and youth experience are no longer supplements to clinical practice. They are now part of the core model.
Two Feathers’ approach also celebrates “indigenous giftedness” and “the importance of understanding the good life, the human way—in Hupa Language K’winya’nya:n-ma’awhiniw—to live in balance and harmony with the world by having honor and respect for community members, the environment, self, ancestors, and creation” (per a 2025 report to the James Irvine Foundation).
Two Feathers also developed a theory of change that more clearly equalizes and integrates clinical care and cultural/human development programming. Within its human development programs, Two Feathers has expanded programs promoting mentorship and job training, as well as programs to address bullying and self-harm in schools (including programming with a strong LGBTQ+/2Spirit focus), increasing youth self-efficacy through cultural teachings that emphasize kindness.
Moorehead noted, “We have gone from crisis intervention to approaching mental health more holistically. We give students options. If a student [is struggling], we ask: Do you want a clinician or cultural program support? We get after the same issues in a more creative way.”
The Youth Ambassador (Leadership Development and Job Training) Program, for example, provides youth ages 15 to 21 the opportunity to develop leadership and advocacy abilities while deepening their connection to others, community, and culture. Activities include peer advising, employment preparation and support, certifications (first aid, food safety), conflict resolution, landscaping and gardening, event planning, youth activities, cultural education, team building, public speaking, and problem solving.
Evaluation data suggest that program participation across Two Feathers’ clinical and human development programs is growing—and that participants are achieving notable gains. In 2018, Two Feathers served 25 youth, but by 2024, Two Feathers had received 247 new referrals, served 289 youth in individual counseling, employed 88 youth through leadership and workforce programs, and engaged 476 community members in cultural activities. Youth participating in leadership development programs reported gains in goal setting, school and workplace engagement; gains in substance abuse prevention knowledge; and reductions in substance use. In communities where mental health crises are endemic, 57 percent of participants reported no mental health challenges in the prior 30 days; 43 percent of leadership and workforce program participants became employed, and 36 percent enrolled in college or trade school (in communities with high baseline rates of unemployment and college enrollment).
As California undertakes a multi-billion-dollar overhaul of its youth mental health system to better serve the 284,000 California children dealing with major depression, the need for effective, culturally grounded models has never been greater. In California, 1 in 5 adolescents has a diagnosed mental or behavioral health condition, and Indigenous youth are at greater risk, statistically. Two Feathers is poised to launch two best practice, holistic wellness centers for youth (one in Hoopa and a second in McKinleyville), and it is well positioned to inform statewide conversations about culturally grounded, community-based mental health models.
As Moorehead noted, “Staff members have remarked that it’s powerful for a Native organization to say ‘Hey—we don’t have to follow. We can be national leaders in mental health; we can be creative, have better outcomes, better systems. We can be a model program not just for Native youth, but for all youth and their communities.’”
“The real test is straightforward: How well does the mission center the community it serves?”
Putting Community at the Center
The journey that Two Feathers took shows how an organization can clarify its purpose by centering community in its mission and work. Revisiting an organization’s focus and strategies can be more than an exercise in language. It is a way to decide whose needs and experiences shape an institution’s direction and, ultimately, whether its work makes a difference. The organization’s experience shows how clarifying who is at the center can reshape programs, strengthen alignment with community needs, and shift outcomes over time.
The real test is straightforward: How well does the mission center the community it serves? Can a community member quote it with a smile? Do the programs address a deficit from the outside in, or does the organization work from within, helping the community fulfill its own aspirations?
Two Feathers’ experience suggests that centering community is not a communications exercise. It is a discipline that cuts across governance, strategy, management, and resource allocation. Centering community means community values and knowledge reshape programs, redirect resources, and ultimately drive decisions.

title: Good News in History, September 18
content:
188 years ago today, the Anti-Corn Law League was established in England by the economics-savvy liberals who understood that protectionism is immoral and useless in benefiting the economy. The League, led by Richard Cobden and heavily influenced by economist Daniel Riccardo, succeeded in seeing the Corn Laws of 1815 abolished, laying out the first laizzez-faire arguments against mercantilism to be heard in Europe, and establishing for all time the case study on their use. READ more about this successful political movement… (1838)
The Corn Laws imposed tariffs on imported cereals into England under the guise of protecting the domestic production (corn meant any grain at the time). As in all economic activity, the Corn Law tariffs had two effects, which renowned French economic journalist Friedrich Bastiat described famously as one which is seen, and one which is unseen.
The tax on imported wheat meant that producers of the more expensive domestic cereals were able to keep their jobs and production methods intact—a perceived good by the British Parliament.
That which was unseen was manifold. They resulted in a rise in the price of bread at a time when British factory owners were trying to reduce costs. It resulted in food scarcity among the poor as bakers and merchants could no longer import cheaper grains from abroad even in times of shortages. It stalled English farmers from further agricultural innovations, or moving into other industries, having a portion of their income all but guaranteed.
It also decreased the demand on manufactured goods, as suddenly the lower and middle classes were paying more for food they had gotten for less prior to the Corn Laws’ enactment. Lastly, as organizer Cobden saw it, it created unnecessary animosity between nations who might otherwise live in greater harmony if trade were partaken freely.
The lessons of the Corn Law were never lost to history, but rather must be reiterated every time a political administration attempts to re-establish protectionism and mercantilism according to naive desires of obtaining that good which is seen: the protection of a domestic market, and ignoring that which is unseen—the burden imposed on the rest of the economy in exchange.
MORE Good News on this Day in history:
- George Washington laid the first cornerstone of the Capitol building (1793)
- Tiffany & Co. was founded in New York City (1837)
- Daniel David Palmer administered the first chiropractic adjustment (1895)
- The Columbia Phonograph Broadcasting System made its broadcasting debut through its network of over 16 radio stations— later it took the name CBS (1927)
- President Reagan announced the destruction of nuclear warheads by US and USSR (1987)
- Ted Turner, the innovative founder of the first cable news network (CNN), donated 1 billion dollars to the UN, to create the United Nations Foundation, a charity that works to help the world’s poor and preserve the environment (1997)
75 years ago today, A Streetcar Named Desire, the film based on the play by Tennessee Williams, premiered in New York City. Starring Vivien Leigh, Marlon Brando, Kim Hunter, and Karl Malden, the film tells the story of a Mississippi southern belle, Blanche DuBois, who, after encountering a series of personal losses, seeks refuge with her sister and brother-in-law in a dilapidated New Orleans apartment building.
Tennessee Williams collaborated with Oscar Saul and Elia Kazan on the screenplay. It received Oscar nominations in 10 other categories (including Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Adapted Screenplay), and won Best Supporting Actor (Malden), Best Supporting Actress (Hunter), and Best Art Direction (Richard Day, George James Hopkins), making it the first film to win in three of the acting categories.
In 1999, A Streetcar Named Desire was selected for preservation in the United States National Film Registry by the Library of Congress as being “culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant”.
In his 2020 autobiography Apropos of Nothing, director Woody Allen praises every aspect of the production. “The movie Streetcar is for me total artistic perfection… It’s the most perfect confluence of script, performance, and direction I’ve ever seen,” he wrote. (1951)
156 years ago today, a party of explorers from the Washburn-Langford-Doane Expedition traveled down the Firehole River and entered the Upper Geyser Basin, where they found an extraordinary natural feature they would call “Old Faithful“. Nathaniel P. Langford, the expedition leader wrote in his journal of the day’s discovery, noting “it spouted at regular intervals nine times during our stay, the columns of boiling water being thrown from ninety to one hundred and twenty-five feet at each discharge, which lasted from fifteen to twenty minutes. We gave it the name ‘Old Faithful.'”
First things first, the regular intervals at which it discharges are due to it being separated from all the “plumbing” of the Upper Geyer Basin’s features. Intervals between eruptions can range from 60 to 110 minutes, averaging 66.5 minutes in 1939, and slowly increasing to an average of 90 minutes apart today due in theory to earthquakes altering the subterranean water table or other features.
In the early days of Yellowstone National Park, Old Faithful was often used as a laundry, with one employee writing… “Old Faithful is sometimes degraded by being made a laundry. Garments placed in the crater during quiescence are ejected thoroughly washed when the eruption takes place. Gen. Sheridan’s men, in 1882, found that linen and cotton fabrics were uninjured by the action of the water, but woolen clothes were torn to shreds.” (1870)
And, 78 years ago today, Margaret Chase Smith became the first woman elected to the US Senate. For more than three decades, she served as a role model for women aspiring to national politics; she was also the first woman elected to the US House of Representatives and the first to have her name placed in nomination for the US Presidency of a major party.
Senator Smith bravely denounced the Communist witch hunt of McCarthyism at a time when others feared that speaking out would ruin their careers. On June 1, 1950, she delivered her courageous 15-minute “Declaration of Conscience” speech, defending every American’s “right to criticize…right to hold unpopular beliefs…right to protest.”
Breaking their paralysis of fear, six other moderate Senate Republicans signed onto her Declaration. She said McCarthyism had “debased“ the Senate to “the level of a forum of hate and character assassination… with the four horseman of… fear, ignorance, bigotry, and smear,” and Republicans had hurled unproved charges with reckless abandon.
[From her speech] “I think that it is high time that we remembered that the Constitution, as amended, speaks not only of the freedom of speech but also of trial by jury instead of trial by accusation. Whether it be a criminal prosecution in court or a character prosecution in the Senate, there is little practical distinction when the life of a person has been ruined… The exercise of these rights should not cost one single American citizen his reputation or his right to a livelihood nor should he be in danger of losing his reputation or livelihood merely because he happens to know someone who holds unpopular beliefs.” (1948)
16 years ago today, 42-year-old Frenchman Philippe Croizon became the first quadruple amputee to swim across the English Channel. He trained for years, hoping to demonstrate the abilities of handicapped people, and finished the swim in under 14 hours. With the aid of paddle-like prosthetics attached to the stumps of his legs, the French swimmer completed his dream of swimming between five continents two years later. (20 10)
80 years ago today, Tonka Trucks was founded. First called Mound Metalcraft, they opened in a metal manufacturing plant in Mound, Minnesota. The three businessmen, Lynn Everett Baker, Avery Crounse, and Alvin Tesch changed their company’s name to Tonka Toys in 1955, using the Dakota Sioux word “Tanka” or Tonka, which means “great” or “big”.
The logo at this time was an oval, showing the Tonka Toys name in red above waves, honoring the nearby Lake Minnetonka.
A Museum in Winifred, Montana has collected more than 3,000 of the metal trucks, bulldozers, cranes, graders, and all varieties of construction vehicles.
The slogan ‘Tonka tough, built to last’ has been proven true as the steel toys are handed down from one generation to the next—and still holding up. (1946)
And, 176 years ago today, Harriet Tubman fled the plantation where she was enslaved, escaping to freedom in Philadelphia. Traveling at night so she would not be seen by slave catchers, she followed the North Star that guided her 90 miles toward the Mason-Dixon line. Once passing over that border from Maryland into Pennsylvania, she would be free.
The first person to help her was a white woman who was a Quaker. She sheltered her the first night and gave her instructions on where to go next. Tubman is quoted in a biography, as saying, “When I found I had crossed that line, I looked at my hands to see if I was the same person. There was such a glory over everything; the sun came like gold through the trees and over the fields, and I felt like I was in Heaven.”
Born into slavery, the five-foot woman named Araminta (‘Minty’) Ross grew to be strong and determined. She earned extra cash for her escape by working even longer than she was required to on the Poplar Neck Plantation in Dorchester County, Maryland. Because all her family and friends were still enslaved, she subsequently undertook 13 perilous missions back to the state to bring more than 70 people to freedom and help them find work…
Having changed her name to Harriet Tubman, she traveled in extreme secrecy, staying with members of the Underground Railroad—to which the original Quaker woman belonged. The network provided safe houses and transportation for fugitive slaves. Tubman (who came to be known as ‘Moses’) “never lost a passenger.”
During the American Civil War, she served as an armed scout and spy for the Union Army, advising officers on how best to attack the South. In her later years, Tubman was an activist, with her friend Susan B. Anthony, in the struggle for women’s suffrage, and established schools that would educate freedmen in South Carolina. After her death at age 90 or 91, she was buried in a ceremony with full military honors. (1849)
SHARE The Milestones, Memories, and Moments…

title: The ‘troubled’ class assignment that changed Lee’s teaching career
content:
The ‘troubled’ class assignment that changed Lee’s teaching career
When Lee Casuscelli got her first job out of teachers college in the 1980s, she was given what might be termed a challenging first assignment at The Grange Public School in south-west Sydney.
“She just got given the troubled class, I guess they called it, and no teacher really was able to do anything with these kids,” says her daughter Lauren Casuscelli. “They couldn’t really sit still at the start, they were jumping out of the windows and it was a bit chaotic.”
But Lauren says her mother gave her students 100 per cent of her focus. Attendance soon improved, the class became much more settled, and students were able to learn. “She just saw them as kids, not their disability,” Lauren says.
That class at The Grange Public about 40 years ago would become the first step in a long and dedicated career working to improve the lives of students with disabilities and autism.
When Casuscelli died suddenly in a car crash in February, it prompted an outpouring of grief in the Camden community and across the state.
Local MP Sally Quinnell told NSW parliament that hundreds of parents had paid their respects to Casuscelli, describing how she had “helped their children to grow and how she supported families with children with additional needs”.
That legacy was honoured on Tuesday at Parliament House in Canberra at an event held by Schools Plus, an education not-for-profit, with the inaugural Lee Casuscelli Excellence in Special Education Award.
Early in Casuscelli’s career, understanding of autism was much more limited both in schools and the general community. She developed numerous programs and initiatives to support students with autism.
One of those programs was called Tool Time, which she established at Our Lady Help of Christians in Rosemeadow in the 2000s. In one-hour classes, she helped equip specific groups – such as teen boys – with practical tools to navigate the world.
The junior group would cover topics such as how to make a friend, how to keep a friend, and the sorts of social skills people with autism might struggle with. There was also advice for their parents.
She went on to become the principal of Aspect Western Sydney School and Aspect Macarthur School before joining Schools Plus as its director of education.
The inaugural winner of the award is Dr Dawn Grant-Skiba, principal of Warrah Specialist School in Dural. The $50,000 prize includes $20,000 for a teacher fellowship, which is 12 months of professional development, including national networking and master classes.
A further $30,000 will enable Warrah Specialist School to expand innovative approaches that improve outcomes for students with disability and diverse learning needs.
Schools Plus chief executive Sherrill Nixon said: “We are delighted to recognise Dawn, whose work reflects so many of the values Lee held so strongly.”
Grant-Skiba, who was born in Jamaica, has worked across mainstream and specialist support schools in her 26-year teaching career. She says an early experience as a 12-year-old helping older women in her community learn to write their names and develop basic numeracy skillis has been a strong influence.
“The ability to do that has changed their lives,” she says.
She said while she was happy to teach students who learnt easily, she got the most joy from students who needed her more. “My creative juices flow, I get excited when they read a word, when before, they couldn’t recognise a letter.
“Those formative years really inspired me when I did come into teaching, to always look for the underdogs that others didn’t see as much.”

title: Το πρόγραμμα ChildSay για μία πιο φιλική προς τα παιδιά Δικαιοσύνη είναι μια από τις πιο ωραίες δράσεις του υπουργείου, λέει ο Φλωρίδης
content:
Ένα ντοκιμαντέρ που φωτίζει τα ορόσημα μιας διαδρομής σχεδόν ενός αιώνα, αλλά και την πρωτοπορία, και τη φροντίδα για τον άνθρωπο και την κοινωνία.
Το πρόγραμμα ChildSay για μία πιο φιλική προς τα παιδιά Δικαιοσύνη είναι μια από τις πιο ωραίες δράσεις του υπουργείου, λέει ο Φλωρίδης


Το πρόγραμμα ChildSay για μία πιο φιλική προς τα παιδιά Δικαιοσύνη είναι μια από τις πιο ωραίες δράσεις του υπουργείου, λέει ο Φλωρίδης
Το πρόγραμμα ChildSay αποτελεί την πρώτη ολιστική παρέμβαση στη χώρα μας η οποία βάζει τα παιδιά στο επίκεντρο των αποφάσεων που τα αφορούν μέσα από έρευνα, εκπαίδευση επαγγελματιών και ένα εθνικό σχέδιο δράσης για μία πιο φιλική προς τα παιδιά Δικαιοσύνη
«Είναι μια από τις πιο ωραίες δράσεις του υπουργείου και ελπίζουμε πάρα πολλά στην υλοποίησή του», επισήμανε ο υπουργός Δικαιοσύνης Γιώργος Φλωρίδης, κατά την έναρξη της εκδήλωσης «ChildSay – Ενσωματώνοντας τη φωνή των παιδιών στη λήψη δικαστικών αποφάσεων για την επιμέλεια» που διοργανώθηκε από το υπουργείο Δικαιοσύνης και υλοποιείται στο πλαίσιο του ευρωπαϊκού προγράμματος «Πολίτες, Ισότητα, Δικαιώματα και Αξίες». Ουσιαστικά το καινοτόμο αυτό ευρωπαϊκό πρόγραμμα αποσκοπεί σε μία πιο φιλική προς τα παιδιά Δικαιοσύνη.
Ειδικότερα, κάθε χρόνο χιλιάδες παιδιά στην Ελλάδα περνούν μέσα από τις διαδικασίες λήψης αποφάσεων επιμέλειας και γονικής μέριμνας, χωρίς η γνώμη τους να ακούγεται ή να λαμβάνεται υπόψη σοβαρά, κάτι που είναι σε βάρος της ψυχικής υγείας και των δικαιωμάτων των ανήλικων παιδιών.
Έτσι, το πρόγραμμα ChildSay που είναι ένα συγχρηματοδοτούμενο από την Ευρωπαϊκή Ένωση έργο, αποτελεί την πρώτη ολιστική παρέμβαση στη χώρα μας η οποία βάζει τα παιδιά στο επίκεντρο των αποφάσεων που τα αφορούν μέσα από έρευνα, εκπαίδευση επαγγελματιών και ένα εθνικό σχέδιο δράσης για μία πιο φιλική προς τα παιδιά Δικαιοσύνη.
Αφορά παιδιά ηλικίας από 6 έως 10 ετών, γονείς, εισαγγελείς, δικαστές και δικηγόρους, αλλά και επαγγελματίες, όπως είναι αστυνομικοί, συμβολαιογράφοι, δικαστικοί επιμελητές, κοινωνικοί λειτουργοί και ψυχολόγοι.
Στο πρόγραμμα αυτό, συνολικής διάρκειας υλοποίησης 24 μηνών, συμμετέχει το υπουργείο Δικαιοσύνης ως εταίρος, με στόχο να ενσωματωθεί ουσιαστικά η φωνή και τα δικαιώματα των παιδιών στις αποφάσεις της επιμέλειας σε ευθυγράμμιση με τα διεθνή πρότυπα Δικαιοσύνης φιλικής προς το παιδί. Ακόμη, το ChildSay αξιολογεί την ισχύουσα νομοθεσία, εκπαιδεύει δικαστές, δικηγόρους και ψυχολόγους σε παιδοκεντρικές πρακτικές.
Ο κ. Φλωρίδης στον σύντομο χαιρετισμό του έκανε αναφορά σε μια απόφαση του Ευρωπαϊκού Δικαστηρίου Δικαιωμάτων του Ανθρώπου, η οποία δημοσιεύθηκε τον Σεπτέμβριο του 2025 και αφορούσε προσφυγή κατά της Ελλάδος. Όπως εξήγησε, το Ευρωπαϊκό Δικαστήριο Δικαιωμάτων του Ανθρώπου σημείωνε ότι χρειάζονται ορισμένες προϋποθέσεις ώστε ένα δικαστήριο να μπορεί να ακούσει τα παιδιά και συνέχισε: «Σε αυτή την απόφαση αναφέρεται επί λέξει: “Οι προαναφερθείσες προϋποθέσεις είναι καλά ορισμένες στο ελληνικό νομικό σύστημα. Σύμφωνα με τη νομολογία του Αρείου Πάγου, όπως παρουσιάζεται από την Κυβέρνηση, ένα δικαστήριο υποχρεούται να ακούσει ένα παιδί μόνο εφόσον θεωρεί ότι το παιδί διαθέτει την απαιτούμενη ωριμότητα. Δεν απαιτείται ειδική αιτιολογία για την απόφαση σχετικά με το αν το παιδί διαθέτει την απαιτούμενη ωριμότητα, η οποία καθορίζεται με ελεύθερη εκτίμηση των αποδεικτικών στοιχείων».
«Δηλαδή, η νομοθεσία η δική μας περιλαμβάνει τις προϋποθέσεις για να ακουστεί ένα παιδί. Τι σημαίνει αυτό; Σημαίνει ότι το ελληνικό νομικό σύστημα είναι θωρακισμένο στα θέματα αυτά. Τι μένει; Να δώσουμε ένα ουσιαστικό περιεχόμενο σε αυτές τις δυνατότητες του ελληνικού νομικού συστήματος, όπως αυτές αποτυπώνονται στους νόμους και έχουν διαπλαστεί και από τη νομολογία των ελληνικών δικαστηρίων. Και εδώ είναι που το πρόγραμμα αυτό μπορεί να προσφέρει πάρα πολλά. Και επειδή έχουμε ήδη πέντε χρόνια από την εφαρμογή κάποιων αλλαγών στο Οικογενειακό Δίκαιο, τις οποίες αξιολογούμε διαρκώς, πρόθεσή μας είναι, να συστήσουμε άμεσα μια επιτροπή που να τις δει ώστε να πως τα ελληνικά δικαστήρια αντιμετώπισαν με βάση τις νομοθετικές αυτές αλλαγές τα θέματα των παιδιών και κυρίως τι προβλήματα έχουν ανακύψει από τη νομοθεσία αυτή. Άρα αυτά τα συμπεράσματα που θα εξαχθούν στην πορεία από τη δουλεία αυτής της ομάδας θα είναι πάρα πολύ χρήσιμα για την αλλαγή που σκοπεύουμε να κάνουμε σε κάποια ζητήματα και κάποιες πλευρές του Οικογενειακού Δικαίου», είπε ο υπουργός Δικαιοσύνης.

Από την πλευρά της η προϊσταμένη της γενικής διεύθυνσης ειδικών νομικών ζητημάτων του υπουργείου Δικαιοσύνης Ευτυχία Κατσιγαράκη, αναλύοντας το πρόγραμμα, μεταξύ των άλλων, ανέφερε: «Αυτό ευρωπαϊκό πρόγραμμα εστιάζει σε ένα ιδιαίτερα ευαίσθητο, πολυπαραγοντικό και κατεπείγον κοινωνικό ζήτημα: την προστασία της ψυχικής υγείας και των δικαιωμάτων του παιδιού κατά τη διαδικασία λήψης αποφάσεων επιμέλειας και γονικής μέριμνας. Στον πυρήνα των οικογενειακών διενέξεων, όταν ένας γάμος ή μια συμβίωση φτάνει στο τέλος της, τα παιδιά συχνά βρίσκονται δίχως δική τους βούληση στο επίκεντρο μιας διαμάχης».
«Ένα διαζύγιο μπορεί πράγματι να διαλύει τη νομική σχέση δύο συζύγων· δεν πρέπει όμως, σε καμία περίπτωση, να διαλύει την αίσθηση ασφάλειας, τη συναισθηματική σταθερότητα και το μέλλον ενός παιδιού. Πίσω από κάθε δικόγραφο, πίσω από κάθε δικαστική απόφαση επιμέλειας ή επικοινωνίας, δεν υπάρχουν μόνο νομικοί ισχυρισμοί, δικονομικοί κανόνες και αντιμαχόμενα επιχειρήματα. Υπάρχουν άνθρωποι, υπάρχουν φοβισμένες ψυχές, υπάρχουν οικογενειακές ιστορίες και, πάνω απ' όλα, υπάρχουν παιδιά. Και η δικαστική απόφαση δεν εξαντλείται μέσα στην αίθουσα του δικαστηρίου. Μεταφέρεται την επόμενη μέρα στο σπίτι, στο σχολείο, στις παρέες, στην καθημερινή ζωή του παιδιού. Γίνεται καθοριστικό κομμάτι της προσωπικής του ταυτότητας και εξέλιξης», συμπλήρωσε.
