title: Del cuidado infantil a la corresponsabilidad
content:
Especialista en Políticas Inclusivas para la Red CCE por la Primera Infancia.
Hace poco más de dos décadas, la Organización Internacional del Trabajo impulsó el concepto de trabajo decente para colocar a las personas en el centro del desarrollo económico. La propuesta era sencilla y al mismo tiempo transformadora: el empleo no debía medirse únicamente por su capacidad de generar ingresos, sino también por las condiciones de dignidad, protección, igualdad y bienestar que ofrece a quienes trabajan.
Desde entonces, la conversación ha evolucionado. Si durante buena parte del siglo pasado la preocupación principal fue proteger a las personas dentro de los centros laborales, hoy las organizaciones enfrentan una pregunta mucho más compleja: ¿cómo responder a las necesidades de quienes, además de trabajar, cuidan?
Es en este sentido que las prácticas amigables con la familia representan una de las expresiones más avanzadas de esta evolución. Su valor no radica únicamente en mejorar las condiciones laborales, sino en reconocer que el desarrollo de la primera infancia depende del bienestar integral de madres, padres y cuidadores.
Lo que comenzó con iniciativas orientadas a la lactancia, las licencias parentales o la flexibilidad laboral ha terminado revelando una realidad más profunda: el bienestar de niñas y niños está estrechamente vinculado con las condiciones de vida de quienes los acompañan, educan y protegen.
Esa ha sido, precisamente, una de las principales lecciones de los primeros cinco años de trabajo de la Red CCE por la Primera Infancia. A través de la promoción de prácticas amigables con la familia, la Red ayudó a posicionar dentro del sector empresarial una convicción fundamental: la primera infancia no es un asunto exclusivo de las familias ni de las políticas públicas. También es una responsabilidad compartida por las organizaciones donde millones de personas desarrollan su vida laboral.
Sin embargo, la experiencia acumulada durante este periodo ha mostrado que los desafíos que enfrentan las familias trabajadoras son más amplios de lo que inicialmente parecía. Las condiciones que permiten cuidar adecuadamente no dependen únicamente de una licencia o de una prestación específica. También están relacionadas con la calidad de los entornos laborales, las oportunidades de desarrollo, la posibilidad de conciliar responsabilidades personales y profesionales y la manera en que las organizaciones comprenden el bienestar de las personas.
En este punto la conversación sobre cuidados comienza a expandirse.
Durante años, buena parte de la atención estuvo enfocada en visibilizar los efectos que la maternidad y las tareas de crianza tienen sobre la participación laboral de las mujeres. Y con razón. La distribución desigual de las responsabilidades de cuidado sigue siendo uno de los principales factores que limitan la igualdad de oportunidades.
Pero la evolución de esta agenda permite observar un fenómeno más amplio. Cuidar no es una actividad asociada únicamente a la crianza. Millones de personas acompañan diariamente a familiares enfermos, personas con discapacidad o integrantes del hogar que requieren apoyos temporales o permanentes. Reconocer esta realidad no debilita la agenda de igualdad; por el contrario, la fortalece porque amplía nuestra comprensión sobre quiénes cuidan y qué condiciones necesitan para hacerlo mejor.
La corresponsabilidad surge precisamente de esa reflexión. Mientras el cuidado siga siendo interpretado como una responsabilidad individual o familiar, seguirá concentrándose en unos cuantos. En cambio, cuando se reconoce como una necesidad social indispensable para el bienestar colectivo, aparece la oportunidad de distribuir mejor responsabilidades, recursos y apoyos entre familias, empresas, comunidades y Estado.
Desde esta perspectiva, la primera infancia deja de ser solamente una población objetivo para convertirse en el resultado esperado de un ecosistema más amplio de bienestar. Las prácticas amigables con la familia adquieren entonces una nueva dimensión: ya no son únicamente beneficios laborales, sino herramientas concretas para traducir principios de derechos humanos, trabajo decente, igualdad y desarrollo infantil en políticas empresariales de corresponsabilidad.
Los hallazgos compartidos durante la Cumbre 2025 de la Red CCE por la Primera Infancia y los aprendizajes derivados del estudio Empresas que Cuidan apuntan justamente en esa dirección. Más que documentar buenas prácticas, ambos ejercicios han contribuido a ampliar la conversación sobre el papel que pueden desempeñar las empresas en la construcción de entornos donde las personas puedan desarrollarse, trabajar y cuidar en mejores condiciones.
Esa puede ser una de las aportaciones más relevantes de la siguiente etapa. No se trata de abandonar la causa de la primera infancia, sino de comprenderla en toda su dimensión. Si el bienestar infantil depende del bienestar de quienes cuidan, entonces fortalecer a las personas cuidadoras también es una estrategia para impulsar el desarrollo de niñas y niños.
Por ello, el reto de los próximos años no será únicamente multiplicar programas o beneficios corporativos. Será consolidar una cultura empresarial que reconozca el cuidado como una dimensión estratégica del desarrollo económico y social. Esta es, precisamente, una de las conversaciones que comenzará a tomar forma en la Cumbre 2026 de la Red CCE por la Primera Infancia: cómo evolucionar de una agenda centrada en prácticas específicas hacia una visión más amplia de corresponsabilidad.
Porque el cuidado no es un asunto privado ni una carga individual. Es una inversión social que fortalece a las personas, mejora la productividad, favorece la inclusión y genera condiciones para un crecimiento más sostenible.
Hace cinco años, la pregunta era qué podían hacer las empresas por la primera infancia. Hoy la pregunta es más ambiciosa: ¿cómo pueden contribuir a construir entornos donde el trabajo y el cuidado se fortalezcan mutuamente y donde el bienestar de las personas se convierta en una ventaja para toda la sociedad?

title: Brazil protects 1.6 million acres, creates 4 Amazon reserves, and expands Caatinga park
content:
More than 1.6 million acres of Brazilian ecosystems have been placed under protection, expanding conservation efforts in a country considered one of the most ecologically important on Earth.
The newly protected area spans parts of the Amazon and the Caatinga. The measures aim to preserve biodiversity while supporting local communities and Indigenous territories.
Here's what to know
According to an Instagram post from actor and environmental advocate Leonardo DiCaprio, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva announced on September 8 that four Sustainable Development Reserves would be established in the Amazon and that Sete Cidades National Park in the Caatinga would be enlarged.
All four reserves are in the region around the BR-319 highway, and they are meant to safeguard biodiversity while helping defend Indigenous Peoples' ancestral territories.
In Piauí, Sete Cidades National Park is being expanded by more than 17,000 acres (6,900 hectares). DiCaprio said the added protection benefits threatened species, including the endemic Cerrado Little Brown Bat.
Altogether, these new protections total more than 1.6 million acres (676,000 hectares).
More background
This step follows Brazil's establishment of the Rio Tanaru Indigenous Peoples National Park in June 2026.
Protecting intact ecosystems can preserve wildlife habitat, store planet-cooling carbon, and ease pressure from destructive land use.
Sustainable Development Reserves are designed to both conserve nature and to support the people who live in and depend on these landscapes. That can help traditional and local communities maintain livelihoods tied to standing forests, rather than seeing those areas cleared or degraded.
Healthier forests help regulate rainfall, stabilize regional climates, and protect freshwater systems that millions of people rely on directly or indirectly. Stronger protection for Indigenous territories also aligns with long-standing evidence that Indigenous stewardship is among the most effective forms of conservation.
What's being done?
The designations also come with major funding commitments. DiCaprio said more than $47 million is tied to sustainable forest management, along with more than $46 million for restoration and territorial initiatives.
The money is expected to help pay for territorial protection, restoration work, community-led projects, and forest management.
DiCaprio also said the designations received support from @andesamazonfund, Re:wild, @artintoacres, @bezosearthfund, @moorefound, and the Wyss Foundation.
He wrote that these are "important efforts to protect critical ecosystems while supporting the communities who live in and depend on them."
Where can I learn more?
Brazil's new reserves are part of an effort to slow deforestation, repair damaged landscapes, and rebuild the country's environmental vigor. The stories below look at how policy shifts, better monitoring, and reforestation work are affecting the Amazon and other ecosystems across Brazil.
• Across the Amazon, surging deforestation spurred the Brazilian government into stronger conservation action.
• Brazil's native seed networks face obstacles even as its 30-million-acre reforestation plan moves forward.
• In Brazil, improved monitoring helped the Atlantic Forest reach its lowest deforestation in 40 years.
Protected areas tend to have the biggest impact when enforcement, restoration, and tangible political support back them.

title: Entre descobertas históricas e pioneirismo, Fiocruz foi fundamental para consolidação do SUS
content:
A história da Fundação Oswaldo Cruz (Fiocruz) confunde-se com a própria trajetória do desenvolvimento da ciência e da saúde pública no Brasil. Nascida na Fazenda de Manguinhos, no Rio de Janeiro, a instituição construiu uma trajetória secular marcada por descobertas científicas, combate a epidemias e inovação tecnológica a serviço do Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS).
Origens e a Reforma Sanitária no Rio de Janeiro
A trajetória teve início em 25 de maio de 1900 com a criação do Instituto Soroterápico Federal, criado para fabricar soros e vacinas contra a peste bubônica sob a direção técnica do bacteriologista Oswaldo Cruz e direção geral do Barão de Pedro Affonso. Ao assumir a direção geral em 1902 e, em seguida, a diretoria geral de Saúde Pública em 1903, Oswaldo Cruz liderou campanhas sanitárias que erradicaram a febre amarela e a peste bubônica da capital federal.
As medidas sanitárias enfrentaram forte oposição popular, culminando na Revolta da Vacina em 1904 após a instituição da obrigatoriedade da vacina antivariólica. Apesar dos reveses políticos, o Instituto expandiu sua atuação pelo interior do país por meio de expedições científicas pioneiras.
Rebatizada como Instituto Oswaldo Cruz em 1908, a instituição ganhou projeção internacional. Um dos marcos científicos mais importantes ocorreu em 1909, quando Carlos Chagas descreveu o ciclo completo da tripanosomíase americana (doença de Chagas). Em 1920, Chagas assumiu o Departamento Nacional de Saúde Pública, reorganizando os serviços sanitários em todo o território nacional.
Pioneirismo científico
Ao longo do século XX, a instituição acompanhou as profundas transformações políticas do país. Em 1937, iniciou a produção da vacina contra a febre amarela em parceria com a Fundação Rockefeller, tornando-se posteriormente responsável por cerca de 80% da produção mundial desse imunizante. Em 1954, foi criada a Escola Nacional de Saúde Pública (Ensp), que mais tarde receberia o nome do sanitarista Sergio Arouca, cujos estudos foram fundamentais para desenhar as diretrizes do SUS.
Durante a ditadura militar, a instituição sofreu o “Massacre de Manguinhos” em 1970, episódio em que dez renomados cientistas tiveram seus direitos políticos cassados e foram aposentados compulsoriamente. No mesmo período, a instituição foi reestruturada, passando a denominar-se Fundação Oswaldo Cruz em 1974. Em 1976, foram criados os laboratórios de Bio-Manguinhos e Far-Manguinhos, impulsionando a produção de vacinas, diagnósticos e medicamentos para a saúde pública.
Com a redemocratização na década de 1980 e a gestão de Sergio Arouca, os cientistas perseguidos foram reintegrados. Em 1987, equipes da Fiocruz alcançaram outro feito histórico: o primeiro isolamento do vírus HIV na América Latina.
Expansão, inovação e resposta a emergências sanitárias
No século XXI, a Fiocruz consolidou sua expansão nacional e internacional. A Fundação inaugurou novas unidades regionais (como a Fiocruz Ceará), escritórios no exterior (Moçambique), o laboratório permanente Fioantar na Antártica e o Canal Saúde. Na área de pesquisa, realizou o sequenciamento do genoma da vacina BCG em 2006. Em 2016, a socióloga Nísia Trindade Lima tornou-se a primeira mulher eleita presidente na história da instituição.
A Fiocruz manteve papel de destaque no combate a emergências de saúde pública, atuando na pandemia de Influenza A (H1N1) em 2009 e na epidemia de zika e microcefalia (2015/2016), na qual identificou a presença do vírus em casos da má-formação congênita e desenvolveu kits de diagnóstico diferencial.
O combate à covid-19
Ao comemorar 120 anos em 2020, a Fiocruz foi nomeada referência da OMS para Covid-19 nas Américas. Em resposta à crise sanitária, construiu um complexo hospitalar de emergência em menos de dois meses, produziu testes moleculares em larga escala e coordenou o ensaio clínico internacional Solidariedade no Brasil.
Por meio de acordo de transferência tecnológica com o Reino Unido, a instituição assumiu a produção da vacina contra a covid-19, entregando mais de 150 milhões de doses ao SUS em 2021. Em 2022, disponibilizou as primeiras doses da vacina produzidas com o Ingrediente Farmacêutico Ativo (IFA) 100% nacional, garantindo a autossuficiência do Brasil. A instituição também assinou parcerias para a produção local de antivirais orais e desenvolveu testes diagnósticos múltiplos para vírus respiratórios.

title: Beyond politics: What defines leader’s legacy?
content:
In the 9th century, Cordoba, Spain, used oil lamps along its public streets. By 1417, London Mayor Henry Barton ordered people to start hanging lanterns outside their homes. As the imperative to lighten up communities evolved, by 1792, engineer William Murdoch invented practical gas lighting that made use of coal gas and by 1807, Frederick Albert Winsor introduced the first public gas street lighting. This was on Pall Mall in London.
Around the world, some of the most enduring legacies have been built not merely through wealth or political influence, but through a sustained commitment to improving lives. Through the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Bill Gates has committed more than US$100bn to global health, development and other philanthropic causes. Warren Buffett has pledged tens of billions of dollars to philanthropy, while MacKenzie Scott has directed billions of dollars in largely unrestricted grants to organisations working across education, health, equity and community development. Their examples reinforce a universal truth: the highest expression of leadership is not accumulation, but contribution. Increasingly, global best practice measures influence not simply by the titles people hold, but by the lives transformed, opportunities created, and systems strengthened.
It is a habit of mine to occasionally stroll through social media, observing the conversations, ideas and actions shaping our society. On one such occasion, I found myself on the social media page of Hon. Engr. Aderemi Abass Oseni. As a development enthusiast who keeps contributing my quota to nation-building through the Akin Fadeyi Foundation, my work has largely centered on institutional collaborations with government agencies, development partners, multilateral organisations and civil society organizations. That responsibility requires me to remain non-partisan and refrain from endorsing politicians or political interests. In fact, I have never met Engr. Oseni, nor have we had any prior relationship. But I have always believed that humanity should be acknowledged wherever it is genuinely demonstrated. Good deeds should inspire, irrespective of political affiliation, insofar as we set the boundary that ensures obsequious genuflecting does not constitute moral conflation. Through that lens, I took a closer look at the interventions associated with Engr. Remi Oseni, and I must admit that I was fascinated by the consistency, scale, and developmental orientation of his philanthropy.
In a political climate where public confidence is often tested by unfulfilled promises, citizens are becoming less interested in grand declarations and more interested in evidence. Leadership should ultimately be evaluated by outcomes. Are there more children in school? Are young people finding opportunities? Are vulnerable families living with greater dignity? Are communities healthier, safer, and more economically resilient than they were before? These are the questions that came to mind as I examined the public service record of Oseni. His approach offers an example of leadership that appears to place human development, rather than politics, at the centre of public service.
The evidence is substantial. In March 2026 alone, he disbursed N100 million to 820 traders, artisans, entrepreneurs and vulnerable residents, providing grants of up to N1 million to stimulate small businesses and expand economic opportunities at the grassroots. Barely three months later, another N90m was invested in market traders across the constituency’s nine local government areas to strengthen micro-enterprises and improve household incomes.
Recognising agriculture as both an economic and food-security priority, his office supported more than 7,000 farmers with fertilisers, agrochemicals, farm tools and improved agricultural inputs. His investments have also extended into community infrastructure, including motorized boreholes, solar-powered streetlights, electricity transformers and improved access to clean drinking water. He has also responded to humanitarian emergencies, including a N20 million intervention for traders affected by the Iso Alagbo market fire.
Through the Remi Oseni Foundation, indigent students have received support for WAEC, NECO and JAMB examinations, alongside scholarships and tertiary education support. The Foundation has established the Remilekun Food Bank and subsidized food markets for vulnerable households, while medical outreaches have provided health screenings, medications, eye care and reading glasses for elderly citizens. There is also the N250 million Work Tools Empowerment Programme for members of the Blacksmiths, Welders and Metal Technicians Association of Nigeria, an intervention that is particularly noteworthy because productive tools can generate income beyond the moment of the intervention itself.
These are meaningful interventions, and they deserve recognition. But they also raise a larger question: what happens when philanthropy meets the scale of Nigeria’s needs?
Nigeria’s needs are enormous, and no single philanthropist, however generous, can meet them alone. The latest FAAC figures illustrate the scale of public resources circulating through the federation. In July 2026, the Federal Government, 36 states and 774 local government councils shared a record N3.01tn in revenue.
The Federal Government received N1.15tn, the states received N943.35bn, and the 774 local government councils received N673.65bn. An additional N243.48bn was distributed to benefiting states as 13 per cent derivation revenue. Between January and July 2026, the three tiers of government shared approximately N15.997tn through FAAC. These figures matter because they remind us that Nigeria’s developmental challenge is not simply about the absence of resources. It is also about how resources are prioritised, converted into public goods, targeted at areas of greatest need, measured and institutionalised.
The question, therefore, is not simply whether government has resources. The question is, what are we doing with them?
Because while we applaud individual interventions, the wider Nigerian reality remains sobering. The National Bureau of Statistics’ Multidimensional Poverty Index found that 63 per cent of Nigerians, approximately 133 million people, were multidimensionally poor in its 2022 assessment. Food insecurity remains equally severe. The World Food Programme currently estimates that about 35 million Nigerians are facing acute food insecurity, with millions more living under conditions of severe vulnerability. These are not merely statistics. Behind every number is a household making difficult decisions about food, medicine, education, rent and livelihood.
Nigeria has made important investments in healthcare, and these deserve recognition. The Federal Ministry of Health reports that more than 37,000 health workers have been recruited into federal tertiary hospitals since 2024, while nursing and midwifery enrolment has also been expanded. Yet the deficits remain enormous. According to the Ministry, Nigeria’s doctor-to-population ratio remains approximately one doctor to 5,000 people, compared with a WHO benchmark of one to 600. The nurse-to-population ratio is approximately one to 2,000, compared with one to 300, while health workers remain heavily concentrated in urban areas. Thousands of primary healthcare centres are also not functioning optimally.
Another important dimension is the cost of accessing healthcare. WHO data indicate that household out-of-pocket payments account for a very large proportion of current health expenditure in Nigeria. For many households, therefore, the question is not simply whether a health facility exists, but whether a sick person can afford to use it. Philanthropic medical outreaches matter greatly in such an environment. But the larger challenge is to build systems in which Nigerians do not have to wait for a philanthropic medical outreach to access basic healthcare.
The same principle applies to security. Nigeria continues to confront terrorism, banditry, kidnapping, communal violence and other forms of insecurity. The consequences extend far beyond the immediate victims. Security is also an economic issue, a food-security issue, a youth issue and a development issue. A farmer who cannot safely access his farm cannot produce food. A trader who cannot safely transport goods cannot grow a business. A child who cannot safely travel to school cannot fully benefit from education. This is why development interventions cannot be treated as isolated sectors.
And then there are our young people.
Nigeria is a profoundly young country. UN population data places Nigeria’s 2025 population at approximately 237.5 million, with about 48.8 million people aged 15–24. The broader youth population is considerably larger, especially when considering the commonly used 15–35 age bracket. This is not merely a demographic statistic. It is Nigeria’s greatest economic opportunity, or one of its greatest risks.
Empowering young Nigerians should therefore go beyond periodic cash rollouts. Cash assistance can provide immediate relief, but skills create earning capacity. Vocational training creates employability. Apprenticeships create pathways. Access to markets creates businesses. Industrial policy creates jobs. An economy that can absorb the energy and creativity of millions of young people creates dignity at scale.
This is where I believe Nigeria needs to think much more boldly.
We need to examine our macroeconomic architecture: how we produce, what we produce, how we finance production, how we support agriculture, how we build manufacturing, how we develop human capital, how we attract investment, how we create jobs, and how we connect local enterprises to national and international markets.
This is where China’s development experience offers useful lessons, not because Nigeria should copy China, but because it demonstrates what can happen when economic transformation becomes a long-term national project. Over roughly four decades, China lifted close to 800 million people out of extreme poverty. The World Bank attributes this transformation to a combination of broad-based economic growth, market-oriented reforms, agricultural productivity, industrialisation, infrastructure development, urbanisation, education, targeted poverty reduction and effective governance.
The lesson for Nigeria is not simply to give people money.
It is to create an economy in which people can produce, participate and prosper.
Our ageing population also deserves far greater attention. Nigeria is a young country, but it is also ageing. The population aged 60 and above is projected to grow substantially in the coming decades. That means how we care for our elderly is not a distant problem. It is already here.
Nigeria has taken important institutional steps. The National Senior Citizens Centre Act 2017 established the National Senior Citizens Centre, with a mandate covering the health, social inclusion, dignity, security, productive participation and wellbeing of older Nigerians. Nigeria has also developed a National Policy on Ageing and a Strategic Roadmap on Ageing 2022–2032.
But policy architecture must ultimately translate into lived reality. Research continues to identify gaps in healthcare access, financial security, social protection and elder care. Nigeria’s contributory pension system also does not cover every older person, particularly those whose working lives were spent outside the formal sector.
This is where philanthropy, government and the private sector can converge.
Why shouldn’t Nigeria have properly equipped geriatric homes and community-based elder-care centres? Why shouldn’t corporations include senior-care facilities in their social investment portfolios? Why shouldn’t governors and local government chairmen institutionalise programmes for older citizens within their jurisdictions? Why shouldn’t faith organisations, foundations, development partners and private companies sponsor meals, healthcare, mobility support, companionship and assisted living for vulnerable seniors? Why shouldn’t we train and certify a new generation of professional geriatric caregivers?
We can. And we should. The world already offers models we can learn from.
Canada provides an instructive example. Its approach is not limited to building institutions for older people. Canada places significant emphasis on ageing in place, helping older people remain safely and independently within their homes and communities for as long as possible. Home and community care can include nursing, personal care, physiotherapy, social work, meal delivery, housekeeping, transportation and respite support for caregivers, while long-term care facilities provide more intensive assistance where people require round-the-clock support. Canada also provides income support through programmes such as Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement for eligible seniors.
Denmark offers another useful model. Municipalities have significant responsibility for elderly care, including home care and care accommodation. Older people who cannot safely manage independently can receive appropriate housing, assisted living or nursing-home accommodation based on assessed need. Municipalities can also provide respite and relief for family caregivers.
Neither model is perfect. That is not the point. Best practice does not mean perfection. It means continuously building better systems.
These models point towards something Nigeria can adapt: care should not depend entirely on whether an individual has a generous relative, a benevolent politician or a philanthropic benefactor. There should be a system.
And this brings me back to Oseni.
I applaud his work. I applaud the interventions. I applaud the generosity. I applaud the attention to traders, farmers, artisans, students, vulnerable families, and elderly citizens.
But I am also quick to make a larger observation.
The next stage is institutionalisation.
The next stage is a more concerted, data-driven architecture that captures areas of need, identifies who is being left behind, measures outcomes and institutionalises interventions.
Imagine a constituency-level needs and vulnerability architecture that maps households facing food insecurity, unemployed and underemployed young people, persons with disabilities, older persons living alone, children at risk of dropping out of school, communities without functional healthcare, farmers affected by insecurity, entrepreneurs requiring productive assets and communities lacking water and sanitation.
Imagine that data being updated regularly. Imagine interventions being designed around the evidence. Imagine every naira spent having a measurable social return.
That is how philanthropy begins to evolve from generosity into development architecture.
A philanthropist could build a geriatric home. But a stronger intervention might be to build a geriatric-care system involving government, corporations, hospitals, universities, NGOs, faith institutions and trained caregivers.
This conversation should not be directed at philanthropists alone. Governors and local government chairmen should take a cue. The latest FAAC figures demonstrate that resources are reaching all three tiers of government. The 774 local governments alone received N673.65bn from the July 2026 allocation. A philanthropist could distribute food. But an even stronger intervention might combine emergency food support with agricultural productivity, food-processing enterprises, cold-chain infrastructure, market access and nutrition programmes.
A philanthropist could give young people cash. But a more transformative model could combine start-up capital with vocational training, tools, apprenticeships, market access, mentorship and procurement opportunities.
That is the difference between relief and resilience.
Fadeyi, the executive director at www.akinfadeyifoundation.org, writes via [email protected]

title: From your bin to cash: the hidden economy of waste picking
content:
For thousands of waste pickers, discarded plastic bottles, milk containers, cardboard and other recyclable materials are not junk but a source of income.
At least 15,000 waste pickers are recorded in the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) programme in Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal.
EPR is a mandatory environmental policy approach that holds producers, importers and brand owners legally accountable for the entire lifecycle of their products.
Sifiso Gumbi, a waste picker and founder of Urban Surfer, an organisation for waste pickers in Gauteng, said polyethylene terephthalate (PET), found in clear cold-drink bottles, is among the most valuable and widely recovered plastics.
“The everyday items include Coca-Cola bottles and other fizzy-drink bottles, which are PET,” Gumbi said. “Milk containers are HDPE, or high-density polyethylene. Flexible plastics, such as wrapping or plastic shopping bags, are usually LDPE [low-density polyethylene] and can also be recycled. But among those plastics, PET bottles are the most valuable.”
From two-litre cold-drink bottles to milk containers, yoghurt tubs and cardboard, household waste can have economic value long after it has been discarded. But that value depends on the material, where it is collected and constantly changing market conditions. Gumbi said PET currently fetches about R3.50/kg, down from about R7/kg six to eight months ago.
“Recycling is also subject to fluctuations like any other market because the recycling items that they recover are actually commodities.”
Packaging manufacturers should be held accountable for the products they put into the market. If the market is low for a particular plastic, it can end up in landfills, rivers and dams
— Sifiso Gumbi, a waste picker and founder of Urban Surfer
Musa Chamane from GroundWork Friends of the Earth said recyclable prices were also affected by broader economic conditions, including transport costs.
“The price of recyclables that waste pickers are relying on to make a living does get affected by markets,” Chamane said. “Mainly because if the petrol price has risen, like it’s been going up, that means the person who buys those materials from waste pickers has to factor in the transport costs.”
He said aluminium cans could previously fetch about R14/kg but dropped to around R10/kg when market conditions deteriorated.
Both Gumbi and Chamane said prices paid to reclaimers by buyback centres were not regulated, though discussions around regulation were under way.
Chamane said falling prices could force waste pickers to hold on to recyclable materials until conditions improved.
“When the market crashes, they sometimes have to pause working. They will stop even selling their stuff, maybe stashing the items at home, waiting for the market to recover,” he said.
Not all plastics are equally valuable.
Gumbi said multi-layered packaging, including some washing-powder packets and snack packets, could be particularly difficult to recycle because there is little or no market for them.
When material has little economic value, reclaimers have less incentive to collect it, meaning some plastics can ultimately end up in landfills, rivers and dams.
“Packaging manufacturers should be held accountable for the products they put into the market,” Gumbi said. “If the market is low for a particular plastic, it can end up in landfills, rivers and dams.”
The recycling industry in South Africa will not exist without waste pickers. But waste pickers are the least paid people in the value chain
— Musa Chamane from GroundWork Friends of the Earth
A reclaimer can collect between 80kg and 400kg of material a day, depending on where they operate, the materials available and their strategy.
Daily income can range from about R100 to R1,000.
Those operating in wealthier areas such as Sandton, Hyde Park, Sandhurst, Houghton and Linden may encounter more valuable discarded goods, including electronics and other unwanted household items.
Gumbi said EPR initiatives had provided some support.
Through Polyco, a non-profit company focused on making waste a valuable resource that works for South Africa’s economy, more than 600 reclaimers had received training, trolleys and protective equipment.
An EPR payment platform for glass had about 1,000 reclaimers and had paid about R2m in incentives to reclaimers and buyback centres over eight months.
“[But] the waste picker incentive is not enough. It’s only 15 cents a kilo,” Gumbi said.
Chamane said EPR implementation “has been flawed because of such gaps”, arguing that registered waste pickers should receive EPR-linked payments when they sell qualifying packaging materials at registered buyback centres.
“There is a loophole in the system,” he said. “The recycling industry in South Africa will not exist without waste pickers. But waste pickers are the least paid people in the value chain.”
Behind every plastic container is a market, a worker and a chain of buyers.
Whether it becomes income or waste again depends on its material, its market value and whether the recycling system can support its recovery.
Gumbi said solving plastic pollution requires action at the personal, business and government levels to reduce waste and improve recycling.

title: The bird that changed Ecuador: how a chance discovery of a rare species helped to save many more
content:
I have to confess that I rarely enjoy birding in montane cloud forests. The birds that live in these mountainous, cool and humid habitats are masters of disguise, usually passing themselves off as a leaf or other form of foliage. But if I want to see antpittas – elusive, ground-dwelling birds that rarely show themselves – then I have no choice.
So, on a cool, cloudy morning my guide, Juan Carlos Crespo, Fredy Ramón Castillo, a local ranger, and I are standing on a steep, muddy path close to Tapichalaca Lodge, 2,500 metres above sea level in the eastern Andes, waiting for the jocotoco antpitta to emerge from the undergrowth.
Fortunately, antpittas have a soft spot for food, especially the large, juicy earthworms Castillo has placed on a low branch nearby. He calls the bird, with increasingly loud and urgent shouts of “venga, venga!” (“come on, come on!”). The minutes tick by, until I begin to wonder if this is a lost cause.
Then, out of nowhere, a plump, thrush-sized bird with a chestnut back, grey front, black crown and white face-patch materialises just a few feet away. It proceeds to gulp down the earthworms as if it has not eaten for days.
I have seen a lot of different birds, but never one that so changed the course of bird conservation. In November 1997, a group led by the influential US ornithologist Robert Ridgely was exploring this area of southern Ecuador to see what they could find.
As they ascended a forest trail at dawn, they heard the sound of a bird in the far distance. As Ridgely recalled many years later, “It had this crazy call, sounding like an owl; but we had no idea what it was, and to be honest I never thought we would find out.”
Ridgely walked ahead of the group, and heard the sound much closer than before. He recorded the call and played it back to the mystery creature, which came crashing through the dense bamboo, right out into the open.
“I knew right away that this was something really special, which no one apart from the local people had ever seen – an entirely new species to science.” It was, in fact, one of the greatest ornithological breakthroughs of the late 20th century: while new species are sometimes discovered, they are rarely so large, noisy and so obviously different from other members of their family.
Talking to local farmers, Ridgely discovered that they were familiar with the bird, which they had named “jocotoco” to represent its loud, barking call. Two years later, the species was officially described, and named the jocotoco antpitta; the scientific name, Grallaria ridgelyi, commemorating its proud discoverer.
Ridgely soon realised that if the bird was to be saved from extinction its forest home needed to be urgently protected. He and a group of like-minded friends created an organisation dedicated to saving the bird and its habitat, raising funds from donors in the US and Europe to buy and restore the land. In 1998 the Jocotoco Foundation was born.
Today, the foundation protects and manages 19 reserves throughout Ecuador, covering about 50,000 hectares (193 sq miles), and manages a further 82,000 hectares of privately and communally owned land. Together, these sites are home to more than 1,350 species of birds – that’s 80% of all those found in Ecuador, and an astonishing one in eight of all bird species on the planet, as well as many other plant and animal species. The foundation also works closely with nearby communities, employing local people as park rangers – many of whom grew up on the land they now protect – and through jobs in wildlife tourism.
The model for the foundation’s reserves is simple and very effective. First, it restores habitat by planting a variety of native trees and other plants, or in some places simply allows the vegetation to regenerate on its own. Park guards, all of whom come from local communities, protect the reserves against illegal incursions such as cattle grazing, logging and poaching, aided by new technology including camera traps and audio recorders.
They also use these to monitor the fortunes of key species, while providing nest boxes to encourage them to breed, making up for the loss of natural tree cavities while the old-growth forests are being restored.
A recent study at Canandé, in the Chocó region of north-west Ecuador, revealed that even after deforestation, nature can recover very rapidly. The study showed that in just three decades – a single human generation – of being managed for biodiversity, formerly cleared lands have recovered 90% of the biomass – the weight of all animals – and 90% of the number of species found in nearby mature forests. While the new mix of species is not fully the same as in a mature forest, 75% of the original species present in an old-growth forest have returned.
Mike Parr, the president of the American Bird Conservancy, has no doubt about the importance of this work. “Beyond safeguarding Ecuador’s rarest birds, migrating species and incredible overall biodiversity, Jocotoco’s strategic integration of ecotourism, public awareness, community engagement and scientific research are world class. They have done an amazing job covering the previously unprotected endangered species of Ecuador.”
During recent visits to Ecuador I have visited 10 of the foundation’s reserves, including those in the Chocó region north-west of Quito and Copalinga in the Amazon foothills, along with the Los Petreles reserve on San Cristóbal Island in the Galápagos, a refuge for a critically endangered seabird, the Galápagos petrel.
On a visit to Buenaventura reserve, a restored cattle ranch in the western foothills of the Andes, we went in search of an even rarer bird: the El Oro parakeet. This charismatic parrot was only discovered as recently as 1980, and has a tiny home range, with fewer than 1,000 individuals.
Another early start took us to an open area of grassland and scattered trees where the birds are known to gather. Moments later, we heard a raucous call, and there they were: several flocks totalling about 20 of these emerald-green birds, the males with a distinctive red forehead.
But even this memorable moment was eclipsed by my visit to the Chakana nature reserve, more than 4,000 metres above sea level in the páramo grasslands of the high Andes – yet just an hour south-east of Quito. On an unexpectedly fine and sunny day, against a stunning backdrop of the snow-capped Cotopaxi volcano, we enjoyed closeup views of the Ecuadorian hillstar, a specialist high-altitude hummingbird, along with nine Andean condors soaring right around us, before they rose high into the clear blue sky.
Numbers of the Andean condor, the world’s largest flying bird by a combination of weight and wingspan, have fallen rapidly in recent years, due mainly to deliberate poisoning. But here, these mighty raptors are now returning to their ancestral home.
Dr Martin Schaefer, chief executive of Jocotoco, believes that even in these dark times there is room for optimism. “The power to restore what we have lost is in our hands.”
Ian J Davidson, Americas regional director for BirdLife International, agrees. “By creating a network of protected habitat ‘arks’, Jocotoco has given these remarkable species a genuine chance not only to endure, but to recover and expand beyond their remaining strongholds.
“Their work stands as a global conservation success story, an inspiring example of what determination, science and long-term stewardship can achieve for nature.”
At a time when President Trump has withdrawn US government funding for conservation projects around the world, the Jocotoco Foundation is a classic model of how scientists and local people can work together to save endangered birds and the precious places where they live.
This article by Stephen Moss was first published by The Guardian on 13 September 2026. Lead Image: Thirty years after a US ornithologist first sighted a jocotoco antpitta, the foundation he set up to restore biodiversity is a model for conservation globally.

title: Translational Hepatology From Bedside to Global Policy: How Robust Clinical and Translational Research Reshapes Global Practice Guidelines and Patient Outcomes.
content: Over four decades, translational hepatology has evolved from empirical observations into an evidence-driven discipline. This review synthesizes key bedside discoveries, mechanistic studies, prospective cohorts, cross-regional health-economic evaluations, and landmark randomized controlled trials (RCTs) by our team that have helped to reshape regulatory drug approvals, Boxed Warnings, and international practice guidelines across APASL, AASLD, and EASL. First, clinical trials established the biphasic model and risk predictors of immunosuppression-induced hepatitis B virus (HBV) reactivation, proving that pre-emptive nucleos(t)ide analogue (NUC) prophylaxis prevents liver failure and antineoplastic disruptions. Second, multinational Phase III registration trials of finite 48-week pegylated interferon alfa-2a (Peg-IFN α-2a) in chronic hepatitis B (CHB)-combined with intrahepatic cccDNA kinetics, adoptive immunity transfer, and 30-year Asia-Pacific Markov health-economic modeling-established response-guided rules and validated finite Peg-IFN switch/add-on strategies as clinically dominant and cost-effective. Third, prospective cohorts uncovered direct-acting antiviral (DAA)-induced HBV reactivation during HCV clearance, establishing mandatory regulatory Boxed Warnings and pre-DAA screening. Fourth, the Phase III HIMALAYA study and pooled Greater China (Mainland China, Hong Kong, Taiwan) cohorts validated the STRIDE regimen (single-dose tremelimumab plus regular durvalumab) as frontline dual immunotherapy for unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (uHCC), establishing marked survival benefit in HBV-predominant populations (median OS 25.26 vs. 14.09 months) alongside a vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-free standard for cirrhotic portal hypertension within APASL guidelines. Finally, translational insights across metabolic dysfunction, COVID-19, ACLF, artificial intelligence (AI), and functional cure frameworks inform the APASL 2026 "treat-all" CHB paradigm.

title: Food security is a global security imperative
content:
Recent disruptions—from extreme weather events to geopolitical tensions affecting international trade—have underscored a fundamental reality: no nation, regardless of its wealth or geography, can secure its food future alone.
Building resilient food systems requires far more than increasing agricultural output. It requires open and reliable trade, secure maritime routes, scientific innovation, sustainable water management, and strong international partnerships.
Together, these elements place food security at the intersection of economic resilience, sustainable development, and global stability.
These realities have shaped the United Arab Emirates' approach to food security. Despite its arid climate, water scarcity, and limited arable land, the UAE has treated food security as a strategic national resilience priority – one that extends well beyond agricultural production.
Through the National Food Security Strategy 2051, the country is strengthening food resilience by diversifying international supply sources, facilitating reliable food trade, expanding sustainable domestic production, strengthening strategic preparedness, reducing food loss and waste, and developing supply chains capable of withstanding future shocks.
Innovation is central to this vision. The UAE continues to invest in controlled-environment agriculture, hydroponics, vertical farming, precision irrigation, artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and other climate-smart agricultural solutions.
UAE-based companies are developing large-scale vertical farms that produce fresh produce in controlled environments while using significantly less water and land than conventional agriculture. These technologies can increase productivity while easing pressure on scarce water resources.
This transformation is not only about technology. Through initiatives led by the National Agriculture Centre and programmes supporting young and female farmers, the UAE is building national capabilities, fostering agricultural entrepreneurship, and strengthening the human capital needed for a competitive and future-ready food economy.
This approach also reflects a broader economic vision. Through the UAE Food Cluster Strategy, the country is connecting agriculture with advanced manufacturing, biotechnology, food processing, logistics, and research to build a more integrated and competitive food ecosystem.
The 2026 Emirates Agriculture Conference and Exhibition brought together farmers, industry, investors, researchers, and government across the food value chain, reflecting an approach that sees food security not only as a resilience priority, but also as a driver of innovation, investment, skilled employment, and economic diversification.
The UAE’s experience also reflects a wider reality: national resilience depends on the resilience of the global food system. Modern agriculture relies on uninterrupted access to fertilizers, seeds, animal feed, energy, and efficient global logistics networks.
Disruptions to maritime routes or supply chains can quickly affect food availability, drive up prices, and threaten the livelihoods of millions—particularly in countries that depend heavily on imported food. Safeguarding the continuity of these flows is therefore not only an economic necessity; it is a humanitarian responsibility.
Nowhere is this interdependence more evident than in the Strait of Hormuz. This vital international waterway is a global lifeline, carrying approximately one-fifth of global energy supplies and around 30 per cent of the fertilizers essential to global food production.
Any disruption to such a critical artery is therefore not a regional concern alone. Its effects can reverberate through global markets and supply chains, with the greatest consequences often falling on vulnerable, food-import-dependent countries.
This wider responsibility has also shaped the UAE’s engagement through multilateral institutions. On 28 April 2026, the FAO Council adopted by consensus a UAE-led decision addressing the implications of supply chain disruptions in the Gulf region for global food security and agriculture.
The decision called for preventing the politicization of food and agricultural supply chains and strengthened the FAO’s role in monitoring disruptions, providing timely market information and early warnings, and supporting countries in building more resilient agri-food systems.
But resilience cannot be built through preparedness alone. We must also transform how food is produced, financed, and brought to the market, while confronting the growing pressures of climate change and resource scarcity.
The UAE has advanced this agenda internationally by placing food systems at the heart of the global climate conversation.
COP28 marked an important shift: for the first time, food and agriculture were given a prominent place within the climate agenda, reinforced by the Emirates Declaration on Sustainable Agriculture, Resilient Food Systems, and Climate Action.
Endorsed by 159 Heads of State and Government, the Declaration reflected a growing recognition that climate action cannot be separated from how the world produces, distributes, and consumes food.
COP28 also paired political ambition with practical investment, including the USD 200 million UAE–Gates Foundation partnership to accelerate agricultural innovation and strengthen the resilience of smallholder farmers in the Global South.
COP28’s broader legacy was equally significant. Hosted by the UAE, the conference brought 198 Parties together to agree on the landmark UAE Consensus, setting out an ambitious climate agenda to keep the 1.5°C goal within reach.
The Consensus provided an ambitious response to the Global Stocktake and a clear plan to close critical gaps by 2030.
It called on Parties to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems to reach net zero, encouraged economy-wide Nationally Determined Contributions, and set a new target to triple renewable energy capacity and double energy efficiency by 2030.
It also built momentum behind a new architecture for climate finance. The significance of this outcome extends beyond climate policy.
Aligned with the visionary leadership of the UAE, the COP28 Presidency marked a turning point in the effort to achieve tangible and essential progress on global climate action while advancing sustainable economic and social development.
It demonstrated the value of bringing countries together around practical solutions, shared ambition, and collective action.
That same emphasis on turning innovation into practical solutions is increasingly important across Asia. In 2026, the UAE contributed USD 1.5 million to an agricultural innovation fund administered by the Asian Development Bank to help scale proven technologies for farmers across Asia and the Pacific.
The initiative supports tools ranging from artificial intelligence and satellite monitoring to more efficient use of agricultural inputs, demonstrating how international partnerships can turn technological innovation into practical gains for farmers and food systems.
For the UAE and Indonesia, this agenda carries particular relevance.
Indonesia is among the countries in which these agricultural innovations are intended to be scaled, creating a practical foundation for our two countries to deepen cooperation in agricultural technology, investment, knowledge exchange, and resilient food systems.
As two countries deeply connected to international trade and regional supply chains, the UAE and Indonesia share a strong interest in ensuring that food systems remain productive, sustainable, and capable of adapting to future shocks.
No country possesses all the answers to today's complex food security challenges. Every country, however, has knowledge, innovation, and experience to contribute.
Governments, international organizations, research institutions, development partners, and the private sector each have a role to play – from strengthening agricultural resilience and safeguarding supply chains to ensuring that innovation reaches the communities that need it most.
The future of food security will therefore depend not simply on producing more food, but on building systems that can withstand and adapt to a more uncertain world.
That means using water and natural resources more responsibly, keeping global trade and supply chains open and reliable, investing in innovation, and strengthening cooperation across countries and sectors.
Ultimately, success must be measured by a simple test: whether food remains available, accessible, and affordable—particularly when shocks occur.
In an increasingly interconnected world, no nation can secure food security alone. It is a shared responsibility — one that demands sustained cooperation, practical action, and collective leadership.
*) Abdulla Salem AlDhaheri is Ambassador of the United Arab Emirates to the Republic of Indonesia and the Democratic Republic of Timor-Leste (Non-Resident)

title: Partnership with Qatar a key pillar in addressing global humanitarian crises, says UNHCR official
content:
Representative of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) to Qatar Ahmed Lotfy Mohsen has affirmed that the strategic partnership with Qatar serves as a pivotal pillar in addressing global humanitarian crises.
Speaking to the Qatar News Agency (QNA), he stated that Qatar – represented by government bodies and charitable institutions – has, through its close co-operation with the UN agency, provided financial contributions totaling $440mn since 2010.
These funds, Mohsen said, have supported protection programmes and provided life-saving assistance to forcibly displaced persons worldwide.
He added that Qatar’s support extends beyond the financial realm to include logistical and in-kind assistance.
This includes, the official said, facilitating the transport of relief supplies to acute crisis zones – such as Afghanistan and Lebanon – as well as playing a prominent diplomatic role in fostering the stability and dialogue necessary for implementing voluntary return and local integration programmes.
On the actual impact on the ground, Mohsen noted that the support included $40mn provided through the Qatar Fund for Development (QFFD) since 2019 in the form of flexible, unearmarked funding.
This, he said, granted the UNHCR exceptional flexibility to respond rapidly to emergencies and direct resources toward the most underfunded operations, thereby ensuring the continuity of essential services such as healthcare, education, and shelter.
Regarding innovative financing tools and Islamic philanthropy, Mohsen noted that total contributions from Qatar – comprising Zakat and voluntary charity – since 2018 have amounted to nearly $145mn.
This includes a strategic agreement signed by Qatar Charity (QC) last June to contribute $10mn to the Global Islamic Fund for Refugees (GIFR).
The UN official stated that the 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) – convening under the theme Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All and coinciding with the 75th anniversary of the 1951 Refugee Convention – marks a pivotal moment to reflect on the legacy of international protection and to reaffirm the commitment to upholding the dignity and rights of the forcibly displaced.
He added that escalating global humanitarian challenges and the unprecedented number of displaced persons necessitate active international solidarity and the building of effective partnerships.
Mohsen pointed out that the strategic partnership between the UNHCR and Qatar serves as a successful, real-world model of constructive co-operation between governments and international organisations in addressing complex humanitarian crises.

title: From Karnataka Midwife To Padma Shri: Remembering Sulagitti Narasamma’s Extraordinary Journey
content:
Sulagitti Narasamma, a traditional midwife from Karnataka, spent nearly seven decades helping women through childbirth, drawing on knowledge she learnt through observation, experience and her grandmother, Marigamma. Born on 16 June 1920 in Thimmenayapete village in Pavagada, Tumkur district, Narasamma began learning childbirth practices as a young girl by accompanying her grandmother, who was also a midwife. She later became known as ‘Sulagitti Narasamma’, with ‘sulagitti’ being the Kannada word for a traditional midwife.
She travelled across villages and remote communities to assist women in labour, including difficult deliveries. Her work continued despite social rejection and caste barriers. She was recognised with the Vayoshreshtha Samman in 2013, Karnataka’s Rajyotsava award the same year, an honorary doctorate from Tumkur University in 2014 and the Padma Shri in 2018. She died on 25 December 2018, aged 98. Looking back on her life, Narasamma described midwifery as a sacred responsibility and said, “The work of a Sulagitti was given to me by God.”
Not Just A Profession
Narasamma’s relationship with midwifery began within her family. Her grandmother Marigamma had worked as a traditional midwife in the village of Madakasira after being widowed at a young age. She did not charge families for her services. Instead, villagers supported her with food, clothing and the implements she needed. Narasamma accompanied her grandmother when she went to assist women in childbirth and gradually absorbed what she observed.
The apprenticeship shaped the way she later understood childbirth. She learnt to use her hands to assess the baby’s position and sense when birth was approaching. She also learnt about traditional herbs and plants, including knowledge shared by communities she encountered during her work. Narasamma recalled that she was still an adolescent when she delivered her first baby. Her aunt-in-law, Kanumakka, went into labour while other women in the neighbourhood were away at work.
Narasamma summoned a young girl for assistance and delivered the baby. According to Narasamma’s account, Kanumakka blessed her afterwards and encouraged her to continue the work. Over time, Narasamma’s reputation spread beyond her village. Families travelled to seek her help, while she herself travelled by foot, bullock cart and other vehicles to reach women in labour. She was sometimes called upon for difficult births, including by a Brahmin doctor who, according to Narasamma, sought her assistance after hospital medicines and injections had not helped.
Crossing Social And Geographical Boundaries
Narasamma’s work was not always accepted by the people around her. Some members of her family considered midwifery ‘polluting’ work, while her husband’s income from selling buttermilk was affected as some people stopped buying from him because she continued her work. She also encountered caste-based restrictions. In some upper-caste homes, she was asked to conduct deliveries in courtyards, while strict social boundaries governed who could enter certain homes. Yet Narasamma continued to help women regardless of their caste or community. She recalled travelling through heavy rain and difficult terrain to reach the temporary settlement of a nomadic tribal community near a forest.
The journey took several hours, but she eventually reached the woman in labour and safely delivered the baby. Narasamma also described how she viewed women’s suffering during childbirth as something shared across social divisions. Her understanding of service extended beyond delivery itself. In her recorded consent statement, she spoke about advising pregnant women and new mothers about diet and breastfeeding, while also recalling traditional knowledge of herbs, leaves and roots.
She strongly rejected the practice of blaming women who could not conceive. She argued that responsibility should not automatically be placed on women and said both husband and wife should be considered. Her statement reflected the values she had developed through decades of lived experience. “Under no circumstance should the woman be called ‘barren’,” she said in the account.
The Logical Indian’s Perspective
Sulagitti Narasamma’s story is not only about childbirth. It is also about how knowledge is learnt, preserved and passed between generations. Her training did not take place in a classroom; it began by watching her grandmother and developed through years of experience within the community. Her story also shows how care can cross boundaries created by caste, geography and social convention.
At the same time, traditional practices and community knowledge should be understood responsibly alongside the importance of safe, evidence-based maternal healthcare. Narasamma herself described her work through the language of service and compassion, saying, “Delivering a woman from labour pain is more sacred than a puja.” Her life invites us to look beyond formal recognition and ask what happens to valuable community knowledge when the people who carry it are no longer there to pass it on.
How can we preserve such lived knowledge while ensuring every mother has access to safe and dignified healthcare?

title: Gebärdensprache: Kaum Lehrkräfte
content:
Spanisch, Italienisch, Latein – oder Gebärdensprache: Mit dem Schuljahr 2026/27 ist die Österreichische Gebärdensprache (ÖGS) erstmals als zweite lebende Fremdsprache im Lehrplan der AHS-Oberstufe verankert. Wählen können das Fach alle Schülerinnen und Schüler, unabhängig davon, ob sie hören oder nicht, und auch ohne Vorkenntnisse. Ab dem Schuljahr 2029/30 soll die Matura in ÖGS möglich sein.
In der Praxis ist von der Reform in Vorarlberg allerdings noch nichts zu sehen. „Derzeit wird an keiner Vorarlberger AHS-Oberstufe Österreichische Gebärdensprache als zweite lebende Fremdsprache oder als Wahlpflichtfach angeboten“, teilte Christian Kompatscher vom pädagogischen Dienst der Bildungsdirektion auf Nachfrage des ORF Vorarlberg mit. Laut ORF-Recherchen bildet Vorarlberg damit gemeinsam mit dem Burgenland das Schlusslicht.
ÖGS steht für Österreichische Gebärdensprache – die eigenständige Sprache der Gehörlosengemeinschaft in Österreich.
Andere Länder starten in Etappen
Anderswo läuft der Unterricht zumindest punktuell an: In Linz startet das Körnergymnasium, in Wien ist der Bildungsdirektion ein Standort bekannt, in der Steiermark gibt es einen ÖGS-Kurs am WIKU Graz. In Tirol wird die Entscheidung den Schulen selbst überlassen, Kärnten und Salzburg wollen ein Jahr später starten – dort sind Lehrkräfte noch in Ausbildung.
Der Grund für die Zurückhaltung ist überall derselbe: Es fehlt an qualifiziertem Personal. Ein eigenes Lehramtsstudium für Gebärdensprache gibt es in Österreich nicht, auch Unterrichtsmaterial für Kinder und Jugendliche ist rar. Am LZH haben viele Lehrkräfte und Pädagoginnen und Pädagogen eine Zusatzqualifikation im Bereich ÖGS, ein Lehramt hat im Dienststand der Bildungsdirektion aber nur eine einzige Person.
Ausbildung in Vorarlberg wenig attraktiv
„Wie bei allen Spezialisierungen, die nur einen kleinen Teil der Schülerinnen und Schüler unmittelbar betreffen, sind die Aus- und Fortbildungsangebote in Vorarlberg wenig attraktiv, da oft lange Anreisen in Kauf genommen werden müssen“, erklärt Kompatscher. Dazu komme: Unterrichtet eine gehörlose ÖGS-Lehrkraft, braucht es unter Umständen eine zweite sprechende Person mit ÖGS-Kenntnissen in der Klasse. Konkrete Planungen für das kommende Schuljahr liegen nicht vor, das Thema soll bei der Dienstbesprechung der AHS-Schulleitungen im Herbst zur Sprache kommen.
Kindergarten am LZH wird eingestellt
Während an den Gymnasien nichts weitergeht, wird das bestehende Angebot am LZH umgebaut: Der Kindergarten für Hör- und Sprachbildung in Dornbirn wird mit dem Kindergartenjahr 2027/28 eingestellt und in ein mobiles Unterstützungsangebot übergeführt. Das haben Land und LZH am Dienstag bekanntgegeben. Derzeit werden dort sieben Kinder begleitet – Kinder mit schweren Hörbeeinträchtigungen, Kinder mit zusätzlichen Behinderungen sowie hörende Kinder gehörloser Eltern.
Ein Teil der bisherigen Mittel soll künftig rund 1.970 zusätzliche Stunden audiopädagogischer Frühförderung ermöglichen. „Unser Ziel ist, dass Kinder mit Hörbeeinträchtigungen möglichst selbstverständlich am Bildungs- und Betreuungsangebot in ihrer Gemeinde teilhaben können“, sagt Soziallandesrätin Martina Rüscher (ÖVP). Die Mittel des Sozialfonds würden gezielt in den Ausbau der mobilen Frühförderung überführt, das sei „ein weiterer konkreter Schritt in Richtung eines inklusiven Bildungssystems“.
„Bedauern“ am LZH
Am LZH fällt die Reaktion gemischt aus. „Wir bedauern, dass der Kindergarten künftig nicht mehr in seiner bisherigen Form an unserem Standort weitergeführt wird“, sagt Johannes Mathis vom Landeszentrum für Hörgeschädigte. Man werde die Neuausrichtung aber „konstruktiv mitgestalten“. Angebote, die es bisher unter einem Dach gab – Psychologie, Therapie, Soziale Arbeit, HNO und Hörtechnik – stehen den Kindergartenkindern künftig nicht mehr direkt am Standort zur Verfügung. Die mobile Unterstützung werde dennoch „in hoher Qualität“ erbracht.
Vorbild ist „JUMI – Jupident mobile Inklusion“: Seit dem Betreuungsjahr 2023/24 unterstützt ein mobiles Team der Stiftung Jupident Kinder und Fachkräfte direkt in den Kindergärten. Das Land beruft sich zudem auf Artikel 24 der UN-Behindertenrechtskonvention und auf die Sozialfondsstrategie 2030.
Eine Wochenstunde in Dornbirn
Die Schule am LZH bleibt bestehen: Sie steht Kindern von sechs bis 14 Jahren aus ganz Vorarlberg offen, unterrichtet wird bei Bedarf bilingual, dazu kommt eine Wochenstunde ÖGS-Kurs. Rund 60 Kinder mit Hörbeeinträchtigung besuchen die Schule von der ersten bis zur achten Schulstufe, weitere rund 50 werden in Regelklassen an Volks- und Mittelschulen begleitet. Jährlich erhalten fünf bis zehn Jugendliche mit Hörbeeinträchtigung an AHS, BMHS und Berufsschulen eine Förderung.

title: Bill Seeking to Punish the Use of Animals as Weapons of War in Colombia Advances
content:
Last April, the Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP), which emerged from the peace agreements with the FARC guerrilla group, and the University of Essex, in the United Kingdom, published a report stating that during the 2017-2026 period, more than 100,000 animals had been affected in the context of the armed conflict in Colombia, many of them because they had been used as weapons of war by irregular armed groups.
The list of incidents in which animals are used by illegal armed organizations to attack the Colombian Armed Forces is long. Now, these animals are about to have specific legal recognition in the country, thanks to a bill that seeks to criminalize these practices and establish reparation measures for the affected fauna and ecosystems.
Recognizing Animals as Victims of the Armed Conflict
The plenary session of Colombia’s Senate has just given its approval to a proposal presented by Senator Esmeralda Hernandez (from the Historic Pact party), thus surpassing the first two debates, and it is now preparing to face the final two debates in the House of Representatives.
The bill proposes including in the Criminal Code the use of animals as instruments of war, a conduct that is not expressly contemplated under the crime of using booby traps. In an interview with Semana magazine, Hernandez explained that the measure would cover cases of animals used to transport explosives, torture or threaten people.
“The crime of using booby traps exists, such as what happened to [former Vice President German] Vargas Lleras with the loss of his fingers, because the bomb arrived in a book. […] But animals were not included. So what we are doing is criminalizing and including them,” the senator said.
“We have managed to get the Senate plenary to approve our bill to criminalize the use of animals as instruments of war (e.g. donkey bombs) and recognize them, together with nature, as victims of the armed conflict,” Hernandez celebrated on her social media accounts.
The animal rights organization Plataforma Alto supported the initiative and rejected the use of animals in the armed conflict: “Animals deserve full protection and respect, not to be used as tools of war. They are sentient beings, not weapons,” it said.
The impacts include both the direct use of animals by armed groups and the damage resulting from bombings, contamination, pipeline explosions and other actions that affect ecosystems. Senator Hernandez pointed out that more than 44 species are threatened by the effects of the war.
Animals Are Not a Subcomponent of the Environment
The proposal includes protection measures, symbolic reparation, historical memory and the recovery of threatened species. It also contemplates restoring and reforesting areas affected by the conflict.
The report by the JEP and the University of Essex, titled “Invisible Damage. Violence Against Animals in the Armed Conflict in Colombia (2017-2026),” maintains that the development of international humanitarian law, criminal law and human rights law — designed to mitigate and put an end to the worst impacts of social conflicts on human beings — has left animals aside for too long.
It also questions the notion that animals can only be conceptualized as property or as a subcomponent of the environment.
On the contrary, the report helps dispel any uncertainty about the existence of widespread and serious harm to animal populations in the context of the Colombian armed conflict. It found that, during the period studied (2017-2026), at least 100,252 animals have been affected in the context of the armed conflict in Colombia.

title: Environmental Justice Starts in City Hall
content:
‘Whose Movement Is It?‘, a series co-produced by NPQ and the Environmental Justice Oral History Project, is a call to action for those at the forefront of environmental justice decision-making, drawing on insights, hopes, and visions for the future from some of the foundational women organizers of the environmental justice movement.
The United States used to spend an average of about three billion dollars in weather disasters per year. Over the last five years, that average has climbed to 18 billion annually, with 28 billion in 2023 alone. Cities are at the forefront of the destruction, facing more environmental pressure than they’ve seen in the last 50 years. In the past year, floods have shut down subways and highways in New York, heat waves have overwhelmed power grids in Austin, and wildfires in Los Angeles have choked entire regions with smoke and heat; all issues that have significant implications for local infrastructure.
Environmental justice depends on shifting that power upstream by making community input part of decision-making, rather than asking them to react after the fact.
State and local governments account for roughly 75 percent of public infrastructure spending in the United States, and zoning authority largely rests with municipalities. Cities decide where housing is built, where industry operates, where waste facilities are placed, and which neighborhoods receive flood protection or transit expansion. With this in mind, and in the face of newer and harsher climate disasters, cities will increasingly need to use their authority to adapt to an ever-changing future of climate change, a responsibility that carries with it the weight of decades of infrastructural inequity. This also means cities will need to do a better job of centering community voices and input in their processes, from the start rather than as an afterthought or checkbox at the end of decision-making.
Where Climate-Preparedness, Community Input and Development Clash
The agencies responsible for decades of flood-vulnerable growth are now deciding how to protect against it. In Houston, the same planning commission that approved dense residential development in flood-prone corridors also oversees the city’s 2017 post-Hurricane Harvey resilience investments. The situations are similar in cities like Charleston, South Carolina—now tasked with implementing resilience strategies like the Dutch Dialogues Charleston as a citywide flood mitigation effort. New Orleans and other low-lying coastline parishes in Louisiana, once the trail of plantation slavery, are now serving as a pathway for climate disaster, and so many more. Localities are being forced to carry the responsibility of responding to growing environmental strain while building resilience to ever-worsening climate disasters while guiding economic and infrastructural growth. This dual responsibility can force cities to make high-stakes choices in the blink of an eye, a process that often contradicts the participatory planning needs of the communities they serve. When the focus is on expediency— how fast can debris be cleared, how quickly can funds be distributed, how quickly can new housing be built—the communities most affected by these quick choices are left out of the decision-making process.
And when community input is limited to late-stage hearings or short public comment periods, the direction has already been set. Environmental justice depends on shifting that power upstream by making community input part of decision-making, rather than asking them to react after the fact.
When the focus is on expediency—how fast can debris be cleared, how quickly can funds be distributed, how quickly can new housing be built—the communities most affected by these quick choices are left out of the decision-making process.
Historically, the benefits and burdens of economic growth have not been shared evenly; low-income communities and communities of color have faced and continue to face higher exposure to pollution, flooding, and industrial infrastructure, even as cities promote green futures. These decisions have intergenerational effects on air quality, housing stability, property values, and public health outcomes. This can be seen in the Snow Hill neighborhood in Roseboro, NC, where Sampson County’s 1,300-acre municipal solid waste facility, equivalent in size to 990 football fields, is the direct result of rushed and racialized planning. Snow Hill has campaigned for over 50 years against North Carolina’s largest landfill. Residents demanded the County Board of Commissioners address the asbestos and toxic sludge being dumped, reportedly causing shortness of breath and headaches, while water pollution has plummeted residents’ land values. However, the Board sidelined their concerns as they favored the economic benefits of the facility as a funder of local fire and ambulance services.
A very different part of the country, , experienced a very similar problem with missing community participation in what became one of the biggest water crises in the country. Without warning or consultation, and as a cost-cutting measure for the city, Flint residents saw a switch in their water source from Lake Huron to the more corrosive waters from the Flint River. What followed was the corrosion of pipes, seeping lead into drinking water, and resulting in years of poisoning thousands of already vulnerable people.
