As federal funding becomes less consistent amid longstanding environmental harm and new climate threats, the clear path forward for municipal governments is to move from consultation to collaboration, shifting their priorities from developer-driven to community-driven. This is a practice that acknowledges that communities do, in fact, know what’s best for themselves; after all, it is the residents who know best where traffic and pollution are concentrated and where health burdens are the highest.
Municipal governments hold real power over how environmental risk and protection are distributed across neighborhoods, and right now that power matters more than it has in decades.
Self-Determination Across Cities
Across the country, cities like Baltimore are growing and redeveloping under banners such as sustainability and revitalization, doing so with a focus on co-creation and community-ownership. Organizations like Climate Mayors, C40 Cities, and ICLEI are re-committing their infrastructural and economic development towards a green future.
And community-based organizations are more than ready to take up the torch of facilitating those partnerships. In New York City, UPROSE Brooklyn has spent years building climate resilience plans in the Sunset Park neighborhood grounded in residents’ knowledge of the waterfront, the area’s industrial mix, and the community’s vulnerabilities. Those plans have shaped citywide climate policy from the ground up.
Another example we can look to is Minneapolis. The Green Zones program targeted North and South Minneapolis, the neighborhoods carrying the heaviest pollution burdens, and gave residents formal decision-making roles in setting priorities for tree canopy expansion, cleaner transit, and industrial pollution reduction. The city funded community liaisons, translated materials, and held meetings in neighborhood spaces rather than the city hall. And in Portland, OR, the city’s Environmental Justice Action Plan requires city bureaus to consult with frontline communities before finalizing environmental decisions, embedding community review directly into the bureaucratic timeline rather than appending it at the end. These partnerships work because they begin before decisions are made.
Municipal governments hold real power over how environmental risk and protection are distributed across neighborhoods, and right now that power matters more than it has in decades.
With the federal government pulling back from environmental enforcement and climate funding, cities are absorbing responsibilities that used to be shared. Community input must be built into the early design of zoning changes, redevelopment plans, and resilience strategies. Community input is not a procedural nicety; the communities most exposed to environmental harm are also the ones who understand it most intimately. Giving them real power in these decisions is not just the equitable choice. It is the smarter one.

title: Por qué las guacamayas rojas dejan morir a sus crías y cómo una científica peruana intenta salvarlas
content:
Las guacamayas rojas son aves tropicales emblemáticas cuyas poblaciones están disminuyendo. Para cambiar el destino de la especie, los científicos están trabajando para contrarrestar un método de crianza letal que condena a muchas crías a la muerte.
Parker ni siquiera había abierto los ojos cuando una mano lo arrebató de su nido.
Era una mañana de lunes de noviembre de 2018 en la Reserva Nacional de Tambopata, en lo profundo de la Amazonía peruana; la cría, todavía sin plumas, estaba débil y baja de peso, apenas más larga que un dedo medio. Era el menor de cuatro hermanos y, por ello, estaba casi con toda seguridad condenado a morir de hambre.
Al pie del árbol se encontraba Gabriela Vigo-Trauco, la científica peruana que orquestó este rescate.
Después de estudiar a estas aves por más de dos décadas, Vigo-Trauco había descubierto que las guacamayas rojas dejan morir de hambre a sus crías más jóvenes a propósito.
La científica de la Universidad Texas A&M pudo comprobar que casi ninguna de las terceras y cuartas crías en nidadas de varios huevos sobrevive, y que alrededor del 25% de las segundas crías sufre la misma suerte.
Este método de crianza brutal fue, en su momento, una estrategia de supervivencia.
Ahora, se ha convertido en un obstáculo importante para la recuperación de esta especie en declive, víctima de la caza furtiva y la tala, las cuales han llevado a una de sus subespecies al borde de la extinción en todo México y Centroamérica.
Este método de crianza brutal fue, en su momento, una estrategia de supervivencia.
Ahora, se ha convertido en un obstáculo importante para la recuperación de esta especie en declive, víctima de la caza furtiva y la tala, las cuales han llevado a una de sus subespecies al borde de la extinción en todo México y Centroamérica.
En 2017, Vigo-Trauco puso en marcha una misión de rescate muy poco habitual, y fue gracias a esa estrategia que dio con el polluelo al que le dio el nombre de Parker.
Su objetivo era reclutar parejas de guacamayos rojos silvestres para que actuaran como padres adoptivos de las crías condenadas.
Al convencer a las aves silvestres de asumir esta tarea, esperaba probar una nueva vía de salvación para las crías desatendidas de Perú, y para la especie en su conjunto.
¿Por qué las guacamayas rojas descuidan a sus polluelos más pequeños?
Es imposible no ver a las guacamayas rojas. Su plumaje carmesí resalta sobre el verde del bosque, y sus graznidos se escuchan mucho antes de verlas.
Cada hembra puede poner hasta cuatro huevos por temporada, pero por lo general solo una o dos crías llegan a volar fuera del nido.
"Los padres, y en particular la madre, dejaban de lado [al más pequeño]", afirma Vigo-Trauco, codirectora de The Macaw Society, una organización peruana de conservación que reveló este comportamiento tras instalar cámaras en los nidos en 2007.
"El polluelo pasa frío y grita; cuando llega el padre, alimenta a la madre y a las [primeras y segundas] crías, pero deja al tercero gritando".
No se observó acoso entre hermanos ni que estuviera relacionado con la disponibilidad de alimentos en el área. Entonces, ¿por qué descuidan los padres a sus crías más pequeñas?
Vigo-Trauco opina que a los padres les resulta difícil atender a crías que se encuentran en etapas de desarrollo distintas. Incluso una diferencia de cuatro o cinco días en la eclosión puede ser determinante, porque los polluelos necesitan regímenes de alimentación, hasta temperaturas de nido, muy distintas.
Los padres se ven obligados a elegir, explica. Si se esfuerzan demasiado por alimentarlos a todos, corren el riesgo de que ninguno sobreviva.
Cómo ayudan los padres de acogida de animales silvestres
Para las poblaciones relativamente saludables de guacamayas rojas de la Amazonía peruana, la pérdida de los polluelos más jóvenes tiene menos repercusiones.
Pero en países donde los conservacionistas pelean en contra de cazadores furtivos y madereros por la supervivencia de cada ave, Vigo-Trauco dice que la muerte de así sea un puñado de polluelos es un desastre.
Criar a mano a los polluelos rechazados es una solución posible.
Sin embargo, pueden pasar entre un mes y medio y tres meses hasta que puedan emprender el vuelo.
Además, los loros criados en cautividad tienen tasas de supervivencia notoriamente bajas: les cuesta alimentarse en libertad, identificar a los depredadores y formar bandadas.
Por eso es que el equipo de Vigo-Trauco recurrió a la idea de usar padres adoptivos silvestres.
Después de capturar a Parker en 2018, el equipo de Vigo-Trauco lo alimentó a mano en su estación de campo durante tres semanas, siguiendo un horario riguroso de intervalos de dos horas.
Igualmente, examinaron los nidos del bosque para encontrarle al polluelo una familia adoptiva adecuada que le enseñara a desenvolverse como un ave silvestre.
Esta técnica había sido probada anteriormente por avicultores que criaban guacamayas en cautividad —entorno donde las condiciones están controladas y el intercambio de nidos implica simplemente cruzar un pasillo con el polluelo—, y también se basa en experimentos realizados con otras aves silvestres, como las cotorras hombroamarillo en Venezuela durante la década de 1990.
Finalmente, el 22 de diciembre se puso a Parker en un nido nuevo y su madre adoptiva, Tambo, empezó a acicalarlo de inmediato.
Pocos meses después, pudo emprender el vuelo. Fue apenas el cuarto polluelo en conseguirlo después de décadas de observaciones de nidos silvestres en Tambopata.
El equipo obtuvo resultados parecidos con otros 25 polluelos rescatados entre 2017 y 2019.
Otros tres fueron adoptados con éxito, pero no lograron independizarse (ya que murieron a causa de un rayo, un depredador y una enfermedad).
Ya en 2019, Vigo-Trauco se sentía más segura: "Me sentía como si estuviera jugando ajedrez: moviéndome de un lado a otro para ver qué era posible".
Las deficiencias del sistema de acogida
Aunque la crianza en condiciones silvestres facilita el avance, trae consigo muchos desafíos.
Es una labor costosa.
Durante su experimento de tres años en Tambopata, Vigo-Trauco pudo contar con fondos suficientes para cubrir los salarios, el alojamiento y el equipo de un equipo de 20 personas.
Pero dice que que una iniciativa así de ambiciosa "no es fácil de replicar".
Además, es una tarea difícil de llevar a cabo.
Rony García-Anleu es director de investigación biológica de la Wildlife Conservation Society en Guatemala.
Fue pionero en la implementación del método de adopción en las últimas poblaciones de guacamaya roja que quedan en el país y coautor del artículo de Vigo-Trauco sobre la crianza por padres adoptivos.
Sin embargo, la última vez que el equipo de García-Anleu introdujo un ave en un nido de acogida en Guatemala fue en 2019.
La crianza por padres adoptivos en estado silvestre requiere de una sincronización perfecta, según cuenta.
Es necesario adentrarse kilómetros en la selva para localizar un nido con un polluelo en peligro y, después, encontrar una pareja con un nido adecuado que esté vacío o uno que contenga un polluelo de edad parecida.
En cambio, su equipo les enseña a las guacamayas a volar, a alimentarse y a establecer vínculos sociales dentro de una jaula de grandes dimensiones, para después liberarlas cuando están listas.
Volando hacia adelante
A pesar de sus defectos, la técnica de crianza en libertad está sirviendo de base para el trabajo con otras especies de loros, desde Argentina hasta Centroamérica, señala Vigo-Trauco.
Además, desde 2020 ha estado probando una variante: prescindir por completo de la fase de crianza a mano y trasladar los polluelos de un nido a otro tan pronto como nacen.
Este nuevo enfoque exige un mayor seguimiento, pero necesita menos cuidados intensivos para los recién nacidos, lo que reduce los costos operativos.
De igual manera, ya ha dado resultados positivos en el segundo año del proyecto: se logró intercambiar con éxito los polluelos de dos nidos —cada uno con dos crías de edades muy dispares— para que los padres pudieran criar a dos polluelos de edad similar.
Vigo-Trauco cree que esto podría abrir la puerta a fomentar esta práctica en lugares con menos recursos.
"Es gratificante ver que nuestra población, relativamente más sana, nos permitió convertirnos en una fuente de conocimiento para otros", afirma Vigo-Trauco.
En cuanto a Parker, logró dejar el nido y alzar el vuelo.
El equipo de Vigo-Trauco volvió a verlo en septiembre de 2019; ya era un guacamayo joven y seguro de sí mismo que volaba junto a sus padres adoptivos y su hermano.

title: SPOTLIGHT: Health policy trailblazer Precious Matsoso credits patience, faith and The Beatles
content:
Leading negotiations on the world’s first pandemic treaty, South African health policy trailblazer Precious Matsoso dealt with “occasional adversarial and intense engagements” by bursting into song. In her melodious church voice, Matsoso sang All You Need Is Love by The Beatles, imparting a message of co-operation to delegates from 194 countries gathered in Geneva, the headquarters of the World Health Organization (WHO).
She recalls: “It was very funny because a Brazilian delegate was saying, ‘Why are we treating each other like this?’ And that’s when I sang that song.” There was also a moment, she says, where she sang the theme song of the movie Mission Impossible.
After 30 years of negotiating health policy on national and global levels, Matsoso says: “When elephants fight, the grass suffers. Here, patients suffer.” She is referring to vulnerable sick people slipping between the cracks, with life-and-death stakes, as health sector stakeholders clash.
Following her three-year tenure as co-chairperson of the International Negotiating Body for the WHO Pandemic Agreement, earlier this year TIME magazine named Matsoso on both its TIME 100 Health 2026 and 100 Most Influential People in the World 2026 lists.
A collective refusal
In her acceptance speech, Matsoso distilled the aim of the pandemic treaty as “a collective refusal to repeat the devastation and inequities we witnessed during Covid-19”.
Driven by the memory of how African countries were pushed to the back of the queue for diagnostics, protective equipment and medicine during Covid-19, the deliberations saw her speak up for equitable access to (and local manufacturing of) pandemic-related health products.
In her speech following the TIME accolades, she added: “[The world] had vaccines in just under a year, an unprecedented achievement in research and development. But half the world, notably Africa, lacked access to diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccines. That was not an accident. That system was designed for charity after the fact, not equity from the start.”
This, she said, is what the pandemic agreement intends to fix.
The pandemic treaty was adopted in May 2025 with a working group still drafting final aspects such as an annex on “pathogen access and benefit sharing”. According to a WHO statement in July, this is “a system that enables the rapid sharing of pathogens with pandemic potential while ensuring the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from their use, including pandemic vaccines, diagnostics, and therapeutics”. To Spotlight, Matsoso says this final section is “arguably the most important test of whether global health rules can alter power relations”.
Our interview is happening inside a central city hotel near the Cape Town International Convention Centre, where earlier in the day she delivered a plenary speech on the pandemic treaty at the World Congress on Public Health.
Matsoso’s CV is a long document detailing countless leadership roles in South Africa and at global health bodies, and many awards over the years, including the South African Medical Research Council’s Lifetime Achievement Award last year.
Presently, she heads the Health Regulatory Science Platform at the University of the Witwatersrand, where she works adjacent to Professor Helen Rees, founder and director of the Wits Reproductive Health and HIV Institute and chair of the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority. The two collaborated in the past, shaping South Africa’s medicine landscape in the time of HIV and Aids denialism.
Soweto childhood filled with music, science and uprisings
Across a pin-cushion protea in a vase, Matsoso recounts her Soweto childhood: how it was filled with music and science. Her father, a self-taught mechanic, and her mother, a maths teacher, loved music and their home echoed with anything from Bach and Tchaikovsky to The Beatles and Tom Jones, she says.
At 15-years-old Matsoso witnessed the 1976 Soweto student uprisings, she says, a pivotal moment that forced her into early political consciousness. In high school, she relished science and particularly chemistry, which she excelled at and taught to her classmates.
“There was somebody called William Smith who used to run Star School [science supplements published in The Star newspaper], it was incredible,” she says.
“He made organic chemistry easy. I loved chemistry very much, but also wanted to be in the health sector. And so pharmacy was the nearest thing.”
Matsoso turned down a bursary in computer science at the University of the North in Polokwane (now the University of Limpopo), in favour of studying toward a Bachelor of Pharmacy at the same university, thanks to funding from a family friend in Soweto. But soon campus politics would force her to Cape Town, where she finished her degree at the University of the Western Cape. Reflecting on student uprisings and her activism at the time, Matsoso says: “The police were looking for us, we were on the run. It was a very sad time, I lost my friend, they killed him during detention.”
In time, her other qualifications would include a diploma in Health Management from the University of Cape Town and a Master of Laws in Healthcare Law and Ethics from the University of Dundee in Scotland.
Health reforms and Aids denialism
In 1995, after having worked as a public sector pharmacist, including at Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital in Soweto, and in the private sector as a pharmacy owner, Matsoso was recruited to head pharmaceutical services at the newly established National Department of Health under then health minister Dr Nkosazana Dlamini Zuma.
Here, Matsoso was in charge of managing drug procurement for the public sector, formalising South Africa’s National Drug Policy in 1996, and also for compiling the country’s Essential Medicines List that same year. With pride she recounts: “I was appointed in 1995, and the Essential Medicines List was produced in 1996. The very first one. And since, it has grown from strength to strength.” The Essential Medicines List is a list of medicines that are considered vital for the health of the country, like antiretrovirals or insulin. The health department undertakes to supply medicines on this list to the public health sector, normally via tenders.
In 1998, she stepped into the demanding role of registrar of the Medicines Control Council, today called the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority. Her appointment followed what some described as a purge of senior leadership at the MCC in early 1998. Highly respected leaders like Peter Folb and Johan Schlebusch were forced out following their decision to suspend a clinical trial of Virodene, a toxic industrial solvent pushed by a group of Pretoria researchers as a cure for HIV. (The affair is set out in detail in chapter 8 of Nathan Geffen’s book Debunking Delusions.)
To Spotlight, Matsoso relays four highlights of her time as registrar of the MCC.
Firstly, she says she refused to register Virodene.
“[Professor] Helen Rees was the chair [of the Medicines Control Council] at the time and I was the registrar. I refused. So we didn’t register it,” says Matsoso.
Secondly, she says she approved the antiretroviral Nevirapine for the prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, and thirdly she granted “special permission” for the import of Daphnach, the generic antifungal used to treat oral thrush which often leaves people living with advanced HIV unable to swallow or eat.
“The tablets that Zackie Achmat and them [Aids activists with the Treatment Action Campaign] brought into the country from Thailand, those were difficult times,” she says, chuckling dryly.
And fourth – “the most significant and which almost got me into trouble, was that the MSF [Médecins Sans Frontières] wanted to conduct a study using cheaper generic antiretrovirals in Khayelitsha. So I approved it, and I was told to withdraw the approval by [then] trade and industry minister Alec Erwin. And I said ‘Well, there’s nothing in the law that says I must withdraw.’”
Early Pepfar negotiations
In 2003, Matsoso was involved in negotiations around the establishment of the United States President’s Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar), an aid initiative estimated to have helped save in the region of 26 million lives. The Trump administration has over the last year and a half scaled Pepfar back dramatically.
Matsoso recalls chairing a meeting on the creation of Pepfar in Gaborone, Botswana: “During the Bush era [former American president George W. Bush], there were debates about why the US was establishing a parallel process when we had the Global Fund. I was chairing, and civil society and the US government were fighting in the room. I said: ‘I’m going to kick all of you out of this room, because this meeting is about HIV/Aids. We are not going to do this in my meeting.’ So I was very firm. And the meeting was a big success.”
The global stage beckons
Eventually she was forced out of her job at the MCC.
“So while I was busy, I get a call on behalf of minister Manto [then health minister Dr Manto Tshabalala-Msimang] that I’m basically fired. I think it was just harassment. But anyway, I applied for a job at the WHO as a director of Public Health Innovation and Intellectual Property. That’s why I left and I went to Geneva for six-and-a-half years.” She took along her children, then aged 18 and 13, saying: “My son and daughter were able to integrate, making friends with children from different parts of the world.”
In this role, Matsoso remembers chairing negotiations through the night to establish a health emergency programme, post-Ebola: “It was difficult. We negotiated through the night for two days. On the first day, we finished at about 9pm; on the second day at about 6am…”
A new health minister
Back in South Africa in 2010, Matsoso was appointed director-general of the country’s health department under the new health minister, Dr Aaron Motsoaledi – a job she would stay in until 2019. This saw her commute between the administrative offices in Pretoria and Parliament in Cape Town up to twice a week. A highlight of this time, she says, was driving the establishment of South Africa’s first independent Health Ombud within the Office of Health Standards Compliance. In 2016, Professor Malegapuru Makgoba would assume this role. He has since been succeeded by Professor Taole Mokoena.
Reflecting on creating new health policy, she says: “In legislative drafting, political parties rarely agree. Because you introduce the law, you have to defend it, sell it, and get them to support the legislation. It’s a different set of skills. Sometimes you face people with limited technical understanding who speak politically. You have to maintain your cool, be patient, and help them understand. In both multilateral and national settings, there is one key ingredient: patience. You must be patient.”
After hours
Given her negotiating skills, from where does her grasp of humanity stem? “Well, I go to church,” says Matsoso.
“I’m very spiritual, people don’t know this because it’s my private space. I also have a group of women that I work with. We have an orphanage that we support in Atteridgeville [a township in Pretoria]. So we’ve seen those children grow up. At the end of each year, we throw them a Christmas party and buy them clothes.”
The well-travelled health diplomat cites some of her favourite countries to visit as Zambia and Japan. Reading and books are central, too.
“So in my bedroom, I have shelves of books within easy reach. This is apart from the bookshelves in my study,” she says.
Earlier this year, Matsoso ended her TIME magazine acceptance speech with words that might well capture her ethos: “To science that is rigorous and accessible,” she said. “To policy grounded in evidence and empathy, and to global health systems where every frontline worker is protected, and to a fairer and safer world.” DM
This article was first published by Spotlight – health journalism in the public interest. Sign up to the Spotlight newsletter.

title: Orgullosamente de Tepito: la Galería José María Velasco cumple 75 años
content:
Orgullosamente de Tepito: la Galería José María Velasco cumple 75 años
El recinto conmemorará su aniversario el 7 de septiembre con actividades dirigidas principalmente a niñas y niños.
- Redacción AN / HG
El 7 de septiembre de 1951 abrió sus puertas la Galería José María Velasco y desde entonces se ha dedicado a mantener un vínculo estrecho con el barrio de Tepito y sus habitantes.
Concebida como parte de un proyecto de galerías populares impulsado por Fernando Gamboa (1909-1990), destacado museógrafo, pintor y promotor cultural mexicano, la Galería José María Velasco surgió con la vocación de acercar el arte a comunidades populares. De las tres galerías creadas originalmente bajo este concepto, es la única que permanece activa.
En entrevista con motivo de este aniversario, su director, Luis Miguel León Cornejo, destacó que una de las claves de la permanencia del recinto ha sido la relación que ha construido con sus habitantes. “El barrio se apropió de ella”, señaló al referirse a la manera en que el espacio se convirtió, con el paso de las décadas, en un lugar de expresión para artistas y habitantes de Tepito.
Esta relación estará presente en la programación conmemorativa, que tendrá como uno de sus principales públicos a las infancias del barrio. El lunes 7 de septiembre, de 9:00 a 13:30 horas, la galería abrirá sus puertas para realizar 7, 5 a festejar con los amigos, jornada en colaboración con el Museo de Arte Moderno, el Museo Nacional de Arte, el Museo de Arte Carrillo Gil y el programa cultural Alas y Raíces.
La actividad reunirá talleres y experiencias participativas dirigidas a grupos escolares de la Escuela Primaria Luis G. León, con el propósito de acercar a niñas y niños a distintos lenguajes, colecciones y prácticas de los museos, así como fortalecer el vínculo entre estas instituciones y Tepito.
El Museo de Arte Moderno participará con Postales para un refugio, taller inspirado en la obra La balada de Frida Kahlo, de Alice Rahon; el Museo Nacional de Arte, con Carteles, colores, caminos y una ciudad para compartir, a partir de la exposición México: ruta y destino; mientras que el Museo de Arte Carrillo Gil presentará Sensorialísimo: Un viaje al interior del museo, experiencia vinculada con la exposición Cúmulos y Variaciones. Lecturas de la Colección MACG.
A celebrar con el barrio
Por su parte, la Galería José María Velasco ofrecerá Cháchara de curiosidades, actividad en la que objetos antiguos serán el punto de partida para que las infancias exploren, mediante el juego y la participación, nuevas historias y significados de aquello que forma parte de su vida cotidiana.
La celebración continuará con otras actividades relacionadas con la memoria y la vida cultural de Tepito. Entre ellas se contempla un homenaje al artista Daniel Manrique, cuya trayectoria y trabajo comunitario mantienen una estrecha relación con el barrio y con la propia historia de la galería. Asimismo, se prevé la presentación de un libro sobre Tepito, en fecha próxima.
Para León Cornejo, llegar a 75 años representa reconocer la perseverancia de una institución que ha mantenido sus puertas abiertas y que continúa trabajando de manera cercana con sus públicos. Enfatizó que la conmemoración está pensada principalmente para quienes habitan el barrio y para las nuevas generaciones que hoy se acercan al arte.
El espacio celebrará así 75 años de trayectoria con una jornada dedicada a las infancias y a la comunidad de Tepito, como parte de una historia que ha vinculado al recinto con artistas, habitantes y distintas generaciones.
La Galería José María Velasco se ubica en Peralvillo 55, colonia Morelos, alcaldía Cuauhtémoc, Ciudad de México.

title: Another plan unveiled to tackle long-standing issues in Port Augusta
content:
Taskforce to tackle crime in Port Augusta welcomed by Indigenous elders who remain critical over lack of consultation
In short:
The state government will establish a taskforce to address crime and violence in Port Augusta.
It joins a number of programs that have been attempted since the City Safe Program was axed in 2020.
What's next:
Few details on how the taskforce will function have been released with representatives from several government departments, the local member and the Port Augusta Council to discuss next steps at a closed door meeting on Friday.
Aboriginal leaders and those on the front line of Port Augusta's long-standing crime and violence issues have seen attempts to address it come and go.
As another plan is unveiled, this time a government taskforce, there is optimism but also some frustration over a lack of Indigenous consultation.
Barngarla elder Aunty Linda Dare says crime and violence is on the rise.
"As far as I'm concerned, the state needs to come and sit down with the community, because we are the ones that see it on a day-to-day basis," she said.
"They need to come and sit down, have a forum with us so we can put our opinions across to them."
For Kuyani and Adnyamathanha elder Malcolm "Tiger" McKenzie, the lack of political presence in the neighbouring Aboriginal community of Davenport is an issue that needs to be addressed.
He said repeated invitations to visit the community had been ignored.
From alcohol to illicit substances
The introduction of heavy restrictions on alcohol in 2022 was another positive step that those on the front line welcomed.
Restrictions included limits on the volume of takeaway alcohol as well as an ID scan process to ensure those limits were followed.
However, Alinda Hogg, the project coordinator at Stepping Stones – an Aboriginal drug and alcohol service provider – said the problem had shifted over the past two years as methamphetamine use increased.
She said a colleague told her a client was using methamphetamine as ID was not needed to purchase the substance.
In April this year Port Augusta Council issued a public safety notice, warning residents about the uptick in discarded needles.
Both Ms Hogg and Aunty Linda Dare said methamphetamine was fuelling more crime than alcohol now.
Danger of rhetoric stoking racism
Eli Partridge and Christian Khan, two Indigenous youth advocates, have warned that rhetoric regarding spikes in "crime", "substance abuse" or "anti-social behaviour" can turn into an attack on "young Aboriginal men".
The two 19-year-olds are both part of the Davenport Community Alliance, which was set up in late 2024.
Both say they have lived experience of being profiled, and that it has had a devastating impact on young men.
Mr Partridge says at times he's wished that his skin was lighter.
Mr Khan expressed a similar experience of feeling "ashamed of just walking around".
The pair say there was no easy answer, but praised initiatives like Mangrove Court — particularly as the program involves supporting the family units of young offenders.
"Sit with them, find out why they're doing these things, how we can remove them from that place," Mr Khan said.
History of programs in Pt Augusta
It's not the first attempt to address longstanding issues in Port Augusta.
In 2020 the Port Augusta City Safe Program was axed with the then-council stating that it was not core council business.
The program had run for 11 years, using security officers and a K9 unit to help reduce crime and violence.
Ms Hogg said it was effective at diffusing situations without needing police.
"They'd come in and calm things down … [people] didn't feel as threatened … it's not as confrontational with them," she said.
"It was pretty sad to see them go."
Aunty Linda Dare expressed similar sentiments and said there was an immediate increase in violence once the program was discontinued.
"The K9 guy, he was brilliant and I've got to give it to him," she said.
"He actually stopped a lot of fights."
In 2021 the Port Augusta Responsible Communities (PARC) was established replacing the City Safe Program.
That too lost the support of council before a government changeover in 2022 saw its end.
In 2024 $12 million was allocated for three years, from both the state and federal governments to form the Port Augusta and Davenport Community Safety and Wellbeing Plan.
There has been little detail released as to how the taskforce will function, with representatives from several government departments, the local member and council meeting on Friday to discuss next steps.
The taskforce is designed to complement the work that has already been launched by the state and federal government's Wellbeing Plan.
This includes Mangrove Court, which began in March to address the causes of youth offending.
Both elders say measures to address Port Augusta's level of crime need to have measurable KPIs that can be easily reviewed.
Breaking down barriers
Looking over the derelict buildings and overgrown sporting grounds of the long-defunct training grounds in Davenport fills Tiger McKenzie with deep sadness.
He fondly remembers how the facility and adjoining football and cricket pitch allowed Indigenous and non-Indigenous people to mingle and connect.
"They engage … those non-Aboriginal people engage with Aboriginal people to understand Aboriginal people," he said.
"Then they become mates."
Before its closure roughly 15-20 years ago, Mr McKenzie said it was a great meeting place, with teams travelling from Roxby Downs, Leigh Creek and Copley to play sport and socialise.
On nearby dunes people would "light a fire and cook kangaroo".

title: Mural contra a hidrovia Araguaia-Tocantins é inaugurado no Rio de Janeiro
content:
Quem passa pela região do Catete, na zona sul do Rio de Janeiro, pode se surpreender com um mural de 11 metros de altura que destaca três mulheres representativas da população local formada por indígenas, quilombolas e ribeirinhos no rio Tocantins. A obra foi inaugurada nesta segunda-feira (31) com o objetivo de chamar a atenção sobre os impactos da hidrovia Araguaia-Tocantins para a população local.
O mural é de autoria da artista indiana Shilo Shiv Suleman, fundadora da Fearless Foundation for the Arts. Desde 2012 ela percorre o mundo para registrar a força feminina, denunciar injustiças ambientais e conectar povos. Ao longo dos anos, a Fearless se tornou um coletivo de artistas que já produziu 95 murais.
“Desenvolvi uma metodologia para que a escuta da comunidade esteja retratada no mural produzido e ela possa se reconhecer. Ao mesmo tempo que denunciamos o modelo do agronegócio aqui no Brasil, na Índia, há protestos semelhantes acontecendo contra o projeto de interligação dos rios Ken e Betwa”, contou Suleman ao Brasil de Fato.
Antes de chegar ao Rio, o coletivo de artistas esteve na Vila Tauiry, no Pará, onde produziu, a partir da escuta das moradoras, um mural dedicado ao Pedral do Lourenção, formação rochosa do rio Tocantins ameaçada pelo projeto da hidrovia.
“Um dos nossos principais objetivos é visibilizar essas lutas no Norte do país. Uma vez que o próprio Estado brasileiro é responsável pela construção de inúmeros grandes empreendimentos que desconsideram completamente as pessoas que vivem nesse espaço”, disse a representante da Aliança Chega de Soja, uma das organizações idealizadoras do projeto.
Lilian Terena, representante da Articulação dos Povos Indígenas do Brasil (Apib), elogiou a força da imagem por entender que a presença de mulheres dentro de seus territórios é a solução para a crise climática, além de indicar respeito aos povos indígenas.
“As pessoas podem olhar para a gente e achar que só estamos brigando por um pedaço de terra. Não. Para nós, o nosso território é sagrado. É a nossa vida. E a continuação do planeta vem de dentro dos territórios”, defende.
De acordo com a resolução 169 da Organização Internacional do Trabalho (OIT) obras de grande impacto em populações locais devem passar por consulta desses povos.

title: Women behind the lens: ‘The women are moving towards the church, but it is not the final destination’
content: South African artist Puleng Mongale explores how her childhood church still connects her to the women of her family, not through religion but shared history and memoryThis image, called Holy Gang, combines an image of a church in my mother’s home town, Fateng-tse-Ntsho, in Free State province, South Africa, with self-portraits of me, multiplied to form a group of women. Although at first glance the women are moving towards the church, it is not the final destination.Positioned higher, beyond the church, is what appears to be a rising sun. For me, the sun represents a place where I can meet and be with my ancestors beyond religious limitations, even though they were members of the church and I am not. Continue reading...

title: Jonah: An uncomplicated man surrounded by highly complicated situations
content:
Vea Mafile’o isn’t particularly interested in rugby and jokes that before the advent of AI it would take her a whole afternoon to write an email.
Yet the 44-year-old film director has just completed the most arduous and lucrative assignment of her career – enapsulating the complex life story of the rugby star and Tongan legend, Jonah Lomu.
On Thursday, Lomu, a new documentary about the All Blacks winger, is being released nationwide. UK production company Sylver Entertainment made Lomu, having previously produced documentaries about US tennis legend John McEnroe and British racing driver Damon Hill.
Mafile’o laughs: “I’m not a great talker and a worse writer, one of those people who has to Google-check spelling and even then Google doesn’t recognise the words. I even did that once trying to spell ‘because’.
“I’m artistic and dyslexic. I love drawing, creating, filming, letting things speak for themselves. If I want to tell you something, I’m not going to talk it or write it. I’m going to talk in pictures and say, ‘Look, here it is’.”
For co-director and lifelong rugby fan Irishman Gavin Fitzgerald the project was an obvious fit. Mafile’o arrived later, with trepidation.
“When I say I’m not a rugby fan, I wouldn’t say in my spare time, ‘hey let’s go to a rugby game’, but I do feel some loyalty to it,” she explained.
”My father, Saia Mafile’o, was a First XV coach. He went to school with Amanaki Palavi, who coached Jonah at Wesley College. Later Tonga College played Wesley. I have a little brother who just scored a contract in France, so it has always been in my environment.
“If you’re making stories about people, you need the right people in place. Gavin was encyclopaedic on rugby detail; however, Sylver probably realised that culturally and around Jonah’s family, it would be easier if someone knew all the nuances.
“There have been all kinds of different films made about Jonah that mostly focused on just his rugby and a sanitised narrative of that. I feel like this was the opportunity to share something different about the man.”
Lomu differs from other films about Jonah because his Tongan family is much more present than in previous efforts. Jonah’s brother John Lomu supplied 160 VHS tapes of privately captured family footage, much of it never seen before.
“It was really fascinating because at the time, late 80s, early 90s, it was very rare for there to be a camera around,” Mafile’o said.
“The footage covers a wide scope of people and places, a snapshot of Tongan migration life growing up in South Auckland. We’re very lucky to have the opening of Lotofale’ia, the church he went to. The big Wesleyan church, Tuingapapai, is also there, with a whole lot of rugby games and private, intimate moments. I would love to transcode all the tapes and return them to the family in a more compact form, but that’s another time and budget process.”
More crucially, his mother, Hepi, is interviewed in Tongan. This has never happened before.
In 2019, Mafile’o made a critically acclaimed film, For My Father’s Kingdom, that debuted at the Berlin Film Festival. The film about her father Saia raises thorny questions about the relationship between money and the church in Tongan culture and addresses tensions within Mafile’o’s family, including Saia’s marriage. They attend a Misinale, an annual church festival and fundraising event in Tonga, an experience that almost resembles an open catharsis.
Mafile’o believes Lomu was a similar experience for members of Lomu’s family.
“Everything that I went through with putting my own family on the line, maybe that’s something that they see and understand: I’m not about to throw people under the bus,” Mafile’o said.
“From the first day that I met Hepi to more recent trips to their house, there has been this energy shift; the confidence has grown, she smiles because at first she was weary and pretty dam scary,” she quipped.
The movie does not feature Jonah’s wife Nadine or his two sons; an offer was made for them to be involved, but declined.
On July 29, a historic, free public premiere of the film was held at the Teufaiva Rugby Stadium in Tonga, which Hepi attended. A massive crowd of over 8,000 attended, the first time a major production company has allowed such an event in the Pacific Islands.
Mafile’o believes the event has been “magic” for the Lomu family, “unlocking doors,” reopening old connections and developing new ones. She hopes the story will inspire a new generation. Lomu was a trailblazer for superstar Tongan athletes like Jason Taumalolo and Daniel Tupou.
And though reluctant to admit it, Mafile’o is a trailblazer herself. She was raised on a dairy farm in Hamilton before moving to Auckland. Her first serious job was as a scuba diver before she undertook a Bachelor of Visual Arts at the University of Auckland, graduating in 2006. Her paintings have explored natural and man-made environmental issues in Tonga. An early success was the Digital Kava Circles video installation series featuring interviews she conducted in Tonga in 2006 following the death of King Tāufaʻāhau Tupou IV.
Fast forward a decade and with her sister, Emily, she founded Taro Patch Creative, a Pacific-led creative agency, studio, and community trust in Papatoetoe, Auckland. According to its website, it “functions as a safe, culturally grounded space for Māori and Moana Pasifika artists, filmmakers, and storytellers to connect, run creative workshops, host events, and preserve cultural identity.”
For My Father’s Kingdom (co-directed by her husband Jeremiah Tauamiti) came from the studio, as did Lea Tupu’anga/Mother Tongue, which is about Katherine, a young speech therapist of Tongan and European heritage who lied about her Tongan language skills to work with Siaosi – an elderly Tongan patient with aphasia who lost his ability to speak English. It was chosen from 17,000 submissions to play at the 2024 Sundance Film Festival.
In 2021, Mafile’o etched her name in history as the first Pacific female director of a prime-time TV drama in New Zealand with The Panthers. Set in Auckland in 1974, The Panthers focuses on how a group of Polynesian students and young people of the street, led by Tongan student Will ‘Ilolahia, formed a revolutionary movement called the Polynesian Panthers, drawing inspiration from the American Black Panther Party. The mini-series is set against the backdrop of racial tensions between European and Pasifika New Zealanders during the dawn raids on overstayers under Prime Minister Sir Robert Muldoon.
For one deeply rooted in Tongan culture and storytelling, what was the most interesting thing Mafile’o learned about Jonah Lomu?
“Jonah was a very uncomplicated person, but almost everyone and every environment around him was highly complicated,” Mafile’o responded.
“He always had a drive and a bigger purpose, and I think that’s something people just don’t really understand: that he did the mahi, he did the work, he’s just not naturally talented, he actually was so dedicated, so young.
“When the All Blacks lost the Rugby World Cup semi-final to France in 1999, Jonah stayed out on the field an hour after every player had left, signing autographs. There’s a great humility in that. Or in Tonga we would call that living by one of the four main pillars of Fā Kavei Koula.”

title: Pacific chiefs to attend Māori Queen's second koroneihana
content:
Pacific chiefs to attend Māori Queen's second koroneihana
The bond between the Pacific and the whare ariki o Te Wherowhero (the house of chief Te Wherowhero) continues to grow stronger ahead of reigning Māori Queen Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po's second koroneihana (coronation) celebrations, a Kiingitanga spokesperson says.
Pacific traditional leaders to gather at Maori koroneihana
Ariki (chiefs) from across the Pacific will congregate onto Tūrangawaewae Marae (the official headquarters of the Kiingitanga)later this week, embodying an age-old connection, through whakapapa (genealogy), reo (language) and culture.
Kiingitanga spokesperson Rahui Papa said the ancient connections between the Kiingitanga movement (Māori King movement) and the great houses of the Pacific was solidified nearly 100 years ago.
"In the 1940's, Princess Te Puea went with the then Princess Piki, who later became Te Arikinui Dame Te Atairangikaahu, [and] they travelled extensively across the Pacific," Papa said.
"They met with Queen Sālote and attended the double weddings of her sons. They met with Pa Ariki in the Cook Islands, in Aitutaki, [meeting chiefs] in Samoa, in Tonga, and in various places across the Pacific."
Papa said Te Arikinui Dame Te Atairangikaahu played a role in establishing the South Pacific Forum, now know as the Pacific Islands Forum, which was having its annual leaders meeting in Palau this week.
"In the times of Te Arikinui Te Atairangikaahu, they set up the South Pacific Forum with big names, like Malietoa (Tanumafili II) of Samoa, Ratu [Sir Kamisese] Mara of Fiji, the King of Tonga Tāufaʻāhau Tupou IV. A whole lot of those connections are still happening today."
Papa shared a fond memory from Te Atairangikaahu's silver anniversary in 1991, the familial connection between all the chiefs from across Polynesia, Micronesia and Melanesia who attended the celebration.
"I think it was Uncle Koro Wētere [who] talked about the Pacific Ocean as it laps the shores of all of our cousins countries as well as Aotearoa as the connector. Those waves, that ocean was the connector of us, not just in a physical sense, but in a cultural and spiritual sense as well."
He said Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po has visited and hosted these ariki at various Kiingitanga events during her two years as arikinui, continuing the legacy her tupuna (ancestors).
"Like Queen Sālote and King Tōfa'ahau. With Ratu Mara, for example, and [Ro] Lady Lala [Mara] who have passed, now their son has taken a leadership role within the [Great] Council of Chiefs in Fiji," Papa said.
As the new generation of ariki continue to stoke these fires of connection, Papa believed it could be an example the world could take note of.
"With the wars that are happening around Europe and in other places, the Pacific holds a very, very special key to world nationhood, to world whanaungatanga (relationships).
"I think that there are beautiful examples that we can share with the world in the hopes of bringing everyone into the cultural dynamic that is just part of our DNA."
The ariki are scheduled to be welcomed on Friday morning with Governor-General Dame Cindy Kiro leading the group onto the atea.

title: Amid war, Ukrainian soldiers celebrate love at ritual wedding
content:
Amid war, Ukrainian soldiers celebrate love at ritual wedding
KYIV – As twilight settled on a hillside by the river near the eastern Ukrainian front, two soldiers exchanged wedding vows during a Slavic ritual honouring ancestors and fallen warriors.
Torches lit the way for the 30-year-old groom, known by the call-sign Ice, and the 32-year-old bride, Khomochka, through the woods to the altar as fellow soldiers formed a guard of honour.
“Before our brothers-in-arms and ancestors, before those no longer with us and those who stand before us, we speak this oath,” they said in unison as the ceremony began.
Combining pagan Slavic traditions and Orthodox Christianity, the Mysteriya ritual revived by the Azov brigade serves as the formal ceremonial framework for the unit’s most significant moments.
Branches were draped with colourful ribbons and ritual wreaths, while bonfires blazed high, ready for the military brotherhood to gather around them.
The ceremony also drew uninvited guests.
Right before the event started, several long-distance drones, usually sent to strike enemy territory, buzzed over the gathering.
Celebrations still went ahead.
More than 4½ years into Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, moments of peace and joy have become especially valuable to the soldiers.
“Events like this show that not everything ends with war – that life goes on,” said Dmytro Rogoziuk, the commander of the 60th Brigade.
“To be honest, for me personally as a commander, there are very few events that bring genuine joy.”
‘I swear’
Though they had been legally married for a year, the couple saw the paperwork as a mere formality, compared with the solemn vows they exchanged before fellow soldiers with whom they had fought for a decade and shared life-and-death risks.
Their daily reality was now manpower shortage, Russian offensives, lack of leave, dangerous rotations to the front lines and reports of their friends’ deaths.
While the exact death toll of this war is unknown, various estimates suggest the casualties number in the tens or even hundreds of thousands.
Khomochka managed the unit’s medical service, carrying the heavy load of trying to save the wounded.
“She’s unstoppable, like a live wire,” said Ice, whose blue eyes – which gave him his call-sign – warmed up when he looked at his wife.
He ended his vows saying: “Your honour shall become my honour; your home shall become my home.”
Khomochka repeated, word for word.
With one voice, they declared to the assembly.
“Such is our word, such is our oath. I swear!”
Their friends and brothers-in-arms loudly proclaimed they accepted the oath.
“If we don’t live here and now, then when should we live, when we are in a state of war?” Khomochka said. AFP

title: For the First Time, the World Will Officially Honor Indigenous Women and Girls, Following Decades of Advocacy and Campaigning LED by the Women Themselves
content: For the First Time, the World Will Officially Honor Indigenous Women and Girls, Following Decades of Advocacy and Campaigning LED by the Women Themselves Country Global agnes Wed, 09/02/2026 - 08:46 Issues Human Rights Program 5 Main Image MEDIA CONTACTS Violeta Sánchez I violeta@colmenalab.com I +593 98 496 1077 Fabio Víquez I fabio@colmenalab.com I +506 87089747 *** PRESS RELEASE FOR IMMEDIATE DISTRIBUTION*** For the first time, the United Nations is officially commemorating the International Day of Indigenous Women and Girls, 40 years after Indigenous organizations and movements established September 5 as a day of advocacy and recognition. The solutions developed by Indigenous women in their communities address structural challenges in education, health, well-being, conservation, and culture. This year, the 14th Indigenous Women’s Leadership Award recognizes four initiatives from Fiji, India, Kenya, and Ecuador that use sports and ancestral games as tools to expand opportunities, strengthen participation, and protect well-being, ecosystems, and culture. In New York, Indigenous women leaders from Asia, Africa, the Americas, the Pacific, and the Arctic are meeting with government delegates and civil society representatives to advance three priorities: direct funding, effective participation, and decision-making power. New York, September 2, 2026 – After four decades of organizing and advocacy, Indigenous women are reaching a historic milestone: for the first time, the United Nations will officially commemorate the International Day of Indigenous Women and Girls on September 5. This milestone comes with a political agenda focused on direct funding for their organizations, effective participation in decision-making, and the implementation of international commitments to protect their rights. On this first official commemoration, the International Indigenous Women’s Forum (IIWF) calls on Member States, multilateral organizations, cooperation agencies, and global civil society to translate these commitments into concrete policy action: 1. Ensure direct funding for organizations led by Indigenous women through dedicated mechanisms such as the AYNI Fund, which facilitate access to resources and strengthen their capacity to decide how those resources are used. 2. Implement General Recommendation No. 39 of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) in national legislation and public policies, ensuring effective mechanisms to protect the rights of Indigenous women and girls. 3. Ensure the full and effective participation of Indigenous women in decision-making on governance, conservation, development, and other policies that affect their lives and communities. These demands are being brought to a high-level international forum. On September 9, FIMI and UN Women will bring together in New York official delegates from various countries, representatives of civil society organizations, and Indigenous women leaders from Asia, Africa, the Americas, the Pacific, and the Arctic for a meeting that places these priorities at the center of the international conversation. The agenda responds to deep economic, educational, and labor disparities affecting Indigenous women across different regions of the world. There are approximately 238.4 million Indigenous women worldwide, and 18.3% of them live on less than $1.90 per day, compared with 6.8% of the non-Indigenous population. In terms of education, 53.5% of employed Indigenous women have no formal education, a proportion that reaches 89.9% in Africa. In Latin America and the Caribbean, 82.6% of the Indigenous population works in the informal sector, —31.5 percentage points higher than the non-Indigenous population. “Behind these figures are Indigenous women and girls who continue to face barriers to education, access to health care, decent work, and participation in decisions that affect their lives. Recognition by the United Nations matters because it can help change that reality, but its true value will lie in what happens next: in the policies, resources, and opportunities that reach Indigenous women,” emphasizes Teresa Zapeta, Executive Director of IIWF. These demands are the result of decades of organizing, training, and advocacy. From Indigenous women’s participation in the 1995 Beijing Conference to the creation of their own networks and mechanisms for global coordination, this journey has enabled them to bring their demands to international forums and train new generations of women leaders. Through its Global Leadership School, IIWF has supported capacity development for more than 140 women leaders from 40 countries, and through the AYNI Fund, it supports initiatives led by Indigenous women worldwide to strengthen their autonomy and community-based responses. “We organized because it was necessary to make ourselves visible, to be heard, and to be respected,” says Tarcila Rivera Zea, founder and president of IIWF. This first official commemoration also brings renewed attention to the historical origins of the date and the legacy of Bartolina Sisa, a Bolivian Indigenous leader of the Aymara people who played a central role in organizing and leading Indigenous resistance to colonial rule before being executed on September 5, 1782. Since 1983, Indigenous organizations and movements have commemorated the anniversary of her death as the International Day of Indigenous Women and Girls. The date honors the memory of a woman who exercised political leadership while underscoring a demand that remains as relevant today as ever: that Indigenous women be recognized as leaders with the power to shape the future of their peoples. The Indigenous Women’s Leadership Award recognizes four initiatives turning sport and traditional games into tools for community transformation As part of the first official observance of the International Day of Indigenous Women and Girls, FIMI is presenting the 14th Indigenous Women’s Leadership Award, recognizing initiatives led by Indigenous women that are driving change in their communities and strengthening their capacity for collective action. This year, the award honors four initiatives from Fiji, India, Kenya, and Ecuador that use sport and traditional games to create opportunities, promote well-being, protect ecosystems, advance education, and keep cultural identities alive. The award will be presented on September 5 in Cambodia, at a ceremony led by renowned Indigenous leader and global activist Joan Carling. “Indigenous women and girls are not only confronting the challenges of our time—they are exercising their agency and leadership to create solutions rooted in their knowledge, cultures and communities. Their innovations are advancing the well-being of their peoples, protecting nature and strengthening future generations. As we celebrate the International Day of Indigenous Women and Girls, we must recognize their leadership, support their initiatives and ensure they have the resources and decision-making power to take their solutions further,” says Joan Carling, Indigenous leader and global activist. A soccer field in India, a hockey field in Fiji, a match in Lamu, and traditional games in a Kichwa community in Ecuador may seem like local stories. But the issues they address are global: education, health and well-being, violence prevention, equal opportunities, biodiversity, and climate change. Their experiences show how community-led solutions can offer models for other contexts. INDIA | Soccer as a Gateway to Education In Assam, Girls for Goals, an initiative of Purva Bharati Educational Trust works with Adivasi girls and girls from tea plantation worker communities, using soccer to support their well-being and keep them engaged in school. The initiative supports 100 girls and also works with 200 parents to challenge gender norms that limit their participation. Some participants are also beginning to receive training in advocacy, public speaking, and governance. In 2025–2026, a statewide tournament brought together 58 teams, showing how a soccer field can become a space where a girl can begin to imagine new possibilities for her future. “The field becomes a training ground for public life. When an Adivasi girl learns to call for the ball, she learns to make her voice heard at home, in her community, and in public spaces,” says Bulbuli Gorh, co-director of programs at Purva Bharati Educational Trust. KENYA | The Field as a Space for Collective Care In Lamu, Awer Women Empowerment uses soccer and beach soccer to work with women and girls who have experienced violence and conflict. Here, sport serves as a tool for mental health and psychosocial support: playing together helps restore connections, strengthen self-esteem, rebuild trust, and rediscover a sense of belonging. The field thus becomes a space for collective care, where well-being is addressed not individually, but through the community. “Safety is a precondition for healing. For participants who have experienced violence or war, having a safe and consistent space is necessary before they can begin to process their experiences,” says Alice Atieno, director of Awer Women Empowerment, Kenya. FIJI | Hockey Can Also Protect Ecosystems In Fiji, the iTaukei Women in Conservation Youth Club works with iTaukei girls and young women to expand access to hockey and create new opportunities for participation. Between 2024 and 2025, the number of girls’ teams participating in the national school competition increased from 9 to 15, while some young women are finding pathways to become coaches, referees, and role models for other girls. Through sport, participation on the field becomes connected to ecosystem protection and community engagement: taking the field can also mean gaining the tools to play a more active role in caring for the places where they live. “FHF also recognizes that women’s leadership must grow alongside participation. Training young women as coaches, referees, and officials will help build a stronger and more sustainable pathway for hockey,” says Rosyln Delaivoni, Monitoring and Evaluation Officer at the iTaukei Women in Conservation Youth Club, Fiji. ECUADOR | Ancestral Games as Living Memory In Camuendo a, Kichwa Otavalo community, AWAK is reviving ritual and traditional games such as chunkana, curiquingue, kari atallpa shina, and encender la vela. Over the past eight years, these practices have become a way to strengthen cultural identity while also addressing current challenges such as self-care, community mental health, and violence prevention. The initiative now reaches four Kichwa communities and seeks to pass on knowledge held in the memory of grandmothers to girls and young women. “The game gives us back sovereignty over our bodies and the right to joy, allowing women to take on leadership roles that were previously denied to them,” says Paccha Yarina Moreta Cañamar, coordinator of AWAK. The four recognized initiatives show that Indigenous women are already creating solutions within their communities. The next step is to ensure that those creating these solutions also have direct access to the resources and decision-making power needed to determine how they are sustained, strengthened, and brought to other contexts. Because the solutions already exist; what is still missing is for the women creating them to also have a say in their future.

title: Maasai culture: Keeping pace with change
content:
Dar es Salaam. While many modern societies have traded traditional ecological knowledge for rapid industrialisation, the Maasai people of East Africa remain one of the most culturally resilient communities on the planet.
This comes even amid reports from human rights organisations and Indigenous advocates warning that their traditional pastoral lifestyle and ancestral culture face an unprecedented existential threat, primarily driven by forced displacements, state-led conservation policies, and climate change.
Further, governments argue that human and livestock populations create environmental pressure on vital wildlife and UNESCO World Heritage ecosystems.
Conversely, advocates state that displacing pastoralists severs their spiritual and economic reliance on cattle, summarizing the process as "killing culture"
But even so, the Maasai’s ability to withstand the encroaching pressures of climate change and land loss is not a matter of luck, but the result of a "sophisticated system" of living that treats the environment and human existence as a single, inseparable unit.
At the heart of this resilience are three fundamental pillars or "legs" as explained in an exclusive interview by one of the renowned elders, defining the Maasai philosophy of being, belonging, and becoming.
According to an adjunct faculty member at the Arusha Climate and Environmental Research Centre (ACER), Mr Alais Morindat and a respected Maasai elder, the community’s life is balanced on three vital legs.
The first pillar is Natural Resources, encompassing the trees, water, pasture, and the diverse landscapes of the highlands and lowlands.
“This pillar is viewed as a divine gift, maintained through a deep understanding of the relationship between the sky and the ground,” he said.
The second pillar is Livestock, the primary livelihood and symbol of wealth that depends entirely on the health of the rangelands.
The third pillar, he said, is Society and Culture, the human element that interprets and manages the other two.
The resilience of the Maasai stems from the absolute interdependency of these pillars. Mr Morindat warns that if the pillar of natural resources collapses due to factors like climate change or land grabbing, the livestock pillar will inevitably fall, leading to the total collapse of Maasai society, history, and culture.
“Unlike communities that have abandoned their traditional roots, we the Maasai recognise that our survival is tied to the physical land we occupy; to lose the land is to lose the very "mark" that makes us a distinct people,” he explained.
The sacred bond with the land
A key reason the Maasai believe so fiercely in their specific land—and not "anywhere else"—is their spiritual interpretation of the ecosystem, often described as "God above and God below".
In this worldview, the sky (God above) is the source of influence, while the ground (God below) is where the divine responds through moisture and rain.
“This philosophy creates a closed loop of accountability and reverence; we do not see the land as a commodity to be traded, but as the literal manifestation of God’s response to our needs. This spiritual connection fosters a "conserving community" by nature,” he said.
Director of ACER, Dr Emmanuel Sulle, notes that the Maasai protect trees and natural resources because they know their entire livelihood depends on them. “They have even developed scientific methods for cutting trees and managing pastures through oral knowledge passed down through generations,” he told The Citizen. This, the researcher said, is why mobility was historically their key strategy; “if rain failed in one area, they moved to another, always following the "response" of God on the ground.”
Today, however, as borders and land laws restrict movement, their resilience has shifted toward restoration and "staying put" to heal the land they still hold.
Many outsiders have historically viewed the Maasai as "rigid" or "people of the bush" who are difficult to change. However, Mr Morindat insisted, the reality is that they are "intelligent creatures" who use their three-pillar system to survive under "huge constraints" that would break less organised societies.
“Our resilience is not about refusing to change, but about changing in a way that preserves our core,” insisted Mr Morindat.
Working with ACER, the Maasai are now bridging the gap between indigenous knowledge and modern science. They are adopting more resilient livestock breeds, such as the Sahiwal, which can thrive in smaller geographical areas while providing higher yields.

title: Displaced by a typhoon, Taiwan’s Bunun people fear for the future of their culture
content:
- More than a hundred Bunun Indigenous people were forced to resettle in lowland areas after 2009’s Typhoon Morakot destroyed the only road leading to Tengjhih, their mountain settlement, in southern Taiwan.
- The Bunun, who believe the connection to their ancestors is a pillar of their identity, still wish to return to their ancestral land, saying it would allow them to preserve rituals and traditional knowledge.
- Each year, however, climate change is making rainfall more destructive, wreaking havoc on efforts to rebuild and reopen the road to Tengjhih.
- Indigenous communities have heavily criticized the government’s resettlement program, under which families receive ownership of the apartments they are given, but not of the land on which the buildings stand.
TENGJHIH HAMLET, Taiwan – Nestled high on a mountain slope in southern Taiwan, Tengjhih was a key settlement of the Bunun Indigenous people. Today, however, little remains but memories of the hamlet.
Wild grass sprouts around abandoned houses. Stray dogs have made the empty streets their territory. The children’s toys and chairs scattered across the ground hint at a hurried departure.
Bunun leader Dahu Ismahasan is visibly moved as he looks at what is left of his village.
“When we were children, we played here. We were happy, innocent,” he says.
But “now the village is destroyed,” says Dahu, who is president of the Bunun tribal council.
Dahu and fellow villagers had to leave Tengjhih in the wake of Typhoon Morakot, which killed 755 people in 2009 across Taiwan. The deadliest storm in the island’s recorded history brought torrential rainfall, causing floods and landslides primarily in mountainous Indigenous territories.
At the time, Indigenous peoples accounted for only 2.1% of Taiwan’s total population; yet in the aftermath of Morakot, around 70% of areas deemed unsafe by the government were located in Indigenous territories.
Nobody in Tengjhih died during Morakot, but the typhoon destroyed the only road leading to the hamlet.
With Tengjhih declared a “high-risk zone”, authorities in 2009 began permanently resettling its 150 residents, mostly in surrounding lower-elevation areas like Kaohsiung, Taiwan’s third-largest city, and Liouguei District, Dahu says.
Morakot also displaced other highland Indigenous communities such as the Tsou, the Paiwan and the Rukai. Like the Bunun, they were also resettled in lower-altitude areas.
Typhoon season typically runs from July through September in Taiwan. Climate change has led to more destructive levels of rainfall during these months, wreaking havoc on efforts to rebuild and reopen the road to Tengjhih.
Authorities halted repairs shortly after a typhoon in 2012 washed away a section of the road. Attempts to fix the route faced another setback in 2021, also due to extreme weather.
In 2023, 14 years after Morakot, the road was finally rebuilt. But just a few months later, another typhoon washed it away. Repeated torrential rains, intensified by climate change, saturated the mountain soil, triggering landslides and putting the settlement at risk. In 2025, another typhoon tore away yet another section of the mountainside.
Preserving cultural heritage
Dahu, 60, now lives in Liouguei, but still makes occasional trips to his ancestral home to reconnect with the mountain.
It is a risky journey. To reach Tengjhih, he has to drive along an alternative mountain road that’s narrow and has no safety barriers.
On the way back, he makes a stop at the neighboring hamlet of Erjituan to visit his 85-year-old mother, Clrenge Ismahasan. Erjituan and Tengjhih are two of the three hamlets that make up Baoshan village, home to the Tengjhih Forest Recreation Area.
In a school classroom, Clrenge and two other elderly Bunun women sit at a table drawing as they listen to traditional Indigenous songs.
Dahu’s mother, who moved to Erjituan after Morakot, still has vivid memories of the day the typhoon struck. “That day, it was pouring,” she tells Mongabay. “Everything was flooded. We couldn’t get down from the mountain.”
She remembers that in Tengjhih, people grew corn, millet and beans. “The men would go hunting and come back two or three days later.”
When asked what they miss most about their ancestral home, the women all look down at their drawings and give no answers.
“It’s too painful for them,” Dahu says. “They know they will never see the village again in their lifetime.”
For the Bunun people, the connection to ancestors is a pillar of their identity. Dahu, who now lives in Liouguei, says returning to their ancestral land is important, as it allows them to preserve traditional rituals and knowledge, from hunting and gathering to cultural practices and ways of teaching younger generations.
Nearly 20 years after the typhoon, Dahu and other villagers still regularly write to the local government to make their case. They are still hoping — and fighting — to return home.
“If this village disappears, our people will disappear too,” Dahu says.
Clrenge says she harbors the same wish. “If we can’t return to the village, who is going to pass on these practices?”
Back in Tengjhih, Saminat Maliklan is one of five residents who still refuse to relocate, choosing to stay in her small wooden house that was spared by the typhoon.
As she prepares tea made from leaves picked from her garden, she looks at her 11-year-old granddaughter visiting from Kaohsiung, a city around 60 kilometers away.
To preserve her culture, Saminat, a Bunun cultural guide, teaches traditional songs and the Bunun language to children in the community.
“I pass on everyday Bunun practices to my granddaughter: carrying wood, pulling weeds, planting things,” she says. “And when it comes to language, I try as much as possible to speak with her in our mother tongue.”
Fading connection
Traditionally, young Bunun people would leave the mountains to study at secondary schools and universities in the lowlands, then return to the village to settle down and start families. However, they no longer have that choice.
“Today, when they come back, there is no village and no work,” says 55-year-old Saminat.
Instead, they are uprooted from their ancestral land, she adds: “They have to adapt to an unfamiliar environment, and their ties with elders gradually fade. Our rituals and ceremonies are disappearing.”
Tengjhih’s economy mainly relied on tourism and agriculture. Morakot and successive typhoons have not only destroyed the access road but also forced the government to indefinitely close the surrounding Tengjhih forest area, which supported livelihoods.
For people like Bi’ Ismahasan, who grows tea and coffee in a settlement near Tengjhih and runs a small business catering to tourists, these sources of income are no longer viable.
“When a major typhoon hits us, I have no income for the entire year,” says the 70-year-old woman. “In 2026, I lost my entire harvest. Every year is worse than the previous one.
“I lost all the customers who used to come to visit Tengjhih. Today, I survive on government assistance.”
Her children and grandchildren all now live in Kaohsiung.
“In the cities, young people from the same communities form associations and organize cultural activities so they don’t forget our seasonal rituals,” Bi’ tells Mongabay. “But deep down, I’m afraid that the emotional connection will slowly fade.”
There are also worries of spiritual disconnect. “Our children will no longer be able to bury us in the mountains,” Dahu says. “And our souls will not be able to return to our ancestral land. We will be condemned to wander far away. It’s truly pitiful, isn’t it?”
No prior consultation
In 2005, four years before Morakot, Taiwan passed the Indigenous Peoples Basic Law, of which Article 21 explicitly establishes the principle of “free, prior and informed consent” (FPIC) for Indigenous tribes. It stipulates that the government must consult with tribes and obtain their consent before carrying out development projects on Indigenous lands.
“But in the case of the Bunun, the relocation of the villages was decided without prior consultation,” says Tunkan Tansikian, a Bunun and an Indigenous rights and policy scholar at National Dong Hwa University. “This naturally led to a loss of trust in the government.”
A report published in April 2022 by Taiwan’s Control Yuan, the government’s audit office, recommended incorporating Indigenous perspectives and traditional knowledge into the reassessment of sites at risk from natural disasters. The government responded with reforms, which the Control Yuan summarized in a report in May 2026. However, the document does not list all at-risk settlements and does not name Tengjhih.
Indigenous communities have heavily criticized the Morakot resettlement program. Families receive ownership of the apartments they are given, according to news reports, but not of the land on which the buildings stand. As a result, they cannot sell, expand or rebuild their homes.
“The purpose of the resettlement program was to persuade residents to abandon their mountain villages, which were considered dangerous, in order to reduce safety risks,” Tunkan says.
“For Indigenous peoples, however, land is a core part of their culture, rather than being treated as a tradable and easily relinquished commodity, as mainstream society does.”
The Taoyuan District Office, which oversees Tengjhih, has ruled out allowing the Bunun to resettle in their ancestral home.
“The site is not suitable for habitation due to landslides, and the option under consideration would be to let residents build a temporary shelter there for short stays, without settling permanently,” it tells Mongabay.
Dahu disagrees, saying that authorities have cited no in-depth geotechnical study to justify their refusal, instead simply invoking the risk of landslides.
After years of campaigning, he eventually secured the construction of an alternative road that would provide, at least, access to the settlement. It is scheduled to open in January 2027, he says. Despite the hope it has brought, continued climate instability makes its opening uncertain.
“We still have hope,” Dahu says. “The wind and rain won’t last forever. One day, the road will be better, and the lives of the people here will be better too. We keep that hope in our prayers.”
Banner image: Taiwan’s Bunun leader Dahu Ismahasan stands with the damaged road to Tengjhih in the background on Aug. 6, 2026. Image by Aylin Ho for Mongabay.

title: Eric Terena, el DJ indígena que denuncia el silenciamiento de la Amazonía | ENTREVISTA
content:
- El DJ y productor sonoro y musical Eric Terena fue uno de los ponentes de la conferencia TEDxAmazônia, que se realizó del 27 al 30 de agosto en Baños, Ecuador.
- Pertenece al pueblo indígena terena, de Mato Grosso, Brasil, desde donde empezó una carrera en el activismo y la comunicación para defender los derechos de los pueblos indígenas.
- En entrevista con Mongabay Latam, cuenta que en ese camino entendió que la preservación de los sonidos de la Amazonía y la música indígena contribuyen a cuidar la existencia de los pueblos.
- Ahora lleva DJ sets con estos sonidos a todo el mundo, mientras construye nuevos proyectos destinados a fortalecer a los artistas indígenas.
En un escenario en el que cada ponente contó con un guión y una ficha nemotécnica, Eric Terena improvisó su charla. Era el tercer día del TEDxAmazônia y había escuchado a líderes indígenas amazónicos hablar sobre sus pueblos y las iniciativas que están llevando a cabo para defenderlos de las industrias extractivas. Sintió que el texto lleno de datos científicos que había preparado no tenía cabida.
Leer más | Día Internacional de los Primates: tres proyectos para salvarlos del tráfico y la pérdida de hábitat
Entonces habló sobre el vínculo entre el sonido y el origen del pueblo terena, al que pertenece, en Mato Grosso, Brasil. “El pueblo terena se organiza a través del canto de nuestros chamanes”, dijo ante un público de 200 personas. Vestía un traje negro y usaba una gran corona de plumas rojas que se extendía hasta su espalda.
“La música está relacionada con la cura, hoy queremos que se entienda como el canto sagrado del pueblo terena”, continuó. Sin embargo, las lenguas de los pueblos indígenas, materia prima de esos cantos, están amenazadas por la migración inducida por el cambio climático, como lo confirmaron científicos neozelandeses en un estudio publicado en 2024.
Además, las máquinas que deforestan, minan y extraen recursos de los territorios indígenas generan un impacto sonoro que Terena llama “masacre acústica”. Esta disrupción afecta a los procesos ecológicos, aseguró.
Por eso, desde hace unos seis años se dedica a registrar los sonidos, la música y los cantos de los pueblos indígenas amazónicos para preservarlos y así mantener la continuidad de las culturas, contó en conversación con Mongabay Latam, tras su charla.
Su trabajo en la defensa de los derechos de los pueblos indígenas comenzó mucho antes. A los 19 años se unió al Movimiento Indígena del Clima de Brasil y después se convirtió en miembro fundador de Mídia Indígena, un colectivo de comunicación indígena. Desde ese espacio se vinculó con el diseño de sonido para reportes, películas y campañas.
Después dio el salto como DJ, actividad que le ha servido para hacer “artivismo” y, al llevar los sonidos de la selva a todo el mundo, demostrar que los pueblos indígenas amazónicos existen y siguen defendiendo sus territorios. Ahora, con 32 años, busca crear oportunidades para más artistas indígenas.
Mongabay Latam se reunió con Terena en Baños, Ecuador, donde se realizó la quinta edición del TEDxAmazônia, la primera fuera de Brasil.
