—¿Cómo sonaba el pueblo terena antes?
—El pueblo terena tenía una tradición muy importante: cantábamos y también creábamos nuestros propios medios para cultivar la comida y mantener la sociedad más involucrada colectivamente.
Esto parte de la mitología del pueblo terena, porque Yurikoyuvakái nos sacó de un hoyo y nos enseñó a usar el fuego, a organizarnos, y también nos enseñó la parte más importante, que es involucrarse como una sociedad con dos mitades, que son los xumonó, más asociados a las bromas y a la fiesta, y los sukirikionó, que se enfocan en la estrategia, en entender la tecnología para la construcción de la sociedad indígena terena y dejar un legado milenario de adaptación.
Hoy estamos enfrentando los fuegos y la demarcación de las tierras de los pueblos terena. Antes nosotros teníamos una región muy grande donde vivíamos y ahora vivimos en una reserva mantenida por el Gobierno hasta que el Estado demarque nuestros territorios. Somos 2000 habitantes indígenas en mi comunidad y vivimos en 30 000 hectáreas, no más.
Entonces esto ha cambiado toda la realidad, incluida la preservación de nuestra identidad, porque no podemos manejar nuestros instrumentos, porque no hay más árboles ni la piel para hacer el tambor que guía nuestra danza. No hay animales por cuenta del fuego y por las haciendas y monocultivos cerca de nuestros territorios.
Eso ha cambiado mucho cómo nuestra visión se está adaptando en esta realidad contemporánea que vivimos. A pesar de estos problemas, estamos ahí cultivando y manteniendo laboratorios con jóvenes, por ejemplo de cine, y también haciendo monitoreo de territorio con drones y micrófonos para medir la densidad sonora de nuestros territorios, o sea, avanzamos mucho, pero todavía tenemos mucho por luchar.
—¿Desde cuándo viven en una reserva?
—Desde 1988, cuando la Constitución de Brasil estableció que el Estado debía demarcar y devolver las tierras indígenas en cinco años. Ya pasaron más de 35 años y estamos esperando que la Justicia brasileña nos reconozca legalmente como parte de este territorio. Esta lucha es transversal e involucra muchos saberes.
—¿Eso quiere decir que ha vivido toda su vida en una reserva?
—Yo viví en la reserva hasta los 8 años y después fui a la ciudad, porque mi familia creó una asociación en la capital [Campo Grande], donde creamos la primera institución urbana indígena de Mato Grosso del Sur.
Sigo teniendo una casa en la comunidad igualmente, pero vivo como una doble vida. Voy a la ciudad por la universidad, por el trabajo y por los DJ sets. Regreso a mi comunidad donde tengo una casa especial para grabar los sonidos. Además, hay un estudio para monitoreo de la biodiversidad.
—¿Cómo graba? ¿Se interna en la selva para registrar sonidos?
—Antes grababa con una [grabadora] Zoom. Ahora para el diseño de sonido uso micrófonos y amplificadores para grabar desde los bosques directamente. También invito a artistas para una inmersión y ellos producen música tradicional y también con instrumentos, semillas. Tengo todo lo que necesito para grabar desde hace dos años.
Además, tengo un proyecto de bioacústica con el que se hace monitoreo. Tenemos cajas con micrófonos instalados que capturan no solo sonidos, sino también frecuencias. En la computadora procesamos los datos de las frecuencias y recreamos la densidad sonora del ambiente. Podemos saber si hay fuego o deforestación.
El único problema es que no tenemos muchos fondos para implementarlo en más territorios. Logramos tener esto en nuestra comunidad, pero también en algunas partes de Ecuador para un test.
El próximo paso es conectar la herramienta a internet inalámbrico. Por el momento el único camino es usando el wifi de Elon Musk y no queremos estar con Starlink en estos territorios porque los datos son muy sensibles, principalmente si nosotros estamos identificando frecuencias de mineros, deforestación, motosierras.
—¿Ya descubrieron deforestación, minería?
—En nuestra comunidad no hay minería, pero hay minería amparada por el Gobierno en Corumbá, una ciudad muy cercana. En nuestras comunidades hay deforestación, incendios y también mucho ganado, o sea, eso es complicado porque hace un cambio a un escenario climático devastador.
Las áreas que no están dentro de nuestros territorios están como desiertos, no hay sonidos. Esto empieza a amenazar nuestros territorios porque la invasión avanza ilegalmente. En otros territorios, que antes eran haciendas y que nosotros retomamos, sembramos árboles e hicimos agroforestería. El escenario estaba cambiando, pero para medir el sonido hay que tener puntos referenciales y recién empezamos. Calculamos que en los próximos 10 años sabremos qué cambió.
—¿Cómo se ven esas frecuencias de la deforestación, de la ganadería?
—Tenemos un plugin para medir las frecuencias y podemos ver que la frecuencia está cambiando. En momentos está roja por cuenta del sonido alto y en otras ocasiones está verde porque el sonido es directo.
Lo más complicado es que al estar en una comunidad muy cerca de la parte urbana, a veces tenemos ruidos externos. O sea, esos sonidos externos también están incomodando y cambiando la biodiversidad. Como dije en la presentación, a veces no hay comunicación entre los animales, no hay reproducción y esto daña todo un ecosistema porque estos animales se van a alejar, van hacia un área muy aislada de nuestra comunidad. Este impacto es más inmediato, podemos mirarlo sin este equipamiento.
—¿Qué significa el silencio para el pueblo terena?
—El silencio responde a un mecanismo de silenciamiento. Hay un mecanismo de silenciamiento para destruirnos o perjudicarnos. Para nosotros no hay silencio, hay otro ruido más bajo, hay ruido de la naturaleza. Muchos dicen que van al bosque para estar relajados y escuchar el silencio de la naturaleza, pero la música de la naturaleza es muy alta.
En los pueblos indígenas, a medida que crece la ciudad, que avanza la ganadería, los incendios, hay más silencio. Hay un sonido de desierto, con más vientos, más insectos que están cerca de los monocultivos y que están ocupando el sonido de la naturaleza.
—¿Cómo reacciona su comunidad a su música?
—Les gusta porque la parte más contemporánea ya está en nuestro territorio hace años. Ya hay un forró terena. El forró es un estilo de música para bailar en pareja. También hay otros estilos como el sertanejo de Brasil o el reguetón de América Latina, pero con artistas indígenas. Además, hay otros ritmos dominados por indígenas, quienes están grabando en sus propios idiomas.
O sea, no inventé nada nuevo, pero estoy muy popular porque estaba involucrado en festivales de música electrónica, o sea, estaba haciendo world music y conectando con diseño de sonido, con muchas películas.
La comunidad se siente representada. Mi familia tradicional viene de un grupo de chamanes musicales y mis primos también tienen bandas, grupos de rock, pero no son tradicionales. Yo solo sigo este camino porque tengo una conexión más sagrada con la tradición. También son muy felices porque cuando estoy en Brasil hay fiesta.
—En su música hay sonidos del bosque, hay voces, cantos, ¿qué otros sonidos están?
—Como tenemos micrófonos sensibles, también grabamos, por ejemplo, palos, porque la humedad de cada región puede producir palos que al chocar hacen sonidos diferentes y crean frecuencias especiales.
Con Sarayaku estuve inmerso y aislado grabando un par de días en los bosques con Taki Supay, un rapero indígena, para que no produzcamos solamente rap, sino que el BPM [Pulsos Por Minuto] sea el mismo de la sensación de estar dentro de la comunidad. Sarayaku está como a 90 BPM.
—¿Midió la frecuencia?
—Sí, en el compás, cuando escuchas los pájaros, están en calma, pero con los kuikuro, con los karapó [pueblos indígenas de Brasil] pasó a ser más rápido, como 120 o 130 BPM.
Entonces no estoy dedicado directamente a un estilo. No hago tecno, no hago electro, no hago electronic dance music, yo soy indígena y busco crear música en el ritmo de la comunidad, en el tempo de la comunidad, ya sea que esté en la Amazonía o como ahora que estoy produciendo con músicos de Otavalo [de los Andes de Ecuador], que tienen un ritmo más parecido a la cumbia. Entonces hago arreglos y busco instrumentos que se traduzcan directamente a la identidad del pueblo con el que estamos creando la música.
—¿Cuál es el BPM del pueblo terena?
—Ahora es como 62. Antes coexistía en mayor medida la música de baile en pareja tradicional y la música de los chamanes, que tiene 30, 60 BPM y a veces no tiene constancia, es muy aleatorio.
—¿Cómo reacciona el público a su música?
—¡Dios mío! Las personas me abordan después del concierto y me dicen que nunca escucharon los sonidos de la Amazonía. Se emocionan mucho, es muy impactante porque hay mucha gente que no conoce de la Amazonía, que no sabe de su existencia. Fui a 26 países de Europa y de África, y solo cuando me ven con las plumas se dan cuenta de que la Amazonía y los pueblos indígenas todavía existen. Ahora saben que estamos fortalecidos por la música.
—¿Qué proyectos está preparando?
—En este camino con comunicadores indígenas y otros grupos estuve visitando comunidades de América Latina y escuchando que ha pasado lo mismo, porque ellos estaban perdiendo sus idiomas y necesitaban comunicación para resguardarlos.
Filmamos, grabamos y tenía esta sensibilidad para la música. O sea, después de completar las campañas para ayudar y fortalecer la identidad musical local, empecé a crear estos bancos de sonidos de cada comunidad para, en el futuro, intentar hacer colaboraciones que amplifiquen la lucha con el apoyo de colaboradores externos.
Fue un desafío hasta hace un mes, cuando se concretó un proyecto. Teníamos la idea de crear una plataforma musical y de sonido pública para que el mundo pueda acceder legalmente a los archivos y no sean robados por plataformas de la industria musical que explotan la cultura. Este es un mecanismo para que tengamos herramientas para encontrar sonidos directamente y conectar con las comunidades.
—¿Esta herramienta ya está al aire?
—No, estamos produciéndola junto con Lanceros Digitales. Ellos están programando el diseño de la plataforma, va a ser open source. Son indígenas y creemos que así no vamos a ser distorsionados por la industria.
El proyecto inicial es identificar artistas, chamanes y personas que han hecho música sanadora para cuidar y curar personas. Estamos catalogando sonidos. Vamos a avanzar también a tener una plataforma de artistas, pero no como las plataformas conocidas, que son agresivas, pagan poco y sacan mucha plata. No queremos eso, queremos que todos los derechos sean de las comunidades.
Vamos a tener artistas de toda América, desde Canadá hasta la punta de América del Sur, pero también sabemos que hay artistas en África, estamos hablando con samis del norte de Europa y con gente de Asia también. Intentamos tenerlo para febrero de 2027.
Vamos a coordinar con las comunidades para que ellos no sean dañados en ningún momento. Y quizás si hay algún riesgo, vamos a parar y reconstruir, porque queremos avanzar con las comunidades de América Latina para mantener este legado.
—¿Qué le gustaría hacer en el futuro?
—Tengo otros proyectos, pero este de amplificar y crear oportunidad para otros [músicos] indígenas creo que va a ser un gran proyecto de mi vida para crear un legado en un camino donde las personas van a querer seguir después y también replicar esto en sus comunidades, porque nosotros somos creadores, pero no impedimos que otros también creen.
Los sueños van a seguir. Para mi pueblo el sueño es muy importante para guiar nuestro camino. Yo no soñé hasta ahora qué va a pasar en el futuro, hasta que no tenga un sueño, seguiré en este proyecto.
*Imagen principal: Eric Terena es activista del pueblo terena y DJ. Trabaja con sonidos amazónicos. «La idea es que hagamos canciones, que nos encontremos haciendo revolución musical», afirmó. Foto: cortesía Eric Terena

title: Indigenous ‘turtle women’ help vulnerable reptiles recover in Ecuadorian Amazon
content:
On the banks of the Aguarico River in the Ecuadorian Amazon, a group of Indigenous Siekopai women are combining traditional knowledge and modern technology to help a threatened native turtle recover.
Their efforts center around charapa turtles (Podocnemis unifilis), also known as the yellow-spotted Amazon River turtle, Mongabay Latam’s Astrid Arellano reported. The animal’s populations have declined due to hunting adult turtles, harvesting eggs from nests and pollution from garbage, oil and gasoline.
“Sometimes we see plastic, garbage bags,” Janeth Piaguaje, a Siekopai community leader of the project, told Mongabay Latam. “We also see dead animals floating down the river. We can’t control all of that, but we do make a significant effort to clean the beaches where we work.”
Boat traffic is also eroding riverbanks, and climate change has caused water levels to rise, flooding the flats where turtles make their nests. Charapa turtles are listed as vulnerable by the IUCN, the global conservation authority.
To help the turtles recover, a group of seven Siekopai women, who call themselves Tari Nomiowa’i, or “turtle women,” patrol the riverbanks looking for turtle tracks and nests. When they find nests, the women carefully collect the eggs, a skill Piaguaje said she learned from her father.
“He taught me how to handle the eggs, how to see on what dates and in what months the turtles lay their nests,” she said.
The women document the date, time, location and number of eggs in each nest using the Epicollect5 app, a field data collection tool.
Then they take the eggs to an incubation facility where they are protected from predators, flooding and pollution. Once the eggs hatch, the women continue to care for the baby turtles for another month, feeding them cassava, sweet potato and taro leaves.
Their painstaking work has paid off. Over the 2025-26 nesting season, the women collected 235 eggs and successfully hatched and released 208 hatchlings into the Aguarico River over March and April this year. The group invited the local community, including schoolchildren, to participate in the turtle release and attend workshops.
“A little girl said, ‘I’m going to take care of them, I’m going to tell them not to touch the eggs,’” Piaguaje recalled.
A driving force behind the work of the Tari Nomiowa’i is their culture and the ancestral belief that the turtles are a link between the visible and spiritual worlds, each swimming with protection from Koouwajëo, the spiritual chief, mother and ancestral guardian of the turtles.
“I want Koouwajëo to be proud,” said Piaguaje. “When we protect turtles, we don’t just care for a species; we honor the spirits of the river, strengthen our culture and maintain the sacred pact between our community and nature.”
Read the full story by Astrid Arellano in Spanish here.
Banner image: The Tari Nomiowa’i women collecting charapa turtle (Podocnemis unifilis) eggs, taking data and measuring the nest. Image courtesy of CI Ecuador.

title: Michael Painter put Indigenous land rights at the center of conservation
content:
- Michael Painter, an ecological anthropologist who joined the Wildlife Conservation Society in 1997, spent much of his career working at the intersection of conservation, Indigenous land rights, and rural development.
- In Bolivia, he helped strengthen partnerships with Indigenous organizations in the Gran Chaco and Greater Madidi, including efforts that supported the titling and management of large Indigenous territories.
- Painter later worked within WCS to advance a human-rights-based approach to conservation, including safeguards for research involving people and stronger recognition of Indigenous rights and governance.
- Painter died on February 11, 2026.
In the Bolivian Chaco, the Isoceño Guaraní did not need conservationists to tell them that their land was under pressure. Agricultural settlement was pushing into the region, and their organization, the Capitanía de Alto y Bajo Izozog (CABI), had its own territorial aims. What outsiders could provide was scientific expertise, legal support, money, and access to institutions that could help turn those claims into recognized rights.
Working with the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS), CABI developed the proposal for Kaa-Iya del Gran Chaco National Park, which Bolivia created in 1995. At 3.4 million hectares, it was enormous even by the standards of South American protected areas. CABI became its co-administrator. The partnership also helped develop a mechanism for securing Indigenous land under Bolivia’s agrarian reform law. It was used to title 273,000 hectares for the Ayoreode and 560,000 hectares for the Isoceño Guaraní, as well as land for 43 Chiquitano communities. WCS says the process helped establish precedents for Indigenous land titling elsewhere in Bolivia.
Michael Painter arrived at WCS in 1997 to direct the Kaa-Iya project. For an ecological anthropologist, its implications were hard to miss. Conservation did not have to mean setting land aside and then persuading the people living around it to cooperate. Indigenous organizations could be conservation partners in their own right, with territorial goals, political interests, and knowledge of their own. A useful role for an organization such as WCS was sometimes to strengthen their ability to deal with governments, companies, donors, and conservationists themselves.
Painter, who died on February 11th, 2026, had reached that point by a circuitous route. He earned a Ph.D. in anthropology from the University of Florida and joined the Institute for Development Anthropology in Binghamton, New York. He studied rural development: settlement in Bolivia’s lowlands, the Chapare development program, land degradation, class formation, and the forces determining who used land and how. In 1985 he published a study of ethnicity and social class in Santa Cruz; other work examined agricultural development and settlement in the Chapare.
He also worked as an adviser to Botswana’s Department of Wildlife and National Parks, evaluating community-based natural-resource management. The subjects shifted, but his preoccupation did not. Land use was shaped by economics and power as much as by ecology.
In 1995 Painter and William Durham of Stanford University edited The Social Causes of Environmental Destruction in Latin America. The book rejected explanations of environmental damage that rested mainly on population growth. Unequal access to land, poverty, concessions granted to powerful interests, and other social relations could create incentives for destructive land use. Social equity, the editors argued, had ecological consequences.
Kaa-Iya gave Painter a chance to apply such thinking. He was interested not simply in consulting Indigenous people, but in who possessed the information and authority needed to make decisions. Indigenous technicians were trained to gather and interpret ecological data. An organization able to produce evidence of its own was in a stronger position when governments or companies arrived with competing claims about what should happen to its land.
The approach carried into the Amazon. Painter became WCS country director in Bolivia and later Peru, then directed its Amazon program. Around Greater Madidi, WCS worked with protected-area authorities while also supporting Indigenous organizations seeking control over neighboring territories. By 2008, 372,000 hectares of the Tacana I Indigenous Community Land had been titled, most of it alongside Madidi. Other work involved Lecos territories and the management of Madidi and Pilón Lajas.
The paperwork could be difficult and the stakes high. Zulema Lehm of WCS Bolivia remembered Painter guiding colleagues through the “complex process” of obtaining the title for Tacana I. Years later, she was still using materials he prepared on research ethics when training WCS partners.
Painter eventually moved from running field programs to trying to change some of the practices of conservation organizations themselves. In 2009 he joined WCS in New York, where he worked on Indigenous partnerships, livelihoods, rights, and what became a human-rights-based approach to conservation. He helped establish the Conservation Initiative on Human Rights and represented WCS in it. He also helped create the organization’s Institutional Review Board for research involving human subjects and chaired it from 2018 until 2025.
This was not always an easy fit for an institution built around wildlife science. Conservation projects had political consequences whether scientists intended them to or not: they affected access to land and resources and could strengthen one group at the expense of another. Painter argued that conservationists therefore had to pay attention to rights, governance, and the quality of people’s lives.
In a 2014 commentary for Mongabay, he argued that protected areas remained essential but were insufficient. Conservation also depended on what happened beyond their boundaries, particularly on lands managed by Indigenous peoples and local communities. Recognizing their land and resource rights could both protect biodiversity and build political support for conservation.
In later writing, he argued that conservationists and human-rights advocates had interests in common. In a Scientific American essay published in 2017, he described biodiversity loss as a “double injustice”: ecosystems were degraded, but so were the lives and livelihoods of Indigenous and traditional peoples who depended on them.
He was no romantic about partnerships. Years of development work had made him skeptical of projects that assumed conservation and economic development would naturally reinforce one another. Interests could clash. Participation could be promised while decisions remained with outsiders. The harder task was to build institutions capable of negotiating those disagreements.
Painter briefly left WCS in 2015 for the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, where he worked on its Andes-Amazon Initiative. He returned two years later and, with David Wilkie, helped lay the groundwork for what became WCS’s Rights and Communities Program.
Colleagues repeatedly described the same manner behind this work. Lilian Painter recalled his “pragmatism, patience and generosity” and his ability to navigate difficult situations and build alliances. John Polisar, whose jaguar work in the Gran Chaco followed years later, said much of it might not have been possible without the partnerships Painter had helped put in place.
WCS colleagues did not learn of Painter’s death until late August, more than six months after he died. Its announcement described a man who had become a sounding board for staff wrestling with social research, Indigenous partnerships, and questions of rights. Lehm put it more simply. She had grown accustomed to knowing that Mike was there, “always available to kindly answer any questions.”

title: No More Speeches, Pres Ali: Put Guyana’s Indigenous Wealth in Indigenous Hands
content:
As Guyana commemorates Amerindian Heritage Month, the nation must pause and reflect honestly on the condition, aspirations and future of its First Peoples. Last evening, I listened carefully to the address delivered by President Irfaan Ali at Whirl Wind Village, Sophia. While speeches and expressions of appreciation for Indigenous peoples are important, our First Peoples deserve far more than ceremonial words. They deserve meaningful action, economic empowerment, ownership and opportunities capable of transforming their communities for generations to come.
Amerindian Heritage Month should not be reduced to a period when politicians visit Indigenous communities, deliver speeches, celebrate their culture and make promises. It must be a time when the country asks a fundamental question: What tangible economic opportunities are being created to place Indigenous people in control of their own future?
One area where the Government of Guyana can make a significant difference is Indigenous tourism ownership. Guyana possesses extraordinary natural beauty, wildlife, rivers, forests and Indigenous cultures with enormous potential for sustainable tourism. Yet too often, the greatest economic benefits from tourism flow to businesses and investors from outside the communities where these attractions are located. That approach must change.
The Government should establish an Indigenous Tourism Ownership Programme designed in consultation with Indigenous leaders, village councils, communities and other stakeholders. The objective should be straightforward: Indigenous communities should not merely participate in tourism; they should own it.
Under such a programme, the Government could provide initial capital financing, technical assistance, training and business support, while the Indigenous village or community retains ownership of the enterprise. The programme could support village-owned eco-lodges and guest houses, tour boats and river excursions, birdwatching and wildlife businesses, Indigenous craft and cultural shops, fishing and angling tours, jungle and forest excursions, cultural and heritage experiences, traditional food and culinary tourism, and nature tours, community transportation services, camping and adventure-tourism facilities, as well as traditional arts, music and cultural performances.
These would only be starting points. The communities themselves should determine which businesses are appropriate for their environment, culture and aspirations. Nobody in Georgetown should be deciding from an office what an Indigenous community needs or what kind of enterprise can succeed in that community.
This is the fundamental change Guyana needs. Our Indigenous brothers and sisters should not always be treated as beneficiaries of Government programmes. They should be owners, entrepreneurs, employers and investors in their own communities.
Imagine a village owning an eco-lodge where visitors stay. The village owns the property and the boats. The village employs the tour guides, produces and sells its crafts, provides the food and conducts the cultural tours. The village earns the revenue, and that revenue is reinvested into education, healthcare, infrastructure, youth programmes and further economic development. That is what empowerment should mean.
The Government has an important role to play, but Government assistance must not become Government ownership. Initial capital could come through a dedicated Indigenous Tourism Development Fund, providing grants or low-interest financing for viable community-owned projects. However, the Indigenous community must retain ownership and have a meaningful say in how the enterprise is managed.
Such a programme would require proper governance, transparent accounting, professional training and business development support. Indigenous entrepreneurs should receive training in hospitality, accounting, marketing, digital commerce, tour management, environmental conservation and customer service. The Government can also assist communities in accessing international tourism markets and developing partnerships with airlines, hotels, travel agencies and online booking platforms. But the Indigenous community must remain at the centre of the enterprise.
Any serious Indigenous development programme must be designed with Indigenous communities, not merely for them. The Government must sit down with village councils, Indigenous leaders, young people, women, entrepreneurs, traditional leaders and community members and ask what they want for their communities, what businesses they believe can succeed, what resources they already possess, what support they need and how their culture and traditions can be protected while creating economic opportunities.
Development cannot be imposed from Georgetown. It must be built in partnership with the communities themselves. The people who live in these communities understand their land, rivers, forests, traditions and challenges better than any consultant or politician.
There is also another issue that must be confronted honestly. Our Indigenous people must not become political decorations. Every political party should respect the fact that our First Peoples are citizens of Guyana whose dignity, livelihoods, culture, land, education and economic future must be placed above partisan politics.
Indigenous communities should not only be remembered during elections, political rallies or Heritage Month celebrations. They deserve attention every day of the year. Guyana must move beyond the politics of photographs, speeches and promises. Our Indigenous people deserve measurable results. They deserve businesses, jobs, modern infrastructure, quality education, healthcare, reliable transportation and connectivity. They deserve opportunities for their young people to remain in their communities because they can build prosperous lives there. Above all, they deserve ownership and dignity.
The Government of Guyana has an opportunity to demonstrate that Amerindian Heritage Month can become more than a month of speeches. Let it become the beginning of a new national policy of Indigenous economic ownership. Let the country establish community-owned tourism enterprises, put capital into the hands of Indigenous communities, train Indigenous entrepreneurs, create opportunities for Indigenous youth, strengthen village economies and protect Indigenous culture and the environment while creating sustainable income.
When tourists travel into Guyana’s hinterland, the Indigenous communities whose lands, rivers, forests and cultures make the experience possible must be among the principal owners and beneficiaries of that tourism economy. It is not enough for outsiders to profit while the communities receive occasional employment, small contracts or ceremonial recognition.
President Irfaan Ali and the PPP Government have an opportunity to move from words to action. Amerindian Heritage Month should not end with another speech. It should begin with a programme, a budget, a timeline and measurable results.
Our First Peoples have contributed to the story of Guyana since long before the modern State existed. Their culture, knowledge, traditions and relationship with the land are an indispensable part of our national identity. We must therefore ensure that their future is not determined by dependency, political promises or outside ownership.
Let Guyana build Indigenous communities that own, operate and benefit from the economic opportunities within their own homeland. Let the country stop repeatedly failing its First Peoples. Let their livelihoods, culture, dignity and future be paramount.
Amerindian Heritage Month must be about more than remembering our First Peoples. It must be about empowering them and not to subject them.
Pt.Ubraj Narine, JP, COA
Former Staff Sgt.(GDF), Mayor
City of Georgetown

title: After two years on the throne, Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po is forging her own path
content: Today is the second day of the second anniversary of the coronation of Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po. Known as Koroneihana, the four-day event sees people from around the country, and the world, gather together at Tūrangawaewae Marae to celebrate the coronation of Te Arikinui. Yesterday, hapū and iwi from around Tainui waka gathered to honour their loved ones. Today, iwi from across Aotearoa will do the same. Tomorrow, leaders from around the world, MPs and other politicians will arrive. On Saturday, Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po will deliver a much-anticipated speech to the nation. Following her father’s death in August 2024, Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po spoke publicly for the first time at last year’s Koroneihana. She used the opportunity to outline her priorities as the successor to her father’s throne. The economic prosperity of Māori was the main theme, signalling what was to follow over the next 12 months. Since her father’s passing, Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po has continued with the expected roles and responsibilities of the Kīngitanga. The regular annual events of poukai throughout Waikato, manu kōrero and kapa haka competitions, gala dinners, and Koroneihana preparations have consumed much of her time since her ascension to the throne. But Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po has also set her own direction for the Kīngitanga movement. A highlight of her reign so far has been the launch of an iwi-backed $100m sovereign wealth fund, announced at the Ōhanga ki te Ao economic summit held in Waikato last November that brought together leaders from Australia, Europe, North America, Asia, and the Pacific. “Every opportunity must deliver real outcomes for our people and solid returns that grow wealth for generations to come,” she said during her speech at the event. The fund forms a key part of a wider strategy for the development of the Māori economy, now estimated to be worth approximately $126bn. Aligned closely with Waikato-Tainui, the Kīngitanga is combining its forces with other major political and strategic leadership bodies, sector-specific collectives and advocacy networks and major iwi post-settlement governance entities to work towards a burgeoning Māori economy and mana motuhake for Māori. Kuini Nga wai hono i te po at the Ōhanga ki te Ao summit held in November 2025. (Image: Kiingitanga). “Ōhanga Ki Te Ao is a chance to achieve our economic aspirations independently of government in our pursuit of self-determination, sustainable futures and thriving peoples,” Nga wai hono i te po said during her maiden speech as monarch. The economic focus builds on the legacy of Kīngi Tūheitia Pōtatau Te Wherowhero VII, the father of Nga wai hono i te po. Tūheitia was a strong advocate for kōtahitanga, national unity, social justice, and indigenous cooperation across the Pacific – a legacy that Nga wai hono i te po has continued during her reign. Among her many regular commitments, Nga wai hono i te po has continued to foster positive relations between the Kīngitanga and leaders around the Pacific, including travelling to Rarotonga, where she met with the Ui Ariki – the traditional leaders of the island – alongside members of the Cook Islands government. In May, she travelled to the United Kingdom where she met Prince William and became the first Māori monarch to meet a British royal at Windsor Castle. She also spoke at the First Nations Major Projects Coalition conference in Canada, highlighting the need to protect the taiao, grow indigenous economies and uphold the right of indigenous nations to lead. A trip to Dubai was also led by Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po to promote the sale of Māori grown kiwifruit into the market. The initiative, supported by a $5m investment fund, aims to assist Māori kiwifruit growers as they look to double their exports to the region over the next decade. Beyond economics and international visits, Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po has emphasised the need for preservation of the natural environment. At the royal regatta dinner at Tūrangawaewae Marae in March, she issued an urgent call to action to restore balance between humanity and ecosystems, noting that “the natural world is constantly speaking through rivers, land, winds, and oceans – and it is time to listen”. Kiingi Tuheitia smiles at the Kiingitanga 165th anniversary event at Tamaki Paenga Hira/Auckland Museum in December 2023. (Photo: Kiingitanga Facebook) Kuīni Nga wai hono i te po is scheduled to deliver her Koroneihana speech on Saturday afternoon. With an election looming, and two particularly strong candidates standing in the Hauraki-Waikato electorate – Labour’s Kingi Kiriona and Te Pāti Māori’s Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke, both with strong links to the Kīngitanga – many will be watching closely to see whether the Māori monarch endorses a candidate or party. Her speech is otherwise likely to echo last year’s one, calling for greater economic independence and a strengthening of Māori independence through a thriving Māori language and environment – all of which, she says, will support Māori wellbeing. As Nga wai hono i te po continues to create her legacy, the role of the Kīngitanga in today’s society will continue to evolve. Established in 1858 to unite Māori tribes, halt land sales to European settlers, and protect indigenous autonomy, the challenges the Kīngitanga and te ao Māori now face have shifted, but kotahitanga remains pivotal in the journey towards mana motuhake.

title: The Missing Colors of Black American Pigment-Making
content:
The Missing Colors of Black American Pigment-Making
George Washington Carver is remembered as an innovative agricultural scientist, but his overlooked artistic work places him in a lineage of Black American natural dyeing traditions.
This article is part of a series focusing on underrepresented craft histories, researched and written by the 2025 Craft Archive Fellows, and organized in collaboration with the Center for Craft.
As one of humanity’s oldest crafts, natural pigment-making occupies the intersection of science, agriculture, and art. It requires curiosity and ingenuity to see a marigold flower, for instance, and know that it can stain fabrics with beautiful shades of mustard yellow to gold; to know, as our ancestors did, that they also have anti-microbial and anti-inflammatory properties. The blue color of denim traces its roots to indigo, a dye crop cultivated and processed by West Africans and their descendants throughout the Atlantic world. The global indigo trade that made blue textiles possible was deeply intertwined with enslaved labor and African dyeing knowledge.
Indigo is just one of many plant and mineral dyes that Africans and Black Americans have cultivated and used to create an array of colors. Bògòlanfini, also known as mudcloth, is one such earth-based color tradition dating back to the Bambara people during the 12th century in present-day Mali. The word itself describes the process: “Bògò” means “clay” or “mud,” “lan” means “by way of,” and “fini” means cloth in Bambara — “mud by way of cloth.”
Despite its foundational role in art and everyday life, natural pigment-making remains largely absent from institutional craft archives. As a researcher and environmental designer, I am deeply invested in Black people’s relationships to plant dyes, sustainable materials, and natural fibers. Yet, in searching for these histories, it seems that the archives fail to fully document the depth and breadth of this knowledge. What I found instead reminds us that pigment-making is an environmental craft tradition worthy of preservation, study, and contemporary revival.
Chemical-derived dyes were discovered accidentally in 1856, though plant-based dyes continued to be used well into the 20th century. Before then, the colors of textiles, art, and painted surfaces relied on natural dyes and pigments from local ecologies. Why do we celebrate finished works while overlooking the craft traditions — and people — that produced their color?
Despite the histories of plant dyes and pigments, I have not found any archives devoted specifically to natural color-making by Black folks in the United States. What I did find was that a celebrated historical figure’s pigment-making was one of his many great achievements, yet is often overshadowed by his other scientific contributions.
George Washington Carver is widely remembered as an innovative agricultural scientist whose research transformed Southern farming through crop rotation, soil restoration, and resource conservation. Born into slavery in Missouri in the early 1860s, Carver was motivated by a desire to support poor Black farmers still living with the economic devastation of slavery and sharecropping. He believed that scientific knowledge and creative practice should be accessible to everyone.
While Carver’s scientific accomplishments are well documented, his artistic and material practices have received far less attention. He was an accomplished artist, craftsperson, and natural pigment maker who understood resourcefulness as both necessity and a way of life. He believed people could make use of the materials available around them. As he notably advised, "From what you have, make what you want." One of the few moments when Carver's artistic work received widespread recognition came in a November 1941 Time magazine profile that described him as the "Black Leonardo." The article coincided with the opening of the George Washington Carver Museum and Archives at Tuskegee University and noted that the institution housed 71 of Carver's original paintings, many created with paints he and his assistant made from peanut oil, Alabama clay, and vegetables.

title: Young artists at the Santa Fe Indian Market are just beginning
content:
Kalle Benallie
ICT
Young artists at the Santa Fe Indian Market were recognized for their work as emerging talent at one of the most prestigious Native art events of the year. For many, it’s already a lifelong passion.
Sixteen-year-old Aydrian Day, Ho-Chunk/Anishinaabe/Lakota, took home the Best of Class in the 17-years-old and under class. It’s Day’s fourth time being honored as Best of Class and said he was honored to be recognized for his hard work by the market.
“I felt really grateful for my family to bring me all the way to Santa Fe, and give me all the stuff I need, and to give me the opportunities to come to Santa Fe and be a good artist,” Day said.
He made a Lakota shell penny dress, entitled “Wambli Gleska Win,” that represents the tradition of giving a dress to a woman that you respect and admire. Day made the dress to honor his great-grandmother, whom he’s very close to, and his 1-year-old goddaughter.
It took Day more than two years to make because he’s still in high school and can’t bead full-time. He first started beading seriously when he was 7 years old, where he began entering different art markets.
“I was always watching my parents. I’d be playing around with my toys or something and they’d always be beading and making their outfits and regalia and beading in the background,” Day said. “So I would see them doing that and it was just natural.”
His main inspirations are his parents and great-grandmother. Over the years he’s been able to connect to other artists who have shared their knowledge with him and considers them like friends, aunties, uncles, older brothers or grandmas.
“Just made that many deep relations coming to art markets,” he said. “I feel like it’s really cool because we can all bond over all our artistry and how we make our stuff.”
He mainly gravitates toward beading and with the recent piece, he mixed in quillwork. Day also likes to paint and occasionally does ledger art, following in the footsteps of his father.
“I’m trying to soak up all the knowledge I can so I can carry on all these traditions. I can teach my kids and my grandkids how to bead or how to quill and how to shell and how to make their own regalia too,” he said. “Just to be proud of who we are. I never want my next generation of kids to be shameful at all or have any nervousness to be who they are.”
Day encourages young artists to do art and learn a craft because it’s another way to connect to your culture and stay on a good path. The Anishinaabe call it the Red World.
“To not get distracted with any other kind of ways you can go with life that aren’t as good, and this definitely helps with all those distractions and it can be a good livelihood for many people,” he said.
Other categories Day won at the market include: first place in boundary, second place in beadwork and quillwork and best of division through ages 14-to-17.
Twelve-year-old Jaquelyn Patricio, Acoma Pueblo, won first place in the pottery category, non-burnished (matte), either painted or undecorated, and second place in the pottery figures category and the Anita Day Memorial Award to Encourage the Work of a Youth Potter.
It was her first time at the Santa Fe Indian Market and she was surprised that she won.
“I started making pottery when I was 9-years-old. Just watching my dad and sisters make pottery, so I thought I could try too. It’s kind of like playing with mud or slime,” she said in an email.
The design of the pottery submitted represents the mountains and rain.
“We need the rain to give moisture to the land and for the animals to drink,” Patricio said.
She said the process of creating pottery takes three to seven days, depending on the weather and what she plans to make. She hand coils it, lets it dry, makes a shape, lets it dry again, scrapes it and takes out any bumps.
“If it’s raining the pot takes longer to dry. Once the pot is dry, I then shine it with a white slip and use a shiny rock to make it shine,” Patricio said.
Then, she outlines a design with a pencil, beginning at the bottom and sections it off into fours and uses a paintbrush made of human hair and starts filling it in.
“I admire my dad Robert Patricio’s work and my sisters, Felisha, Kylie, Juanita, and TobieMae. Their shapes, styles are all different. The designs that they create are from long ago. I also admire what my ancestors made long ago,” Patricio said.
She plans to continue to make pottery and make figures that’s made before like a set of cups that have faces on them.
“My advice for other young Indigenous potters would be to always keep trying and don’t give up. You can improve as the years go by if you stick at it,” Patricio said.
Nine-year-old Nanibah Little, Diné, won first place in the painting category of the youth division and best of division for ages 9 and under.
She shared a booth with her dad and grandpa at the market; who are both artists in their own right. Her dad does painting and her grandpa makes sculptures.
Her inspiration was her cat and her grandma’s cat, Sebastian.
“He reminds me about Tuba City [Arizona] and my grandparents,” she said.
It took her about three weeks to paint her cat Sebastian, using a sketch that was drawn from a photo.
“I like to paint because I like spending time with my dad painting together. Since my dad is an artist. When I won the competition, he was really proud of me,” she said.
A copy of her painting was sold to a collector. Next year she’s thinking of drawing another cat of hers named Tigger or make a sculpture out of cardboard to submit to the Santa Fe Indian Market.
Other pieces of art she’s made are a rubberband car for a science project and toys like a paper-folded doll house with different paper figures: cats, a duck, a potato, a bunny and more.
She likes using recyclable materials like paperclips, popsicle sticks, tape, cardboard, plastic, tape and paper.
“I like crafting more too because when I’m crafting sometimes or drawing – sometimes when I get sad or I get mad, I just draw craft or paint,” Little said.

title: Four hours under the rubble, 97 years above it
content:
National
Four hours under the rubble, 97 years above it
Guna Maya Bohara was rescued from an elderly care home where she had lived for more than a decade. But her survival was only the latest chapter in a life marked by loss, resilience and a family she built around herself.Aarya Chand
Guna Maya Bohara sometimes sings at night. It is the same bhajan—Hare Ram, Hare Krishna—that she used to sing during her stay at the elderly care home and during temple visits. Sometimes after singing, she asks a question: “Why did the water hit me?” The 97-year-old has asked the question more than once.
Apart from that, however, Bohara has mostly stopped speaking. Bohara is currently receiving treatment at Bir Hospital in Kathmandu. Her arms and legs have turned black and blue. She sometimes moves suddenly, almost involuntarily. She lies still for a while. Then another movement breaks the stillness. Doctors have diagnosed her with acute stress disorder.
On the morning of August 26, Bohara was in her room on the ground floor of the elderly care home at Devighat, a riverside town in Nuwakot. She was unaware that a glacier had collapsed high in the Himalayas. The collapse triggered a landslide, sending water and debris thundering down into the Trishuli River. The furious waters reached the ground floor, where Bohara was. It pushed her to the edge of the ground floor and left her there. The current was less intense on this side of the floor, witnesses say. Some of those caught in the current did not survive.
Nepal Police and Nepali Army personnel worked for about four hours to reach her, clearing rubble carefully so as not to injure anyone still buried beneath it. Bohara’s relatives also rushed to the site. They brought a JCB excavator. With it, they worked together to move the debris away, inch by inch — moving, moving, moving, Dipak, Bohara’s great nephew, remembers, until there was space to lift her clear in its bucket.
Last Wednesday’s floods, however, were only the latest of Bohara’s ordeals in her long life.
At 97, Bohara has outlived her husband by 81 years. She was eight when she married him in Nuwakot’s Suryagadhi, at a time when child marriage was common practice. At 83, she chose on her own to move into a nursing home—Senior Citizens Welfare Foundation—in Devighat, close enough that her nieces could visit daily. She liked it there, among people her own age and looked forward to birthdays—her own and other residents—celebrated together.
By her twenties, she had already outlived nearly everyone who shared her blood: her husband, eight years into their marriage; both her parents, four years after that; her only brother, sometime later.
She never had children of her own.
What she had instead was her husband’s family, his three brothers, their wives, and in time their children. She raised thirteen nephews, twelve nieces as her own, sending every one of them to school, packing roasted maize for their lunch. Dipak says her family regards women of her generation as having quietly carried entire households through decades few now remember.
Bohara is the last of her generation left in the family.
Physically, she has proved more resilient than her age might lead one to expect. She has a pre-existing disability in her legs and an injury to her hand, caused by the torrents of water, is still being assessed, a CT scan and an X-ray pending. She survived on fruit juice for the first two days and has since moved to milk and full meals, Dipak said.
Of the people who share Guna Maya Bohara’s blood, none remain. Of the people who call her family, the nephews and nieces she once packed lunches for, there are twenty-five now, and they take turns at her bedside, waiting.
Dipak said that Bohara has not stopped asking, “Why did the water hit me?” He has tried to explain to her—more simply than what actually happened—that a lake, Gosaikunda, had burst far above them. She seems to understand, for a while. But hours later, she asks again: “Why did the water hit me?”

title: What even is an ‘Asian’? And why are we bundled together?
content: Tze Ming Mok introduces a new book that explores through art, activism, research and lived experience what it means to be Asian in Aotearoa. The following has been abridged from the original introduction to Between Dreams. During the “Inv-Asian” migration wave of the early 1990s, you could see the Asians at school clustering together in class and lunch break. We didn’t know if we liked each other yet, because we didn’t speak the same languages or dialects. There was just an unspoken agreement that we wouldn’t try to hurt each other. This is how you make friends, I think. Spivak’s strategic essentialism is one way of Being Asian, but it also requires thinking through what your strategy is in aid of. To not get bullied, yes. What about the rest? Can we imagine something better? To make a real life for ourselves, with agency, humanity and validation of our specificity? What even is an “Asian” and why are we bundled together, at lunch, in statistics, in books, in a blur of ill-fitting stereotypes? On the streets of Aotearoa, “Asian” is a racialised term specific to East Asians or “yellow” Asians. Meanwhile, Stats NZ defines “Asian” through a far vaster sweep of continental geography that takes in 60 percent of the world’s population – from Samarkand to Chennai, from Pyongyang to Bali. What about West Asia? You’ll have to ask the Iranians. At a grassroots organisational level, pan-“Asian” community activism in the diaspora is often based on strategic alliances within state-determined funding of diversity, policy and community initiatives – the confines and definitions of which can be grating. But activism and community work inside these confines can also be generative, collaborative and specifically dependent on articulating difference within our tenuous alliance. We grind away for recognition of the term “Asian” as not simply inherently absurd, but – in the way we need to use it – as inherently diverse. We do so in order to deploy it meaningfully in public policy, in political analysis, in collective struggles and in our histories of ourselves. “Asians” do not always have a shared ethnic history, language, religion, tradition or migration cohort. Oft-times, our homelands have been or are still at war with each other, even as others cannot tell us apart in the suburbs of Auckland. But more often, we do have a common history or experience of migration, arrival, settlement and daily life that has been governed by a racial and colonial logic marking us out for a clear purpose, which I will state bluntly: To return an advantage to colonial capital through replacing more expensive and better-organised labour. The historical arrival of Asian peoples in Aotearoa is inseparable from the British drive for colonial expansion through Oceania, with New Zealand being just one outpost. Aotearoa Asians inhabit multi-levelled, multi-cohort, multinational diasporas connected by what Ballantyne would call the “webs of empire” – the giant bureaucracy of governance and trading interests – or what Wallerstein would call the capitalist world system – where legacies of racial ideologies, oppressive rule, and extraction of value from bodies and stolen lands in one part of the system wash up repeatedly on the shores of another. Asian presence in Aotearoa is often the historical result of being filtered along these webs, in order to return value to the imperial centre. The historical transportation of Asian bodies to the Caribbean, South-East Asia and the South Pacific, including Aotearoa, was required to extract valuable material and agricultural resources from freshly acquired colonial lands – sugarcane, cacao, rubber, tin, gold. A century later, national immigration policies extract valuable human resources from the erstwhile Asian periphery and reallocate it to the neocolonial core that has grown up around the New Zealand settler state – nurses, doctors (including my parents in the 1970s), builders, teachers, IT workers. Stories of New Zealand Asian achievement and nationalist dedication abound, but leave a bitter taste. Audre Lorde says you cannot dismantle the master’s house using the master’s tools. But, we whisper to ourselves, with our postcode envy from Mount Roskill to Botany, but – but – but what if I am the tools? Is this all we have been doing this whole time? Tooling away industriously, hewing to the structure of white supremacy? Inhabiting the role of “middleman minority” used by the white state as a political, economic and administrative buffer against other groups denied power? To the contrary, this book shows how organising, agitating, joining rebel alliances and going in deep cover to challenge the dominant order has also always been the story of Asians in Aotearoa. Much of our early story here takes place at the shifting borders of the periphery, where existing accounts repeatedly reveal natural alliances between those who were “together on the margins”. This includes ease of intermarriage between Asian labour and Indigenous people under white colonial rule that excluded and oppressed them both, as shown by the commonplace nature of Chinese ancestry among Aotearoa Samoans due to the history of indenture, or the well-documented whānau relationships and community connections between Māori and early Asian market gardeners similarly marginalised within the Pākehā settler-state. Stories in Between Dreams include the recent reconnection between old-generation Chinese and the iwi who extended kaitiakitanga to the Ventnor remains, as explored by fourth-generation Chinese New Zealander Christopher Fung, bringing this relationship full circle over a century. Matua Moana Jackson’s example of the Taranaki Parihaka exiles in the caves of the South Island creating a protective cordon around Chinese gold miners inspired activist group Asians Supporting Tino Rangatiratanga (ASTR) in their kaupapa of reciprocity, mutual aid and solidarity with Māori. Fung is one of several ASTR alumni and affiliates who are contributors to this book, and to the 2021 public submissions on the New Zealand history curriculum consultation that inspired it. Rev. Mua Sofi Strickson-Pua (right) and his younger brother Sofi Ulugia-Pua outside their childhood home in Scanlan Street, Grey Lynn, 2019. (Photo: Taylor Aumua) Post-war social movements had undercover Asians working alongside Māori and Pasifika in new ways. In their story of their Chinese-Samoan father – the unionist, community leader and broadcaster Sofi Pua – activists Mua Strickson-Pua and Sofi Pua Junior sense the echoes of indenture in Sofi Pua Senior’s advocacy against the Dawn Raid deportations, and their own protests against the Springbok tour. As part of a 1970s intellectual and radical milieu, Pua was a friend of James K Baxter, as was former Jerusalem commune member “Burma Bill” Maung, a political exile and former senior Burmese government administrator. Maung famously leveraged his cultural capital and high-level connections to become an intermediary between the New Zealand government and dispossessed Māori in gangs in the 1970s. Instead of representing the interests of the white elites as a middleman, Maung literally acted as an agent of Black Power. The removal of New Zealand’s informal “White New Zealand” immigration policies in 1987 led to a rapid increase in Aotearoa’s Asian population. This initially led to an ugly surge in anti-Asian racism in the 1990s, mirroring that of a century earlier. In the 1990s, Manying Ip, a 1970s generation Hongkonger and academic, was the most prominent anti-racist advocate to speak out against this backlash, although the Chinese community in particular was split between new migrants with little political voice, and older communities trying to distance themselves from the new “rich foreigners” being targeted. This new idea of “rich Asians” taking over Aotearoa was a totalising fantasy intended to mobilise the savage political force of racial resentment. This fantasy has been erasing the reality of Asian working-class and migrant labour struggle for decades. In a unique and important contribution to Aotearoa’s history scholarship, unionist Sun-Min Elle Park and curator/union delegate Grace Gassin highlight our long history and ongoing record of fighting for workers’ rights in Aotearoa, both within and outside of a trade union movement that has not always welcomed us as members. Grace Gassin, editor of Between Dreams. (Photo: Supplied) Aotearoa Asian communities built and consolidated throughout the 2000s, creating new alliances across the migrant cohorts, with a crucial bridging role played by 1.5-generation migrants coming to adulthood. The increasing ease of online communication had coincided with a demographic tipping point, and previously isolated progressive and radical Asians rapidly began forming networks throughout media, academia, community-based activism, the public and third sector, and the arts – a critical and diverse “Embedded Asian Underground”. At this point in 2026, the majority of Asians in Aotearoa have no direct ancestral or familial connection to early Asian settlers and their stories of survival and solidarity. Post-1987 community histories underline the modernity of the Asian diasporas. Staying connected to identity in a politically and socially conscious sense is less about upholding an unattainable ideal of cultural and linguistic authenticity frozen in time, and more about continuing to engage in solidarity with the contemporary social and political life of countries in the Asian region itself – as much a part of normal day-to-day life as the extended family group-chat. The nature of Ong & Nonini’s diasporic “ungrounded empires” should not only be seen as the transnational relationships created by capital flows – but also networks of resistance to dictatorship, authoritarianism and colonial capitalism. Stories and objects from these newer generations in this collection show that to be Asian in Aotearoa is to also participate and resist in ways that are specific to Asia and the Asian regional context. Sometimes this relates to the West’s imperialist or neoimperialist legacy of war, as Rebekah Jaung explores in her chapter on the memorialisation of the Korean war. Sometimes it is about our own homelands’ imperialism over others in the region. Pan-Asian solidarity here is a precarious balance between historical colonisers and the historically colonised, transported to a new colonial framework in the Pākehā settler state. The Asian region’s geopolitical shifts in the last twenty years have ensured that bland liberal generalities are inadequate for even understanding what has historically been the largest single Asian population in Aotearoa, the ethnic Chinese. In a piece that strikes at the heart of the matter, former journalist Keith Ng reflects on his return to Hong Kong to join the city-state’s 2019 street revolution – a final mass show of defiance and identity before the descent of a new Iron Curtain. The first Lennon Wall along the stairway to the Hong Kong Central Government building in Admiralty, 2014. (Photo: Wikicommons /Wpcpey CC SA.) New moves from the old Biggest Empire in the region may already be splitting “Asian” solidarity unless we redefine the terms on which solidarity is based. Aotearoa has seen emerging, contingent alliances between those affected by the Chinese government’s new claims on the Chinese diaspora, and by its repressive rule at home. Similarly , those against the current Indian government’s turn to Hindutva fundamentalism, its persecution of Muslims, and the dismantling of Asia’s oldest secular democracy, have been coming together in a rebel alliance. We are still part of an intergenerational struggle to build, win and maintain post-Cold War democracy across East, South and South-East Asian countries, and to uphold those values in the diaspora. “Out here”, these once regional progressive solidarities have transformed into a global, transdiasporic collectivity – sometimes jokingly referred to as the Milk Tea Alliance, or simply the Asian anti-authoritarian left. As I write this, a quarter of a century after the historical turning point of 9/11, we are witnessing a global resurgence of the far right, a collapse in democratic political norms, and a rapid decline in reality-based social and political discourse in the West. Political institutions only upheld by convention have proved no match for bad actors capitalising on the rapid peak and decline of the mass public sphere promised by social media. The canaries in the coal mine are dead; fascism is here. More Reading Yes, the post-war consensus has collapsed. But that consensus – around liberal democracy, human rights and a humane welfare state – was never one that extended to Asian countries or Asian people. We had to fight for it, and some of us fought and lost – if not us personally, then our parents, our grandparents, our aunts and uncles, our cousins, our old neighbours and our friends. Aotearoa needs, right now, to learn from those of us who know what it is to fight for justice and lose. To give up and leave. We’ve seen things you people wouldn’t believe. We have gathered like dew, disappeared like mist and re-formed as tears. All these “losers” and descendants of losers can tell you what the true cost of surviving is. But some also still hold on to what drove us to get into trouble in the first place, and what the purpose of survival is at all: to keep our identity, our values, and our stories alive. Even if it has to be in some other place – even in some place like this. Between Dreams: Resistance and Representation in Asian Aotearoa edited by Grace Gassin ($50, Te Papa Press) is available to purchase from Unity Books. Gassin is delivering the Julie King Memorial Lecture at WORD Christchurch on Sunday August 6, details here.

title: Tammy Eagle Bull Is Weaving Indigenous Design Into Modern Architecture
content:
As extreme weather intensifies and America’s housing crisis deepens, it’s becoming clear that the conventional ways in which we build new structures are no longer working. In response, some architects are starting to place greater weight on weaving resiliency, cultural literacy, and a deep understanding of the natural environment into their work.
Tammy Eagle Bull has been advocating for these practices for decades. As the first Indigenous woman licensed to practice architecture in the United States, she has spent her career incorporating the historical and cultural knowledge of Indigenous tribes into her work. For many years that has meant designing for tribal communities, like the Porcupine School on South Dakota's Pine Ridge Reservation, which was the state's first LEED Silver-certified school, or the Oglala Lakota Artspace, which was designed around the Lakota belief that stars are connected to "sacred histories, stories, and knowledge." Still, she knew these approaches weren’t only relevant to tribal projects. "There's an [Indigenous] philosophy and methodology and pedagogy that is very applicable to everything that architects and designers do," Eagle Bull tells TIME.
Where conventional architectural practices are often guided by technical factors like zoning, Eagle Bull takes a different approach. "I like to go further back into the deep temporality of the site,” she says. “What was it originally? Who lived here? How did they live?"
She says this is especially important when thinking about extreme heat in a place like Phoenix, which had a record 113 consecutive days of 100-plus degree temperatures in 2024. "People are like, 'This is so inhospitable. It's too hot. People can't thrive here,'" she says. "[But] people did. They had thriving cities, they had agriculture, and they were able to sustain life. And so, if we look back, we can see that living in modern day Phoenix shouldn't be such a struggle. There were strategies that were employed to manage water and to manage heat."
These design principles are at the root of many modern models, says Eagle Bull, such as the “Passive House” concept, in which the built environment is crafted to work with things like weather systems and wind flows, and “life-centered design,” which takes local ecology and circularity into consideration. "The heart of all that is really what Indigenous design has been practicing for millennia," she says.
As a professor of practice at Arizona State University’s Design School, Eagle Bull is helping educate the next generation of architects in these design principles. For example, some of her students recently imagined solutions for unhoused Indigenous populations in Phoenix, focusing on how shelters might be deployed quickly and safely while still centering Native culture and practices. One idea floated was co-housing, which isn't typically embraced in shelters, where men and women tend to be separated. But Eagle Bull argues these kinds of approaches have their place. "There are a lot of times where it's an extended family, maybe the son's taking care of the mother or the grandmother," she explains. "So the idea is being flexible, employing different strategies and ideas in a balance that can work best for whatever situation."
In 2025, Eagle Bull became the director of a new Master's program at ASU. The M.S. in Indigenous Placekeeping and Design was founded by Wanda Dalla Costa, the first First Nations woman to be a licensed architect in Canada and a leading figure in Indigenous design in North America. It is one of only a handful of degree programs in the U.S. that focuses on both the history and practical application of Indigenous design. "There are a lot of things that we can learn from [Indigenous] cultural practices," Eagle Bull says. "They can help us not only manage the ecology and environment, but also how people exist with each other and thrive and create places that support who they are and support their community."

title: In Ghana, larger-than-life coffins tell the stories of the dead
content:
Funerals
Frederick Teiko Ofori spent a large portion of his life with a guitar in his hands, so when the Ghanaian musician died in a road accident, his family decided that the instrument should accompany him on his final journey.
His coffin was built in the shape of an enormous guitar.
The coffin stood out at his funeral on Saturday in Adjen Kotoku Amoama, on the outskirts of Accra, among bright red flowers, a portrait of the 40-year-old and the mourners gathered under canopies to shade themselves from the sun.
Yet it was also par for the course in a country where celebrations of life often include such intricately crafted tributes to the deceased.
In Ghana, particularly among Ga communities around the capital, "figurative" or "fantasy" coffins, as they're known, offer fantastical, yet intimate, send-offs.
Fishermen are buried in massive, human-sized fish or canoes, farmers in cocoa pods, drivers in cars and religious figures in Bibles.
Ofori left behind a wife, a young family including a child born just a week before the funeral, and a musical legacy abruptly cut short.
But even in death, the guitar remained part of his identity.
The huge wooden instrument carrying his body was made by Daniel Oblie Mensah, known by the cheery nickname "Hello", a veteran coffinmaker who has spent more than three decades turning people's professions, passions and status into their final resting places.
"Anytime someone commissions me to do a coffin in the profession of the deceased, it excites me," Mensah, 54, told AFP.
"It helps me truly honour the deceased and the family."
The modern tradition of sculptural coffins emerged among Ga craftsmen around Accra in the middle of the 20th century, partly inspired by the elaborately shaped palanquins used by local chiefs.
Today, the objects occupy an unusual niche of contemporary art, quickly disappearing underground despite painstaking, finely tuned craftsmanship.
Some end up displayed in museums, however, including a guitar-shaped coffin by Ghanaian artist Paa Joe, on loan to New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art.
A teacher's final pen
Samuel Commey Tetteh lay dressed in white before his funeral began, visitors greeting elders at the family home before approaching the body of the man known throughout the community as "Teacher".
Tetteh, born in 1943, had taught in Paanor, in Ga South, outside the capital, for more than half a century, his family said.
The quiet of the early morning eventually gave way to pounding music as mourners filed in. Then came Tetteh's coffin -- a giant pen.
Again, it was Mensah's work. It took about two weeks.
A sheep was slaughtered and its blood applied to the coffin, the solemnity of the funeral rites taking precedence over the fun of the coffin.
And then, the pen was buried, Mensah's work disappearing into the ground.
At workshops around Accra, dozens of other lives wait to be translated into wood.
Some customers arrive carrying a photograph of exactly what they want. Others simply describe the life of the deceased.
Then the craftsmen let their imaginations run riot.
One of the most difficult designs that carpenter Lawrence Okoe Anang remembers was a crocodile, commissioned more than a decade ago for a priest in Ghana's Volta Region.
His father made the coffin, while the younger Anang, then still learning the trade he started training for at age 10, helped around the workshop.
Worldwide interest
Coffins typically fetch around 10,000 Ghanaian cedis ($900), said the 26-year-old, who now runs the workshop with his younger brother.
Pieces intended for exhibitions cost more, because craftsmen use more durable materials, intended to last decades under the museum lights.
The industry remains heavily dependent on skills passed down through families, though it has changed considerably since earlier generations worked with hand tools.
Modern equipment has sped up production, wood supplies have become more reliable, and overseas commissions for museums and collectors have helped grow the trade.
The ability to turn ordinary timber into a fish, aeroplane, Bible, pen or guitar raises questions over what to call the people who make them.
Anang considers himself a carpenter, coffin maker and artist, rolled into one.
At Ofori's funeral, however, those kind of playful questions seemed distant.
Around his grave stood the people the musician had left behind.
They gathered around the guitar.
Then, it was lowered out of sight.

title: Mali: Mariam Bagayoko continues to impress on stage aged 88
content:
Music
At the age of 88, renowned singer Mariam Bagayoko still has the energy to perform traditional Malian songs with a strong stage presence. She says it's a lifelong passion.
"From the time I was very small, I began singing in the way of my community. Even before I could speak properly, I would join the women’s evening gatherings around the pounding mortars and sing with them," Bagayoko explains.
Bagayoko has spent her life championing traditional music far beyond Mali and fighting to preserve it in the modern world. She's disappointed that the original rhythms are evolving.
"Today, the n'goussoumbala and the yabara [traditonal musical instruments, ed.] are still present in our music. But the rhythms of our homeland are no longer there. The new generation has modernised them and adapted them to the rhythms of other countries. As a result, they are gradually losing their intrinsic value and the original rhythms are falling into oblivion. Worse still, during competitions they now only play the rhythms of neighbouring countries," she says.
Alhtough her father was initially against her musical ambitions, she has been supported by her children, and hopes they will carry on her legacy.
''I leave my legacy to the children. They will know how to sing in my absence. Only last night, my daughter sang and danced in front of the audience just like I do. She climbed onto the balafon to dance, then carried on dancing on solid ground as well; it was unforgettable. If they don’t stray from the path and aren’t ashamed of it, the next generation is assured."
In 2025, she was given a lifetime achievement honour at the Aga Khan Music Awards in London, having been selected from more than 400 candidates globally.

title: Zerstörtes jüdisches Erbe: Die Mission des Ivan Glasenberg
content:
Zerstörtes jüdisches Erbe: Die Mission des Ivan Glasenberg
Der frühere Glencore-Chef hat es sich zur Aufgabe gemacht, die Erinnerung an die jüdische Kultur in Litauen am Leben zu erhalten. Unterwegs mit dem charismatischen Manager zum Ort seiner Vorfahren, wo nun ein Museum der Superlative steht.
Etwa eine Viertelstunde vor der Landung zeigt Ivan Glasenberg aus dem Fenster des Embraer-Geschäftsflugzeugs. «Schaut mal, wie schön», sagt er mit Blick auf die weite, dünn besiedelte Landschaft Litauens mit Wäldern, Seen und Ackerflächen. Glasenberg wirkt emotional. Es ist das Land seiner Vorfahren, das er erst im Alter von 54 Jahren zum ersten Mal betreten hat – und das ihn seither nicht mehr loslässt.
Glasenbergs Grosseltern wanderten 1936 von Litauen nach Südafrika aus, sein Vater war damals sechs Jahre alt. Die Familie entkam dadurch dem Holocaust, der 160 000 litauischen Juden das Leben kostete und eine ganze Kultur eliminierte.
Bei seinem ersten Besuch in Litauen 2011 war Glasenberg von dieser Geschichte derart berührt, dass er es sich zur Aufgabe gemacht hat, die Erinnerung an dieses Verbrechen wachzuhalten.
Landung auf einem Nato-Militärstützpunkt
Bisher hat Glasenberg nie über seine Familiengeschichte geredet und stets vermieden, dass sein Name im Zusammenhang mit seinen Aktivitäten in Litauen genannt wird. Dabei zeigt dieses Engagement eine ganz andere Facette des mächtigen Geschäftsmanns, der Glencore zu einem der grössten Rohstoffkonzerne der Welt machte und jahrelang eine Reizfigur für linke Politiker und NGO war.
Nach einigem Zögern hat Glasenberg der NZZ angeboten, ihn nach Litauen zu begleiten, an einen Gedenkanlass zum 85. Jahrestag der Erschiessung von über 600 Juden in Šeduva, dem Städtchen seiner Grosseltern. Das sei eine gute Gelegenheit, um seine Familiengeschichte und sein Engagement zu verstehen, sagt er.
So sitzen wir an diesem Dienstagvormittag in einem Flugzeug mit Destination Šiauliai, ein Nato-Militärflugplatz im Norden Litauens. Auf der riesigen, gespenstisch leeren Militärbasis fühlt man sich bereits mittendrin in der bewegten Geschichte dieses Landes: Das Areal diente den Nazis als Luftwaffenstützpunkt, im Kalten Krieg bauten es die Sowjets zu einer wichtigen Basis aus, mit zwei über drei Kilometer langen Landepisten und einem gigantischen System von Bunkeranlagen. Dass heute die Nato hier Kampfflugzeuge stationiert hat, um Putin von einer Ausweitung des Kriegs abzuhalten, ist von aussen nicht zu sehen: Die Maschinen sind unter zeltartigen Unterständen verborgen.
Vom Flugplatz dauert es etwa eine halbe Stunde nach Šeduva, einer Kleinstadt mit rund 2300 Einwohnern. Anfang des letzten Jahrhunderts war hier die Hälfte der Bevölkerung jüdisch. Auch die Vorfahren Ivan Glasenbergs wohnten in diesem Schtetl, wie die jüdisch geprägten Landorte genannt wurden; seine Grosseltern führten einen kleinen Lebensmittelladen.
Viele wanderten nach Südafrika aus
In den Jahren vor dem Zweiten Weltkrieg setzte eine Auswanderungswelle ein, hauptsächlich aus wirtschaftlichen Gründen, zum Teil aber auch wegen des aufkommenden Antisemitismus. Viele reisten wie Glasenbergs Grosseltern nach Südafrika, wo der Goldboom eine gute Perspektive versprach und die Apartheid-Regierung um weisse Einwanderer buhlte. Dies hat Auswirkungen bis heute: Von den rund 50 000 Juden in Südafrika haben 80 bis 90 Prozent litauische Wurzeln. Ivan Glasenberg lebte bis zu seinem Umzug in die Schweiz 1991 in Südafrika, wo seine Eltern ein Grosshandelsunternehmen für Reisegepäck führten.
In Šeduva war bei Kriegsbeginn 1940 der Anteil Juden durch die Auswanderung bereits auf ein Drittel gesunken. Ende 1941 gab es gar keine Juden mehr. Alle 600 bis 700 verbliebenen waren erschossen worden, nur ganz wenige entkamen.
Was in Šeduva vorgefallen ist, ist kein Einzelfall – in den über 200 Schtetln des Landes passierte Ähnliches. Die meisten Juden Litauens waren bereits umgebracht worden, bevor die Nazis Ende 1941 die ersten Vernichtungslager einrichteten und an der Wannseekonferenz im Januar 1942 den Holocaust organisierten. Was in Šeduva allerdings anders ist: An dem Ort gibt es seit einem Jahr ein grosses Museum, das an das ausgelöschte Leben und die damaligen Verbrechen erinnert.
Es ist nicht einfach ein weiteres Museum zur jüdischen Geschichte, sondern ein Bau, der in jeder Hinsicht den Anspruch hat, herausragend zu sein. Das beginnt bei der Architektur, den Baumaterialien, dem Park und natürlich der Ausstellung, die mit ihren multimedialen und interaktiven Elementen international neue Standards setzt. Es scheint, als ob hier Geld keine Rolle spielt.
Im ersten Jahr lockte das Lost Shtetl Museum im litauischen Niemandsland bereits 100 000 Besucher an.
