title: Sale of 100-year-old Vancouver church reflects hard choice facing many congregations
content:
Sale of 100-year-old Vancouver church reflects hard choice facing many congregations
Many are facing a difficult decision: Continue despite waning attendance or close and sell their place of worship to a more prosperous congregation or to a property developer?
On a warm July day outside a church at 12th Avenue and Trimble in Vancouver, a small crowd gathered for a brief ceremony that was bittersweet for some but exciting and promising for others.
In the early afternoon, Rev. Richard Watson, representing West Point Grey Presbyterian Church, handed a symbolic cardboard cutout key to Pastor Joseph Concepcion of the Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ (4th Watch) and, with it, ownership of the 100-year-old landmark.
It was a day of celebration as children paraded with red-and-yellow balloons while parishioners crowded around, and photographers and videographers captured the moment.
Now a minister at Kerrisdale Presbyterian Church, Watson prayed the new parishioners would continue ministry there for another 100 years.
The three-lot prime location in affluent Point Grey had just sold for $6.4 million, even though a year earlier a developer offered $7.5 million and, two years ago, it was listed at $10 million.
Ian Rokeby, chair of the committee overseeing Presbyterian real estate in the Lower Mainland, said after initial expectations that the church would be demolished and redeveloped, he is glad it is being passed to another congregation — one that is growing.
“The number of worship spaces in the Lower Mainland is diminishing every year, so we were anxious,” Rokeby said. “One of our priorities is to preserve houses of worship.”
When it closed three years ago, West Point Grey Presbyterian had only 19 people attending. With dwindling attendance, the 200-seat church couldn’t afford a full-time minister or keep up maintenance of the aging building.
Many mainline congregations are facing the same difficult choice — continue despite waning attendance or close and sell to a more prosperous congregation or property developer.
“(There are) a handful of people who are doing way too much, and so they actually aren’t doing any outreach in the community, which is one of the primary objectives of the church,” said Rokeby.
It is dispiriting when all a congregation can manage to deal with is broken plumbing, he said.
Many congregations are relying more on rent revenue to cover the costs of building maintenance, pay the pastor, minister or priest, and finance community outreach.
When Jeff Rock, coordinating minister at Canadian Memorial United Church in Vancouver, was ordained 15 years ago it wasn’t unusual for 90 per cent of a congregation’s income to come from tithes or offerings.
Now, he said, that number has dropped to 50 per cent, with the other half coming from rent.
In Vancouver’s competitive land market, churches often rent space to daycares, community events, concerts and support groups.
“I get a request for space usage almost every day. People are just desperately looking,” he said. “A lot of spiritual communities have found themselves becoming, really, rental agencies.”
According to Statistics Canada, religious demographics in B.C. have changed over the decades. Between 2011 and 2021, the proportion of people identifying with mainline Christian denominations has decreased, with Anglicans down 42.9 per cent, United Church members down 49 per cent ands Presbyterians down 40 per cent, since 2011.
Anglicans in that decade dropped to 2.8 per cent of the B.C. population from 4.9 per cent, United members dropped to 2.6 per cent from 5.1 per cent, and Presbyterians dropped to 0.6 per cent from one per cent.
Over that period, the proportion of the B.C. population identifying as “non-religious” or secular grew from 44.1 per cent to 52.1 per cent.
Other denominations are offsetting the decline.
For example, the proportion of people identifying as Sikh increased 25.5 per cent, the number sayibg they were Muslim was up 44.4 per cent, and the number of Hindus was up 54.5 per cent respectively.
The Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ (4th Watch) in Vancouver has grown, despite those identifying as Pentecostal or other charismatic denominations also dropping 42.9 per cent since 2011.
Rock said that over the past decade places of worship have felt the same financial squeeze as many households and residents.
Attendance levels drop and people who still attend church are not able to donate as much as before, he said.
“I’m lucky that I’m in a spiritual community that’s vibrant and is thriving. But I know many of my neighbours are feeling that attrition rate more and more.”
Ownership out of reach
When Watson handed over the key of the Presbyterian church, one door closed while another opened for another congregation. But the prospect of church ownership is out of reach for many religious groups.
Growing congregations look, often for years, to purchase places of worship. Many are priced out of the market entirely. With few churches available, their capacity to grow and practise their faith hinges on whether congregations selling their churches view the property as financial assets or as community institutions.
Growing congregations often don’t have the capital to buy, and they are purchasing from a limited supply of land that is also sought after by other congregations and property developers.
Rokeby said many religious communities have “dreams” of owning a place to worship, but “no cash.”
Devin Roberts, the church realtor representing the Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ, compares those congregations that are growing to the average millennial unable to break into the housing market. If they can’t afford to buy, their only option is to rent. But renting comes with its own challenges.
Compared to Vancouver, Surrey and Maple Ridge, where zoning is more flexible, Roberts said Burnaby, the Tri-Cities, Pitt Meadows, Mission and White Rock have stricter regulations that limit where congregations can gather in commercial areas.
“A big fat ‘no’ to anything other than an actual church building,” Roberts said.
The Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ had not had a permanent home since it was established in Vancouver nearly 26 years ago. Members gathered in hotels, industrial and commercial buildings, and even in family homes.
For eight years, Pastor Miziel Rivera searched for a permanent place for her congregation in New Westminster, Richmond and Surrey. When they did find a potential location in Surrey, another congregation outbid them by $1 million.
When they gathered Sundays at a hotel, a volunteer had to arrive at 6 a.m. to set up chairs, musical instruments and the pulpit. For weekday services, when the hotel wasn’t available, congregants would gather in restaurants or parishioners’ homes.
Founded in the Philippines in 1977, the Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ has grown steadily in Vancouver since the 1990s. As more people joined and the congregation grew from 80 to 100, hotel space became inadequate.
At the first meeting after the Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ purchased the church, everyone was in tears, Rivera said.
“We’ve been negotiating, and it was a back and forth. I’m just grateful to West Point Presbyterian Church. (They were) very patient with us,” Rivera said.
However, without the financial support of the global Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ denomination they are a part of, Rivera said they wouldn’t have been able to purchase the church.
Of the more than 30 congregations that Philippines-based Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ has across Canada and the Caribbean, only three own their places of worship, in Edmonton, Toronto and, now, Vancouver. It was hardest to find a church in Vancouver, said Concepcion, who serves as the church’s Canada district coordinator.
It’s difficult for congregations to host events, programs and fellowship without a space of their own, he said. “I believe that these programs in the church help believers to mature and grow and to be connected.”
Unlocking revenue to continue
While the Point Grey church sale represents a continuity of faith, other church sales represent a combination of faith and property development.
Acquiring and consolidating lots for a traditional land assembly is costly and difficult for developers. Collaborating with a church is relatively simple and a more attractive form of property development, according to Tim Law, a lawyer at Lawson Lundell in Vancouver.
Law, himself a regular churchgoer, said property development, whether for social or market housing, is a way for congregations to “unlock” revenue and continue.
Lawson Lundell posted in February 2026 about the opportunity congregations have to redevelop their property for major projects. They said congregations with old or aging churches can build new developments to help pay for new facilities and infrastructure.
Marcela Corzo, the founder of LinkQuest Development, said religious institutions in Vancouver are sitting on more than $3.4 billion in asset value, giving congregations a unique opportunity to continue their worship and mission.
The common denominator for congregations deciding to redevelop their land is the age of their churches, she said. “They have 100-plus years of lifespan, and they are coming to an era when they need to spend a lot of money in capital expenditures. More than 50 per cent (of places of worship) are facing very expensive capital expenditures.”
Tim Dickau, director of the non-profit Citygate Vancouver and former pastor of Grandview church, said congregations aren’t just developing property to keep their lights on.
Citygate works with a community network to support social programs, including by helping churches better utilize their properties to engage in neighbourhoods. For many congregations, Dickau said, it’s part of a larger mission to support community.
Rock said redevelopment projects represent a balancing act between competing interests. For example, in a space that might have housed an education wing or gym, a congregation might choose to partner with a developer to prioritize condos or commercial space instead.
For example, Oakridge United Church, which redeveloped in 2018 to include 49 residential units and a coffee shop, now has fewer rental spaces than before, said Rock.
“I think most churches that do some kind of a redevelopment are downsizing their space rather than creating more community spaces for rent,” he said.
One municipality encouraging property development at places of worship is Burnaby. It allows up to six storeys of housing if it’s for uses such as dormitories, supportive and transitional housing, and non-market housing. If congregations or property developers want to build higher than six storeys and include market-rate housing on the property, they need approval from council.
“They really see churches as a low-density use with kind of underused land,” said Roberts. “They really see housing as a big issue. They don’t see churches as a big issue.”
Carl Isaak, city liaison to the Burnaby Housing Authority, said the city is prepared to allow even more housing to be built on place-of-worship property if community amenities are built with it. Isaak said the density of the residential housing is “essentially unlimited” provided churches and developers include community benefits and amenities reflective of the development potential.
One door closed, another opened
In Point Grey, the Presbyterian church tried for more than two years to sell. When the property was listed at $10 million near the peak of the booming real estate market, there were discussions about developing housing while retaining a place of worship on the property.
As the property market cooled, they eventually received an offer for $7.5 million from a developer. Zoning allowed for up to six dwellings in a small apartment building, or eight rental homes. But if they agreed to the sale, the church would have to take on risk for rezoning of the property, Rokeby said.
Eager for a clean sale, the church approached Leonardo Di Francesco and Rav Rampuri, two church realtors with more than 30 years experience. The two helped find the Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ. They say they have sold nearly 100 churches to Christians, Sikhs, Muslims and others, sales that reflect shifting religious demographics and immigrant trends of the past three decades.
But it’s difficult for local congregations to break into a market with such limited supply, they say. When a church does become available, many don’t have enough capital to purchase, or can’t get financing.
Francesco said banks are hesitant to give loans to religious institutions. “If they foreclose on a church, it will be all over the newspaper.”
It leaves congregations like Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ, which exist within large international groups, and property developers as the only customer base for the region’s expensive places of worship.
For six months, the two groups negotiated before settling on $6.4 million, which was $3.6 million less than the original listing price.
Rokeby said they accepted the offer for several reasons: the cooling property market, fatigue from the length of the sale, and the opportunity to have their church pass to another congregation.
Buying a church was the conclusion of a long-held dream, says Wilma Calica, a member of the Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ and one of those at July’s key-exchange ceremony.
There are “no words” to describe how she feels, she said, adding that congregants are “overwhelmed” with happiness.
After the key exchange, and before entering the church sanctuary, Concepcion prayed with the congregation.
He prayed for church communities to grow, for the few to become many: “This is not material treasure. This is not money. These are people … I pray that this place will be filled with rare, beautiful — not material things, not beautiful clothes — (but) beautiful people.”
On Sept. 27, The Pentecostal Missionary Church of Christ in Vancouver will celebrate 26 years.
It will also be the first time they celebrate an anniversary in their new church. The first time in a place of their own.
Marc Guido Bolen is a 2026 recipient of the Langara College Read-Mercer Journalism Fellowship. This feature was produced through the fellowship.

title: Fiction: A low-caste woman in Tamil Nadu’s Tranquebar is introduced to Christianity in 18th century
content:
Pecchi could not have guessed that the parangi who was leading her to this strange place was Schwartz – a man whose footsteps would later leave wide imprints on the soil of Thanjavur, whose name would one day be whispered as the shepherd of a new faith. For nearly 40 years, since Bartholomaeus Ziegenbalg had planted the first fragile seed of the Lutheran Mission in Tranquebar, Christianity had tried to push its tender roots into the hard earth of the south. The missionaries came from Denmark and Halle, carrying their strange books and stranger hopes – hoping to “rescue the heathen from darkness, to nurse their souls into salvation.”
But the land was old, its gods older still. The missionaries soon discovered that the people here clung fiercely to their pantheon, like children clutching the many fingers of one mother.
It was only with Schwartz’s arrival that the mission felt a new wind fill its sails.
Pecchi walked behind Schwartz towards the great doorway of the New Jerusalem Church, and a faint shiver passed through her. It was not entirely fear, nor entirely wonder, but something born of the two – like standing close to the sea at dusk, unsure whether to step back or forward.
“Have you been inside before?” he asked.
She shook her head, eyes moving slowly along the vastness of the structure.
It dawned on her that the parangi and his group were preaching a new religion, and she was entering a temple of this new faith. She had seen the temple at Godhanamangalam from outside. It looked large. She did not know much about the gods resident in the temple. Kadamban had said they were powerful gods, but they understood only the language of the Brahmins; Muthalamman was the goddess assigned to their caste. But Kadamban wasn’t happy with Her. Either She wasn’t as powerful as the Brahmin gods or didn’t take Her job seriously. Why else would they have to struggle for a living whilst the upper caste didn’t?
Now, faced with the enormous stone ribs of this church, the old temple seemed suddenly small, almost shy of its own shape and size.
After Bernt, Pecchi was no longer uncomfortable with white men, but this religion was strange. Rumours stirred in her memory – that parangis mocked the village gods, ate beef, drank liquor by the barrel and never washed after defecation. Yet, no rumour could explain the gentleness with which this white man placed a hand on her shoulder.
“My name is Schwartz,” he said. “You are safe here. This is God’s house.”
But she could not shake off her unease.
“My husband…” she began, “will you find out when he returns? He left five days after the Purattasi full moon.”
“We shall try,” said Schwartz. “First, you must eat.”
The moment he mentioned food, the world inside her collapsed into its oldest need. Fear, doubt, memory – all these could wait; hunger could not.
Just as she and Muthu received a cup of kanji and a sliver of fried fish, a woman hurried up to Schwartz, breathless in panic.
“Pastor! A pregnant woman – suddenly in labour – something is wrong.”
Schwartz’s voice was soft but firm. “Mariam, under the eye of the Lord, no one remains forsaken.”
“She cannot be moved,” Mariam insisted.
“Then you must help her, and we shall pray.”
Pecchi felt her fingers twitch – the instinct rising like a buried memory.
“I‒I can help,” she said timidly. “I am a maruthuvacchi.”
Schwartz turned to her with gratitude that warmed the cold air of the church.
“God indeed sends His servants at the right hour.”
The labour was long and dangerous. The baby pressed downwards too early; the mother’s breath trembled like a lamp flame. Pecchi’s hands moved steadily, though fear gnawed at her – fear of failure, fear of her ill luck. Between contractions, she whispered prayers to Muthalamman. She worried if the White God at the church would take offence at her calling her goddess. Would there be a clash between the gods? She didn’t know.
After hours of sweat and trembling effort, the newborn’s cry cut through the room – a perfect, unbroken flute. The mother’s exhausted smile glowed faintly in the lamplight.
For Pecchi, it felt as if a window had opened in her life and a soft wind had entered.
“You are blessed in your work,” Schwartz told her, his voice full of relief. “Truly, the Lord’s servant.”
Her heart brimmed with a pride she had not known in years.
“You haven’t had anything to eat! Will you please have your kanji?” Schwartz asked. Muthu wore a contented look, having had her meal.
Schwartz waited until she had eaten and then spoke gently: “If God has given you such hands, should they not serve the poor, serve His flock?”
Pecchi didn’t understand.
“I am asking if you’d want to work as a maruthuvacchi at the church?” he said.
“But I haven’t learned enough,” Pecchi said modestly.
“You could learn from a senior siddha vaidyar. The church will arrange that. You could work in our medical room,” said Schwartz.
So, she had found work; therefore, food.
Pecchi instantly promised Muthalamman two bottles of liquor. She had to find a way to settle her escalating dues.
The apothecary was a retired Dutch sailor who used vinegars and herbs with European names. The locals weren’t impressed. Some prescriptions went right against traditional wisdom. People were appalled that he should be prescribing a chalk mixture with opium, considered poison, to treat loose motion.
Samuel Benjamin Cnoll, a German scholar of palm-leaf texts, had been urging Schwartz to find a native healer. “The land already knows its cures, we must learn from them,” he had said.
A healer for women’s diseases would be a good start, Schwartz felt. That would bring in the female crowd. Women always seemed to want more from the gods than men.
So Pecchi joined the small medical hut beside the church. She inhaled foreign scents, ran her fingers over jars of rose-hip syrup and lavender balm, learning their temper as she matched them with the leaves and roots she had known since girlhood. Soon she was blending potions of her own, a union of western mixtures and forest remedies, and mothers began to arrive – women who trusted another woman’s ear, another woman’s hands.
Muthu, quick and eager, began to assist: crushing herbs, carrying warm water, wiping wounds with a tenderness that reminded Pecchi of her own mother. Mariam occasionally came to help; she had many other things to do.
Excerpted with permission from The Grammar of Silence: Five Centuries. Three Women. Towards Liberation, R Seshasayee, Rupa Publications.

title: Nepal floods: No bodies to cremate, kin burn kusha effigies as hopes fade for missing
content:
TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWAKOT): Families in flood-ravaged Nuwakot and Rasuwa who could not find missing relatives — or their bodies — began performing symbolic cremations with human-shaped effigies made from kusha, a sacred grass used in Hindu rituals.
After days of searching hospitals, morgues, riverbanks and recovery lists, relatives lit the effigies on pyres at cremation sites so they could begin mourning.
In Nuwakot, families gathered along Trishuli river for the rites as priests shaped bundles of kusha to represent the missing person, placed them on wooden pyres and guided relatives through the same rituals normally performed over a body.
Families from Rasuwa, one of the worst-hit districts, also began holding such funerals or travelling to cremation grounds after repeated searches failed to locate their kin.
Rozel Shrestha, 12, performed the rites for his father, Krishna Shrestha, 37, who disappeared in Rasuwa.
Krishna’s brother Jeevan Shrestha said the family had searched widely before accepting that they might never recover his body.
“We searched everywhere, went to morgues across the country, but could not find his body,” he said. “The family eventually decided we had to perform our traditional rituals to liberate his soul.”
Relatives of Raj Kumar Shrestha, 30, performed his last rites with a kusha effigy after searching for six days. The family had received a photograph of a body resembling him and travelled to Simtar in Nuwakot, but the body had already been moved.
They could not trace it afterwards. Nirajan Poudel of Bidur municipality performed rites for five relatives — his parents, uncle, aunt and cousin — after none could be found.
Similar scenes later unfolded at Pashupati Aryaghat in Kathmandu, where more than 100 kusha effigies were cremated in a single day. Tapindra Prasad Timalsina was among those who performed last rites there for Sabin, 21. A priest prepared the effigy and relatives poured water over it before Timalsina lit the pyre. “It weighs heavily on my heart,” he said.
Devmani Bhattarai, a professor at Nepal Sanskrit University, said Hindu scriptures permit families to perform last rites with an effigy when a body cannot be recovered and there is clear evidence that a relative was swept away or if an entire settlement was destroyed. “If the body has not been found, there is no time to wait,” he told TOI on phone.

title: El rap indígena se convierte en un escudo para defender la Amazonía ecuatoriana
content:
- Jóvenes de diferentes nacionalidades indígenas de la Amazonía ecuatoriana apelan a la música para denunciar los impactos de las actividades extractivas en sus territorios.
- Cada tema es interpretado en la lengua originaria de su autor y algunos tienen subtítulos y pasajes en español para tender un puente hacia oyentes de otras culturas.
- Mongabay Latam presenta las historias de cuatro raperos indígenas: Willan Gualinga (Taki Supay) de la nacionalidad kichwa de Sarayaku; Misael Elías Criollo Grefa (Misa17), a'i cofán; Raúl Vargas (Robenban), kichwa de Pastaza, y Tzitzanu, sapara.
- Con su música están llegando a escenarios nacionales e internacionales: el tema “Ingi Tsampi”, de Misa17, suma más de 400 000 visualizaciones en TikTok a un mes de su lanzamiento.
La primera vez que Willan Gualinga se subió a un escenario fue en su comunidad, Sarayaku, en la Amazonía ecuatoriana. Recuerda que le sudaban las manos, le temblaba el cuerpo y su boca no podía pronunciar todas las palabras que se amontonaban en su mente. Tres años después de su debut, se presentó con la misma canción en el Festival Rizoma 2026, en la ciudad amazónica de Puyo, donde ya no eran decenas, sino miles de espectadores los que coreaban sus letras en idioma kichwa.
Esta vez su cuerpo se movía al ritmo y, sobre todo, con la fuerza necesaria para acompañar el mensaje que estaba transmitiendo: “Allpamanda kawsay manda jatarishun” o “levantémonos por la tierra y por la vida”, en español. Este es el nombre de su primer tema y la frase que repetía a todo pulmón durante su presentación. La canción se enfoca en los relatos de los abuelos sobre los orígenes de Sarayaku y, al igual que sus otras composiciones, pone el foco en las amenazas a su pueblo.
“A través de la música podemos transmitir los conocimientos de nuestros antepasados y, sobre todo, defender el territorio”, dice este joven de 23 años, conocido artísticamente como Taki Supay. Como él, una nueva generación de artistas amazónicos están usando el rap como una herramienta para visibilizar las amenazas que afectan a los diferentes pueblos y nacionalidades indígenas de la Amazonía ecuatoriana y, sobre todo, para demostrar por qué es necesario proteger la selva.
Leer más | Eric Terena, el DJ indígena que denuncia el silenciamiento de la Amazonía | ENTREVISTA
“El rap es hablar de lo que sientes, de lo que está pasando y de nuestra lucha”, agrega Misael Elías Criollo Grefa, más conocido como Misa17. Él es el primer rapero de la nacionalidad a’i cofán de Ecuador y su tema “Ingi Tsampi” ya suma más de 9000 visualizaciones en YouTube y más de 400 000 en TikTok a un mes de su lanzamiento.
En el sur de la Amazonía, las letras del grupo Zona Verde, compuesto por Raúl Vargas (Robenban) y Alejandro Moya (Naruman), impulsan las demandas de sus comunidades kichwa y shuar de Pastaza por el acceso a agua limpia. En la misma provincia, pero en el territorio sapara, Tzitzanu rapea en contra de la industria petrolera y a favor de mantener viva su cultura.
Todas estas canciones transmiten su amor por los ríos, la selva, los animales y todo lo que les rodea. Pero, sobre todo, están basadas en las experiencias que vivieron los cantantes desde que eran niños, cuando empezaron a acompañar a sus padres y abuelos en la defensa de su hogar, en su oposición a diversas actividades extractivas que dejaron sus impactos ambientales en el territorio.
Cada uno canta en su lengua, lo que para ellos representa otra forma de resistencia, de mantenerse fieles a su identidad y de llevar sus saberes a otras partes del planeta. Aunque el rap de los cinco ya ha trascendido fronteras, el camino no ha sido fácil. La ausencia de estudios de grabación en la Amazonía y los altos costos de producir los videos son algunos de sus obstáculos.
A eso se suman los riesgos de exponerse públicamente a los impactos que generan las actividades económicas que quieren instalarse en sus territorios y que, según dicen, los convierte en blanco fácil de agresiones o represalias. Sin embargo, estos jóvenes confían en que esta nueva forma de resistencia, a través del arte y sus rimas, en lugar de traer más enfrentamientos, será motor del cambio que llevará el mensaje a un público más amplio, despertará conciencias y motivará a otros jóvenes a involucrarse en la defensa de la Amazonía.
Rapear para sobrevivir
A Carla Vera, docente universitaria y periodista musical, no le sorprende que el rap haya ganado popularidad en estos territorios. “Es un género que se acopla a la potencia de los discursos y de la resistencia indígena. Va en contra de la opresión, promueve la liberación, es directo y genera ese sentimiento de empoderamiento en quienes lo hacen y en quienes lo escuchamos”, dice.
Para entender el contenido de sus canciones hay que remontarse a sus orígenes. El rap surgió en el Bronx, uno de los distritos marginales de Nueva York, en la década de los 70. Las rimas cargadas de mensajes de protesta contra la situación del país, en un contexto de racismo, precarización laboral y maltrato policial, irrumpieron en la escena musical.
En la actualidad, este género mantiene esa esencia y la connotación política de sus mensajes. Para Vera, también es entendible que el rap esté ganando más popularidad en este momento, ya que responde a las amenazas crecientes que enfrenta la Amazonía.
Según datos de MapBiomas, recopilados por la Fundación Ecociencia y entregados a Mongabay Latam, el 71 % de la minería en Ecuador se encuentra en la región amazónica. De esta, casi la mitad (44.5 %) está en territorios indígenas. Por otro lado, las concesiones petroleras están en el 63 % de los territorios de pueblos y nacionalidades amazónicas.
Leer más | Ecuador: juez ordena frenar minería en el río Ortega y nombra a una comunidad como su guardiana
“No quiero ver nuestros ríos contaminados, no quiero ver nuestra selva acabada, no quiero enfermedades por la culpa del petróleo, no quiero ver más muerte en mi territorio”, rapea Misa17 en su canción “Ingi Tsampi”, que significa “nuestra selva” en su lengua A’ingae. Con una camisa que conserva la forma y los rasgos de su vestimenta tradicional, pero más holgada, para darle un toque más urbano, y con el número 17 atrás, Misa lanza una frase tras otra sin detenerse a respirar.
Este joven de 19 años nació en Dureno, una comunidad a’i cofán ubicada en Sucumbíos, en el norte de la Amazonía, que se ha opuesto al ingreso de las empresas petroleras Texaco y la estatal Petroecuador.
Uno de los rostros más visibles en esa resistencia fue su tío, Eduardo Mendúa, quien fue asesinado en febrero de 2023. “Eduardo vive y la lucha sigue, fuerza, fuerza en honor a nuestro líder”, recita Misa17, mientras detrás de él, en el video musical, aparece una imagen del difunto defensor.
Desde que empezó a escribir sus canciones, hace dos años, ha encontrado un refugio en el rap. Al reconocerse como una persona más reservada, la música se ha convertido en el canal perfecto para expresarse. Aunque al inicio sus padres no lo apoyaban en este camino, al ver su esfuerzo y sus resultados, ahora son sus principales seguidores.
Gracias a su videoclip, el mensaje de este rapero ha llegado a otros países. “El mundo se va a dar cuenta de todos los problemas que pasamos en mi comunidad y algún día llegará más ayuda”, dice con una sonrisa, confiado de que sus deseos se convertirán en realidad.
Robenban también espera que, a través de sus canciones, se pueda difundir la importancia de proteger la selva, especialmente la cuenca del río Puyo, que es el que pasa por su hogar, la comuna San Jacinto, en Pastaza. Actualmente, las comunidades de esta zona están impulsando una acción de protección para exigir la descontaminación de este cuerpo de agua, afectado sobre todo por las descargas de aguas residuales.
Junto con Naruman, Robenban está escribiendo una canción sobre esta problemática y espera publicarla en los próximos meses. Su idea es narrar los impactos en la salud de las comunidades y en el turismo, que es su principal fuente de ingresos. En sus otras canciones, Robenban ya abordaba temáticas similares. “Se escucha el llanto de los peces mientras los ríos se secan”, rapea en su tema “Decepcionado y triste”, que es una crítica a los gobiernos por destruir la selva y “crear guerras”.
Leer más | TEDxAmazônia llegó a Ecuador para reunir a científicos, artistas y líderes indígenas
El contenido romántico era el que más le llamaba la atención cuando inició su carrera, pero al ver los procesos de resistencia de sus mayores, decidió enfocarse en “promover la protesta consciente para defender la selva a través de la música”. Al escuchar a unos amigos improvisar canciones, conoció lo que era el rap. Así, empezó a imitarlos, sin imaginarse que, una década después, tendría seis temas propios en YouTube.
Su afición se convirtió en una profesión hace seis años, cuando conoció a Naruman, de nacionalidad shuar, y formaron Zona Verde, un nombre que hace alusión a su hogar. El grupo ya se ha presentado en diversos escenarios de la Amazonía y en ciudades de la costa ecuatoriana como Guayaquil. Además, cuentan que tienen seguidores en países como Colombia y Estados Unidos, que les envían mensajes y están pendientes de lo que pasa en sus territorios. “Queremos que los niños y la gente adulta llegue a entender que vivimos gracias a la tierra, a las aguas, a los árboles y no debemos destruirlos más”, explica este rapero kichwa de 28 años.
Una lengua universal
Al tener un integrante shuar y otro kichwa, las canciones de Zona Verde tienen frases en ambas lenguas y en español. En el caso de Gualinga (Taki Supay), sus letras son exclusivamente en kichwa y en el de Misa17, sus rimas son en a’ingae, con subtítulos y algunos fragmentos también en español. “Este ritmo me gustó apenas lo escuché, pero quería hacerlo en mi idioma”, asegura este rapero a’i cofán, cuya lengua está en peligro de desaparecer. Él está convencido de que esta es una forma de incentivar a los más jóvenes a seguir practicándola.
A Tzitzanu le ocurre algo similar, ya que el sapara también está en riesgo de extinguirse. Las manifestaciones culturales de esta nacionalidad, que vive en la frontera entre Ecuador y Perú, fueron proclamadas en 2001 como Obra Maestra del Patrimonio Oral e Inmaterial de la Humanidad por la Unesco.
Su lengua fue reconocida como un repositorio de saberes y “memoria viva de toda la región”. Cuando integraron la lista de la Unesco, sólo cinco personas, de más de 70 años, hablaban el sapara a la perfección. Ahora, solo queda una abuela.
Tzitzanu es parte de la nueva generación de jóvenes sapara que están aprendiendo su lengua con el fin de evitar que desaparezca. Cuando era un niño, acompañaba a su padre, que es maestro de la lengua sapara, a las distintas comunidades de esta nacionalidad para entregar libros, diccionarios, rompecabezas y juegos para motivar a las personas de este territorio a que retomen este elemento trascendental de su cultura. Ahora, se esfuerza por mantener su lengua viva a través del rap.
Sin embargo, para este joven, de padre sapara y madre achuar, es importante rapear en varias lenguas para que el mensaje llegue a más personas. “Hablar en nuestro idioma es interesante, pero nosotros tenemos claro lo que pasa y lo que necesitamos es dar a conocer nuestra visión al mundo de afuera”, explica.
Tzitzanu, que significa “el primer hombre que llegó a la tierra a enseñar la ciencia y el arte”, honra su nombre desde 2015, cuando un primo le enseñó lo que era el rap y desde ese momento decidió que esa sería su arma para defender sus derechos y los de su hogar, que forma parte de la Comunidad Ecológica Cultural Yakuruna, un proyecto de turismo vivencial ubicado en la Amazonía de Ecuador, en la provincia de Pastaza.
“Me gusta porque puedes expresar muchas cosas en poco tiempo”, cuenta el cantante de 28 años. La oposición a los impactos del petróleo en su territorio también es uno de los temas protagonistas en sus canciones. “Somos una revelación, evolución, revolución en contra de su traición, explotación y destrucción”, se escucha en “Enraizate” o “Aiteka kaja pawetsa kaje” en sapara.
Contagiar las rimas
Tzitzanu también busca que otras personas de su comunidad ingresen al mundo del rap. Por eso, les comparte canciones de otros raperos y les explica el impacto que pueden tener estas letras.
Por su parte, Gualinga dice que “hay que dar un mensaje más claro, que muestre cómo todo está cambiando y cómo podemos perder nuestro conocimiento”. Este joven kichwa conoce de cerca lo que es la oposición al establecimiento de las actividades extractivas en territorio indígena. Su comunidad, Sarayaku, ha sido reconocida internacionalmente por resistirse al ingreso de una empresa petrolera, que intentó instalarse sin consultar a su pueblo.
El caso llegó a la Corte Interamericana de Derechos Humanos, que en 2012 emitió una sentencia en la que se reconocieron violaciones a los derechos colectivos de este pueblo.Ya han pasado más de 14 años y aún no se ha cumplido con algunos puntos de la sentencia, como el retiro de los explosivos que la empresa instaló en 25 000 hectáreas del territorio de la comunidad.
Gualinga tenía nueve años cuando se emitió la sentencia y ese fue uno de los eventos que le marcó, ya que le ha impulsado a buscar más formas de dar a conocer lo que está pasando en su tierra.
“Mi sueño es tener un estudio en Sarayaku donde los jóvenes puedan venir a hacer música y grabar lo que realmente les apasiona”, cuenta este rapero que conoce de cerca las dificultades de producir estos materiales en la Amazonía.
Tanto Gualinga como Tzitzanu, Robenban y Misa17 cuentan que el proceso para publicar un video o grabar sus canciones es costoso, necesitan equipos que no son comunes en la zona y tienen que viajar a ciudades como Puyo o Lago Agrio, ya que solo ahí están los estudios.
Esto se ha convertido en un obstáculo para que estos artistas publiquen sus canciones. Misa17, por ejemplo, ha escrito 12 temas, pero ha logrado sacar un video. El objetivo de todos es buscar formas de instalar más estudios cercanos a las comunidades para motivar a los niños a seguir este camino. “Vamos a crear una comunidad de raperos para seguir resistiendo”, dice orgulloso el cantante a’i cofán.
Su anhelo es que los niños de las comunidades ya no necesiten de ídolos externos, como fueron para ellos Canserbero o Santa Fe Klan. Con cada verso en kichwa, a’ingae, shuar o sapara, esta generación está construyendo sus propios referentes y demostrando que la selva también se defiende con música. El mayor desafío ahora, dice Gualinga, es perder el miedo, no solo a presentarse en los escenarios, sino a recitar con fuerza su mensaje.
*Imagen principal: Willan Gualinga, conocido como Taki Supay en el mundo artístico, se dedica al rap desde hace tres años para difundir los conocimientos ancestrales de su pueblo, al igual que las amenazas que los acechan. Foto: cortesía Willan Gualinga

title: 300 mensen herdenken Joodse slachtoffers van razzia in Marollen in 1942
content:
Zo'n driehonderd mensen hebben donderdagavond deelgenomen aan een herdenkingsmars in de Marollen in het teken van de slachtoffers van de grote anti-Joodse razzia die op 3 september 1942 in de wijk begon.
300 mensen herdenken Joodse slachtoffers van razzia in Marollen in 1942
Lees ook: 76-jaar oude Razzia tegen Joden herdacht
Vierentachtig jaar na de feiten in de Marollen kwamen buurtbewoners, nabestaanden, verenigingen, kunstenaars en andere Brusselaars opnieuw samen om de slachtoffers te herdenken.
De mars vertrok om 19.00 uur in de Vossenstraat en trok vervolgens door de Huidevettersstraat en de omliggende straten. Op verschillende plaatsen werd halt gehouden bij de zogenaamde struikelstenen, herdenkingsstenen die herinneren aan Joden die vanuit de Marollen werden gedeporteerd en vermoord werden in Auschwitz of in andere nazivernietigingskampen of werkkampen.
Kunstenaars spraken de namen van de Joodse slachtoffers uit, samen met de datum van overlijden. Daarop volgde telkens een gezamenlijk "Présent". Dit gebeurde vaak aan het huis van de Joodse slachtoffers zelf.
Het initiatief van de mars kwam er op vraag van Richard Kalisz, die voor het project onder andere kunstenaar en acteur Sam Touzani en filmmaker Luc Dardenne samenbracht.
Verschillende artiesten namen deel aan de avond. Ook muzikaal was er een belangrijke rol weggelegd voor de herdenking.
Barbarij
De organisatoren benadrukten dat de herinnering aan de razzia's en de Holocaust geen zaak van één gemeenschap is. "Omdat de herinnering aan de barbarij de hele mensheid aangaat", klonk het bij de organisatoren.
De mars eindigde aan de ingang van de Huidevettersstraat, waar het toekomstige herdenkingsmonument voor de slachtoffers van de razzia's werd voorgesteld.
Het ontwerp heeft de vorm van een betonnen kubus op menselijke schaal. Een spleet die door het monument loopt, verwijst naar de historische en menselijke breuk die de Shoah heeft veroorzaakt.
Het monument moet, samen met de bestaande struikelstenen, een blijvende plaats krijgen in de openbare ruimte en toekomstige generaties herinneren aan wat zich in de Marollen heeft afgespeeld.
De herdenkingsmars bracht donderdagavond uiteindelijk ongeveer 300 mensen samen, onder wie Brussels burgemeester Philippe Close (PS) en OCMW-voorzitter David Weytsman (MR).
