“Surgió a partir de una sensación muy concreta: había muchas ganas de involucrarse, pero pocos lugares reales para hacerlo, sobre todo desde el interior y sin pertenecer a estructuras tradicionales, o espacios muy cerrados y elitistas”, asegura Uriel. “Es el proyecto por el que puedo madrugar, sacrificar planes, ocupar fines de semana enteros en reuniones y, aun así, sentirme feliz. Dormirme con la sensación de estar construyendo algo que vale la pena para otros jóvenes. Y la sensación de estar dejando un camino”.
“En la práctica, el IAEPG funciona como un espacio de producción y formación: escribimos artículos y documentos de análisis, organizamos charlas y encuentros, impulsamos instancias de debate y articulamos con organizaciones, embajadas y actores institucionales. Buscamos que los jóvenes aprendan a poner sus ideas en palabras, a sostenerlas con argumentos y a participar del debate público con responsabilidad”, continúa Uriel.
“La idea empezó a tomar forma a mediados de 2025 y se lanzó oficialmente en octubre de ese año. El principal desafío fue armar un equipo que creyera en una propuesta nueva, sin financiamiento, sin certezas y con mucho trabajo por delante, era difícil que se sumen, con, con la incertidumbre de no saber si eso iba a prosperar, si iba a fracasar, si merecía invertir el tiempo ahí. Muchos dudaron, otros rechazaron la propuesta. Hasta que aparecieron las personas indicadas. Compañeros que se sumaron sin garantías, con entusiasmo y convicción. Sin ellos, el IAEPG no sería nada. Todos trabajamos sin recibir nada a cambio, más que la satisfacción de no quedarnos con los brazos cruzados, algo que no es poco: jóvenes empujando para el mismo lado”.
“Cuando abrimos la convocatoria de voluntarios, una respuesta me quedo marcada para siempre fue: Cuando tengas algo importante que decir, pero hables bajito, buscá un buen amplificador. Creo que el IAEPG puede ser ese amplificador. Ahí entendí todo. Ese es el camino, sigamos por acá. Esta es nuestra misión”.
Tener foco y hacerse cargo de las preguntas incómodas: “Muchos jóvenes sienten que la escuela no les habla”
Uriel recuerda con orgullo a ese niño parlanchín que alguna vez fue, jugando en los médanos de su amada Pinamar, teniendo conversaciones eternas con sus abuelos y pretendiendo ser un señor con un discurso importante para transmitir al mundo. Mucha agua corrió bajo el puente y, sin embargo, su travesía recién comienza.
Lleno de propósitos para su querida Argentina y para el mundo, Uriel confía en este presente como trampolín hacia un futuro diferencial. Hoy IAEPG, como impulsor de sus sueños, reúne a más de veinte jóvenes de distintas provincias, entre ellas Córdoba, San juan, Buenos Aires, CABA, Chaco, Santa fe y Jujuy, y traspasa fronteras, con integrantes de Chile y Venezuela.
“Diferentes ideas, contextos y miradas, pero con una misma voluntad: hacer. Son jóvenes muy distintos entre sí, con diferentes ideologías, distintos pensamientos, contextos y realidades muy diversas, pero con ganas de hacer, aportar y sumar”, asegura Uriel, quien recientemente creó asimismo FOCO, un observatorio de educación: “porque la educación atraviesa todo y, sin embargo, rara vez se la piensa escuchando a quienes la viven todos los días. Se habla sin haber pisado una escuela y ver las condiciones reales de aprendizaje, se toman decisiones sin tener en cuenta los recursos y las herramientas de los directivos”.
“FOCO busca hacerse cargo de las preguntas incómodas: por qué muchos jóvenes sienten que la escuela no les habla, cómo se pierde el sentido de estudiar, qué pasa cuando aprender compite con el hambre, la precariedad o la incertidumbre. Pensar la educación hoy exige ampliar el dialogo. No alcanza con hablar de escuelas, contenidos o calendarios. La educación ocurre en territorios rurales y en márgenes urbanos, en contextos atravesados por la pobreza, la violencia o el conflicto, en espacios donde el acceso al conocimiento es frágil o directamente inexistente. Ocurre también en centros de estudiantes, organizaciones juveniles y experiencias comunitarias que muchas veces suplen ausencias estructurales del Estado. Se juega en sociedades donde persiste el analfabetismo, donde miles de estudiantes abandonan sin que el sistema registre su ausencia, donde la expectativa se erosiona y el sentido de aprender se vuelve difuso”.
“A quien está del otro lado, mi mensaje es: no quedarse de brazos cruzados. Ver un problema y hacer algo, aunque cueste, aunque al principio no te escuchen, aunque no te entiendan. En el camino uno se cae, se equivoca, aprende y se encuentra con personas que valen la pena”, dice Uriel, pensativo. “Y decirlo claro, los jóvenes no somos solo el futuro. Somos el presente. Somos muchos en todo el país con ganas de involucrarnos. Solo necesitamos que alguien nos escuche y nos tenga en cuenta”, concluye.
*
Si querés compartir tu experiencia de regreso podés escribir a argentinainesperada@gmail.com

title: For Whose Dear Sake Our Fathers Died: Priya Hajela on the trauma, contradictions of colonial history
content:
In the late 1970s and early 80s, in a school hall at The Lawrence School, Sanawar, students would rise together and recite Rudyard Kipling’s “The Children’s Song” — a pledge of loyalty to a motherland, sung in memory of fathers who had died defending it. Scattered through the rows were children who had recently lost fathers of their own, in wars with Pakistan. When the verse about fallen fathers landed, they would cry, and they would leave the hall. Priya Hajela, then a student at the school, never forgot it. “It made a huge impact on me,” she says.
Decades later, that hymn gave her the title of her new novel. For Whose Dear Sake Our Fathers Died, published by Speaking Tiger, follows four generations of the Uppal family across nearly a century of upheaval, beginning after the death of Maharaja Ranjit Singh and ending before the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
Speaking to The Indian Express, Hajela says her working title was Battle Lines, but once she finished the manuscript, she realised the book’s emotional charge was the relationship between fathers and sons. “The title has to touch the heart,” she says.
Hajela came to fiction rather late in life after a corporate career spanning 22 years. At 48, she pursued an MFA in creative writing at Goddard College in Vermont, which she completed in 2017, leading her to excavate the histories of her family and her people.
Born in Punjab, she was sent to boarding school at a young age and then moved to the United States at 17. Growing up, she could read Gurmukhi, but could not speak Punjabi fluently.
Her intention, she says, was never to study history for its own sake. “What drives me is actually to get an understanding of who I am and where I come from.”
Story continues below this ad
For Whose Dear Sake Our Fathers Died is a prequel to her earlier novel Ladies’ Tailor, which dealt with the aftermath of 1947. This time, the story is told through Beant Kaur as she pieces together the half-remembered life of her grandfather, Balwant Singh Uppal. “History talks about the leaders,” she said. “It doesn’t talk about what happened to the common man.”
A father’s death, a son’s dilemma
Balwant is where the novel’s central contradiction lives. He despises the East India Company as an “evil force,” but is willing to die for a British officer he personally serves.
The Calcutta army killed Balwant’s own father, a force made up overwhelmingly of Indian troops fighting under British command, says Hajela. “He wonders, are they my enemy, or are the British my enemy?” she says. “Yes, the British were leading, but there were so few of them.”
With the Sikh army his father died fighting for now dismantled, and farming crushed under rising taxes, joining the British Indian Army was the only option for Balwant.
Story continues below this ad
Hajela recounts the anguish of the Ferozepur Regiment, where Sikh soldiers were ordered to fight rebels who looked and spoke like them. They were so similar that they tore their turbans off, only to be torn apart on the battlefield. She says soldiers would turn their faces away as rebels were tied to cannons and blown apart. “There was definitely this massive guilt,” she said. “Is it really necessary? Yes, they rebelled. But to go to this length?”
Reading against the record
Getting the texture of this period right meant refusing to trust any single account, Hajela said. History written by the winners reads differently from history written by the losers, and until Independence, she points out, Indians lost at nearly every turn: the 1857 uprising, both Anglo-Sikh wars.
She found Indian-authored histories often eager to recover heroes and martyrs, while British accounts carried the victors’ biases, and she read the two against each other. Amarpal Singh’s histories of the first and second Anglo-Sikh wars became a key source; Singh, a computer engineer by training who became absorbed in this history, has also traced Sikh war memorials standing today in French fields from the First World War.
For the on-the-ground reality of 1857—what it actually felt like inside the Lucknow residency during the siege—Hajela turned to diaries written by British women, texts she found freely available.
Story continues below this ad
When the narrator doesn’t know everything
With all that research, Hajela’s first draft read like “a history textbook.” Her fix was to strip the story down to Balwant’s own limited vantage point.
“He does not know the rationale, and he does not know what’s happening elsewhere,” she says. “He is observing what is happening before him. And that is what he’s going to tell his granddaughter.”
She draws a direct line to her next project, a work of non-fiction on the Sikh Gurus. Guru Gobind Singh died in 1707, she said, but the Suraj Prakash, the chronicle by Kavi Santokh Singh that documents his life, was not written until the early 1800s.
For a century in between, the stories survived only by being retold and performed, gaining and shedding details with each telling. Hajela insists that the absence of a contemporaneous written record doesn’t make those stories less true.
Story continues below this ad
What’s left to fight for
Asked what she hopes readers take from the book, Hajela hopes it is the idea to “open your eyes, be aware, and find something to stand behind.”
She says the recent Gen Z student protests in Delhi against paper leaks were an example of the kind of stories worth telling.
“The world is becoming really strange,” she said. “You can’t just coast. Believe in something and believe strongly, and then do something for that cause.”
It’s advice Balwant himself gives his grandson in the novel: there may be no grand battles left to fight, but that doesn’t mean inaction is an option.
Story continues below this ad
Whether that instinct to act and pass the story on will survive in a generation fixated on their phones rather than a grandfather’s chair, Hajela isn’t sure. But she hopes the book does what that hymn in the Sanawar Hall once did to her: land somewhere and start a conversation.

title: Indu Mitha’s love story carried Bharatanatyam across Partition, kept it alive in Pakistan
content:
The life and times of Bharatanatyam exponent Indu Mitha, who passed away in Dublin at 97 last week after a brief illness, came with numerous twists and turns. The kind that seem as though lifted off a page-turner. Except that Indu’s story isn’t fiction.
In 1951, four years after the bloody Partition, a 22-year-old Indu, daughter of a Bengali-Christian philosophy professor, Gyanesh Chandra Chatterjee, whose family had moved to Delhi from Lahore after Partition, decided to move to Karachi against her parents’ wishes and married a Pakistani army officer, Aboobaker Osman Mitha. The two had met at her uncle’s house party shortly after Partition. A few days later, he saw her again. “I took one look, and my heart turned over… I knew this was the girl I must marry,” wrote Mitha in his memoir years later.
Mitha’s family was as opposed to the match as Indu’s, on grounds of culture and religion, especially amid the divisive space that the Subcontinent had become then. Indu’s older sister, Uma Chatterjee, was married to director Chetan Anand then, which was also not comforting for Mitha’s family, who considered a life around films hardly respectable.
Indu with her husband former Major General of the Pakistani Army, Aboobaker Osman Mitha (Credits: Instagram/ tehreema_mitha)
But despite all odds, Indu crossed over and married Mitha, and the two had three daughters in the following years.
When Indu came to Karachi from Delhi, she brought an unlikely inheritance: Bharatanatyam, the dance form she had imbibed in Delhi and Chennai. Indu had studied philosophy at Delhi University while training in Bharatanatyam under Lalitha Shastry. Shastry was from the first batch of Kalakshetra and had learned under the aegis of Bharatanatyam icon Rukmini Devi Arundale.
Alongside, Indu also studied modern and creative dance with actor and dancer Zohra Sehgal and her husband, Kameshwar Sehgal, at their Zoresh Institute in Lahore while her family still lived there.
Mitha, from a wealthy Bombay family, had joined the British Indian Army in 1942 after graduating from the Indian Military Academy, Dehradun, and served with the Parachute Regiment in Myanmar (Burma then) during the Second World War. After his family moved to Pakistan, Mitha was, in 1954, tasked with setting up the Special Service Group (SSG) of the Army, with help from US Special Forces. He is still known as the ‘Father of the SSG’.
Story continues below this ad
But Bharatanatyam, the art form from Tamil Nadu, was not an obvious choice for a woman making a life in Pakistan, particularly when the country’s cultural ideas became only more conservative with time, mainly in the 1980s. But Indu persisted, and for the next seven decades taught generations of students an art form whose cultural home was far away in the temples and courts of South India — first in Karachi, then in Lahore and later in Islamabad. She taught over 2,000 students. Some of her noted disciples include Amna Mawaz Khan, Iftikhar Masih and her daughter Tehreema, who now runs a dance academy in the US.
“To me, her greatest contribution was teaching young girls in schools in Lahore, who got exposure to Bharatanatyam and later teaching students at her academy, even though there were very few,” says noted Pakistani classical dancer, actor and social activist Sheema Kermani, 75, who was also seen performing classical dance in Ali Sethi’s popular Coke Studio song, Pasoori.
Against all odds
Indu began by teaching dance at Lahore Grammar School and later taught in cantonment houses, schools and academies; performed in drawing rooms and on stages; trained dancers who wanted to and could learn, including her daughter and choreographer Tehreema Mitha. Indu also formed an academy, Mazmoon-e-Shauq, later.
She also experimented with the form’s musical and literary vocabulary, using North Indian instruments and music and setting Urdu poetry to Bharatanatyam, partly because she could not remember all the songs as she was not fluent in Tamil, Telugu and Sanskrit and could not find South Indian orchestras, and partly because she felt that the dance needed to speak to those around her. She translated some of what she remembered into Urdu. This was pioneering work. She was presenting Faiz through Bharatanatyam, rare even in India.
Story continues below this ad
Then came the Zia-ul-Haq years, which were particularly difficult for the arts, especially dance. It was now incompatible with the State’s attempt to define a new Islamic identity. But despite severe odds and many curbs, Indu refused to give up dance and continued to teach. She did so more privately then.
Her daughter’s arangetram in 1986 at the Goethe Institute, as no one else would agree to give them space, took place during the Zia regime. With the organisers providing no help, Indu and Tehreema had to sweep the stage before the performance. Indu contributed to numerous choreographies of Tehreema, including one where a pregnant woman, deserted by her beloved, wants to have the baby.
“This woman’s character is unlike the traditional woman in the classical Bharatanatyam repertoire, who either pines for her lover or portrays her heartbreak… the choreography breaks that mould of traditional Bharatanatyam repertoire and of the female character by raising this unconventional theme and by inherently questioning social mores,” writes Indu’s student Feriyal Aslam in her dissertation Choreographing [in] Pakistan: Indu Mitha, Dancing Occluded Histories in ‘The Land of the Pure’.
‘The spark of an artiste’
Noted Pakistani Kathak dancer Nahid Siddiqui, who trained under Pandit Birju Maharaj in Delhi in the mid-1970s before moving to the UK during General Zia-ul-Haq’s period of martial law, met Mitha in Islamabad at a workshop she conducted at Indu’s academy.
Story continues below this ad
“The spark of an artiste is her life. In a place like Pakistan, where the promotion of classical dance is difficult, and there’s hardly any encouragement, one loses one’s spirit. So, I do think Indu ji felt isolated. But I always saw a sense of calm and peace on her face. She was a very fine woman, always in a sari, and she would almost always attend my performances in Pakistan. But all of us who dance and are from Pakistan have suffered a lot,” Siddiqui, who has been living in exile in London since her popular 13-episode show Payal was taken off the air after six episodes in 1978, says.
But despite this, Indu persevered, teaching those who were willing and making a place for Bharatanatyam in a country where its presence was often complicated.
Bharatanatyam exponent Indu Mitha. (Credits: Instagram/ tehreema_mitha)
Sheema Kermani, one of Pakistan’s most prominent classical dancers and choreographers and the founder of the feminist cultural group Tehrik-e-Niswan, met Indu in 1984 after she returned from India after training at Delhi’s Shriram Bharatiya Kala Kendra, where she learned Bharatanatyam under Leela Samson, Kathak under guru Ram Mohan and Odissi under guru Mayadhar Raut.
“I had just come back to Pakistan and was looking for other dancers in the country. Most dancers (like Siddiqui) had left by then. So, from Karachi, I went to see her in Lahore. I tried to understand how she managed. Indu ji didn’t perform very much and mainly taught. Once I invited her to Karachi to act in a play and she did. When I went to India again in 1988 and came back with more training in Odissi, she was very interested in learning about it,” says Kermani, now 75.
Story continues below this ad
Indu also appeared in the documentary ‘How She Moves’ (2020), which followed her and her students as she prepared for what was intended to be her final recital. Indu, however, later objected to the film, writing that the film represented the filmmaker’s ideas, and not hers.
Mitha was awarded the Presidential Award for Pride of Performance in August 2020 for her exceptional contributions to classical dance and the arts.

title: Fukushima’s Old Farming Rituals Come to Life in Haga Hideo’s Photography
content:
Photography as a Bridge to a Vanishing Time
Fukushima’s Old Farming Rituals Come to Life in Haga Hideo’s Photography
Guideto Japan
Lifestyle Culture- English
- 日本語
- 简体字
- 繁體字
- Français
- Español
- العربية
- Русский
Worshipping Tanokami: The Deity of Abundant Harvests
Before becoming a professional photographer, the pioneering folklore photographer Haga Hideo (1921–2022) worked as a translator at a news agency. That career came to an end in 1952 when the agency disbanded. For a change of scene, he headed to Fukushima Prefecture, where his father was from. While staying with relatives in what is now the city of Iwaki, he encountered a New Year ritual performed among farming families.
Prior to Japan’s rapid economic development in the years after World War II, folk beliefs in the tanokami rice deity were alive and well in many parts of the country. In Fukushima, the family patriarch and his eldest son would gather the straw from the rice harvested the previous fall to create a yorishiro, an object to beckon a deity, to welcome Shōgatsu-sama, the spirit thought to bring bountiful crops. In spring, this spirit would reappear in the rice paddies to make the rice ripen; it would then leave after the fall harvest, returning to the mountains where it dwelled.
The idea of an invisible deity responsible for the bounty of nature inspired Haga, who turned his camera lens to deity-welcoming ceremonies and their carefully crafted ritual implements and offerings. Casting a closer eye on this unadorned spiritual culture, he was reminded of marebito, the concept of a divine spirit visiting from the “other world” that he had learned about from the folklorist and ethnologist Orikuchi Shinobu (1887–1953) during his university studies.
Passing On the Traditions of Iwaki
In the foreword to Tanokami: Nihon no inasaku girei (Deity of the Rice Paddies: The Rice Cultivation Rituals of Japan), Haga’s first collection of photos taken in Iwaki, he explained why he had chosen to pursue this work there.
“For 2,000 years, the Japanese people have grown rice, around which the belief in tanokami and associated rituals has developed. Many Japanese customs and myths have been influenced by tanokami, providing insight into how rice cultivation rituals are reflected in daily life and social structures . . . Today, modern science has made good harvests possible without the intervention of tanokami. Progress in agricultural technology and the modernization of farm life are rapidly eroding traditional village society, in which religious beliefs, crop production, and entertainment were intertwined. This is a last opportunity to record the rituals associated with rice production for posterity.”
As Haga had foreseen, the rituals around rice growing were rapidly becoming simplified or had disappeared altogether. Meanwhile, the significance of rites centering around tanokami, such as Hiroshima Prefecture’s Mibu no Hana Taue and Ishikawa Prefecture’s Oku-Noto Aenokoto, has been recognized with their collective inscription by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Haga, who made recording folklore for posterity his lifework, passed away in 2022 at the age of 101.
Iwaki, where Haga got his start as a folklore photographer, is today on the verge of losing its traditional farming culture. The Iwaki City Museum of Folklore and Traditional Housing, which opened in 1999, is leading efforts to preserve what is left of those traditions. The museum collects and displays all manner of artifacts related to local life.
Five traditional thatched-roof houses, dismantled and transported from various parts of Iwaki, have been re-erected in the museum’s vast grounds. Meticulously preserved, they reproduce a premodern farm village. On display inside the houses are farming tools of the era; visitors can also try their hand at working in the fields and paddies outside. Iwaki schoolchildren visit here as part of their social studies lessons, and on weekends, adults can participate in workshops to learn about the local culture.
In the summer of 2026, Haga’s son Haga Hinata visited the folklore museum to donate 46 film rolls’ worth of digitalized photo data, to help teach local history. Sorting through the collection, the museum selected photos of folklore entertainment that had died out more than 30 years before, including them in a special exhibit during the summer.
According to curator Ōta Yūhi, “Photos depicting farming in Iwaki in the postwar years are very rare, and they are invaluable for scholarly research. For example, the folklorist Seki Keigo [1899–1990] remarked that he had understood narikizeme, the act of hitting a fruit tree with a knife to cast a spell to ensure a bountiful crop, from a written description, but that Haga’s photo was the first time he had actually seen the action performed.”
A special exhibit planned for the fall on the theme of “straw” features donated photos illustrating Shōgatsu-sama, torigoya, and other traditions. The photos will also be used for school lectures by outside speakers and are included in the Iwaki Digital Museum showcasing cultural resources. Haga says “I’m very happy that the folklore museum values local folklore and that I was able to entrust it with my father’s photos.”
Rich Folklore Traditions Live On
Haga also called on the Fukushima Museum in Aizu-Wakamatsu to donate the digitalized contents of 138 rolls of film containing photos taken throughout the prefecture. His father’s photos had been included in an exhibition that traveled to Beijing and Rome in 2012, the year after the Great East Japan Earthquake. Haga’s presentation took place on the occasion of the return of the exhibition to the Fukushima Museum.
At the ceremony, Ōsato Masaki, the museum’s curator in charge of folklore, displayed the actual ritual implements and crafts that the photos had recorded. He explained: “Along with actual physical examples, photos are vital for explaining traditional rituals. Haga Hideo’s photos, especially those in which he focused on capturing the essence of those rituals, are priceless.”
In addition, several film strips were digitalized in chronological order, giving a good idea of the sequence of events taking place. The 1960 photos showing festivities in the town of Miharu are particularly interesting.
One sequence shows the moment a bride enters the groom’s home, a once-in-a-lifetime occasion. According to Ōsato, “Haga must have negotiated beforehand with the family, since he took photos from inside the home.” He expressed surprise that the sequence of photos “shows the go-between and a female neighbor removing the bride’s umbrellalike wicker headgear and guests chanting the celebratory ‘Takasago’ song from the nō play of the same name. These are the kinds of photos depicting a ceremony that one might expect to see in school textbooks on folklore.”
Presenting the collection, Haga said, “Fukushima’s festivals are an important element in human relations. They haven’t really been in the public eye since the March 2011 earthquake, but I hope that these photos will make local people proud of their folk culture.”
A similar collection of digitalized photos, taken in the 1950s, was gifted to Kagoshima Prefecture’s Amami Ōshima in the summer of 2025; activities relating to the collection have been ongoing there. The Amami Museum held an exhibit commemorating the donation of the photos this summer and is also planning a traveling exhibition to other parts of Japan, starting with Kobe, targeting former residents of Okinoerabujima, one of the Amami islands. Perhaps a similar activity can be organized in Fukushima to communicate the local culture to younger generations.
(Originally published in Japanese. Reporting and text by Fujiwara Tomoyuki of Nippon.com. Banner image: A man carrying the straw bundles used in the Shōgatsu-sama New Year ritual, at left, and a man striking a fruit tree in the narikizeme rite. © Haga Hideo.)

title: The God who lived in our conscience
content:
The house is humming. The family is gathering. The old toys are coming out.
And Papa is about to build a universe.
Janmashtami in our home was never simply a festival we observed. It was a world we assembled.
Every year, Papa—my father, Deepak—would help us build the jhanki. From trunks and cupboards came old toys, some handed down from my grandparents’ generation, their paint faded, their limbs occasionally loose, their faces carrying the strange solemnity of objects that had survived more childhoods than one.
Little cows. Little cowherds. Little people. Little gods.
Krishna. Radha. The gopis. Animals. Deities.
An entire civilisation waiting patiently in boxes for someone to bring it back to life.
And for a few enchanted days every Janmashtami, that someone was us.
My brother Samir and I, my sister Seema, and our cousins Sumita, Sangeeta and Raghav gathered around the grown-ups with the seriousness children reserve for projects adults mistakenly imagine are merely play.
Our Bhua, Deepa, was there. Her husband, our Phuphaji, Hargobind Bhatnagar. Our mother, Sunita. Papa, Deepak.
And above all, in the great constellation of my childhood memory, there was Dadi, Kamla Bhatnagar.
Her husband, my paternal grandfather, Bade Papaji, was Bhagat Saran Bhatnagar. They belonged to that generation that seemed to carry libraries in their memories and histories in their habits.
But Dadi did something remarkable.
She told us mythology without demanding that we surrender our minds.
Who knew a grandmother could be so cool?
She did not tell us these stories as if curiosity were a sin. She taught us to wonder, to question, to listen, to imagine.
Mythology, she seemed to suggest, was not the enemy of science. Science was not the assassin of mythology.
Both were humanity’s attempts to understand what it could see and what it could not.
Sometimes mythology reached towards a truth before science had found the language to explain it. Sometimes
science arrived centuries later and illuminated what mythology had been trying to imagine.
Sometimes they disagreed.
Sometimes they danced.
And sometimes they simply stood across the room from one another, equally aware that humanity still knew very
little about the mystery of being alive.
For us, however, the mystery of Janmashtami began with atta.
The Yamuna flowed through our jhanki, made from kneaded flour.
We shaped riverbanks and bends with our hands. We painted them with watercolours—blue for the river, brown for the earth, green for the trees.
Give a child flour and water, and he will make geography.
Give him an old toy, and he will make history.
Give him a shoebox and a mirror, and he will make the weather.
Papa, Samir and I did exactly that.
The greatest thrill of Janmashtami for me was our sound-and-light drama. We took a shoebox and turned it into a primitive projector. We found mirrors, reflective glass, coloured cellophane, scraps of plastic, anything that could catch or bend light.
Blue became night.
Silver became lightning.
Grey became rain.
Darkness became danger.
Light became revelation.
We created monsoon storms with mirrors and scraps.

And somewhere in the middle of all that glorious amateur theatre, Papa would begin the commentary.
Then Dadi would add something.
Bhua would remember another version.
Phuphaji would interrupt.
Someone would correct someone else.
Someone would laugh.
And the story of Krishna would rise from the floor, the walls and the flickering light.
We were not reading mythology.
We were staging it.
There was Kansa—evil, frightened, furious Kansa, haunted by the prophecy that a child would one day bring about his end.
There was the prison.
Devaki.
Vasudeva.
The newborn Krishna.
A child whose first breath was taken in captivity.
And then came the great crossing.
Vasudeva carrying the baby in a tokri.
The storm.

The river.
The danger.
The darkness.
The desperate journey towards safety.

title: Karnataka Vet Spends Life Savings to Build a 600-Tree Gene Bank for Rare Mangoes
content: At the edges of forests, along village boundaries, and in old backyard orchards across Karnataka, wild mango trees cling to a shrinking place in the landscape. Unlike the polished, uniform fruits that fill city stalls, these mangoes are smaller, sharper, more aromatic — fruits that carry the weight of local memory. On a 5.4-acre plot in Kukkila, nestled within Vitlapadnur village of Bantwal taluk in Dakshina Kannada, rows of young mango trees rise like verses in a living manuscript. Each sapling bears a name — often remembered only by the older generation of farmers — and carries with it the story of a coastal landscape once rich with hundreds of naada mavu, local mango varieties now fading into obscurity. At the heart of this green archive stands Dr P Manohara Upadhya — a veterinary surgeon by profession, and a gentle conservationist by passion. Welcome to the world of wild mangoes of Karnataka. The Mangoes that almost disappeared In Karnataka’s lush Malnad and coastal regions, mango trees are more than just fruit-bearing trees. Many varieties are closely tied to the villages and families where they originated, carrying with them stories, traditions and the unique flavours of their home regions. But that sense of familiarity is under strain. Old trees are being felled, farms are shifting, and traditional food habits are fading. In many places, native mangoes vanish simply because they are deemed inconvenient or less profitable than standardised commercial crops. On a 5.4-acre plot in Kukkila, nestled within Vitlapadnur village of Bantwal taluk in Dakshina Kannada, rows of young mango trees rise like verses in a living manuscript. Farmers are generally reluctant to cultivate wild varieties, since the market favours fruits that sell by standardised names rather than for their uniqueness. Climate stress compounds the decline — irregular rains, sudden heat, and disease weaken flowering and fruit set, leaving harvests uncertain year after year. The loss is more than agricultural; it is cultural. Each fallen tree erases a local name, a flavour, a seasonal memory. For families who have relied on the same tree for generations, this is not just decline — it is a quiet erosion of identity. Yet across Karnataka, farmers, conservationists, nurseries and researchers are working to ensure these mangoes do not disappear. A living archive in Kukkila On Upadhya’s 5.4-acre plot in Kukkila, that effort has taken root in the form of Maavu Mantapa — a mango gene bank raised using his life’s savings. Its name in Kannada evokes both “mango” (maavu) and a sheltering pavilion (mantapa). The idea is simple but powerful: collect and grow varieties before they are lost, give each one a place, and preserve the living tree rather than merely its memory. By May 2026, Maavu Mantapa had already grown into a living archive with 600 trees, of which 430 were indigenous and 170 were Indian hybrid and exotic mango varieties. Each sapling bears a name and, often, a story of where it came from. As Dr Upadhya explains, the work is far from finished. Once the trees begin yielding, each will be carefully documented in an ongoing study. That process has already begun, with five plants bearing fruit this year and another hundred expected next seasons. On Upadhya’s 5.4-acre plot in Kukkila, that effort has taken root in the form of Maavu Mantapa — a mango gene bank raised using his life’s savings. Supporting him is NaaMaaMi — Naada Maavu Mitraru, or “friends of local mangoes” — a dedicated team that helps identify and track species across the region. What stands in Kukkila is therefore more than an orchard. It is an attempt to keep Karnataka’s disappearing mango vocabulary alive — one tree, one name and one variety at a time. Each mango carries a story Across Karnataka, the names of these mangoes are rooted in the places where they grew. There is Otte Maavu from Kukkalli and Kuri Tale from Anavatti, both grown in Hosanagar. Belur in Sagara taluk is known for Apple Raja, a mango prized for its crisp bite. Ripponpet has its own favourites, including Kubera and Swastik, while Hosanagara is home to Apoorva. Further towards the coast, Puttur is known for Puttur Master, also called Bolwar Kasi. Near Kundapur, the Narayana Kini mango from Kota adds another distinctive flavour to Karnataka’s rich collection of traditional varieties. Uttara Kannada has its own collection of distinctive mango varieties. Maani Bhatta comes from Kumta, while Gidugana Mane and Varate Guduga are found around Sirsi. Karwar’s Kodibag is known for Kari Ishaad, while Sullia has its own local variety called Nekkare. Some mangoes are valued for their ability to bear fruit throughout the year. Sagara’s Kattinakere and Mangaluru’s Derebail are both all-season varieties that can keep households supplied with mangoes year-round. Yadehalli and Gilalagundi, grown near Anandapuram, are also known for their all-season harvests. Beyond their names and flavours, these mango varieties embody practical traits prized by growers. Kadugaayi is pickled raw when the fruit weighs around 1.5 kg, helping preserve it for longer. Kuchgaayi is preserved whole in brine, extending its shelf life beyond mango season. Bolwar Kasi is known for its disease resistance and fast growth, while Baaymane Kasi produces exceptionally large ripe mangoes, weighing between 700 grams and 1 kg. Sundar is remembered for its heavy yield and importance to local households. Across Karnataka, the names of these mangoes are rooted in the places where they grew. Veteran journalist Shree Padre, who is the editor of Adike Patrike, a Kannada monthly farm magazine dedicated to farmers and rural communities, shares: “These wild mangoes weave together Karnataka’s cultural tapestry — where land, lineage, and tradition meet in orchards that embody identity as much as they yield fruit. They are more than mangoes; they are living legacies, each bite carrying the flavour of its soil and the memory of its people.” The orchard is only the beginning The preservation of these varieties is not confined to Kukkila. Across Sirsi, Karwar, Shivamogga, Dakshina Kannada, Belur, Gadag and other parts of Karnataka, custodian farmers continue to grow and care for lesser-known mango varieties. In his fifties, Rajendra Hindumane is a celebrated farmer from Hosahalli village near Jog Falls in Shivamogga district, Karnataka. Renowned for his integrated farming system and for cultivating more than 1,200 varieties of exotic fruits, spices, and medicinal plants, he also proudly nurtures 40 Appemidi mango trees on his two-acre farm. These trees, rooted in the heritage of Malnad, are tended with care by Rajendra alongside his teenage daughters, making the orchard both a family endeavour and a living legacy. Kannangi Seshadri (74), a farmer from Kannangi village in Shivamogga, cultivates 20 Appemidi mango trees on his 68-acre farm, alongside arecanut, jackfruit, black pepper, and nutmeg. He explains: “Naada mavu thrive in the Malnad region, unlike Raspuri or Alphonso. They bear fruit at the onset of the monsoon in June, just as the rains arrive.” Farmer Mapalathota Subraya Bhat of Markanja village, near Sullia in Dakshina Kannada district, has preserved 80 wild varieties on his land. Eight years ago, Sameer Patil planted 500 Appemidi plants in Lakkalakatti village in Ron taluka of Gadag district, which receives scanty rainfall, unlike the coastal areas. “Its ability to flourish in arid and semi-arid regions prompted me to plant this new crop, and I am getting good harvests,” he said. Together, these farmers are doing something crucial: keeping varieties in cultivation rather than allowing them to survive only as memories of older orchards. Saving a tree is not enough; Its important to grow more For a rare mango variety to survive, protecting an old tree is only the beginning. It also needs to be propagated and planted elsewhere. Ananthmurthy Javali was among the first to collect scion cuttings from forests and develop them into mother plants in his nursery. Ananthmurthy Jawali in his nursery Today, he maintains over 400 mother plants of Appemidi mango at Ripponpet village, making him a key figure in safeguarding this heritage fruit. His work ensures that rare mango genotypes are not lost to deforestation or neglect, keeping Karnataka’s mango heritage alive. “I have lost count of wild mango saplings I have sold over the years. It may be over 50,000,” he says. The scale of that propagation offers these varieties a chance to move beyond the trees where they were first found. “We grow these varieties more for their emotional value than for demand. There are very few takers, and growers rarely ask for them. But when dedicated mango enthusiasts visit our nursery, we suggest unique types like Apple Raja, Varate Guduga, or Kadugaayi, highlighting what makes each special,” says Amogh Javali, who co-runs the three-decade-old Ankur Farm and Nursery with his father, Ananthmurthy. In 2025, Ananthmurthy was honoured with the Plant Genome Saviour Farmer Recognition Award by the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Authority (PPV&FRA). The award recognised his conservation of Appemidi mango, jackfruit, and other rare fruit species — cementing his role as both an innovator and a custodian of biodiversity. What researchers are trying to save While farmers and nurseries are keeping these mangoes alive on the ground, researchers are working to understand and conserve the diversity within them. Appemidi mangoes, in particular, are valued for their use in pickles, with fruits and leaves carrying distinct aromas. Sade midi is the plain variety, Jeerige midi has the aroma of cumin, and Karpoor midi has the aroma of camphor. Comprehensive surveys have been conducted across Karnataka, and over 200 local Appemidi mango genotypes have been collected and conserved in the field gene bank of ICAR-IIHR. Characterisation of these varieties is currently underway at the Institute. It has also developed cryopreservation techniques to store their pollen for future breeding, and supported efforts to secure a Geographical Indication (GI) tag to protect their identity. By working closely with farmer groups in Shivamogga and Sirsi, it has helped graft and propagate rare types, ensuring both cultural preservation and livelihood support. “While wild mango diversity exploration has not been specifically conducted in the coastal regions of Karnataka, Appemidi mango varieties native to the Western Ghats region have been conserved,” says Dr M Sankaran, Principal Scientist & Head, Division of Fruit Crops, ICAR-IIHR, Bengaluru. Researchers studying coastal Karnataka have confirmed just how variable these native mangoes are. A detailed assessment of wild genotypes in the region found major differences in fruit weight, stone weight, pulp percentage, peel percentage, and leaf traits, proving that this is a broad and valuable genetic pool. “Wild mangoes of the Western Ghats are known for their distinctive flavours, tastes, and scents,” the study notes, underlining why scientists consider them important conservation material. This diversity could also prove valuable for the future. Researchers see Appemidi germplasm as a potential resource for breeding disease-resistant and climate-resilient mangoes — connecting the conservation of traditional varieties with the challenges facing agriculture today. From farms to gene banks and orchards The conservation effort is also moving beyond individual farmers and nurseries. In a village of Karnataka’s Mandya district lies the 15-acre Bada Bagh, a living archive of forgotten mangoes. Its custodian, Syed Ghani, tends to varieties that are commercially unknown yet centuries old. Within its groves stand between 100 and 119 distinct types — many found nowhere else. Ghani recalls how this orchard once supplied fruit to the palaces of the Mysore maharajas and even to Tipu Sultan himself. After years of painstaking effort, he succeeded in registering 116 of these trees as indigenously collected plant material, securing their place within India’s protected genetic heritage. The Sirsi-based College of Forestry, too, has helped popularise wild mangoes by moving them from backyard and traditional use into formal conservation, research, and nursery propagation. It has also worked with farmers, NGOs, and forest departments to keep these indigenous mango varieties in cultivation rather than letting them disappear. The influence of such conservation efforts has extended into public spaces as well. The preservation of these varieties is not confined to Kukkila. In 2025, when Mangaluru’s Pilikula Golf Club set out to plant 4,000 native saplings — among them 180 varieties of wild mango — after clearing the acacias, they turned to the Kodagu-based Chirgura Nursery. These saplings, carrying the genetic legacy of landscapes from Kasaragod to Uttara Kannada, many of them endangered, are now poised to take root in a new public space. From individual farms to nurseries, research institutions and public landscapes, the effort is creating more places where Karnataka’s rare mangoes can survive. More than a mango For generations, these trees have existed quietly at the edges of farms, in backyards and along forest landscapes. Their value was not always measured by how much money a fruit could fetch in a market. It lived in the first mangoes of the monsoon, in pickle jars that lasted beyond summer, in local names passed from one generation to another, and in the knowledge of farmers who knew which tree flowered when, which fruit stored well, and which variety could withstand a particular landscape. Today, that knowledge is finding new life in conservation orchards, nurseries, farms and gene banks. The work is not about replacing commercial mangoes. It is about ensuring that Karnataka does not lose the extraordinary diversity that existed alongside them. And with farmers planting new saplings, nurseries propagating rare varieties, researchers conserving their genetic material and institutions creating new spaces for them to grow, these mangoes are no longer surviving only in memory. From Kukkila’s Maavu Mantapa to scattered orchards across the Ghats, Karnataka’s wild mangoes remind us that heritage is not past — it is living: fruits that bind food, ecology, and memory. In a land dominated by commercial varieties, these treasures endure for their distinctive character, rooted deeply in the Western Ghats. To protect them is to safeguard biodiversity and, just as importantly, a way of eating, remembering, and belonging.

title: Sacks, Matkas & Bows Become Sports Gear at Madhya Pradesh’s Baiga Olympics
content: There are no synthetic tracks here. No floodlit stadium. No branded jerseys, expensive sports shoes or professional training camps. Instead, there are gunny sacks, earthen pots, ropes, bows and arrows, mud, wooden sticks and the physical skills that have travelled through generations of the Baiga community. In Baihar, in Madhya Pradesh’s Balaghat district, these everyday objects become sporting equipment during the Baiga Olympics — a tribal sporting and cultural festival designed around the traditional games of the Baiga people. The event was first organised in Baihar in 2015 by the Balaghat Tourism Promotion Council, with the stated aim of showcasing traditional Baiga games and helping conserve the community’s cultural heritage. Later editions have brought together Baiga participants from Madhya Pradesh and neighbouring states. A 2020 edition, for instance, was planned over three days and invited Baiga communities from parts of Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Jharkhand and Andhra Pradesh. But who are the Baigas? The Baigas are one of Madhya Pradesh's Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs)-a special category created to identify tribal communities facing particularly severe socio-economic and infrastructural disadvantages. India currently recognises 75 PVTGs across 18 states and the Union Territory of Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The classification has historically been based on indicators including low literacy, economic vulnerability, geographical isolation, dependence on subsistence livelihoods, and stagnant or declining population trends. The Baiga are among the PVTGs listed in Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. The term itself has an important history. These communities were earlier officially referred to as “Primitive Tribal Groups”, but the terminology was changed to PVTG in 2006–07 because the word “primitive” was considered inappropriate and value-laden. They have traditionally lived in close relationship with the forests of central India, particularly across areas of Madhya Pradesh and neighbouring Chhattisgarh. In Madhya Pradesh, large concentrations of the community are found in districts including Mandla and Balaghat. Their relationship with the forest goes well beyond livelihood. Baiga communities have traditionally depended on forest resources for food, medicine and other necessities, while maintaining extensive knowledge of local plants and their uses. And then there are the games. Long before the word "Olympics" was attached to them, many of these activities were simply part of community life. The Baiga Olympics takes those games out of the village setting and puts them into a common arena. So, what exactly happens at the Baiga Olympics? The answer is wonderfully different from what one might expect from a conventional sporting meet. Take Bora Daud. Instead of sprinting down a professional track, participants climb into gunny sacks and race. The humble sack becomes the equivalent of a piece of sporting equipment. Then there is the Matka race, where participants race while balancing earthen pots. It turns an everyday object into a test of balance, coordination and speed. From Matka Daud and Bora Daud to Bhalafenk, Dhanushbaan, Kabaddi and Kho-Kho, the games blend tradition with sport. Photograph: (Madhya Pradesh Tourism/Shutterstock) Bhalafenk, or spear throwing, draws on the physical precision associated with traditional hunting skills. Dhanushbaan, involving the bow and arrow, is another important traditional contest. The Madhya Pradesh government lists it among the Baiga Olympics' traditional "hunter games". There is also Vajni Khel, described as a traditional form of wrestling; Rassa-Kashi, the tug-of-war; and running events including relay and Tritangi races. The official list of competitions has included Matka Daud, Bora Daud, Tritangi race, relay race, Bhalafenk, Vajni Khel, Lipa-Poti, kabaddi, kho-kho, volleyball, Rassa-Kashi and Dhanushbaan. Earlier editions have also featured games such as Gobardanda. What do you need to compete? Not much by modern sporting standards. A sack for Bora Daud. An earthen pot for the Matka race. A spear for Bhalafenk. And, most importantly, the knowledge of how to use them. A special torch also forms part of the event. According to the Balaghat district administration, the torch travels through different districts before reaching Baihar, with a promotional vehicle accompanying it and inviting Baiga youth to participate. The event was first organised in Baihar in 2015 by the Balaghat Tourism Promotion Council. Photograph: (Government of Madhya Pradesh) The participants, too, are not necessarily professional athletes. The Ministry of Tourism describes the event as one where both young and older members of the Baiga community can participate, rather than restricting competition to trained athletes. A participant does not need years of specialised coaching, a sponsorship deal or access to a stadium. A skill learned through community life can become the basis for competition. Why does something like this matter? Because indigenous cultures can disappear quietly. The Baiga Olympics offers one way of keeping some of those practices visible. People from Baiga community are all set to welcome you to take a sneak peek into their world with Baiga Olympics, Balaghat. The 3 day fiesta from 4th-6th Jan will showcase the rich culture of Baiga tribes of Madhya Pradesh.#MPTourism pic.twitter.com/nsFQWyLVUD — Madhya Pradesh Tourism (@MPTourism) January 2, 2020 There is also an important question of dignity. For years, tribal communities have often been represented primarily through poverty, remoteness or deprivation. The Baiga Olympics attempts to shift the frame. An Olympics without an Olympic-sized budget That may ultimately be the most compelling part of the Baiga Olympics. The event borrows the language and spectacle of a global sporting competition, the torch, competitions, teams, spectators and prizes but changes the meaning of what counts as an athlete and what counts as sport. The Baiga Olympics does not attempt to reproduce the world's Olympics in a forested corner of Madhya Pradesh. It builds a sporting platform around what the community already knows. Sources: ‘Balaghat to host two-day Baiga Olympics to promote tribal culture’: By Hindustan Times, Published on 18 March 2015 ‘Baiga tribe: cuisine and culture’: By Madhya Pradesh Tourism, Published on 12 May 2022 ‘Baiga Olympics’: By Government of Madhya Pradesh

title: Que nous dit le folklore ? Il révèle des facettes méconnues des récits autochtones, négligées depuis des générations.
content:
Cet article s’inscrit dans la série « Droits des peuples autochtones » du Spotlight de Global Voices d’août 2026. Cette série donne un aperçu de la vie et des expériences des peuples autochtones afin de créer des liens entre les régions, de placer leurs vécus au cœur du récit et de partager les histoires de dirigeants, de militants, de membres des communautés et bien d’autres encore. Vous pouvez soutenir cette couverture en faisant un don ici.
Enfant, je m’asseyais avec ma grand-mère près d’un borais (un petit pot en terre servant à faire du feu) durant les rudes journées d’hiver. J’écoutais ses récits de personnages bienveillants ou maléfiques — djinns, esprits, fantômes, sorcières et sorciers, arbres, oiseaux et animaux — qui revêtaient une importance particulière dans la culture et la tradition tharu. Elle chantait des chants populaires avant de m’en expliquer le sens.
Je n’avais jamais envisagé de documenter le folklore autochtone tharu avant le départ de ma grand-mère. Maintenant qu’elle n’est plus parmi nous, ses précieuses paroles de sagesse me manquent profondément. Heureusement, j’ai eu l’occasion de collaborer avec Amrit Sufi et Subhasish Panigrahi, qui non seulement documentent la culture orale en Inde, mais ont aussi inspiré et aidé de nombreuses personnes passionnées de culture et de traditions à documenter leurs propres cultures.
Documenter le folklore autochtone demande du temps. Il faut d’abord passer du temps auprès des communautés pour qu’elles se sentent suffisamment en confiance pour partager leurs contes, leurs chansons, leurs expressions et leurs idiomes, sans oublier leurs expériences personnelles.
En documentant la culture orale tharu dans l’est du Népal, j’ai découvert de nombreux éléments fascinants qui, s’ils étaient étudiés plus en profondeur, révéleraient des facettes méconnues des récits autochtones.
Morangsair : un chant de migration saisonnière
En enregistrant un chant populaire appelé « Morangsair » ou « Morangesari », encore chanté dans l’est des plaines du sud du Népal, j’ai découvert la migration saisonnière de jeunes hommes quittant le district de Saptari, à l’extrême est de la province de Madhesh, pour se rendre dans le district de Morang, dans la province de Koshi, à l’est du Népal, une région plus fertile qui offrait du travail à ceux qui souhaitaient gagner un peu plus d’argent.
Le district de Sunsari, nommé d’après la rivière Sursair — aujourd’hui appelée « rivière Sunsari » — faisait partie du district de Morang avant 1962. Aujourd’hui, pour rejoindre Sunsari, autrefois rattaché à Morang, depuis Saptari, il faut traverser deux rivières : la rivière Koshi et la rivière Sunsari. À cette époque, avant la construction des ponts, le trajet était bien plus difficile.
Ce chant populaire est la plainte d’une jeune femme qui supplie son mari de ne pas partir à Morang. Elle évoque la forêt dense, le climat chaud et la rivière Sursair, qu’il devrait traverser pour s’y rendre. Pourtant, le chant ne mentionne pas la rivière Koshi, la plus grande du Népal, qui se trouve avant la rivière Sunsari sur le chemin menant à Morang.
Dans la vidéo ci-dessous, Chandrakala Chaudhary, originaire d’Itahari dans le district de Sunsari, interprète « Morangsair », également appelé « Morangesari » :
En approfondissant mes recherches, j’ai appris que le cours actuel de la rivière Koshi se situait autrefois plusieurs kilomètres plus à l’est. Dans sa partie indienne, la rivière a déplacé son cours de près de 100 kilomètres vers l’ouest. Le Gange est également appelé « Sursuri » ou « Sursari » dans le Guru Granth Sahib, un texte sacré hindou. Les rivières Sursair et Koshi finissent toutes deux par rejoindre le Gange.
Biyahi : quand une rivière porte le nom d’une femme mariée
En discutant avec Mahabir Chaudhary, un aîné tharu du district de Saptari, au Népal, j’ai découvert un fait intéressant : une rivière et l’un de ses affluents portent des noms issus de mots tharu désignant une femme mariée.
La rivière a été rebaptisée « Behai » par des administrateurs népalophones. Pourtant, selon des aînés tharus, son nom d’origine est « Biyahi », qui signifie « première épouse » en tharu kochila, ou tharu oriental. Un affluent nommé « Samdahi » alimente cette rivière. « Samdahi » signifie « deuxième épouse » en tharu oriental. Après leur confluence, les rivières Samdahi et Biyahi poursuivent leur cours sous le nom de Biyahi.
Sabudana ke gachhi : le motif de tatouage qui raconte l’histoire des perles de sagou
De nos jours, le sabudana, ou sagou, vendu sur les marchés est principalement fabriqué à partir de l’amidon de racine de manioc. Pourtant, autrefois, les perles de sagou étaient aussi préparées à partir de la moelle des palmiers sagoutiers. J’ai découvert ce procédé lors d’un entretien avec des femmes âgées parlant le tharu oriental. L’une d’elles m’a montré un tatouage ressemblant à un palmier et m’a expliqué qu’il s’agissait du sabudana ke gachhi. « Gachhi » est le mot tharu pour « arbre ». Elle m’a également confié que le sabudana était autrefois fabriqué à partir d’un palmier.
J’ai ensuite approfondi mes recherches et découvert qu’autrefois, on abattait les palmiers, en extrayait la moelle riche en amidon du tronc, puis on la transformait pour fabriquer des perles de sagou. Cette tradition perdure encore dans certains pays d’Asie du Sud-Est.
En documentant la culture orale tharu, j’ai recueilli bien d’autres récits qui méritent d’être portés à la connaissance d’un public plus large.
Mais je cherche encore à me remémorer les histoires que me racontait ma grand-mère, lorsque nous étions assises près du feu pendant les froides journées d’hiver.

title: 32º Grito dos Excluídos e Excluídas une moradia, terra e vida das mulheres nas ruas de Porto Alegre
content:
Porto Alegre recebeu, nesta segunda-feira (7), a 32ª edição do Grito dos Excluídos e Excluídas, mobilização que ocupa as ruas do país desde 1995 como contraponto popular aos desfiles cívico-militares do Dia da Independência. Neste ano, o lema nacional da caminhada é “Na defesa da Terra, da Paz e da Moradia, erguemos a voz: Mulheres Vivas e Soberania!”, tema que orientou falas, cânticos e apresentações ao longo de toda a manhã.
A concentração começou em frente ao Instituto Federal de Educação, Ciência e Tecnologia do Rio Grande do Sul (IFRS), na rua Coronel Vicente, no Centro Histórico, marcando a defesa da educação pública e gratuita como um dos eixos da atividade. De lá, os manifestantes seguiram em caminhada até a rua Barros Cassal, no bairro Floresta, em frente ao Cibai Migrações e ao Assentamento 20 de Novembro, onde ocorreu o ato político e cultural que encerrou a programação.
Moradia como eixo da mobilização
A pauta habitacional atravessou praticamente todas as falas do ato. O encerramento em frente ao Assentamento 20 de Novembro não foi escolha aleatória: o empreendimento é fruto de 20 anos de organização de famílias sem-teto e está com a obra em fase final de conclusão.
Ceniriani Vargas da Silva, conhecida como Ni, integrante do Movimento Nacional de Luta pela Moradia (MNLM), destacou o significado de realizar o encerramento naquele endereço. “Esse grito para nós foi bem importante porque também traz a pauta da habitação como algo central”, afirmou. Segundo ela, a mobilização também reuniu as lutas pela terra, pela paz e pela soberania e o enfrentamento à violência contra as mulheres, tema que, avaliou, precisa estar presente em todos os espaços.
Segundo Ni, a inauguração do assentamento está marcada para 22 de novembro, com festa que deve incluir atrações musicais e interdição da rua para a celebração. “Vai ser uma festa linda, histórica para marcar essa grande conquista do movimento popular organizado”, disse. Para ela, o empreendimento também demonstra a capacidade do cooperativismo e da autogestão de produzir moradias de qualidade.
A questão habitacional também apareceu associada às famílias atingidas por desastres climáticos no Rio Grande do Sul. Leonardo Maggi, da direção estadual do Movimento dos Atingidos por Barragens (MAB), afirmou que grande parte da população atingida segue sem moradia definitiva. Enquanto o governo trabalha com a necessidade de 22 mil casas, o movimento calcula que pelo menos 50 mil unidades precisam ser construídas.
“A nossa estimativa é que mais ou menos metade das famílias ainda estão fora dos cálculos de habitação”, disse Maggi, atribuindo a estimativa a levantamentos do próprio movimento e da Confederação Nacional dos Municípios, além de dados do Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE).
Maggi citou o caso de Lajeado, no Vale do Taquari, onde, segundo ele, mais de 600 famílias estariam vivendo em abrigo mantido pela prefeitura, embora o município reconheça oficialmente 176 famílias na lista de habitação. “Existe uma incoerência, uma inconsistência no que está sendo feito. Dinheiro tem, só faltou decisão da parte das prefeituras de aplicar o dinheiro que o governo federal mandou para resolver os problemas dos atingidos”, avaliou.
A secretária executiva da Cáritas do Rio Grande do Sul, Jacira Teresinha Dias Ruiz, relacionou a pauta habitacional à Campanha da Fraternidade deste ano, que tem como tema o direito à moradia digna. Para ela, a conquista do Assentamento 20 de Novembro mostra o papel da organização popular na garantia desse direito. “E ela não acontece sem luta. O movimento de luta pela moradia é uma grande experiência, um grande exemplo de conquistas ao longo dos anos, até chegar a esse resultado dessa cooperativa habitacional”, afirmou.
Feminicídio e violência contra as mulheres
O enfrentamento à violência contra as mulheres foi tratado como um dos pontos centrais da edição deste ano do Grito, em referência direta ao lema nacional. De acordo com um dos informes transmitidos durante a concentração, houve um ato específico em memória das mulheres mortas por feminicídio, com a canção “Maria” e um minuto de silêncio pelas vítimas.
Chirlei Fischer, da direção estadual do Movimento dos Trabalhadores e Trabalhadoras por Direitos (MTD), apresentou dados sobre feminicídios no estado e no país neste ano. Segundo ela, 52 mulheres já foram mortas no Rio Grande do Sul e 834 no Brasil.
“Nós mulheres trabalhadoras do campo e da cidade estamos sofrendo muito com a violência”, declarou. “Precisamos denunciar esse feminicídio que cada vez mais cresce, que cada vez mais nos ronda, e dizer que o direito das mulheres precisa ser alcançado.” Fischer também associou a violência de gênero à falta de acesso a moradia, escola e trabalho remunerado digno.
Na mesma direção, Juliana Bergmann, da coordenação do Levante Popular da Juventude, apontou um crescimento nos casos de feminicídio no estado neste ano. Para ela, levar esse debate ao Grito dos Excluídos reforça uma pauta historicamente vinculada à classe trabalhadora e aos movimentos sociais. “É fundamental para varrer o discurso de ódio da internet, das ruas e das casas das nossas companheiras”, afirmou.
Leonardo Maggi, do MAB, relacionou a pauta a um caso ocorrido dentro do próprio movimento. Há quatro anos, segundo ele, uma coordenadora da organização em Porto Alegre foi assassinada pelo marido. “Trazer essa pauta, que é tão forte para todo o povo gaúcho, é muito importante para nós”, disse.
Soberania e disputa eleitoral
Parte das falas relacionou a data à disputa em torno de projetos de país, em ano de eleições gerais. Tomaz Brunet, da direção estadual do Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra (MST), afirmou que a soberania brasileira vem sendo pressionada por forças internacionais, inclusive por meio de tarifas e outras medidas econômicas.
“Mais do que nunca, neste dia em que comemoramos a nossa independência, a gente precisa reafirmar a força do povo brasileiro e reafirmar que é ele que deve dar a direção do seu país, e não outro povo”, afirmou Brunet, que também destacou a presença das cozinhas solidárias no ato.
Amarildo Cenci, presidente da Central Única dos Trabalhadores do Rio Grande do Sul (CUT-RS), defendeu a permanência da mobilização mesmo em um contexto de governo federal identificado por ele como mais favorável às pautas populares. Para Cenci, a existência de um governo progressista não elimina a necessidade de pressão social por direitos.
“A gente continua na luta por direitos, por moradia, por paz. A paz significa direitos, educação de qualidade e moradia para as pessoas. Nós precisamos que os ricos sejam tributados e que o trabalhador e a trabalhadora permaneçam e entrem cada vez mais no orçamento”, disse.
Cenci lembrou ainda que a mobilização se manteve em edições anteriores mesmo em contextos políticos mais adversos. “Não me lembro de ter faltado um grito, mesmo em épocas em que a gente fazia com meia dúzia de pessoas, em ambientes mais difíceis, de neoliberalismo”, afirmou.
Território indígena e disputa de memória
O ato também reservou espaço para a fala de representantes de povos indígenas. Laércio Guarani, professor de história na retomada Nhe’engatu, em Viamão, relacionou a mobilização à disputa por território e por direitos historicamente negados às comunidades indígenas.
“Nossos direitos, dos povos indígenas, estão sendo atacados a todo momento. A gente vem de uma retomada, de um espaço onde a gente teve que fazer um movimento de retomar, onde um dia foram nossos também esses espaços”, disse.
Guarani também chamou atenção para a ocupação histórica do território onde hoje está construída a capital gaúcha. “A grande Porto Alegre também é uma grande aldeia indígena, para quem não sabe. A gente está em cima de uma aldeia, de um cemitério indígena, neste momento”, afirmou.
Encerramento com teatro e cozinhas solidárias
A programação em Porto Alegre foi finalizada com apresentação teatral do grupo Panapana e almoço preparado pelas cozinhas solidárias presentes no ato, formato que se repetiu em outras edições da mobilização no estado.
A caminhada em Porto Alegre integrou uma mobilização nacional que teve atividades em 18 estados e no Distrito Federal, além de programações realizadas ao longo da semana anterior em cidades como Lajeado, no Vale do Taquari, onde o ato coincidiu com os três anos da enchente de 2023, e Santa Cruz do Sul, integrada ao desfile cívico local.
O Grito dos Excluídos e das Excluídas surgiu a partir de debates da Semana Social Brasileira, promovida pela Conferência Nacional dos Bispos do Brasil (CNBB) em 1993 e 1994, e teve a primeira edição nacional em 7 de setembro de 1995.

title: Inaugural Indigenous food summit in Portland in September
content:
Nika Bartoo-Smith
Underscore Native News + ICT
PORTLAND, Ore. — A group of Indigenous organizations around the Portland metro area felt inspired by the first Indigenous foods expo last year in the Northwest. They decided to bring something similar to their own city.
Starting with a budget of zero dollars, and less than a year to plan, that dream has turned into a reality with the inaugural Indigenous Food Summit on Sept. 9 and 10. The event will be held at the Native American Student & Community Center at Portland State University, hosted by the Northwest Indigenous Food Sovereignty Alliance and other community groups.
Expecting around 300 people, the conference is completely free and open to the public.
Beyond programming, such as “wild food preparation” and “cougar hide tanning,” meals, coffee and snacks will also be provided to attendees; highlighting local Indigenous-owned companies. There will also be a marketplace of Indigenous vendors.
Over the course of the two-day summit, community members are invited to come learn and share knowledge focused around food sovereignty.
“I think it’s really important for folks to have those conversations about what food sovereignty looks like for themselves in their own communities or their organizations, whatever that looks like,” said Emma Johnson, Cowlitz, Indigenous Traditional Knowledge & Cultural Knowledge coordinator at Portland State University. Johnson helped organize the summit.
“I think that’s the power behind that term is that you get to define it for yourself, and it boils down to, in some form, managing your own food systems.”
Planning the summit
Over a dozen organizations are involved, including the university’s Indigenous Traditional Ecological & Cultural Knowledge program, Native American Youth and Family Center, OSU Extension and many others.
Organizing this summit meant putting together different sources of funding, Gina Mengwasser, Western Cherokee Nation of the Baysville Band, Health Equity manager at the center. This came primarily through grants, and organizers volunteering spare time to turn the vision into reality.
“It’s been chaotic, and not in a bad way. It’s just in a ‘whoa, are we going to pull this off way?’ And we’re pulling it off,” Johnson said.
The agenda includes dozens of different workshops for attendees such as pressure canning, growing first foods, tea blending and so much more.
The day before the summit Growers Food Safety Training will offer a course geared toward supporting Indigenous food growers in learning safe practices to grow, harvest and handle produce.
Planning a free summit was also crucial to organizers.
“This is a shared knowledge. We don’t want to charge for our knowledge,” Mengwasser said. “It’s supposed to be shared, and we want to do that for our community. And if we have the ability with some of our funding, we want it to be free.”
While this event is the first of its kind in Portland, organizers are aiming for this to become an annual or biannual event.
Organizers hope the summit is also a place of building community connections and continued food knowledge sharing beyond this event. And a space to learn about other resources and spaces in community centered around food sovereignty.
“I’m hoping for joy,” Johnson said, “obviously more connections and just like that inspiration to know that different avenues for food sovereignty projects are possible.”
For questions about the summit email NIFSA503@gmail.com.
This story is co-published by Underscore Native News and ICT, a news partnership that covers Indigenous communities in the Pacific Northwest.

title: Gabriela García narra en fotolibro una crónica familiar marcada por el EZLN
content:
“He estado dividida en dos mundos”, de ahí surge Hay pájaros en el alambre, editado por Hydra
Lunes 7 de septiembre de 2026, p. 5
Gabriela García Rivas, cineasta y narradora visual, tuvo que superar miedos, sacudirse silencios, develar secretos de más de 30 años y aceptar que “he estado dividida en dos mundos”, los cuales dieron forma al fotolibro Hay pájaros en el alambre, tras explorar el archivo fotográfico de sus padres, que participaron en la construcción de un sistema de salud comunitario en Chiapas, antes y después del levantamiento del Ejército Zapatista de Liberación Nacional (EZLN) en 1994.
Desde esa doble mirada, de la pequeña que nació y vivió en esa región a la mujer adulta, decidió “recontar y resignificar su historia”, así como “el vínculo con mis padres (Gabriel García Salyano y Georgina Rivas Bocanegra), la memoria de un territorio en disputa y lo que fui siendo entre esas imágenes”.
La autora puntualizó: “el movimiento zapatista puede contar su historia sin mí, pero yo no puedo contar mi historia sin ese levantamiento” insurgente.
En Hay pájaros en el alambre, desarrollado en el programa Incubadora de Fotolibros 2023, de Hydra –que produce desde la experimentación con narrativas y procesos híbridos–, “se aborda, mediante textos (en español e inglés) e imágenes, una reflexión única y personal acerca del movimiento revolucionario más importante de la segunda mitad del siglo XX en México”, historia de la que la familia de García Rivas es un testimonio vivo.
El fotolibro fue presentado por la autora el sábado pasado en la librería Hydra, donde estuvo acompañada por la fotógrafa y cineasta Maya Goded, así como por Ana Casas Broda, codirectora de Hydra Editorial.
En ese acto se abordó el proceso creativo de García Rivas, se recordó el arduo trabajo de sus padres, se recorrió su trayectoria en distintos formatos y se habló de la superación de sus miedos, así como del derecho de contar una historia, aunque haya pájaros en el alambre.
“Es un libro especial que aborda el zapatismo desde una perspectiva personal y poética; había una narrativa compleja, la cual trabajó Gabriel en la Incubadora sin politizarla; fue increíble, porque las primeras páginas del libro provienen de rollos que fueron revelados 30 años después de que fueron tomados por su papá, y ella los vio por primera vez aquí”, recordó Casas Borda.
Destacó que “ha sido importante la experimentación con materiales y formas de impresión, desde duotono hasta cuatro tintas en offset. En coherencia con la temática del libro, en la producción se experimentó con papeles locales comunes, los cuales tienen diversos usos, que enriquecen la narrativa con diversas texturas, gramajes y pequeñas imperfecciones”.
Maya Goded aseguró: “desde que conocí a Gabriela entendí sus silencios, que aprendió desde chiquita. Ella sentía que su historia no era tan importante por lo grande del movimiento zapatista; sin embargo, reflexionó, sintió y cuestionó. Me emociona que esa niña y su voz, que se mantuvo callada durante tanto tiempo, se quitó los escombros y etiquetas que no dejaban que emergiera”.
En entrevista, Gabriela García, nacida en Chiapas y egresada del Centro de Capacitación Cinematográfica, explicó que la génesis del fotolibro fue la idea de hacer un documental sobre el Islam y su llegada a San Cristóbal de las Casas, justo con el inicio del movimiento zapatista.
“Necesitaba imágenes de la toma de San Cristóbal, el primero de enero de 1994. Entonces pregunté a mi papá, quien había trabajado durante años en las comunidades, si sabía quién podía darme material de archivo. Él, muy quitado de la pena, respondió: ‘allá en el cuarto de las chácharas hay un par de cajas de cartón, chécalas; tomé unas fotos, si te sirven son tuyas’.
“Había un montón de sobres y diapositivas, donde estaba documentado desde el primero de enero y los 15 días siguientes que hubo un cerco militar”. García rescató ese material del polvo y de los hongos causados por el paso del tiempo y se encargó de digitalizarlo.
Al adentrarse en el acervo se dio cuenta de que “además de ese registro, también estaban los procesos comunitarios de capacitación de promotores de la salud y de la construcción, antes y después del zapatismo. Mi padre trabajaba en la zona de Guadalupe Tepeyac, en Las Margaritas; se dedicaba a la formación de promotores de salud, pues había gran mortalidad infantil”.
El peso de los secretos
En esa cotidianidad “crecí con bajo perfil, en silencio, muy en la onda de proteger una vida, la de mi familia y mis afectos. En realidad eran secretos; de repente me di cuenta de que me comenzaban a pesar. Tenía un cuerpo muy aprendido a sobrevivir, enfocado en la vigilancia”.
En la publicación “busco capturar no sólo los momentos significativos de la vida comunitaria, sino también las experiencias y emociones de mi infancia, vivida entre la resistencia y sus silencios”.
El fotolibro presenta material fotográfico de Gabriela García, quien también devela sus propias imágenes, cuyo registro es muy similar a lo que hacían sus padres, pues “trabajo en una organización de parteras tradicionales; documento los procesos organizativos y de aprendizaje”.
García Rivas es narradora visual; su práctica se desplaza entre el cine, la fotografía, la escritura y el trabajo con archivos. En su obra explora las formas de vulnerabilidad social y la relación entre entorno, experiencia individual, memoria e identidad.
Ha dirigido cortometrajes y los ha presentado en festivales nacionales e internacionales. Su ópera prima, El silencio es bienvenido, formó parte de la competencia Premio Mezcal del Festival Internacional de Cine en Guadalajara 2017.

title: Lambayeque teje su historia: cuando el patrimonio cultural se convierte en emprendimiento
content:
La historia y el patrimonio ancestral de Lambayeque encontraron una nueva forma de expresión a través del tejido. La colección “Esencia ancestral: tejiendo nuestra cultura lambayecana”, creada por la artesana Mari Carolina Reaño Sánchez, convirtió emblemáticos personajes de la cultura regional en piezas de amigurumi y obtuvo el primer puesto del XIII Premio Nacional de Diseño de la Artesanía Peruana, en la categoría innovación en la artesanía.


La propuesta de la creadora del emprendimiento Marigumi lleva a personajes como el Señor de Sipán, la Sacerdotisa de Chornancap y el Sacerdote Guerrero desde el ámbito arqueológico y museístico hacia una expresión artesanal contemporánea, con el fin de acercar la historia y la identidad lambayecana a las nuevas generaciones.
La colección se presenta en la exposición temporal “Esencia ancestral: tejiendo nuestra cultura lambayecana”, inaugurada el 31 de agosto en la sede de la Dirección Desconcentrada de Cultura (DDC) Lambayeque, en Chiclayo, donde permanecerá hasta el 15 de setiembre.
En la muestra no solo se presentan las piezas ganadoras de Mari Reaño, sino que reúne también obras de destacados artesanos de la región, quienes comparten sus conocimientos, tradiciones y costumbres como una expresión viva del patrimonio cultural lambayecano.
Habla la artesana
En diálogo con la agencia Andina, Mari Reaño explicó que cada pieza es elaborada de manera artesanal con hilo de algodón y puede demandar aproximadamente un día de trabajo. Sin embargo, los diseños con mayor complejidad requieren más tiempo debido a la cantidad de detalles que deben ser reproducidos.
“Uno de los mayores retos fue representar al Señor de Sipán, debido a la complejidad de su vestimenta y a los diversos símbolos que caracterizan al personaje. Cada elemento fue trabajado cuidadosamente mediante la técnica del crochet para mantener los detalles de la representación”, afirmó.
La artesana informó que la historia de Marigumi comenzó hace seis años con la elaboración de muñecos tejidos, pero con el tiempo el emprendimiento tomó una nueva dirección: utilizar la artesanía como una herramienta para preservar la memoria, revalorar las raíces culturales y transmitir la historia de Lambayeque, a través de las manos de sus artesanos.
Nuevas propuestas
“Esencia ancestral” también incorpora nuevas propuestas, como personajes en formato de llavero y piezas acompañadas de bases de madera con grabados láser personalizados. Entre las creaciones destaca una representación del papa León XIV en amigurumi, como parte de las nuevas propuestas desarrolladas por la artesana.
Para Reaño, el reconocimiento nacional demuestra que Lambayeque puede innovar sin dejar de lado sus raíces y que la cultura también puede convertirse en una oportunidad para generar emprendimientos sostenibles y nuevas fuentes de ingreso.
Su propuesta parte de una idea central: el patrimonio no tiene por qué permanecer únicamente detrás de una vitrina. También puede convertirse en una experiencia cercana y tangible que las personas puedan llevar a sus hogares, conocer y valorar.
La exposición incorpora piezas de otros artesanos lambayecanos y destaca, entre ellas, un manto inspirado en la Sacerdotisa de Chornancap, tejido por integrantes del taller Artesanas del Corazón.
La exposición
