Puede visitar la muestra hasta el 15 de setiembre, de 08:30 a 17:00 horas , en la sede de la Dirección Desconcentrada de Cultura Lambayeque.
Más que una colección de muñecos tejidos, “Esencia ancestral” plantea una nueva manera de contar la historia: transformar los símbolos de una de las culturas más importantes del Antiguo Perú en piezas artesanales capaces de conectar pasado y presente.
“Cuando tejemos nuestra cultura no solamente unimos hilos, unimos pasado, presente y futuro”, resumió Reaño, quien apuesta por que la artesanía lambayecana siga creciendo y demostrar que el patrimonio cultural puede ser innovación, identidad y motor de emprendimiento.

title: Prisoner of war's sister urges Australians to remember horrors of Sandakan
content:
Boyup Brook's vow to never forget the WWII horrors of Sandakan
In short:
The small WA town of Boyup Brook has held an annual memorial service for the victims of Sandakan Death Marches for more than 30 years.
June Edwards lost her brother Bill to the horrors of the notorious Japanese Prisoner of War camp.
The Sandakan death marches in WWII are described by the Australian War Memorial as the greatest single atrocity committed against Australians in war.
The last words 101-year-old June Edwards has from her brother Bill Beard are a scrawled note sent from the Sandakan prisoner of war camp in 1945.
Private Beard simply wrote: "Today is my birthday."
He is among the hundreds of Australian soldiers who never made it home from the notorious Japanese internment camp.
After the fall of Singapore in 1942, nearly 2,500 Commonwealth troops became Japan's prisoners of war on the Malay-Indonesian island Borneo.
In what became known as the Sandakan Death March, the Japanese forced more than 2,000 sick and weak prisoners to march 260 kilometres across Borneo in the final year of the war.
Those too weak or otherwise unable to continue were killed, with many of the bodies never recovered.
Just six soldiers survived the horrific treatment inflicted by their captors.
The local connections left a particular mark on the small town of Boyup Brook, about 260km south of Perth, which falls silent each year to remember one of the most brutal chapters in Australia's military history.
Fate shrouded in mystery
Ms Edwards said in the two years after Singapore fell, her family did not know what happened to Bill, who came from the nearby town of Worsley.
Then they received a telegram that he was a prisoner of war.
She said her mother knew her son would never return when his photo fell from the wall.
"We had hopes of him coming back," Ms Edwards said.
"But Mum said ... he'll never come back, I know from his photograph he'll never be back."
The family later discovered he had died from malaria on July 10, 1945, just a month before the end of the war.
Town's dedicated commemoration
Boyup Brook locals built a dedicated Sandakan war memorial in the early 1990s, one of the first in the country outside of Sydney.
A service is held on the second Tuesday in September each year.
Late resident and former POW Ted McLaughlin wanted to pay tribute to his good mates who died in Borneo.
When the horror of what had happened in Sandakan emerged after the war, Joe McLaughlin said his father became dedicated to ensuring those men were never forgotten.
"It took a while to find out how his mates died, and he said he must remember them,"Mr McLaughlin said.
In addition to the memorial service, the town sponsors a local student to travel to Malaysia each year, alongside historian Lyn Silver, to learn the history.
Remembrance critical
Ms Silver said the horrors of Sandakan were covered up after the war, and should never be forgotten.
"The number who died and the manner of death were so horrific," she said.
"When this was all discovered by investigators, a conscious decision was made not to give out any details to prisoners of war's families because it was too distressing."
Ms Edwards was still brought to tears at the memory of her brother, and the cruelties he suffered.
At 101, she concedes this year's service at Boyup Brook could be her last.
But she was touched to see new generations learning the history of Sandakan.
"The schools come down with their choirs and all the young ones are there," she said.
"They've got to hold them to let people know."

title: Preserving Ernie Barnes’s Legacy in Paint Tubes
content:
Preserving Ernie Barnes’s Legacy in Paint Tubes
The late artist and athlete who rendered joyous scenes of Black life, dance, and motion is the subject of renewed institutional attention as his daughter, Erin Barnes, works to conserve his studio practice.
When artist Ernie Barnes died in 2009, his daughter Erin was left to sort through the vestiges of materials the Los Angeles-based painter and professional football player had accumulated over his decades-long art practice.
There were canvases, sure, but also paint tubes, brushes, and containers Barnes kept in the garage that he used as his studio to create vibrant, kinetic scenes of Black church gatherings, football games, and nightlife during the Jim Crow era, including his iconic work “The Sugar Shack” (1976), making him one of Southern California’s most beloved artists.
For years, Barnes stored her father’s partially squeezed containers of Liquitex, Grumbacher, and Winsor & Newton acrylic paint and thought little about it until about a year ago, when she began to realize the materials were integral to commemorating his legacy.
“I realized how much of the physical studio still existed through the paint tubes and brushes, and I felt a responsibility to preserve them as part of a record of his historical practice,” Barnes told Hyperallergic. “These tubes are the physical remnants of his creative process.”
Black figurative painters such as Jacob Lawrence, Amy Sherald, and Kerry James Marshall have been widely celebrated by museums and institutions in the last decade. Barnes isn’t always mentioned in the same breath as other contemporary art stars despite the $15.3 million sale of “The Sugar Shack” in 2022. (Its buyer, energy trader Bill Perkins, told the New York Times that “for certain segments of America, it’s more famous than the ‘Mona Lisa.’”)
That could soon change. A major documentary about Barnes’s life, Who is Ernie Barnes, was announced in July, and the Canton Museum of Art in Ohio recently opened a special exhibition celebrating his work, Good Times: The Artistic Journey of Ernie Barnes, on August 18. Some of Barnes’s works will also be on display at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, which opens to the public on September 22.
Barnes grew up in Durham, North Carolina, under Jim Crow segregation, learning about art from books and catalogs because museums did not allow Black people to enter them. Encouraged by his mother, he sketched throughout his childhood and attended North Carolina College (now North Carolina Central University) on a football scholarship.
Barnes proved to be a gifted athlete in college and was drafted into the NFL, where he played for five seasons. But he never put aside his art and often made pencil or charcoal sketches of other players while he was on the sidelines during a game.
“His teammates were in awe of how he could come up with an idea and sketch it right away,” Thaleen Barnes, Ernie’s second wife, told Hyperallergic. “When we went to places, he watched how people walked, their mannerisms, and how they talked. He was interested in their body, their form and movement. Just looking around the world that we lived in was an inspiration for him to sketch.”

title: The Pine Trees That Would Not Leave Me
content:
The Pine Trees That Would Not Leave Me
While visiting the Lebanese mountain town Dhour El Choueir, I couldn't shake off a painting and a poem I had translated two decades earlier.
Six years ago, on August 4, 2020, a massive explosion at the Port of Beirut killed more than two hundred people, wounded thousands, and devastated large parts of the capital.
This August, sitting with a friend at a family-run restaurant amid the pine trees of Dhour El Choueir, a mountain town overlooking Beirut, I found myself unable to shake off a painting and a poem I had translated two decades earlier.
Lebanese painter Moustafa Farroukh’s watercolor “A Group of Pines in Bekfaya” was painted just a few miles from here in 1936. Born and first trained in Beirut under the painter Habib Serour, Farroukh later studied in Rome and Paris before returning to establish his practice in his native city. Through portraits and idealized landscapes, he offered a vivid vision of Lebanon’s people and terrain. Farroukh became a foundational figure in modern Lebanese painting, his art helping shape a visual language for the country while its political and cultural identity was still taking form under the French Mandate.
The painting of the pine grove was seared into my memory when I first saw it in 2003 in a catalog accompanying a Sursock Museum exhibition of Farroukh’s works. (The watercolor was on loan from the private collection of Emile Nasrallah.) Sursock itself later became a victim of the Beirut Port explosion. The blast shattered its stained-glass windows and damaged the historic building as well as dozens of artworks. The museum reopened on May 26, 2023, with five exhibitions, one of them titled Beyond Ruptures.
In August 1937, the Armenian poet Vahan Tekeyan was also here in Dhour El Choueir when he wrote the sonnet “To a Lebanese Pine Tree.”
I reconnected with the sonnet after returning home. I corrected a few errors in my translation, adjusted the wording and rhythms, and tried to bring the English closer to the movement of Tekeyan’s Armenian.
Here is the translation as I read it now, at twice the age I was when I first attempted it, with many more years of witnessing Lebanon from near and far.
To a Lebanese Pine Tree
By Vahan Tekeyan
Dhour El Choueir, Lebanon, August 1937
Your pain unfolds from the past, O soft-shadowed
pine tree… Barely risen from the ground
you have lost your maiden branch, the trace of which
appears on you, dried and jutting, like a severed arm.
Then countless others followed it, one after another…
Until, once they thought your trunk had grown large enough,
they let your upper branches sprout and thicken,
and slowly adorn themselves with translucent tresses.
And upon them too, how many fresh traces of the saw —
all your grandchildren and great-grandchildren, dead too soon,
whose open grave you have become beneath the skies…
But you do not at all inspire, O green tree of the mountains,
with memories of so many victims, any thought of mourning;
you ever bring forth new life and sway in joyous mood…
Born in Constantinople in 1878, Tekeyan came of age in an Armenian literary world that would be shattered during his lifetime. Poet, editor, teacher, and public figure, he belonged to a generation whose intellectual and literary lives cannot be separated from the violence that dispersed Ottoman Armenians across new geographies.
By 1937, Lebanon had become one of the epicenters of Armenian revival in the Middle East. Survivors of the Armenian Genocide had reconstituted community life away from their ancestral towns, rebuilding around churches and secular institutions.
Tekeyan participated directly in this process of revival. In September 1937, he became the first editor of a new Armenian newspaper in Beirut, Zartonk (“Awakening,” still published today). Tekeyan included “To a Lebanese Pine Tree,” written the previous month in Dhour El Choueir, in the paper’s inaugural issue, nestled among news items ranging from the upcoming parliamentary elections in French Mandate Lebanon and domestic politics in Palestine to the Spanish Civil War and Mussolini’s visit to Germany.
For all the Armenian resonances of Tekeyan’s wounded tree, the poem is emphatically Lebanese. Reading it in Lebanon in August 2026, I was struck less by what the pine might stand for than by how closely its contradictions seemed to belong to the country around me.
The poem begins with history lodged in the body. “Your pain unfolds from the past,” Tekeyan tells the tree.
The first wound appears low on the trunk. The lost branch resembles a human limb, its trace “dried and jutting, like a severed arm.” Before long, the instrument of amputation appears explicitly: the saw.
The mutilations accumulate. “Then countless others followed it, one after another.” Yet the tree continues upward. Its higher branches are eventually allowed to sprout and thicken, adorning themselves with “translucent tresses.” Tekeyan lets us glimpse flourishing before making us look again: those branches, too, bear “fresh traces of the saw.”
And then Tekeyan shifts the metaphor. The injured body becomes a genealogy. Its branches are its “grandchildren and great-grandchildren, dead too soon.” The ancestor remains standing as its descendants disappear around it.
Tekeyan then reverses the natural order of generations: The ancestor becomes the grave of its descendants, “whose open grave you have become beneath the skies.”
Everything in the sonnet seems to carry us toward grief.
Until it doesn’t.
“But you do not at all inspire,” Tekeyan writes, “any thought of mourning.”
And he tells us why: “You ever bring forth new life.”
In writing and conversation about Lebanon, the word “resilience” is tossed around liberally. But endlessly celebrating people’s resilience can normalize what they are repeatedly forced to endure.
No less common in Western media is the portrayal of Lebanon as hedonistic: its nightlife and crowded beach clubs, where the party continues amid economic collapse and political crisis. For decades, such coverage has treated the revival of Beirut’s bars and clubs as evidence that the country is “back.”
It is a seductive shorthand. But like the celebration of resilience, this framing romanticizes precarity and escapism while obscuring the scars of war and the uneven costs of crisis.
Tekeyan’s pine offers us something more compelling. Farroukh’s pines, in turn, offer a key to reading the poem.
Farroukh’s trees stand together.
Seen in this light, what is often flattened into hedonism may instead be understood as one manifestation of solidarity: an insistence on gathering with friends and family against the odds, even while bearing the traces of violence.
My grandparents were child survivors of the Armenian Genocide who found refuge in Lebanon, where my parents and I were born. I grew up during the Lebanese Civil War and came of age in its aftermath. When I first translated Tekeyan’s poem in 2003 and encountered Farroukh’s painting in the exhibition catalog that same year, I was still living there. Three years later came another war. Soon thereafter, I moved to the United States.
But it was only in Dhour El Choueir, in August 2026, that the poem and the painting came together for me, revealing something about Lebanon beyond the familiar scripts.
The wounds remain. The tree sways.
Acknowledgment: The author would like to thank Rowina Bou Harb, Head of Archives at the Sursock Museum, for her assistance.

title: Indonesia turns to Indigenous data to map customary lands
content:
Indigenous peoples in Indonesia have long faced a basic problem: Data on their communities, cultures and customary territories are scattered across government agencies and civil society organisations, making them less visible in spatial planning and permitting.
The Indonesian government is trying to address that gap by integrating data from the Ministry of Culture, the Ancestral Domain Registration Agency (BRWA) and the country’s largest Indigenous peoples’ alliance, AMAN, in a dataset covering 3,857 Indigenous communities.
The government says the integrated data will strengthen policymaking and protection of Indigenous peoples. BRWA says the bigger significance could be spatial: Customary territory maps, which can show the ancestral lands, traditional territories, languages and more of Indigenous peoples, could eventually become part of the government’s geospatial data and potentially be visible in spatial planning and permitting.
BRWA was established in 2010 by Indigenous and civil society organisations, including AMAN, to document and register customary territories amid the government’s slow progress in recognising Indigenous peoples and their lands.
The new integrated dataset was launched on Aug. 19 in Jakarta. Before the launch, data on Indigenous peoples had been scattered across various ministries, institutions and civil society organisations, according to Restu Gunawan, the Ministry of Culture’s director general of cultural and traditional protection.
“
By integrating customary territory maps into. One Data Indonesia, the spatial information about these territories becomes part of the hundreds of IGT [thematic geospatial information] maps held by the government.
Kasmita Widodo, head, Ancestral Domain Registration Agency (BRWA)
The differences matter, he said during the launch: Even a difference of one community in the datasets could translate into thousands of hectares of difference when it comes to customary territories.
Didik Darmanto, director of religion, culture, youth and sports at the Ministry of National Development Planning, or Bappenas, cited the Kulawi Indigenous community in Central Sulawesi as an example.
Bappenas has data on the community, which is spread across several villages, while another dataset from the Ministry of Forestry also refers to Indigenous legal communities. Bappenas therefore needs to establish whether the different datasets refer to the same Indigenous community, Didik said during the launch.
One problem is that the different government datasets do not yet have a common “primary key” that would allow officials to establish whether records from different agencies refer to the same entity, he said.
Culture Minister Fadli Zon said the integration would make it easier for the government to coordinate policies and interventions aimed at protecting Indigenous peoples, their cultures and customary territories.
“Our weakness is indeed data,” he said during the launch event. “Data may look easy, but it turns out that we still cannot get it in order. If the data are not in order, policy interventions will also be inadequate. This is what is now being integrated.”
The database is intended to capture cultural aspects as well, including Indigenous languages, manuscripts, rites, local foods, traditional knowledge, folk games, oral traditions and other cultural expressions.
Fadli said the Ministry of Culture was ready to become the data custodian for Indigenous peoples, although BRWA says the formal process for determining the custodian still involves the country’s Geospatial Information Agency, or BIG.
Customary maps
The 3,857 community records are already the result of synchronising the three sources, according to BRWA head Kasmita Widodo. But integrating customary territory maps into Indonesia’s broader official geospatial architecture requires another process involving BIG, he said.
The government’s national data governance system, One Data Indonesia, is intended to make data across government more accurate, up to date, integrated and shareable. Bappenas manages the central One Data Indonesia secretariat.
“By integrating customary territory maps into One Data Indonesia, the spatial information about these territories becomes part of the hundreds of IGT [thematic geospatial information] maps held by the government,” Kasmita told Mongabay.
During the launch, AMAN handed over 2,284 customary territory maps covering 36.6 million hectares. The maps are spread across 32 provinces and 209 districts and cities.
BRWA’s latest figures show that of the 2,284 customary territories it has registered, 418 have received recognition from local governments, covering about 7.54 million hectares (18.3 million acres).
The maps have a spatial dimension and could eventually become part of the government’s official thematic geospatial information, Kasmita said.
That would make Indigenous peoples and their territories more visible in government planning and permitting, he said.
At present, Kasmita said, a customary territory map does not necessarily appear as a layer in the government’s online permitting system if that territory has not been registered or integrated.
Therefore, a company seeking a permit could potentially not encounter a customary territory layer even if Indigenous peoples claim that territory.
With the integration of the data and the submission of the customary territory maps, Kasmita said he hopes Indigenous territories can eventually be incorporated into permitting, development planning and spatial planning.
“[Customary territories] have to become one of the important layers” in district and provincial spatial plans, he said.
But the maps will not automatically become part of Indonesia’s broader geospatial system simply because they have been synchronised, Kasmita added. BIG will need to go through a process to determine who is custodian of the data, based on proposals from the relevant ministries and institutions.
Recognition still lags
The integration could make Indigenous peoples more visible in government data, but it does not itself grant legal recognition to their communities or customary territories.
Furthermore, only 332,661 hectares (822,000 acres) had so far been recognised as customary forest, Kasmita said.
The problem is compounded by Indonesia’s sectoral system, in which different agencies have authority over different types of land.
Kasmita said that customary territories can fall inside state-designated forest areas, where the Forestry Ministry has authority; or in non-forest areas classified as APL or Other-Use Areas, which fall under the Ministry of Agrarian Affairs and Spatial Planning/National Land Agency.
He said BRWA had previously pushed the Ministry of Home Affairs to become data custodian because the ministry works with local governments on matters such as regional regulations and regent decrees concerning Indigenous peoples. The ministry has not taken on that role, he said.
The deeper problem is that Indonesia still lacks an effective system for recognising Indigenous peoples and resolving competing claims over their territories, Indigenous advocates say.
Erasmus Cahyadi, deputy secretary general for advocacy, politics and law at AMAN and chairman of the substantive team of the coalition overseeing the Indigenous Peoples Bill, said the newly launched data answered questions that had remained unresolved for more than two decades.
Indonesia’s 1945 Constitution recognises the existence of Indigenous peoples, he said, but Indonesia still lacks a system for determining who they are and where they live.
The new data provide visibility into Indigenous peoples’ existence, their identities and the extent of their territories, he added.
But recognition remains difficult.
“For more than a decade, we have become accustomed to complicated procedures for recognising Indigenous peoples,” Erasmus said. “In this complicated process, the burden of proof lies with Indigenous peoples, while the authority to grant recognition lies with the government.”
He said recognition procedures often avoid rather than resolve underlying conflicts, particularly where customary territories overlap with forest areas or other land uses.
That recognition gap is one reason Indigenous advocates have continued to push for a comprehensive Indigenous Peoples Law, which has been under discussion for 16 years. Government officials, including Fadli and the chairman of the House of Representatives’ Legislative Body, Bob Hasan, have said they hope the bill can be enacted in 2026 or 2027.
For Indigenous peoples, however, the law needs to do more than establish another recognition procedure. It must also address the underlying legal and tenure problems on the ground, Erasmus said.
Without that, the Indigenous Peoples Law would not be of much use, he said.
Rukka Sombolinggi, secretary general of AMAN, said Indigenous peoples’ rights remain largely confined to constitutional recognition, without a comprehensive law translating those rights into a system for living alongside the state.
“So to this day, customary territories have not been recognised, Indigenous peoples have not been protected, and their authority to govern and manage themselves has not been protected,” she said during the launch event.
She cited roughly 11 million hectares (27 million acres) of customary territory that she said had been seized in the name of development during the 10 years of former President Joko Widodo’s administration from 2014 to 2024.
When Indigenous peoples resist the loss of their territories, they can face division, criminalisation and, in some cases, violence, she said.
The data initiative could help change that by making Indigenous communities and their territories more visible to government, Rukka added.
That visibility also matters for environmental protection, she said. Indigenous knowledge has an important role in protecting ecosystems and helping communities restore damaged nature.
“The easiest way out of the crisis is to protect the guardians of the Earth, who protect the best remaining places, from the mountains to the sea,” Rukka said.
Research has similarly linked secure Indigenous and community land rights with better environmental outcomes.
Indigenous Peoples and local communities hold or manage large portions of the world’s land, while Indigenous territories contain a substantial share of the planet’s remaining biodiversity.
For Rukka, however, better data are only a first step.
“Hopefully, today will open a new door toward a better life, with Indigenous peoples becoming part of Indonesia and Indonesia being present among Indigenous peoples,” she said. “May Indigenous peoples experience complete freedom.”
This story was published with permission from Mongabay.com.

title: De oceaan is geen scheiding maar een brug op het literaire festival Read My World
content:
De oceaan is geen scheiding maar een brug op het literaire festival Read My World
Geeft een relevant perspectief ter verduidelijking. Beweringen worden geredigeerd voor leesbaarheid en evidente onjuistheden
Literair festival Dichter Theoresia Rumthe en mensenrechtenactivist Defe Wabiser willen via verhalen uit West-Papoea en de Molukken bruggen slaan met ‘broeders en zusters’ in Nederland.
Het zal 2017 zijn geweest, rekenen ze terug. Toen troffen Theoresia Rumthe en Defe Wabiser elkaar toevallig in een bibliotheek annex boekwinkel in Bandung, West-Java. „Soms heb je van die mensen waarvan je voelt dat ze later nog eens je pad zullen kruisen”, zegt Wabiser over de ontmoeting. En zo geschiedde. Bijna tien jaar later werken de twee vrouwen uit het oosten van Indonesië – Rumthe van Maluku (de Molukken) en Wabiser van West-Papoea – samen aan het literaire festival Read My World, dat vanaf donderdag in Amsterdam plaatsvindt.
Rumthe is dichter en leidt een literair platform. Wabiser zet zich als activist in voor bescherming van het leefgebied van inheemse volken. Read My World focust dit jaar op de Molukken en West-Papoea en naast gasten uit beide delen van Indonesië zijn ook schrijvers en kunstenaars uit de Molukse en Papoeaanse diaspora en van daarbuiten uitgenodigd. Het festival beoogt met verhalen, gedichten en andere kunst en cultuur een brede uitwisseling tussen de beide volkeren, hun diaspora en andere geïnteresseerden te bevorderen.
Gedeelde geschiedenis
In ‘Oceanic Solidarity’ vonden Rumthe en Wabiser een overkoepelend thema, vertellen de co-curatoren in een videogesprek. „De oceaan is de plek waarover vanaf 1951 zo’n 12.500 Molukse KNIL-soldaten en familieleden uit de Molukken en andere delen van Indonesië met hun gezinnen naar Nederland werden gebracht”, zegt Rumthe. Het Koninklijk Nederlandsch-Indisch Leger (KNIL) bestond uit Nederlandse en inheemse militairen en vocht om koloniale belangen te beschermen. „De zee werd zo een brug, een plek die onze geschiedenis draagt. De zwart-wit foto’s van die reis laten ons die geschiedenis steeds opnieuw beleven.” De dichter ziet de oceaan door die gedeelde geschiedenis niet als „iets dat ons scheidt, maar juist als iets dat ons verbindt.”
„Voor mij is de oceaan een universum dat we delen”, zegt Rumthe. „De oceaan is niet alleen een fysiek gegeven, maar staat ook voor kennis; het staat voor een thuis, een cultuur, maar ook migratie, geschiedenis en diaspora.” Onder jonge kunstenaars in Indonesië bestaat een sterke wens om verbonden te zijn met „de broeders en zusters in Nederland”, merkte Rumthe eerder bij een literair festival dat ze op Ambon organiseert.
Het is niet alleen de verbinding met de voormalige kolonisator en de Molukse en Papoeaanse diaspora (die begin jaren zestig in Nederland arriveerde nadat Nederland Nieuw-Guinea als kolonie had opgegeven) die inmiddels in Nederland leeft, ook gemeenschappen in Indonesië zijn onderling altijd met elkaar verbonden door het water. „In onze cultuur is de oceaan vanzelfsprekend gemeenschappelijk”, zegt Rumthe. „Bij de oceaan zijn mensen nooit alleen. Ze leven er samen, ze vissen er samen. Ze helpen elkaar.”
Gemeenschappelijke vijand: de VOC
Verbindingen tussen de Molukken en Papoea bestaan ook dankzij het water en gaan ver terug, weet Wabiser. „Onze voorouders stonden begin 1600 voor een gemeenschappelijke vijand, die heette de VOC.” De Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie, de handelsonderneming die in de 17de en 18de eeuw met grootschalig geweld onder meer grondstoffen en specerijen uit Azië haalde en verhandelde, kwam niet naar Papoea maar wel naar de Molukken. Deze twee gebieden dreven handel met elkaar. „Maar de VOC probeerde dat bestaande handelssysteem te vernietigen en conflict te creëren tussen de koningen van Maluku en mijn voorouders in West-Papoea”, vertelt Wabiser.
Ook vandaag de dag zijn er gemeenschappelijke vijanden die de bevolking van Papoea en de Molukken bedreigen, ziet Wabiser in haar werk. Het wordt inheemse gemeenschappen heel moeilijk gemaakt om hun mensenrechten op te eisen. „Tegelijkertijd geeft de Indonesische regering juist heel makkelijk concessies af voor palmolieplantages in de gebieden waar zij leven.” Ze bouwen die op moerassig gebied en hebben dus materialen nodig om wegen aan te leggen. En die zijn niet voorhanden in Papoea dus die halen ze van de Kai-eilanden, waar kakak [oudere zus] Theoresia’s familie vandaan komt.”
Vrijheden onder druk
Indonesië bevindt zich op een moeilijk moment, vertellen Rumthe en Wabiser. Hun (t)huis wordt op allerlei manieren bedreigd. Vrijheid van meningsuiting en andere vrijheden staan onder druk en net als in Europa brandden de afgelopen maanden ook in Indonesië talloze hectaren natuurgebied af. Dat komt naast klimaatverandering door de activiteiten van de Indonesische staat en diens zakenpartners, die natuurgebieden openstellen voor palmolie- en suikerrietplantages en mijnbouw. Plantages zijn extra vatbaar voor brand en zodra concessies aan bedrijven zijn afgegeven is onduidelijk bij wie de brandpreventieverantwoordelijkheid ligt.
Wabiser hoopt dat ze kunnen bouwen op de samenwerking van hun voorvaderen uit de tijd van de VOC, want de strijd tegen de verwoesting van een leefgebied is al eens eerder gevoerd. „Wat in West-Papoea gebeurt, gebeurt ook in andere delen van Indonesië. Omdat de vrijheid van meningsuiting beperkt is, is het veiliger om via kunst ons thuis en onze cultuur te beschermen.” Zo nodigde Wabiser Samuel Yohanes Glenn M uit, een kunstenaar die met natuurgeluiden en het verzamelen van Papoeaanse culturele objecten zijn cultuur levend wil houden en er opnieuw betekenis aan wil geven.
Tijdens Read My World wil Wabiser nieuwe verbonden smeden met de Papoeaanse diaspora en andere geïnteresseerden, „vrienden die dezelfde waarden en principes hebben om ons thuis te beschermen en die dat ook via kunst doen.”

title: ¿Quién llegó primero? Los dos significados de “indígena” en Europa
content:
Esta entrada es parte de la serie «Spotlight» de Global Voices de agosto de 2026, «Derechos indígenas«. Esta serie ofrece una visión de las vidas y experiencias de los pueblos indígenas con el fin de establecer vínculos entre regiones, destacar las experiencias indígenas y contar historias de líderes, activistas, miembros de la comunidad y otras personas. Puedes apoyar esta cobertura con una donación.
Para muchos europeos, la palabra “indígena” evoca dos significados muy distintos. Uno refiere a comunidades lejanas, en parte ficticias y profundamente romantizadas, que defienden sus tierras de los colonizadores; una imagen adquirida a través de relatos de aventuras de la literatura popular, novelas, películas e historietas europeas y estadounidenses. El otro significado es mucho más cercano a su realidad: reclamos nacionalistas de ser “autóctonos”, supuestos descendientes de los habitantes “originales” cuya sangre está ligada al suelo de su país, acompañados de argumentos de que los “otros” (por lo general, pueblos vecinos o migrantes recientes) llegaron después y, por ende, tienen menos derechos sobre el mismo territorio. Los Balcanes son un ejemplo especialmente contundente de cómo estas ideas pueden coexistir y ser objeto de abusos, aunque no constituyen una excepción exclusiva de tal región.
Una distinción importante suele perderse con facilidad en la traducción. En el uso internacional de los derechos humanos, los pueblos indígenas no son simplemente aquellos que pueden demostrar que sus antepasados llegaron primero. No existe una definición universal única, pero el concepto abarca autoidentificación, continuidad histórica con sociedades precoloniales, instituciones culturales o políticas diferenciadas, un vínculo estrecho con la tierra y experiencias de conquista o marginación.
Según explican los científicos sociales Maykel Verkuyten y Jochem Thijs de la Universidad de Utrecht, la autoctonía y el nativismo político funcionan de manera distinta: dividen a los habitantes en una población “anfitriona” natural y “huéspedes” condicionales. La creencia en la autoctonía —que un país pertenece a sus primeros habitantes— “puede ser una razón aceptable para exigir la propiedad colectiva de un territorio, y este reclamo puede tener consecuencias negativas para los recién llegados”, explicaron. “Los niños podrían razonar que un lugar pertenece a su grupo porque ‘nosotros’ llegamos primero y, por lo tanto, desarrollar actitudes negativas hacia otros grupos”.
Un ejemplo clave de cómo la cultura popular moldea la percepción en este ámbito es el caso de los nativos o indios norteamericanos.
Una versión europea del Lejano Oeste
Mucho antes de la televisión por cable e internet, los europeos ya habían construido su propio Oeste norteamericano, en parte gracias a las novelas de Karl May (1842-1912), que leían adultos y niños, que se convirtieron en un elemento infaltable en las bibliotecas familiares en Alemania y Austria, y en toda Europa, incluida Yugoslavia. May no había visitado el Oeste americano antes de escribir sus historias más famosas; y aun así, su héroe apache Winnetou moldeó las ideas sobre los nativos norteamericanos durante generaciones. Por ejemplo, en Macedonia del Norte muchas mujeres que nacieron en la década de 1970 se llaman Vineta en su honor.
Las adaptaciones cinematográficas basadas en la coproducción de varios países europeos, así como festivales y parques temáticos, ayudaron a mantener vivo este mundo imaginario, tal como se retrata en el siguiente video que acompaña al artículo de The New York Times “Perdidos en la traducción: La fascinación de Alemania por el Viejo Oeste norteamericano”:
Las representaciones de los nativos norteamericanos creadas por Hollywood no respondían a una fórmula única e inmutable. Muchos de las primeras películas del Oeste retrataban a los pueblos indígenas como anónimos “salvajes indios despiadados” (expresión extraída de la Declaración de Independencia de Estados Unidos), al punto de llegar a la caricatura. Películas posteriores los presentaron como víctimas de la conquista o como grupos étnicos y personas reconocibles con virtudes, defectos e intereses contrapuestos. Películas como Un hombre llamado Caballo, Pequeño gran hombre, Soldado azul y Las aventuras de Jeremiah Johnson son un ejemplo de este cambio en la década de 1970. Para la década de 1990, Danza con lobos y El último mohicano reflejaron la llegada de esta visión empática al público masivo, aun cuando la figura del “buen salvaje” terminó convirtiéndose en otro estereotipo.
Las historietas del Oeste europeas, incluidas obras maestras como la francesa Blueberry o la belga Comanche, siguieron trayectorias similares y, al igual que los antaño populares spaghetti westerns, los cómics del Oeste italianos tuvieron una evolución muy parecida. Series como Tex, Zagor, Historia del Oeste y Ken Parker se nutrieron del cine al tiempo que desarrollaban personajes indígenas diversos. Aunque continuaban siendo fantasías europeas, la mejora en las tramas convirtió a los pueblos originarios en actores de la historia, en contraposición a ser un simple telón de fondo o un enemigo único y sin rostro. En Yugoslavia, donde los cómics italianos tenían una enorme base de lectores, su lenguaje moral se volvió familiar para varias generaciones.
Anticolonialismo local
Los lectores yugoslavos no se limitaban a consumir aventuras traducidas. Dado que las importaciones de Occidente no bastaban para saciar el apetito por las historietas, la producción local se desarrolló en el período entre las dos guerras mundiales y continuó durante la era de la Yugoslavia socialista.
Por ejemplo, el dibujante Andrija Maurović (1901-1980) creó una amplia gama de cómics de aventuras y del Oeste de gran factura visual. A partir de 1978, la editorial Dnevnik de Novi Sad, encargó a guionistas y dibujantes locales la creación de episodios con licencia de El gran Blek, conocidos popularmente como Yu Blek. Asimismo, las editoriales Forum y Marketprint produjeron cómics de Tarzán entre 1983 y 1990, que se incorporaron a la franquicia global. Se trataba de una historieta comercial, distribuida en un país que se enorgullecía de haber sido cofundador del Movimiento de Países No Alineados y que celebraba públicamente su solidaridad con las luchas anticoloniales. Las giras de Tito por África y Asia proyectaban mensajes de paz y alianza con los Estados recientemente independizados. En este contexto, las historias sobre la resistencia a la conquista resonaban con la narrativa fundacional yugoslava de antifascismo partisano, liberación y coexistencia:
Esto hace que la década de 1990 resulte especialmente incómoda de recordar. Muchos que adoptaron o facilitaron las políticas nacionalistas se habían criado bajo los valores de “hermandad y unidad”, la solidaridad anticolonial y los héroes populares que protegían a los oprimidos, lo que demuestra que la infusión de los derechos humanos en la cultura popular no constituye una vacuna contra el fanatismo.
El discurso anticolonial perdura en la política nacionalista contemporánea, aunque a menudo de forma selectiva. Los crímenes coloniales de Occidente se invocan para retratar a “Occidente” como intrínsecamente ilegítimo y para responder a las críticas contra Rusia apelando al whataboutism (la falacia del “y tú más”), mientras que la conquista rusa a lo largo de Asia central, el Cáucaso y Siberia —y, más tarde, la rusificación de los pueblos asiáticos y europeos— queda fuera del encuadre.
Vojislav Šešelj, criminal de guerra condenado, ofrece un elocuente ejemplo serbio: tras describir a Estados Unidos como un Estado construido mediante la destrucción de su población nativa, instó a los serbios estadounidenses a votar por Donald Trump, en gran medida por la postura de este respecto a Rusia. El servicio de verificación de hechos Istinomer documentó luego la amplia mitología que los medios serbios construyeron en torno a Trump.
Variaciones de estas narrativas también están presentes en otros países de los Balcanes, contraste que se volvió más marcado tras la propia retórica expansionista de Trump respecto a Groenlandia y el canal de Panamá. Cuando la violencia colonial solo importa si la comete un adversario geopolítico, el anticolonialismo se convierte en una coartada en lugar de un principio.
Autóctonos en casa
Desde el proceso de construcción estatal del siglo XIX hasta la desintegración de Yugoslavia, las historias nacionales en pugna buscaron raíces cada vez más profundas. “Autóctono” se convirtió en un elogio, mientras que “recién llegado” o “huésped” pasó a ser una acusación. Los reclamos de quién llegó primero no causaron la violencia de manera mecánica, pero sirvieron para cubrir moralmente la asimilación, la expulsión y la limpieza étnica: si a los vecinos se los consideraba intrusos temporales, su expulsión podía presentarse como una restitución antes que como una injusticia. Las investigaciones sobre la formación de los Estados posotomanos demuestran cómo el desplazamiento, la redistribución de tierras y la homogeneización nacional estuvieron entrelazados desde fines del siglo XIX.
A partir de ese momento, los nacionalistas balcánicos tradujeron reiteradamente los relatos de continuidad en “derechos históricos”. Como herederas de entidades políticas antiguas o medievales, las naciones modernas supuestamente tenían derechos prioritarios sobre sus territorios. La Grecia moderna fue un ejemplo temprano, mientras que las historiografías rivales posteriores vincularon a serbios y búlgaros con imperios medievales, a los rumanos con la continuidad daco-romana y a los albaneses con la ascendencia iliria. La reciente “antigüización” afirmó la continuidad de los macedonios étnicos modernos con el reino de Alejandro Magno.
Sin embargo, los mapas de derecho histórico raras veces coincidían con las poblaciones mixtas que habitaban el territorio. La asimilación forzada, la migración forzada, el intercambio de poblaciones o la limpieza étnica fueron instrumentos fundamentales en construir los Estados-nación balcánicos desde la independencia de Grecia hasta las secuelas de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, y resurgieron más tarde durante las guerras yugoslavas (1991-2001). El vocabulario resurgió tras un incidente internacional en 2014, cuando un dron desplegó una pancarta que llevaba literalmente la palabra en inglés autochthonous (autóctono) sobre un mapa de la “Gran Albania” durante un partido de fútbol para la Eurocopa entre Serbia y Albania en Belgrado.
La investigación genética ha aportado a estas narrativas un vocabulario nuevo y aparentemente científico. Descubrimientos legítimos sobre el linaje —o estimaciones comerciales presentadas como ciencia— se interpretan de forma selectiva como prueba de que una nación moderna desciende directamente de una población antigua. Por ejemplo, la difusión en línea de las afirmaciones de teorías conspirativas pseudohistóricas que vinculan directamente a los serbios contemporáneos con la cultura prehistórica de la cultura Vinča —a los que califica como “el pueblo más antiguo de Europa”— contradice la evidencia científica sobre las migraciones eslavas.
Asignar a las etnias macedónicas y griegas porcentajes rivales de ascendencia genética del “antiguo ADN macedonio” reduce historias complejas y compartidas a meros certificados de autenticidad. La incertidumbre científica y siglos de mestizaje desaparecen; luego, se utilizan cifras seleccionadas para tildar a los vecinos de menos autóctonos, extranjeros o incluso racialmente inferiores. La genética de poblaciones puede arrojar luz sobre las migraciones y la ascendencia, pero no puede transformar culturas prehistóricas en naciones modernas ni decidir quién tiene mayores derechos sobre un territorio.
La movediza frontera entre “anfitrión” y “huésped”
Los Balcanes constituyen un caso dramático de cómo el odio justificado al nativismo contribuyó a alimentar guerras reales, pero “justificaciones” similares surgieron en otros lugares. Los movimientos contra los migrantes en Francia, Gran Bretaña o Alemania no necesitan atribuirse la descendencia de los primeros habitantes para llegar a una conclusión semejante: los recién llegados tienen menos derechos que los “nativos”.
El término Gastarbeiter de la Alemania occidental, que significa “trabajador huésped”, plasmó esta contradicción. A partir de la década de 1960, se reclutó a trabajadores de los Balcanes y Turquía porque se les necesitaba, pero no se asumió que obtendrían la residencia permanente ni la ciudadanía por naturalización. Incluso sus hijos y nietos podían ser tratados como huéspedes, mientras que los migrantes anteriores o sus descendientes pasaban a formar parte del “nosotros” consolidado y rechazaban a quienes llegaban después.
Por lo tanto, la paradoja más profunda es europea, no exclusivamente balcánica. En las historias sobre el Oeste norteamericano, “haber llegado primero” suele identificar a un pueblo desposeído que merece protección. En la política nacionalista, esa misma idea puede ser invocada por un grupo dominante como una licencia para excluir.
La historia y el sentido de pertenencia a una tierra son importantes, pero no deberían convertirse en un escalafón de la valía humana ni en un título de propiedad para la dominación étnica. La verdadera prueba de humanidad comienza cuando las personas cuyos derechos están en juego no son figuras lejanas en una película o en un cómic, sino los vecinos actuales.

title: My area of joy in Madras was Egmore : Y. Gee Mahendra
content:
I was born and brought up happily in Madras. My area of joy was Egmore, my grandparents’ house. It was opposite Museum theatre – a very special place in my life. The green space behind the theatre used to be our play area. That was our Amazon, our Congo. I was Tarzan and Phantom there.
In the evenings we would watch plays at the theatre. It was also where my career in theatre started in 1961. My parents lived in Nungambakkam and I visited them in the weekends. It was a very small house, but it was where the Nungambakkam Ladies Club held there meetings, the Padma Seshadri Bala Bhavan School was started, and the United Amateur Artistes’ drama rehearsals used to happen in the evenings. Though my father was an ordinary government servant, since he was a theatre personality, I had the opportunity to meet many actors including Makkal Thilagam Sivaji Ganesan, Gemini Ganesan and Savithri Amma.
In the 1960s - 70s the Marina beach used to have this famous eatery. I would have watched Kadhalikka Neramillai 20 times just to see the Marina beach. My cinema career too started in Madras. It made me a big actor. The city taught us a lot of values, it taught us friendship. There was an innocence about Madras that is lacking in Chennai. Sadly, we have started to fight for survival here.
(As told to Deepa H Ramakrishnan )
Published - September 09, 2026 12:49 am IST

title: 40 anos de resistência camponesa: como o movimento Tèt Kole Ti Peyizan Ayisyen mobiliza a luta no Haiti
content:
Em outro contexto, seriam dias de festividades no Haiti, com centenas de camponeses vindos de todo o país, homens e mulheres, jovens e veteranos, reunidos para celebrar a luta e reafirmar o compromisso. Mas, neste mês de setembro de 2026, não haverá nenhum grande evento para celebrar os 40 anos de existência e resistência do Tèt Kole Ti Peyizan Ayisyen, organização camponesa de abrangência nacional.
Com as estradas do país bloqueadas pelas gangues e um clima especialmente tenso na região da capital, a situação atual do país não dá abertura para realizar as comemorações que a data merecia. Nem por isso o marco passará em branco. No lugar da festa, serão realizadas dezenas de assembleias locais ao longo dos próximos meses, promovendo momentos de reflexão, crítica e autocrítica junto com a base.
O Tèt Kole trabalhou desse jeito desde sua criação, em setembro de 1986. Como movimento reivindicativo camponês, promove a organização popular, a formação de base e a defesa dos direitos da população rural contra o jugo do imperialismo e das elites do país.
“O nosso objetivo concreto é chegar a uma sociedade sem favores. Uma sociedade em que as pessoas possam viver como pessoas. Uma sociedade em que quem trabalha é quem come. (…) Ainda não chegamos a isso. Mas, justamente por isso, não podemos desanimar, nem desistir”, resume Jean-Jacques Henrilus, um dos fundadores da organização, membro da Coordenação Nacional.
Ao mesmo tempo em que instiga a olhar para frente, ele ressalta que seria injusto minimizar as árduas conquistas das quatro décadas passadas: “Hoje, temos a capacidade de mobilizar povo nos 10 departamentos do país. Isso é um primeiro ponto. Segundo, a gente conseguiu incentivar os camponeses a sentarem juntos, trabalharem juntos, comerem juntos, serem solidários entre eles para enfrentar as doenças, a morte ou a exploração do Estado.”
Membro da Direção Executiva, Pierre-Mary Louis concorda e acrescenta: “Se hoje os camponeses têm direitos, podem falar livremente, mobilizar-se, dizer o que eles querem e não querem, o Tèt Kole contribuiu muito nisso, por meio das formações que fazemos e do acompanhamento contínuo em todos os cantos do país.”
O começo antes da oficialização
Foi na ditadura de François e Jean-Claude Duvallier (de 1956 a 1986) que o Tèt Kole foi gestado, muito antes do seu nascimento formal. Na época, os camponeses eram as primeiras vítimas da repressão exercida pelos poderes locais, junto com as milícias e os paramilitares conhecidos como “Tonton Makoute”.
“Eles prendiam os camponeses por qualquer motivo, batiam neles, os encarceravam e os obrigavam a vender sua terra, seus animais, seus porcos, para serem soltos”, lembra-se Jean-Jacques Henrilus.
Nos anos 1970, as primeiras reuniões começaram a acontecer junto às comunidades de base da Cáritas de forma clandestina, uma vez que havia restrições às liberdades de associação e expressão. “Tivemos que usar a própria roça como espaço para construir o movimento. A gente fazia mutirões, capinava, plantava e, depois disso, na hora do almoço, na sombra de uma árvore, fazíamos a reunião. Porque era impossível fazer isso em outro local”, conta Henrilus.
À medida que o movimento foi crescendo, as estratégias se multiplicaram, com encontros de vários dias, acampados no mato ou nos canaviais, ou até mesmo em Porto Príncipe. As reuniões aconteciam em voz baixa, sem canto nem tumulto. Cada participante tinha uma hora específica para chegar e ir embora, a fim de evitar a aglomeração na rua.
Com a queda do regime de Duvallier, o Tèt Kole pôde finalmente organizar o seu primeiro encontro nacional em 6 de setembro de 1986 e oficializar seu nome. Mas, mesmo com a volta da democracia, a marginalização e a violência sistêmica contra a população camponesa continuaram.
Violências sistêmicas
O Haiti, que se libertou da colonização com uma revolução que pôs fim à escravidão, nunca conseguiu levar a cabo uma reforma agrária com devida redistribuição de terras. Até hoje, as maiores parcelas estão nas mãos de grandes proprietários, das igrejas ou do Estado, mantendo os camponeses em situação de arrendamento ou como trabalhadores precarizados.
Quando o povo se organiza, a repressão não demora. Foi o caso do massacre de Jean Rabel, em 23 de julho de 1987, quando 139 camponeses foram assassinados, a mando das elites locais, por reivindicarem um pedaço de chão. O movimento Tèt Kole não tinha sequer um ano de existência formal. Longe de se deixar abater, ele continuou ao lado das famílias no enfrentamento ao Estado. Hoje, aquela região é um exemplo de conquistas em termos de luta pela terra e organização popular.
As frentes de trabalho do Tèt Kole são muitas, do local ao internacional. Começam com a busca por direitos fundamentais (como o acesso a documentos de identidade e serviços básicos, muitas vezes negados às populações que vivem em zonas mais recuadas) e vão até a promoção da agroecologia, soberania alimentar, educação popular, preservação ambiental, economia social e solidária, igualdade de gênero, além da defesa incondicional da soberania do país e do seu povo contra todas as formas de ingerência imperialista.
A nível internacional, o Tèt Kole se articula dentro de organizações como CLOC-Via Campesina, Alba Movimentos e a Assembleia Internacional dos Povos (AIP), que compartilham os mesmos objetivos estratégicos contra um inimigo comum. Ele sustenta também um vínculo especial com o Movimento dos Trabalhadores e Trabalhadoras Sem Terra (MST) do Brasil, que, desde 2009, mantém uma brigada permanente de militantes no Haiti.
“A nossa parceria não se baseia em projetos ou aporte financeiro. É uma relação de irmandade. Uma relação de luta, de troca, de solidariedade”, relata Pierre-Mary Louis. “E isso é uma prova de que, nessa dinâmica de globalização da nossa luta, qualquer organização de qualquer país pode levar [a outro país] sua essência, suas ideias e sua solidariedade, do jeito que o MST faz.”
De ruim para pior
Paradoxalmente, depois de tantos avanços e tantas lutas, parece que a conjuntura do país nunca foi tão dramática. A crise de segurança e, em especial, a quase impossibilidade de deslocamento dentro da ilha têm como consequência um empobrecimento generalizado das famílias de pequenos agricultores. “Os camponeses precisam levar sua produção ao mercado local ou nacional, onde eles trocam ou vendem seus produtos para comprar o que lhes falta em casa. Porém, faz cinco anos que essa relação está praticamente cortada”, explica Louis.
As atividades de organização dos movimentos também são diretamente afetadas por essa situação, que impossibilita, por exemplo, assembleias gerais ou grandes mobilizações a nível nacional. A instabilidade impede qualquer planejamento, assim como o custo disparatado das passagens aéreas para viajar de Norte a Sul.
Mais grave ainda é a situação do Centro Nacional de Montrouis, que o movimento vem construindo ao longo de 15 anos, numa região hoje dominada por gangues armadas. O local era o principal centro de formação do Tèt Kole, erguido numa área de 14 hectares dedicados à agroecologia. Em 2024, ele foi invadido e saqueado, e hoje se encontra absolutamente inacessível para os membros da organização.
Dessa crise multifacetada, a direção do movimento faz uma análise aprofundada e histórica, rejeitando as respostas precipitadas ou superficiais. A violência, segundo eles, não é o feito de alguns bandidos locais que podem ser derrotados com uma intervenção estrangeira, por mercenários estadunidenses ou por uma falsa troca de governo. Ela faz parte de um projeto global e geopolítico de recolonização do Haiti, de exploração do seu povo e dos seus bens naturais – projeto implementado por aqueles mesmos que agora pretendem trazer soluções.
“As gangues foram criadas nessa lógica, por setores mafiosos nacionais e internacionais que precisavam exercer uma dominação sobre o povo haitiano, especialmente sobre as massas dos bairros populares, sobre os camponeses no meio rural, criando uma situação de pobreza, de miséria, de confinamento, para mantê-las sob dominação imperialista”, explica Jean-Jacques Henrilus.
Por isso, críticos à realização de eleições em um contexto tão antidemocrático consideram que a saída está numa mudança estrutural da sociedade, na construção de um novo Estado em que o poder esteja realmente nas mãos e a serviço do povo. “O Tèt Kole está engajado numa dinâmica que almeja uma mudança de Estado. Uma mudança radical, ou seja, não apenas trocar as pessoas que estão ali, mas sim construir um Estado popular, um Estado socialista capaz de assumir suas responsabilidades em prol do país e de todas as pessoas”, afirma Pierre-Mary Louis.
Henrilus complementa que essa criação de um novo Estado, de uma nova nação, realmente soberana, só pode partir da organização popular, único caminho possível “para reivindicar, para exigir, para enfrentar, para batalhar contra esse sistema de opressão. Porque, se a gente não se unir para acabar com ele, para arrancá-lo pela raiz, (…) a nação está perdida, a pátria está perdida, e nós estamos perdidos enquanto povo”.

title: 'We will sow' — Odesa farmers defiant in face of relentless Russian assaults
content:
'We will sow' — Odesa farmers defiant in face of relentless Russian assaults
Volodymyr Varbanets, 76, a farmer, stands in the grain warehouse in Odesa Oblast, Ukraine, in August 2026. (Karina Piliuhina / The Kyiv Independent)
ODESA OBLAST — Volodymyr Varbanets sinks his hands into a mound of wheat, letting the golden kernels slip between his fingers.
This year brought an unusually good harvest, the best since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion, he says. Behind him, hundreds of metric tons of wheat, barley, lentils, and peas fill the farm's warehouses.
"But we cannot sell it," he sighs.
For more than 20 years, Varbanets has worked this land, sowing and harvesting crops across 206 hectares. At 76, he still climbs behind the wheel of his tractor or combine. Three of the men who once worked on the farm have been mobilized, leaving him, his son, and another worker to tend the fields.
Normally, by late August, trucks would already be carrying his harvest from the farm to the three deep-water ports of the Greater Odesa logistics hub about 50 kilometers south. From there, it would be loaded onto commercial cargo vessels and shipped across the Black Sea to markets worldwide.
"We cannot sell it."
But this year, the harvest remains in the warehouse.
Since mid-July, Russia has intensified its attacks on Odesa's ports and adjacent infrastructure. Although the ports remain technically open, fewer ships now dare to enter this new maritime kill zone.
"The ports are almost blocked," says Dmytro Barinov, president of the Ukrainian Ports Association Ukrport.
'Ship Hunting' Campaign
On July 13, a Russian strike on a Togolese-flagged cargo vessel killed five people and injured 10 as it unloaded mineral fertilizers at the port of Odesa.
Six days later, three Russian cruise missiles struck the Golden Leo, a civilian bulk carrier loaded with corn, shortly after it left Chornomorsk. The attack killed 10 people, including nine crew members from India and Syria, and a Ukrainian maritime pilot. The damaged vessel sank a week later in the Black Sea.
"The corridor is not working, the ports are standing still, nobody is taking grain."
Both ships were traveling the maritime corridor used by merchant ships to reach Greater Odesa's three deep-water ports: Odesa, Chornomorsk, and Pivdennyi. Ukraine established the maritime corridor in August 2023, after Russia did not renew the agreement that Turkey and the United Nations had brokered separately with each side to allow for the export of grain from Ukrainian ports. Ukrainian strikes on Russian naval facilities and warships opened up the corridor for commercial shipping.
Barinov describes the increase in Russian attacks on civilian commercial vessels in the Black Sea this summer as a systematic targeting campaign rather than sporadic hits.
"It's ship hunting," says Barinov.
In July, 169 vessels entered the ports of Greater Odesa. By late August, only one or two ships a day were arriving, according to Barinov.
Container lines were among the first to suspend calls, he says. Their ships run on fixed schedules and cannot afford to wait indefinitely for safe passage. Bulk carriers transporting grain or iron ore have more flexible schedules, but Barinov says even those operators are increasingly reluctant to enter Odesa.
Some shipowners have offered crews substantially higher pay to make the journey, he adds. But at some point the problem is no longer one of schedules, freight rates, or insurance premiums.
"They are afraid for their lives," Barinov says. "It's not a matter of money."
Working at a loss
The drop in traffic has come at the height of Ukraine's harvest season.
Between Aug. 1 and Aug. 26, Ukraine exported around 1.42 million metric tons of agricultural products, around one-third of the possible export volume with full logistics access, the Agriculture Ministry estimates. Grain was hit hardest, with exports at 822,000 metric tons, around one-fifth of the potential volume.
"The corridor is not working, the ports are standing still, nobody is taking grain," says Varbanets, looking at his harvest. "And if somebody does take grain, then it is for next to nothing."
Last year, he says, even the cheapest wheat sold for around Hr 11,000 ($265) a ton. Today, buyers are offering him roughly Hr 3,500 to 4,000 ($84 to $96). Lentils that previously sold for around Hr 25,000 ($602) a ton now fetch about Hr 15,000 ($361).
At the same time, the farm's costs for diesel, fertilizer, and spare parts have risen.
"We are not even working for zero," he says. "We are working at a loss."
Varbanets still needs to pay his workers and taxes, and settle with the owners of the land he leases. In a few weeks, he has to sow again.
read also
The grain can be kept in his warehouse for about a year, Varbanets adds. But it has to be moved regularly to preserve its quality; at his farm, he uses a loader to shift it from one part of the warehouse to another.
"Grain has to be constantly in motion," he explains.
The grain elevators have little room for new deliveries. Until enough ships arrive to carry the stored grain away, they cannot empty, leaving farmers with fewer places to send their harvest.
No Good Alternative
Ukraine has other routes for moving its exports, but none match the capacity of the deep-water ports around Odesa.
Ukraine’s Danube ports of Izmail and Reni became crucial after Russia's 2022 blockade and, as ships retreat from Greater Odesa, have taken on more traffic. For farmers like Varbanets, rerouting grain to the Danube means a much longer and more expensive journey.
Izmail is roughly 400 kilometers away from his farm, and Varbanets estimates that the cost of transporting grain there can amount to 30-35% of the grain's sale value, before accounting for delays.
The Danube ports are smaller and constrained by the Sulina Canal, which limits the size of vessels that can reach them. Barinov says ships carrying around 5,000 to 7,000 metric tons can use the route, a fraction of the capacity available at Greater Odesa's deep-water terminals.
"Nobody is taking grain."
Moving the cargo of a single 100,000-metric ton capacity ship overland would require roughly 5,000 trucks, each requiring a driver, documents, fuel, and a border crossing, Barinov adds.
The Danube route offers no escape from Russian attacks either. Russia has repeatedly targeted ports and logistics infrastructure there, leaving Ukraine's backup route slower, smaller, and exposed to many of the same dangers as Odesa.
By the end of August, around 70 vessels were waiting to enter the Sulina Canal en route to Ukraine's Danube ports. The shift has kept some exports moving, but it has also shown how quickly alternative routes become congested when traffic is diverted from Greater Odesa.
Romania's port of Constanta is another option. Ukrainian cargo can reach it by rail or road. While Constanta already handles Romanian and other European exports, border capacity, railway links, and cargo transfers all create additional bottlenecks for Ukrainian cargo.
read also
Defending the corridor
What keeps the corridor open at all is a force of Ukrainian Navy patrol boats that work around the clock, serving as mobile air-defense groups along the coast. Each vessel covers an assigned sector, monitoring the waters, detecting and neutralizing explosive devices, watching for unmanned boats, and shooting down low-flying Russian attack drones.
When an incoming aerial threat is detected, Yevhen, a 32-year-old serviceman of the Ukrainian Navy identified by first name only for security reasons, puts on his body armor and helmet, climbs into the turret, and takes his position at the machine gun.
Shahed drones have chased their boat more than once while they were out at sea, he says.
"We fired back," says Yevhen, who served in the airborne forces before joining the Navy. He never expected to end up at sea.
"I can't swim," he adds with a smile.
But the boats' machine guns offer little protection against missiles launched from occupied Crimea and Russia. Crews increasingly face jet-powered Shahed variants and Banderols, which travel faster than conventional Shaheds and are harder to intercept.
Russia sends alternating types of drones and missiles at intervals of 30-minutes to an hour, says Oleh Zasyadvovk, a captain 2nd rank and communications officer with the Ukrainian Navy.
"There is no period of more than an hour without an alert," he says. "The tactics change almost every day."
During particularly demanding shifts, Yevhen says, he spends more than 24 hours at sea and goes for as long as two days without sleep.
The next harvest
For Varbanets, the lack of viable alternative routes is becoming more pressing as storage space dwindles. His wheat, barley, lentils, and peas already fill most of the warehouse space, while the next harvest approaches.
"There will be nowhere to pour the sunflower," he says.
On his way to the sunflower fields, Varbanets passes the village cemetery where four Ukrainian flags mark the graves of local men killed fighting in the war. One of them grew up with his grandson, who worked on the farm as an agronomist and is now serving in the military.
Further along the road, the war has cut through the farmland. The soil is charred where a Russian drone shot down nearby crashed and burned. The crash sparked a fire that burned around 600 hectares of land and damaged the tree lines that protect the soil from wind and snow in winter, Varbanets says.
Asked whether he will replant the burned fields, he answers: "What else can we do? We will sow."

title: ¿En qué parte del Perú será día NO laborable este 8 de setiembre y por qué?
content:
Cada 8 de setiembre, mientras el calendario avanza con normalidad para gran parte del país, una región se detiene para rendir homenaje a una tradición religiosa. La fecha no corresponde a un feriado nacional, sino a un día festivo religioso no laborable establecido para esa jurisdicción. La medida fue dispuesta por el Gobierno Regional como parte de las celebraciones dedicadas a Nuestra Señora de Cocharcas. Así, las calles y actividades de la región adquieren un ritmo distinto marcado por la festividad. Para sus habitantes, la jornada representa una pausa vinculada con la fe y las costumbres locales.
La precisión resulta importante porque el descanso no se aplica de manera general en todo el territorio peruano. Se trata de una disposición de alcance regional, ligada específicamente a la conmemoración de Nuestra Señora de Cocharcas. Mientras en otras zonas las actividades continúan con su rutina habitual, en esta región la fecha adquiere un significado especial. La celebración combina tradición religiosa e identidad local, convirtiendo el 8 de setiembre en una jornada esperada por la comunidad. Más que un feriado para todo el país, es una fecha que mantiene viva una tradición arraigada en su propio territorio.
Esta es la región que celebra en honor a la Virgen de Cocharcas con peregrinaciones y procesiones
Cada 8 de setiembre, Apurímac cambia el ritmo de sus calles para recibir una de sus celebraciones más emblemáticas: la Festividad de Nuestra Señora de Cocharcas. En medio de la devoción, los pobladores se reúnen para rendir homenaje a la llamada “Mamacha Cocharcas”, una figura profundamente arraigada en la identidad regional. El corazón de esta tradición se encuentra en el Santuario de la Virgen de Cocharcas, en el distrito del mismo nombre, provincia de Chincheros. Allí, la fe congrega a familias y visitantes que llegan para participar de una jornada cargada de simbolismo. Cada año, el santuario vuelve a ser escenario de una historia que se niega a desaparecer con el paso del tiempo.
La festividad guarda más de cuatro siglos de historia y conserva una particular mezcla de expresiones religiosas y culturales. Las prácticas de la tradición católica conviven con manifestaciones propias del mundo andino, creando una celebración que refleja la diversidad de Apurímac. La devoción hacia la Virgen se transmite de generación en generación y permanece como parte de la memoria colectiva de sus habitantes. Con el paso de los años, la fiesta ha mantenido su esencia y continúa reuniendo a la comunidad alrededor de sus creencias. Así, cada 8 de setiembre, la “Mamacha Cocharcas” vuelve a ocupar el centro de una celebración donde la fe y la cultura caminan juntas.
La celebración reúne a miles de peregrinos durante la festividad con actividades culturales y tradicionales
Desde temprano, la devoción comienza a sentirse en cada rincón de la festividad de la “Mamacha Cocharcas”. Las misas y ceremonias religiosas reúnen a los fieles, mientras las peregrinaciones acercan al santuario a devotos que llegan desde distintos puntos del país. Luego, la imagen de la Virgen recorre las calles en una procesión acompañada por cantos, música y muestras de fe. A su alrededor, las danzas tradicionales y los conjuntos andinos llenan el ambiente de color y movimiento. Entre la celebración religiosa también aparecen ferias gastronómicas, artesanales y diversas actividades culturales.
La fiesta se convierte así en un punto de encuentro para miles de peregrinos que llegan con la esperanza de renovar su devoción y mantener viva una tradición de generaciones. Desde Apurímac, Ayacucho y Cusco hasta Huancavelica, Junín y Lima, los visitantes emprenden el viaje para participar de esta celebración. Cada delegación llega con sus propias costumbres, sonidos y expresiones culturales, que terminan formando parte de una misma jornada. El santuario recibe entonces a una multitud unida por la fe y la tradición. En Cocharcas, la celebración demuestra que la devoción también puede convertirse en una poderosa expresión de identidad cultural.
Conoce el origen del culto a la Virgen de Cocharcas gracias a Sebastián Quimichu en el siglo XVI
En Cocharcas, provincia de Chincheros, la historia de la Virgen se entrelaza con la fe católica, las tradiciones andinas y el relato de un hombre que decidió emprender un largo camino en busca de alivio. El origen de esta devoción se remonta a finales del siglo XVI y tiene como fecha emblemática el 12 de septiembre de 1598, cuando, según el inventario turístico del Mincetur, habría sido entronizada la Virgen en este pueblo. Con el tiempo, en ese mismo escenario se levantaría el santuario que hoy recibe a miles de creyentes. La imagen guarda además una estrecha relación con la Virgen de Copacabana, venerada a orillas del lago Titicaca. Sus semejanzas recuerdan el vínculo entre ambas expresiones de devoción.
En el centro de esta tradición aparece Sebastián Martín Asto, conocido como Sebastián Quimichu, un poblador de Cocharcas que, según los relatos conservados, padecía una enfermedad que afectaba uno de sus brazos. Ante la imposibilidad de trabajar, emprendió un viaje hasta el santuario de Copacabana con la esperanza de encontrar una respuesta a su padecimiento. La tradición cuenta que, después de pedir la intercesión de la Virgen, recuperó la salud y decidió agradecer el milagro de una manera especial. Prometió entonces llevar una imagen de la Virgen hasta su pueblo natal para compartir aquella devoción con su comunidad. El relato quedó registrado en un manuscrito de 1625, una de las primeras fuentes vinculadas con el origen de esta historia.

title: Inaugural Indigenous food summit in Portland in September
content:
Nika Bartoo-Smith
Underscore Native News + ICT
PORTLAND, Ore. — A group of Indigenous organizations around the Portland metro area felt inspired by the first Indigenous foods expo last year in the Northwest. They decided to bring something similar to their own city.
Starting with a budget of zero dollars, and less than a year to plan, that dream has turned into a reality with the inaugural Indigenous Food Summit on Sept. 9 and 10. The event will be held at the Native American Student & Community Center at Portland State University, hosted by the Northwest Indigenous Food Sovereignty Alliance and other community groups.
Expecting around 300 people, the conference is completely free and open to the public.
Beyond programming, such as “wild food preparation” and “cougar hide tanning,” meals, coffee and snacks will also be provided to attendees; highlighting local Indigenous-owned companies. There will also be a marketplace of Indigenous vendors.
Over the course of the two-day summit, community members are invited to come learn and share knowledge focused around food sovereignty.
“I think it’s really important for folks to have those conversations about what food sovereignty looks like for themselves in their own communities or their organizations, whatever that looks like,” said Emma Johnson, Cowlitz, Indigenous Traditional Knowledge & Cultural Knowledge coordinator at Portland State University. Johnson helped organize the summit.
“I think that’s the power behind that term is that you get to define it for yourself, and it boils down to, in some form, managing your own food systems.”
Planning the summit
Over a dozen organizations are involved, including the university’s Indigenous Traditional Ecological & Cultural Knowledge program, Native American Youth and Family Center, OSU Extension and many others.
Organizing this summit meant putting together different sources of funding, Gina Mengwasser, Western Cherokee Nation Batesville Band, Health Equity manager at the center. This came primarily through grants, and organizers volunteering spare time to turn the vision into reality.
“It’s been chaotic, and not in a bad way. It’s just in a ‘whoa, are we going to pull this off way?’ And we’re pulling it off,” Johnson said.
The agenda includes dozens of different workshops for attendees such as pressure canning, growing first foods, tea blending and so much more.
The day before the summit Growers Food Safety Training will offer a course geared toward supporting Indigenous food growers in learning safe practices to grow, harvest and handle produce.
Planning a free summit was also crucial to organizers.
“This is a shared knowledge. We don’t want to charge for our knowledge,” Mengwasser said. “It’s supposed to be shared, and we want to do that for our community. And if we have the ability with some of our funding, we want it to be free.”
While this event is the first of its kind in Portland, organizers are aiming for this to become an annual or biannual event.
Organizers hope the summit is also a place of building community connections and continued food knowledge sharing beyond this event. And a space to learn about other resources and spaces in community centered around food sovereignty.
“I’m hoping for joy,” Johnson said, “obviously more connections and just like that inspiration to know that different avenues for food sovereignty projects are possible.”
For questions about the summit email NIFSA503@gmail.com.
This story is co-published by Underscore Native News and ICT, a news partnership that covers Indigenous communities in the Pacific Northwest.
Correction: The story has been updated to reflect the correct spelling for the Batesville Band of the Western Cherokee Nation.

title: Sharpeville massacre, 66 years on: Families still wait for justice
content:
Sharpeville massacre, 66 years on: Families still wait for justice
More than six decades after police opened fire on protesters, survivors and relatives are taking their fight to court.
Sharpeville, South Africa – Paulina Mathinye was five years old when her father left home for a meeting near the police station in Sharpeville, a township south of Johannesburg.
She remembers waiting for him to return.
“I’ll go run to him,” Mathinye recalled thinking. “He will pick me up like daddies always do with their beloved daughters.”
He never did.
On March 21, 1960, Mathinye’s father joined other men from the community at a gathering protesting apartheid’s pass laws, which required Black South Africans to carry documents restricting where they could live and work.
“There was a meeting here at the old police station, so he accompanies those fathers to the meeting. But then he never came back.”
Police opened fire on the protesters that day in what became known as the Sharpeville Massacre.
Apartheid-era police records put the death toll at 69 and the number of injured at 180. Research published in 2024 using police records found that as many as 91 people may have been killed and 238 injured. The higher figures are also cited by lawyers representing Sharpeville survivors and families.
The massacre became a defining moment in South Africa’s struggle against apartheid. March 21 is now commemorated as Human Rights Day, and South Africa’s democratic Constitution was signed in Sharpeville in 1996.
But for the families of those killed and injured, the consequences did not end that day.
More than six decades later, survivors and relatives are seeking redress through the courts.
Lawyers for Human Rights has filed an application in the Gauteng High Court challenging the continued existence of the Indemnity Act 61 of 1961, an apartheid-era law that the applicants say prevented survivors and dependants of those killed from pursuing civil and criminal proceedings arising from the massacre.
The applicants are also seeking certification of a class action involving survivors who were shot and dependants of those killed.
For Mathinye, the legal fight is inseparable from the life that followed her father’s death.
He had been the family’s breadwinner. After he was killed, her mother worked as a domestic worker to support five children.
“We sometimes go to bed with empty stomach. We sometimes go to school and when we come back from school we find nothing to eat.”
There was no electricity, and sometimes her mother could not afford even a candle for the children to study.
“There was no light. There was no library. Struggle even to buy a candle, a mere candle.”
Mathinye wanted to become a teacher.
She stayed in school and applied to study further, but her family could not afford it. She eventually began working while still young to help support her mother and siblings.
When she encounters people she went to school with who became teachers and nurses, she thinks about the life she might have had.
“If my father was not shot, maybe I was going to be one of those people… Maybe by this time I would be a teacher.”
Why now?
The effort to seek redress is not new.
Charne Tracey-Mamdoo, a lawyer in the Strategic Litigation Programme at Lawyers for Human Rights, told Al Jazeera that victims and families attempted to pursue claims soon after the massacre.
“Immediately after the Sharpeville massacre, victims and families did attempt to pursue these sorts of claims, but they were barred because in 1961 the apartheid government enacted the Indemnity Act.”
The applicants argue that the Act created a legal barrier to civil and criminal proceedings arising from conduct covered by the legislation.
The current case challenges that barrier.
Lawyers for Human Rights is asking the High Court to declare the Indemnity Act unconstitutional and invalid. It is also seeking certification of a class action for survivors who were shot and dependants of those killed.
The applicants must first persuade the court to grant the constitutional relief they seek and certify the proposed class action. If the case proceeds, individual claims for damages could then be pursued.
More than 70 survivors and relatives have expressed support for or interest in the proposed litigation, according to Lawyers for Human Rights.
Tracey-Mamdoo said lawyers had spent years locating surviving victims and witnesses, reconstructing claims and gathering historical and expert evidence.
