The survivors’ age has added urgency. Many of those directly affected by the massacre are now elderly, and some who spent decades seeking redress have died without seeing the matter resolved.
An inheritance of loss
Ishmael Poho was six years old when his father left home for a community meeting on March 21.
Poho wanted to go with him.
“He said, ‘No, I’ll come back. You need to stay home.’”
Poho saw his father again briefly that day.
“That was the last time I saw my father that day.”
It took his mother three days to find his body.
According to Poho’s account, related partly through an interpreter, his mother searched police stations before eventually finding him among bodies that had been placed in garages.
“At that station, there were vehicle garages as part of the building and the infrastructure. However, bodies were piled up or stacked up in those garages,” the interpreter said.
His father’s death changed the family’s circumstances.
His mother had never worked and did not speak English. She eventually found work as a domestic worker in a nearby white neighbourhood. As the children grew older, they also worked to support the household.
Poho, now 72, thinks about the people he went to school with who became teachers, nurses and other health professionals.
“If my father was alive, I would have been different. My life would have been different from the life I have lived.”
For Mauleen Maine, the loss began before she was born.
Her uncle was 23 when he was killed.
According to family history passed down by her grandmother, he had returned from a night shift, gone to buy bread and then returned to the meeting.
He had been the family’s breadwinner.
After his death, Maine’s grandmother struggled financially and eventually sold liquor to survive. She died without seeing the matter resolved.
Maine’s parents later continued seeking redress. They too died without seeing justice.
Now Maine, 62, is continuing the effort.
She told Al Jazeera through an interpreter that compensation alone would not be enough. Her family also wants better housing and educational opportunities for their children.
For families like hers, the question is not only what was lost in 1960, but what might have been different in the decades that followed.
What would justice mean?
For Vincent Thamae, a member of Voices of Sharpeville who has worked with survivors and families, the case cannot be reduced to compensation.
“It’s not a question of the amount of money. It’s the question of how much does it need for a change in the lives of the victims and survivors?”
Thamae argues that the effects of the massacre reached beyond those who were shot.
“The victims were not only those who were shot,” he said. “We maintain even the whole township was a victim.”
Lawyers for Human Rights says the plaintiffs also want dialogue with the South African government about appropriate reparations and recognition.
The formal court case, however, is narrower. The applicants are challenging the Indemnity Act and seeking relief that would enable the proposed class action to proceed. The court has not yet ruled that the Act is unconstitutional, nor has it determined that the government is liable to compensate the applicants.
That distinction matters because Sharpeville occupies a powerful place in South Africa’s democratic identity.
It is remembered every year as a symbol of the struggle for human rights.
For some of the families who lived through the massacre, however, remembrance has not amounted to redress.
Lawyers for Human Rights says 51 Sharpeville survivors were formally awarded reparations through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission process.
Poho had expected the democratic government to address the concerns of survivors and families.
“We were happy that a Black government had stepped into office, and we were hopeful that our issues would be met and, you know, justice realised, only to realise it became worse. Nothing ever came.”
The government respondents will have an opportunity to respond to the application before the High Court considers the relief sought.
There is no clear timetable for the proceedings.
For Tracey-Mamdoo, the age of the survivors makes the case urgent.
“They’ve already waited a very long time for this to happen and we are doing everything we can to just kind of move that process forward.”
Mathinye is now 71. Poho is 72.
Their fathers died more than six decades ago.
Their families have lived with the consequences ever since.
Children grew up without fathers. Breadwinners were lost. Educational opportunities disappeared. Mothers struggled to keep households afloat. And in some families, the next generation inherited not only the consequences of the massacre but also the fight for redress.
Sharpeville is remembered as a turning point in South Africa’s history.
For these families, the story remains unfinished.
And Mathinye is still asking the question she has carried since she was five.
“Why did they shoot my father?”

title: Hero’s welcome for Amai’s Cook Out winner
content:
Obey Musiwa, Harare Bureau
HARARE has welcomed home Edith Takasimba, winner of the 2026 Amai’s Traditional Cookout Competition national finals held at Mbizo Stadium in Kwekwe, Midlands Province.
Takasimba was welcomed at a ceremony in Harare yesterday, with provincial leaders describing her victory as a demonstration of how traditional knowledge and skills can contribute to women’s empowerment, cultural preservation and tourism development.
The national finals, held under the Ministry of Tourism and Hospitality Industry, showcased the enduring value of indigenous culinary knowledge, while highlighting traditional cuisine as an important component of Zimbabwe’s heritage and tourism economy.
Minister of State for Provincial Affairs and Devolution for Harare Metropolitan Province, Senator Charles Tawengwa, said the province had closely followed the competition and was proud of Takasimba’s achievement.
“The competition was not simple and was not easy, and we admired the courage that Takasimba showed to go all the way and bring the trophy and certificate back to Harare,” he said.
“We celebrate this as Harare province, and we encourage other women to remain open to such opportunities for empowerment.”
Harare deputy mayor and Ward 7 (Mt Pleasant) Councillor Rosemary Muronda commended the standard of the competition, describing the innovation displayed by contestants as impressive. “Women came out in their numbers to take part in these competitions and produce various traditional recipes.
“This is a nutritious heritage that will safeguard lives and remain relevant even as the world moves further into the digital age,” she said.
Takasimba said her journey from the community level to the national finals required determination and sacrifice.
“I started at JC Hall and progressed to Highfield, where we got all our motivation, and it was so hard, but we were told nothing is impossible.
“In Warren Park, they taught us to simply be ourselves, and that is where I got to number one,” she said.
She credited her family, the community and the First Lady’s Office for supporting her throughout the competition.
“When I reached the provincial round, I also got number one. At the national finals, our supporters brought us stoves and ovens, and I want to thank the women who stood by us.
“I hardly had time with my family; sometimes the ingredients we needed would only arrive late at night, and we would wait for hours. It was a very difficult time, but we pushed through.”
Dr Mnangagwa’s Amai’s Traditional Cookout Competition was launched in 2019 with the support of chiefs’ wives and has grown into a national programme promoting indigenous cuisine and skills. The competition now brings together women, churches, students, professional chefs, persons with disabilities and inmates, with exhibitors from all 10 provinces participating this year. The programme has also provided a platform for communities to preserve traditional culinary knowledge while creating opportunities for empowerment and participation in the tourism sector.

title: A Little-Known Fact: Pakuri’s Lands Stretch Across Two Regions
content:
A little-known fact about Pakuri, better known as St Cuthbert’s Mission, is that the country’s only titled Indigenous community in Region Four actually stretches across two administrative regions.
The Amerindian Peoples Association (APA), in an update on its ongoing community outreach, said part of Pakuri’s titled lands lies in Region Five, even though the community itself is recognised as the only Indigenous village in Region Four.
Located along the Mahaica River, Pakuri is primarily home to the Lokono people and is one of Guyana’s best-known Indigenous communities. Its relative proximity to Georgetown has also made it an important centre for Indigenous culture and heritage.
The APA said Pakuri’s circumstances are notably different from those of many hinterland communities.
“Unlike several of the hinterland regions, where numerous Indigenous villages are spread across large territories, Pakuri is recognised as the only Indigenous village in the Demerara-Mahaica Region.”
But the community’s administrative geography is more complicated than its designation as a Region Four village might suggest.
“But many of you may not know that the village straddles two regions! Part of Pakuri’s lands falls within Administrative Region Five (Mahaica-Berbice). So if you didn’t know, now you know!”
The revelation highlights an important distinction between administrative boundaries and Indigenous land ownership in Guyana. While the country is divided into ten administrative regions for purposes of governance and public administration, Indigenous communities may hold titled lands extending across those regional boundaries.
Pakuri’s location and history have given it particular cultural significance. The community, historically known as St Cuthbert’s Mission, is associated with the Lokono nation and is frequently identified as a cultural centre because of its accessibility from the coast and Georgetown.
The APA’s latest update came as its outreach team moved from Region Three into Region Four after spending longer than initially planned in Region Three.
With characteristic humour, the organisation acknowledged the extended stay.
“We know we said we were overnighting in Region Three, but spent more than one night there. So, we will just pretend that it was just one long night.”
The APA then announced its move into Region Four and drew attention to Pakuri as a significant Indigenous community in the region.
“Today, we are moving on to Region Four, and we are sure many of us also know of the only titled Indigenous Community in the Region, Pakuri or commonly known as St Cuthbert’s Mission.”
The community’s lands crossing into Region Five means that, despite Pakuri’s recognition as Region Four’s only Indigenous village, its territorial footprint does not fit neatly within a single administrative boundary.
The detail is more than a geographical curiosity. It is a reminder that the history, land rights and territorial realities of Guyana’s Indigenous communities can extend beyond the administrative lines used to divide the country.

title: 9/11 firefighter's son spends months bringing steel from World Trade Center across US
content:
The steel 'embodies his soul': 9/11 family takes World Trade Center beam across US
Stephen Siller Jr. was just 9 months old when his firefighter dad died on 9/11.
On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, 34-year-old New York City firefighter Stephen Siller had just finished his overnight shift when he heard a call come in on the scanner.
"He immediately knew something was awry," so he drove to his firehouse in Brooklyn, his son, Stephen Siller Jr., told ABC News.
"When he got there, he realized his whole unit had responded [to the World Trade Center]," Siller Jr. said. "So he grabbed his gear, threw it in his truck and started to make his way to the World Trade Center. But on 9/11, they shut down every entryway into Manhattan."
He parked his car by the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel, Siller Jr. said, put about 60 pounds of gear on his back, and ran through the tunnel to the South Tower of the World Trade Center.
Stephen Siller was among 343 New York City Fire Department members killed on 9/11. He was survived by his close-knit siblings, his wife Sally, and his five children, including Stephen Jr., who was 9 months old.
Siller Jr., now 25, doesn't have his own memories of his father, but he's poured his energy into honoring those who died on 9/11. And to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks, he spent the last four months bringing a 16,900-pound steel beam from the World Trade Center to dozens of cities across the U.S. in hopes that seeing a piece of history up close will help Americans remember, learn and be inspired.
The Steel Across America campaign allows the public to "put their hand on that steel and feel the loss and sacrifice that was made that day -- the sacrifice of first responders and their loss, the loss of innocent people who just went to work," Stephen Siller Jr.'s uncle, Frank Siller, told ABC News.
9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan,” a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept.11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live.
Siller Jr. described the entire tour as "incredibly powerful."
At the first stop, ground zero, a firefighter whose entire unit was killed on 9/11 "walked up to the steel and he put his hand on it, and he was overcome with emotion," Siller Jr. recalled. "You could just immediately see tears rushing down his face. And he started to hug the steel like he was hugging his friends he lost 25 years ago."
To Siller Jr., the steel represents the more than 1,000 bodies never recovered from the World Trade Center -- including his father's.
"Who they are is ingrained in that steel, what they did is ingrained in that steel. It holds the memory of that day," he said. "It's the most overwhelming piece of history I've ever come across."
The beam represents "resilience, strength, but also sacrifice," Frank Siller added. "... Ground zero is my brother's burial place, obviously. But the steel has his -- embodies his soul, and the souls of so many."
As Siller Jr. spent his summer traveling the U.S., from Oklahoma to California to Mount Rushmore in South Dakota, he said he was surprised by how many people had personal connections to the terror attacks, like the police officer he met in Seattle whose uncle was killed on 9/11.
"And we had thousands of people show up to 35 events across the country who may not have had a connection to 9/11," he added, "but for them, they wanted to mourn that day, they wanted to make sure they never forgot."
"Everywhere we went was incredible -- the support, it was mind-boggling," Siller Jr. said. "In Texarkana, a small, little town in Texas, we had about 1,000 people show up to an event. It was unbelievable. You know, companies letting all their employees out of work to go see this piece of steel."
Siller Jr. found one of the most memorable stops to be Emma E. Booker Elementary School in Florida, where President George W. Bush was reading to students on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, when he learned of the attacks.
"We normally have stairs that go up to the steel truck," Siller Jr. explained, but on this May visit to the school, it was pouring rain.
Still, the children "were begging the firemen, 'Hey, can we get up? We just want to touch the steel,'" Siller Jr. said.
As the kids were lifted up, they began "praying over this steel," he recalled.
"Little kids who understand that, you know, this is a sacred piece of history ... it once held up the Twin Towers, it once held floors and walls, and now it holds the gravity of that day," he said.
"I was really shocked at how interested they were," he said.
To Frank Siller and Siller Jr., educating the next generation was a key goal of the Steel Across America campaign.
"These kids were incredible; they were patient ... and they consistently showed up," Siller Jr. said. "No matter where we were in the country, there were families there, which was beautiful -- fathers and mothers wanting to teach their kids."
"I was 9 months old on 9/11 -- if you were born after me, and not in New York City, you know, there's a high chance that you have no real understanding of that day," he continued. "It's important that that lesson is taught to these kids -- there's so much to be pulled from the sacrifices made."
The Steel Across America campaign is part of the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, started by Frank Siller in honor of his brother's run from the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel to the World Trade Center. The foundation supports military members, first responders and their families across the U.S. The foundation is currently providing wounded veterans and first responders with mortgage-free, specially-adapted smart homes.
"We didn't let Stephen just perish in that rubble and let that story end there. No, we took his act of courage and sacrifice and said, 'We're going to do good with it,'" Frank Siller said.
"Would Stephen make that run again through the tunnel, knowing he was gonna die? I think he knew he was gonna die," Frank Siller said. "At the very least, he knew it was a strong possibility that he might not be coming home. And to think that he did that, knowing how much he loved Sally and his kids, people like that are few and far between. ... And it's got to be recognized and never forgotten."

title: Meet the chefs who kept Ground Zero workers fueled after the 9/11 attacks
content:
Meet the New York City chefs who kept Ground Zero workers fueled after the 9/11 attacks
Members of "Operation Chefs With Spirit" reflect on the tragedy 25 years later.
Chef Don Pintabona spent years cooking up the finest dishes for celebrities, Wall Street brokers and other VIPs at the Tribeca Grill in downtown Manhattan, but nothing could have prepared him and the rest of the city's restaurant community for their biggest job.
In the hours after the World Trade Center was attacked and destroyed on Sept. 11, 2001, Pintabona said he and many other chefs, caters, food service workers and others all yearned to help the city in some capacity with their skills, but didn't immediately know how.
But through quick thinking, organizing and the generosity of thousands New Yorkers, Pintabona and the other restaurant members put together a massive operation that fed Ground Zero workers around the clock for two months after the attacks.
"Everybody kind of just said, 'Okay, let's jump in,'" Pintabona, 66, told ABC News.
He and other volunteers of "Operation Chefs with Spirit" said that even though 25 years have passed since the attacks, the memories of those weeks are still fresh, as is the sense of awe at how they put the operation together.
Turning the page on a tragedy
Pintabona said he had a desire to do something after the attacks to help the city, but it was a little piece of paper that came to him serendipitously that sparked his idea for the operation.
On Sept. 11, he said he watched the destruction of the towers from the roof of his home in Brooklyn, which was so close that pieces of paper debris from the towers were floating in the air near him.
One of those was a "P" page from a dictionary and when Pintabona picked it up he said he noticed that one side of the page had words with negative connotations, such as pesky, while the other side had words such as persevere, perseverance, persistence.
“9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan,” a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept.11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live.
"I mean, in my mind, this came straight from heaven, that through the perversion, you gotta persist, you gotta persevere," he said. "So those words were banging around my head for the days and weeks and just trying to figure out how can I live up to this."
Pintabona said the next day he was able to get to his restaurant, and he started cooking with what he had in his kitchen. He then brought the food to Stuyvesant High School in lower Manhattan, which was one of the staging areas for first responders.
"We had just floods of people coming in to attack the food," he said adding that the meals were gone in a matter of hours.
Pintabona said he wanted to continue to feed more people but transporting the meals through the streets, which were damaged and restricted to first responders and the National Guard, would be a challenge. He said he had a eureka moment during a cigarette break while watching the Hudson River.
"I saw a barge…And I said, 'Holy s---, this is it. We've got to feed everybody by boat,'" he recalled.
A crew assembles, quickly gets into action
Pintabona told ABC News he found that that other chefs in the city were also interested in feeding the Ground Zero workers and they all put their heads together.
He soon started calling up several contacts within the food industry, the city government and the owner of Spirit Cruises, which operated city sightseeing and party cruises lines, and things quickly began to fall in place.
Spirit provided three boats, one at Chelsea Piers that would be used to cook and prepare the meals, another to transport the food to Ground Zero, and a third, a triple decker, stationed in Battery Park City near the pit that was used for the workers to eat and rest.
The city's top chefs, such as Charlie Palmer, Danny Meyer and Daniel Boulud, and food workers and volunteers would be doled out with tasks with everything from cutting veggies to organizing forks, spoons and plates.
Jim Stewart, a longtime food service coordinator who had experience coordinating food operations at the Meadowlands and other big clients, jumped in when Pintabona made the calls for help. Stewart said he too was compelled to do something after the attacks.
"I think at that point, having something to do was sort of helpful, and it gave you some sort of purpose in a very difficult situation," Stewart, 66, a Navy veteran, told ABC News.
Stewart used his connections to secure food from the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, which was still in fridges following the end of that year's U.S. Open.
Stewart and Pintabona estimated that the food from the tennis center could serve 75,000 meals, but that was all eaten within three days.
Fortunately, they weren't the only New Yorkers who were willing to share from their fridges. Stewart recalled how a whole slew of Downtown Manhattan restaurant staff, from small Chinatown restaurants to larger, more elite eateries like the ones under B.R. Guest, were calling him up and ready to offer their food.
"So they would be bringing down enormous amounts of food packages to go. All the cooks from down there, they brought meals for like 200 people without question for a month," Stewart said.
"I would get a call, and they would go, 'At the airport, there's two pallets of beef from Texas.' It was not just New York," Stewart added.
Pintabona said that thousands of New Yorkers arrived at Chelsea Piers ready to volunteer, even those who never cooked a meal in their life.
Although Pintabona had to turn many would-be volunteers away because of space and logistics issues, he said he worked out to tailor their skills to fit the operation.
"When they would come on, I would try to talk to as many as possible. 'Okay, you work at Smith Barney in the accounting department? You know what? We need you to help us inventory the food that comes in off the trucks,'" he recalled. "A lot of people, obviously servers and whatnot, food service people, I would put them front-facing on the buffets, you know what they're used to."
Megan Murphy was a full time bartender at Rue 51 in Manhattan on Sept. 11 and she told ABC News she immediately answered Stewart's call. She helped to serve the food and coordinate with other volunteers right at the pit.
"It was my call to duty," Murphy, 51, told ABC News while holding back tears. " I had been doing something because I was helpless. I felt helpless and I just wanted to help. I just want to be…I just needed to be there."
'Nourishing more than their stomachs'
By Sept. 14, the operation had kicked off and the volunteers were ready to go and the first set of food was delivered to the pit.
The boats would sail from Chelsea Piers nearly 2 1/2 miles south to Ground Zero with a team of volunteers and return back for another round and the operation would continue 24/7.
Workers still had soot on them and looked liked they hadn't slept in days but they gladly accepted the meals and cherished the time to step away from the terrible scene.
Pintabona said massage therapists joined in on the volunteering and provided the crews with free massages to ease their muscles.
He said the meals definitely helped the pit workers have the energy to push through with their work, but the chefs and volunteers all felt that their service meant a lot more than a free lunch.
"You'd see the looks on the faces of people that came in, if they'd been on the pile for God knows how many hours and starving and then they got to sit in a clean environment and then talk to other first responders," he said.
"So that was the most amazing part of the effort," he added, "[It] kind of nourished a lot more than just stomachs."
Murphy, who continued to bartend at night during her volunteer time, said that many who came down to help went beyond just serving food and in many cases offered the pit crews a place to unwind and let out their raw emotions.
"I would make an effort just to go to everyone and talk to them, and let them talk to me about the experience," she said.
"If after lunch they could walk out and I could walk out with them and they were smiling and getting off their shift and made it a better day, that was what I was there to do," Murphy added.
The volunteers and chefs said that while they pushed forward with the operation, with some sleeping on the boats, the stress and hard work did compound.
Fortunately, the volunteers had each other's backs, according to Pintabona and Stewart.
"It got so ridiculous that one day Jimmy was working the phones and, you know I just had this stupid, selfish craving for a Krispy Kreme doughnut," Pintabona recalled.
"I said, 'All right, let's call this guy.' We called them, and the next day a whole truck with like 20 rolling racks of Krispy Kreme donuts showed up," Stewart said. "So [Pintabona] looked at me and was like, I should have known better."
Looking back 25 years later
The operation ended after roughly two months and roughly a million meals after the Red Cross came in and took care of meals for the Ground Zero pit crew. But Pintabona said that the crew didn't grow apart.
He organized a Christmas party at Cipriani in Soho for all of the volunteers and their families and many stayed in touch in the last 25 years.
Stewart said he was humbled by the outpouring of support from not only New Yorkers, but people throughout the world who heard about the feeding operation and were moved.
"I have these pictures that were sent to me from a class where the children, they drew cartoons," he recalled. "They said like, 'Keep going. You're doing great.' You know, 'thank you for your efforts.'"
Murphy said that she is still emotional thinking back to the weeks after the attacks, but the memories of selfless New Yorkers always stand out.
"New York is strong, New Yorkers are strong," she said.
Pintabona agreed and said for him it all came back to that floating dictionary page and that push to persevere.
"You have to turn the page and stay on the positive side. So that's kind of what I've learned through this experience," he said.

title: Woolly dog pelt returns to Coast Salish territory for the first time
content:
Woolly dog pelt returns to Coast Salish territory for the first time
The only surviving woolly dog pelt tells a story of vibrant cultural values
His name was Mutton. Although he died in 1859 at the tender age of 18 months, Mutton is a survivor who has returned to his ancestral territory to be studied, and welcomed with respect by Coast Salish artisans and community members.
Mutton, a woolly dog, whose hair was used in Salish and Makah weaving, was the companion of naturalist and ethnographer George Gibbs, who worked on the Northwest Boundary Survey in the 19th century.
Mutton’s pelt, the only surviving pelt of the woolly dog, is on loan to the Museum of Anthropology at the University of B.C. from the Smithsonian Institution until August 2027.
In his field notes, Gibbs recorded that Mutton grew ill and died around 1859. Those notes, and the pelt, along with other wildlife specimens, were sent to the Smithsonian at the end of the expedition Gibbs was part of. The pelt was carefully preserved, but lay forgotten in a drawer until it was rediscovered around the year 2000.
Jordan Wilson, curator of Pacific Northwest and Contemporary Indigenous Art at the Museum of Anthropology, unveiled the pelt on Tuesday, after local Indigenous community members had time to visit and spend time with their returning canine ancestor.
The woolly dog, which has a fox-like face and a brown button nose, appears in rare historical photographs, in sketches by artist Paul Kane, and on woven Skokomish/Twana baskets. But the breed itself vanished some time around the late 1800s.
Stories of a fluffy, white dog whose soft fur was sheared and collected like wool to be used in traditional weaving, have been passed down through oral traditions by Coast Salish community members for over 100 years since its disappearance.
“This is the only existing pelt of a now-extinct breed of dog that was once selectively bred here in the Coast Salish region and the neighbouring territories of the Interior Salish and the Makah people. Our ancestors bred these dogs for their fur to be used in weavings, robes and other textiles,” said Wilson.
“Early historical accounts from Capt. George Vancouver and Simon Fraser make reference to Indigenous peoples travelling in canoes with woolly dogs, so we have a sense that the dogs travelled with our ancestors as they moved throughout their respective territories,” said Wilson.
The pooches were kept separate from other village dogs so their beautiful pelts would not be compromised by cross-breeding to preserve the integrity of their fleece. “There was a very selective breeding process that ensured the quality of the fur,” said Wilson.
According to a study published in the research journal Science in 2023 after Mutton’s genome was sequenced, the dogs had a distinctive curly undercoat. They were pampered, regarded as “people,” “relatives” and members of the family, loved and cared for, combed, and fed a special diet of salmon.
Genomic testing on Mutton and other breeds from Coast Salish territories show that woolly dogs were present for at least 5,000 years before European colonization, possibly up to 15,000 years.
The woolly dogs were much more than companions. Their cloud-like hair was spun and woven into traditional blankets, supplementing other materials such as waterfowl down and fluff from plants like cattails and fireweed.
According to Debra Sparrow, a Musqueam master weaver, her grandfather Ed Sparrow told her that, “Every village had (woolly dogs), that they were like gold because they were mixed with the mountain goat and then rove and spun.”
“Research is still ongoing doing testing on existing Salish blankets and other weavings,” said Wilson.
Settler colonialism impacted the way of life that protected these pups, including the management of their breed. They did not survive the social conflicts and cultural interruptions that came with the Gold Rush, the establishment of the Indian Act, the potlatch ban, and assimilation.
The significance of this pelt isn’t just about the extinction of a species, said Wilson. “It also speaks to the lives of our ancestors, their relationship with the more-than-human world, and their teachings and knowledge that continue to be passed forward.”

title: Cinta muestra la conexión entre un corredor rarámuri y Antonin Artaud
content:
Martes 8 de septiembre de 2026, p. 7
Los sueños como puentes que unen a dos diferentes culturas son el tema principal en la filmografía del mexicano Federico Cecchetti, quien en su cinta titulada Jíkuri: Viaje al país de los tarahumaras, muestra la conexión que tienen un corredor rarámuri y un poeta francés.
La película narra la visión del dramaturgo y director escénico Antonin Artaud, asombrado con los rituales rarámuris y la experiencia de un corredor de la comunidad, quien crea un lazo espiritual con el también poeta.
Artaud hizo un viaje a la sierra tarahumara en 1936 para conocer los usos del jíkuri, que en la cultura rarámuri es el nombre sagrado que se le da al cactus del peyote, cuya experiencia describió en el libro D’un voyage au Pays des Tarahumaras (Viaje al país de los tarahumaras).
“Tras leer el libro, me identifiqué mucho con Artaud y su historia: cómo fue a buscar la esencia del arte y el teatro que, según él, estaba ligada con los ritos de las culturas originarias. Ya tenía experiencia con los wixáritari en una película. Me había acercado mucho al chamanismo y los sueños; cuando leí el libro, me pareció brutal.
“Al pueblo se le llama de dos formas, hago el paréntesis porque es importante decir que para ellos la palabra correcta es rarámuri, pero yo lo dejé tal y como se nombra en el libro: tarahumaras”, explicó el director Federico Ceccheti en entrevista con La Jornada.
El filme se estrenará en salas mexicanas el 17 de septiembre, en el contexto del 90 aniversario de la visita que hizo Artaud al país y los 130 años de su nacimiento en Marsella.
En su recorrido, la cinta formó parte de la Competencia Mezcal de la edición 39 del Festival Internacional de Cine en Guadalajara y en la selección oficial de ficmonterrey 20, en 2024.
“He tenido muchas experiencias con el jíkuri: primero con amigos en plan desmadroso. También lo probé en las peregrinaciones con los wixáritari, curiosamente ahora con los tarahumaras o rarámuris lo tratan de una manera muy diferente, como un ritual supersagrado; para la gran mayoría de ellos es un ritual casi satánico.
“En la sierra si hablas del jíkuri es como una palabra prohibida que asocian con el diablo; son muy pocos los chamanes que lo siguen, es un ritual que está prácticamente extinto, muy pocos lo conocen, pero es un espíritu y maestro que te puede otorgar muchos dones, pero si no sigues sus reglas, te puede robar el alma.
“Cuando hacen su ritual, casi no lo consumen, lo importante es que el cactus esté presente en la danza y ellos entran en trance solamente al bailar con los cantos del chamán. Así están toda la noche, invocando al espíritu, pero sin comer la planta.
“Hasta el final de la ceremonia se dividen el jíkuri, hacen una agüita, lo disuelven y entre todos se lo beben, pero es una microdosis la que consumen”, compartió Cecchetti.
Grandes personajes
La cinta es producida por Machete Films y está protagonizada por el actor francés François Negret y el corredor rarámuri José Cruz Apachoachi, además de pobladores de esa comunidad en Chihuahua. “Los dos fueron grandes personajes. François Negret parece la encarnación de Artaud, un actor superintenso que lleva todo al límite.
“Traía esa intensidad en su ADN. Cuando lo contacté, me confesó que siempre había querido interpretar al poeta francés, fue el mejor Artaud que pudimos haber elegido. José Cruz Apachoachi, el protagonista rarámuri, tiene carisma y un corazón enorme, se da a querer muy fácilmente y creo que la cámara lo quiso mucho, desde su sonrisa y mirada.
“Los actores tienen códigos de vida completamente opuestos, fue como hacer la encarnación del viaje que vivió Artaud, que fue una colisión y que poco a poco se entretejió y se convirtió en esta colaboración y en este aprendizaje, hubo escenas que nos costó mucho trabajo hacer.
“Conforme avanza la historia, crece una confrontación entre ellos y en el set realmente se dio. Esto nos enriqueció mucho”, agregó el cineasta.
El largometraje es la segunda entrega de la trilogía que concibió Cecchetti sobre las culturas originarias del país. La primera fue El sueño del Mara’akame (2016), que aborda la historia de un joven que quiere convertirse en músico y con la cual obtuvo un premio Ariel por ópera prima, categoría en que también ganó en el Festival Internacional de Cine de Morelia en 2017.
Cecchetti estudió dirección cinematográfica en el CUEC-UNAM y en el Centro Sperimentale di Cinematografia de Roma, Italia y recibió en dos ocasiones el apoyo del Fondo Nacional para la Cultura y las Artes.
“Es clara la continuidad entre El sueño del Mara’akame y Jíkuri..., son muy distintas, pero nacen de esta curiosidad de encontrar la mística de las comunidades originarias. Ambas películas tienen en común el jíkuri. “Si bien la manera cómo ritualizan la planta es diferente, también la unen con los sueños, que es uno de mis temas principales, y para las dos culturas tienen un gran peso, lo mismo que para el surrealismo, por eso en la cinta el puente que se crea entre rarámuris y Artaud es por medio de este ambiente onírico”, finalizó el director.

title: Opinion: On Sept. 11, the memorial ceremony at Peace Arch reminds us that some things rise above borders
content:
Opinion: On Sept. 11, the memorial ceremony at Peace Arch reminds us that some things rise above borders
Opinion: Canadians and Americans gather at the annual ceremony to honour those who answered the call, support those who continue to serve, and demonstrate that some values transcend borders
On Sept. 11, 2001, the world changed forever. Like millions of people, we watched in disbelief when we learned that thousands of innocent lives had been taken in acts of unimaginable violence. We watched in disbelief as first responders rushed toward danger while others fled. Many never came home.
Twenty-five years later, those memories remain vivid. But equally enduring is something else: the extraordinary spirit of service, courage and unity that emerged in the days, weeks and years that followed.
That is why Canadians and Americans gather beneath the Peace Arch to remember.
The annual Northwest 9/11 Memorial Ceremony has never simply been about looking back. It is about honouring those who answered the call, supporting those who continue to serve, and demonstrating that some values transcend borders.
This year marks the 25th anniversary of 9/11, and that milestone carries particular significance.
A generation has grown up with no personal memory of Sept. 11. Many of the young police officers, firefighters and paramedics attending our ceremony were children, or not yet born, when the attacks occurred. Yet they understand the responsibility they have inherited: to remember those who came before them and to uphold the ideals of public service, sacrifice and courage.
This year’s ceremony will be especially meaningful as we welcome four first responders who served in New York City on Sept. 11, 2001. Their presence reminds us that history is not confined to books or documentaries. It lives in the experiences of those who answered the call that day and in the commitment they continue to demonstrate decades later.
Their stories are deeply personal, but they also belong to all of us.
Over the years, this ceremony has grown into far more than an annual commemoration. It has become a gathering of communities, agencies and individuals who understand that service knows no borders. Canadian and American first responders work together every day. Border officials cooperate to protect our shared communities. Military personnel train alongside one another. These partnerships endure because challenges do not stop at the border, and neither does the willingness to help.
This year, that message carries added significance. Canada and the United States are experiencing a period of heightened economic and political tension, with trade talks having broken down and disagreements testing a relationship that has long been among the closest in the world. Those differences are real, and their consequences matter to people and communities on both sides of the border.
But moments of disagreement can also remind us of what should never be lost. The relationship between Canadians and Americans has always been about more than governments, trade agreements or the political issue of the day. It has been built over generations by neighbours, families, communities and people who have repeatedly stood together when it mattered most.
When police officers from Vancouver stand beside retired members of the New York Police Department, when firefighters from British Columbia honour colleagues from the FDNY, and when border officers from both nations stand shoulder to shoulder beneath the Peace Arch, they demonstrate something profoundly hopeful: friendship, cooperation and shared purpose endure.
That message is every bit as important today as it was 25 years ago.
Guy Morall is founder of the annual 9/11 Memorial Ride in B.C. Henry Hollander is a retired deputy chief, North Whatcom Washington Fire and Rescue. Cody Stamberger is from the Ferndale Washington Fire and Rescue. Tim Armstrong is a retired chief, New Westminster B.C. Fire Service. Howard Blank is a Vancouver-based entertainment executive and philanthropist.
More than 400 first responders, military and border services personnel, public officials and members of the public are expected to gather beneath the iconic Peace Arch at the Canada-U.S. border, at 11 a.m. on Friday, Sept. 11 for the Northwest 9/11 Memorial Ceremony.

title: A family of seven, a photograph we found in Nepal: Their story
content:
If destruction had a colour in Nepal, it would be the colour of mud. The muddy Trishuli that crashed down on homes and people, the buildings torn apart and caked with mud all the way up to the fourth floor, the trees with their exposed roots choked with shredded and clumped clothes, all covered in mud. And then, a dash of colour — a family of seven staring out of a photograph, smiling, joyous.
We found the photograph at the foot of a tree. It was the only sign of life in Betrawati, a village around 80 km north of Kathmandu that was among the hardest hit by the flash floods that struck the country on August 26. Most people here were either on the list of the dead or missing, or had left for relief camps or the homes of their relatives in the higher reaches. We took photographs of that moment and moved on.
The smiles in the photograph stayed. It’s the only time since we arrived that we had seen smiles that weren’t wistful or painful. The questions remained, too. Who could the family be? Were they still together? Had time, and distances, done what they do to relationships? Had the flood separated them? Where were the children? The ones in the foreground, in the red and blue dresses, with matching hair-bands? The matriarch in the back row?
The date on the photograph said July 1, 2009. There was little to go by.
⠀
The search for a family of seven
Four days later, we returned to Betrawati to look for the family.
A two-wheeler ride on the highway that usually takes less than two hours from Kathmandu took us more than six hours, as our SUV lumbered through backcountry trails of mud and stones, weaving through forests and mountain routes.
Betrawati, a village split between Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts in central Nepal, stands on the confluence of the mighty Trishuli and the gentler Falakhu river. It is home to the Uttar Gaya temple, a holy pilgrimage site for people from Nepal and India. The historical 1792 Treaty of Betrawati, which ended the war between Nepal’s Gorkha Kingdom and China’s Qing Dynasty, was signed here.
Story continues below this ad
Little had changed at Betrawati since our last visit. Only a few buildings stood in what seemed like a vast ocean of mud. Remnants of life had been washed up onto the terrace fields where villagers once grew maize and paddy — mangled trees, a school bag, a stray slipper, pillow covers, a mannequin. An auto rickshaw was lodged precariously high on one of the trees that still stood, its twisted canopy holding the vehicle along with boulders and large portions of concrete walls. A school bus now stood nose-down in the mud.
Visuals of a school bus swept away after the Nepal flash floods (Express photo by Tashi Tobgyal)
An eerie silence had settled over what was once a bustling pilgrimage destination. Only the hiss of the muddied river as it flowed nearby, and the muffled conversations of the few police personnel on duty with their sniffer dogs, hoping to find signs of life in the rubble. The only other people were those looking for their family members. They walked around with heads lowered, eyes scanning the slush and the debris. Like us, all of them held a photograph or two, asking anyone they encountered if they had seen the people they were looking for.
According to Nepal’s Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, as of September 8, 5,326 people remain missing since the floods, and 1,357 are confirmed dead.
Chini Maya Thapar Magar’s house, on the side of the Bhote Koshi river in Rasuwa district (Express photo by Tashi Tobgyal)
On the road leading to the village, we waved down a few cars and motorbikes and asked about the photo, but got no leads. Enquiries at a few open shops yielded no results. Then, someone suggested that we go to the relief camp a little down the hill, where some villagers had taken shelter.
Story continues below this ad
The camp, with a dozen blue and green tents, had been set up by Chinese relief organisations on what used to be paddy terrace fields. It now sheltered around 70 people who had fled from neighbouring villages.
We approached a group of older men sitting in a circle and smoking. They shook their heads as they passed around the photograph we had printed. Our hopes sank. As we were making our way out, stopping every now and then with the photograph, someone exclaimed from behind, “Chini Maya.”
Social worker Ishwar Thapa Magar, 40, it turned out, was a relative of the family. Taking a closer look at the photograph and pointing to the elderly woman in the back row, Magar said, “This is Chini Maya.”
The photograph suddenly came alive. China Maya Thapar Magar, then 51, shared the frame with her daughter Srijana, son Nirmal, daughter-in-law Sunita, granddaughters Sakshi, 10, and Samriddhi, 8, and a relative’s baby.
Story continues below this ad
Everyone was safe, it turned out. Except Chini Maya. She was missing.


(Google Street View of China Maya’s house before the floods)
A festival, and a group photo
At a cafe in Tokha, on the outskirts of Kathmandu, Chini Maya’s granddaughter Samriddhi, now 25, says, “My grandmother hung this photograph on the wall by her bed. I remember the day it was taken.”
October 9, 2009, was a busy day at Chini Maya Thapar Magar’s house, which stood on the other side of the Trishuli river in Rasuwa district. It was the festival of Dashain, one of the biggest festivals in Nepal, a variation of the Dussehra celebrations in India. Her son Nirmal Pyakurel and his family had come down from Kathmandu to celebrate the festival.
Story continues below this ad
The women were racing against time for the morning puja. Srijana, Chini Maya’s daughter, then unmarried, and daughter-in-law Sunita were cleaning and decorating the house, while Chini Maya supervised a simmering pot of khasi ko masu (goat curry). Sakshi, in a blue Chinese silk dress, and Samriddhi, in a blood red one, had got into a fight over their eyeliners.
Everyone was in their best clothes, except Chini Maya, who was still fussing over the khasi curry. An uncle asked them to assemble for a group photo. Nirmal wore a pair of sunglasses, and Srijana put a strand of gajra in her hair. Sakshi and Samriddhi ended their fight just in time and managed to smile.
Chini Maya, still in her nightie, picked up Siyana, a relative’s child whose family was visiting them. The family assembled on the street outside their house and the uncle clicked the photo on a cybershot camera. The camera, however, got the date wrong: 1.7.2009, said the photo when it was finally printed.
Afterwards, the families of Chini Maya’s sisters as well as other relatives and friends came over, and everyone had a good time eating goat curry, drinking Chini Maya’s home-brewed raksi, and playing rounds of the card game teen patti.
Story continues below this ad
At the camp in Betrawati, 60-year-old Dil Bahadur Magar, who is from the nearby village of Kuvindi, says Chini Maya’s father used to run the village flour mill and the family had a prominent house.
“I remember going to their house to get our grains cleaned and sifted,” says Dil Bahadur.
The family had eight daughters, so the girls, including Chini Maya, “grew up like boys”. Chini Maya, the third of the siblings, never went to school, but learnt to be useful around the house, cutting grass for the cattle and collecting firewood.
She married at 21, but her marriage didn’t last. She later built a three-storeyed house by the river and ran small businesses — a utensils shop on the ground floor and rooms for rent on another floor. She would generously hand out her home-brewed raksi, but also sold some part of it.
Story continues below this ad
Chini Maya’s granddaughter Samriddhi says she has always known her grandmother and her sisters to be fiercely independent — “at times, even aggressive”.
She recalls an incident from the 2000s, when the country was under Maoist rule. “Soldiers used to bully villagers a lot those days. Once, at a weekly market in our village, my grandmother got furious when she saw a soldier hitting a villager, so she chased him across the bridge, entered the bus he had fled into, brought him out and thrashed him in public, before the villagers calmed her,” says Samriddhi, who works as a Class 3 teacher while also pursuing a postgraduate degree in sociology.
Social worker Ishwar Thapa Magar with the photo (Express photo by Tashi Tobgyal)
Samriddhi’s mother Sunita, who lives in Japan with her elder daughter Sakshi, spoke to The Indian Express from Tochigi prefecture about how Chini Maya’s house in Betrawati was a huge draw.
“All her children and grandchildren, as well as her sisters and their families, used to gather at her place during festivals. Local politicians would come to her house to eat the fish she cooked and discuss village matters. Her house was where everything happened since it was so large and she loved cooking for everyone,” says Sunita Onta Shreshtha of her mother-in-law.
Story continues below this ad
In 2017, Sunita, her husband Nirmal and elder daughter Sakshi, moved to Japan, where they did a series of odd jobs. Two years later, she says, Nirmal moved back to Betrawati to take care of his mother Chini Maya. Sakshi, now 27, works as a tattoo artist in Japan.
Talking to The Indian Express from her home in Jackson Heights, New York, Chini Maya’s daughter Srijana Deuja, now 40, says her mother and the rest of the family shared a special relationship with the Falakhu river that’s barely 100 metres from the house.
“When Sakshi and Samriddhi were young and came visiting from Kathmandu, they would spend all their time by the river, swimming and making mud houses on the banks,” says Srijana, who works in a beauty salon.
Samriddhi remembers those holidays by the river fondly. “It used to flood then too, but we were never scared. Floods just meant more fish to catch and cook,” she says.
Samriddhi says she has always known her grandmother and her sisters to be fiercely independent (Express photo by Tashi Tobgyal)
The day of the flood, and afterwards
Days before the August 26 flood, five of Chini Maya’s sisters had come to Betrawati for the festival of Gain Jatra.
That day, Chini Maya’s nephew called from Kathmandu and alerted the family of a massive flood that was coming their way. The nephew once worked at a hydropower project, so he knew what he was talking about. Chini Maya hung up, shouted out to her son Nirmal, who was on the floor below, and told him and the others to run. Nirmal ran out, believing his mother, aunts and their elderly domestic help were behind him.
Minutes later, a barrage of water and debris thundered down the Trishuli, surging into the Falakhu. Within minutes, the valley witnessed something unprecedented: a whirlpool of brown water, boulders, and debris, four storeys high, stood churning where the two rivers met.
When he finally reached higher ground, Nirmal looked around for the rest of the family. His mother and their help were missing.
Days later, Chini Maya’s house in the village, though battered, is among the few that still stand. The ground floor is buried under mud. The room on the first floor, where the fridge would always be stocked with her famous raksi, is now bare and knee-deep in mud. Only the ceiling fan, its wings twisted out of shape, remains. A mangled bike has made its way to the second floor, deposited there by the waves.
Days after the tragedy, with no trace of Chini Maya, the family had to make the difficult decision of carrying out her last rites. They had spent the last few days scouring websites with lists of survivors, the missing, and the unidentified dead.
Despite that, says Samriddhi, she hopes her grandmother will turn up one day at Betrawati, walk up to her house by the river. “When you called and asked about Chini Maya, I thought for a minute that she had been found,” she tells us.
Samriddhi says Chini Maya knew the river better than most people. “She used to say, ‘Dui phan ma khola paari pugchu (In two jumps, I’ll cross the river).’ She would also say, ‘Moh maareyo bhani, khola ma morchu (When I die, the river will take me).”

title: ‘Always kind, never argued’: Colleagues on Manipur musician killed in Delhi
content:
Chongtham Vikram Singh grew up in a family steeped in music. His mother Chongtham Kamala, now 85, is one of the defining voices of Manipuri music and cinema. She sang in Matamgi Manipur (1972) — the first Manipuri feature film in which her melodious voice earned her the moniker ‘Lata Mangeshkar of Manipur’.
But Singh set out to build a musical identity of his own and chose the electric guitar to find himself. He went on to become a pioneering guitarist of Manipur’s early rock scene.
Beaten to death in Delhi’s Kilokari village after objecting to a group making noise outside his residence on Monday, the 54-year-old leaves behind a significant musical career that ranged from Manipur’s early Western music scene to years spent teaching and mentoring young musicians in the Capital.
Those who have worked with him – from guitarist Sachidananda Angom to folk musician Mame Khan of Coke Studio India fame – remember him as someone who was “always kind, helpful” and who “never had arguments with anyone.”
Singh is survived by his wife, Joshna, 54, and their son Yaiphaba. The 20-year-old is a law student.
On Tuesday, fellow musicians, family members and well-wishers held a candlelight vigil at the historic Kangla fort in Imphal, demanding justice.
Manipur Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh, in a letter to his Delhi counterpart Rekha Gupta, requested that a fair probe be conducted under the direct supervision of senior police leadership. The Manipur CM also asked for reinforced security measures across Delhi localities with significant populations of students and working professionals from Manipur and other northeastern states.
Story continues below this ad
Originally from Lourung Purel Leikai in Imphal West district, Singh was the eldest son of Kamla and Chongtham Birendra, a medical doctor. A calm Kamla, sitting quietly at the family home, told The Indian Express, “Vikram (Singh) and his brother Vivek always loved to perform as kids. They always participated in school entertainment events.”
Even as he forged a separate path for himself, Singh, for years, accompanied his mother to the radio station – she had gained immense popularity as a broadcast singer at All India Radio (AIR), Imphal – regularly for recordings. The experience left a lasting impression on him. Singh auditioned, too, and was also approved as a child artist at AIR. He would play the accordion then.
“Since his mother was associated with AIR Imphal, he got to meet some of the most significant artistes in Manipur and learned under the tutelage of renowned names,” says Angom, former lead guitarist of well-known band Imphal Talkies and The Howlers.
Singh began as the lead guitarist of famous Manipur band Ultra Vires formed in the late ’80s. He had just finished his class X then. This was a time when rock music was at its peak in the state and Singh immersed himself in the sound. To hone his skills further, he later enrolled at Trinity School of Music in Kolkata, where he studied classical guitar.
Story continues below this ad
He then went on to play with Phoenix (later Phynyx) and then Eastern Dark, remembered for its socially conscious themes. Singh is remembered by his friends and colleagues for his fine, highly skilled guitar playing. Almost two decades ago, Singh moved to Delhi and began giving lessons in electric guitar. This is when Angom became his student.
‘He could really light up a room’
“He would also come down to the studio for the recording of various Imphal Talkies albums. We would often do these informal jam sessions. He was a really good guitarist and, as a person, one of the nicest guys you would ever meet. He was always kind, helpful and could really light up a room. It (his death) is a terrible loss,” said Angom.
When Singh came to Delhi, he began by teaching at Arttree Academy of Music & Performing Arts in Kamla Nagar. Classical guitar instructor Tej Gurung, who teaches at Delhi School of Music, met Singh at Arttree, where the two became colleagues and friends. “He taught electric guitar; I taught classical guitar. He was a wonderful person, the sweetest guy and also a brilliant guitar player. He’s got to be super famous in Manipur because he was very good,” says Gurung.
After a while, Gurung introduced him to Hitesh Madaan, the guitarist for Euphoria — the popular folk rock band formed by Palash Sen in 1988. Soon, Singh began teaching at Madan’s ARIA music school in Rajouri Garden. What was unique about Singh was that teaching, like it is for many musicians, was not a part-time job for him; he really enjoyed helping younger musicians find their own way around the guitar. He also mentored students at home.
Story continues below this ad
Alongside his teaching career, Singh continued playing with various musicians, including Delhi-based classic rock and jazz band Fubar Ghetto. For about three years, he worked as a lead guitarist for Khan, who sang in Zoya Akhtar’s Luck By Chance (2009) and does regular international tours.
“It was very heartbreaking to hear about the passing of Vikram – a really kind and lovely person. Playback singer Chinmayi (Sripada) recommended him to me and he played with me until 2016. I also featured him in two of my videos. We did numerous shows together. A hugely talented person and the favourite artiste of my band, he never had arguments with anyone and was always good to others, besides being a musically brilliant artiste. I don’t understand how some people could behave this way with him. It is just really sad,” Khan told The Indian Express.

title: Back-to-school rituals that help these families calm first-day jitters
content:
This week, Libby Barnicke and her family will engage in what has become, for them, an important tradition. She’ll dress up her two boys in their crisp new school uniforms and line them up on the front porch for their annual back-to-school photo.
It’s a tradition that is replicated in households from coast to coast. For many families, these early weeks of September are a major occasion. The end of summer, and the start of a new year.
“I always view September as the new year. Not January first,” said Ms. Barnicke, who lives in Toronto. “It feels like the beginning. Like a renewal. It’s excitement, but also a lot of anxiousness.”
It’s a month that brings new milestones in many families. The start of a new routine, or adventure, or challenge. A new step toward independence. For many, it will be their first day in a new place.
The Globe and Mail spoke with four families experiencing “first days” this week. Here’s what they told us about how they feel, and how they’re preparing:
First day of kindergarten: Aadhya Trivedi, 4 years old
Aadhya is a chatty preschooler who lives in Toronto with her family. She knows how to spell her own name, and how to count to four fingers when asked her age. She likes rainbow-coloured tutus, chapatis with curried vegetables and reading books with her mom. When she grows up, she plans on being a doctor and also a princess.
What she’s most excited about
Aadhya’s older brother already attends the school where she’s headed, so he’s given her some ideas on what to expect.
“Kindergarten,” she said, “is where you help your teachers. Cleaning. Putting books away. Sitting in the circle.”
She’s most excited to see the school library, which her brother has described in great detail. She can’t wait to pick out her own books and bring them home.
What she’s worried about
Aadhya will miss the comforts of daycare. “The teachers love me a lot. I love my teachers a lot.”
She’ll miss her daycare friends, too. “I love my friends,” she said. “We hug with each other and hold each other’s hands.”
She’ll be parting ways with almost all of them. Most are heading off to a different school, so she’ll have to make new friends. When asked if this makes her nervous, she gives the tiniest nod.
“The new friends might hate me, and might not love me,” she said. “They might not want to be best friends with me.”
How the family is preparing
“She’s already been in the daycare setting, so the routine is kind of the same,” said her mom, Sonali. They’ve been working as a family to drill the importance of that morning routine in to their children: Of waking up by a specific time and leaving plenty of room each morning to get ready and out the door without feeling rushed.
Beyond that, Sonali said she’s been focused on preparing Aadhya for the practical challenges of kindergarten such as how to get through a full day without an afternoon nap, how to recognize her own name at her cubby and how to tell the difference between her stuff and all the other kids’, which often look similar.
Aadhya is also practicing how to open and close her own lunch bag and food containers. It’ll be her first time bringing lunch from home, and she’ll have to figure out how to navigate that. “It’s all about keeping things simple and accessible,” said Sonali.
First day rituals
Each year, Sonali asks family and friends to send in short video messages for the kids with their well-wishes for the new school year. She compiles all of them into a larger video that the family watches the night before school. They make popcorn, settle into the couch and make a night of it.
“It’s a tradition that we all look forward to,” Sonali said.
The transition from summer to a new school year is always an anxious, nerve-wracking time. “And, honestly not just for the kids,” she said.
“It’s emotional for the parents too – seeing your babies going out into the world.”
First day of middle school: Taylor, 12
Until recently, Taylor attended a co-ed, public Catholic school in Toronto, where he lives with his family. But this week he is moving to an all-boys, private middle school that is connected to a high school. So he’ll be sharing the halls for the first time with kids who are much older, ranging from Grade 7 all the way up to Grade 12.
What he’s most excited about
Taylor is an athlete who plays soccer, football and hockey. “Any sport, basically.” So he’s looking forward to the new sports and activities available.
“It’s a lot bigger than my [former] school, so there’s lots of different types of activities and clubs,” he said. “It’s just a totally different environment.”
He’s also looking forward to the fact that he’ll be joined by many of his existing friends who are moving to the new school alongside him.
What he’s most worried about
“Probably the exams.” The curriculum in middle school, he expects, will be much more intense.
How they’re preparing
This week will represent a big step into independence for Taylor, said his mom Libby. Instead of getting dropped off and picked up by his parents each day, he’ll be responsible for getting himself to and from school.
For the first time, Taylor will have to navigate public transit on his own. He’ll also have to figure out where to buy his snacks after school, and how to pay for them. The family is having to discuss, for the first time, questions such as whether he’s ready for a debit card or a cellphone.
“It’s a change in tide,” said Libby. “We’re having meaningful conversations about what the new routine is going to look like – early adult conversations, I would say.”
Back to school rituals
This will be the seventh year that Libby has lined up her boys for their back-to-school photo (they missed one year because of the pandemic). “It’s just always been a marker for me to show the progress – to show just how big they’re getting.”
Still, beyond the anxiety and the nerves, she said, there’s a lot of excitement.
“I think there’s something very joyful about coming of age, and moving on,” she said. “I just can’t wait to see what he does with this next chapter.”
First day of high school: Arshia Purohit Singh, 13
At first glance, Arshia seems like a typical Vancouver teenager. She likes sushi and swimming, music by Olivia Rodrigo and Sabrina Carpenter and books from the popular ‘Powerless’ YA series by Lauren Roberts.
But, if you spend just a minute talking to her, it’s clear that she’s no ordinary kid. Arshia was the valedictorian at her elementary school and runs her own small business online. She organizes fundraisers for the local children’s hospital and intends to be a lawyer one day – after graduating from Harvard Law School, of course.
She’s made the difficult decision to attend a different high school (which, in her Vancouver school district, is grades eight through 12) than all of her friends. She’s opting instead for a school with an International Baccalaureate program, which she considers more academically challenging.
What she’s most excited about
Arshia is looking forward to the idea of a challenge. Of more intense classes, and the chance to join the basketball team, the debate club and the students’ council.
“I’m definitely feeling a little bit nervous, but I’m also just really excited for all the new opportunities and all the new people I’m going to meet.”
She’s excited, too, about having a bit more freedom.
“In elementary school, it’s a lot more structured. We were kind of taken to every class, things like that. But in high school, they’ll tell us to go to our different classes, and then it’s just entirely up to us.”
How the family is preparing
The family is big on organization and building good habits. Ever since they were little, Arshia’s mom Sophia Purohit Singh has taught her two kids how to balance their own schedules and make sure they’re staying on top of deadlines.
“The habits were developed way early on, where it was always about keeping yourself busy and organized. Having your own calendar and managing it,” said Sophia. “So there’s not time left over to go on their phone for hours.”
They’ve doubled down on this routine over the summer. Entirely of her own accord, Arshia has been working ahead on her math workbooks (“just to be ready for next year”), and has been talking through with her parents how she might juggle her many new assignments and responsibilities in high school.
Back-to-school rituals
Every year, the family spends at least one day combing through the house to see what school supplies they’ve left lying around.
“It’s stuff we’ve collected over the year, and figuring out how to reuse them,” said Arshia. And then they’ll go back-to-school shopping for everything else.
Back-to-school outfits, said Arshia, “are definitely still a thing.” For her first day of high school, she chose her outfit in advance: A new skirt she bought recently, with a t-shirt and hoodie, in case of cold. “I’m just going to wear what makes me comfortable,” she said.
She knows this is an important moment for her.
“This is kind of a big point of change in my life,” she said. “In a few years, my life is going to change a lot.”
First day of teaching: Nick Erickson, 41
Over the past few decades, Mr. Erickson has been a sawmill worker, a concrete labourer and a logging truck driver. But this week, the father of five from Lake Babine Nation in B.C. will take on a new career: A high-school teacher.
He’s a new graduate of NITEP, the Indigenous Teacher Education Program at the University of British Columbia, where, after going back to school in his late 30s, he recently graduated with a bachelor’s degree in education. He’ll be teaching a small group of Indigenous students, grades eight through 12, at a high school in his community.
“My goal is to give Indigenous students the confidence to go on to bigger and better things. To show them they’re capable,” he said.
“If I can do it at the age of 41, there’s no reason why anybody else can’t do it.”
What he’s excited about
Mr. Erickson can only recall ever having one Indigenous teacher when he was growing up. “It was the only classroom where I felt like I wasn’t really being judged,” he said. Now, he’s excited to be that positive role model for his own students.
“I have a lot of life stories. I’ve had a lot of things happen in my life that I can relate with the kids.”
Plus, as the father of five daughters (who range in age from eight to 25), he has ample confidence and experience in dealing with teenagers.
As a teacher, he said, he won’t be “Mr. Erickson.” Just “Nick.”
“I want to help them and teach them,” he said. “But I also want to learn beside them.”
One more bonus? His wife, Marsha Erickson, completed the NITEP program alongside him. They’ll be sharing this experience as first-time teachers in the community together.
What he’s worried about
“I’m kind of nervous. I’m responsible for these kids. But if I’m my genuine, authentic self, I’m not going to have any problems. I’m just going to be the best person I can in front of them.”
Back-to-school rituals
Each year, the couple has taken back-to-school pictures of their five kids on the deck in front of the house. This year they’ll take photos again – only this time, with the addition of mom and dad.

title: Rare hide from extinct woolly dog bred by B.C. First Nations is on display
content:
After more than 160 years in storage at the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, the only known pelt of an extinct woolly dog is back on Canada’s West Coast.
Woolly dogs were once abundant, bred by Salish and Makah peoples along the Pacific coast for their soft, woolly fur, which was woven into clothing, blankets and robes, according to the Museum of Anthropology at the University of British Columbia.
They had fluffy light-coloured coats, curled tails and pointy, fox-like faces, similar to a Samoyed, only smaller. They were occasionally shorn for their coats, which were often combined with mountain goat hair and the fibres of plants to make a strong, warm wool. They were considered extinct by the late 1800s, according to UBC, though one was photographed in the 1930s.
Now, the only known pelt in existence is on display at the Museum of Anthropology at UBC until September, 2027, on loan from the Smithsonian.
When Atheana Picha first laid eyes on it Friday morning during a special private event for the Indigenous community, emotion welled in her throat. She’d grown up hearing stories of woolly dogs passed down through generations.
“The woolly dogs were a big part of our family life,” Ms. Picha said. “Having met this relative now, who left us 200 years ago, is pretty powerful.”
For generations before European contact, textiles such as robes and blankets that included woolly dog fur were considered prized possessions, and used sparingly to mark significant community milestones such as marriages and funerals.
While woolly dogs largely disappeared more than a century ago, knowledge of their importance was kept alive in Salish and Makah oral history and traditional weaving. Ms. Picha herself learned those stories, and now helps keep the tradition alive.
“When we see a weaving … it’s talking about whose territory we’re on, what history’s here,” she said.
Ms. Picha explained that Salish oral history describes how it was primarily women who cared for the woolly dogs, often keeping them isolated on small islands so they wouldn’t breed with other village dogs used for hunting. They were fed special diets to keep their coats healthy, and shorn about once a year for their fur.
After European contact, the practice of weaving remained an important trade tool for Salish people, but the introduction by settlers of industrially woven fabrics began to erode First Nations’ textile production.
It wasn’t long before colonial laws started banning many Indigenous cultural practices. Residential schools sought to erase Indigenous cultures altogether, said Jordan Wilson, the museum’s curator of Pacific Northwest and contemporary Indigenous art. The federal government’s decades-long potlatch ban, which barred First Nations from participating in traditional ceremonies, was particularly devastating, eroding a central hub for sharing cultural knowledge, he said.
In recent years, interest in woolly dogs and other traditional wool has grown as efforts to revive Salish weaving took off. Ms. Picha is a member of the Tsartlip First Nation on Vancouver Island, and learned traditional Salish weaving from master weaver Debra Sparrow of the Musqueam Nation. In the decades after European contact, the art of Salish weaving was nearly lost. Ms. Picha is part of a new generation of Salish women who are helping to bring it back, and having the chance to see a woolly dog’s fur up close, to feel its curl and texture, is invaluable, she said.
“Seeing the fibres on the pelt, they’re already twisting,” Ms. Picha said, tracing her finger over the pelt’s glass case. “They want to be spun. It’s just hungry to be turned into a blanket, turned into warmth.”
Indigenous repatriation is under way – but gaps remain in measuring progress
The pelt now on display in Vancouver is from a dog named Mutton, who was the companion of naturalist George Gibbs. Mr. Gibbs helped carry out land surveys establishing the Canada-U.S. border in the mid-19th century.
It’s not known exactly how Mr. Gibbs came to own Mutton, but Mutton is believed to have come from near present-day Chilliwack, B.C. Genetic research suggests Mutton lived to be about 18 months old. Mr. Gibbs sent the pelt to the Smithsonian along with other specimens from his time in Salish territory.
According to Mr. Wilson, the loan was made possible because of work by the Stó:lō House of Respect Caretaking Committee, a group of elders and knowledge-keepers from Stó:lō communities in the Fraser Valley and Fraser Canyon area. The group helped advocate for its temporary return.
Mr. Wilson is now part of the team responsible for caring for it. He first saw the pelt himself at the Smithsonian years ago, as part of his professional museum training. It’s one of the innumerable Indigenous cultural items removed from their homelands by settlers and sent to museums across the globe, separating the artifacts from their communities.
He said the opportunity to display the pelt close to its original home, even temporarily, is a major milestone.
“I think this is really important,” Mr. Wilson said.
It’s particularly special for the museum he works at. The Museum of Anthropology is usually focused on human creations and cultures, Mr. Wilson said. Western academia tends to view specimens such as Mutton’s pelt as natural history artifacts, not anthropological ones.
Earlier: Indigenous artifacts at Vatican Museums heading back to Canada after repatriation campaign
But Mr. Wilson said that sort of stark division between the human and natural realms isn’t how Indigenous people view the world, or themselves.
From a genetic science perspective, Mutton’s pelt represents the extinction of a unique breed, one of the many profound impacts of colonialism, he said. But from an anthropological perspective, it represents the generations-long sinew of Indigenous culture and history tying past to present.
“That really speaks to our ancestors’ connections to territory and place and the beyond-human world,” Mr. Wilson said.
Along with all that history, Ms. Picha sees a long-lost family member finally home for a visit.
“Looking at this pelt, I think of all the things that fed this dog to make it stronger,” Ms. Picha said. “I think of all the people that gave this dog a hug during its life, and all those people who fed it and petted it and saw so much joy.”
The pelt will be on display at the Museum of Anthropology on UBC’s campus until the end of August, 2027.

title: In Paash’s village, a fight over the space that keeps his memory alive
content:
Stay updated with the latest - Click here to follow us on Instagram
The words of Avtar Singh Sandhu, better known as Paash, have travelled far beyond Talwandi Salem, his birthplace in Jalandhar district. Nearly four decades after he was killed, his poetry continues to surface wherever people gather around democratic rights and resistance — at farmers’ protests, workers’ meetings, student gatherings and literary forums.
For generations of readers, Paash was not merely a poet who wrote about struggle; he was a poet who participated in it.
Ahead of his birth anniversary on September 9, however, his legacy has become the centre of a dispute in his native village. Tension erupted after the village panchayat allegedly tried to stop members of the Paash-Hans Raj Memorial Committee from erecting a pandal at an eponymous complex for the celebrations. Allegations of manhandling prompted the local administration to deploy police to prevent a confrontation.
The dispute centres around two kanals of land at the entrance of Talwandi Salem, where the Pash-Hans Raj Memorial has stood for 26 years. The committee says the land was allotted to it in 2000 through a written panchayat resolution. The panchayat, however, maintains that the land belongs to it.
The confrontation dates back to early August, when the Paash Memorial International Trust, the Paash-Hans Raj Shaheedi Yaadgar Committee and several unions approached the Nakodar SDM and local MLA with allegations of vandalism. According to their complaint, panchayat representatives broke the locks of the memorial gate. When the committee replaced them, one side of the gate was allegedly removed and panchayat representatives entered the premises and installed swings, pipes and open-gym equipment.
Local administrative officials initially maintained that the land belonged to the panchayat, while indicating that the matter was close to resolution. The dispute flared again when committee members arrived to prepare for Paash’s September 9 birth anniversary. A group led by sarpanch Pardeep Singh allegedly confronted them, including veteran activist Jhanda Singh Jethuke. Committee members alleged that some activists were pushed and that mobile phones were confiscated.
For villagers and Paash’s admirers, the confrontation has taken on a larger meaning. “It is a great disrespect to a great poet, and that too by the people and the panchayat of his own village,” said a local resident.
