title: Stitching the Future: Technology as a Sacred Trust
content:
Stitching the Future: Technology as a Sacred Trust
By grounding our digital strategy in the same values as our ancestors, we can ensure technology serves our school community rather than consuming it.
September 9, 2026
Paul McKinnon / Shutterstock
In an era where artificial intelligence promises to archive human culture at the touch of a button, Indigenous communities face a vital question: Who has the right to own, shape and digitize sacred knowledge?
Long before AI became a headline in education, this question fundamentally reshaped my work as the instructional technology coordinator at Indian Community School. But understanding how to protect our community’s digital future didn’t start in a computer lab; it began in a quiet valley in Wisconsin, with my grandmother’s unfinished quilt and a ribbon skirt workshop that changed everything I knew about knowledge itself.
I grew up in a small rural village tucked into Wisconsin’s Driftless Area, where winding roads disappear between steep bluffs and deep valleys, and every hill seems to reveal another breathtaking view. It was a place shaped not by glaciers, but by time. A landscape as rugged as it was beautiful.
It was also home to my grandmother — a strong cheesemaker’s wife who was, in some ways, the quintessential grandmother figure. She hosted Sunday family dinners, baked fresh bread, volunteered at the local food pantry and quilted with the other ladies from church twice a week. She also cursed like a sailor and wasn’t stingy with her love or hugs.
In my teen years, she became my shelter — a quiet refuge from a chaotic home and a reminder that love exists even in the hardest seasons. When I went away to college, she sent me away with a quilt made just for me, a special gift we all only receive once. As an adult, she became the reason we visited the Driftless Area and was the glue that kept our families together. During that time, she showed that love to my children, who adored her.
After a long stay in a nursing home and years of declining health, my grandmother passed away last year. After her passing, my twin sister and I discovered her last unfinished quilt tucked away in a forgotten storage bin. Her hands hadn’t been able to hold the material or work the sewing machine for a long time, and we thought all the quilts had been claimed. Finding one more, even unfinished, felt like a blessing.
Around the same time, my twin sister and I both signed up for a staff ribbon skirt class where members of the Indigenous community would teach us not only how to make ribbon skirts, but also share teachings about how to wear them respectfully and as true allies. Carrying pieces of our grandmother’s unfinished quilt with us, we set out to create ribbon skirts in her honor.
Before that class, I knew very little about ribbon skirts beyond seeing them worn at school celebrations and community events. I quickly learned they are not tied to a single tribe, but are worn by Indigenous women across many Nations, each with their own traditions, teachings and stories. I also learned that a ribbon skirt is much more than a beautiful piece of clothing. It represents identity, resilience, and the enduring strength of Indigenous women.
Today, communities across North America celebrate Ribbon Skirt Day each January, recognizing not only the skirts themselves, but the right of Indigenous people to wear them with pride after generations of policies that sought to erase their cultures.
What surprised me most was that our class wasn’t really about making skirts. It was about learning the responsibility that comes with them. We learned when it was appropriate to wear a ribbon skirt, what it meant to wear one as an ally, and why those teachings mattered as much as the sewing itself. Anyone can buy a ribbon skirt online, but creating one alongside community members who generously shared their knowledge transformed it into something entirely different. Every stitch became part of a relationship built on trust, respect and a willingness to learn.
That experience changed the way I thought about knowledge itself. I realized that some things are valuable not because they can be owned, bought, or preserved, but because they carry stories, relationships and responsibilities that extend far beyond any one individual. They belong to the communities that shaped them and to the generations who will inherit them.
The tension between owning knowledge and stewarding it sits at the very heart of my work as the instructional technology coordinator at Indian Community School. If knowledge is built on trust and community relationships, then technology cannot simply be an instrument to extract, scale, or monetize data. That conviction was tested in 2021, well before generative AI became a household conversation, when a company approached our language and culture department with an extraordinary proposal.
They offered innovation. A way to immortalize language and culture through “virtual ancestors” — artificial intelligence trained on the stories, voices, and wisdom of living tribal elders. As the instructional technology coordinator, I was initially excited about what an extraordinary opportunity it would be to place our school at the forefront of modern technology!
However, the more my colleagues and I analyzed the pitch, the more our excitement gave way to deep alarm. The offer was riddled with deep red flags: vague promises around intellectual property, zero accountability for data privacy and a predatory push to extract sacred community knowledge. But recognizing those red flags was only half the battle.
Facing a tool this complex also exposed the gaps in my own understanding of artificial intelligence at the time. I realized that properly vetting this proposal and ensuring our school’s technology program moved forward in a good, grounded way required more than just caution. It demanded that I build my own AI literacy so I could stand as an informed guardian for our community’s data.
That 2021 proposal became the catalyst for a journey that has defined my work ever since. Recognizing gaps in my own understanding, I immersed myself in AI literacy, digital ethics and Indigenous data sovereignty frameworks. As we start the 2026-27 school year, AI is no longer a distant possibility; it is actively shaping how stories are told, how knowledge is created and how data is harvested.
In response, my role has evolved from simply managing technology infrastructure to helping our school build an ethical digital sanctuary. We began facilitating professional development sessions that empower our teachers to critically evaluate AI tools through a lens of cultural safety and data privacy. In the classroom, we reaffirmed our dedication to active digital stewardship over passive consumption.
Rather than allowing third-party algorithms to dictate or summarize Native experiences, our students now engage in hands-on digital storytelling, learning how to protect their personal and cultural data while using modern tools to amplify their authentic voices on their own terms.
The core lesson I learned in that ribbon skirt class remains my guiding principle: technology, like knowledge, is only as valuable as the relationships and trust behind it. For educators, leaders, and communities navigating this fast-shifting landscape, maintaining agency over our stories requires asking hard questions before we ever sign a contract or adopt a tool:
- Who owns the data being used to train this system? In my school, we actively reject software platforms that do not explicitly provide full intellectual property rights to the school.
- Does this tool respect the sovereignty and living culture of the community it serves? I work with stakeholders to ensure that software and platforms do not train on student or staff data, and I prioritize tools with the least environmental impact.
- Are we adopting technology to enhance human relationships, or replace them? We prioritize tools that bring elders, teachers and students together in real-world dialogue, using technology as a bridge for connection rather than a substitute for human presence.
When my sister and I stitched pieces of our grandmother’s unfinished quilt into our ribbon skirts, we weren’t just preserving her memory; we were continuing a relationship rooted in love, honor and continuity. That is the true essence of stewardship. When we approach technological innovation not as a rush to extract the future, but as a solemn duty to protect what was handed down to us, we ensure that modern tools honor where we came from. In the age of AI, our responsibility remains unchanged: to stitch technology into the living fabric of our communities in a good way, ensuring our stories remain whole, authentic and undeniably our own.

title: A Homeland Remembered: Crimean Tatars and the Question of Indigenous Identity in Europe
content: A Homeland Remembered: Crimean Tatars and the Question of Indigenous Identity in Europe Country Russia Ukraine agnes Wed, 09/09/2026 - 10:12 Issues Human Rights Program 5 Main Image By Mara Moldavan (CS Intern) For centuries, the Crimean Tatars have lived on the Black Sea peninsula of Crimea, where their language, traditions, and history are closely tied to the land. But since Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, many Crimean Tatars have been forced into exile or now live under occupation. Their situation raises a question that Europe still struggles to answer: what does it mean for an Indigenous People to defend identity, continuity, and political belonging when access to their homeland is disrupted by occupation and war? “Our homeland is Crimea—and no one else's,” says Liudmyla Korotkykh (Crimean Tatar), a lawyer and manager at the Crimean Tatar Resource Center, an organization that documents human rights violations in Crimea. Speaking from Kyiv, where she has lived since leaving Crimea in 2015, Korotkykh describes a Peoples whose identity is inseparable from the land itself.​ ​Who are the Crimean Tatars? The Crimean Tatars are recognized in Ukraine as one of the Indigenous Peoples of Crimea, alongside the Karaims and the Krymchaks. Outside of Eastern Europe, many people are unfamiliar with the idea that Indigenous Peoples live within Europe at all. Korotkykh believes this misunderstanding stems partly from the way Indigenous identity is often depicted. “People often think Indigenous Peoples are those who were colonized,” she explains. “And historically, Europeans were the colonizers. Because of this, many people don’t imagine Indigenous Peoples existing in Europe.” Tatar Youth. Photo by Crimean Tatar Resource Center. A Relationship Rooted in Land Crimea is located on the northern coast of the Black Sea and consists of mountains and prairie lands. Over generations, communities developed ways of living with these environments. “It’s more than territory,” Korotkykh says. “It’s a special way of life.” One example lies in the mountains, where traditional orchards known as chayır rely on natural water flows shaped by the terrain. These mountain gardens allow communities to grow fruit and crops in places where irrigation would otherwise be difficult. According to Korotkykh, the unique conditions of these landscapes produce fruit that is known for its distinct flavor. Even among those who grew up far from Crimea, that connection remains. Korotkykh’s mother was born in Uzbekistan after the deportation. “We grew up hearing stories about Crimea,” she says. “People would say that the fruit there tastes better, that even the sun shines more brightly.” Displacement and Survival In 1944, Joseph Stalin, then leading the Soviet Union, ordered the mass deportation of Crimean Tatars to Central Asia, accusing the entire population of collaborating with Nazi Germany. Families were forced onto trains and deported thousands of kilometers away; many did not survive. For decades afterward, Crimean Tatars weren’t allowed to return. Their culture was suppressed, yet families continued to maintain traditions and language in private, passing them from one generation to the next. Over time, small acts of cultural preservation became forms of resistance. Weddings, for example, took on a significance beyond celebration. In Crimean Tatar communities, large gatherings allowed people to share music, language, and news while raising funds to support cultural activities and the growing movement. During the late Soviet era, Crimean Tatars began returning to their homeland after generations of exile. Many found their homes gone and land ownership uncertain, but through persistence and collective effort, they slowly rebuilt community life. By the early 21st century, Crimean Tatar culture was beginning to reemerge across the peninsula. A Homeland Under Occupation That recovery was interrupted in 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea. In February 2014, thousands gathered outside the Crimean parliament building in Simferopol to support Ukraine’s territorial integrity and protest Russia’s actions. “Crimean Tatars were in the center of opposition to the occupation,” Korotkykh says. In the years that followed, many Crimean Tatar activists and journalists faced arrests and criminal charges widely criticized by human rights organizations. “Russia uses these accusations to create the image that Crimean Tatars are extremists,” Korotkykh says. “But in many cases, people are targeted simply for their activism or for their beliefs.” Despite pressures, Crimean Tatars continue to safeguard their identity. As Korotkykh explains, language remains a powerful marker of belonging: “When you hear Crimean Tatar language or see traditional clothing, you understand you are among your people.” For younger generations, cultural expression has become a form of resistance. “In conditions where political activity is dangerous, culture becomes a way to show who you are. Young people are increasingly interested in traditions because they want to keep that identity alive,” Korotkykh says. What Is at Stake The broader war between Russia and Ukraine has added new pressures to Crimean Tatar communities. After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, reports of arrests and political prosecutions in Crimea intensified. The stakes, Korotkykh argues, extend beyond one community. Crimea’s location on the Black Sea makes it strategically important for the region, and it has become a central element of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. For Korotkykh, the international response to Crimea since 2014 shows just how easily the concerns of Indigenous Peoples can be overlooked in geopolitical debates. “When the occupation began, many people said a full-scale war in Europe was impossible,” she recalls. “But we warned that Russia would not stop in Crimea.” Eight years later, those warnings proved prescient. Only a few hundred thousand Crimean Tatars now live worldwide. Korotkykh worries that continued displacement could slowly fade the identity of Crimean Tatars. “If the world closes its eyes to Crimea,” she says, “our People could disappear.”​ ​ Liudmyla Korotkykh A Future Tied to Home Today, Korotkykh documents human rights violations in Crimea while also advocating internationally for the rights of Crimean Tatars and the other Indigenous Peoples of Crimea. Her work extends to engagement with United Nations mechanisms and international forums, where she brings attention to the situation on the peninsula. Like many Crimean Tatars living outside Crimea, she still has family there. “I’m Crimean Tatar. I’m from Crimea,” she says. “And of course, I want to go home.” Despite the ongoing war and uncertainty about the future of Crimea, Korotkykh remains hopeful that the rights of Indigenous Peoples will play a greater role in shaping Ukraine’s future. In 2021, Ukraine adopted a law recognizing Indigenous Peoples, including the Crimean Tatars, Karaims, and Krymchaks, marking an important step toward acknowledging Indigenous identity within Europe. “Each person can make the world more just,” she says. For the Crimean Tatars, the memory of Crimea continues to shape daily life—whether on the peninsula itself or across the diaspora. Even after decades of deportation, exile, and conflict, that connection endures. Crimea remains not only the land remembered, but the homeland many still hope to return to.

title: Vietnam’s nearly 400-year-old fishing village worships 2 giant whale skeletons
content:
Canh Duong Fishing Village, located in Hoa Trach Commune, is known as one of the eight ancient villages renowned for their long history in the former Quang Binh Province, which was merged with Quang Tri Province to form the new Quang Tri Province in July last year.
Historical records show that the village was founded in 1634, making it nearly four centuries old.
After hundreds of years of making a living from the sea, residents have come to see whale worship as an integral part of the village’s cultural and spiritual life.
Villagers worship two whale skeletons known as ‘Duc Ong’ (the Revered Lord) and ‘Duc Ba’ (the Revered Lady) at Ngu Linh Temple.
According to local villagers, ‘the Revered Lady’ washed ashore in the area in 1809, while ‘the Revered Lord’ came ashore in 1907.
The two enormous skeletons are displayed on wooden platforms inside the temple, with an altar standing between them.
Villagers carefully preserve numerous vertebrae, fan-shaped fin bones and skull bones.
Particularly striking are four curved ribs, each rising more than four meters against the walls.
Their immense size has led locals to compare them to giant elephant tusks.
Dao Van Hai, 69, who is responsible for looking after the temple, said that many parts of the two skeletons were lost or damaged during two wars.
In 2004, Ngu Linh Temple was built to provide a dedicated place to worship and preserve the two remaining skeletons.
Researchers previously collected samples and determined that the ‘the Revered Lord’ skeleton was some 28.8 meters long, while ‘the Revered Lady’ measured around 28.5 meters.
When alive, the two whales may have weighed hundreds of metric tons.
Not far from Ngu Linh Temple lies a cemetery reserved exclusively for whales that washed ashore along the Canh Duong coast.
Dozens of graves have been built much like human graves, each with an incense bowl placed in front of its headstone.
The headstones are inscribed with the whale’s name as well as the date when it was discovered.
Particularly intriguing is the fact that each whale grave has its own distinctive name, including Nam Duong Duke, Young Husband and Princess.
“After the whales are buried, about six or seven years later, the villagers erect stone headstones and give each grave a name,” said Nguyen Mai, a resident of Canh Duong Bac.

title: Colombia’s Indigenous guardians adapt as pressures mount on the ‘Heart of the World’
content:
- Indigenous Wiwa families in Colombia’s Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta are moving farther downslope in an effort to preserve community cohesion amid climate and security pressures.
- The mountain range’s Indigenous nations continue to hold to a “law of origin” that guides their path amid intensifying pressures from armed violence, resource extraction, and climate change.
- Wiwa leaders describe sacred sites, rivers and forests as “living curricula,” inseparable from cultural and ecological responsibilities.
- Recent protections have expanded the protected parts of the Sierra Nevada and prohibited new bids for mining and fossil fuel extraction.
RIOHACHA, Colombia — Amid the low slopes of a tropical dry forest, families from the Wiwa community of Gomke are building a new home.
Their ancestral settlement lies higher on a lush mountain in the town of Dibulla, overlooking the Caribbean coast in Colombia’s Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta.
Across this region, many Indigenous communities have been forcibly displaced by climate-related disasters or uprooted by armed actors. Gomke’s move to lower terrain, however, is described by community representatives as voluntary: a collectively led adaptation strategy to protect social, educational and spiritual cohesion amid intensifying climate pressures and the presence of paramilitary groups.
They call their new settlement Shegunamke.
The Wiwa have also acquired other parcels of land elsewhere in the Sierra, including at higher elevations. “We have left [those] untouched so that rivers, springs and bodies of water do not die,” said Roberto Carlos Coronado Calvo, rector of Shenzhawimaku, the Wiwa educational institution that combines conventional learning with the community’s language, culture, knowledge systems and relationship to the territory.
“If we begin clearing and cutting into the páramo [ecosystem], how can we guarantee life for those living below?”
Across the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, known to its peoples as Gonawindúa, or the “Heart of the World,” the four Indigenous nations of Arhuaco, Kankuamo, Kogui and Wiwa are navigating deep changes driven by agro-industrial expansion, legal and illegal mining (driven by rising global gold prices), the return of paramilitary violence tied to the drug trade, and accelerating climate impacts within and around the Línea Negra, their ancestral network of sacred sites.
These changes are intensifying pressures on ancestral lands and pushing communities to abandon homes, territories, and cultural practices.
Amid all this, the communities can still fall back on the spiritual and political framework known as “the law of origin,” which defines the interdependence of Mother Earth and all forms of life. It offers a way to deal with these changes, resist the pressures, and hold on to fundamental truths about humanity’s relationship with nature, life, and existence.
Knowledge as inseparable from territory
Within this cosmovision, the Sierra is not property or a collection of exploitable resources; for the communities, it’s a single living organism encompassing forests, rivers, wildlife, sacred sites, and human communities.
The law of origin governs this fragile equilibrium. This ancestral code guides the four Indigenous nations of the Sierra in maintaining environmental and cosmic order. As the mountain’s traditional guardians, the four nations view commercial resource extraction as direct violence against Mother Earth.
Mineral and energy resources — gold, coal, oil, gas, salt — are understood as her vital organs; extracting them is thought to degrade the natural architecture sustaining life. Yet they continue to be extracted: data analyzed by the Interamerican Association for Environmental Defense (AIDA) show that at least 120 active mining titles and more than 90 pending applications overlap the Línea Negra.
For Luis Enrique Salcedo Zalabata, governor of the Arhuaco Cabildo of Magdalena and La Guajira, upholding ancestral responsibilities has grown increasingly difficult. When private developments, mining and armed conflict restrict access to sacred sites, and agro-industrial and climate pressures transform surrounding ecosystems, territorial knowledge risks disappearing with the elders who preserve it.
The human consequences became visible in Serankwa in March 2026, when armed clashes erupted over drug-trafficking routes. An explosive dropped from a drone seriously wounded a young Arhuaco man and injured several relatives, according to the victim’s family.
After the military secured the area, the family was evacuated to Santa Marta and dispersed to different medical centers, an Indigenous health care provider, and temporary shelters. That displacement separated them from their crops, sacred places, community authorities, and a territory understood not as property, but as a living body.
“To be a woman is to represent the territory,” said the family matriarch. “It is to represent Mother Earth. When a woman is harmed, it also means that the territory is being harmed.”
Displacements, such as those experienced by the people of Gomke and Serankwa, requires communities to rebuild daily relationships with new landscapes while maintaining their connections to high-mountain sacred sites where pagamentos rituals — offerings intended to preserve ecological and spiritual balance — are performed.
A spiritual resistance
The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta rises from the Caribbean shores to snow-capped alpine summits. Its complex ecosystems of peaks, rivers, forests, sacred sites, animals, and human communities form an interconnected living system. Damage to one part affects the whole, Indigenous authorities say.
Wiwa knowledge keeper Roberto Carlos Coronado Calvo is combining training under traditional elders with studies in traditional education and interculturality. He sees education as central to cultural continuity amid the changes affecting Indigenous lands and societies in the Sierra.
“It allows us to heal the memory,” Coronado said. “It allows us to heal the territory. It allows us to heal the places. And it allows us to heal the languages.”
The Línea Negra’s sacred sites, rivers, forests and winds form what Coronado calls “living curricula.” These places hold knowledge inseparable from the territory and carry practical responsibilities community leaders seek to maintain amid the rapid changes taking place around them.
“At my present level of learning, I hear when the trees or birds speak,” he said. “Birds speak like people. I listen when they tell me what is happening or what is going to happen. That is called listening.”
For Coronado, such listening is not only a spiritual practice but an action guide: it informs land-use decisions such as leaving acquired forest parcels intact to protect rivers and springs.
“Reciprocity. Care for the trees. Care for the waters. Care for Mother Earth,” Coronado said. “We must protect, conserve and nurture that whole system every day.”
Centuries of Indigenous stewardship have produced measurable territorial protections. In 2023, Colombia expanded Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta National Natural Park by 172,458 hectares (426,153 acres), to a total of 573,313 hectares (1.42 million acres).
Developed with the Consejo Territorial de Cabildos Indígenas de la Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, a collective of Indigenous assemblies, the measure recognizes ancestral governance as an effective conservation mechanism.
The park is home to a recorded 3,057 species of wildlife, including 49 threatened species and 126 plant species found nowhere else on Earth. Notable species include the critically endangered blue-billed curassow (Crax alberti), the Andean condor (Vultur gryphus) and the jaguar (Panthera onca). It also protects the headwaters of about 18 major rivers, supplying water to the departments of Magdalena, Cesar and La Guajira.
In 2026, Colombia designated 1.5 million hectares (3.7 million acres) of the Sierra Nevada as the Corazón del Mundo Renewable Natural Resources Reserve. Located within the broader ancestral territory structured by the Línea Negra, the reserve prohibits new applications for mining and fossil fuel extraction.
Colombia’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has pledged to expand fossil fuel production and mining and pursue a harder, more militarized strategy against armed groups. While the former plan goes against the worldview of the Sierra’s Indigenous communities, the latter has found some favor with groups struggling from heightened insecurity.
For Coronado, Indigenous ecological knowledge represents generations of systematic observation that must inform wider society. For that reason, he said, protecting the Sierra Nevada can’t be left to its Indigenous guardians alone.
“When we care for the Sierra Nevada, we care for life,” Coronado said. “It belongs to all humanity. Everyone. And we all have a commitment.”

title: From traditional agroecology to modern practices: the cultivation of native potatoes in the Peruvian Andes
content: IntroductionNative potatoes represent the biocultural heritage of Andean farming communities. Since their origins, they have been cultivated using agroecological terrace farming systems in the Peruvian Andes. This study analyzes how a community is transforming the traditional agricultural system of native potato cultivation in the mountains of Ayacucho through a contemporary model of sustainable development.MethodologyAn ethnographic immersion study was conducted in the indigenous community of Condorcocha (Ayacucho, Peru), which produces native potatoes, with the aim of understanding the dynamics of the social fabric that emerges from the interrelationship between culture, cosmovision and the land, as processes inherent to local production systems.ResultsThe ethnographic analysis identified ten categories organized into three interrelated dimensions: strategic-commercial, associated with planning, value creation, and mutually beneficial strategies; ecocultural, linked to green leadership, ancestral knowledge, and agroecological innovation; and social, characterized by gastronomic partnerships and community cohesion. In summary, these dimensions explain how local actors are transforming their traditional agricultural system through the conservation, promotion, and sustainable commercialization of native potatoes.DiscussionThis study demonstrates that the ancestral agroecological engineering inherited from pre-Inca and Inca civilizations—which integrates terraces, soil management systems, seed conservation, crop diversity, and community organization—constitutes a living and active system in today’s high Andean communities. This historical continuity demonstrates that biocultural heritage can be successfully integrated with contemporary production and marketing strategies, strengthening biodiversity conservation, food security, and sustainable development, in accordance with the Andean principles of reciprocity and respect for Pachamama.

title: Conservation’s Blind Spot: Why Language Matters for Biodiversity
content:
To many visitors a mangrove forest appears as a stretch of trees standing between land and sea. But if you walk through the same forest with a local fisher returning with the tide, a honey collector searching for wild hives, or a boatman who has spent a lifetime navigating its creeks, another landscape comes into view. What seems to be a single landscape is understood as many. Diverse names distinguish places where fish breed, honey is gathered, storm surges lose their force, or tides behave differently.
Across the eastern and western seaboards in India, coastal communities have developed distinct names for tidal forests that reflect ecological function as much as geography. In Bengal, Sundarban evokes a forest historically associated with the sundari tree and its life-sustaining tidal ecology. Along the Godavari–Krishna delta, the Telugu expression mada vanalu refers to brackish tidal forests that nurture fisheries and soften the impact of cyclones. Tamil and Malayali people use terms built around kandal to distinguish salt-tolerant coastal habitats, while related expressions across the Konkan and Gujarat coast identify creek-edge forests, honey-collecting areas, and other ecosystems.
These names are far more than local expressions. They reflect generations of close observation about how the forest functions and how people have learned to live with it.
Much of this vocabulary is quietly disappearing. In administration, education, and even conservation practice, diverse coastal landscapes are increasingly gathered under a single term, mangroves. The forest remains, but the distinctions that once helped people recognize its ecological diversity begin to fade.
Conservation has become notably good at measuring environmental change. Forest cover, species recovery, and habitat loss are monitored with increasing precision. Still, an irony remains. Even as technologies sharpen the view of nature, the ecological languages through which Indigenous peoples have long interpreted these ecosystems and processes are becoming less visible.
Before ecosystems disappear, the ability to read them often begins to erode.
Conservation routinely monitors species richness and habitat extent but rarely asks whether the vocabulary needed to recognize those habitats is itself surviving. That is conservation’s overlooked blind spot. Protecting biodiversity is not only about safeguarding species and habitats; it also requires sustaining the languages that enable people to understand the many distinctions within an ecosystem in the first place. Conservation cannot fully succeed while the ecological languages that make landscapes intelligible continue to disappear.
When Conservation Loses Resolution
Ecologists classify habitats by their vegetation, hydrology, and species, while people who have lived in these landscapes for generations have long relied on another system of classification — language. Their vocabularies did not evolve to describe nature in the abstract. They emerged from everyday interactions. In tidal forests people learn to distinguish places shaped by tides, soils, fisheries, storms, and seasons, allow them to understand differences that matter.
The problem arises when these locally evolved classifications are absorbed into broader, standardized terminology. A common vocabulary undoubtedly makes administration, education, and scientific communication easier. Yet it also carries an unintended consequence: Ecosystems begin to appear simpler than they really are.
India’s mangrove coast illustrates this shift.
These are not simply regional names but ecolexicons that condense generations of environmental observation into everyday language.
As this mosaic of ecological vocabularies gives way to the single label mangroves, something more than linguistic diversity is lost. It’s like reducing the resolution of a satellite image: The coastline remains visible, but its finer ecological distinctions begin to disappear.
This process may be understood as linguistic flattening — not merely a dilution of linguistic richness and a loss of words, but also the gradual loss of ecological resolution. Long before a language falls silent, it can lose the nuances that once helped people read landscapes.
Language as Conservation Infrastructure
Linguistic flattening also weakens the systems that have long governed how people interact with ecosystems.
Language is often treated as a medium of communication, yet in many Indigenous societies it functions as something more fundamental. It carries practical rules, ethical obligations, and ecological boundaries that are learned not from policy manuals but through everyday speech, stories, and customary practice. In this sense, language is part of conservation infrastructure.
The Māori understanding of harakeke (New Zealand flax) offers a striking example. The central shoot, or rito, represents the child, while the surrounding leaves symbolize parents and grandparents. This is more than a metaphor. The vocabulary itself shapes harvesting practices: Inner shoots are never cut, because removing them threatens the life of the plant. Only the outer leaves are taken, allowing regeneration to continue. Even the flowering stalks (kōrari) are managed with care so that nectar remains available for native birds, supporting pollination and the wider ecosystem.
This appears to be a biocultural expression but in practice is a sophisticated system for managing relationships between people and nature. The language does not simply describe ecological relationships; it instructs people how to behave within them.
Similar patterns are found across Indigenous societies, where names, stories, and customary expressions regulate seasonal harvesting, identify sensitive habitats, and define responsibilities towards land and water.
Conservation recognizes the value of Indigenous knowledge, yet it often overlooks the languages through which that knowledge is organized, remembered, and transmitted. Protecting place-based knowledge while allowing the languages that sustain it to disappear is rather like preserving a library after removing its catalogue. The books may still exist, but their meaning becomes increasingly difficult to recover.
Vanishing Languages, Vanishing Environmental Archives
Modern conservation depends heavily on data. Satellite imagery tracks forest loss, climate models project future change, and ecological surveys measure species abundance with precision. Yet most of these records span only a few decades. They rarely capture and interpret the much longer histories through which communities have understood environmental changes.
That longer record often survives in language. Across Indigenous societies, names for plants, animals, winds, tides, and seasons are not arbitrary labels but accumulated observations refined over generations. They preserve knowledge of when rivers shift their course, when particular fish arrive, how flowering responds to rainfall, which plants indicate groundwater, or where storms repeatedly reshape the coast. Much of this information was never written down because it did not need to be. It remained alive in speech, memory, and everyday practice.
When a language slips away, the environmental archive becomes fragmented, and we lose part of nature’s archive. Individual observations may still be recorded by researchers, but the wider system that connected them — linking species, habitats, seasons, and human experience — is gradually lost.
Conservation then faces an unusual paradox. We invest heavily in collecting new ecological data while allowing centuries of carefully accumulated environmental knowledge to disappear unnoticed.
Seen in this light, language loss is not simply a cultural concern. It also represents the quiet erosion of one of conservation’s oldest and least recognized ways of understanding nature. Protecting biodiversity therefore also means sustaining the living archives that have preserved ecological memory across generations.
Conservation Literacy Beyond Species Lists
Conservation governance has made important progress globally in recognizing Indigenous peoples as partners in biodiversity protection. The Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework calls for respecting and applying traditional knowledge in biodiversity governance, while IPBES has repeatedly shown that indigenous and local knowledge strengthens conservation outcomes. Likewise, UNESCO’s International Decade of Indigenous Languages (2022–2032) emphasizes that these languages sustain knowledge systems shaped through long relationships with place.
Yet an important gap remains. Conservation frameworks celebrate traditional knowledge but rarely ask how that knowledge survives across generations. Knowledge does not exist independently of the language through which it is observed, evolved, organized, and passed from one generation to the next. A conservation strategy that values Indigenous knowledge while overlooking Indigenous languages risks protecting the product while allowing the process that continually renews it to fade.
This calls for a broader understanding of conservation literacy. Alongside species inventories, habitat maps, and ecological monitoring, conservation should also recognize the value of ecolexicons, the place-based vocabularies that enable Indigenous communities to distinguish habitats, seasonal change, and ecological processes.
Supporting community-led language documentation, multilingual ecological education, and regional diversity of Indigenous vocabularies are therefore not simply a cultural exercise. It strengthens the knowledge infrastructure of future generations to interpret and care for the landscapes they inherit.
Reading Nature Before It Falls Silent
Biodiversity conservation has long measured success in hectares restored, species recovered, and habitat protected. These remain essential benchmarks. Yet this understanding argues that another measure deserves attention: whether the languages that enable communities to understand, interpret and care for those landscapes are also surviving.
A forest is more than the trees it contains. It is also the vocabulary through which generations have learned to read its tides, seasons, species, and silences.
The next frontier in conservation is not simply protecting more land but protecting the many ways in which people understand that land. Every ecological language that survives preserves a way of noticing what others might overlook while their disappearance reduces the world’s ability to see nature in all its complexity.
Conservation cannot claim to protect the living world if it allows the languages that have long interpreted that world to disappear unheard.
Long before a forest falls silent, its words often do.

title: As guardiãs da fé de todos
content:
Por Jenifer Alexandre*
Durante séculos, quase toda cidade brasileira conheceu ao menos uma mulher capaz de unir fé, cuidado e conhecimento ancestral. Eram elas, as rezadeiras e benzedeiras: referências de cuidado, espiritualidade e solidariedade. Hoje, porém, a presença dessas mulheres se torna cada vez mais rara.
Muitas envelheceram sem conseguir transmitir seus saberes às novas gerações. Outras foram silenciadas pelo preconceito religioso, pela urbanização acelerada e pela ideia de que apenas o conhecimento científico possui valor. Aos poucos, aquilo que antes fazia parte do cotidiano popular corre o risco de sobreviver apenas na memória dos mais velhos.
Falar sobre rezadeiras e benzedeiras é também falar sobre etnociência: o reconhecimento dos conhecimentos produzidos pelos povos por meio da experiência, da oralidade e da convivência com a natureza, conforme o estudo Identidades étnicas e etnociências nas práticas de rezadeiras, de Graciela Souza Almeida e Natalino Perovano Filho.
Mesmo com as particularidades que distinguem o saber acadêmico e o saber popular, é impossível negar a riqueza existente nesses conhecimentos tradicionais, pois, durante muito tempo, diferentes pessoas e comunidades guardaram práticas de cuidado desenvolvidas a partir da observação das plantas medicinais, das crenças espirituais e coletividade.
No entanto, reconhecer a importância delas não significa negar a ciência ou substituir tratamentos médicos. Pelo contrário, significa compreender que diferentes formas de conhecimento podem coexistir e dialogar. A medicina popular e os saberes tradicionais fazem parte da formação histórica e cultural do Brasil. Ignorar isso é apagar parte da identidade do próprio povo brasileiro. Embora essas práticas sejam frequentemente associadas às mulheres, também existem homens que exercem esse ofício e participam da preservação desses saberes tradicionais.
Contudo, destaca-se a atuação feminina devido à sua expressiva presença histórica e cultural nesse contexto. Essas mulheres representam muito mais do que práticas religiosas. Elas preservam uma memória coletiva construída por meio da oralidade. Cada reza aprendida com a mãe ou com a avó, cada planta colhida no quintal, cada orientação dada a quem chega em sofrimento faz parte de um patrimônio imaterial que resiste há séculos, de acordo com as autoras Danielle Gomes do Nascimento e Maria Ignez Novais Ayala.
Desse modo, o desaparecimento gradual dessas pessoas revela também uma transformação profunda nas relações sociais. Muitos jovens já não aprendem as rezas, não conhecem as ervas medicinais e sequer conhecem mulheres que exerçam esse papel.
Esse processo de esquecimento não está relacionado apenas às transformações religiosas ou ao avanço da ciência, mas também à desvalorização de práticas culturais que, durante séculos, constituíram importantes formas de cuidado, acolhimento e transmissão de saberes. Soma-se a isso o desconhecimento sobre a importância histórica dessas práticas e, por vezes, a falta de reconhecimento das mulheres que dedicaram suas vidas ao cuidado da comunidade. Ou seja, mais do que o desaparecimento de um ofício, observa-se o enfraquecimento de um patrimônio cultural construído ao longo do tempo, cuja preservação depende do respeito à memória, à diversidade de saberes e às experiências compartilhadas pelos diferentes grupos sociais.
Ademais, embora muitas vezes tratadas como se fossem a mesma coisa, rezadeiras e benzedeiras possuem diferenças sutis. Conforme a pesquisada Alaíze dos Santos Conceição, no seu artigo Notas sobre religiosidades populares no Recôncavo, as rezadeiras estão mais ligadas às orações e pedidos de proteção espiritual. Já as benzedeiras, além das rezas, costumam utilizar ervas, ramos, gestos e sinais da cruz em seus rituais de cura. Em comum, ambas carregam um conhecimento transmitido entre gerações, resultado da mistura entre tradições indígenas, africanas e portuguesas que ajudaram a formar a cultura brasileira.
Mulheres que se apoiam na fé: na própria fé e no poder do acolhimento. Recebem em suas casas, sem cobrar nada, aqueles que chegam carregando dores, medos e esperanças como as guardiãs da fé de todos. Para elas, cada pessoa atendida é acolhida com carinho e respeito, como alguém da própria família. Suas mãos, acompanhadas por orações sussurradas, buscam sempre o bem-estar de quem as procura. Dona Maria e Dona Maria Matias são exemplos dessas mulheres, cujo acolhimento se revela não apenas em suas palavras e gestos, mas também na serenidade de seus olhares.
No entanto, muitas das práticas que fazem parte desse ofício ainda passam despercebidas e raramente são reconhecidas como patrimônio cultural ou como formas legítimas de conhecimento ancestral. Entre elas estão o acolhimento de pessoas em momentos de sofrimento físico e emocional, a escuta atenta, os conselhos oferecidos a partir da experiência, as visitas a vizinhos, familiares e enfermos e, sobretudo, o cultivo e o conhecimento das plantas medicinais mantidos nos quintais e transmitidos entre gerações.
Como afirmam as pesquisadoras Nascimento e Ayala, caminhar pelos caminhos da cultura popular significa reconhecer a riqueza de conhecimentos preservados pelas pessoas mais velhas ao longo das gerações. Em acordo com as autoras, as rezadeiras e benzedeiras carregam muito mais do que orações e rituais: guardam memórias, experiências e formas de cuidado construídas ao longo de gerações. São mulheres que mantêm viva uma relação profunda com a escuta, com a fé, com a natureza e com o acolhimento comunitário.
Na perda de uma delas, perde-se mais do que uma prática tradicional. Perde-se uma parte da memória cultural brasileira e uma fonte viva de conhecimentos ancestrais. Portanto, preservar esses saberes é preservar a memória popular brasileira. É reconhecer que a cura também pode nascer da fé, da escuta, do cuidado e da ancestralidade.
Para saber mais
ALMEIDA, Graciela Souza; PEROVANO FILHO, Natalino. Identidades étnicas e etnociências nas práticas de rezadeiras. ODEERE: Revista Internacional de Relações Étnicas, v. 6, n. 2, 2021. DOI: https://doi.org/10.22481/odeere.v6i2.9750
CONCEIÇÃO, A. S. Notas sobre religiosidades populares no Recôncavo. Revista Discente Ofícios de Clio, v. 2, n. 2, p. 99, 11 jun. 2018. DOI: https://doi.org/10.15210/clio.v2i2.12918
DO NASCIMENTO, Danielle Gomes; AYALA, Maria Ignez Novais. As práticas orais das rezadeiras: um patrimônio imaterial presente na vida dos itabaianenses. Nau Literária, v. 9, n. 2, 2013. DOI: https://doi.org/10.22456/1981-4526.43698
*Jenifer Alexandre é mestre em Biodiversidade e formada em bacharelado e licenciatura em ciências biológicas pela Universidade Federal da Paraíba (UFPB).
**A opinião contida neste texto não necessariamente representa a linha editorial do Brasil de Fato.

title: Final preparations for the Reed Dance under way
content:
Final preparations are under way as thousands of AmaZulu maidens are expected to participate in this weekend’s uMkhosi woMhlanga, the Reed Dance, at the eMashobeni Royal Palace in uPhongolo in KwaZulu-Natal.
About 30 000 maidens are expected to take part in the traditional annual cultural ceremony which celebrates AmaZulu culture and promotes purity and self-respect amongst young women.
Among those preparing for the event is authorized maiden minder, Staff Ndlovu, who is responsible for more than 200 maidens from KwaMashu in Durban.
“Regarding the buses, we usually go to the bus owners and go with them to have the bus checked in Verulam. There is someone who goes underneath the bus and inspects the vehicle. As we are travelling with the girls, we usually tell them that even though you are leaving home and your parents are here, you have to respect everyone. You have to respect the young and old, and when the minders talk to you, you must always remain humble.”
Twenty two-year-old Slindelo Myeni from Mkhuze, who has been attending the Reed Dance for 10 years, says they get to learn important life lessons whenever they meet and gather as maidens.
“The Reed Dance is a time for us to celebrate our day as maidens because it’s one of the few places where we get to meet each other. The AmaZulu King has invited us to celebrate with him, receive his blessings and get his advice. What we learn each year is different, and every message gives us an opportunity to learn, grow and become better young women.”

title: For First Nations, Trump’s lake renaming is much ado about Niiganii-gichigami
content:
Lake Ontario is Niiganii-gichigami in the Anishinaabemowin language. Elders tell me the lake was always known as this.
But what, exactly, is in a name?
For First Nations people, I know that regardless of which community you are from, names have meaning. They can provide information, and signify respect. So when an American President renames a body of water on an angry whim by writing “Lake America” over “Lake Ontario” on a map with a marker, it means nothing to us – those who have lived here since before all these lines were drawn and borders created.
Mr. Trump loves to recolonize. He did it to the Gulf of Mexico in January, 2025, when he renamed it the Gulf of America. He also changed the name of the Alaskan mountain Denali, which had been reverted to that traditional Koyukon Athabascan name under Barack Obama, to Mount McKinley. But the Anishinaabeg have lived in and around the Great Lakes since well before Canada or America was a country. In Anishinaabemowin, the “Great Lakes” are Nayaano-nibiimaang gichigamiin: the five freshwater seas. Niiganii-gichigami, our name for Lake Ontario, translates to “the leading lake.” “Ontario,” meanwhile, comes from either Wendat or the Haudenosaunee word “kanadario,” referring to beautiful or sparkling water; the Haudenosaunee, the people of the long house, also live here, and the Wendat were an Iroquoian speaking nation.
Rift with Canada shows potential to become a pressing U.S. election issue
My friend, Dehaeho:węhs Amos Key Jr., is a Faith Keeper from Six Nations of the Grand River in Ohsweken. When I asked him what Ontario means, he said: “When you study the etymology of our Haudenosaunee languages, and you add the suffix ‘ri:io to a word or phrase, it gives it the meaning of something being very precious, coveted and gifted from Shögwayadisöh, our Creator.” The French picked it up and the name has been in use since 1641, noted Prime Minister Mark Carney, who schooled the U.S. leader about the origins of the name on X. “The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” he said. “We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
The Prime Minister was right to brush off Mr. Trump’s silly stunt – especially during an escalating trade war. The fact that Mr. Trump was focused on such colonizing tactics shows you where his head is at and what his ambitions are.
But this is what we know: An American President can never take away the name of a lake that was never his in the first place. Water can’t be owned. Water is alive. It has spirit. It ebbs and flows and it fills our bodies. Water gives us life and it can take it away. Renaming our beautiful, glimmering and wide Niiganii-gichigami “Lake America” means nothing to any of us living here in Canada.
In a trade war, can you shop your way to patriotism?
Mr. Trump’s childlike act has only mobilized Canadians, and brought us closer together. Suddenly, those who live here are getting a taste of the threat of colonization. Indigenous people have experienced this before, more than 150 years ago. We know how this playbook goes. But this time, those who colonized our ancestors are being threatened alongside us.
This is a tiresome fight, and Indigenous peoples have seen it all before. We are so done with those that come from foreign lands to take our water, our critical minerals, our sense of self. They will not tell us who we are. It makes sense that it was Manitoba’s Anishinaabe Premier, Wab Kinew, who pushed back when the Prime Minister asked the provinces to return American alcohol to liquor-store shelves ahead of the since-scuttled deal. “Very wise people have said you can’t get a good deal with a bad person,” the Premier said. We still have agency, Mr. Kinew said, so we don’t have to give in to a bully and make a deal that leads us down the wrong path, even if it hurts: “I think we should fight.”
Canadians now have a choice. They can look inward. Buy food grown on this land. Change habits. Learn and embrace true history, not deny it. Be proud of the Indigenous peoples who have taken care of the waters, the Earth, the animals. Recognize our collective history by, among other things, supporting Orange Shirt Day on Sept. 30. And we can act like we say we are: Canadians who say “Ontario” and “Niiganii-gichigami,” because the whims of an American politician mean nothing to those of us with long memories.

title: Princess Anne reunited with childhood riding teacher
content:
Princess Anne reunited with childhood riding teacher
- Published
The Princess Royal has been reunited with a former Windsor groom who taught her to ride more than 70 years ago.
Barbara Rosen, 94, said Princess Anne was three and her brother King Charles was five when she began working at Windsor Castle in the 1950s.
The pair met when the princess visited The Nicky day centre in Crumpsall as Manchester Jewish Community Care marked its 75th anniversary.
Rosen said they had a "really nice chat", adding: "We both remembered one another."
She said she was the first female groom to work there, at a time when the role had previously been carried out by men.
"They were just children," Rosen said of Anne and Charles.
"I used to ride with them and teach them how to ride."
She recalled the children's ponies, William and Greensleeves, and said she travelled with the Royal Family and the ponies to Sandringham and Balmoral.
Rosen said she worked as a groom for about seven-and-a-half years before leaving after she married.
During their reunion, she said she and the princess recalled people and places from their time at Windsor and looked through old photographs.
They also spoke about three-day eventing, in which the princess later competed.
David Delew, chief executive of Manchester Jewish Community Care, said the meeting was one of the highlights of the Royal visit.
He said Princess Anne spent longer in the centre's reminiscence room than he had expected as the pair talked about "the old days, the different horses and the family".
The charity was established in 1951 as the Manchester Jewish Blind Society and now provides care, support and community services.
During the visit, Princess Anne also met members, staff and volunteers, viewed refurbishment plans for The Nicky and unveiled a commemorative plaque.
Rabbi Daniel Walker described her visit as a "wonderful expression of solidarity" and said the community was "extremely grateful" for the support it had received.
The King visited the nearby Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue in October 2025 following the attack there earlier that month.

title: Thousands support petition against proposed amendments to Treaty references in legislation
content:
Thousands support petition against proposed amendments to Treaty references in legislation
A Ngāti Kahungunu petition calling for a halt on government plans to amend references to Te Tiriti o Waitangi in legislation has attracted more than 20,000 signatures.
Ngāti Kahungunu chair Bayden Barber told RNZ that any legislative or constitutional changes affecting Te Tiriti should involve genuine consultation with Māori and the public.
Iwi representatives are planning to deliver the petition to Parliament on horseback, with the first group of riders departing Friday morning from Waimārama Marae.
Barber said Waimārama was the home of Harawira Mahikai Te Tātere, a Ngāti Kurukuru chief who signed Te Tiriti o Waitangi at Waipūreku in 1840.
"We will ride from Waimārama, and connect with riders from Heretaunga, Ahuriri and Wairoa at the Tukituki River. From there, we'll travel through Havelock North.
"We will continue through Ngāti Kahungunu heartland, travelling past Pukehou marae, on to Waipawa, Waipukurau, Rākautātahi, Tāmaki-nui-a-Rua (Dannevirke) and Te Whakaoriori (Masterton)."
Barber said the trek aims to send a simple yet powerful message that cannot be ignored.
"We want to send a message to this Government that we are serious about protecting Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the founding agreement of this country. Not only to this Government, but whoever is there come November 7."
"Te Tiriti o Waitangi is what makes our country unique - the coming together of two peoples, Māori and Pākehā, working for the benefit of all - and it must be upheld. If you haven't already signed the petition, please do."
Te Taiwhenua o Tāmaki nui a Rua representative and Ngāti Kahungunu deputy chair Hayden Hape said this petition is important given the current climate.
"This petition is especially important as we have experienced continued attacks on Te Tiriti o Waitangi within government legislation, basically absolving the government of its responsibility to uphold Treaty precepts and principles."
Government response
In a statement, Minister of Justice Paul Goldsmith said the Government does not agree or accept its legislation is weakening Treaty obligations.
"Over the last 30 or 40 years, Parliament has made all sorts of references to the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi. Sometimes it's 'honour', or 'have regard to', or 'give effect to', or 'take into account'.
"We need to create some consistency here, in the interests of increasing certainty and supporting compliance. A core foundation of our success as a nation is predictability in the law."
Barber said the horse trek will bring together tangata whenua, whānau, hapū, iwi and supporters from across the lower North Island in a highly visible journey to deliver a message that Te Tiriti o Waitangi must be protected.
The riders are expected to arrive in Wellington next Tuesday where the petition will be presented to Ikaroa-Rāwhiti MP Cushla Tangaere-Manuel at midday on the steps of Parliament, with the intention of presenting it to the House later that afternoon.

title: This Red-Ant Chutney Has Different Names Across India. Gordon Ramsay Just Put It in the Spotlight
content: In June 2026, Jharkhand Tourism shared a social-media video of Gordon Ramsay tasting the state’s red-ant chutney, describing his reaction as “absolutely delicious”. The clip brought fresh attention to a food that may look unusual to an outsider but has long been part of Indigenous diets across eastern, central and northeastern India. For communities living around forests in Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal and Arunachal Pradesh, the red weaver ant is not something encountered as a culinary dare. It can be food, a seasonal forest resource, a traditional medicinal ingredient and, in some places, something that can be sold in local markets. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Jharkhand Tourism (@jharkhandtourism) And there is no single red-ant chutney. The same species appears in different food traditions, carrying different names, recipes and meanings depending on where you are. The ingredient is the red weaver ant, Oecophylla smaragdina. Demta and Hau in Jharkhand In Jharkhand, red-ant chutney is known by local names including Hau, while Demta is also used in some communities. The ants and their eggs are collected from tree nests and prepared with ingredients such as chillies, salt, garlic, ginger and coriander. The chutney is eaten with everyday foods rather than reserved as a novelty. Local accounts describe it being served with maaru-bhaat, puffed rice and vegetables. Bastar has its Chapda Travel west into Chhattisgarh, and the preparation takes another name. Red-ant chutney is particularly associated with Gond communities and is commonly known as Chapda, Chhapra or Chapura, depending on the locality. A 2024 review in Nature journal, “Bio-economic potential of ethno-entomophagy and its therapeutics in India,” documents the consumption of red ants among tribal communities in Chhattisgarh and notes that red-ant chutney is popular among Gond communities. The same review records red ants being consumed across several districts of Odisha, including Koraput, Kandhamal, Keonjhar, Sundargarh and Mayurbhanj. They may be roasted, eaten with rice, or fried with salt, chillies, spices and mustard oil. Bengal has Kurkut The tradition becomes particularly interesting when it reaches Jhargram in West Bengal. A 2020 study titled “On the Use of Red Ant Oecophylla smaragdina by the Indigenous People of Binpur, Jhargram, West Bengal,” by Atanu Mitra, Angsuman Chanda and Srimanta Kumar Raut, documented the practice in the Purnapani and Jorum forests of Binpur. The researchers had been visiting tribal settlements in the area since 1994, documenting how local people collected, prepared and used ants. Here, the red weaver ant is locally called Kurkut. What looks like one dish from a distance is actually a network of regional food traditions shaped by forests, seasons and local knowledge. Photograph: (IndiaToday) The study found that Indigenous people collected the ants and larvae between September and February, when large numbers of nests could be found in trees. The insects were used as food, medicine, and a commercial product. The recipe offers another glimpse of how local knowledge changes with geography. Researchers recorded a chutney made by grinding the ants with chilli, mint, onion, ginger, garlic, cumin, mustard oil and salt. Another preparation involved pounding the ants with onion, chilli, mustard oil and salt. It was eaten with rice for two or three days. Some families also boiled the ants and ate them directly. In Mayurbhanj, it is Kai In Mayurbhanj, Odisha, the red weaver ant is known as Kai, and the preparation is Kai Chutney. Here, the tradition has received formal recognition. On 2 January 2024, Similipal Kai Chutney of Odisha received a Geographical Indication registration. The official Intellectual Property India database lists the Mayurbhanj Kai Society Limited as the applicant and records the product as a registered food product from Odisha. Further east, it is Tonge and Babuk The tradition does not end in eastern India. In Arunachal Pradesh, Oecophylla smaragdina is one of the preferred edible insects among tribal communities. The ant is locally known by names including Tonge and Babuk, and both adult ants and larvae are consumed. One ant, several food cultures Put these regions together, and the map looks different. Hau or Demta in Jharkhand. Chapda in Chhattisgarh. Kai in Odisha. Kurkut in Jhargram. Tonge or Babuk in Arunachal Pradesh. The clip brought fresh attention to a food that may look unusual to an outsider but has long been part of Indigenous diets. Photograph: (Image enhanced with AI) The names change. So do the recipes and the communities that prepare them. What remains is the red weaver ant and a body of knowledge about collecting it, preparing it, and using it. That brings the story back to Gordon Ramsay. His reaction makes for a compelling social-media moment. But for generations, Indigenous people have known where these ants build their nests, when they are available, how to collect them, and how to turn them into food. Sources: ‘On the use of red ant Oecophylla smaragdina by the indigenous people of Binpur, Jhargram, West Bengal’: By Atanu Mitra, Angsuman Chanda and Srimanta Kumar Raut, Published in 2020 ‘Nutritional and anti-nutritional composition of Oecophylla smaragdina (Hymenoptera: Formicidae) and Odontotermes sp. (Isoptera: Termitidae): Two preferred edible insects of Arunachal Pradesh, India: By Jharna Chakravorty, Sampat Ghosh, Karsing Megu, Chuleui Jung, V.Benno Meyer-Rochow, Published on 2 July 2016 ‘If you are protein deficient, then definitely eat the chutney of 'Demta Ants', it not only tastes good to the tribals but also takes care of their health’: By Ravi Sinha, Published on 18 November 2022

title: Tái hiện đồ chơi Trung thu xưa giữa lòng Hà Nội
content:
Tái hiện đồ chơi Trung thu xưa giữa lòng Hà Nội
Tối 10/9, hàng chục món đồ chơi Trung thu truyền thống được phục dựng và trưng bày tại triển lãm "Lưu trăng".
Triển lãm thuộc chuỗi hoạt động văn hóa Tết Trung thu 2026 do Ban quản lý hồ Hoàn Kiếm và phố cổ Hà Nội phối hợp Câu lạc bộ Đình Làng Việt tổ chức tại Trung tâm Văn hóa Nghệ thuật.
