title: Farmer's legacy lives on in wildflower he discovered before tragic death
content:
Farmer killed fighting WA bushfire honoured by planting of native flower he discovered
In short:
A West Australian farmer killed fighting a bushfire last year has been honoured for his discovery of a potentially new plant.
Mark Mudie discovered an unusual red-flowering hakea during seeding season about two years ago.
What's next?
Work is underway to determine the taxonomy of the plant, which locals hope will be named in Mr Mudie's honour.
A West Australian farmer who died fighting a devastating bushfire has been posthumously honoured with a native flowering plant he discovered two years before his death.
Ravensthorpe Shire deputy president and farmer Mark Mudie died in December last year while battling a blaze at West River that destroyed more than 5,000 hectares of farmland.
The plant, believed to be a hybrid species of hakea, is being planted today in Ravensthorpe, about 500 kilometres south of Perth, to remember and celebrate his life.
Mr Mudie's son Nathan said his father often wandered the bushland around the community, drawn to region's native flora.
"I remember the day dad found it, driving in the truck during seeding, and he called me up and said, 'I found a plant that I've never seen before'," he said.
"I didn't think much of it, but he was very excited about it and got some samples taken away.
"It was a bit of a rare thing to have out in our area, but Dad was very proud to find it."
Sitting adjacent to the Fitzgerald River National Park, the region's biodiversity attracts visitors from around Australia every year for its natural wildflower displays.
Nathan Mudie said the flowers were one of his father's passions, which he often shared with the family.
"He quite enjoyed the wildflower season in Ravensthorpe and used to always pick a bunch of wildflowers and bring it back home for Mum," he said.
"He was right into his wildflowers."
Plant returned to family
Ravensthorpe Wildflower Show and Herbarium coordinator Sue Leighton said Mark Mudie would often send her photos of flowers he saw to learn their names.
When he discovered the unusual hakea, she was one of the first people he called.
"He sent me a photo and said, 'Sue, I don't know what this is, I've never seen it before?'"Ms Leighton said.
"He sent a picture of this hakea that was about two-and-a-half metres high and about two-and-a-half wide and full of big blooms on it."
Ms Leighton said three of the herbarium staff went out to examine the plant and take cuttings for further examination.
"One taxonomist has said that it's just a subspecies of another one, but there's never been any seed on it at all, so we do believe it is a hybrid," she said.
"I've got those two plants that Kings Park has given us, and we're doing a ceremony planting of the one that will go in the herbarium garden at Ravensthorpe, and the other one will go to his wife, Elaine."
Kings Park senior plant breeder Digby Growns said it was an impressive specimen, and worthy of horticultural attention.
"It was covered in these globular flowers, similar to Hakea laurina, and we presumed it was a hybrid with that species and another unknown species," he said.
Mr Growns took several cuttings in a bid to propagate the plant.
"First to bring it into cultivation and protect it, given there was only a single plant," he said.
"And then to have a look at it, to see if there was any opportunity for making it commercially available."
Mudie Surprise
Ms Leighton said it could take years for the taxonomy of the plant to be finalised, but the herbarium was hoping, in time, the hakea could be named in honour of Mark Mudie.
"If it was something that could be grown as a hybrid, it could be given a name," she said.
"It won't have a species name on it, it will just have a trade name ... It could be called Mudie Surprise."
Nathan Mudie said with just the planting of the hakea, the remembrance and recognition of his father's discovery had touched the family.
"It's a very nice tribute that the community and everyone's decided to do, and for us as a family, it was very, very touching for us, and it's very nice to be here," he said.
"I think he'll be very proud of that and of how the community rallied together, and it shows the person that he was."

title: Seaman’s Schnapps reaffirms cultural heritage commitment
content:
Seaman’s Schnapps has reaffirmed its commitment to preserving Nigeria’s cultural heritage through its sponsorship of the 2026 Ekimogun Festival in Ondo Kingdom.
The annual festival, also known as the Ogun Festival, celebrates Ogun, the Yoruba deity associated with iron, war and creativity, and attracted traditional rulers, dignitaries, indigenes, tourists and Nigerians in the diaspora.
According to a statement, Seaman’s Schnapps served as the lead sponsor and official prayer drink at the festival, which featured traditional prayers, drumming, carnivals, cultural displays and community competitions.
On the eve of the grand finale, the Seaman’s Schnapps team visited the Osemawe of Ondo Kingdom, Oba Victor Kiladejo, presenting him with an honorarium and a specially commissioned portrait as a gesture of respect for the traditional institution and the Ondo heritage.
The brand also organised an Ayo Olopon competition at Odo Ajomu, drawing participants and spectators while promoting the traditional board game. Its Prayer Hut provided another point of engagement for festival-goers, while a branded media wall showcased its new 20cl product alongside the traditional 3cl offering.
The grand finale featured a cultural troupe supported by Seaman’s Schnapps, which performed traditional dances and eulogies around the Osemawe’s Palace. The brand also supported pounded yam and eating competitions, with winners receiving gifts.
Speaking at the festival, Senior Brand Manager, Nigeria Distilleries Limited, Nnenna Uche-Onyenacho, said the celebration reflected the values associated with the brand.
“The Ogun Festival is a celebration of strength, creativity, and identity, values that are at the very heart of what Seaman’s Schnapps represents as Nigeria’s original prayer drink. We are honoured to stand with the Ekimogun people in preserving and promoting a heritage that belongs not only to Ondo but to all Nigerians,” Uche-Onyenacho said.
She added that the brand’s involvement went beyond commercial visibility and sponsorship.
“Our presence here is not about a logo on a banner. It is about being part of a living culture and helping to preserve and pass it on to future generations,” she said.
Marketing Manager, Nigeria Distilleries Limited, Gbemileke Lawal, said the company’s continued support for the Ekimogun Festival and other cultural celebrations reflected its commitment to treating Nigerian culture as a living expression of national identity.
The Osemawe called on governments at all levels to intensify efforts to preserve indigenous heritage, while urging state and local authorities to support and institutionalise local festivals to boost tourism and cultural development.
The Speaker of the Ondo State House of Assembly, Olamide Oladiji, described the festival as a symbol of the identity and values of the Ondo people, while palace spokesperson, Chief Wole Benson, said Ondo City embraced a carnival atmosphere throughout the celebration.
Seaman’s Schnapps said its continued support for cultural festivals formed part of its broader effort to promote authentic Nigerian culture and encourage younger generations to embrace their heritage.

title: The Boruca Peoples’ Non-Linear Path to Self-Determination: Defined by Community Resilience
content: The Boruca Peoples’ Non-Linear Path to Self-Determination: Defined by Community Resilience Country Costa Rica agnes Tue, 09/08/2026 - 09:11 Issues Human Rights Program 5 Main Image By Iza Harris The Boruca Peoples have faced immense imposition from outsiders since the Spanish conquest in the 1500s, spanning from colonialism to the current governance structure under the Democratic Republic of Costa Rica. Costa Rica became an independent state in 1838, though Indigenous communities there did not receive legal recognition until 1977 and did not gain the right to vote until 1994. Despite some legal progress toward recognizing the need for self-determination and representation of Indigenous Peoples, the federal government has essentially carried the torch of the conquistadors. Currently, governance operates through Integral Development Associations (ADIs), local governing bodies intended to represent each Indigenous territory. Within Boruca communities, the ADIs have encouraged passivity—a stark contrast from the communal ethos that has long been central to Boruca life. Carlos Morales Lázaro (Boruca), a former ADI vice president, says that the government’s failure to implement legal procedures to protect Indigenous Peoples’ rights and defense against invading Peoples is “proof of institutionalist racism, a relic of colonialism... which presents this country as an ecologist’s paradise to the outside world while failing to seriously protect ethnic groups who follow a model of ecologically sound agricultural practices.” Brún̈cajc community leader José Ángel says that before the installation of the ADI, both designated Boruca territories (Rey Curré and Boruca Village) were governed by an active citizenry who were keen to work on communal projects and mutual aid and devoted to raising future leaders. The majority of Borucan community members agree there has been a retreat from community engagement as power became concentrated within the development organization. In Boruca Village, there was a time when various committees would work in tandem. When public streets and spaces needed cleaning, for example, the town would get together in the hundreds and do their share. It was more than just working together to solve problems; it was a time of celebration and joy in shared spaces. “We had more autonomy before today, [whether] there were problems or times of celebration. It was a communal decision where different committees worked together,” Ángel affirms. The day before we spoke, Ángel recalls that heavy rains nearly washed the village’s bridge away. Before the ADI, everyone would have been energized to resolve the issue, to bring shovels and machetes and cut down nearby trees to fix the problem. Now, he says, “the municipality’s machinery comes, it gets fixed. And if not, no one helps.” The sense of responsibility to participate in civil services has been snuffed out by bureaucracy, while the disconnect between organizations has grown. Now, each enterprise within the territory receives funding that must be accounted for and solely distributed toward the needs of each individual organization—an approach that inhibits cross-collaboration and resolution of issues. “This type of regulation killed the form of organization that the town had,” Ángel says. Ángel’s comments reflect the sense that laws and regulations applied to the Indigenous territory are “closing us off,” reducing community participation to individuals doing their day jobs and returning home without an interest in further resolution of issues. Years ago, he worked as a teacher in the local reservation school. At that time, he says, teachers had the power and influence to teach the importance of communal thinking and action within the classroom. Now, however, a culture of passivity has infiltrated the schools, and teachers are no longer personally invested in creating future leaders in their students. “If they were to train leaders [today],” Ángel says, “they would be leaders who are just looking around to see what they can grab, how they can benefit from being there.” The underlying sentiment of Ángel’s comments is that imposed governmental structures have usurped the sense of communal responsibility, heightening individualistic, self-serving, and financial motivations of people throughout the governing body and town. As a result, people are less willing to participate in projects without compensation. The Indigenous collectivist mindset has been eroded by the disease of the capitalistic mindset, which has been imposed on these Indigenous territories. Despite the growing distance between governance and community, there are still occasions where the Boruca Peoples are exercising communal identity and the power exerted within it. One such example is the community’s fierce fight against the development of the Diquís Dam, a project proposed by the Costa Rican Electricity Institute (ICE), a state-owned utility. The project was initially proposed in the 1970s, then redesigned and publicly launched in the mid-2000s, designed to be the largest dam in Central America. It would have had a catastrophic impact on terrestrial and marine ecosystems, causing flooding and disruption to the Boruca community in Rey Curré. The fight against the installation of the hydroelectric dam was waged by Maria Lázaro’s activist grandfather, Don Christiano Lázaro. In a 2024 article in "Terralingua," she detailed the beginning of the fight: “In 1978, the Peoples of Ujarrás, Salitre, Cabagra, Térraba, Boruca, and Yímba Cájc took over the civic center of Buenos Aires canton as a form of protest and rejection of the project.” This mass mobilization of people included Indigenous leaders, community members, and various organizations who refused to be the victims of a massive imposition on their lands. The original project was projected to “displace 1,600 persons, including 500 Indigenous people.” Rafael González. Artisan and Elder Rafael González was one of the community members opposing the project; he participated in the various peaceful marches to Buenos Aires and La Merced Park in San Jose to the Legislative Assembly and the Presidential Palace. González spoke of the various community groups that spearheaded the resistance to the megaproject, such as the Mujeres con Espíritu de Lucha, or Women with a Fighting Spirit, as well as other men’s groups. He remarks that this $2.5 billion project would have only harmed local communities while lining the pockets of national institutions and international contractors. “The greed for money that comes along...that’s what spreads. Good ideas, good deeds are thrown in the trash,” he says. There was plenty of back-and-forth regarding the legality of the project. In 2011, the Constitutional Court determined that it was constitutional “as long as the Indigenous communities were consulted within a period of six months from the notification of the ruling.” Yet, no consultation was conducted, and therefore, the condition necessary to proceed was not met. The Indigenous communities involved were not interested in the offers made to relocate them in exchange for well-paying jobs. Speaking for the community, beloved Terriba martyr Jehry Rivera, now deceased, said, “We don’t believe in the promises of employment for Indigenous Peoples, as up until today it had been demonstrated that all the qualified and best paid personnel have been brought from the outside. Indigenous workers are used only to break rocks.” The community’s fight was aided by the ADI, which filed a lawsuit against ICE, forcing workers off their land. The lawsuit corroborated that a consultation process never took place. Eventually, the fight was won, and in 2018, the project was indefinitely halted. The dynamics at play show the strength of the Boruca in their conflicts with neighboring Indigenous communities. The ADI played a role, yet was not the utmost factor of importance in pushing for the rights legally granted to Indigenous Peoples within their territories. Leaders throughout the Boruca community hope that in the future, Boruca youth will be trained to be invested in their community and traditions. Morales Lázaro notes how vital it is that the Boruca Peoples find ways to maintain their identity and to critically reflect on the imposed and adopted forms of education taught to their children. “We must not forget that [imposed] education tells us that learning happens within four walls. But the Indigenous way of life has always been to learn by observing, by example,” he says. “Young people need to be trained, and more importantly, to gain experience” in local organizing and communal activity, so that “when we older people aren’t here anymore, they will continue the defense of rights.” Maria, who is young and community-oriented, is frustrated with the lack of involvement of her Boruca peers in the fight for their human rights and representation. Her approach is to follow in the footsteps of her justice-seeking, community organizer grandfather, and to join her peers across Salire, Terriba, and other Indigenous communities. She acknowledges that the objective of the state government is to divide so Indigenous people don’t see their collective needs, because “all their fights are connected.” Fortunately, having inherited her grandfather’s temperament and sense of duty, she is carrying the torch for the shared struggle of a resilient and culturally vibrant community. -Iza Harris is a recent graduate from Pitzer College with a Bachelor of Arts in International Political Economy whose work centers on justice, indigeneity, and decolonial perspectives as pathways toward a more environmentally conscious, caring, and equitable society. During her time at Pitzer, she studied abroad in Nepal and Costa Rica, conducting in-depth research with the Raute and Boruca Indigenous communities to uplift the voices and perspectives of communities whose experiences are often unheard or dismissed.

title: Former classmates reunite as primary school turns 100
content:
Former classmates reunite as primary school turns 100
- Published
It is a school that gave shelter in the devastating Belfast Blitz during World War Two.
And Euston Street Primary School in inner east Belfast is now celebrating its 100th birthday.
It was officially opened in July 1926, just in time to admit pupils for the new school term.
And a century on, the school has opened its doors and classrooms to welcome back many former pupils to celebrate the big birthday.
Among them were Barbara Best and Rosaleen Gilpin, who have been lifelong friends since they met at Euston Street as pupils in the 1940s.
Both, who are now 83, started the school in 1947.
"I started at the same time as Rosaleen, and we've been friends ever since," Barbara told BBC News NI.
Being back in their old classroom triggered many memories, even if things have changed.
"The classroom assistant was a bamboo cane in the corner," Rosaleen said.
"The teachers were strict but they were very good to try and help people from the area to do well."
So was Rosaleen caned at school?
"Well, I've been known to be," she laughed.
For Barbara, the school library was her favourite place.
"You were allowed to go there on a Friday after school, and I remember going down there and thinking 'oh, so many books, great'," she said.
"It was lovely."
And Rosaleen still has a family connection to the school.
Showing her and Barbara round was her granddaughter Sarah McCrossan, who now teaches there.
"It's crazy to think that I'm working in the same place that she came as a child and walked in the same corridors," Sarah said.
"She said that the behaviour management strategies were very different, she said she was sent to the principal's office many times to get the cane which obviously doesn't happen anymore.
"This school is obviously in the middle of a big community and the community is so good to the school and the school is so good to the community."
And in World War Two the school saved many members of that community during the Belfast Blitz.
In April 1941, a German bomb fell on nearby Thorndyke Street, killing many residents including those taking refuge in an air-raid shelter.
So Euston Street Primary's basement became the main air-raid shelter for the local community.
The school sustained damage in a later bombing raid, but the basement kept people safe.
During the anniversary open day, many current and former pupils signed their names on the walls of the historic basement corridors.
Colin Johnston also has a continuing family connection to the school, as his granddaughter Poppy Anderson is a pupil.
Colin attended from 1965 until 1972 and was back being shown round by Poppy.
For him, the technology Poppy uses in school is the biggest difference from his own schooldays.
"All the i-Pads and all that they have now, there was nothing like that in my day," he said.
"It's a big change, it's really modern now."
"I remember my first class down in room five, Miss McConnell, and it was a great school."
He said the school was vital to the local community.
"They cannot do without the school," he said.
"As you see even today, the school dinners and all that and the other things that the school runs it's superb."
And for acting head-teacher Laura Rainey that sense of community was part of the reason for big celebration.
"We've welcomed past pupils, past staff and past governors," she said.
"It's been really lovely just to hear lots of positive memories, happy memories.
"And also some memories that you wouldn't hear nowadays about maybe the cane being used and just how things have changed.
"It's so special to have those stories and that legacy.
"We actually have families that have had four generations come through the school. That says everything."

title: Kushe Aunshi honours fathers, keeps ancestral traditions alive
content:
Visual Stories
Kushe Aunshi honours fathers, keeps ancestral traditions alive
Devotees across Nepal marked the Hindu festival with offerings to their fathers and rituals to remember departed ancestors.Deepak KC
Hindu devotees across Nepal observed Kushe Aunshi on Friday, honouring their fathers and paying tribute to deceased ancestors.
The festival is traditionally marked by children offering their fathers their favourite foods and expressing love, respect and gratitude.
Those whose fathers have died gathered at sacred sites to perform rituals including shraddha, tarpan and pindadan. At Gokarneshwar Mahadev Temple in north-eastern Kathmandu, popularly known as Uttar Gaya, devotees performed the rites on the banks of the Bagmati river.
Large numbers of devotees also visited the Pashupatinath Temple and other religious sites across the country.
Also known as Gokarne Aunshi, the day holds a dual significance in Hindu tradition, celebrating the bond between children and their fathers while providing an occasion to remember and honour departed family members.
Kushe Aunsi falls on the new moon day of the Nepali month of Bhadra. The day is also associated with the collection of kush, a sacred grass used in Hindu rituals throughout the year.
Here are photos of devotees who gathered at the Gokarneshwar Temple to perform rituals for their deceased fathers.

title: Twilight fandom helps fund Quileute Tribe’s move to higher ground
content:
This story was originally published by Underscore Native News.
Lyric Aquino
Underscore Native News + Report for America
This story is part of Underscore Native News’ reporting that explores and amplifies Indigenous climate solutions, through the Indigenous Climate Solutions Cohort. Underscore is part of a five-newsroom grant supported cohort with the Indigenous Journalists Association (IJA) and Solutions Journalism Network’s Climate Beacon Newsroom Initiative.
To many Indigenous people and Twilight Saga super fans, it’s no secret the Quileute Tribe was not compensated for the representation of its people in the popular fantasy books and subsequent films.
The Quileute people’s likeness is used throughout the franchise even as their traditional lore is misrepresented. In both the novels and movies, Quileute tribal members are portrayed as shape-shifting werewolves, often referred to as “dogs,” who are forced to cut their hair despite it being culturally significant to remain intact. The stories have been criticized for perpetuating harmful stereotypes of Indigenous people.
The tribe has found itself in an unusual spotlight: receiving global attention for a pop-culture phenomenon that amassed over $3.3 billion at the global box office without being given compensation.
“Many supporters and scholars have raised conversations about cultural representation and compensation. The Quileute Tribe did not receive royalties from the Twilight franchise despite the use of elements inspired by Quileute culture and identity,” the tribal council told Underscore Native News in an email. “Conversations about this issue have helped spark broader discussions about Indigenous representation, cultural respect, and ethical storytelling.”
Now, Twilight fans are trying to rectify the lack of financial compensation by raising funds for the Quileute Tribe’s Move to Higher Ground Project through varied creative means. From raffles, to a personal donation from the CEO of a large makeup company, to creating social media videos about the project, fans are trying to find any way they can to make a difference.
The urgent need to move
Located along the western edge of the Olympic Peninsula, the Quileute Tribe’s coastal town La Push sits at the mouth of the Quillayute River. Home to fewer than 400 people, the quaint town is just one small section of the former 800,000 acres the tribe inhabited pre-colonization.
But after signing over their land in exchange for health, education and job training as well as reserving hunting, fishing and gathering rights in their “usual and accustomed places,” the Quileute Tribe was left with a tiny parcel of land in a tsunami zone. That land has been slowly withering away due to coastal erosion, exacerbated by climate change.
“Living in a tsunami zone at the edge of the Pacific Ocean, a catastrophic earthquake can wipe out our community in less than 10 minutes — an entire generation of the Quileute people will cease to exist,” state tribal officials said on the tribe’s Move to Higher Ground Project website.
In a 2023 report from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), scientists stated rising sea levels are a direct result of the planet’s rising temperatures melting snow glaciers and ice sheets, which add water to the ocean. Additionally, as water temperatures continue to warm, the volume of the ocean increases due to thermal expansion. Over time, the changing waters, intense storms and winds have led to the erosion of La Push’s shores, leaving hardly any barrier between the ocean and their land if a tsunami were to occur.
After years of lobbying the federal government for acreage, in 2012 President Barack Obama signed legislation that returned around 280 acres of Olympic National Park land to the tribe. The returned land is being used for the Quileute’s Move to Higher Ground Project, a multi-year development of an upper village located outside of flood and tsunami zones.
In 2022, phase one of the development was completed when the Quileute Tribal school was built some 250 feet above sea level. Eventually, the upper village will hold homes, an elder center, cultural facilities, tribal government offices, emergency services, parks and open spaces.
But the Move to High Ground Project is just one of many in the Pacific Northwest, including the Quinault Nation, which estimates it will cost $450 million to move its entire lower village, Taholah, a half-mile away. Similar to Quinault, the Quileute are looking for ways to continue the funding to move their citizens to safety.
“The Move to Higher Ground initiative is a multi-phase, long-term relocation effort, meaning funding needs evolve as each stage progresses,” the Quileute tribal council told Underscore. “Because development occurs in stages and depends on grants, infrastructure costs and construction timelines, the total remaining fundraising goal is ongoing rather than a single fixed number.”
The power of fandom
Twilight carries a complicated legacy when it comes to representation of Indigenous people, an issue not lost on some longtime fans like Kayla Parker. Like many preteens of the era, her obsession started in the sixth grade, when she began reading the first Twilight young adult novel.
Enraptured by the drama, edginess and whimsy of the vampire-werewolf-romance saga, she became obsessed with the franchise.
“I read the first book, bawled my eyes out, because I was like, ‘Why will a hot, rich vampire not make me immortal and give me superpowers? This is so rude. Edward Cullen should be in love with me,’” Parker said. “I was miserable.”
In 2007 she picked up the second book in the series and immediately lost interest in the plot.
“I picked up ‘New Moon’, and it’s not even about Edward, it’s about Jacob. I was sickened, I was disgusted. I was like, ‘never mind. I’m not reading this, I can’t do it.’ So then I put it aside. I did not continue reading and I did not continue watching the series.”
But in 2015 she binged the films and devoured the four books in the series, reigniting the brief obsession that had consumed her preteen brain.
But something didn’t sit right with her, particularly the parts involving the Quileute tribe. As she grew up, Parker felt uneasy about the use of the Quileute tribe’s likeness without permission and compensation. As an avid reader and consumer of the Twilight books and films, she wanted to help right the wrongdoing of the Quileute people in her own way — through social media.
Parker now serves as a moderator for a Facebook group called “Twilight Shitposting,” created in 2020 for and by fans of the book and film series to engage with each other through jokes, memes and general conversation around the topic. Six years later, the group has amassed more than 820,000 followers and is responsible for raising $117,000, according to group moderators, for the Quileute’s Move to Higher Ground Project.
Parker said the moment the group started to gain a large following she thought she could use the group’s platform to raise funds for the tribe.
“I do believe in the power of social media. I do believe in the power of collective action. I do believe in the power of reading and media, and in the things that we read and consume,” Parker said.
Starting in September 2021, the Facebook group moderators organized an online fundraiser event, encouraging members to donate at least $1 to the Move to Higher Ground Project. That first year, $6,000 was raised, with many donating more than just the dollar. Those who donated were entered into a raffle for prizes such as book covers, getting an admin to approve a post in the group, and a copy of “The Twilight Saga: The Official Illustrated Guide.”
In the years that followed, Parker said fans have offered illustrations, merchandise, art pieces and more to be part of the prize pool for future raffles.
By 2025, the annual fundraiser had gained so much popularity that the moderators gave the first 600 donors a spot on a raffle wheel to win one of 112 prizes and raised $37,000.
“I feel like, in reality, we’re doing something very small. We didn’t start anything, we didn’t originate anything,” Parker said. “We’re really just trying to shine a light on things that have already existed.”
Reflecting on fandom culture, Parker said connection from stories is inherently human.
“I think that human beings are naturally hardwired to find community and to find connection,” she said. “The power of storytelling has been as pervasive as it has been because stories are really what connect people… Twilight is what it is — it is a story.”
Parker hopes people who were associated with the Twilight franchise see the fundraiser and use it as an opportunity to make reparations to the Quileute people.
“We would love it if we could get the attention of people like Stephanie Meyer that would kind of be like, ‘Oh, you know what, maybe I should have done that. Maybe I should use my money to put it back to some people that I should have consulted with, I should have talked with,’” Parker said.
Underscore Native News reached out Stephanie Meyer, author of the Twilight Saga for comment. She did not respond to the request.
The makeup mogul
Twilight fans can choose from a vast array of licensed merchandise: socks, backpacks, bedsets, jewelry, clothing and much more. A popular trend in recent years has been makeup collaborations with brands such as ColourPop Cosmetics and Glamlite Cosmetics.
However, many fans boycott officially licensed materials because of the franchise’s history with the Quileute Tribe. When Gisselle Hernandez, CEO and founder of Glamlite Cosmetics, announced the release of her Twilight collection on Valentine’s Day in 2025, she was shocked to see so many fans talking about the Quileute Tribe and their history.
“When I started my partnership with Twilight through Paramount, I wasn’t aware that the movies and the books had been based on real people,” she told Underscore Native News.
When fans asked her if she was going to donate to the tribes, Hernandez, who had little knowledge of the Quileute people, began looking into the tribe and their Move to Higher Ground Project.
“Anything that is important to my audience is important to me,” she said. “And so I took it upon myself to begin the research.”
After learning about the history of the Quileute people and their tense history with the franchise, Hernandez reached out to the tribal council to ask for a meeting to learn more and make a personal donation. When she heard back, she immediately canceled everything she had lined up for the week and made the seven hour journey to La Push.
“I became really involved. I really wanted to be able to meet the tribe in person because I wanted to hear firsthand from them, from tribal leaders, exactly what is happening,” she said. “Why do they need these funds? And so they could share their story with the world.”
Hernandez said she was awe-struck by the beauty of La Push and the warmth of the tribe, a place and people she didn’t know were real just months prior. In her time with the Quileute Tribal Council, she took a tour with Chairman Rio Jaime and heard about the need for funds to Move to Higher Ground.
She was moved when Jaime said as a kid he used to have to do evacuation drills in case a tsunami hit. As she toured the reservation, Hernandez filmed a TikTok to help amplify the tribe’s efforts, reaching 1.3 million followers on Instagram, Tiktok and Facebook once it was posted.
“One thing about me is when I make a donation it’s never just writing a check and handing it over to people,” she said.
Hernandez also brought attention to the tribe’s rich tourism history that existed before Twilight, encouraging people to stay at the resort on Quileute lands. But after she personally donated an undisclosed five-figure sum to the tribe and released her video, Hernandez says she faced harsh backlash from the licensor of Twilight.
“By choosing to make a personal donation to the Quileute tribe, I lost certain partnerships because it was frowned upon,” she said. “Before I made the donation, I knew of the consequences and what the retaliation would be moving forward, and I still decided to do it. I believe in doing good. I believe in doing what’s right, even if it means losing opportunities and losing certain partnerships.”
Underscore Native News reached out to Paramount Pictures for comment and they did not respond to the request.
While Hernandez had plans to live out her Twilight-fantasy through releasing a makeup collection for each book, her licensing partnership quietly ended, with an announcement about the collection leaving, and after March 31, 2026, Hernandez said Glamlite Cosmetics is no longer allowed to sell anything Twilight related.
Hernandez said companies who have entered into similar licensing agreements have been offered the same choice, though she did not name those companies.
“There’s plenty of other brands that received the same restrictions and they had the same opportunity to make the donations,” she told Underscore Native News. “And instead they chose to just follow protocol, look the other way and use the story of the Quileute Tribe to make [a] profit and completely ignore an entire population of people and benefit off their name, off their story, without making that donation, just because it means it was going to be frowned upon.”
Creative fundraising to make every dollar count
In January 2026, romance author Kelsey McKnight hosted a unique fundraiser for the Move to Higher Ground Project, raising over $1,000 by raffling off a character based on the winner to be featured in the second book of her vampire romance trilogy, “Bound by Blood.” The raffle was posted on her Instagram and TikTok, as well the “Twilight Shitposting” Facebook page.
A fan of Twilight for over two decades, McKnight said her love for the franchise didn’t mean she couldn’t critique the way the Quileute people were portrayed in the books and films.
“I didn’t have the cultural knowledge that I could have or that I should have when I was younger, and I just enjoyed the books and the movies and went on with my day,” she said.
McKnight was moved by the Quileute tribe’s Move to Higher Ground effort. And, as an avid fan of the Twilight franchise, she felt like she could help right the wrongs of consuming media without a second thought by bringing funds and awareness to the initiative.
“I’m a very small fish,” she said. “If I was a big fish, like ColourPop Cosmetics, I would funnel some of that money into the group of people that [were] fetishized.”
For a little over a week, fans donated in increments of $5 per entry. McKnight hand wrote onto raffle tickets the 600 names of eager vampire-loving fans hoping to become a character in her trilogy.
After she drew a name from her Nosferatu popcorn bucket, McKnight reached out to the winner, sent her the first book, “These Immortal Vows,” and began crafting the character of the winner for her second book. With so much enthusiasm over the raffle, McKnight added a couple of small bonus winners and featured them in the second book as well.
As she begins preparations to write the third book in her trilogy, McKnight plans to do a similar raffle but on a larger scale to support the Move to Higher Ground Project.
“It happened very quickly, and it was over very quickly, but I’m hoping that at some point I can figure out a way to do something that’s a little bit bigger,” she said. “I was pleasantly surprised that there was so much interest in that particular form of fundraising. So it is something that I think would be really helpful to do for me in the future, as far as using my work to raise awareness in a creative way.”
Phases and the future
Although the legacy of the Twilight franchise is complex, Quileute tribal officials told Underscore Native News they’re thankful for fans supporting them and their movement.
“Twilight fans from around the world have shown up in meaningful ways,” the tribal council wrote in an email. “Many have turned awareness into action through donations, advocacy, and helping spread the word about the Move to Higher Ground initiative. Many fans’ donations reflect a broader desire to acknowledge Indigenous communities and support real-world needs connected to popular culture narratives.”
As an ambitious long‑term relocation effort, the project’s timeline is expected to last many years and will constantly be evolving. Development will occur in stages and depend on grants, infrastructure costs and construction timelines. Throughout the process, donations from fans will be essential for housing, community facilities and safety infrastructure.
“For all of us involved with the Move to Higher Ground initiative, the support from fans has been a powerful example of how pop culture can inspire real-world compassion and action,” the tribal council wrote. “We want everyone to know that we see you and we truly appreciate you. We see and hear your genuine desire to learn about who we are and how you can support our real life challenges.”
“Whether a donation is large or small, every single one matters,” the council continued. “What means the most to us is knowing that fans are giving what they can from the heart, and that kind of support is something we will never take for granted.”
Correction: The story previously stated the Quileute Tribe was not consulted during the creation of the Twilight Saga. Those references have been removed in response to the tribe’s clarification that filmmakers did consult them, although they did not receive compensation.

title: ‘I’m coming home’: Last words haunt a 9/11 daughter 25 years later as she builds a legacy in his honor
content:
"I'm getting out. I'm coming home."
Those were the final words of William Lawrence Fallon Jr. before he was killed in the 9/11 terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center 25 years ago.
He worked as an IT manager for Cantor Fitzgerald and was just 38 years old when he was killed.
I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES
His daughter Kayla Fallon Smith was 8 years old when she learned her father would not be coming home.
Before the attacks, Smith, now 33, said her father – who always commuted into work early – would call the house phone in the morning to wish her and her sister well before they would head to school.

📸 Instagram: kelsiecairns_tv
🎥 Facebook: Kelsie Cairns
He went in early so he could leave earlier in the afternoons to take her to dancing school after her school day.
"That was the kind of man he was. I remember he would get up and work out in the morning before even going to work, so you'd hear the weights dropping in the house. I do remember that as a kid," Smith said.
Those quick and light-hearted morning phone calls to his daughters set the tone for the day.
"He would tell us what the skyline looked like. Sometimes it would be cloudy below him and he couldn't even see the street, but it'd be sunny up there," she said.
FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE
Smith remembers hearing her father's voice for the last time on Tuesday, Sept. 11, 2001.
"I spoke to him on the house phone that day, as I always did," she said, to which he said on the phone, "Have a good morning," she said.
"I'm sure I said something like, 'I love you, have a great day'," Smith said.
Her dad called again that fateful morning – sometime after the first tower was hit.
SALVATION ARMY RESPONDER OPENS UP ON 9/11 CANCER BATTLE, PHONE CALL THAT CHANGED HIS LIFE
This time, her mother answered the phone.
"He said something to the degree of, 'I'm getting out, I'm coming home,' and that was it," she said.
Smith's mother replied and said, "What are you talking about?" He responded and said, "Turn on the news."
After that he hung up.
9/11 DEATH TOLL KEEPS GROWING DECADES LATER AS TOXIC EXPOSURE HAUNTS SURVIVORS
His family never heard from him again.
"Those words haunt me a little bit," Smith said. "Every year, grief is different. It doesn't go away. It's a myth when people say that time heals all wounds; it doesn't."
In the last 25 years of growing up without her father, Smith has turned her pain and grief into purpose. She's devoted her life to helping others living with grief and mental struggles.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Smith is a licensed mental health counselor who founded Trails of Purpose – a nonprofit organization that provides free mental health counseling and equine-assisted therapy to military members, veterans, first responders and their families.
"As I was getting my graduate degree, I started to experience equine-assisted therapy, and I really—it just clicked for me," she said.
She went on to say, "I never experienced that as a kid, and I had a lot of trauma therapy growing up. The resources were abundant for 9/11 victims, and I never experienced equine therapy."
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
She started her organization in 2019.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
"I needed a place to just be when my brain always felt on fire. I think I've created that, and it's seeming to resonate with other people."
Trails of Purpose has offered 30,000 hours of free mental health counseling and equine-assisted therapy to military members and first responders.
"The horses, and the connection that they have when when words don't seem to to come, the horses can just be with you," she said.

"I created the thing that I think I needed: community and understanding, and a place that's safe, and quiet, and a respite," she said.
As she helps others heal, Smith said she'll never stop sharing her father's story.

title: Desolador panorama del trato que reciben los jóvenes indígenas en el sistema de justicia australiano
content:
Este artículo es parte de la serie Spotlight de Global Voices de agosto “Derechos indígenas”. Esta serie ofrece una visión de las vidas y experiencias de los pueblos indígenas, de las conexiones a través de regiones, experiencias indígenas y contar las historias de líderes, activistas y miembros de la comunidad y más. Puedes apoyar este reportaje con una donación.
Mientras los activistas continúan luchando por eliminar la desigualdad en la comunidad indígena en Australia, una reciente actualización de la Comisión de Productividad del Gobierno australiano muestra un panorama sombrío de la desigualdad dentro del sistema de justicia, sobre todo para los jóvenes indígenas. El informe es parte del Acuerdo Nacional para Cerrar la Brecha, que busca «hacer posible que los aborígenes e isleños del Estrecho de Torres y los Gobiernos trabajen juntos para dejar atrás la desigualdad que viven los aborígenes e isleños del Estrecho de Torres y lograr resultados de vida iguales a los de todos los australianos».
El informe señaló que la detención de indígenas está en aumento, mientras que hay una enorme desproporción de jóvenes de las Primeras Naciones en el sistema penitenciario australiano:
The rate of First Nations prisoners jumped to more than 2,500 per 100,000 adults in 2025 and up from more than 2,300 a year earlier and more than 550 in 2019.
… First Nations youths remain heavily over-represented in detention, with 25.7 children aged 10–17 per 10,000 in custody on an average day in 2024-25 and ‘‘no change from the baseline’’ towards the target of a 30 per cent cut by 2031.
El índice de prisioneros de las Primeras Naciones pasó a más de 2500 cada 100,000 adultos en 2025, de más de 2300 un año antes y más de 550 en 2029.
…los jóvenes de las Primeras Naciones siguen siendo abrumadora mayoría en las detenciones, con 25,7 niños de entre 10-17 años cada 10,000 en arrestados en un día promedio entre 2024 y 2025.
El Servicio Legal para Aborígenes e Isleños del Estrecho de Torres resaltó que, en comparación con el promedio de otras poblaciones, a los jóvenes de las Primeras Naciones lo detienen sin sentencia mucho más tiempo:
The average length of time spent in unsentenced detention was 57.2 days, with the highest average in Queensland at 96.3 days and Victoria at 81.1 days.
El promedio de tiempo de arresto sin sentencia fue de 57.2 días; el promedio más alto es el de Queensland con 96.3 días y Victoria con 81.1 días.
El gerente general del Servicio Legal para Aborígenes e Isleños del Estrecho de Torres, Nick Espie, fue incisivo con los últimos hallazgos:
The data shows that yet again, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children — who have had no finding of guilt against them — are being locked up at alarming rates and for alarming amounts of time.
The evidence is clear that when a child spends time behind bars, it increases their likelihood of reoffending. Not only is this approach cruel and damaging to our children and their families, governments are spending almost AUD 3,200 on locking up children, a measure we know makes communities less safe.
Los datos muestran que, una vez más, los niños aborígenes e isleños del Estrecho de Torres —a quienes no se los ha declarado culpables de ningún delito— son detenidos a un ritmo alarmante y por una preocupante cantidad de tiempo.
La evidencia es clara. Cuando un niño pasa tiempo tras las rejas, aumenta la probabilidad de reincidencia. No solo este planteamiento es cruel y perjudicial para nuestros niños y sus familias, los Gobiernos están gastando casi 3200 dólares australianos en encerrar niños, una medida que sabemos que hace mas inseguras a las comunidades.
En mayo de 2026, la Oficina de Derechos Humanos de Naciones Unidas se refirió a este problema y destacó que:
The UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination today expressed alarm over the persistent overrepresentation of Indigenous children in Australia’s criminal justice system, warning that this reflects systemic and structural racial discrimination against Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.
… In several states and territories in Australia, the minimum age of criminal responsibility is lower than the threshold under international human rights law and standards, and in some cases is as low as 10 years old.
Hoy, el Comité para la Eliminación de la Discriminación Racial de la Naciones Unidas ha expresado alarma acerca de la gran desproporción de niños indígenas en el sistema de justicia penal australiano, y advierte que esto refleja discriminación sistémica y estructural contra las comunidades aborígenes e isleñas del Estrecho de Torres.
… En varios estados y territorios de Australia, la edad mínima de imputabilidad es más baja que el límite bajo la ley internacional de derechos humanos, y en algunos casos llega a los 10 años.
El Servicio Legal para Aborígenes e Isleños del Estrecho de Torres fue una de las más de 200 organizaciones que firmaron una carta abierta para el primer ministro australiano, Anthony Albanese, que llamaba al Gobierno a tomar acción de manera urgente:
From coast to coast across our lands, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children are being criminalised and imprisoned at alarming rates because of political point-scoring rather than evidence-based reforms.
This is an emergency.We… are urging you to call an emergency summit on youth justice, so that key decision makers in government can listen to the voices of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander legal experts and leaders in a setting where community-controlled organisations lead the discussion.
De costa a costa a lo largo de nuestra tierra, a los niños aborígenes e isleños del Estrecho de Torres se les criminaliza y encarcela a un ritmo alarmante por buscar rédito político en lugar de reformas hechas con datos contrastados.
Esta es una emergencia.Los instamos a convocar a una cumbre de emergencia para darle justicia a los jóvenes, para que quienes toman decisiones en el Gobierno puedan escuchar las voces de los expertos legales y líderes aborígenes e isleños del estrecho de Torres en un ámbito donde las organizaciones controladas por la comunidad dirijan la discusión.
Amnistía Internacional Australia inició su campaña Kids Need Better en agosto de 2026, que pide justicia por los jóvenes indígenas:
Únete a a la nueva era de nuestra campaña de justicia para los jóvenes indígenas.
————-
📣¡Esta noche es la gran noche! ¡Confirma tu asistencia en el enlace en la biografía!Nos vemos en línea esta noche para escuchar al tío Rodney Dillon, a Kacey Teerman, a Anne Hollonds y a Satara Uthayakumaran.
Acompáñanos mientras damos a conocer la visión detrás de la campaña, lo que hemos aprendido al trabajar junto a las comunidades de las Primeras Naciones, nuestros simpatizantes y expertos, y cómo juntos podemos construir un futuro en el que cada niño sea tratado con dignidad y humanidad.
Rodney Dillon, anciano de la Nación de Palawa en lutruwita (Tasmania), presentó la campaña en este video:
El video presenta algunas soluciones que llevarían al sistema penitenciario de Australia a ser más justo:
We’re calling on governments to establish enforceable minimum standards for the treatment of children in custody, raise the age of criminal responsibility to at least 14, invest in Indigenous-led community solutions, and end harmful detention practices. Because every child deserves dignity, care and the opportunity to thrive.
Pedimos que los Gobiernos establezcan parámetros mínimos ejecutables para el trato de los niños detenidos, que aumenten la edad de imputabilidad a los 14 años como mínimo, que inviertan en soluciones comunitarias y que detengan las prácticas de detención dañinas. Porque los niños merecen dignidad, cuidados y la oportunidad de prosperar.
La petición en línea de Amnistía Internacional destaca algunas novedades de algunos Gobiernos y estados. Por ejemplo:
In the Northern Territory, the minimum age a child can be imprisoned has been lowered to 10, spit hoods have been reintroduced, and children continue to be held in overcrowded youth detention centers and police watch houses. Almost every child in detention is First Nations.
En el territorio norte, la edad mínima de imputabilidad en la que un niño puede ser detenido bajó a 10 años, han vuelto a usar capuchas antisaliva y a los niños los siguen deteniendo en comisarías y en centros de detención para jóvenes que están sobrepoblados. Casi todos los niños detenidos son de las Primeras Naciones.
Las capuchas antisaliva son riesgosas y hasta mortales, y fueron prohibidas en el territorio norte junto con las sillas de sujeción luego de una escándalo nacional en 2017, pero luego fueron restablecidas en 2025.
En 2025, el informe de la Comisión de Derechos Humanos australiana, «Help Way Earlier!», mostró un panorama perturbador de cómo el sistema de justicia australiano maltrata a los niños:
On an average day, 4,542 children across Australia were under youth justice supervision.
57 percent were Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children
Indigenous children were 23 times more likely to be under supervision and 28 times more likely to be in detention than non-Indigenous children
En un día promedio, 4542 niños en Australia están bajo supervisión de la justicia juvenil.
El 57% son niños aborígenes e isleños del Estrecho de Torres.
Los niños indígenas son 23 veces más propensos a estar bajo supervisión y 28 veces más propensos a ser detenidos que los niños no indígenas.
Los principales hallazgos incluyen:
Many children in contact with child justice systems have experiences of poverty, violence, abuse, intergenerational trauma, mental health issues, homelessness, drug and alcohol abuse, and neurodevelopmental disabilities.
Many are in the child protection systems or living in out-of-home care.
If children at risk are supported earlier on — whether in the community, in detention, or when released from detention — they are less likely to be involved in criminal activity, keeping them and our communities safe.
Muchos niños en contacto con los sistemas de justicia infantil viven la pobreza, violencia, abuso, trauma intergeneracional, problemas de salud mental, situación de calle, adicción a las drogas y al alcohol, y discapacidades de desarrollo neurológico.
Muchos están en el sistema de protección de menores o viven bajo tutela fuera del hogar.
Si los niños en riesgo tienen apoyo temprano —ya sea en la comunidad, durante su detención o cuando son liberados— es menos probable que terminen involucrados en actividades delictivas, preservando su seguridad y la de las comunidades.
Anne Hollonds, ex comisionada nacional para la infancia de Australia, explicó el informe en este video:
Estos informes sostienen firmemente que las medidas duras y punitivas no están funcionando. Detener un niño por un año cuesta un millón de dólares australianos (700,000 dólares estadounidenses), y los detractores argumentan que es momento de intentar algo diferente.
Aunque algunos estados tienen diferencias y otras iniciativas para reducir las detenciones de jóvenes indígenas, los activistas aseguran que no hay progreso suficiente para reducir esta vergüenza nacional.
El senador Malarndirri McCarthy, ministro federal para los indígenas australianos, urge a los Gobiernos estatales y territorios a hacer más.
State and territory governments must also back in their commitments under the National Agreement with investments and policies that improve outcomes for First Nations people.
Los Gobiernos estatales y territoriales también deben respaldar sus compromisos en virtud del Acuerdo Nacional con inversiones y políticas que mejoren la situación de los pueblos de las Primeras Naciones.
La presentación del seminario web de la campaña de Amnistía Internacional incluye pedidos de jóvenes en prisión en Australia. Se puede ver el video de 50 minutos debajo.

title: The Prime Minister’s Literary Award winners include a collective Yolŋu novel – and a murder trial
content:
This year’s winners of the Prime Minister’s Literary Awards query the instability of Australian identity. And the winners of the fiction and nonfiction prizes both point to the cruel legacy of European invasion and colonialism.
A brave and moving historical Yolŋu novel, A Piece of Red Cloth, has won the fiction prize. It was collectively authored by Yolŋu knowledge holders Merrkiyawuy Ganambar-Stubbs, Djawa Burarrwanga and Djawundil Maymuru, and novelist Leonie Norrington.
A pioneering collaboration between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal writers that honours Yolŋu ancestors through the eyes of their descendants, it represents a healing opportunity for Australian culture. As Norrington says, “Aboriginal people, since the first invaders came, have been trying to say, ‘Look, we have a really wonderful way of understanding the world, and you can learn from it.’”
Described by the judges as “a profound work of remembrance, fusing oral history, novelistic technique and deep cultural knowledge”, this innovative book also received this year’s Australian Book Industry Award for Social Impact Book of the Year. It has been shortlisted for multiple prizes.
The nonfiction prize winner, Walkley Award-winning journalist Kate Wild’s The Red House, is a gripping exposé of race and power within contemporary Australia – explored through the tragic killing of Kumanjayi Walker in 2019, and the subsequent murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. It’s also no stranger to literary prizes, having won this year’s Age Non-fiction Book of the Year.
Play, emotion and imagination
Turkish–Australian Ender Başkan’s playful and expansive Two Hundred Million Musketeers has won the poetry prize. Rohan Howitt’s consideration of Australia’s claims to the Antarctic, The Southern Frontier, was awarded the Australian history prize.
Both prizes for younger readers went to verse novels. Drift by Pip Harry, which follows two 14-year-olds as they navigate fitting in and deal with anxiety (and bees), won for young adult literature. And Song of a Thousand Seas by Zana Fraillon, which looks at friendship and different brains through the eyes of an octopus, won for children’s literature.
These are stories about kin, culture and belonging, migration, settlement and territorial rights. They pick at the loose threads of psychological and physical definitions of what it means to be Australian. Their fresh perspectives explore and interrogate ideas of home and nationhood, ownership and entitlement – with imagination, rigour and heartfelt emotion.
The awards, delivered by Creative Australia, boast the biggest prize pool in the country. The winners of each category receive A$80,000, with A$5,000 each for shortlisted writers.
‘True history’ as fiction
A Piece of Red Cloth, set in the 1600s, tells the story of Batjani, a Yolŋu elder trying to protect her beloved granddaughter, Garritji, from Makassan trepang fishermen on the coast of Arnhem Land. The story opens up a complex and unfamiliar chapter of pre-colonial Australian history.
For hundreds of years, trading between Yolŋu and seafarers from the port of Makassar, now eastern Indonesia, took place without issue. But when European merchants claimed the region as the Dutch East Indies, a new chapter of brutality was introduced.
The Makassan traders adopted the cruel tactics of their colonisers, and began plying Yolŋu men with opium and alcohol. In exchange, they claimed the young women and children, and took them for sex-trafficking, until the the elder Yolŋu women rose up in protest.
The novel reimagines these facts as Batjani does her best to protect Garritji, who is approaching womanhood, from the fishermen. “It’s a true history,” says Ganambarr-Stubbs, whose own grandmother was snatched in a similar scenario. “Wider Australia should learn more about the history – all the histories – because that’s how all of us came to be here now.”
Nonfiction: ongoing race inequity
The Red House highlights the ongoing inequities of race in Australia. In her investigation of the legacy of Australia’s colonial past, journalist Kate Wild seeks ways to break the cycle of dehumanisation and state violence that continues to plague this country.
With precision and care, she recounts the confrontation between Walker and Rolfe in an isolated desert community, and tracks the aftermath of Rolfe’s high-profile, emotionally charged court case. Her report reveals the depth of Australia’s damaged and unresolved relationship with its First Nations peoples.
An outsider, she nevertheless finds ways to integrate Warlpiri and Luritj perspectives with care and respect, laying down a challenge to those involved in the work of communicating First Nations stories.
Her book was praised by the judges as a work “of great listening” that “embeds the reader in a supratemporal zone beyond Western ideas of time, history and narrative in order to trace repeating patterns of violence, rhetoric, pain and anger”. It represents a nuanced, compassionate contribution to a critical ongoing national conversation about race, culture, history and entitlement.
A story of transgenerational trauma, difficult questions and unfinished business, Wild’s work takes on issues that many Australians still prefer to avoid or deny. It presses for an end to a situation that appears to have no resolution.
Poetry: fatherhood in an uncertain world
With his debut poetry collection, Two Hundred Million Musketeers, Ender Başkan captures the intensity of parenting young children within an increasingly uncertain world.
Fatherhood impacts his work, friendships and creative practice in inner-city Melbourne. It alters his awareness of social and political concerns, and shifts his attention from the past and the present into the future.
Dealing in connection and bustling with life, Başkan’s poems reflect on his childhood, his grandparents’ exile from Türkiye (where Başkan returns, with his young family), and on being Turkish. He explores his responsibilities to child-rearing and housekeeping, the need to earn a living and to care for older generations.
Başkan has been critically hailed as a writer whose “main point is that poetry can and should be fun”. He won the 2021 Overland Judith Wright Poetry Prize, and the 2025 Anne Elder Award.
His work continues the legacy of migrant poets that included his close friend and mentor, the late Ania Walwicz. According to the judges, Başkan offers “an invitation to explore what might be possible if a line were to stretch between one person and another”.

title: Indigenous fisherwoman finds ‘lost’ spinach pipefish, not seen by science in 40 years
content:
Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries.
On the final day of a two-week expedition, where researchers were searching for a “lost” species along Papua New Guinea’s Sepik River, Helen Asu arrived with two small, greenish-brown fish. She had caught them while fishing for prawns with an umben, a traditional hand net, near Imbando village in East Sepik province.
They were spinach pipefish (Microphis spinachioides), a species known only from the Sepik and not recorded by scientists since 1985, reports Mongabay’s Spoorthy Raman.
“It was honestly an incredible moment,” said Jerrica Agebigo, a researcher at the Papua New Guinea University of Technology and the New Guinea Binatang Research Centre, who led the expedition. “When Helen showed the fish to us, I immediately realized that we had found something very special.”
The spinach pipefish is a freshwater relative of seahorses and seadragons. It grows to about 15 centimeters (6 inches) and uses its elongated snout to catch small prey. Its coloring helps conceal it among water lilies and other plants along the banks of the Sepik, Papua New Guinea’s longest river.
Almost everything else about it remains uncertain. The specimen used to describe the species was held at Hamburg’s natural history museum, but was destroyed during the second world war. When the fish was last assessed for the IUCN Red List in 2016, it was classified as data deficient. It later became one of the 10 most sought-after species on the “Lost Fishes” list, compiled by SHOAL, Re:wild and the IUCN Freshwater Fish Specialist Group. The wider list includes more than 300 freshwater fishes missing to science.
Agebigo’s team, made up of local scientists and community members, set out in June to learn whether the pipefish still survived and, if so, what threats it faced. Along the Sepik river they showed pictures to residents and asked fishers whether they recognized it. On June 18, Asu supplied the answer.
The rediscovery will allow scientists to begin filling gaps in knowledge left by four decades without a confirmed record of the fish.
“The fact that a species could go without a confirmed record for around four decades — and then be found through the daily activities of a local fisher — is a powerful reminder of the importance of local ecological knowledge,” Agebigo said. “Without Helen’s knowledge, experience and willingness to help us, we may not have found the species.”
Read the full story by Spoorthy Raman here

title: 9/11: I want my dad to be remembered as the hero he was
content:
9/11: I want my dad to be remembered as the hero he was
- Published
Ever since he was a young boy and his father relocated to the USA, Godwin Forde had dreamt of living there too.
In September 2001, he was finally old enough to fly out on his own and visit his dad, Godwin Forde senior, and make plans to finish school in the States.
He never got the chance.
His father was one of 67 British people who died in the deadly al-Qaeda attack on the World Trade Centre on September 11, 2001.
Godwin's sister Charlene, then 19 years old, had just moved to live in New York with her dad a week before.
Instead of the happy family reunion they'd always imagined, Godwin's first trip to the US was spent searching New York in vain for the father he'd waited years to reconnect with.
On the day of the attacks, Godwin recalled that he had just returned from school and was planning to go out with his friends, when his foster mum asked him to stay in and wait for a phone call from his sister.
"I took a seat, the news was on, and you could see all the images," he recalled.
Godwin, who is from north-west London, felt uneasy because his dad and sister were living in New York, but as he wasn't aware his father was working in one of the twin towers, he had no reason to be unduly concerned.
Godwin senior worked in security, and had previously worked at Fox News and on the David Letterman show.
He was a fairly well-known figure, often spotted in the background of TV programmes, once reportedly even making a cameo appearance on the FX TV Show Breakfast Time.
But unknown to Godwin junior, he'd recently been promoted to head up a security team on one of the upper floors of the South Tower at the World Trade Centre.
When his sister Charlene rang from New York, she was worried.
"She was explaining that, she hadn't heard from Dad yet. No-one had seen him, and no-one else had heard from him.
"At that point, I just wanted to get to her, to make sure she was OK," explained Forde.
"It was a waiting game."
Godwin flew over to New York two weeks later, and the teenagers searched for their father together, putting up posters, ringing helplines, heading to the pier where there were camps of people anxiously waiting for news of relatives.
They were mostly alone, with some help from the Red Cross.
It wasn't until the end of October that year that they got confirmation that their father hadn't survived.
"We finally got the death certificate. We had to plan a memorial. We couldn't even plan a funeral. We had no body, no belongings."
The siblings eventually heard two stories about what might have happened to their dad.
One of them came from a colleague who was with him at the time when the attacks happened, and she had made it out.
Godwin had the chance to speak to her.
"They used to call him Mr G, she told me. He told her to go and find her way out, but he said he needed to stay to clear everyone and anyone else he could find."
There was also another version of the story.
"One story I heard was that he'd made it out, heard more people were inside so he ran back in, and that's when the building collapsed. But then the other story was that he didn't actually come out at all, and he stayed in, ferrying whoever he could to the exits.
"Either way, both stories are heroic however you look at it."
Since Godwin Forde's death, nothing for his son has been the same.
"I didn't manage to move to the States. That plan got completely derailed. Other goals I had at the time also changed."
What happens for him on September 11th each year, when images of the attacks fill our screens?
"I normally leave the country for a month if possible, and kind of disappear off the grid," he says.
"This year I'm here, and I'm kind of just going through the motions, really."
It's hard to explain to anyone what he has suffered and what he is still suffering, because who else can really understand?
"There is only a select few people who know. It's not something I discuss," he explains.
"Something like this you can never get used to. Having someone taken away like that, you never really get over it."
'Lucky to be half of what he was'
For Godwin there are still mixed emotions about what happened.
There is undoubtedly a sense of deep pride and love for his father.
There is the grief and sadness.
But there are conflicting emotions too.
"There are times when you do get upset and angry at him based on the fact that we are here, and he could have come home.
"But at the same time I do understand that he did his duty and I feel like I would have probably done the same thing."
Godwin would like his father to be remembered as the "hero that he was".
"Someone that would literally go out of his way for anyone," says Godwin.
"I would be lucky if I could be just half of what he was."

title: En el Ateneo Luis Mariano Rivera de Carúpano rindieron honor a la Virgen del Valle
content:
El Ateneo Luis Mariano Rivera de Carúpano, municipio Bermúdez del estado Sucre, rindió homenaje a la Patrona de Oriente, la Virgen del Valle, con una velada cultural que incluyó la celebración de una Rucaristía, que presidió el presbítero Jesús Villarroel, párroco de la catedral; además de una exposición de imágenes de "Vallita" hechas por artistas locales; así como una muestra de danza, cantos y para cerrar un galerón.
Auristela Tenías, comisionada de Turismo y Cultura de la institución dijo que pidieron a la Virgen que sea inspiración para un Carúpano más humano y cristiano.
La velada contó con la participación de los grupos de danza Expresión Dramática Octágono, Fundación Niño Jesús, la Escuela de Ballet y Danza Domingo Renault y la escuela de ballet y danza Lucy Cordero de la Casa de la Cultura de Playa Grande.
Resaltó la realización del galerón infantil con la Fundación Cultural Guaraúnos, con cinco niños que cantaron décimas a la Santa Virgen. También contaron con la participación del grupo de cuerdas del ateneo, el cantante Elías Rodríguez y la cultora Catalina Núñez.
Recordar
Por su parte, el padre Jesús Villarroel señaló que a la Virgen del Valle no se le celebra solo un día, sino que es una devoción constante para los orientales.
“Este día nos expresa que la Virgen del Valle no es un día, es todos los días. Para los orientales esta celebración se prolonga, por eso hoy seguimos celebrando la fiesta de nuestra madre”.
Villarroel recordó a los fallecidos por los terremotos y pidió orar por ellos, “Pedimos por tantos hermanos venezolanos fallecidos y también recordando todo este acontecimiento que vivió nuestro país”, señaló.
