title: Ecuador: el conflicto de tierras comunales detrás de la detención del dirigente indígena Julián Cruz
content:
- El ex presidente de la Comuna Ancestral Chojón fue detenido el 20 de julio de 2026 tras ser acusado de hurto.
- Su detención se dio en medio de una disputa territorial con una camaronera.
- En 2012, la comunidad recibió su título comunal ancestral, pero una sentencia encontró que el Ministerio de Agricultura concesionó parte de esas tierras a compañías acuícolas.
- El dirigente está detenido en la Penitenciaría del Litoral, que enfrenta graves problemas de violencia carcelaria, insalubridad y hacinamiento.
El 9 y 10 de septiembre se llevó a cabo la audiencia en etapa de prueba por el caso de hurto de camarón contra Julián Cruz, dirigente indígena de la isla Puná, en Guayaquil. Detrás de su detención, el pasado 20 de julio, existe un conflicto por tierras ancestrales entre la Comuna Ancestral Chojón y empresas camaroneras. Una de esas empresas es Naturisa SA, la misma que lo acusó ante las autoridades. Su defensa dice que él no ordenó el supuesto robo, no participó del hecho y que no estaba en la isla ese 21 de junio de 2023.
Telmo Jaramillo, abogado del Comité Permanente por la Defensa de los Derechos Humanos (CDH), relata que hasta el momento, dos abogados de la empresa rindieron sus testimonios durante la reciente audiencia. El letrado sostiene que los hombres no presenciaron los hechos, pero señalan a Cruz como culpable. Sin embargo, dice Jaramillo, en el contrainterrogatorio no demostraron que tienen pruebas de su participación, como imágenes de cámaras, ni de que el dirigente haya dado la orden a otros comuneros. Mongabay Latam intentó comunicarse con un representante de la compañía pero no recibió respuestas sobre este punto del conflicto.
Leer más | Perú: último ataque a Olivia Bisa vuelve a exponer debilidades en la protección a líderes indígenas
Cruz, presidente de la Federación de Comunas y Organizaciones del Pueblo Punae (FECOOPE) y ex dirigente de la comuna, asistió de manera telemática a la audiencia, ya que desde ese 20 de julio está recluido en la Penitenciaría del Litoral. La cárcel enfrenta problemas de hacinamiento e insalubridad “muy duros”, en palabras de Billy Navarrete, presidente del CDH, y es uno de los principales escenarios de la violencia carcelaria en el país.
Bandas armadas controlan la penitenciaría y están extorsionando a los familiares, afirma el abogado. “Les estamos orientando en relación al control criminal que hay en la cárcel. Lo que ahora nos preocupa es que se garantice la vida y la integridad física a los privados de libertad”, dice. La audiencia continuará el 25 de septiembre.
El conflicto de tierras se remonta a 1996, cuando camaroneras se instalaron en la zona. “Cuando recién vinieron, construyeron piscinas, talaron mangles, árboles, montañas, removieron una loma que era patrimonio. Todo eso denunciamos, pero no se sacó nada”, dice a Mongabay Latam Pedro Cruz, hermano de Julián y presidente de Chojón.
“No existe ningún conflicto con la comuna”, asegura vía correo electrónico César Palma, representante de Naturisa, pues “ya existe un pronunciamiento judicial sobre el tema”. Se refiere a una acción de protección que en primera instancia reconoció la violación de los derechos comunitarios, pero en segunda instancia revirtió la decisión inicial.
“Se trata de una disputa de tierras que, por la intervención de organismos del Estado, correspondería ser conocida en la vía contenciosa administrativa”, se lee en la sentencia. Para Jaramillo, los jueces de la Corte Provincial “no se pronunciaron sobre el fondo del conflicto, como sí lo hizo el juez de primer nivel”.
“Paralelamente, como elemento intimidatorio, surge el delito de hurto. No nos queda duda de que es una estrategia de la camaronera para debilitar el reclamo de la comuna, para debilitar a sus dirigentes”, afirma Billy Navarrete, presidente del CDH.
La entrada de las camaroneras a Chojón
La actividad camaronera llegó a la zona en la década de 1980, cuando la comunidad impulsó la construcción de piscinas administradas por la Asociación 24 de Septiembre, relata Galo Plaza, investigador del desarrollo rural y técnico de territorios de la Confederación de Nacionalidades y Pueblos Indígenas de la Costa Ecuatoriana (CONAICE).
Puná es una de las parroquias más pobres del cantón Guayaquil, con acceso limitado a servicios, como agua potable, educación y salud, describe Navarrete. “De esto se aprovechó la industria camaronera para cooptar a la población y sus dirigentes”, añade.
La asociación operó con normalidad hasta 1996, cuando uno de sus representantes habría cedido varias hectáreas a un inversionista a través de una empresa privada.
El 31 de diciembre de 1996, la fuerza pública ingresó a Chojón, allanó viviendas y detuvo a 13 hombres y una mujer. Estuvieron detenidos cerca de tres meses, cuentan Pedro Cruz y Plaza, quien ha acompañado a la comunidad por varios años y también levantó una memoria escrita de este hecho, a la que accedió Mongabay Latam.
«Se los trató de piratas venidos de Durán. Ahora se los acusa de hurto», señala comparando aquellos hechos con la actual denuncia contra Julián Cruz.
Para 2009, las piscinas de la empresa ya ocupaban cerca de 100 hectáreas con 13 piscinas camaroneras, reportó El Universo.
Entre 1985 y 2016, Puná perdió 5648 hectáreas de manglar, mientras la superficie ocupada por diferentes empresas camaroneras aumentó en 7013 hectáreas, según un estudio que analizó el avance de la industria en la isla de aproximadamente 92 000 hectáreas.
«Tenemos varios años luchando, peleando con invasores, gente que no es de la isla, nos han invadido, se apropiaron de tierras», dice Pedro Cruz.
El Estado concesionó parte del territorio ancestral a camaroneras
Chojón forma parte de la parroquia rural Puná, en el golfo de Guayaquil. Con cerca de 250 habitantes, es una comunidad ancestral reconocida por la Secretaría de Gestión y Desarrollo de Pueblos y Nacionalidades. En 2012 se oficializó el título comunal por 209.31 hectáreas.
Tras varias idas y vueltas administrativas, de las 209 hectáreas tituladas, la comuna conserva solo 61, según consta en la acción de protección. “Estas tierras ancestrales han sido adjudicadas arbitrariamente por el MAG”, asegura Plaza.
En la sentencia que otorgó la acción de protección a la comunidad el 6 de junio de 2023, se ordenó dejar sin efecto la resolución de Rectificación de Providencia de Adjudicación a favor de Naturisa. “[Esta acción] vulneró el derecho de las comunidades, pueblos y nacionalidades en la garantía de la propiedad imprescriptible, la indivisibilidad” del territorio, se lee en el documento.
Leer más | Cuando el zoológico se convierte en laboratorio: la ciencia que revela especies invisibles
También dejó en firme la adjudicación de las 209 hectáreas a favor de la comunidad y ordenó la restitución inmediata de las tierras ancestrales. Además, dispuso el desalojo inmediato de personas ajenas a la comunidad del territorio comunal.
Por eso, se ordenó que Naturisa repare y/o compense a la Comunidad Ancestral Chojón. Por último, se ordenó que el MAG y la Subsecretaría de Tierras y Reforma Agraria publiquen en sus páginas web institucionales disculpas públicas a la comunidad por la vulneración de sus derechos constitucionales.
No obstante, esto quedó sin efecto tras la sentencia de segunda instancia. Palma, representante de Naturisa, explica que “existe un acuerdo emitido por la Subsecretaría de Acuacultura que estableció que tal área corresponde a superficie considerada zona de playa y bahía, como tal, [son] terrenos que solo pueden pertenecer al Estado”. Sobre esta área, Naturisa asegura tener un acuerdo de concesión.
Mongabay Latam solicitó la versión del MAG, vía el Portal de Transparencia de la Defensoría del Pueblo, pero, a pesar de las insistencias vía correo electrónico y vía mensajería, no recibió respuesta hasta la publicación del artículo.
Denuncia de hurto y acuerdo con la comunidad
El 21 de junio de 2023, la empresa envió una carta a José Antonio Camposano, entonces presidente de la Cámara Nacional de Acuacultura, en la que denunció un intento de invasión y robo de 30 000 libras de camarón. Miembros de la comuna y otra camaronera fueron señalados como responsables.
El 22 junio, 16 días después de que se aceptara la acción de protección, Naturisa presentó la denuncia contra Julián Cruz en la Fiscalía General del Estado, según se documenta en el Módulo de Información de Noticias de Delito de la institución. En ese entonces, Cruz era el presidente de Chojón.
Esa misma fecha, el líder dirigió una carta a Camposano en la que calificó la denuncia de Naturisa como “temeraria y calumniosa”. Mongabay Latam accedió a las cartas de ambas partes.
A pesar de estas acusaciones, en octubre de 2025, la compañía firmó un acuerdo con el pueblo indígena por los “evidentes errores cometidos al momento de haberse otorgado la adjudicación en favor de la Comuna Chojón” y con el fin de “evitar nuevos equívocos en cuanto a la ocupación del área de zona de playa y bahía que actualmente tiene Naturisa y que por adjudicación le corresponde a la Comuna Chojón”.
El CDH envió a Mongabay Latam este documento, que está notariado en el cantón Guayaquil. Este medio llamó y envió emails insistentemente a César Palma para consultarle sobre su participación en el acuerdo y sobre el avance del cumplimiento de los términos, pero no respondió a la solicitud.
En el acuerdo consta que la empresa se comprometió a entregar a la comunidad 130 000 dólares, a realizar obras de mejoramiento de las piscinas comunitarias contiguas a Naturisa y a no continuar con la acusación particular presentada ni a ejecutar impulso alguno del proceso judicial propuesto en contra de Julián Cruz.
“Si hubo hurto, ¿cómo llega la empresa a un acuerdo?”, cuestiona el abogado Jaramillo. La comunidad, por su lado, se comprometió a no presentar acciones de índole administrativo o judicial relacionados con los terrenos que ocupa la compañía Naturisa.
Un caso “sin indicios”
Jaramillo asegura que el fiscal no tiene ninguna versión que diga que Cruz estuvo presente el día de los hechos ni que dio la orden para cometer el hurto. Además, según el testimonio del líder indígena, no estuvo ese día en isla Puná, pues estaba viajando de regreso de Quito. El abogado también afirma haber conversado con varios comuneros que ratificaron esa versión. Tampoco se ha demostrado, enfatiza, que personas de la comuna fueran las responsables de extraer el camarón.
“A mi criterio, nunca existieron indicios, pero el juez llamó a Julián a juicio, por eso el caso pasó al tribunal penal y nos encontramos en esta instancia”, detalla el abogado.
La Fiscalía General del Estado dijo a Mongabay Latam que el expediente contra Cruz se originó por un Parte Informativo de la Armada elevado al Fiscal de Delitos Acuáticos del Guayas, con los camarones y la embarcación como elementos que sustentan la denuncia. La entidad no dio más detalles.
En el parte, al que accedió Mongabay Latam, se describe que Naturisa alertó al ECU911 sobre un supuesto robo. Después, guardacostas interceptaron una gabarra con tres camiones que transportaban 20 280 libras de camarón. En el documento no se nombra a Julián Cruz.
Su nombre se vinculó formalmente en la audiencia de formulación de cargos, el 23 de abril de 2025. El 21 de julio de 2025, Naturisa presentó la acusación particular, dos años después del hecho. Sin embargo, la Justicia dispuso que se haga un reconocimiento de firmas el pasado 20 de agosto, pero los representantes de Naturisa no acudieron, de acuerdo con el abogado. Mongabay Latam no pudo corroborar este punto con la compañía debido a que su representante no respondió las reiteradas llamadas.
Detenido y sin visitas
Julián Cruz está en el pabellón 10 de la Penitenciaría del Litoral, que a pesar de estar militarizada, sigue bajo el control de grupos armados, afirma Navarrete del CDH. Sus familiares fueron extorsionados y solo una vez que pagaron, Cruz pudo ingresar al pabellón.
La familia se ha unido a plantones organizados por el Comité de Familiares de Personas Privadas de la Libertad para exigir la aprobación de listas que permiten el ingreso de víveres y útiles de aseo para los presos, algo que el Estado no puede garantizar en la actual crisis carcelaria, explica Navarrete.
Mientras tanto, su hermano denuncia que no han podido visitarlo, debido a que las visitas están restringidas por tratarse de una cárcel militarizada. Miembros de la comunidad y organizaciones de defensa de derechos humanos se reunieron en Guayaquil para asistir a la audiencia de juicio.
Mientras tanto, Jaramillo espera que la comunidad se mantenga unida y solidaria con Julián Cruz. Está seguro de que se conseguirá la libertad del dirigente, pues cree que los elementos de Fiscalía “son débiles” y que la entidad “parece que ha actuado cercana a los intereses de la empresa”.
Pedro Cruz concluye con un reclamo: “Nosotros queremos que él esté acá y que ellos desalojen nuestro territorio”.
*Imagen principal: Julián Cruz fue presidente de Chojón y ahora preside la Federación de Comunas y Organizaciones del Pueblo Punae. Foto: cortesía CDH

title: Rebelião da 3ª idade: a geração que revolucionou os costumes hoje luta por direitos e inclusão
content:
Um em cada cinco habitantes do Rio Grande do Sul tem 60 anos ou mais. Estamos falando de mais de 2 milhões de pessoas. E Porto Alegre é a capital brasileira com maior número de sexagenários e de homens e mulheres além dessa idade. Justamente aqui acaba de surgir uma iniciativa voltada à defesa da justiça, da dignidade, da autonomia e da vida mais plena possível para os velhos e velhas.
É o MOVER, o Movimento da Velharada Rebelde. O grupo lançou um manifesto afirmando que palavras como “velho” e velha” não os assusta. Adiante, afirma: “Somos os velhos e velhas do século 21, integrantes de uma geração que sonhou em mudar o mundo e que revolucionou os costumes”. Com convicção, acentua: “Fomos jovens rebeldes e não abrimos mão da nossa rebeldia”.
Amplo, o manifesto do MOVER trata desde a luta por aposentadorias decentes e do reajuste regular do salário-mínimo até a qualificação das casas de repouso, passando pela discussão do chamado “testamento vital” quando o idoso ou idosa decide o destino do seu corpo.
São inúmeras bandeiras onde não falta aquelas que acenam ao “mundo além de nós”, ou seja, às grandes questões que convulsionam a vida em sociedade e o futuro do planeta.
Nesta semana, De Fato recebe as jornalistas Rosina Duarte e Cristina Pozzobon, duas das fundadoras do MOVER, onde elas também questionam o uso de eufemismos para designar os mais velhos como “Melhor Idade”.
O podcast De Fato é uma produção do Brasil de Fato RS em parceria com o SindBancários de Porto Alegre e Região.
Todo sábado, um entrevistado ou uma entrevistada debaterá os principais fatos em destaque no Rio Grande do Sul, no Brasil e no mundo.

title: ‘Gaton – A Força da Terra’, livro de Kapri Padilha, reúne memória e resistência Kaingang
content:
Foi entre amigos, familiares, estudantes e professores que ocorreu, nesta quinta-feira (10), o primeiro de três encontros de lançamento de “Gaton – A Força da Terra”. Escrito pela indígena Kaingang Kapri Audisseia Nascimento Padilha, o livro foi apresentado na Faculdade de Educação da Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), em uma atividade mediada pela filósofa Magali Mendes de Menezes. A publicação aborda a memória, a espiritualidade e a trajetória de resistência do povo Kaingang e apresenta reflexões e ensinamentos da mãe da autora, a cacica Iracema Gãh Té Nascimento, liderança política e espiritual indígena.
A autora, Kapri Padilha, explica que o incentivo para escrever o livro nasceu da trajetória da família na luta constante por direitos. “A minha inspiração foi a nossa caminhada… Ela não é fácil. A luta por território é constante e árdua, porque sempre temos que estar lutando e batalhando, mas minha mãe nunca levou para esse lado de tristeza, de briga. A força da Gâh Té me inspirou… Ela traz essa força da terra com ela. Traz a sabedoria, os nossos mitos, através dos nossos mais velhos, que é a nossa raiz”, comenta.
Outros dois eventos estão previstos para este mês. No domingo (13), o bate-papo acontecerá na Aldeia Gãh Ré, no Morro Santana, às 15h. O último encontro de lançamento ocorrerá na quarta-feira (16), no Instituto de Filosofia e Ciências Humanas da UFRGS, das 14h às 16h, com mediação da antropóloga e colaboradora do livro Geórgia Macedo. Os dois encontros terão a participação da autora e da cacica, com entrada gratuita.
Força da terra
A obra é a primeira publicação de Padilha e reflete sobre a relação dos povos indígenas com a terra, a memória e o futuro, mesclando cultura, educação e história para contar a caminhada da cacica Iracema na defesa e retomada dos territórios ancestrais e na luta pelos direitos dos povos indígenas. Ressalta, ainda, a importância de que as histórias indígenas sejam contadas pelos próprios autores e traz aspectos da cosmologia Kaingang, como a profunda relação do povo com a terra, compreendendo o território não apenas como espaço rural, mas como lugar de luta por direitos, memória, espiritualidade, ancestralidade e vida.
O livro é uma publicação bilíngue, na língua Kaingang e em português, com tradução da autora e do irmão, Adilson Karinde Nascimento Padilha. A cacica Gãh Té explica que a ideia de produzir a obra nas duas línguas surgiu da própria mistura familiar, que reúne indígenas e não indígenas. A produção envolveu a participação de integrantes do povo Kaingang, principalmente da comunidade da Aldeia Gãh Ré, onde a autora reside, no Morro Santana, em Porto Alegre, além dos territórios em São Leopoldo e Canela.
A publicação também contém fotografias do acervo pessoal da família e ilustrações dos netos da cacica Iracema, produzidas a partir da escuta das histórias da avó em oficinas de desenho.
Para a autora, tanto o processo de escrita quanto o de escolha do material que entraria na obra foram bastante desafiantes. “Eu escutava a Gãh Té e, ao mesmo tempo, escrevia. Só que a comunidade inteira estava em dúvida sobre o livro… Então ficamos sempre conversando sobre. E só depois decidimos e chamamos a professora para fazer uma oficina com as crianças. Foi um desafio, porque a gente tem tantas coisas para poder mostrar… A verdade, bem sincera, é que foi bem difícil para poder selecionar o que é mais importante porque tudo ali é importante para nós”.
A obra levou mais de dez meses para ser produzida e foi idealizada por mãe e filha, em conjunto com as antropólogas Geórgia Macedo, que colaborou na escrita, e Ana Letícia Meira Schweig, responsável pela edição e pelo projeto gráfico.

title: “Woven Letters” exhibition brings Moroccan carpets to Gouda museum
content:
From September 26, the Gouda Museum in the Netherlands will host the first solo exhibition dedicated to Mina Abouzahra, a Dutch designer of Moroccan origin.
Titled Woven Letters, the exhibition will showcase furniture and carpets that weave together Moroccan craftsmanship and Dutch design, each telling personal and cultural stories.
At its heart, the exhibition challenges the notion of Moroccan carpets as mere decorative objects. In Amazigh tradition, textiles are imbued with rich symbolism, representing femininity, fertility, marriage, protection, and death.
Woven by women, each piece becomes a record of an intimate story, with life’s major stages expressed through motifs and colors in a visual language passed down through generations.
The exhibition will feature several new creations, including Bénédictions, a cabinet rich with symbolic meaning. Traditionally, this piece of furniture accompanies a young Moroccan bride’s transition to independence, serving as the only personal item she takes when leaving her family home.
For this project, Abouzahra collaborated with two Dutch craftspeople: Tsugi Woodworks, which crafted the wooden structure using Japanese joinery techniques without glue or nails, and Het Borduurburo, which produced the embroidery adorning the textile panels.
Other notable pieces include the Sofa Goity, a stack of mattresses that pays tribute to family ties and intergenerational living in Morocco, and the Abouzahra X Rietveld chair, a reinterpretation of a design by Wim Rietveld, son of renowned designer Gerrit Rietveld. This piece combines the austerity of postwar Dutch design with the richness of handwoven Moroccan textiles.
The centerpiece of the exhibition is the monumental tapestry Lettre, which draws on a tradition specific to Taznakht. When a young Amazigh woman marries and leaves her family, she remains without direct contact with them for a year.
During this period, she weaves a tapestry in which colors and symbols express her inner state. Her father visits her only once before taking the work back to her mother, who “reads” the woven letter through the language of weaving.
The exhibition complements Murs des Merveilles, the Gouda Museum’s major autumn exhibition devoted to the history of local weaving. For this occasion, Abouzahra worked with Gouda communities to create contemporary cushions woven in Taznakht, reinterpreting the traditional cushions of the city’s guilds.
This project creates an unexpected link between Dutch textile history and Morocco’s living weaving tradition, made all the more significant by the fact that nearly one in 10 Gouda residents has roots in the northern Rif mountains and Amazigh culture.
About Mina Abouzahra
Born in the Netherlands to Moroccan parents, Mina Abouzahra grew up between two cultures. During her studies at the Higher School of Wood and Furniture, she discovered the traditions of her parents’ homeland, a craft heritage that continues to shape her work today.
Her creations are now part of several museum collections. In 2022, she received the Dutch Creativity Award and the European Design Award. “Through my work, I preserve my cultural heritage and express my Moroccan identity,” she said.
Since 2013, Abouzahra has run a design studio between Amsterdam and Taznakht in southern Morocco, where she collaborates with a cooperative of women weavers who preserve centuries-old Amazigh traditions. She also advocates for fair working conditions and fair pay for these craftswomen.

title: Comunidades religiosas de matriz africana entregam carta-compromisso a candidatas
content:
A candidata à reeleição para deputada estadual Marina do MST (PT) e Anielle Franco (PT), candidata a deputada federal, assinaram nesta quinta-feira (9) uma carta de compromisso com os povos e comunidades tradicionais de matriz africana. Entre os principais compromissos estão a promoção do respeito a essas comunidades e combate ao racismo religioso.
O ato aconteceu no Quilombo da Gamboa, recentemente contemplado em edital da Minha Casa, Minha Vida Entidades, e reuniu cerca de 100 pessoas. Entre as lideranças religiosas estavam o Pai Anderson de Bamboxê e a Mãe Roberta.
O Rio de Janeiro tem uma das maiores populações de praticantes de religiões de matriz africana do país. Segundo o Censo 2022, 2,59% dos fluminenses com 10 anos ou mais se declaram praticantes de Umbanda ou Candomblé, o segundo maior percentual entre os estados.
Compromisso
Para Marina, o documento representa uma agenda construída coletivamente pelos povos de terreiro e deve orientar a atuação política em defesa de seus direitos.
“Essa carta-compromisso que vocês estão entregando, que vocês elaboraram coletivamente, pode ser considerada como programa dos povos e comunidades tradicionais de matriz africana do Estado do Rio de Janeiro. Esse documento tem que servir para orientar a nossa luta nos territórios, na busca por direitos e na construção de políticas públicas”, afirmou Marina do MST.
:: Quer receber notícias do Brasil de Fato RJ no seu WhatsApp? ::
Já Anielle Franco, ex-ministra da Igualdade Racial, destacou a importância de transformar os compromissos assumidos em ações concretas de enfrentamento ao racismo religioso e de defesa da democracia.
“O que está em disputa aqui não é só a nossa liberdade e o combate à intolerância e ao racismo religioso. É a nossa soberania e democracia”, completou Anielle.

title: En Arizona inició la construcción del muro fronterizo de Trump pese a la oposición de la tribu Tohono O’odham
content:
La construcción de un nuevo tramo de 100 kilómetros de muro fronterizo con México, impulsada por la administración del presidente estadounidense, Donald Trump, comenzó en Arizona pese a la oposición de la Nación Indígena Tohono O’odham, que considera que el proyecto viola su soberanía.
Tohono O’odham cree que el nuevo tramo de muro amenaza el medioambiente y resulta innecesario ante la caída del “95 %” en las detenciones migratorias en ese sector.
“Siempre hemos protegido nuestra tierra, nuestra comunidad, mucho antes de que esta nación fuera establecida y aún hoy nuestro deber es seguir protegiendo la tierra”, dijo a EFE Verlon José, presidente de ese territorio tribal, sobre el proyecto Tucson 5.
Por décadas, este resguardo indígena que comparte parte de la frontera entre Arizona y México se ha opuesto a la construcción de un muro físico dentro de su territorio, al considerar que afectará el tránsito de sus propios miembros, muchos de los cuales viven a ambos lados de la frontera y la cruzan con frecuencia para participar en ceremonias religiosas, peregrinaciones o visitar a familiares.
La comunidad también advierte que la construcción del muro podría destruir sitios ceremoniales considerados como “sagrados” y cementerios ancestrales.
La Nación Tohono O’odham interpuso una demanda contra el proyecto, al considerar que la construcción de una barrera de doble capa de acero y concreto, de unos 9,1 metros de altura, viola su soberanía al alterar los límites de sus terrenos, pero el pasado agosto una jueza federal en Washington falló en contra de la tribu al determinar que no pudo demostrar que el gobierno de Trump estuviera violando su soberanía.
La decisión se basa en un decreto emitido en 1907 por el entonces presidente de Estados Unidos, Theodore Roosevelt, que establece una franja de terreno de 18,3 metros de ancho a lo largo de la frontera con México, desde California hasta Nuevo México, considerada como “terreno de uso federal” con el propósito de combatir el narcotráfico.
Despliegue operativo y reclamos por derechos ancestrales
Semanas después de ese fallo, contratistas y agentes armados de la Oficina de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza (CBP) se presentaron de forma sorpresiva a finales de agosto dentro del territorio tribal.
De acuerdo con CBP, actualmente se realizan trabajos de medición y toma de muestras de tierra en el área, donde ya se observa la presencia de maquinaria pesada.
El comisionado de CBP, Rodney Scott, anunció la reactivación del proyecto Tucson 5, que, según aseguró, permitirá “cerrar” uno de los corredores irregulares más utilizados para el tráfico de drogas y de inmigrantes indocumentados en la frontera con México.
Sin embargo, José indicó que siempre la Nación Tohono O’odham ha cooperado con el gobierno federal en la vigilancia de la frontera, permitiendo la entrada de agentes de la Patrulla Fronteriza y cooperando con sus operaciones de seguridad nacional.
“En los últimos dos años los arrestos se han reducido en un 95 %, no vemos por qué la necesidad ahora de construir el muro”, enfatizó.
“Esto no se trata de la construcción de un muro o de seguridad nacional, se trata de la violación de los derechos de la Nación Tohono O’odham, su cultura y sus sitios ancestrales”, dijo a EFE la congresista de Arizona Adelita Grijalva.
Grijalva junto con otros congresistas demócratas han hecho un llamado a CBP pidiendo un alto a la construcción del proyecto.
Alerta ambiental en el manantial de Quitobaquito
En medio de la disputa se encuentra el manantial de Quitobaquito, en el sur de Arizona, y aunque está fuera del territorio indígena, es un sitio de importancia cultural para este pueblo, que lo consideran un lugar sagrado.
Además su laguna, que está en terrenos del gobierno federal, es un refugio para especies amenazadas, entre ellas la tortuga de Sonoyta y el pez pupo de Quitobaquito.
José asegura que el resguardo mantiene su lucha legal en los tribunales y ha apelado la decisión de la corte.
También señala que miembros de la tribu observan diariamente los trabajos que realizan los contratistas y agentes de CBP, y que algunos incluso encienden fogatas por las noches para llevar a cabo ceremonias pacíficas.
“Existe una gran frustración, pero también desilusión por la falta de respeto a nuestra cultura, es como si nuestras creencias y nuestros antepasados no tuvieran ningún valor”, lamentó José en declaraciones a EFE.

title: 2 Negrense national artists: One painted people’s struggles, the other lit the stage
content:
AT A GLANCE
- Nunelucio Alvarado and Teodoro Hilado were named among the National Artists for 2025, recognizing their significant contributions to art and theater in the Philippines.
- Alvarado, a social-realist artist, has dedicated over five decades to portraying the lives of ordinary people, while Hilado, known as the 'Father of Philippine Lighting Design,' pioneered technical direction in theater.
- Both artists have left a lasting impact on their communities, with Alvarado continuing to live among those he inspires, and Hilado being honored posthumously for his innovative work in enhancing theatrical storytelling.
NEGROS OCCIDENTAL, Philippines – One is 76 and living with dementia in his hometown, where for more than five decades he turned his art toward the lives and struggles of people around him. The other died in 2015, after a career devoted to an aspect of theater most audiences rarely see but experience in every production.
Nunelucio Alvarado, fondly called “Maestro Nunelucio,” and Teodoro “Teddy” Ledesma-Hilado were named among the 10 National Artists for 2025 in Proclamation No. 1414 announced by Malacañang on Wednesday, September 9.
Their recognition brings together two very different lives in art. Alvarado is the social-realist artist from Sagay whose provocative works became a quiet form of social revolution, while Hilado, the Silaynon known as the “Father of Philippine Lighting Design,” pioneered lighting design and technical direction in the Philippines.
For Helen Arguelles Cutillar, Sagay’s tourism and information officer, Alvarado’s life is itself a canvas.
“He is peerless,” Cutillar said. “He touched people’s lives, especially the poor in so many ways.”
Alvarado has no college degree. Yet for more than five decades, he etched his mark in visual arts, building a body of work centered on social realities and the lives of ordinary people.
His recognition, however, is not being seen in Sagay as a distinction that belongs to him alone.
Sagay Mayor Leo Rafael Cueva said the honor also belongs to the communities whose lives and struggles have been at the heart of Alvarado’s work.
“Maestro Nunelucio showed that an artist does not have to leave his community behind to create work that matters to the nation and the world,” Cueva said. “He brought his art back to Sagay, shared it with our children and communities, and helped make art part of everyday life here.”
“We now have a national treasure living with us. He is a true gem in the field of arts,” Negros Occidental 2nd District Representative Alfredo Marañon III said on Thursday, September 10.
Alvarado is living with dementia, and his wife, Rosalia “Sally” Alvarado, spoke on behalf of the family as the country recognized his contribution.
“We hope his legacy of bringing art and the love for art into the community will continue for generations to come,” she said.
The Metropolitan Museum of Manila hailed the declaration of Alvarado as a national artist, saying it highlighted his work depicting the lives and struggles of communities in Negros.
It said Alvarado has been known for his social realist works rooted in the sugarlands of Negros, with recurring images of sakadas and sugarcane reflecting exploitation, hardship, resistance, survival and hope.
The museum, which holds Alvarado’s works in its collection, said his art has given voice to local communities and helped bring their experiences and stories to a wider audience.
“Immortalizing his agrarian activism in his work, Alvarado continues to spread his philosophy that art belongs to the people and his advocacy for the active involvement of art and grassroots communities in the Philippines,” read part of the museum’s statement.
The museum also celebrated the declaration of another national artist, Imelda Cajipe-Endaya (visual arts), whose works are also in its collection.
The museum said Endaya is known for her textured mixed-media works using everyday fabrics and objects, and for an artistic practice focused on Filipino identity, human rights, feminism, overseas Filipino workers, environmental issues and peace.
“Their works have illuminated the realities, struggles, and aspirations of local communities and through their art and advocacy, Cajipe-Endaya and Alvarado have made impactful contributions to Philippine art and inspire future generations to learn and appreciate the stories that shape them as Filipinos,” it said.
If Alvarado brought art into the life of his community, Hilado devoted his career to the technical side of theater.
The Silay-born artist was named a national artist for theater, specifically for technical direction, 11 years after his death at 77, recognizing a career that helped establish technical direction as an important part of theater from the wings.
Hilado pioneered lighting design and technical direction in the Philippines and became known as the “Father of Philippine Lighting Design.”
He helped professionalize the technical side of the performing arts, using light, space and technical direction to enhance storytelling.
When he served as technical director at the Cultural Center of the Philippines, Hilado mastered a minimalist approach to theater, using lights and space to heighten storytelling. His work created atmospheres that captivated audiences and helped raise the standards of local productions to an international level.
Silay Mayor Joedith Gallego asked Silaynons to celebrate Hilado’s recognition.
“He [was] an exceptional artist behind theater lighting and productions,” Gallego said.
Hilado was the third national artist from Silay, according to Solomon Locsin, chairman of the Negros Occidental Historical Council. Before him came Leandro Locsin, who was declared a national artist for architecture in 1990, and Agnes Dakudao-Locsin, national artist for dance in 2022.
In Sagay, the recognition of Alvarado brings national attention to an artist whose work has remained closely tied to his community. And in Silay, Hilado’s posthumous recognition honors a career devoted to the technical craft of theater.
Their lives in art were different. One continues to live with the community that became central to his work; the other is remembered for a career that helped shape how theater was presented to audiences.
Aside from Alvarado, Hilado and Endaya, the other 2025 national artists are as follows:
- Gabriel “Gabby” Formoso – architecture
- Rafael “Nonoy” Catalino Froilan – dance
- Maria Beatriz “Patis” Fabella Pamintuan Tesoro – design and allied arts
- Armando “Bing” Lao – film and broadcast arts
- Gregorio Brillantes – literature
- Nicanor Tiongson – literature
- Alfredo Buenaventura – music
– Rappler.com

title: Yosemite National Park highlights Indigenous arrowhead crafting
content:
There is a simple reason why Indigenous arrowhead crafting has remained largely the same for thousands of years—if something works, it works. The earliest examples of these lethal tools date back around 74,000 years ago to Stone Age Ethiopia, but the skill is still practiced today by trained artisans around the world. Yet, the process isn’t only a matter of breaking rocks into sharp-edged projectiles.. As Yosemite National Park officials recently highlighted, there is more to this very specific technique called knapping.
Proper knapping largely hinges on choosing the correct stones. These usually include chert, flint, and most notably obsidian due to their surgically sharp fracture lines. Artisans then slowly and purposely break off flakes of rocks to shape them into not only aerodynamic arrowheads, but knives, scrapers, and spear points.
Interestingly, obsidian isn’t native to the Yosemite, yet the region’s Indigenous communities have prized the material for generations. The volcanic glass was introduced into the area via ancient trade routes that crossed over the Eastern Sierra’s Mono Lake in present-day eastern California near the Nevada border. Tribes separated by hundreds of miles relied on these and similar exchange networks to swap tool materials for animal skins, medicinal plants, as well as nutritious pine nuts and acorns.
Yosemite’s earliest Indigenous communities initially knapped obsidian into larger points for spears and spear throwers known as atlatls. As hunting technology evolved over hundreds of years towards a reliance on bows and arrows, the obsidian points shrank in size to make them more aerodynamic.
The national park celebrates the ancient tradition of knapping at its annual Knap-In event, which includes demonstrations, workshops, and other hands-on opportunities. While this year’s Yosemite Knap-In took place in August, numerous others are held across the United States throughout the year.

title: Americans mark 25 years since the Sept. 11 attacks
content:
Americans commemorated the 25th anniversary of 9/11 on Friday, remembering the shock, the dead and the sweeping consequences of the al-Qaeda attacks on symbols of U.S. might and prosperity.
The milestone anniversary brought memorial rituals – wreath-laying, flag-flying, moments of silence, vigils and readings of victims’ names – and volunteer projects in tribute to a day that about half of U.S. adults remember as the most historic event of their lifetime, according to a new poll. On Sept. 11, 2001, al-Qaeda extremists hijacked four commercial jets and crashed them into New York’s World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing nearly 3,000 people.
Elsie Caldwell carried a photograph of her son Kenny Caldwell to the trade centre to hear his name and all the others read aloud Friday morning. She last spoke to him that morning a quarter-century ago.
“Mom, I just want to let you know that I love you,” Caldwell said he told her in a final phone call. She is one of many relatives of victims whose remains never were recovered.
Trump attends Pentagon observance
The attacks brought down the World Trade Center’s twin towers – icons of U.S. economic power, and among the tallest buildings on Earth – and blew a hole in the Pentagon, the U.S. military’s fortress-like headquarters near Washington. The fourth plane was headed for the nation’s capital, officials concluded, but the aircraft went down in Pennsylvania after passengers and crew members stormed the cockpit and fought the hijackers.
“Sept. 11 reminded us of the terrible power of hate,” President Donald Trump said Friday at the Pentagon’s anniversary ceremony Friday.
“The 25 years since have shown us the even greater power of the American spirit to endure and prevail, and to win,” added the Republican, who was in his native New York on 9/11.
Former President George W. Bush, who was in office on 9/11, and ex-Presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama and Joe Biden and current Vice-President JD Vance convened for the observance at the National Sept. 11 Memorial in New York. Other administration officials went to the Flight 93 National Memorial in Pennsylvania.
At ground zero, a new tribute to those who fell ill
For Angilic Casalduc, attending the New York commemoration “helps to show you’re not alone.” She lost her mother, Vivian Casalduc.
“There’s no timeline for grief, and unfortunately, no one can say how can you can grieve, but coming here once a year makes it feel just a little bit better,” she said.
Traditionally, there are no political speeches at the ground zero commemoration, where victims’ relatives read aloud the long list of names and added personal messages. They thanked first responders and the military, talked about their loved ones’ lives, and mentioned family milestones they’ve missed. Many of those who spoke were too young to have met the relatives they lost.
The ceremony has long been punctuated with moments of silence at key points in the attack timeline and this year organizers added another moment to honour people who were exposed to the clouds of toxic dust released by the twin towers’ fiery collapse and have since died of cancer and other illnesses. Questions remain about how many people developed health problems linked to the dust.
The impact of 9/11 endures
How 9/11 is still claiming its first responders.
Reuters
It’s a reminder of how the attacks’ long shadow has reached into many corners of life in the U.S. and beyond.
The U.S.-led global war on terrorism included invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan – the latter Washington’s longest war – and detentions and harsh interrogation of terror suspects in an international network of secret CIA prisons. The U.S. found and killed al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden in Pakistan in 2011, but accused 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed still awaits a trial 23 years after his capture.
The attacks changed U.S. air travel, prompted new federal surveillance and intelligence-gathering powers and banking regulations, and generated ongoing debate over the balance between security and freedom. The Department of Homeland Security, many state anti-terrorism laws and billions of dollars in state and local counterterrorism funding all are post-9/11 creations.
So, too, is the culture of individual vigilance summed up by the slogan “ if you see something, say something.”
Sept. 11 generated a wave of patriotism that propelled some Americans to join the military, fire departments, police forces or other public agencies.
Casey Kloepfer became a New York police officer this June. He was 4 when his father, Officer Ronald Kloepfer, was killed at the trade centre.
“It’s big footsteps to fill, but it’s definitely something that I take very seriously and want to continue to honour him and be the best police officer I can,” the 29-year-old, who wears his father’s badge number, said by phone this week.
New York’s mayor comes under scrutiny
Amid the calls to service and for national unity that many remember, the attacks also fanned mistrust, prejudice and hate crimes directed at Muslims.
In the quarter-century since, Muslim Americans have played a growing role in public life from statehouses to Congress to New York City Hall, where Zohran Mamdani is the city’s first Muslim mayor. Yet he faced some criticism for attending the anniversary ceremony at ground zero, something his predecessors have done for years.
Some complaints came from Republican ex-Gov. George Pataki and 9/11 victims’ relatives, who cited among other things past remarks that some of Mamdani’s political associates have made about the attacks. Former Mayor Rudy Giuliani, a Republican, also inveighed against Mamdani attending, though the two shook hands Friday as they and other officials awaited the start of the observance.
Mamdani, a Democrat, said earlier this week that he loves the city and country and wants the anniversary to focus on victims’ families, first responders and New Yorkers who helped one another after the attacks, which he called a “horrific act of terror.” The 34-year-old mayor was an elementary school student in New York on 9/11.
Times Square billboards pause advertisements
Remembrances extended far beyond the attack sites, including beams of light projecting from New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, a stair climb at Mississippi State University’s football stadium and a ceremony at Honolulu’s 9/11 memorial.
Sept. 11 isn’t a federal holiday, but Congress has designated it both Patriot Day and a National Day of Service and Remembrance.
“One appropriate way to remember is by serving,” says Jay Winuk, who lost his brother Glenn Winuk and then co-founded the volunteer organization 9/11 Day with friend David Paine. The group helps people find volunteer opportunities and this year arranged for dozens of Times Square billboards to pause their advertising at 9:11 a.m. Friday.
Instead, they simply displayed the time.

title: Wonden na 25 jaar nog vers: '9/11 is geschiedenis waar we nog middenin zitten'
content: Na 25 jaar zijn de wonden van nabestaanden, overlevenden en hulpverleners nog altijd vers. De Amerikanen die de aanslagen op 11 september 2001 van dichtbij meemaakten, leven nog iedere dag met de gevolgen ervan. Vandaag was voor hen een dag van leven en dood, van leven en overleven, en van leven met de gevolgen. Een dag van verdriet en herinneren. En van opkrabbelen na die allesverwoestende terroristische aanslagen. Voor velen begon ook deze dag als elke andere. "Iedereen vecht voor die ene vrije parkeerplek, en dan de trein in", vertelt Stanley Praimnath. Net als 25 jaar geleden haasten forenzen zich voor de trein naar Manhattan, bij het station op Long Island waar we hem ontmoeten. 'Ga terug naar je kantoor' Hij was altijd vroeg op zijn werk, ook die dag. "Ik stuurde een team aan, probeerde het goede voorbeeld te geven", zegt hij. Toen hij de lift uitkwam, ging de telefoon. "Eerst mijn moeder, toen mijn broer. Stan, ben je oké?, vroegen ze. Ze hadden tv gekeken." Stanley had toen nog niet door wat zich in de andere toren van het World Trade Center had afgespeeld, hij zat in de lift toen het gebeurde. Al snel werd duidelijk dat een vliegtuig de noordelijke toren had geraakt. "Ik zei: ik ga nu naar huis." Het gebouw is veilig, klonk het uit de mond van een beveiliger. Sirenes loeiden, vergezeld door een boodschap via de intercom: "Ga terug naar je kantoor", hoorde Stanley. Kort daarna vloog een tweede vliegtuig de zuidelijke toren in, waar Stanley voor de Japanse Fuji Bank werkte, op de 81e verdieping. "De hele verdieping was aan stukken gereten, alsof er een gigantische sloopkogel doorheen was geraasd." Gordon Felt hoorde het van een collega, zette de televisie aan. Hij zag het tweede vliegtuig de zuidelijke toren invliegen. "Toen wisten we dat het geen ongeluk was en dat we werden aangevallen." Even later belde zijn schoonzus. Zijn broer Edward was onderweg van New York naar San Francisco met vlucht 93. "Ze vertelde dat ze niets van hem had gehoord. Zodra ze meer hoorde, zou ze het ons laten weten." Kleine keukenbrand Bij brandweerman Bill Hayes ging die ochtend ook een alarm af. Een kleine keukenbrand: iemand had het fornuis aan laten staan. Terwijl Bill aan het blussen was, viel zijn oog op de televisie, die nog aanstond. Hij zag dat na de torens ook het Pentagon was geraakt. "Ik gaf het door via mijn portofoon. De bevelvoerend officier zei: 'Wie zei dat? Herhaal die melding!'" Alle brandweerlieden werden gemobiliseerd, ook Bill. "Ik sprak een bericht in voor mijn vrouw. Terwijl ik dat deed, ging het alarm opnieuw af. Het laatste wat ik nog kon zeggen was: 'We gaan die kant op'." Later vertelde zijn dochter dat een ouder tegen haar had gezegd: 'Je vader is misschien wel dood'." Ze was toen 9 jaar oud. Stanley stond toen net weer buiten, zwaargewond. Op miraculeuze wijze was hij als een van de weinigen in de nok van zijn toren ontsnapt aan de dood. Zijn eerdere schreeuw om hulp was gehoord door Brian Clark, die drie verdiepingen hoger werkte. Samen zijn ze aan de vuurzee ontsnapt. Ze hadden de lange weg van 1.620 traptreden naar beneden afgelegd voordat de zuidtoren, een klein uur na de inslag, ineenstortte. Voor Bill moest het werk toen nog beginnen. Drie dagen lang was hij bezig. Overlevenden vond hij niet meer in het puin op Ground Zero, de plek waar de Twin Towers stonden. Al noemt hij die zelf liever anders: the pit (de kuil). 'Kunt u me nog horen, meneer?' Gordon kreeg opnieuw een telefoontje. Vlucht 93 is neergestort in Pennsylvania, overlevenden zijn er niet. Het belletje van zijn broer Edward naar de meldkamer van 911, vanuit het toilet, bleek een van de laatste tekenen van leven uit het vliegtuig. "Er is een kaping gaande", klonk het. "Kunt u me nog horen, meneer? Hallo?" Toen werd het stil op de lijn. "Ik heb er één keer naar geluisterd", zegt Gordon daarover. "Dat is niet iets wat ik nog een keer zou willen doen." Voor de familie van zijn broer, ook voor Gordon, begon het toen pas. "Wonden helen niet", zegt hij. "En misschien willen we ook helemaal niet dat ze helen. We willen niet vergeten wat we zijn kwijtgeraakt. Maar vlucht 93 is ook een verhaal van enorme moed, hoop en inspiratie." Gordon, Stanley en Bill, alle drie leven ze nog elke dag met de gevolgen van de aanslagen. Wonden werden littekens, Stanley worstelde lange tijd met een schuldgevoel. Waarom overleefde hij het en veel van zijn vrienden en collega's niet? In zijn geloof vond hij een antwoord: genade van God, concludeerde hij. Hij ging studeren en werd predikant. Leukemie Ook werd hij meermaals ernstig ziek. 11 september 2020 kreeg hij de diagnose leukemie. "Die dag moet mij niet", lacht Stanley. Of de ziekte gerelateerd is aan 9/11? "Sommigen zeiden van wel, anderen niet." Ook kreeg hij een vierdubbele bypass. "Mijn zus zei ooit: 'Stan, je hebt meer levens dan een kat'. Ik zei: 'Katten krijgen negen levens en gaan uiteindelijk gewoon dood'." Ook Bill kampte met gezondheidsklachten, de reden waarom hij na decennia bij de brandweer en in het leger vroegtijdig met pensioen ging. "Kanker, twee keer, gerelateerd aan het WTC", zegt hij. Zijn belangrijkste les? "Niets is vanzelfsprekend", zegt hij. "Probeer goed te leven want je weet nooit wat er de volgende dag gebeurt." "Ik denk niet dat ik een held ben, maar ik heb wel met helden gewerkt", zegt Bill. "Ik wou dat we meer mensen hadden kunnen redden. Maar we hebben alles gedaan wat menselijkerwijs mogelijk was." Voor Gordon staat voorop dat het verhaal van 11 september niet mag worden vergeten. "Het is geschiedenis waar we tot op de dag van vandaag nog middenin zitten", zegt hij. "We dragen dit verhaal in ons hart en op onze schouders. Dat blijven we doen zolang we kunnen, maar er komt een dag dat wij er niet meer zijn. Dan moeten anderen het verhaal oppakken en verder dragen."

title: South Africa: Thousands of Zulu women gather for reed dance ceremony
content:
Tradition
Bright outfits and dancing filled the streets of Ingwavuma, in South Africa's southeastern KwaZulu-Natal province on Saturday, as thousands of young zulu women gethered to take part in the annual Reed Dance ceremony.
Every September, young women, locally known as "maidens", head to the royal palace to present a long reed to Zulu King Misuzulu kaZwelithini.
For participant Sno’thando, the event is a way of preserving tradition.
"We are here to be taught how to respect ourselves, our bodies, and remember our culture and preserve it for the coming generations," she says.
For the participants, the reed is a symbolic gesture implying their commitment to maintaining a tradition passed down through generations.
Participants aso view it as a way of looking after themselves. Cebisa Ntshangeni says "it's important because this continues to encourage us to look after ourselves, we love it and most of the time it's in your heart that when you are a maiden you must look after yourself until its time to get married."
The event is also attended by members of the royal family, traditional Zulu regiments and instructors who accompany the participants. Among those who gathered for the ceremont on Saturday is 71-year-old Mam’Mahlinsa, who came with girls from her region.
"My name is Mom Mahlinza, and I am responsible for the girls from Elangeni here in Ngwavuma. Today we are here accompanying the girls [ed. maidens], in this celebration of the reeds, here in Ngwavuma, whereby the young ones, the ‘pure’ girls who have looked after themselves as maidens, come here to the royal house to bring “Ngangezwelakhe” [ed. the King] the reeds , showing that they are still looking after themselves as maidens, and remain like that," she says.
Singing and dancing took place throughout the ceremony. The yearly gathering remains an important expression of Zulu cultural identity, bringing together generations and preserving a tradition that has been ongoing for centuries.

title: After nearly 50 years, this master craftsman is hanging up his tools
content:
After nearly 50 years, this master craftsman is hanging up his tools
Craftsmen of Tasmania's heritage construction trade have had a busy month inside a 146-year-old church in Campbell Town.
A solid plasterer, a stained glass worker, and a heritage building specialist have been working together to help restore the former Brickhill memorial church.
Gavin Merrington, 64, expects it will be his last major restoration project.
After nearly 50 years spent repairing stained glass in buildings across Tasmania, he's preparing to hang up the tools — for the big jobs at least.
Original stained glass restored
The Campbell Town project, in Tasmania's midlands, hasn't been a small task.
The church's original High Street-facing main window had never been replaced, and after nearly 150 years, the soft lead holding the glass together was well and truly breaking down.
"The putty under the lead starts to wash out and then the water gets in, and they just degenerate," Mr Merrington said.
"You could see a few broken [pieces], but when you pull them out they start to separate and there were heaps broken."
Mr Merrington was able to track down the exact type of glass used in the original windows.
Intricate pieces were then hand-painted and fired in a kiln, with the process repeated many times until the desired colour and effect were reached.
That was done for "maybe 90 pieces", he said.
Based out of his studio in South Hobart, the work on the main windows at Brickhill took 10 weeks.
The glass was then carefully transported to Campbell Town, placed in a wooden crate and secured with screws before being levered 5 metres off the ground to where it needed to be fitted.
"If you touch it on the scaffold you're likely to break something, and they're very heavy too, so it's a matter of being careful and having lots of hands on the windows to get them up," he said.
Leadlighting around the world
It was a newspaper ad that inspired Mr Merrington to pick up the trade of leadlighting at the age of 16.
He has spent much of his career working on church windows, a passion that has taken him around the world.
After being awarded a Churchill Fellowship in 2014, Mr Merrington travelled to Europe to learn from global experts in glazing and glass preservation — skills he brought home to Tasmania.
"Coming back it was just sort of reiterated, we're on the right path and we're looking good as far as the skills that are being disseminated around Australia,"he said.
"Australia is quite up with world trends as far as conservation."
Mr Merrington lists Launceston's Holy trinity church and Hobart churches St Mary's cathedral and All Saints as some of his favourite projects he has worked on.
Heritage trades 'quite a community'
Heritage building specialist Peter Evans, who has also been working on the Brickhill project, first met Mr Merrington 20 years ago on a different church restoration.
He said that was typical of Tasmania's heritage trades, with many of the people working on these buildings having known each other for decades.
"It's quite a community; we all rely heavily on each other," he said.
"All the people I work with, a lot of our relationships go back 35 to 38 years."
A fifth-generation Campbell Town local, Mr Evans said the region was dotted with Victorian farmhouses and churches that kept him and his team of six busy.
"[There was] such a flurry of buildings [built] in the 1830s, so this area here through to Hobart, but particularly the Midlands," he said.
"It's good to be able to take our part in preserving these buildings, and we'll hand over to the next generation, mainly just keeping them watertight and sound."
An unlikely owner
Ohio-born Matt Collins always wanted to buy a church.
After moving to Australia in 2017, he set his sights on Brickhill.
Built in 1880 with money left by former convict-turned-merchant Joseph Brickhill, the church was deconsecrated in 1964.
Since then, it has been a wool museum, a co-working space and now operates as short-stay accommodation.
"I think there is a duty and responsibility when you own or steward a building like this one to preserve it because it has such a rich history, relevance and significance to the local community,"Mr Collins said.
"I'm really, really honoured that I've had Gavin and his team come and work on this building, with all the years of experience and knowledge that they have."
Future of heritage crafts
After Brickhill, Mr Merrington is stepping back from major restoration work, but he is not walking away from the craft entirely.
He will continue working on smaller jobs and consultancy work.
Mr Merrington said he was confident his heritage trade was in safe hands.
"I've got an employee who will keep going after me hopefully, and he's got all the skills so that's really good,"he said.
Mr Merrington said while it was a "shame so many churches are being sold", having people such as Matt committed to restoring them was "better than it could have ever been expected", even compared to remaining in the church's hands.
He said after nearly 50 years of travelling the state, he was looking forward to a break.
"A few holidays, spend some time with the wife and the grandkids, that kind of thing," he said.

title: Un jeune de 17 ans à la tête d’une exposition très atypique à Halanzy
content:
Un jeune de 17 ans à la tête d'une exposition très atypique à Halanzy
Elle retrace l'histoire d'Halanzy et de la Gaume pendant la deuxième guerre mondiale. Un jeune de 17 ans est à la manœuvre.
- Publié le 11-09-2026 à 15h16
C'est une exposition atypique qui est proposée au Cercle Saint-Rémy d'Halanzy. Elle sera inaugurée ce samedi matin à l'issue de la cérémonie au monument aux morts d'Halanzy qui débutera à 10 h 30. Elle se poursuivra ce dimanche et tout le week-end prochain.
L'exposition propose un thème général inédit, celui de la libération de Musson, d'Halanzy et de la Gaume, par la 5ème division blindée américaine au mois de septembre 1944, mais aussi de la suite du parcours de ses soldats qui ont poursuivi leur mission en traversant l'Allemagne jusqu'aux portes de Berlin. Objets de collection, témoignages, films, reportages, armes, véhicules de l'époque… mais aussi l'essayage des uniformes et du barda des soldats pour se rendre compte de l'effort que représentaient leurs déplacements. Plusieurs autres animations sont également prévues.
Gabin Pinsoni, 17 ans, est à la tête de l'exposition
Autre côté atypique de l'événement, il est dirigé par Gabin Pinsoni, un Mussonnais de 17 ans en rhéto à l'école secondaire Ello de Differt, anciennement Institut de Nazareth et Cardijn-Lorraine. "Mon papa est un collectionneur dans l'âme et consacre ses recherches et sa passion à la première guerre mondiale. Son travail m'a toujours intéressé et j'ai décidé de le suivre, mais en me branchant sur la deuxième guerre mondiale. Nous avons consacré tous nos loisirs à chiner dans les brocantes et à visiter les musées, principalement le War Museum de Bastogne. J'y ai fait beaucoup de rencontres, notamment celle de Johan Hissette, qui malgré ses 43 ans, est devenu mon meilleur ami et qui m'a beaucoup aidé dans la préparation de mon exposition."
Le jeune Gabin a limité son exposition à tout ce qui tourne autour de l'histoire locale et des villages gaumais. "Dans mon esprit, il n'a jamais été question de vouloir refaire une énième histoire de deuxième guerre mondiale ou de revenir sur des épisodes qui ont fait l'objet de nombreux films, comme le débarquement en Normandie. Il y a bien les musées de Latour et de Diekirch dans notre région, mais moi ce qui m'intéressait, c'était de transmettre aux habitants d'Halanzy et de Gaume, la mémoire de ce qui s'est passé dans leurs villages et dans leur région à cette époque, mais aussi de rendre hommage à ces soldats anonymes et inconnus venus de la côte ouest des États-Unis, qui ont traversé l'Atlantique pour nous délivrer. J'espère que les gens de nos villages seront nombreux à s'intéresser à ce pan de leur histoire au travers de cette exposition."

title: These girls fear new child protection laws will lead to 'lost generations'
content:
Tiwi Island teenagers reflect on changes to NT child protection laws
Surrounded by the ocean, where eucalypt forest stretches from the sand to meet the sky, the Tiwi Islands are a living library for the young people who call it home.
Etched into the landscape are guides on how to live off the land and language that describes their way of life, all of which has taught kids their traditional customs over generations.
The island and its community hold the knowledge that tells the story of each family and how they're connected.
But there are fears these connections to kin and culture are under threat.
These fears are acutely felt by 17-year-old Tiwi Island girls Shanina Kantilla and Tahni Thompson, who are cousins on their mother's side.
Even when they're hundreds of kilometres from home, the islands are never far from their minds.
Shanina recalls a happy childhood spent camping, hunting, swimming and fishing.
"It's very important, especially starting from a young age, learning about our culture, skin groups and also our country … where we inherit our tribes, the sacred sites, ceremony," she said.
Tahni also feels a deep connection to being Tiwi, having returned after spending part of her childhood in Darwin.
"It's like my safe place. Whenever I go to other places, I always feel homesick," she said.
Life on the Tiwi Islands
The Tiwi Islands is known for many things — vibrant artwork, secluded fishing spots and die-hard footy fans — with some of Australia's most renowned AFL players coming out of the region.
"We have a local league of AFL and it gets really hectic around those times," Tahni said.
Tiwi culture is also embedded in the girls' schooling, with weekly lessons on country.
But the real tutoring starts young and comes from within families — grandparents, parents, aunties and uncles.
Shanina's pride in her family traditions shines through as she explains how she's been taught to take wood from the local paper bark trees to weave into baskets.
"We scrape all the wood out and when we're done, we have to boil it and then we fold it, and let it sit for about two, three hours," she said.
"Once it dries up, we come back and start doing our traditional paintings."
Both girls are well aware past government policies prevented this cultural knowledge from being passed down.
"Since the missionaries came, they just changed everything," Tahni said.
"Some of the kids on the other island, [due to] the [Stolen] Generations, don't really speak Tiwi."
From the early 1900s, Catholic missions on the Tiwi Islands controlled much of daily life, influencing where people lived, who they married and the upbringing of their children.
For many families, the policies disrupted the transmission of language, cultural practices and traditional knowledge.
Today, cultural disconnection can take different forms.
Tahni knows this firsthand. Growing up away from her homelands, she felt as though a part of her identity was missing until she returned to the Tiwi Islands.
"I wouldn't want to be taken away from my family," she said.
"I would want to stay with them forever."
Deflating the 'political football'
On the other side of the territory's coastline, as thousands gathered for the Garma festival, First Nations people voiced fears of a renewed threat to kinship systems and culture.
Just weeks before, the Northern Territory government announced changes to child protection laws which critics said weakened the Aboriginal Child Placement Principle.
National Indigenous children's commissioner Sue-Anne Hunter was among those fearing it would lead to more children removed from their communities.
"I'm not here in a battle, I'm here to protect our children and make sure they're safe," she said.
"I feel like it's a bit of political football for everybody, and that's not what our kids should be."
The child placement principle aims to keep Aboriginal children connected to family, community and culture when they enter care.
It prioritises placing children with family in the first instance, then the child's own First Nations community and then other First Nations carers.
But under the NT changes, introduced after the death of Kumanjayi Little Baby, the government no longer needs to try to place a child with their community or a First Nations carer if they can't be placed with family.
Sue-Anne Hunter sees devastating echoes of the past.
"No-one is saying that our children need to be unsafe. If a child needs to be removed, then that's the fact. The thing is that culture is part of safety. It's their identity," she said.
"Maybe they [the NT government] need to have a discussion with some Stolen Generation people about how being disconnected affected their lives."
Ms Hunter spent much of her time at Garma hearing directly from young people, many of whom told her they were anxious about the changes.
"It's front of mind for youth as well," she said.
"We need to be investing in the front end. Family support, getting into families early, not waiting until we're ready to remove them."
A spokesperson for the NT government denied the changes were weakening protections for Aboriginal children.
"These reforms — designed after extensive consultation — created a Universal Child Placement Principle so the same strong provisions apply to every child," they said.
"Additional provisions have been retained for Aboriginal children that reflect their cultural needs and connection to family, community and country."
Child protection isn't the only policy change adding to Ms Hunter's workload.
In recent years the NT lowered the age of criminal responsibility and reintroduced spit hoods, the NT, Victoria and Queensland removed the principle of detention as a last resort for children, Victoria and Queensland brought in "adult crime, adult time" laws and nearly all jurisdictions tightened youth bail.
Ms Hunter said she wished the politicians who attended Garma, including NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro, had asked the next generation what they thought of the changes.
"There are a whole lot of people here ready to give some solutions, have some discussions, but it just doesn't seem to be happening," she said.
"It would have been nice if [Ms Finocchiaro] was able to stay, maybe go into the youth forum and listen to the kids."
The NT government spokesperson said lowering the age of criminal responsibility to 10 was about "early intervention and community safety".
"Strong families, cultural connection and early intervention are the best way to break the cycle of youth crime, alongside clear consequences when offending occurs," they said.
'They are just little kids'
Inside the youth forum, Tahni and Shanina reflected on family and friends who had been caught up in the justice system or removed from their families.
"Those ones that are under Territory Families [in out-of-home-care], they don't know our culture much because they only come once a year for a visit around the community," Shanina said.
"It's hard for them to know who their family is, who they are, and their culture … I feel for them."
They were also worried about children as young as 10 being held responsible for crimes.
"Ten years old, they're not really teenagers yet, they are just little kids. They aren't mature enough [to understand]," Tahni said.
"Instead of sending them away, just discipline them on the island and that way they can learn from their mistakes instead of getting them sent off somewhere else.
"[Juvenile detention is] pretty traumatic, and they'll have to carry that trauma for the rest of their lives."
The cousins say there are deeper issues affecting young people and punishment isn't the solution.
"I think younger children have to do counselling, talk about their feelings … instead of getting frustrated. That causes a lot of problems," Shanina said.
As the youth forum began to wind up, Tahni shared her message for the NT government.
"Our voice matters," she said.
"We don't want [Stolen Generations] to happen again.
"If we didn't have culture, we wouldn't know our identity. That's why it's important for us to learn at a young age.
"[Otherwise] there might not be any Tiwi people left. There will just be lost generations."

title: Joe Salgado virou à direita no 11 de setembro e sobreviveu
content:
Um carro dos bombeiros, uma ambulância e um veículo de socorro ajudam a compor um solene triângulo, palco da homenagem da comunidade portuguesa às vítimas dos ataques de 11 de setembro. Ao final da tarde de sexta-feira, ouve-se português na confluência da Ferry Street com a Wilson Avenue, em Newark, New Jersey. Manhattan fica a meia-hora. Estes portugueses, que hoje colocam a bandeira nacional a meia-haste, também têm uma história para contar.
É o caso de Joe Salgado, um dos poucos sobreviventes portugueses do 11 de setembro. Trabalhava no 47.º andar da Torre Norte e conseguiu escapar do edifício com vida. Tinha chegado cedo ao trabalho no banco First Union. “Era um dia lindo. Lembro-me tão bem”, afirmou à Rádio Observador, entrevistado na emissão especial desta sexta-feira à tarde em Nova Iorque. Aos 65 anos, Joe Salgado recorda vividamente essa terça-feira, dia 11 de setembro de 2001. “Chegava cedo ao banco, entre as 7h30 e as 8h00. Dependia do trânsito, mas era um dos managers e, como manager, queria sempre chegar antes do pessoal”. Nesse dia fatídico não foi diferente.
Tinha começado uma reunião há poucos minutos quando sentiu um estrondo que fez abalar a torre. Do piso onde estavam, não se aperceberam logo do que tinha acontecido. Teria sido um embate na torre, mas pensaram num pequeno avião ou helicóptero. Mesmo assim decidiram começar a descer as escadas. Foi quando chegaram ao 22.º andar que ouviram muito barulho. Foi o momento em que o segundo avião se despenhou contra a torre sul.
Quando chegaram ao piso zero havia mais do que uma saída. Quatro colegas decidiram virar à esquerda. Joe e mais três funcionários viraram à direita. “Ainda hoje não sei porquê. Não sei por que virei à direita”, admite. Mas essa decisão salvou-lhe a vida. Os quatro colegas que foram pelo outro lado já não conseguiram sair.
Joe Salgado cruzou a rua e olhou para as torres. A segunda começou a ruir. “Começámos a correr pela rua abaixo o mais rápido possível. Não conseguíamos ver nada, tal era o pó nos olhos. Um bombeiro deu-nos uma garrafa de água, limpámos a cara e fomos a pé até Brooklyn”. Só mais tarde encontrou uma cabine telefónica e ligou para casa — para dizer que estava vivo. Durante todo esse tempo não faziam ideia se Joe tinha escapado. “Quando chegámos a Staten Island, houve uma carrinha que nos viu e parou. Viu que estávamos cobertos de pó e levou-nos a New Jersey”. Por essa altura, o mundo já estava em choque. Joe Salgado ainda não sabia exatamente o que tinha acontecido e só com a família, e com o que ia passando nas rádios e nas televisões, teve a verdadeira noção da tragédia a que tinha conseguido escapar: “Tive uma sensação de gratidão”.
Joe reúne-se todos os anos no dia 11 de setembro com os colegas que estavam juntos naquele dia no escritório. Esteve várias vezes no Ground Zero e assinalou lá o 10.º e o 20.º aniversário, mas não este ano. “Já faleceram 13 amigos. Ainda é um grande choque para todos”, justifica.
“Lembro-me dos apitos dos rádios dos bombeiros que tinham falecido”
Na Ferry Street, a meia-hora de comboio do World Trade Center, o português é uma das línguas mais faladas. Basta olhar para as montras e para as caras. Estamos num pequeno Portugal do outro lado do Rio Hudson. E muitos têm histórias para contar de um dia que não esquecem. É o caso do capitão da polícia de Newark, Maik Alexandre — a mãe não sabia escrever Michael, daí a opção menos óbvia na escolha do nome.
Maik Alexandre, que fala com o Observador impecavelmente fardado, lembra-se desse dia como se fosse ontem: “Estava a ter aulas na Academia de Polícia quando o primeiro avião embateu numa das torres e pensávamos que tinha sido um acidente. Quando o segundo avião se despenhou na torre sul, quase 20 minutos depois, soubemos que estávamos em guerra”.
Maik Alexandre começou por ir no carro da polícia, a fazer de batedor, para que as ambulâncias chegassem o mais rapidamente possível a um dos cinco hospitais que existiam em Newark na altura. “Fiz esse percurso mais de 60 vezes, para trás e para a frente”. Em 2001 tinha apenas 25 anos, mas lembra-se bem do nevoeiro de cinza no Ground Zero: “Não conseguia ver quase nada. O ar estava cheio de pó e vidro.” Depois, o que recorda melhor é do cheiro. “Era o cheiro de um corpo queimado, mas não era um… Eram milhares”.
As recordações vão surgindo à medida que conversa com a Rádio Observador. “Lembro-me dos apitos dos rádios dos bombeiros que tinham falecido. Alguns eram altos, significa que estavam por cima dos escombros. Outros baixinhos. Estavam enterrados e as baterias estavam a descarregar. Por isso, começavam a apitar”. Passados dias, ainda se ouviam esses apitos por entre os escombros.
Nesta emissão especial da Rádio Observador, em Nova Iorque, falámos com muitos portugueses e luso-descendentes. Em três horas de emissão em direto, foram feitas 11 entrevistas, que pode ouvir aqui.
Nova Iorque continua a ser a grande metrópole, uma cidade imensa, inundada de luz, cores, odores, mas tem uma ferida por sarar. Na zona de impacto daquele dia, abre-se um buraco para onde escorre água de forma ruidosa. Os nomes de 2.983 vítimas estão gravados em painéis de bronze do memorial dos atentados de 11 de setembro, onde os discursos estão proibidos. Entre essas quase 3 mil vítimas estão 9 portugueses: António Rocha, Raymond Rocha, Manuel da Mota, Christopher Mello, António Rodrigues, João Aguiar Jr., Dennis Gomes, Carlos da Costa e Mark Jardim.
A emissão especial da Rádio Observador em Nova Iorque teve o apoio da Fundação Luso Americana para o Desenvolvimento

title: ‘The Asholio Heritage’: Documenting history, identity and life of Asholio people
content:
By Prisca Sam-Duru
Presented as a rich and priceless compendium, “The Asholio Heritage,” by an accomplished and seasoned journalist, Ben Adam Shemang, is a historical masterpiece that takes readers on an interesting journey into almost everything they need to know about the Asholio people in Southern Kaduna, Nigeria.
The book by the pioneer Director of Training with the Voice of Nigeria (VON), Shemang who retired as Director of News (VON), brings to light, who the Asholio people are, what stands them out, as well as some of the people’s identity being threatened by modernisation.
In other words, The Asholio Heritage explores the cultural identity, farming practices, and social structure of the people.
Shemang, a graduate of Ahmadu Bello University (B.A. English), who holds postgraduate diplomas in journalism and law, a master’s in criminology and security studies, and currently a PhD student in Criminology and Security Studies, brings his training as a journalist into the compilation.
“The Asholo Heritage,” was published in November 2025 by NIRPRI Publishing Press, Abuja. The 409-page book is a product of profound research on Asholio life, history, culture, tradition, and custom.
The epoch-making history book on the Sholio people, is structured into 22 chapters made up of provocative topics and themes, including the people and history of Sholio, political organisation, clans and rulers, arbitration and alternative dispute resolution, language and linguistic variations, settlement patterns, religious modes of worship, cultural dances, family and marriage systems, games and leisure, music and musical instruments, customary practices, beliefs, economic activities, mathematics/counting, genealogy, etc.
In the “Introduction,” the author explains that the book wasn’t written to cause disaffection or injury to anyone considering that it delves deep into diverse aspects of Asholio people’s ways of life which aren’t documented.
Rather, the book was written “with the intention to provoke “debates, further insights and more literary works by critics, scholars, students, researchers and authors about the people,” adding that it “contains many parts of the history, politics, sociology, geography, economic development, the phonetics and phonology, the language, culture, religion, belief system, architecture etc, of the Asholio people,’ noting that it also provides insight into the Sholio land and immediate neighbours.”
In other words, “The book as it is in my submission, tends to define Asholio people with the hope that incoming authors and researchers can pick aspects or parts of this book and develop them into different books and that will be interesting reading titles in my thinking.”
“The Asholio Heritage” also features the totems and taboos of the Asholio people, such as why females are forbidden from eating eggs. As documented in chapter nineteen, “Way back, when a new house is to be built, it is started with just one stone at the centre of the proposed compound. The stone was called “afang agban”, meaning that the Asholio people started building a new compound with a granary (agban). The emphasis on the granary was the fact that the family must never go hungry.
Chapter one subtitled, “The Asholio People”, dives into who the people are, disclosing that Lutswe was the father, founder, and leader of the Asholio people. “…Lutswe came in the Alutswe clan, people who are said to be the first people to live in what is today known as Sholio land.” According to the author, the Asholio people are divided into four clans- Alutswe, Abvuat, Azam, and Aswua. The clans are listed in order of seniority without any of them being superior to the others.
It is noted in this chapter that modern scholars and colonial records have spelt the names of the clans quite differently without being able to change who they are; all these names refer to the same people who call themselves Asholio.
The author also reveals in the “Introduction” the different names the Asholio people are known with. He wrote, “The people we are talking about call themselves Asholio while outsiders call them Moroa or Marwa. So, some documents will have it as Moroa, Moro’a or Marwa.
In chapter two, titled ‘History of Asholio People,’ Shemang gives profound and diverse accounts of the origin of the Asholio people. Under subtitles such as ‘Vak as origin of Asholio’, ‘Bauchi origin theory’, ‘Origin from colonial sources’ and ‘Zaria and Katsina origin story,’ the book documents the diverse theories and accounts about the Asholio people.
The book captures the ‘Political Organisation’ of the Asholio people in Chapter Four, in which the author traces the leadership structures of the people from the pre-colonial era. Subtitles in this chapter include; ‘Pre-Colonial Period’, ‘Colonial Period’, Post-Colonial politics in Sholio land 1960- date, Asholio (Moroa) Development Association, Sholio Town Hall and Chat Community Bank. He follows this chapter up with “Some of the Paramount Rulers (YAAGWAM) of Sholio”, which is the title of Chapter Five.
While Chapter Nine deals with ‘Language and Linguistic Variations’ of the Asholio people, chapter eleven documents the impact of civilization on the people. The two major impacts are in the areas of cultural erosion and “Changes and substituting names of settlements”.
