The people’s religion and modes of worship, their sacred places and heroes and heroines, diverse cultural dances, family and marriage (which delves deeper into the relationship between grandparents and their grandchildren), games and leisure, the different musical instruments used for entertainment, the different practices, totems and beliefs of the Asholio people, etc, are all captured from chapter thirteen to chapter nineteen. Interestingly, the Asholio people have their own unique mathematics symbols.
This is documented in chapter twenty-one titled, ‘Mathematics (fe) and its importance. This section is presented with two subtitles, ‘Mathematics Symbols’ and ‘Counting in Sholio Language’.
The author’s attempt to make the book appealing to the reader pays off as he employs coloured illustrations, images, and photographs like the one used for the cover page.
He goes further to dedicate a total of sixteen pages in between pages 266 and 267, for photographs and illustrations showing the people’s kitchen utensils, wild fruits, traditional method of storing cold water, how the people dressed in the 70s, traditional dancers, their huts, and a whole lot more.
The ‘References’ section is an indication that ‘The Asholio Heritage’ is a well-researched and referenced book. It is quite suitable for the avid reader and scholars. Any reader who is traditionally and culturally inclined will find the book a historical companion.
As Fr. Benjamin Yakubu Bala, also known as fr. Bamba wrote in the Foreword, Shemang’s book will serve as a rich reference material to many.
“The heritage of a people is preserved in documentation. Unfortunately, there is not much documentation available on Asholio. Therefore, this book is a modest contribution by Shemang in this regard. Considering that there is not much written on the Asholio heritage, the author made good use of oral sources and personal experience and a few available documented sources.
“The author pays tribute to documentation by colonial masters. Some were apt while others contained uncompleted and unbalanced truths. In this book, you will see how the author was able to respectfully blend the colonial narratives with the realistic experiences of the people from local sources,” fr. Bamba wrote.
‘The Asholio Heritage’ is highly recommended to the Nigerian public, particularly every indigenous person of Southern Kaduna. Tourists and tourism entrepreneurs will find it a vital document.
To lovers of history, the book is priceless. It is a must kept on the shelves of homes, schools, and public libraries.

title: Lethbridge firefighters honoured at annual memorial: ‘What we signed up to do’
content:
It’s been 25 years since terrorists attacked the United States by crashing two commercial passenger jets into the World Trade Centres, one into the Pentagon and another that was taken down by passengers over a field in Pennsylvania.
Thousands of people died that day. Many who lived through witnessing it remember the tragedy as if it was yesterday.
“I was still in high school. I was in math class, so I remember exactly where I was,” said Brent Nunweiler.
A few short years later, Nunweiler himself would become a firefighter, saying he was influenced by those in service to change his career plans.
Now, he is the president of the Local IAFF 237 Firefighters Union in Lethbridge.
Far removed from the attacks in the northeastern US, Lethbridge’s brothers and sisters in the red trucks still honour the fallen every year.
“Twenty-five years ago, our profession changed forever,” Nunweiler said. “We’re honoured to recognize those from, not only New York, but our own members here who have given their lives for the community.”
During the annual event, every IAFF member across North America who passed away in the last year is honoured by having their name called.
Get daily National news
In Lethbridge, all local members are read aloud, whether they passed away this past year, or decades ago.
“A lot of those names we read locally I worked with, (my colleagues) worked with. Their families are here, so to let their families know we are still thinking about them and that their service is honoured is extremely important,” said Nunweiler.
Most of the names of people called died, not actively battling a blaze, but to cancer.
It’s a silent killer that has claimed so many firefighters in the years since 9/11, and for generations before the attacks.
“Our risks stay with us long after we stay home. It’s a dangerous profession, one of the most dangerous in the world.
“None of us would choose a different profession, this is what we signed up to do.”
As this year marks a quarter-century since the attacks, it felt different for those involved in the ceremony.
“We always feel it every year, but this year we knew it was in the public awareness and lots of people have that history in their hearts,” said Neil Laboske, commander of the IAFF 237 honour guard.
He says sadness and grief is felt fully, but it’s not the only emotion relit every year on September 11.
“Immediately after the events of 9/11, everybody was very much together and working together on building a future,” he said.
That unity in the face of rubble and smoke defined the days, weeks and years after the attack.
Now, Laboske says it’s more important than ever to remain unified while honouring the fallen.
“We just hope it’s an opportunity for people to stop, look around and remember what’s really important.”

title: Van Akkrum naar Amerika en terug: het bijzondere verhaal van bejaardenhuis Coopersburg – alleen deze zaterdag te bezoeken
content:
Van Akkrum naar Amerika en terug: het bijzondere verhaal van bejaardenhuis Coopersburg – alleen deze zaterdag te bezoeken
Een verslag door een auteur ter plaatse
Open Monumentendag Aan de rand van het Friese Akkrum staat het rijksmonumentale Coopersburg, in 1901 geopend als bejaardenhuis. Een bijzonder gebouw, maar het verhaal erachter is minstens zo fascinerend. Stichter Frank Cooper werd geboren in Akkrum, vertrok naar de VS en maakte daar fortuin. Alleen deze zaterdag, tijdens Open Monumentendag, is Coopersburg geopend voor publiek.
Een groepje keurig geklede ouderen kijkt ontspannen in de camera. Het is 1901, het jaar waarin bejaardenhuis Coopersburg in Akkrum (een Fries dorpje nabij Sneek en Heerenveen) zijn eerste bewoners verwelkomt. Achter hen strekt zich een langgerekt gebouw uit van bruine bakstenen, afgewerkt met witte sierbanden en zwarte dakpannen.
Architectuurhistorisch valt het onder de zogeheten overgangsarchitectuur: een weinig sexy, maar toch veelzeggend hokje tussen de neostijlen en modernere stromingen als jugendstil en art deco. In het midden trekt een statig middendeel met zuilen en torentjes de aandacht. Aan weerszijden daarvan staan tien kleine woningen, elk met een eigen voordeur, erker en gevel. Los van elkaar zouden het haast huisjes kunnen zijn, maar samen vormen ze een imposant en opvallend symmetrisch geheel.
Nieuw leven in Amerika
Coopersburg is het levenswerk van de Friese Folkert Kuipers, die in 1866 via Harlingen in het Engelse Hull op een boot stapte om voorgoed zijn geluk in de Verenigde Staten te beproeven. Het was op z’n zachtst gezegd een roerige tijd toen hij de overtocht maakte: het bloed van de Amerikaanse Burgeroorlog was nog maar net opgedroogd, de toenmalige president Abraham Lincoln was even daarvoor doodgeschoten en in het ‘Wilde Westen’ waren gewapende conflicten tussen het Amerikaanse leger, kolonisten en verschillende inheemse naties nog aan de orde van de dag. Niet zo gek dus dat de ouders van de toen 22-jarige Folkert zijn vertrek met lede ogen aanzagen en hem alvast geld toestopten voor de terugreis. „Maar niets of niemand kon hem tegenhouden”, vertelt Anne Dijkstra, oud-voorzitter van de historische vereniging Akkrum Ald en Nij, lachend. „Hij was een ondernemende jongen, sprak goed Engels en was vastbesloten het te maken in Amerika.”
In New York City werd Folkert opgevangen en gecontroleerd bij Castle Garden op het zuidelijkste puntje van Manhattan – Ellis Island werd pas geopend in 1892 – en verwelkomd door Friezen die al eerder de overtocht hadden gemaakt. De extreme armoede in het 19de-eeuwse New York dwong hem om naar Buffalo te vertrekken, waar hij al snel werk én een vrouw vond. Een Nederlandse zelfs, de in Middelburg geboren Antonetta Gerrardina de Graaff. „Ze trouwden en verdienden een beetje geld met de verkoop van herenvesten die Nettie maakte, waardoor een paar jaar later een grote droom in vervulling ging: een eigen winkel”, gaat Dijkstra verder. „Folkert heeft veel aan zijn eerste vrouw te danken.”
Toch leefde Nettie niet lang genoeg om het grote succes mee te maken; in 1879 stierf ze aan de complicaties van een buitenbaarmoederlijke zwangerschap, nadat ze eerder vijf gezonde kinderen had gekregen. Afleiding voor zijn verdriet vond Frank – Folkert Harmen Kuipers bekt niet zo lekker in de VS, dus logischerwijs had hij zijn naam laten wijzigen in Frank Harmon Cooper – in doorwerken. Samen met mantelhandelaar Henry Siegel opende hij in 1887 zijn eerste grote warenhuis in Chicago. Een grote brand leidde in 1891 tot de opening van een nieuwe vestiging in een gigantisch pand aan een van de hoofdstraten van de stad. En dat succes leidde weer tot een ‘Big Store’ op de plek waar Frank het eigenlijk in 1866 al wilde maken: New York City.
Meet me at the fountain
Met die zaken schreven Siegel & Cooper warenhuisgeschiedenis. Pier van der Heide, bestuurslid van de historische vereniging: „In Chicago verkochten ruim tweeduizend medewerkers meubilair, kleding, kruidenierswaren en boeken. Verder zaten er in het gebouw een bank, arbeidsbureau, telegraafkantoor, dokter, tandarts en kappers – een slimme manier om van een bezoeker ook een klant te maken.” In New York had het warenhuis zelfs een kinderopvang en restaurants. Beide panden waren voorzien van de modernste voorzieningen: draaideuren, roltrappen, liften, elektrisch licht en zelfs airconditioning. Ook trof je in allebei de winkels bij binnenkomst meteen een sierlijke fontein aan. Een herkenbaar ontmoetingspunt voor klanten, waaruit in New York de bekende uitspraak ‘Meet me at the fountain’ voortkwam.
Frank had niet alleen oog voor zijn klanten, maar ook voor zijn personeel. Zo zorgde hij voor een ziekenfonds, sportfaciliteiten, woonruimte voor vrouwelijke medewerkers en zelfs vakantiehuisjes. „Frank H. Cooper is een naam in Chicago die gedurende minstens tien jaar gestaan heeft voor alles wat in de handelswereld modern en up-to-date is. (…) Zijn personeel treedt hij opgeruimd tegemoet en zijn persoonlijke aantrekkingskracht valt op waar hij gaat”, schreef de Chicago Tribune lovend in 1901.
Terug naar Akkrum
Franks groeiende fortuin zorgde ervoor dat hij regelmatig kon terugkeren naar Akkrum. Tijdens een van die bezoeken werd hij getroffen door de zichtbare armoede in zijn geboorteplaats, vooral onder ouderen, en besloot hij dat daar iets aan moest gebeuren.
Tijdens een van de bezoeken aan Akkrum werd hij getroffen door de zichtbare armoede in zijn geboorteplaats, vooral onder ouderen
In 1899 richtte hij de stichting Coopersburg op en vroeg hij gemeentearchitect Folkert Hoekstra om een tehuis te ontwerpen. Vervolgens ging het zeker voor die tijd erg rap: nog geen twee jaar later stond het gebouw er. Op 8 mei 1901 werd Coopersburg officieel geopend, een moment waarvoor Frank met een hele delegatie de oceaan overstak: zijn vijf kinderen en hun aanhang, een handjevol kleinkinderen en zelfs twee kindermeisjes.
Frank bleef ook na de bouw financieel verantwoordelijk voor zijn plan. Om de ouderen te onderhouden stortte hij een flink bedrag in de stichting, die werd bestuurd door regenten die hij zelf aanwees. Dat bestuur kwam samen in de regentenkamer, die zich in het middengebouw bevindt en nog grotendeels in originele staat is. Boven de haard prijken de namen van alle bestuursleden die Coopersburg door de jaren heen heeft gehad.
Uniek is ook het gastenboek dat sinds 1901 prominent op tafel ligt. Alle bezoekers van Coopersburg staan erin vermeld, van bloemisten, bakkers en koopmannen tot een journalist van het Algemeen Handelsblad. Ook aan Frank zelf herinnert de kamer. Aan de muur hangt een schilderij van zijn beroemde Big Store, dat hij liet maken voor zijn vader. Wie goed kijkt, ziet dat de raampjes van het warenhuis zijn ingelegd met parelmoer.
In elke woning – tweeëntwintig in totaal, waarvan twee in het middengebouw – was plek voor twee bewoners. Man of vrouw maakte daarbij niet uit, en ook geloof speelde geen rol. Dat was opvallend voor die tijd. „Hoe de bewoners zelf met die gemengde bewoning omgingen, weten we niet”, vertelt Jan Eijzenga, secretaris bij de historische vereniging. „Maar je kunt je voorstellen dat het niet altijd eenvoudig was om een woning met iemand te delen die je niet zelf had uitgekozen. In het archief hebben we aandoenlijke briefjes gevonden van bewoners die de regenten smeekten om niet bij een bepaalde alleenwonende persoon te worden geplaatst.”
Mausoleum in de tuin
De woningen zijn inmiddels eigendom van een woningstichting en niet te bezichtigen – ook niet tijdens Open Monumentendag. Wel toegankelijk is de weelderige tuin voor en achter Coopersburg, met slingerpaadjes, bruggetjes, een fontein en kruisvormige zonnewijzer. Maar de echte blikvanger staat verderop in de tuin: het mausoleum – ook een rijksmonument – van Frank en zijn eerste vrouw Nettie.
Een opvallende parel tussen het groen, maar bovenal het laatste eerbetoon van hun kinderen aan hun ouders. Het werd door een lokale architect ontworpen in een ingetogen art-nouveaustijl. Boven de zware houten entree zijn de portretten van Frank en Nettie gebeeldhouwd en aan weerszijden staan twee vrouwenfiguren, die rouw en de overwinning op de dood symboliseren. Daarachter liggen de twee grote tombes, uitgevoerd in wit marmer. In die van Frank werd zijn gebalsemde lichaam bijgezet. Nettie, die al in 1879 was overleden, werd uiteindelijk alleen nog met haar botten te ruste gelegd. Normaal blijft het mausoleum gesloten, maar deze zaterdag kunnen bezoekers ook de binnenkant bekijken.
Frank kwam van niks en werd groot in Amerika. Hij heeft daar een enorm leven en imperium opgebouwd, maar is altijd een van ons gebleven
Open Monumentendag op Coopersburg is dit jaar extra speciaal, want het rijksmonument bestaat 125 jaar. In de tuin is daarom een fototentoonstelling te zien met oude beelden van Coopersburg en Akkrum. Ook worden twee splinternieuwe bronzen beeltenissen onthuld van Frank en Nettie, gemaakt door de Friese beeldhouwer Ben van der Geest. Maar waarom is er juist nu zoveel aandacht voor het echtpaar? „We zijn ontzettend trots op deze geschiedenis”, zegt Dijkstra. „Frank kwam van niks en werd groot in Amerika. Hij heeft daar een enorm leven en imperium opgebouwd, maar is altijd een van ons gebleven.”
Misschien is dat wel precies wat Coopersburg zo bijzonder maakt: het gebouw vertelt het verhaal van een man die de wereld introk en er fortuin maakte, maar zijn grootste blijvende stempel juist in zijn kleine geboortedorp achterliet.

title: Widow of Canadian killed in 9/11 wants to ‘redefine’ the day
content:
Maureen Basnicki stands in the dining room of the Albany Club in downtown Toronto on the eve of 9/11, proud of the dinner she has helped organize.
The “Service Day” dinner, she explains, is to show gratitude to service men and women — those who fought for Canada in Afghanistan, supported Canadians after 9/11, and those who continue serve our communities on a day-to-day basis.
Twenty-five years ago, her husband Ken Basnicki, 48, was killed when Al Qaeda terrorists highjacked planes and flew them into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Centre.
Maureen Basnicki, a flight attendant at the time, says she woke up that morning in a small town just outside of Frankfurt where her crew was on a layover.
She says she turned on her television and saw the second plane fly into the south tower.
“You can only imagine my shock and horror knowing Ken was there. I didn’t know which tower he was in, but I knew he was in New York and the rest is history,” she explains.
Because she didn’t have a cellphone at the time and was desperate to speak to Ken, Basnicki says she went down to the lobby of the hotel and asked the concierge if he could call Ken, who did have a cellphone.
There was no response so she begged the concierge to call back and leave him her number at the hotel.
“In any event, my mother-in-law received a call from Ken because he knew I was in Germany and didn’t have a cell phone. I can only repeat his last words to anybody, to his mother. He said ‘Mom, something horrible has happened. The room is full of smoke, the roof is blocked and I don’t know how I’m going to get out. I’m on the 106th floor of the World Trade Centre.’ That’s how definite I was about his whereabouts on that day,” Basnicki says.
Get daily National news
The skies were shut down as a result of the terrorist attack so Basnicki was stuck in Germany for three days, far from New York and the couple’s two children, aged 16 and 21, who were back in Toronto.
“I still get emotional when I think of it. Thankfully, I had a great crew. I got support from other crew members at the hotel, from the German people. People couldn’t do enough for me, but of course, I wanted to be home with my children,” she explains.
Basnicki says their family played the waiting game hoping that Ken would be a survivor.
“I knew when I was trapped in Germany that Ken was never going to come home,” she explains.
In the years since then, Basnicki has worked hard advocating for survivors of terrorism and to change the dialogue on 9/11.
“It’s imperative for me and for history’s sake, for our young people to understand what happened that day was a global event.”
She says while people will “never forget” the hate and the horror of the heinous attack that occurred, she is more of an “always remember” person.
“The outpouring of love and support, the response from Canadians that came in the aftermath, that’s so important. Looking back, 9/11 was an attack on our values, a shared value with the United States. It was an attack on democracy. I like to think we can celebrate our values that day instead of dwelling on the hate and horror,” Basnicki says.
In the room at the Albany Club where the dinner is being held, the tables are decorated with red and white linens and recording artist and anthem singer Robert Pilon is set to perform.
- Edmonton business, hit by crime several times, frustrated with police releasing suspect
- Former Saskatoon massage therapist sentenced to 30 months for sexual assaults
- Alec Baldwin says new documentary on ‘Rust’ shooting shows ‘me at my worst’
- RCMP seize package with $44K worth of cocaine at Manitoba airport
“I was successfully able to get, under the Harper Government on the tenth anniversary, September 11th to be designated ‘National Day of Service'”, Basnicki says.
These are the kind of events that she dedicates her time to now.
“We all want to remember the good memories. I’ve reached a point where you can only imagine how I feel when I see the planes, as a former flight attendant, used as a murder weapon to kill my husband. That visual is hard for me to escape,” she says, her voice cracking.
“I would rather dwell on the aftermath, celebrate with my ‘Come from Away’ family, not to make light of the event but to show off our true values,” Basnicki adds, with a smile on her face.
Basnicki encourages everyone to commemorate 9/11 by doing an act of service, be it participating in the upcoming Terry Fox Run or donating blood.
“Buy a cop a cup of coffee, a firefighter, show your gratitude,” she says laughing.
“Just a small way. Everybody can do that. It took average Canadians to react after 9/11. Go beyond the political rhetoric. Find your own personal capacity, a way of saying ‘we live in a very great country and we love our values here.'”
Basnicki says she misses Ken and knows he would have been proud.
“Ken was a man of service. He coached the kids when he was able to, he put his family ahead of his work, He had his priorities right. He gave to his community, organized community events. We had an annual volleyball tournament, on Labour Day weekend,” says Basnicki.
She says she will continue to work towards advocating for new legislation to combat terrorism but also to remind Canadians to celebrate the National Day of Service.
“For me, it was a death day for my beloved Ken. But c’mon, life is beautiful and I’m very proud of my country.”
Basnicki says she will continue to remember the nearly 3000 lives lost that day, including 24 Canadians, but wants to redefine the day.
“We have yet to define the day. There’s no physical memorial but let’s have a living one.”

title: INDIGENOUS A&E: ‘Unceded’ art, music tour, Apache images
content:
Sandra Hale Schulman
ICT
The latest: Weighty words, new record and tour, bold traditions in art
ART: Exposing performative words
Cahuilla artist Gerald Clarke doesn’t do anything small. As an educator and tribal leader using wit and material innovation to expose historical and present-day injustices, he has previously created two large scale sculptures — a giant 100-foot basket of straw for Desert X and satellite dish baskets made of crushed beer cans for an exhibit at the Palm Springs Art Museum.
Now, in a new series created for the 2026 Converge45 Triennial in Portland, Clarke has created “Between the Lines,” which takes on the by-now-routine land acknowledgments through a 16-foot “rubber stamp” sculpture and stamped branding iron prints contrasting the words “Unceded” and “Sorry.”
The exhibit is on display now through Oct. 17 at the Center for Native Arts + Cultures in Portland, Oregon.
“For several years now, various institutions have implemented a policy of delivering land acknowledgments as part of their practice,” Clarke said in a statement, noting that the Cahuilla Band of Indians is located in Southern California on unceded, ancestral lands.
“Describing the land as unceded is factually correct,” he said. “However, as an Indigenous person from so-called unceded lands, I don’t sense that the weight of the word is really understood or being expressed. While one may know the definition of the word unceded, that doesn’t mean that they can truly understand or comprehend the emotional weight of the word upon the tribal people whose lands have been taken.”
The Land Acknowledgement Series developed with the creation of a maquette for a larger work, “Unceded,” which is in the form of a large rubber stamp, he said.
“I chose the form of a rubber stamp to convey the idea that the word unceded lacks the emotional weight and true recognition of its meaning to Indigenous people,” he said. “I see it as similar to receiving a birthday card from a loved one that is unsigned but is simply stamped with a signature. Lacking the emotional connection that’s being expressed, it becomes meaningless and could even be seen as an aggression or disregard for Indigenous land rights.”
Other rubber stamps spell out “Sorry” and “Stolen,” and a series of prints use black ink on the “Unceded” maquette and red ink on the “Sorry” maquette, Clarke said, to “reconsider the words, their context, and their histories involving settler governments, relationships, and the treatment of Indigenous people.”
MUSIC: Miller takes a head trip
Two-time JUNO winning singer/songwriter/guitarist Derek Miller from Six Nations of the Grand River is a journeyman musician with a knack for guitar-based roots rock with a pop sensibility.
With a new album, “Outta My Head,” he has booked a tour across Canada starting Sept. 18 in Toronto.
He has appeared in the film, “Rumble: The Indians Who Rocked the World,” and on stages all over the U.S. and Canada.
“‘Outta My Head’ is out now, so excited,” Miller said. “First LP on vinyl on the @silverheelsrecords label with 11 songs. I’m really stoked to share this medicine. These songs helped me a lot through life lately, hope they can help you.”
Miller has shared a stage with artists Blood, Sweat & Tears, George Thorogood, Smokey Robinson and The Neville Brothers. Canada’s Olympic Committee, wanting an artist that reflected Canada’s roots, hired Miller to rock the crowds at the closing ceremonies of the Vancouver 2010 Winter Olympics.
In addition to recording with Willie Nelson and Daniel Lanois, Miller recorded for the Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of the American Indian, resulting in the 2016 JUNO-nominated album, “Rumble: A Tribute To Native Music Icons,” covering songs by Link Wray, Redbone, Peter La Farge and many more.
ART: Apache traditions in paint
The Southern Plains Indian Museum in Anadarko, Oklahoma, presents a new exhibition, “Talrick Enjady: Bold Traditions,” celebrating the painting work of Mescalero Apache artist Talrick Enjady.
The exhibition runs through Oct. 16, 2026.
Talrick was immersed in Apache customs and traditions in his upbringing, and he conveys these traditions, experiences, and community values onto his canvases. Each work takes shape through experimentation by sketching on canvas and then adding design to determine the direction of the artwork.
Talrick adds subjects, with enhanced silhouettes of dancers and spirits that are brightly colored for dynamic perspectives. He uses acrylics, graphite, watercolor, pastel, and charcoal, with natural paints from local sources.
While Talrick sees his paintings as traditional, the works also offer a unique view of Apache culture.
A full-time artist since 2022, Talrick has paintings in the Amerind Museum in Dragoon, Arizona, and the Mountain Arts Gallery and Tanner Tradition in Ruidoso, New Mexico.

title: Follow the Flowers, Find Ethiopia
content:
Follow the Flowers, Find Ethiopia
Addis Ababa, September 11, 2026 (FMC) — There is a moment each year when Ethiopia seems to change its rhythm.
The rains begin to loosen their hold. The hills remain intensely green, the air grows brighter, and the countryside takes on the colour of renewal. In towns and villages, preparations gather pace. New clothes appear. Homes are made ready. Songs return to the streets. Families begin their journeys home.
And then the flowers arrive.
The delicate yellow blooms of Adey Abeba have become one of the gentlest signatures of Ethiopia’s New Year. But they are also an invitation—to look beyond a single celebration and discover a country whose seasons are marked not only by weather, but by memory, movement, music, faith, food and the meeting of communities.
For a traveller arriving in Ethiopia at this time of year, the calendar can feel less like a sequence of dates than a route through a living cultural landscape.
The journey begins with Enkutatash, celebrated on Meskerem 1 as Ethiopia enters 2019. It is a day of family gatherings, traditional food, church observances, children’s songs and greetings exchanged between generations. Yet its meaning reaches beyond the festivities. It is one of those occasions when the ordinary social fabric of the country becomes especially visible: families reconnect, neighbours visit, children move from house to house, and communities welcome another year together.
Then the journey continues.
Across Ethiopia, September and the weeks that follow bring a remarkable succession of cultural and religious celebrations. Among them is Gifaataa, the New Year festival of the Wolaita people, celebrated between mid-September and early October. UNESCO inscribed Gifaataa on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2025, recognising a tradition in which people prepare their surroundings, return home to their families and seek reconciliation before the festival begins.
In other communities, the season carries its own ceremonies, music, dances and ways of welcoming renewal. Ethiopia’s cultural landscape is not a single story repeated in different places. It is a collection of stories lived side by side.
That becomes particularly visible as the country approaches Meskel.
In Addis Ababa, the enormous Demera bonfire transforms the heart of the capital into a place of ceremony and gathering. Across the country, the commemoration of the finding of the True Holy Cross brings together people of different ages, backgrounds and communities.
UNESCO inscribed Meskel on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013, noting among its social dimensions the reunion of families, reconciliation and the strengthening of social cohesion.
And when the season moves toward early October, another major cultural moment emerges with Irreecha, the Oromo thanksgiving celebration associated with the close of the rainy season.
It is a time of gratitude, gathering and collective expression, extending the season of celebration beyond the New Year itself.
This is why September in Ethiopia is difficult to describe simply as a holiday season.
It is a cultural passage.
The landscape itself participates. The country is emerging from Kiremt, the main rainy season, leaving the highlands and valleys richly green before the brighter, drier months settle in.
Rivers and waterfalls have been replenished; fields carry the memory of the rains; mountain slopes and rural landscapes appear at their freshest.
For visitors, this creates a rare meeting of landscape and culture.
A journey can move from the ancient streets and distinctive architecture of Harar to the monumental history of Aksum; from the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela to the lakes and highlands around Bahir Dar; from the dramatic landscapes of the Simien Mountains to the Rift Valley and the communities whose traditions give each place its own character.
But the most memorable encounters may not always be found on a monument.
They can happen around a coffee ceremony, at a family table, beside a festival procession, in a marketplace, on a rural road or in a conversation with someone who has a story about the place where they live.
This is where Ethiopia’s heritage becomes more than something to be viewed.
It becomes something to experience.
The country’s cultural wealth also tells a larger story about how Ethiopians have understood community and continuity.
Traditions have carried knowledge across generations—through music and oral history, craftsmanship and architecture, agricultural practices and customary systems, religious observances and communal celebrations.
Some of these traditions have now found recognition on the global stage. UNESCO’s current list includes seven elements associated with Ethiopia, ranging from Meskel and Ethiopian Epiphany to the Gada system, Fichee-Chambalaalla, Gifaataa, Shuwalid and Xeer Ciise.
Yet recognition is not the reason these traditions endure.
They endure because people continue to live them.
That distinction matters.
For Ethiopia, cultural heritage is not simply an inheritance preserved behind glass. It is part of the country’s social sovereignty—the ability of communities to retain their own stories, languages, values and ways of marking life while presenting them confidently to the wider world.
And that confidence gives the country’s hospitality a particular character.
Visitors are not merely being shown Ethiopia; they are being invited into moments that Ethiopians themselves value. The welcome is found in the sharing of food, the ceremony of coffee, the exchange of greetings, the opening of a home and the instinct to gather around occasions that matter.
In that sense, culture becomes a form of diplomacy long before a passport is stamped.
The season also offers a different way of seeing Ethiopia’s history.
A country with some of Africa’s most recognisable ancient monuments is often approached through the lens of the past. But travel through Ethiopia reveals something more dynamic: history is continually being interpreted by people living in the present.
Ancient cities remain inhabited. Religious traditions continue alongside contemporary life. Indigenous knowledge sits beside modern education and technology. Traditional celebrations fill streets that are also part of rapidly changing cities.
The old and the new do not always stand apart.
They share the same landscape.
That may be the most compelling reason to experience Ethiopia now.
The country is not asking the world merely to admire its history. It is revealing how history, culture, nature and contemporary life continue to shape one another.
Follow the flowers, and the road leads to a New Year.
Follow the celebrations, and it leads to communities.
Follow the communities, and it leads to stories.
Follow those stories, and a much larger Ethiopia begins to emerge—one whose identity has been carried across centuries, whose landscapes are entering a brilliant new season, and whose people continue to give their traditions new life.
The flowers will fade.
The celebrations will move on.
But the roads remain open, the mountains remain on the horizon, the coffee will still be poured, and the stories will still be waiting.
This is Ethiopia at the turning of the season: not simply a destination to see, but a country to encounter.

title: Fiction Park: They left a city and found a home
content:
Culture & Lifestyle
Fiction Park: They left a city and found a home
When an old friend tells a family about an empty ancestral property, a family decides to leave Kathmandu and start anew.LB Thapa
The dice of fate had never rolled in Bire’s favour. His insatiable appetite for gambling had finally consumed the last vestiges of his inheritance.
When Bire announced his intention to seek fortune in Kathmandu, Chhabilal, Bire’s elder brother, did not intervene. He simply watched his brother disappear over the horizon, knowing that some journeys must be undertaken alone.
Kathmandu greeted Bire with its characteristic chaos—a cacophony of honking vehicles and the ceaseless rhythm of survival. Bire found himself among the daily wage labourers who gathered at construction sites. He worked hard under the scorching sunlight. He carried bricks and mixed cement under the unforgiving sun, trying to adjust to the new environment.
In the evenings, when the work was done, and the labourers gathered around flickering lanterns to share their meagre dinners, Bire would join them in their rituals of escape. A bottle of local liquor passed from hand to hand, and a deck of cards would appear, the familiar symbols of his downfall drawing him back like a moth to flame. It was during one such evening that he first noticed Sita—not among the drinkers, but moving with quiet grace through the shadows of the labour settlement.
Sita was the daughter of Hom Bahadur, a weathered labourer who had raised his child with values as solid as the walls he helped construct. Unlike many in their circumstances, Hom Bahadur had insisted on education for his daughter. Sita had passed her School Leaving Certificate examination, but the halls of higher education held no appeal for her. She preferred the simple rhythms of domestic life—the warmth of the kitchen, the comfort of her mother's company, the quiet dignity of caring for their modest home.
Bire and Sita’s paths crossed with increasing frequency, their conversations beginning with shy glances and progressing to stolen moments between work shifts. However, Sita, through her own observation, glimpsed the man he could become. When Bire finally gathered the courage to propose, Sita's acceptance came with conditions as firm as the mountain stone that surrounded their village.
"I am also willing to marry you, Bire," she said with unwavering intensity. "But you must forsake three things: the gambling that has destroyed you, the drink that clouds your judgment, and the smoke that will blacken your lungs. These are not merely requests—they are the foundation upon which our life together must be built."
Bire agreed without hesitation, but Sita, wise beyond her years, demanded more than empty promises. She led him to the sacred precincts of Pashupatinath Temple, where the ancient Shiva lingam stands as a silent witness to countless vows. Bire knelt before the lord of destruction and creation, swearing with all the sincerity his soul could muster to honour his word.
When Sita finally confided in her father, Hom Bahadur agreed with her daughter’s decision.
The wedding was modest but filled with joy. Bire and Sita began their married life in a single room in Kathmandu's labyrinthine alleys, their possessions few but their dreams abundant. In that cramped space, Sita insisted on creating a small shrine, a corner of sanctity where she could offer her daily prayers. Bire, who had once lived only for the next gamble, now found himself drawn to the quiet peace of devotion.
Two daughters arrived in quick succession—tiny bundles of joy who filled their parents’ hearts while straining their already limited resources. The single room that had once seemed sufficient now felt like a cage. Bire watched his daughters sleep as Sita performed her evening rituals, and his heart ached for something more—a home where they could breathe, where the sacred could have its own space, where his children could play without knocking against the walls that confined them.
It was during one of his restless walks that Bire encountered Hikmat, an old friend whose own life had taken unexpected turns. Hikmat listened patiently as Bire poured out his frustrations—the impossibility of affording a proper home in the city, his unwillingness to let Sita work while their daughters were so young, the constant pressure that threatened to crush the fragile peace they had built.
"I have an idea," Hikmat said, his eyes gleaming with the light of revelation. "My ancestral village—Timirkot—lies about eighty kilometers from Gorkha Bazaar. We sold our property to a man named Captain Chitra Bahadur, a Gurkha serving in the British Army. He lives in England now and hasn't visited in years. The house stands empty, surrounded by land that once bloomed with abundance. You could live there. The village is nearly deserted now—no one would bother you."
Bire's heart quickened at the prospect. The village life he had known in his childhood called to him like a forgotten melody. He rushed home to share the proposal with Sita, who agreed immediately.
The journey began with a day's rest in Gorkha. The next morning, they boarded a battered jeep that carried them through winding mountain roads, the vehicle groaning with each turn. At Chisapani Bhanjyang, the road ended, and their true journey began.
For twenty kilometers they walked—Bire carrying their belongings, Sita with the younger daughter strapped to her back, the older girl clinging to her mother's hand. The path wound through rhododendron forests and alongside rushing streams, past terraced fields that clung to impossible slopes, and over suspension bridges that swayed treacherously above deep gorges.
When they finally reached Timirkot, Bire had no trouble locating Hikmat's ancestral home. It stood at the edge of the village, a structure of stone and timber that had once been grand but now wore the melancholy of abandonment. Vines crept over its walls, and the courtyard had surrendered to weeds and wild grass. The village itself seemed frozen in time—a handful of houses scattered across the hillside, many of them roofless and decaying, their former inhabitants having fled to the cities in search of opportunity.
But Bire and Sita saw not decay but potential. With determination born of necessity, they set to work. They cleared the undergrowth, scrubbed the stone floors until they shone, and repaired what they could with the limited tools they possessed. Sita cooked their meals over an open fire while Bire worked by the light of their kerosene lantern.
Within weeks, the house began to transform. The barren land around it responded to Bire's labor with generous yields—vegetables of every variety, grains and eventually, livestock that filled the empty stalls. Bire established connections with traders in Gorkha, who made the arduous journey to collect his produce. He was building not just a home but a legacy.
The villagers who remained were curious about the newcomers. Some came to offer help; others simply to observe. Bire received them all with the hospitality. When they asked who he was and how he had come to live in the captain's house, he would smile and say, "This is my home now, and you are all my neighbours."
His daughters grew strong and healthy, their laughter echoing through the valleys. A primary school lay five kilometers away—a journey they would make when they reached the proper age. For now, their education came from their mother's stories and their father's lessons about the land. Sita had never been happier; she had space for her shrine, room to breathe, and the peace that comes from living in harmony with nature.
Then, on an ordinary morning, everything changed.
Bire was working in his fields when he heard angry voices echoing from the house. He dropped his hoe and ran, his heart pounding with a premonition of disaster. When he arrived, he found a distinguished-looking man and his wife confronting Sita, their faces contorted with rage.
"How dare you occupy my property without permission!" the man thundered. "I will summon the police immediately!"
Bire stepped forward, his hands raised in a gesture of submission. "Sir, I beg your forgiveness," he said, his voice steady despite the turmoil within.
"We meant no disrespect. We will vacate your property at once. Please, there is no need for the authorities—we will leave peacefully."
Captain Chitra Bahadur, a British Army officer, was momentarily disarmed by Bire's humility. Sita, meanwhile, had recovered her composure and was already ushering the captain and his wife inside. She offered them fresh yogurt and insisted they rest while she prepared a proper meal. The captain's wife, impressed by Sita's grace under pressure, began to soften.
Over the course of the day, Bire showed the captain the fields he had cultivated, the livestock he had raised, and the repairs he had made to the property.
That night, as the family huddled together in the kitchen, preparing for their departure, Captain Chitra Bahadur and his wife held their own conversation.
The next morning, as the captain and his wife prepared to leave, he called Bire and Sita before him. His stern visage had been replaced by something warmer, something approaching gratitude.
"My wife and I have discussed the matter thoroughly," he said. "And we have reached a decision. You will stay. The property is mine, yes, but I have no intention of living here. The previous caretaker abandoned his duties—he hasn't paid the taxes in two years. You, however, have shown greater care for my land than I could have hoped for. I ask only one thing: pay the taxes promptly and send me the receipts on WhatsApp. Consider this as your home, for as long as you wish."
Bire and Sita stood frozen, the weight of the captain's words slowly penetrating their consciousness. Tears streamed down their faces—tears of relief, of gratitude, of vindication. They had ventured into the unknown with nothing, but they had been rewarded beyond their wildest expectations.
As the captain departed, waving from the winding path, Bire turned to Sita, who was still in tears. Their daughters emerged from the house, their small faces full of curiosity at their parents' display of emotion.

title: Tohono O’odham fight border wall on sacred, sovereign lands
content:
Standing near the pond at Quitobaquito Springs, Lorraine Marquez Eiler, a Hia-Ced O’odham elder, shared how her ancestors held ceremonies at the sacred site — a desert oasis in a national park that the federal government is set to bulldoze for a new border wall.
She pulled out a photo of her great-great grandparents and her great-grandparents, who would walk about 50 miles through the Sonoran Desert to the springs. The O’odham call the water flow A’al Vaipia. She showed the image of her ancestors to a group that included Indigenous leaders and a U.S. congressional representative — all there on Aug. 24 to condemn the border wall construction.
“All of my lifetime of work has been for the memories of my ancestors, of what they went through. With the incoming wall, should it be disrupted?” Marquez Eiler said in a determined voice, speaking of her ancestral lands. “That’s just another slap in the face, as far as I’m concerned, to my ancestors. And so I ask: Why?”
Surrounded by more than 100 community members at a town hall that followed the visit to Quitobaquito, Marquez Eiler hoped the federal government would pause border construction, as it did earlier this month in Texas after public backlash.
Quitobaquito is sacred to the Hia-Ced O’odham, the Tohono O’odham and other Indigenous people in Southern Arizona and México, who have traveled to the site for generations to join religious pilgrimages and ceremonies. They fear the spring is at risk of drying up if another border wall is built on the protected lands about 30 miles west of Tohono O’odham Nation.
The tribal nation is now fighting to halt border construction on two fronts: On O’odham land, where the federal government plans to build a new 30-foot border wall; and on adjacent federal land where another new border fence threatens Quitobaquito.
The projects are part of the Trump administration’s push to spend nearly $50 billion in taxpayer funds on border wall construction.
This is far from tribal citizens’ first fight with the U.S. government over destruction and division of their sovereign tribal lands. From the beginning, people of the Tohono O’odham Nation have lived on lands that had no borders.
When the U.S. and Mexico governments agreed to separate territories, the Tribal Nation wasn’t informed.
For years and until today, O’odham citizens — on both sides of a border they never agreed to — travel freely across their nation. While they have tried to work with border officials to quell crime, they have fought border walls that separate their people and harm their ancestral lands.
The recent fights under the Trump administration have spurred a legal battle and a high-profile standoff between federal agents and law enforcement from the Tohono O’odham Nation. O’odham people are now fighting for tribal sovereignty in the face of a Republican-led federal government arguing for U.S. sovereignty.
Feds already razing the land
In the Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, where Quitobaquito Springs sits about 13 miles west of the Lukeville port of entry, the Trump administration has proposed a 30-foot tall border fence 150 feet from the existing one. Marquez Eiler is worried she will no longer be able to access land that for generations has been part of her Tribal Nation’s religious traditions, if that wall is built.
Parts of Quitobaquito lands originally belonged to a family of Hia-Ced O’odham descent. In 1937, President Franklin Roosevelt signed a proclamation establishing the Organ Pipe National Monument as a way to preserve a vast swath of the Sonoran Desert. The new monument was part of a U.S. National Park Service effort to preserve “ecological wonders of the country,” the agency’s website states.
Now, a few miles east of the pond, construction equipment from federal government contractors sits next to the border, the land around it already cleared. Cactuses along the border are marked with a colored string, and a rope lines the proposed area where a second border wall may be built.
If that line continues west, the Quitobaquito pond is right in its path. If contractors bulldoze the cacti, they will destroy legally protected desert plants. They will destroy flora that is sacred to the O’ohdam people, who traditionally believe that plants and the earth are their ancestors.
When the U.S.-Mexico boundary was created through the 1854 Gadsden Purchase, it divided the Tohono O’odham Nation’s ancestral lands. Today, there are about 3,000 enrolled O’odham citizens living in Sonora, Mexico, and families often cross the border to visit family, visit cultural sites, and for religious ceremonies.
Tohono O’odham Nation sues federal government
About 30 miles east of Quitobaquito — on O’odham land — the administration has also proposed building a 30-foot fence in three areas where the border is currently marked by heavy steel fencing a few feet tall.
In June, the Tohono O’odham Nation filed a lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security in an attempt to block border wall construction on their land.
“While the Nation values its close relationship with the Department, it has long opposed construction of a border wall on the Reservation,” the lawsuit states.
“The Nation understands that construction of the wall would entail significant devastation on the Reservation, including the destruction of mountain peaks sacred to the O’odham,” the suit argues. “It would fray the ties between O’odham communities and families on opposite sides of the border, interfere significantly with O’odham religious rituals and practices, and destroy plant and animal resources sacred to the O’odham.”
The tribal nation’s lawsuit cited instances earlier in the year when federal contractors “destroyed ancestral sites of great importance while constructing the wall” adjacent to O’odham land.
In April, a Department of Homeland Security contractor damaged the Las Playas Intaglio, a 1,000-year-old fish-shaped geoglyph in Arizona’s Cabeza Prieta National Wildlife Refuge that pointed toward the Gulf of California.
Border Patrol continues construction
In a memorandum outlining opposition to the lawsuit, the federal government’s attorneys said the Tohono O’odham Nation failed to show that the border wall construction is being done in excess of the federal government’s legal authority. The document also emphasized the U.S. government’s “preexisting right to secure the border.”
“While the United States has worked — and will continue to work — cooperatively with Plaintiff to promote their shared interest in border security, Plaintiff does not hold veto power over the United States’ sovereign duty to secure its borders,” the memo said.
While waiting for a decision from the courts, tribal leaders put up “No Trespassing” signs on Aug. 7, saying in a news release that border wall contractors who attempted to enter the Tohono O‘odham Nation would be “illegally trespassing.” Early Aug. 25 morning, contractors entered the tribal nation accompanied by about 20 “masked, armed” border patrol agents, according to a news release from the Tohono O’odham Nation.
In an emailed statement to Arizona Luminaria, Rodney Scott, U.S. Customs and Border Protection commissioner, said CBP is moving forward with the federal government’s border wall construction project along the 62 miles that cut through the Tohono O’odham Nation.
“The project will close one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border: remote desert that has facilitated decades of drug loads, migrant deaths, and cartel activity,” Scott wrote.
A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson in the same email said, “the worksites are inside the 60-foot Roosevelt Reservation,” referring to designated land north of the U.S.-Mexico border that the federal government manages.
“This is about tribal sovereignty”
At Quitobaquito Springs, Marquez Eiler, the tribal elder, led U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva toward the pond to share more with the congresswoman about the tribal communities’ fight.
“After standing here today, seeing this land, and directly hearing from the nation, I am more convinced than ever, this is not just a border construction project,” Grijalva said. “This is about tribal sovereignty, it’s about sacred land, it’s about history, culture and spiritual practices of the O‘odham people and others.”
Tohono O’odham Chairman Verlon Jose and Vice Chairwoman Carla Johnson organized the trip to Quitobaquito to stand against the Trump administration’s insistence on building a new border wall.
For the Tohono O’odham and other Indigenous people, the land is their church, where they hold ceremony and prayer, Jose said. The federal government has a history of destroying the O’odham’s sacred land, he added.
When the first border fence went up between 2019 and 2020, contractors blasted through O’odham burial sites on Monument Hill.
“This is not ours to own. It is ours to protect, to protect for the people. To protect for you and I and everyone the creator has placed here on this earth,” Jose said.
“Why do we not want a wall?”
A few hours after their visit to Quitobaquito on Aug. 24, the International Sonoran Desert Alliance, which Marquez Eiler co-founded, hosted a town hall in Ajo, about 40 miles north of the springs. Grijalva, Jose and Johnson shared their efforts to stop the construction projects and listened to residents’ concerns.
More than 100 people filled the Ajo Plaza Rec Hall.
They shared worries over whether the wildlife would survive another construction project – the Quitobaquito pupfish, an endangered species, the Sonoyta mud turtle, the desert caper plant and the Quitobaquito tryonia, a tiny springsnail, call the springs their home.
They criticized the taxpayer cost for the border fence as too high – more than $46 billion in federal funding for projects from California to Texas. They urged Grijalva to push for comprehensive, humane immigration reform instead.
“Why do we not want a wall? Because we are not afraid of who is on the other side,” said Sara Mae Williams, Justice of the Peace in Ajo and a citizen of the Tohono O’odham Nation. “It’s us. It’s our people. It pains me when they try to divide us.”
On Aug. 25, Grijalva and other Democratic federal lawmakers who represent the borderlands – Reps. Veronica Escobar of Texas and Raul Ruiz and Juan Vargas of California – sent a letter opposing the wall to the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of the Interior.
The lawmakers urged the Trump administration to stop further construction of the border wall “until meaningful government-to-government consultation has occurred with the Tohono O’odham Nation and Congress has received a full accounting of the project’s impacts on Tribal lands, cultural resources, and surrounding communities.”
The fight continues
U.S. District Judge Richard J. Leon denied the Nation’s motion for a preliminary injunction on Aug. 14. In a written opinion explaining his decision, the judge said the Tohono O’odham Nation is “unlikely to succeed on the merits because the federal Roosevelt Reservation exists along the international border and, in any event, plaintiff has not established that construction of a border wall will indeed alter Reservation boundaries.”
“The international border is an area of great significance to both the United States and to the Nation,” Leon wrote. “While I have concluded that a preliminary injunction is unwarranted, I fully expect the Government in the months ahead to follow through on its guarantees of consultation and cooperation with the Nation to address the Nation’s concerns regarding border wall construction!”
The Tohono O’odham Nation appealed Leon’s decision to a higher court on Aug. 26. The day after, the Tohono O’odham again asked Leon’s lower court to stop border wall construction while the appeal was resolved. Leon had not responded by Sept. 10, and the federal government has said it plans to fight the injunction and appeal.
“We will not let this destroy our sacred sites, our burial sites, our holy places, the places of our ancestors,” Jose said at the town hall, pausing to stress his sentences. “We will not let it destroy our environment. We will not let it further divide our people. We will not let it divide our reservation.”

title: Museum agrees to return remains to ancestral homeland
content:
Museum agrees to return remains to ancestral homeland
- Published
More than three dozen sets of human remains taken during the British colonial rule of India and Myanmar are set to be returned to their ancestral home by a museum.
Skulls and bones belonging to the Naga people of northeastern India and Myanmar - formerly known as Burma - have been displayed at the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford for more than a century.
In 2020, the museum removed all human remains from public display as part of what the it called a "decolonisation process" - including the ancestral Naga remains.
The museum has now announced that a formal decision has been made by the University of Oxford Council to return the 39 ancestral human remains to their homeland.
"They've been here in a foreign land for more than a century," Dr Vihuto Asumi, President of the Sumî Hoho Naga tribe, said of the remains.
"We believe that their spirits are still not at rest - so by doing this, we believe it will bring spiritual healing, not only to the ancestral remains here but to everyone who died during the head-hunting days."
The Pitt Rivers claims to hold the largest collection of Naga artefacts in the world, most of which were acquired during British colonial rule in India and Myanmar.
Many were acquired by John Henry Hutton, a colonial administrator in the Indian Civil Service and an anthropologist, who handed them to the museum more than a century ago.
Among the museum's Naga collection - which contains several thousand items - are 219 items listed as human remains, 39 ancestral human remains and 178 objects that are thought to contain human hair.
The latest announcement concerns only the ancestral remains, and follows a declaration made by a Naga delegation visiting Oxford in 2025, in which the group requested the objects be returned.
The museum's director, Prof Laura Van Broekhoven, said: "It has been a long journey to get to this moment."
"We know that this week will be one where we will feel both grief and sadness when looking back on that past, and also where hope is possible as we work towards reconciliation and healing."
Following the decision, the Pitt Rivers is now organising an official handover ceremony involving a Naga delegation.
The Naga will then accompany the remains of their ancestors home, with some returning for the first time in more than a century.

title: At 4, he lost his NYPD father on 9/11; 25 years later, he wears his badge
content:
At four years of age, Casey Kloepfer was too young to understand why his father never came home from work. Twenty-five years later, he carries that loss into the same department his father served, wearing his father's badge number and playing for the NYPD lacrosse team his father helped create, states an online report by NYC Government website. For Casey, the connection to his father is not confined to a photograph, a memorial or a family story. It is woven into the uniform he wears and the department he chose to join.
A father lost on September 11
Ronnie Kloepfer was an NYPD officer who was killed in the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. He was among the thousands of first responders who rushed toward danger as others tried to escape. His death left behind a family that, like so many others, had to navigate life without someone who had been at its center. Ronnie's connection to the NYPD extended beyond his work as a police officer. He was also instrumental in establishing the department's lacrosse team, bringing together officers through a sport he loved and the team would eventually become an unexpected bridge between generations.
Following his father's path
A quarter-century after September 11, Casey became an NYPD officer himself. His decision gave a new meaning to a legacy that could easily have remained rooted in the past.
He now wears his father's badge number, carrying a small but deeply personal reminder of the man whose career ended before Casey was old enough to understand it.
Casey is also part of the same lacrosse tradition his father helped establish. Alongside other officers whose families share similar connections to the department, he keeps alive something that began long before the attacks. The significance is particularly powerful because the NYPD's relationship with September 11 did not end when the World Trade Center towers fell. Hundreds of officers who responded that day and worked at Ground Zero in the months that followed have since died from illnesses linked to their service.
A legacy that keeps moving forward
The story of Casey and his father reflects a larger reality within the NYPD. The department has spent 25 years carrying the memory of those it lost while welcoming new generations who were children, or not yet born, when the attacks happened. For younger officers, September 11 can feel like distant history. For families such as the Kloepfers, it remains personal. Casey's uniform, badge number and place on his father's lacrosse team bring those two eras together. Ronnie's life was cut short on September 11, but the things he built did not disappear with him. His son now serves in the department he once served, and the lacrosse team he helped found continues to bring NYPD officers together.

title: A los 84 años sigue trabajando en el campo: la historia de Malena Sanguinetti
content:
La inauguración de la 121ª Expo Rural del Prado tuvo un momento especialmente dedicado a quienes han construido su vínculo con el campo desde lugares muy diferentes. Bajo la consigna “Las Rurales”, la Asociación Rural del Uruguay (ARU) reconoció tres mujeres con historias atravesadas por el trabajo, la producción, la vocación y, sobre todo, la perseverancia.
Las homenajeadas fueron Malena Sanguinetti Ponce de León, Marisa Viera e Isabel Chiarino, y, a su vez, se reconoció la trayectoria del médico veterinario Jaime Castells. Cuatro recorridos distintos, desde generaciones y realidades también diferentes, pero unidos por una vida estrechamente vinculada al medio rural.
Malena Sanguinetti: a los 84 años, sigue al frente del campo
Malena Sanguinetti Ponce de León tiene 84 años y continúa trabajando en el campo familiar en Canelones, a pocos minutos de Montevideo. La historia del establecimiento se remonta a 1907, cuando la tierra fue adquirida por su abuelo, mientras que su padre comenzó a trabajarla tres décadas después.
Pero su propia historia productiva también tiene mucho para contar. A los 70 años, con un campo que mostraba señales de desgaste, encontró nuevas herramientas para transformar el sistema y seguir adelante.
En 62 hectáreas desarrolló un esquema de pastoreo con 70 potreros, con agua y sombra en cada parcela. También buscó mejorar el tipo de ganado, trabajando con animales de tamaño moderado y genética Red Angus. El sistema, además de mejorar la utilización del campo, terminó siendo una herramienta para que pudiera continuar trabajando a una edad en la que muchos ya se han retirado.
Su historia estuvo marcada por aprender haciendo. Malena contó que le hubiera gustado continuar estudiando, pero las circunstancias de la vida no se lo permitieron. Eso, sin embargo, nunca significó dejar de formarse.
“Nunca dejé de aprender a través del trabajo y la experiencia”, expresó. Con esfuerzo, responsabilidad y compromiso, sostuvo, siempre buscó salir adelante y darle lo mejor a su familia.
Incluso dudó antes de aceptar el reconocimiento. Finalmente estuvo en el Prado para recibirlo y convertirse, a sus 84 años, en una de las protagonistas de la inauguración.
Cuatro historias diferentes. Una productora que sigue trabajando a los 84 años; una mujer que encontró en el tambo una oportunidad y hoy lidera un equipo; una cabañera que debió abrirse camino en un ámbito que inicialmente le habían dicho que no era para ella; y un veterinario que después de más de seis décadas de profesión sigue entendiendo el trabajo como una forma de servir a los demás.
Cuatro historias con las que la Rural del Prado eligió, en el comienzo de su 121ª edición, reconocer también a muchas otras que se repiten todos los días en el campo uruguayo.

title: WATCH: Anastasia Fourie shines at Zulu Reed Dance as 30 000 maidens gather in KZN
content:
The uMkhosi Womhlanga is a centuries‑old Zulu custom, revived in the late 20th century, aimed at promoting self‑respect.
Anastasia Fourie, a young debutant from Eshowe, KwaZulu‑Natal (KZN) drew national attention after participating in the 2026 uMkhosi Womhlanga (Zulu Reed Dance) at the Emashobeni Royal Palace near oPhongola, alongside fellow debutant Kelly Kleinbooi from Greytown.
Fourie and Kleinbooi joined around 30 000 maidens at the annual cultural festival, which has become a focal point of public curiosity and debate.
Maidens
From Msunduzi to Richmond, maidens were sent off with prayers, cultural teachings and messages of encouragement from municipal, traditional and community leaders before embarking on the journey to eMashobeni Royal Palace near uPhongolo.
The uMkhosi Womhlanga is a centuries‑old Zulu custom, revived in the late 20th century, aimed at promoting self‑respect, community solidarity, and delaying sexual activity among young unmarried women.
During the ceremony, maidens gather reeds from riverbanks and present them to King MisuZulu kaZwelithini as a pledge of purity.
Zulu culture
Speaking to broadcasters on site, Fourie expressed joy at her initiation into the custom.
“I enjoy really much. It’s an honour to be here with everyone, and it’s a new experience. I like the Zulu culture and how they celebrate it and just the way how everything is done into the culture. Yeah, I like how everything is done here. It’s not bad, but it’s good. They must just celebrate their virginity, happy that they still have it.”
She and Kleinbooi vowed to return to the ceremony every year, describing the journey and its cultural requirements as meaningful to their participation.
Traditional attire
Fourie’s choice to wear traditional attire tailored to her comfort prompted mild debate over dress codes, but attendees and spectators largely welcomed her presence.
The event created a hive of activity in oPhongola, KwaZulu‑Natal, as maidens from across the country paraded before the Amazulu king.
[WATCH] A debutant at the uMkhosi Womhlanga (reed dance), Anastasia Fourie, speaks to #Newzroom405‘s @Lethu_Nxumalo about her experience with the maidens attending the celebration at Emashobeni Royal Palace. pic.twitter.com/BCVJqucIL4
– Newzroom Afrika (@Newzroom405) September 12, 2026
Caution
Mpiyakhe Buthelezi, spokesperson for the king, cautioned against the misuse of photographs taken during the ceremony, warning that images of maidens should not be exploited to degrade participants or misrepresent the event.
“People are not coming here to be embarrassed. They are here to honour culture. We ask that photos not be taken in ways that disrespect the maidens or distort the meaning of the ceremony,” the spokesperson said.
Ubuntu
The annual gathering promotes values including dignity, Ubuntu, respect and abstinence and forms part of broader efforts to encourage social cohesion and the positive development of young women.
The event is supported by the KwaZulu-Natal (KZN) Department of Sport, Arts and Culture on behalf of the provincial government.

title: Bashir Hajiyev highlights revival of Kalbajar at Honey Festival
content:
Bashir Hajiyev highlights revival of Kalbajar at Honey Festival
- 12 September, 2026
- 19:18
It is a source of pride to gather again on this land and take part in an event that preserves Kalbajar's ancient traditions, Bashir Hajiyev, Special Representative of the President of Azerbaijan in Kalbajar district, said.
According to Report's correspondent in Karabakh, he made the remarks at the Second Kalbajar Honey Festival.
"We owe the fact that we are in our native land today to the decisive political will and leadership of the Victorious Commander-in-Chief, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev, the heroism of our martyrs and the bravery of our veterans," Hajiyev said.
He noted that, on the instructions of the head of state, large-scale reconstruction and development work is underway in the liberated territories, settlements are being rebuilt and residents are gradually returning to their native lands.
"Kalbajar is one of the important centers of this large-scale reconstruction process. Life is becoming more vibrant here with each passing day, people are once again working on their native lands and establishing farms, while various events and festivals are being held. All this is a manifestation of the new reality created by the Great Return. The fact that the Honey Festival is being held in Kalbajar for the second time also carries special significance in this regard," he said.
Hajiyev noted that beekeeping is one of Kalbajar's traditional agricultural activities and has long played an important role in employment and the economic life of the district's residents.
"These traditions continue to develop today and are entering a new stage. It is particularly encouraging that beekeepers are expanding their activities and presenting their products at a festival like this," he said.
According to Hajiyev, events such as the Honey Festival are rooted in the hard work of Kalbajar residents, their love for their homeland and attachment to their native land.
"We clearly see these values today in their daily lives and in their enthusiastic participation in this event. Their work and attachment to the land give these events their true meaning. The joy on people's faces shows that such events are an expression of reunion with their land and the new life being built here," he said.
Hajiyev expressed confidence that the Honey Festival would continue to be held as a tradition, expand in scale from year to year and contribute to promoting Kalbajar's agricultural, tourism and economic potential both in Azerbaijan and internationally.
"I would like to thank everyone who contributed to organizing this festival, first and foremost the head of state, as well as our residents, beekeepers, farmers, guests and media representatives," he added.

title: Even after her death, Hana Razga is the glue that keeps her family together
content:
Hana Marta Razga: Feminist. Advocate. Mentor. Community builder. Born May 28, 1947, in London; died Jan 31, 2026, in Edmonton; died of sepsis; aged 78.
Imagine what it must have been like to wake up in Prague on Aug. 21, 1968 when, overnight, thousands of Soviet tanks rolled into Czechoslovakia to extinguish the brief liberalization period known as the Prague Spring.
For 21-year-old Hana Marta Razga, it was a turning point. She left her homeland along with her fiancé Jan Soukup, to courageously forge a new life in Canada, knowing that she might never return home to see her family again.
Born in London to Czechoslovak diplomats, Hana was the fifth of seven children. She lived in England and Hungary, as well as Czechoslovakia as a child. It was an unusual upbringing that exposed her to other cultures, languages and political systems.
By the end of 1968, Hana and Jan had arrived in Canada. They were married in Banff in the spring of 1969 and shortly afterward, settled in Edmonton to start a family. They had four children: Katarina, Jana, Olivia and Alex, before they separated in 1988.
Hana made sure that her children received equal attention and resources. Having four children spread quite far apart in age meant that she was always managing a wide range of interests and demands. She created a monthly “Day Out” where she would take one child out for lunch and shopping for new clothes or toys, on a rotating schedule. This was her opportunity for one-on-one time. It was a day that made each child feel special, seen and heard.
Hana spent her life advocating for fairness and social justice in Canada. She championed women and children throughout her career, her political engagement and her volunteer work. She lived simply and deliberately, mindful of her environmental impact long before “global warming” became a household term. Hana’s dedication to conservation however showed up in quirky ways. Birthday cards arrived with messages written on sticky notes so the card could be reused. And she insisted on flushing her toilet with cold bath water left in the tub.
In 1983, Hana was hired at Transport Canada to create opportunities for women. Her female colleagues became lifelong friends and these feminists helped establish Edmonton’s Canada Place Child Care Society so mothers who worked for the government could have their children cared for in the same building. The centre still operates, over 35 years later.
When Hana retired from public service, she shared her pension with her two unmarried sisters in the Czech Republic. She also began running as an NDP candidate in numerous federal, provincial and municipal campaigns in Conservative Alberta years before the historic NDP win in 2015.
Hana invested thousands of dollars of her own money and countless hours door-knocking to meet constituents. She was deeply disappointed with each loss but she kept coming back because she held a steadfast conviction to her ideals and values. She was stubborn and in it to win.
She volunteered with the Big Brothers Big Sisters of Edmonton, located in what would become her beloved neighbourhood of Riverdale, on the banks of the North Saskatchewan River. She had a deep respect for nature, whether planting seeds in her garden or wildcrafting herbs to make salves and tinctures, she saw plants as healers. Most famously, she was known for promoting her “onion syrup” cough remedy made with chopped onions and honey.
In 1988, Hana received a pardon from the Czechoslovak government, allowing her to return. Since then, she spent many summers with her family in Prague, travelling back for over three decades. Her last trip was four months before she died.
Hana was delighted with the arrival of successive grandchildren. She was intelligent, compassionate, curious, caring and a generous individual who liked things to be her own way. She liked to end her day with a glass or two of prosecco. When travelling across the country to visit family, she would bring a water bottle filled with wine on the Greyhound bus so she could quietly sip as the sun went down.
Even after her death, Hana is the glue that keeps the family connected. Against her lawyer’s advice she named all four children as co-executors of her estate. All are committed to handling her affairs together as a team - Team Hana.
Jana Razga is Hana Razga’s daughter.

title: The Boge-Bada arrives at Era Kone
content:
The Boge-Bada arrives at Era Kone at around 1 pm, welcomed by traditional dancers from Manumanu Island and the Tabu dancing group from the Hanuabada village.
The traditional Hiri Lakatoi is the centrepiece of the annual Hiri Moale Festival in Port Moresby, celebrating the historic trade voyages of the Motu people.
Looking back to the history of the Lakatoi, the first Lakatoi was built by Edai Siabo, from the village of Boera.
According to the legends told, Edai Siabo was returning from a fishing trip when a great eel appeared and dragged him under the water. The eel was believed to be the spirit of the sea.
He returned Edai to the surface of the sea, after instructing him to build a great Lakatoi, to fill it with cooking pots, and to sail westward, following the south-east trade wind called the laurabada in the Motu language.
Obeying the spirit, he built the first Hiri-Lakatoi, named it Bogebada (which means sea-eagle), and had it loaded with pots made by his wife.
He and his friends then sailed up the coast into the waters of the Gulf of Papua. That is where the historical Hiri-Trade Voyage was formed, which is now an important part of the culture of the Motu people.
For months, the Bogebada and its crew were away. The villagers were all convinced the crew had perished. They mocked Edai’s wife and tried to force her to remarry.
Before Edai left, he had instructed her to stay within a corner of her house, not to bathe in the sea, to keep a tally of the days the Bogebada had been gone, to keep her fire burning, and to have her skin tattooed by an old woman.
Failing to stick to this routine would endanger the expedition and the lives of Edai and his men.
One day, a Lakatoi appeared on the horizon and slowly approached the village. It was Bogebada.
Edai was arriving back home, a hero. His wife jumped into the sea and washed away her accumulated dirt, put on her finest costume, walked out onto the verandah of the house, hit it with a stick, shouted, Hedihoroha Bogebada and began dancing in joy.
The traditional Hiri voyages carried the much-prized Motu cooking pots to the people of the Gulf of Papua and brought back plentiful supplies of sago for the Motu.
For the Motu people, along the coast, the land and the sea provided what sustained their families and community. Food was life, food was wealth, food was a symbol of generosity and togetherness.

title: 13 Contestants of the 2026 Hiri Hanenamo are preparing for the official crowning
content:
As the Boge-Bada reached the shores of Era Kone(Ela Beach), the voices of the Hiri Hanenamos shouting the famous ‘Hedi-horo Boge-bada’ echoed along the shoreline of Era Kone.
The 13 contestants are participating in the Hiri Hanenamo Quest, which is the prestigious cultural pageant held during the annual Hiri Moale Festival in Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea.
The 13 contestants, after their official registration had participated in different judging categories, lead-up events and community engagement within their communities, have now reached the peak of the quest, which is the crowning, that will be staged tomorrow, September 13, 2026, at the Sir Herbert Murray Stadium after the last sway (Koea).
Unlike a conventional pageant, the Hiri Hanenamo focuses rigorously on cultural literacy, community leadership, and the preservation of the historic Hiri trade legacy.
These exemplary young women have been formally nominated by their respective local leaders to serve as cultural ambassadors, representing the identity, oral history, and traditional values of their respective Motu and Koitabu villages.
The annual event is organised by the Motu Koita Assembly, in collaboration with the National Capital District Commission and the Hiri Moale Festival Committee.
The 13 contestants for the 2026 quest are:
• Hanenamo 1: Miss Asi Hota — Gaire
• Hanenamo 2: Miss Edna Moi Oala — Boera
• Hanenamo 3: Miss Keruma Asi — Porebada

title: Newman Rodeo's return for first time since 2019 draws 'royalty'
content:
Return of Newman Rodeo draws 'royalty' and riders from far and wide
In short:
The small mining town of Newman has been buzzing in the lead-up to its first rodeo in seven years.
The full-points rodeo drew competitors from across the state, including rodeo royalty.
What's next?
Event organisers and locals hope the event will become a mainstay on the town's calendar.
Rodeo royalty Ariana Rhodes is among the dozens of competitors who travelled from far and wide to compete in Newman's revitalised rodeo.
Eleven-year-old Ariana and her eight-year-old cousin Svetalina Stones trotted their horses around the red dirt arena that reflects the Pilbara town's mining roots.
The pair appeared at home despite it being somewhat different to where they normally ride in Lake Clifton, south of Perth, 1,200 kilometres away.
Newman, deep in the heartland of iron ore country, has not had a rodeo since 2019.
Royalty at the red dirt rodeo
Crowned Rodeo Mini Princess last year, this is Ariana's first Newman Rodeo.
"I'm competing in barrel racing and pole bending," she said.
"My favourite's barrel racing."
Svetalina hopes to follow in her older cousin's footsteps and did not hesitate when asked about her favourite event.
"Barrel racing," she said with conviction.
Newman was the furthest she had travelled for rodeo.
The royal family lived up to their title, taking out medals for their events.
