title: What the commemoration of the 235th anniversary of Bois Caïman means for Haiti’s memory and future
content:
The night of August 14, 1791, marked the beginning of a series of events that changed the world. A large group of enslaved people and rebel leaders met at Bwa Kayiman (Bois Caïman), a historic site located in Haiti’s Northern Department, in the town of Plaine-du-Nord.
Under the leadership of the houngan (Vodou priest) Dutty Boukman and manbo (priestess) Cécile Fatiman — along with key resistance leaders — the gathering brought together enslaved people from different plantations for a clandestine religious and political ceremony. They invoked the lwa and ancestral spiritual forces, seeking their protection and strength for the struggle ahead.
It set in motion the first major anti-slavery movement in Saint-Domingue (which would later become Haiti), as enslaved people fought for their freedom. At that time, the island of Hispaniola was divided into two European colonies: the western part was the French colony of Saint-Domingue, and the eastern part was the Spanish colony of Santo Domingo; the modern republics did not yet exist.
During this time, Saint-Domingue was one of the world’s richest sugar and coffee colonies, built on an economy that depended entirely on the slave trade. To stop this terrible human suffering, enslaved people united to resist one of the most powerful colonial empires of the 18th century.
Coming together to resist
The resulting uprising brought together different groups of enslaved people. The population included Creole enslaved people who were born on the island, spoke Haitian Creole, understood French, and worked as skilled workers (carpenters, blacksmiths, masons, shoemakers, or house servants); “Bossales,” enslaved people who were brought directly from Africa on a négrier (slave ship), endured the hardest labour conditions and suffered brutal physical punishments, yet held onto their African roots, languages, songs, and Vodou traditions, and domestic or “elite” enslaved people who worked in the masters’ homes as servants, cooks, bodyguards, hairdressers, wet nurses, cochers (horse-drawn carriage drivers), or commandeurs (plantation slave leaders).
In this harsh environment, enslaved women often suffered sexual abuse from colonisers, which led to a mixed-race population, while plantation leaders were often forced to enforce rules with great severity. While the plantation owners tried to turn these groups against each other, the movement found strong support in les Nègres Marrons (the Maroons), who escaped the plantations and mines, and fled to the mountains to fight back.
Dehumanising treatment
During this period, plantation slaves made up the overwhelming majority of Saint-Domingue’s enslaved population, performing the most rigorous tasks and working relentless schedules from dawn until well into the night. When they arrived at colonial ports after weeks in the holds of slave ships travelling from Africa to the Americas, they were branded with heated irons as marks of identification and ownership. Branding also marked medical information or past flight attempts.
Enslaved people were routinely beaten with whips and straps made from dried cowhide, which tore through their skin and left large, bloody wounds. Other punishments included being chained in dark basements for several days, often without food. If someone rebelled, an overseer might force another enslaved person to cut off an ear, arm, or leg as a brutal deterrent to others on the plantation.
The most cruel punishments involved public hangings, beheadings, or torture. Recaptured fugitives faced these brutal penalties, and plantation mortality was high. When enslaved people grew too old or sick to perform hard labour, they were often abandoned and left to die, or executed by plantation owners who viewed them as burdens.
In stark contrast to domestic slaves and overseers, who had access to better food, agricultural and mine slaves survived mainly on water and cassava. This, coupled with the terrible labour conditions and widespread dehumanisation, ultimately fuelled the mass collective resistance that resulted in the Bois Caïman uprising.
From fight to freedom
From the mountains, these rebel fighters employed guerrilla tactics. Using weapons like slingshots, knives, machetes, and arrows, they ambushed and attacked colonial soldiers, took their weapons, poisoned water sources and animals, and burned plantations and their houses. Most of the time, these attacks took place at night, while the colonists were sleeping.
They also built a strong intelligence network. From house servants to drivers, enslaved people worked as spies to send information about hidden weapons to rebel commanders, using kònn lanbi (conch shells) and drums to send signals across the mountains. Vodou ceremonies helped prepare the fighters, who bathed in natural plant mixtures and used special powders for protection.
Following the Bois Caïman ceremony, the anti-slavery struggle continued over 12 years through the leadership of key figures such as Toussaint Louverture, Jean-Jacques Dessalines, Henri Christophe, Alexandre Pétion, François Capois, and Jean-Pierre Boyer. Women also played a central role in sustaining this revolution, including Marie-Jeanne Lamartinière, Sanité Bélair, Catherine Flon, and Claire Heureuse.
This movement ultimately led to the Battle of Vertières on November 18, 1803, where the insurgent army defeated the French colonial forces in the western part of Saint-Domingue. This victory brought an end to slavery in the former colony and resulted in the declaration of the first Black republic in the world — Haitian independence on January 1, 1804. Later, during the unification of the island under President Boyer in 1822, slavery was also formally abolished in the eastern Spanish-speaking side. (Under President Boyer, the Haitian government occupied the eastern part of the island, formerly Santo Domingo. This occupation began on February 9, 1822, and ended 22 years later on February 27, 1844, when the eastern side declared its independence from Haiti.)
Modern-day perspectives
To mark the 235th anniversary of this significant historic event at Bois Caïman, on August 14, 2026, various socio-cultural, Vodou, and conference/debate events were organised across the country, including an event in Cap-Haïtien organised by Kenbe Kapow, a collective founded in 2025 by a group of young people. According to Peterson Jules, Kenbe Kapow’s secretary general, who spoke with Global Voices via a WhatsApp call, it acts as an advocacy group to demand accountability from local authorities, raise civic awareness among citizens, and encourage political engagement.
In addition to political leaders, the event brought together public figures from academic, literary, and cultural sectors, and featured patriotic songs, dance performances, and discussions about the role of Bois Caïman in making Haiti the world’s first independent Black republic. Panellists also emphasised the need for national unity to address Haiti’s multi-dimensional challenges — particularly the ongoing political crisis, gang violence, and widespread public despair.
In comparing historical marronage to the country’s present-day challenges, Kenbe Kapow’s Communications Officer Karlin Georges Le Pont highlighted the importance of individual and collective responsibility:
Nou te genyen yon etap mawon, mawonaj kote esklav yo pou te ka soti sou difikilte dominasyon nan chan yo te pran chimen mòn, men yo pa t pran l pou yo te kapab deresponsabilize yo. Se te yon fòm rezistans ke moman an te mande, e pandan yo te nan mawon yo te reflechi sou kouman yo kapab pran libète yo. Si n ap eseye fè yon paralèl ak epòk sa yo, jodi a n ap viv nan yon epòk mawonaj kote ayisyen an mawon tèt li, ayisyen an mawon peyi l, ayisyen an mawon moun li ye a. Kontrèman ak ansyen mawon yo ki te mawon pou te kapab cherche libète, nou menm nou mawon paske nou di nou fatige, nou pap batay ankò. An nou soti nan etap mawonaj la pou nou vin nan etap kongrè a, etap ransebleman an ak tout fòs viv patriyòt nasyon an pou nou chita pou yon Ayiti miyò pou tout moun.
We had a stage of marronage where the enslaved, to escape the harsh domination in the fields, took to the mountains. However, they did not do so to shirk their responsibilities; it was a form of resistance required by that time. While in marronage, they reflected on how to achieve their freedom. Drawing a parallel to today, we are living in a time of modern marronage where Haitians are hiding from themselves, their country, and their identity. Unlike the former Maroons who fled to seek freedom, we flee because we say we are tired and will no longer fight. Let us move past this stage of marronage and enter the stage of the congress — a stage of gathering all the patriotic living forces of the nation to sit together for a better Haiti for everyone.
Politician and former senior state official Sterline Civil stressed the need for civic duty and action over rhetoric, noting that Haitians “must work to show that we are worthy” of the Bois Caïman heritage. “Otherwise,” she claimed, “we will never succeed and will only continue to make grand speeches.”
In a similar vein, architect and local leader Wideline Pierre emphasised the need for unity and shared purpose, suggesting that if Haitians want to emerge from the current social, political, and economic situation, they “must realise that unity, konbit (collective labor), and solidarity are what define us as a people.”
A new Bois Caïman?
Dominique Dupuy, a former minister and Haitian ambassador to UNESCO, suggested:
Se yon dezyèm Bwa Kayiman nou bezwen, se yon dezyèm chita nou bezwen, yon dezyèm gran ransebleman, yon dezyèm gwo konba nou bezwen. Se tout ayisyen nan tout orizon, patisipan yo, sa ki deyò yo, ak vwazinaj nou, zanmi nou, ak kominite nou ki ka leve jou an kò pou Ayiti, pou Ayiti zansèt yo te imajine a, pou Ayiti pitit nou yo merite a, pou yon Ayiti kote nou pap sèlman sibi jou après jou nan chèche lavi, men nan chèche lavi nou jwenn li pandan nou vivan.
We need a second Bwa Kayiman, a second sit-down meeting, a second great gathering, and a second major battle. It is all Haitians from all backgrounds, those present, those abroad, along with our neighbours, friends, and community, who can make the sun rise again for Haiti — for the Haiti our ancestors imagined, for the Haiti our children deserve, and for a Haiti where we do not merely survive day after day searching for life, but where we find life while we are alive.
Rekindling protest
On the actual historic site, the 235th anniversary commemoration involved houngans, manbos, and others from the Artibonite department — a region severely impacted by gang violence — gathering to honour their ancestors. Participants dressed in vibrant Afro-Caribbean attire adorned with vèvè symbols and portraits of lwas.
The atmosphere vibrated with the sounds of traditional instruments, including tanbou (drums), klòch (bells), and chachà (rattles). Spectators came in their numbers to the Bois Caïman grounds, where a stage and loudspeakers set the mood with traditional, rasin, and protest music.
There was a shared spirit of communion through song, dance, and protest. Marching across the site, participants carried banners bearing direct messages and demands: Ayiti pou Vodou, Vodou pou Ayiti (Haiti for Vodou, Vodou for Haiti); Aba Jezi kolon (Down with the colonial Jesus); Nou mande Leta bay peyi a sekirite (We demand that the government provide security for the country); Nou mande pou Leta retire 52/100 li bay legliz nan bidjè a (We demand that the state remove the 52 percent allocated to churches from the national budget); Jezi fè nou esklav, Desalin libere nou (Jesus made us slaves, Dessalines freed us); and Viv Ewò yo (Long live the Heroes).
Despite the historic epic achieved by Haiti’s founders who survived the transatlantic slave trade, defeated Napoleon Bonaparte’s army, and changed the course of history, the battle for true freedom is far from over.
Two hundred and twenty-two years after achieving independence, Haiti remains a unique symbol of human freedom. Yet, the nation still suffers from poverty, chronic political instability, systemic corruption, gang violence, and foreign interference.
Regardless, Haiti possesses the resources needed for its people to live with dignity as the ancestors intended, and the fight for full sovereignty, economic freedom, and social justice remains unfinished.
The greatest challenge for the Haitian people to emerge from this endemic crisis is the need for a new political and economic class, alongside a new model of civil society. This new generation of leaders must have a genuine commitment to Haiti, a clear vision, and the willingness to set personal interests aside to prioritize the nation's well-being.

title: Remembering Taib Andak, the man who helped build Felda
content:
Since its establishment on July 1, 1956, the government agency has transformed Malaysia’s rural landscape, opening up land, creating livelihoods and giving generations of families the chance to build better lives.
That legacy was shaped by pioneering figures who helped turn Felda’s early vision into reality. Among the most important was the late Taib Andak (1916-1997), its first Malayan chairman, whose leadership helped lay the foundations for its success.
Taib was regarded by many as a visionary leader and dedicated public servant. To those who knew him personally, he was also a warm friend, respected colleague and, above all, devoted family man.
His eldest daughter, author and cultural activist Kalsom Taib, remembers him as a man of great honesty who approached his work with a strong sense of duty.
“During Hari Raya, our family would often receive hampers from clients. As children, we were excited because there were chocolates in them.
“But my father would not accept any of them – he would scold the men and make them take everything back. His integrity would not allow him to accept them,” Kalsom, 84, told FMT Lifestyle.
Born in Parit Bakar, Johor during World War I, Taib built a distinguished career in public service, rural development and the corporate sector. His defining role came in 1958 when he was appointed chairman of Felda, succeeding D E M Fiennes.
The agency flourished during Taib’s 13 years at the helm, with more than 100 land schemes established across the country. Most notably, the Felda Taib Andak scheme in Kulai, Johor, became Felda’s first oil palm settlement and was named in his honour.
Taib’s contributions extended well beyond Felda. In 1969, he was appointed chairman of Malayan Banking Bhd (Maybank) and served on the boards of major companies including Sime Darby and Federal Flour Mills.
Kalsom remembers accompanying her father as he travelled around the country to help establish Felda land schemes. He only received a driver later in his career, she recalled, so he would often make the long journeys himself.
“I would accompany him as he drove to these places. It wasn’t like today, where we have modern roads and rest stops. We had to travel along such long and winding roads,” Kalsom recalled.
“I would chat with him to help him stay awake as he drove. Sometimes, he would be so tired that he would stop to take a nap, and I would watch over the car.”
Kalsom describes her father as a man who did his best to instil strong values in his children. Among the most important lessons she learnt from him were to speak up when something did not feel right, and to be grateful for what she had rather than complain about what she did not.
Taib was particularly dedicated to serving then prime minister Abdul Razak Hussein, with whom he shared a close friendship.
“Razak wanted to create jobs for the jobless, land for the landless. He had the vision and my father helped to execute it. They worked very well together.”
While writing her father’s biography, “Taib Andak: In A Class Of His Own” (2008), Kalsom attended a reunion of Felda settlers.
There, she learnt that the opportunities created through Felda had enabled many settlers to send their children to university, with many in turn going on to pursue successful careers.
For her, this was the most meaningful and enduring part of her father’s legacy: the opportunities he helped create continued to transform lives long after his work was done.
Kalsom added, however, that her late father would probably have been saddened by the controversies Felda has faced over the years. Once regarded as a model of land development, she believes the agency is now a shadow of what it once was.
According to her, Taib strongly believed in leading by example and keeping political appointments out of Felda. She believes the departure from these principles has affected the government agency’s performance over the years.
“My father never went to any sophisticated business courses like they have now; yet he was able to lead Felda to success,” Kalsom said in reflection.
“I think it’s because he had a strong value system, which is lacking today. So, we need to follow his example.
“We have so many modern advancements today, but what’s the point if we don’t have our values?”

title: I had to move to Rūātoki to learn te reo Māori. Our tamariki shouldn’t have to
content: Growing up unable to understand her own whānau, Rawinia Higgins went home to Rūātoki and discovered a place where te reo Māori wasn’t simply taught – it was the language of everyday life. Thinking about te reo towns, the theme for Te Wiki o te Reo Māori 2026, my mind goes to Rūātoki – a small town just south of Whakatāne where I learnt to speak Māori. I grew up in an English-speaking home in Wellington. When my native reo Māori-speaking mother and family would get together, they would all be speaking Māori, laughing and sharing stories. I would feel left out because I couldn’t understand and take part in what was being said. When I was around 11 years old, I asked my parents if I could move to Rūātoki – where my mum was from – and attend Rūātoki School. The school was the first officially recognised bilingual school, back in 1978, and was well established by the time I got there in 1985. It was the result of a community where te reo Māori was the norm, staffed by Tūhoe relatives of mine including Koro Whitu McGarvey – who was my teacher – and Tāwhiri and Kaa Williams, among others. It was in this small-town community I learnt te reo Māori – where I was finally able to access the richness of the world that I had been missing. A baptism of fire I won’t romanticise it – learning the language was a baptism by fire. I started out, much to the teasing of my cousins, in the remedial class. I had known of remedial classes at my school in Wellington, but that was for English. At Rūātoki though, the remedial class was for te reo Māori. I still chuckle thinking about it today – it was like living in a parallel universe. What was special about Rūātoki was that it was not only a place where te reo Māori was taught, but also lived in the hearts and homes of the locals every day. That’s the idea behind the te reo towns theme for te wiki this year: to pay homage to those communities who helped create the conditions where te reo Māori could continue to be spoken, learned and lived. They built kōhanga and kura, strengthened whānau and community use of the language, and helped ensure future generations would have access to te reo Māori as a normal part of everyday life. March during Māori Language Week, to demand that the Māori language have equal status with English on August 1, 1980, Wellington. (Photo: Alexander Turnbull Library) It wasn’t consciously political for them and yet it was one of the most politically active decisions they could make. It was about ensuring their children would never have to feel the detachment from culture and community the adults had seen among Māori living in cities. It was about making te reo Māori a normal and natural part of life for younger generations. More than a matter of ‘choice’ It’s important not to simplify this story too much. Rūātoki and other similar communities showed remarkable commitment to te reo Māori, but they were also shaped by circumstance. Around the world, indigenous languages have often remained strongest in communities where people had greater opportunity to live, work and socialise in their own language. Larger towns and cities brought different pressures, with English becoming the dominant language of education, employment, media and public life. This was not a matter of some communities valuing their language more than others or willingly giving it up. Given the choice, most indigenous communities would have wanted to see their language flourish from one generation to the next. The differing fortunes of te reo Māori reflects the uneven impacts of colonisation, urbanisation and social change on people’s ability to use and pass on the language. The lesson is not to romanticise isolation, but to understand the conditions that allow a language to thrive and to recreate those conditions wherever Māori live today. Te reo Māori has come a long way since I went to kura in Rūātoki. It’s now on bilingual signage, in official place names, on our screens, in cafés and restaurants, sports commentary, workplaces and across the public life of this country. Statistics support this, with the 2023 Census recording 213,849 people who could hold an everyday conversation in te reo Māori, up from 185,955 in 2018. That is an increase of 27,894 speakers in five years, and something every New Zealander can take heart in. This growth in visibility is worth celebrating. But visibility is not the same as vitality. A language doesn’t just thrive because it appears on signs, screens or posters. It thrives when people have places to use it, people to use it with, and the words they need for everyday life. Rūātoki, Ōtaki, Matawaia and other te reo towns have always understood this. Te reo Māori grows through whanaungatanga, shared purpose, and communities that make the language normal in the ordinary places where life happens. The gift that Rūātoki gave me Rūātoki didn’t give me just lessons, but a living network of language. The kura mattered deeply, but it was part of something bigger: whānau who spoke, kaumātua who carried the dialect, teachers who believed in the kaupapa, homes where Māori was ordinary, and a community that had decided its children would inherit more than a memory of te reo Māori. There are many te reo towns across the motu, each with their own story, dialect, champions and sacrifices. Rūātoki is just one of them. Ngā Tamatoa and supporters protest at St Kevin’s Arcade, Auckland, 1972 (Photo: John Miller) Te reo towns are not an invention; they are a recognition of communities that have already shown the way. They represent the courage, discipline and love of communities that chose, and had the circumstances, geographical or otherwise, to keep te reo Māori alive in homes, schools, marae and public life. Before there were national strategies and policies, there were communities already doing the quiet, determined work of language revitalisation. They built kōhanga and kura, held hui, corrected and encouraged each other, laughed with each other and kept speaking. They made decisions in kitchens, staffrooms, vans, sports clubs and on marae that would later become a part of a national movement. The challenge now is to keep building the conditions where te reo Māori can live beyond the classroom, ceremony and te wiki. If a language is to thrive, it must have places where it is not only heard but used; not only respected, but shared; not only learned, but lived. I had to go home to find my te reo town. The challenge now is to ensure our tamariki and mokopuna do not have to go searching for theirs. If we keep building the conditions for te reo Māori to thrive, then every town, suburb and community can become a place where the language is not only visible, but ordinary. More Reading

title: Indigenous community trades shark-fishing for conservation in Colombia: 'From hunter to protector'
content:
- In the Colombian department of La Guajira, at South America’s northernmost tip, Indigenous Wayuu fishers from the community of Punta Gallinas are working with marine biologists to conserve and document shark populations.
- Despite a 2021 law banning targeted shark and ray fishing in Colombia, the meat remains a vital protein source in one of the country’s most remote and food-insecure regions.
- Colombian shark conservation initiative Proyecto Puyuii is working with Wayuu fishers to record shark species in the understudied waters of La Guajira, implementing sustainability measures such as larger-mesh nets, safe release techniques, and avoiding longlines.
- With sustainable tourism touted as a potential economic alternative to shark fishing, some fishers argue that compensation will need to be offered before they can afford to stop.
LA GUAJIRA, Colombia — Feet from the ocean, four sharks and a ray lie dead on the wind-battered sand. Above them stands Wilfrido Arends, 46. The blade of a short knife glints in his hand.
Carefully, he bends down to cut a small fin from the underside of one shark — an endangered species known as a blacknose (Carcharhinus acronotus). He hands the sample to a woman next to him, who places it delicately in a vial.
A tape measure is passed over the still glistening back of the dead shark. Each measurement is read out and noted down.
Arends, a fisher from Colombia’s Wayuu Indigenous community, is spearheading shark research and conservation in Punta Gallinas, a Wayuu community where shark meat is part of the traditional diet. Home to around 50 families, the community sits at the northernmost tip of South America.
“If we wipe out our sharks, I think that further down the line we will miss them,” says Arends, who is known locally as “Caracas.”
Together with researchers from Colombian shark conservation initiative Proyecto Puyuii, Arends and other Wayuu fishers are documenting shark diversity in the largely unstudied waters of La Guajira.
“There’s almost no data on anything,” says Diego Cardeñosa, a marine biologist at Florida International University in the United States. A member of Proyecto Puyuii, he has been training Wayuu fishers to record the shark species they catch.
A 2021 law banned shark and ray fishing in Colombia, with a 2024 revision subsequently allowing the incidental bycatch of 15 species. Despite the ban, the meat remains an important source of protein for Wayuu communities across this stretch of arid desert coast — one of the most food-insecure regions in the country.
While commercial poaching is the leading threat to shark populations in Colombia, biologists say that without additional research, even traditional subsistence hunting can increase pressure on sharks, possibly affecting their numbers or threatening endangered species — as happened with overconsumption of turtles.
Proyecto Puyuii aims to promote economic alternatives for fishers, minimize pressure on the local shark population with scientific research, and implement sustainable fishing practices.
The consumption of sharks is accepted by the project, as it is a traditional practice and form of subsistence. But directed shark fishing (generally practiced with longlines in the deeper ocean) is not encouraged. A more sustainable model would limit consumption to incidental bycatch, which depending on the species is not illegal, and include safe release techniques of juveniles.
“If the fisher earns more showing it than killing it, there’s the solution,” says Felipe González, who co-founded the project with Arends over a decade ago. “How do we make these sharks worth more alive than dead?”
‘I gave up shark-directed fishing many years ago’
Like many Wayuu boys in the region, Arends began fishing at the age of 9. As a child, he watched his grandparents hunt shark species ranging from hammerheads to tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier).
“As I got older I took to fishing them too, because it was a custom of the Wayuu,” says Arends, who recalls participating in a once booming trade that saw shark meat and fins exchanged for money, fuel, or resources with buyers in neighboring Venezuela.
“You’d sell it and buy fuel to keep fishing,” he remembers. “We’d buy nets and hooks. That’s how we kept ourselves going.”
At this time, fishers in Punta Gallinas would use artisanal longlines specialized for shark fishing, as well as finer-mesh gillnets that result in higher levels of shark bycatch. According to Arends, the trade began to disappear from Punta Gallinas over a decade ago, before vanishing from the community with the 2021 prohibition.
Local fishers told Mongabay that other Wayuu communities do still participate in a market, with buyers from the towns of Riohacha and Uribia paying around 50,000 Colombian pesos (about $15) per kilo for shark fins.
Though the fin trade is absent in Punta Gallinas, shark meat is still commonly consumed in the community, forming the key ingredient in a traditional dish known as salpicón. Oil is also extracted from the carcasses and used for cooking, while the liver is used in the production of a traditional cough medicine.
Whatever meat is not consumed by the fisher’s own family is typically sold to locally owned hotels and restaurants. Biologists have not assessed the mercury levels (which could be harmful at high concentrations) of shark meat in Punta Gallinas. González says it may be low and is currently not a concern of the project.
“It’s an important protein source,” Arends says, “the first source we have here to feed ourselves and our children is shark.”
Despite the ongoing subsistence use in his community, Arends is determined to promote shark conservation.
“Now I fish mostly with nets — I’ve stopped using what we call the longline, because that fishing is more directed at sharks,” he says. “I gave up shark-directed fishing many years ago.”
Since the early 2000s, Arends has worked on community-based mangrove and sea turtle conservation. Locals report that sea turtles, once a common sight, have disappeared from the area due to overconsumption in local Wayuu communities.
“What happened with the turtles — we don’t want the same thing to happen with the sharks,” he says.
He and other Punta Gallinas fishers began to use large-mesh nets to avoid catching juvenile sharks, focusing instead on other fish species by placing nets away from the open sea, where sharks are commonly found.
If he catches a shark incidentally, it will be released if found alive.
Locals report that these measures have been widely adopted in Punta Gallinas. And, according to Arends, around 17 boats out of an estimated 20 in the community no longer practice shark-directed fishing. Numbers aren’t available on how many have also changed to larger-mesh nets.
“You feel like your programming has been changed — from hunter to protector,” he says. “You feel almost the same as what the animals feel.”
‘A high concentration of shark species’
Though still largely understudied, biologists believe that the waters around Punta Gallinas are likely to contain a wealth of shark diversity.
“In La Guajira and other parts of the Colombian Caribbean, there appears to be a high concentration of ray and shark species,” says Camilo Garcia, professor of marine biology at the National University of Colombia, who mapped the distribution of sharks and rays across the Colombian Caribbean using research data from as far back as the 1960s.
Though his work identified a total of 90 species, he describes the inventory as “incomplete” and believes that further research is needed to establish sustainable catch levels and ensure the sustainability of current and future fishing practices.
In Punta Gallinas, Wayuu fishers have reported the presence of species ranging from tiger and silky sharks to endangered blacknose and the critically endangered smalleye hammerhead (Sphyrna tudes).
Cardeñosa believes that Proyecto Puyuii’s drive to document shark species is a crucial step toward facilitating more informed conservation measures in the future, such as fishing quotas and conservation areas.
As part of the project, Wayuu fishers measure every shark they catch, with dated fin samples passed to Arends for storage.
“This is going to give us a bigger picture of the species composition of the fishery, how much they’re catching and whether it can be sustainable,” Cardeñosa says. “Then we can start to formulate more advanced projects.”
‘What are we going to live off?’
Amid mounting food and water insecurity across La Guajira’s desert coast, a potential transition away from shark fishing is a challenging proposition for some communities. The Wayuu fishers Mongabay spoke to generally consider the 2021 law unfair on communities that still subsist on shark.
Locals report that a lack of rain in 2025’s wet season resulted in widespread plant and livestock death. Luzmila Arends, sister of Wilfrido, reports losing around 247 of her 300 goats after the failed rainy season left little vegetation to feed them. Goats are another common source of meat in Wayuu communities.
Meanwhile, one in three children in the region suffers from chronic malnutrition.
“Many people live off of shark meat,” says Juan Manuel Uriana, 33, leader of the fishers’ association in Bahía Hondita, a larger Wayuu community about 4 miles from Punta Gallinas. “Since there’s no other way for people to live, they do it to survive … they know it’s a crime now.”
According to Uriana, many of the 120 fishers in Bahía Hondita use hooks and longlines to catch sharks and rays, a trade they still rely on for survival.
“You have to compensate people. Then they would stop fishing shark,” he says. “What are we going to live off?”
Proyecto Puyuii members hope that sustainable tourism can provide alternative opportunities. The project is currently affiliated with a Wayuu-run hotel and kite surfing school in the area, a short drive from the famous Taroa sand dunes — a renowned beauty spot.
“The idea is that the money stays in the community,” González says, “that the tourist arrives, sleeps in their guesthouse, eats what they prepare, uses their boats and their guides.”
For some in Punta Gallinas, this has already become a reality.
“I’m earning more now,” says Alexi López, 56, uncle of Wilfrido Arends. Once one of Punta Gallinas’ most prolific shark fishers, he now makes most of his living driving cars and boats for tourists. “It’s easier [than fishing] because I go out, am done in two hours and am back home again.”
Luzmila Arends runs a local guesthouse, which offers visitors the chance to accompany fishers on boat outings.
She hopes that economically viable alternatives will help the community to shift away from a historical dependence on shark meat.
“It’s all culture,” she says. “It’s not that we talk today and tomorrow it’s done, but that people go forwards with that vision for the future. It won’t happen overnight.”
‘Better we release them’
Even amongst those who live off shark fishing, there is evidence of a growing willingness to protect what remains.
“If this project works out, we can participate in conservation, we can work with this,” Uriana says. “The people are open to it.”
In May 2026, fishers in Bahía Hondita caught a large female tiger shark. On opening the animal, they found that it was pregnant. “One of the boys was going to gather [the pups] to take them away,” Uriana says. “I said: no, why are you going to take them? Better we release them.”
According to marine biologists, the protection of young sharks is of particular importance for a sustainable fishery. “More dangerous is fishing juveniles,” Garcia says. “If you catch them, especially before they’ve reproduced, you’re destroying the population directly.”
Using safe release techniques learned from Proyecto Puyuii, Uriana released 43 living tiger shark pups into the ocean.
He speaks from behind dark glasses and the low brim of a cap. “We started releasing them with the children,” he says.
A group of young boys, aged between 8 and 12, watches on as he talks. Uriana gestures to them. “They already know how to fish,” he says.
Back on his fishing boat, Wilfrido Arends scans the horizon, one hand guiding the onboard motor at the rear. A ragged black flag, marking the position of his net, appears from behind the crest of a wave.
Without a word, his 22-year-old son moves to haul it into the boat. He is nicknamed “Caraquitas” (“Little Caracas”) after his father.
“Everything we’ve tried to do is to leave something for our children,” says Arends, whose granddaughter and one of his sons want to become marine biologists. Arends, himself, dreams of one day establishing a shark research center in Punta Gallinas.
“Our ancestors have left this to us,” he says. “We want to leave something better for those who come next.”
This article was originally published on Mongabay.
Featured Image: Euan Wallace/Mongabay

title: 7ª Mostra Pankararu de Música, realizada no Sertão de Pernambuco, abre inscrições para edição de 2026
content:
A 7ª Mostra Pankararu de Música recebe inscrições para a edição de 2026, que acontece de 9 a 12 de outubro, na Aldeia Bem-querer de Cima, no Território Indígena Pankararu, em Jatobá, no Sertão de Pernambuco. A programação reúne música, manifestações artísticas, conhecimentos ancestrais e práticas culturais do povo Pankararu em uma experiência de imersão no território. Os formulários estão disponíveis para o público geral, instituições de ensino e vendedores da comunidade local.
A proposta da Mostra vai além da realização de apresentações musicais. O encontro é organizado como uma etnovivência pedagógica, artística e cultural, criando espaços para a troca de conhecimentos e para o contato com diferentes dimensões da vida no território Pankararu.
Durante os quatro dias de programação, temas relacionados à memória, à educação ancestral, à natureza, à espiritualidade e às práticas de cuidado integram a experiência. A iniciativa também valoriza formas próprias de produção e transmissão de saberes, colocando a comunidade e o território no centro das atividades.
Quem deseja participar da Mostra como público deve preencher o formulário destinado ao público geral. A modalidade é voltada às pessoas interessadas em acompanhar a programação e vivenciar as atividades realizadas no território.
Também há uma inscrição específica para instituições de ensino que pretendem participar com grupos de estudantes. A proposta busca aproximar os conhecimentos construídos no território de outras experiências educativas. No caso de instituições interessadas em permanecer na comunidade durante os dias da Mostra, é necessário fazer contato prévio com a organização por meio dos canais indicados no formulário.
A terceira modalidade de inscrição é exclusiva para vendedores da comunidade local. O cadastro permite a comercialização de produtos durante o evento e não está disponível para pessoas que não fazem parte do território.
A 7ª Mostra Pankararu é realizada em parceria com o Instituto Aió Conexões Pankararu e a Funarte. A iniciativa busca fortalecer uma programação construída a partir do próprio território, valorizando os saberes, as práticas culturais e a produção artística do povo Pankararu.

title: “Les psychiatres et les psychologues m’envoient leurs patients": la médecine ancestrale des guérisseuses mazatèques, un espoir scientifique au Mexique
content:
"Les psychiatres et les psychologues m'envoient leurs patients": la médecine ancestrale des guérisseuses mazatèques, un espoir scientifique au Mexique
Au Mexique, la consommation de champignons hallucinogènes existe depuis des millénaires au sein des communautés indigènes. Mais la science s'intéresse de plus en plus à cette médecine ancestrale qui pourrait aider à traiter certains troubles mentaux.
- Publié le 13-09-2026 à 11h04
D'une main experte, Alejandrina Pedro Castañeda écarte délicatement les broussailles qui recouvrent le pied d'une fougère géante. La végétation est dense dans cette forêt qui recouvre la Sierra Mazateca, une chaîne de montagnes du sud du Mexique. Mais cette Mexicaine de 60 ans la connaît par cœur, elle est née et a grandi à Huautla de Jiménez, un village indigène perché dans ces montagnes habitées depuis des milliers d'années par la communauté mazatèque à laquelle elle appartient. "Regarde", murmure-t-elle soudain, "en voici un. C'est un champignon médicinal."
Du bout des doigts, elle dégage les feuilles qui le recouvrent partiellement, puis coupe sa tige d'un coup sec. Haut de cinq centimètres, sa couleur brune le rend presque invisible à l'œil amateur. "Celui-ci, on le surnomme derrumbe (éboulement en français), car il pousse sur la terre retournée par un glissement de terrain. C'est une espèce qu'on ne trouve qu'ici." Avec 53 espèces de champignons hallucinogènes recensées sur son territoire, le Mexique détient le record mondial et concentre 25 % de la diversité mondiale. Oaxaca, l'État mexicain où se trouve la Sierra Mazateca, abrite 27 espèces à lui tout seul.
Pharmacie naturelle
Alejandrina Pedro Castañeda est guérisseuse, une vocation qui lui a été transmise par sa famille. "Quand j'étais petite, quand on allait cueillir des champignons, on chantait et on récitait une prière pour le premier qu'on trouvait. Puis on communiait, c'est-à-dire qu'on le mangeait. Ensuite, on lui disait : montre-moi où sont tes frères. Ils nous guidaient alors jusqu'à leur famille."
Le peuple mazatèque se soigne depuis toujours grâce aux ressources naturelles qu'il trouve dans la forêt. "Nous n'avons pas de produits chimiques ici, pas d'hôpital, notre pharmacie vivante a toujours été la nature, nous l'utilisons pour prévenir les maladies, pour être en phase avec notre environnement, avec notre corps." Avec précaution, elle arrache une grande feuille d'arbre et enferme le champignon dans cette poche naturelle. "Un seul comme celui-ci ne suffit pas. Pour obtenir un effet, il en faut au moins dix comme ça." Elle le fera ensuite sécher, puis l'utilisera lors des cérémonies, ces rituels de guérison durant lesquels les champignons sont consommés sous supervision d'un guérisseur mazatèque.
Une nouvelle substance psychédélique
Alejandrina Pedro Castañeda n'avait que six ans lorsqu'elle a assisté à sa première cérémonie. C'était avec Maria Sabina, la célèbre guérisseuse mazatèque qui a fait connaître au monde le pouvoir des champignons psychédéliques. En 1957, le magazine américain Life publie un reportage sur Maria Sabina et ses cérémonies. Cette découverte intrigue, et de nombreuses célébrités, comme John Lennon, Jim Morrison ou encore Bob Dylan, voyagent dans la Sierra Mazateca pour connaître Maria Sabina et sa magie.
La consommation de champignons hallucinogènes se démocratise, mais en 1970, le gouvernement américain décide d'inscrire la psilocybine, leur substance active, dans la catégorie la plus restrictive de la législation fédérale sur les substances contrôlées. Le Mexique les classe à son tour parmi les substances psychotropes réglementées en 1984. "Depuis, la psilocybine et les champignons hallucinogènes sont considérés comme dangereux et nocifs, sans aucun potentiel thérapeutique ou médical, précise Rebeca Espinosa, psychiatre mexicaine qui s'intéresse à ces substances depuis plusieurs années. On ne peut donc même pas les étudier via la recherche scientifique au Mexique. Seules les communautés indigènes qui utilisent ces champignons dans leur médecine traditionnelle, comme les Mazatèques, peuvent les consommer."
Intérêt de la science
Rebeca Espinosa et d'autres chercheurs mexicains plaident pour autoriser l'usage des champignons hallucinogènes à des fins de recherche scientifique. Selon la psychiatre, de nombreuses études scientifiques avaient déjà mis en lumière les bénéfices de la psilocybine avant son interdiction, notamment sur certains troubles mentaux. Ces dernières années, la réglementation s'est assouplie aux États-Unis, ouvrant la voie à de nouvelles recherches. "Elles se sont concentrées sur les troubles dépressifs majeurs et l'anxiété associée au cancer ou à d'autres maladies terminales. Dans tous ces domaines, on a obtenu de très bons résultats", affirme-t-elle. La psychiatre s'appuie notamment sur un essai clinique publié en 2021 dans le New England Journal of Medicine, revue médicale de référence. "Des chercheurs ont comparé l'efficacité de la psilocybine à celle de l'escitalopram, l'un des antidépresseurs les plus prescrits actuellement. Après six semaines, 70 % des patients traités à la psilocybine présentaient une réponse au traitement, contre 48 % de ceux ayant reçu de l'escitalopram."
Vers une nouvelle réglementation ?
Ces résultats, comme l'ouverture réglementaire observée aux États-Unis, nourrissent chez Rebeca Espinosa l'espoir d'un changement au Mexique. Ces dernières années, plusieurs initiatives parlementaires ont tenté de faire évoluer le statut de la psilocybine au Mexique. En 2021 puis en 2023, deux propositions ont cherché à autoriser et encadrer son usage scientifique et thérapeutique, notamment contre la dépression et l'anxiété.
Restées sans suite, elles ont été suivies en janvier 2026 d'un nouveau projet visant à reconnaître son potentiel thérapeutique, tout en continuant de la classer parmi les substances présentant un risque pour la santé publique. Si ce dernier projet aboutit, le Mexique pourrait enfin renouer avec ses racines indigènes. En attendant, certains thérapeutes préfèrent orienter leurs patients vers ceux qui savent le mieux, c'est-à-dire les guérisseurs. "Les psychiatres et les psychologues m'envoient leurs patients qui souffrent d'anxiété, d'anorexie, de dépression… Quand ils viennent me voir, on parvient à régler ces problèmes, glisse Alejandrina Pedro Castañeda dans un sourire complice. "C'est ça la médecine du champignon."

title: ‘Mary Leads Us to Jesus’ — Ozigbo
content:
By Nwabueze Okonkwo
ONITSHA — Thousands of Catholics and other Christian faithful from Anambra State and neighbouring states converged on Onitsha to celebrate the birthday of the Blessed Virgin Mary, mother of Jesus Christ.
The event, organised by the Faithspiration Initiative, was themed, “Fill the Jars, Make Room for Fresh Wine,” drawn from John 2:1-11.
The celebration featured the 2026 edition of Ave Maria Praise, performances by gospel artistes, lectures, comedy, prayers and Holy Mass.
The event was held at SS. Peter and Paul Catholic Church, Iba Pope, Awada, Obosi, in Idemili North Local Government Area of Anambra State.
In his opening prayer, the parish priest, Very Rev. Fr. Dr. Aloysius Maduka Agba, prayed for the success of the celebration and journey mercies for invited guests.
Agba, who represented the chief host, the Archbishop of Onitsha, Most Rev. Valerian Maduka Okeke, described the Faithspiration Initiative as a movement comprising young people and adults, including clergy and seminarians, committed to evangelisation and promoting the gospel.
He said the birthday of the Blessed Virgin Mary was worthy of celebration because she was the mother of Jesus Christ, the Saviour of mankind.
Agba also commended the founder of Faithspiration Initiative, Very Rev. Fr. Dr. George Adimike, for his resilience and commitment to the initiative.
In his remarks, former Anambra State governorship candidate, Valentine Chineto Ozigbo, shared a testimony of what he described as a spiritual encounter during a religious event in Portugal.
Ozigbo urged Catholics to embrace Marian devotion and encourage children to pray the Rosary.
“I am not asking you to choose between Jesus and Mary. I am asking you to hold the hand of Mary so that she can lead you to her Son, Jesus Christ.
“Let us spread the Rosary and teach it to our children. Do not be ashamed of your Catholic faith. Do not be ashamed of the Mother Jesus gave us,” Ozigbo said.
He distributed rosaries to members of the congregation and provided his WhatsApp number for those interested in joining the Igbo Rosary and “Songs of Mary” platforms he created on social media.
Delivering the keynote lecture, Rev. Fr. Barr. Johnbosco Igwe, a Catholic priest and legal practitioner, spoke extensively on Marian spirituality.
He identified trust as one of the core spiritual qualities of the Blessed Virgin Mary, citing Luke 1:26-38, where Mary accepted God’s message that she would conceive and bear a child.
Igwe also highlighted gratitude, poverty, contemplation and resilience as other aspects of Marian spirituality.
In his appreciation address, the founder of Faithspiration Initiative, Fr. Adimike, thanked God and the Archbishop of Onitsha for supporting and approving the event.
He described the year’s Ave Maria Praise as outstanding and expressed optimism that next year’s edition would be bigger.
Adimike, who is known for his advocacy for the poor and needy, also commended Agba, popularly known as “Omere Ora,” for hosting the event in his parish.
“I am delighted that everybody is here to celebrate our Mother Mary — Hausas, Yorubas, and Igbos; Christians and Muslims. Everybody is invited to this feast because Our Mother Mary is a Mother to all,” he said.
He appreciated the priests, religious sisters, seminarians, sponsors and benefactors who contributed to the success of the event.
Among those acknowledged were Fr. Pharm. Evaristus Ezeani, Fr. Patrick Egaga, Fr. Simeon Enu, Fr. John Mary Iwe, Engr. Eric Anyamene, Hon. Dubem Obaze, Valentine Chineto Ozigbo, Sir Clement Onyekwelu, Sir Emeka Ezeotu and Prince Chukwuka Onyema.
Adimike also acknowledged members of the Faithspiration Initiative, including Charles Obinna Igwe, Kingsley Ezeudu, Mrs Amara Offor, popularly known as Achallugo, and Amara Dufo.
He further recognised the organisers, including the Awada CWO Zone, Mrs Ifeoma Onwugharam, President, CWO Iba Pope, Mrs Kate Amarachi, members of Catholic Women’s Organisations and Mrs Christiana Obumu Ukandu, who donated the birthday cake in honour of the Virgin Mary.
Highlights of the celebration included the cutting of the birthday cake and the distribution of food, bread and cash gifts to less privileged and vulnerable people across Idemili, Onitsha and neighbouring communities.
Gospel artistes and comedians who performed at the event included Sister Chioma Ezefeta, Sir One on One, Evangelist Onyeka Obiezu, popularly known as “Onye Amuma,” Onu Ndi Aguata and others.

title: La Guadalupe nació entre la ribera del río y la pasión por el futbol
content:
Lugar de tradición en la Magdalena Contreras
Desde niños, sus habitantes jugaron ese deporte en los llanos, adonde acudieron las estrellas de los Pumas
Domingo 13 de septiembre de 2026, p. 25
Enclavada en una zona de obraje, la colonia La Guadalupe da la impresión de que su historia es similar a otros barrios de La Magdalena Contreras: surgió entre lomas deshabitadas que se poblaron de la mano de la industria textilera; sin embargo, aquí los habitantes cobran identidad por sus justas futboleras. Para ellos, este deporte es una forma de pertenencia, una tradición de generaciones, símbolo de distinción e identificación.
De un futbol llanero que practicaron desde la niñez en lotes baldíos de terracería, salió un hombre menudo, férreo defensa que jugaba en la lateral derecha y que, junto con otras leyendas, como Miguel Mejía Barón y Héctor Sanabria, convirtieron a la última línea de los Pumas de la Universidad en una barrera infranqueable: Genaro Bermúdez Martínez, el León de Contreras o el Pelé Mexicano, con el sello de La Guadalupe, marcó la defensa del equipo auriazul de finales de los 70 y principios de los 80 que enorgullece a este lugar futbolero.
Al lado del río Magdalena, donde se instaló la industrial textilera, los obreros de las fábricas construyeron sus viviendas. “Pequeños cuartos de adobe y láminas de cartón, algunos con cercas de sincolote y tejamanil para marcar el límite de los terrenos”, recuerda Encarnación Aguilar, vecino de la colonia y quien portó el número 13 del equipo local.
En apenas nueve hectáreas que la conforman, La Guadalupe es una de las más pequeñas de La Magdalena Contreras; aquellos niños de mediados del siglo pasado veían en todo tipo de terracería enormes canchas de futbol. “Jugábamos descalzos, no había dinero para comprar tenis, mucho menos zapatos de futbol”, platica Encarnación al hacer su remembranza.
Para estos hombres que ya andan entre los 70 y 80 años, la falta de bardas –no sólo en sus hogares, también en las dos escuelas que hay en la colonia: Juventino Rosas y Mariano Abasolo– era una forma de libertad, de vivir “al aire libre”.
El entorno de precariedad lo compensaba la naturaleza: zonas verdes y agua de río que aprovechaban mientras las madres lavaban en el batán, cerca de la corriente del río. En su época de adolescentes, nadaban en la presa y exploraban las cavernas que se formaron en los pedregales, de donde extraían material pétreo y tepetate que esparcían en los pisos de sus viviendas para evitar los lodazales.
El trébol, símbolo de la unión
La colonia estaba dividida en cuatro. Había rivalidad entre los grupos que se formaron, conocidos como los mecánicos, eléctricos y los jugadores. Jóvenes que se juntaron para dirimir sus diferencias en encuentros de futbol y que finalmente conformaron uno solo que representó a La Guadalupe, agrega el veterano jugador.
Actualmente está dividida en secciones, las cuatro tienen a la parroquia de Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe, localizada en la calle Alfonso Priani, de punto central. La primera es de Francisco Villa hasta el Campo Contreras y la primaria Mariano Abasolo; la segunda llega a lo que era la Cooperativa y hoy está un Chedraui; la tercera, a los límites de Santa Teresa, y la última hasta lo que fueron los lavaderos comunitarios, donde se encuentran las oficinas del tan afamado club de futbol La Guadalupe.
La colonia de siete calles principales es un cuadro, “para nosotros son las cuatro hojas de un trébol, que desde hace varios años diseñamos y adoptamos como escudo de identidad para el equipo de futbol de la colonia”, explica Encarnación, fundador del plantel.
A estos jugadores les tocó ver como se cercó con vallas el río Magdalena ante el crecimiento de la inseguridad, cuando surgieron las bandas juveniles en la Ciudad de México. La Guadalupe no estuvo exenta y aparecieron Los Romanos, que a diferencia de Los Panchitos de Tacubaya “estos vecinos se organizaron para defender el territorio”, dice Encarnación.
Tomás Morales, oriundo de la colonia, hijo de obreros textileros, habla con orgullo de su parentesco con el futbolista Genaro Bermúdez, su cuñado, quien empezó en el equipo de La Guadalupe con el número 2, después se fue al Contreras hasta jugar en Pumas al lado de “los grandes: Evanivaldo Castro Cabinho, Hugo Sánchez, Sanabria, Spencer Coelho, Leonardo Cuéllar y más”.
El hombre de 80 años platica sus vivencias de estudiante en cuartos de piedra que caracterizaban a la primaria Juventino Rosas, grupos de 60 niños que abarrotaban los salones y en consecuencia se hizo un anexo para después construir la Mariano Abasolo “de tabique, ya moderna”.
Las familias eran grandes, hasta de ocho hijos por pareja. No tenían luz y se alumbran con velas o lámparas de petróleo. El agua se acarreaba con aguantadores de los bitoques ubicados en Francisco Sarabia y Francisco Villa. Las caminatas eran entre cerros, charcos y caminos enlodados porque todo estaba de bajada, recuerdan los moradores.
En los 70 empezó la urbanización, introdujeron las redes de drenaje y de agua potable. Las calles se pavimentaron y el campo Contreras se oficializó como cancha de futbol. Hasta este punto llegaron los campeones de liga de primera división de 1981: Olaf Heredia, Leonardo Cuéllar, Genaro Bermúdez, Chucho Ramírez, Enrique López Zarza, El Pareja López, Manuel Negrete y El Tuca Ferretti, entrenados por Bora Milutinovic. Los Pumas jugaron con el equipo de La Guadalupe que perdió el partido por una anotación de último minuto, pero al campeón de liga “le costó imponerse a los vecinos de La Guadalupe”, comenta don Tomás.
José Luis Aguilar, segunda generación de fundadores de La Guadalupe, busca conservar su historia, no sólo como una colonia que se construyó con ladrillos, cemento y pavimentación de calles, sino como una comunidad unida que levantó su iglesia, organiza la fiesta cada 12 de diciembre y festeja, en cada una de sus calles, las posadas y donde uno de sus símbolos principales tiene forma de balón, porque ellos son “una colonia futbolera de La Magdalena Contreras”.

title: Mariachi: la tradición que resiste y evoluciona
content:
Mariachi: la tradición que resiste y evoluciona
¡De México para el mundo! Este género musical ha sabido transmitir la esencia de nuestro país a través de sus letras, melodías y la imagen inolvidable del charro mexicano.
Hablar de México sin mencionar al mariachi es imposible. Más que un género musical es un elemento cultural tan relevante, que en 2011 fue reconocido como Patrimonio Cultural Inmaterial de la Humanidad por la Organización de las Naciones Unidas para la Educación, la Ciencia y la Cultura (UNESCO).
Su origen es difuso. Las teorías dibujan sus antecedentes en los conjuntos de cuerdas del occidente mexicano que interpretaban sones, jarabes y otras piezas.
Pese a su presencia en diferentes estados, el título de la cuna del mariachi lo tiene Jalisco, específicamente Cocula, donde es una forma de vida que se manifiesta en sus plazas, monumentos y las generaciones de músicos dedicados a este arte.
Porque más allá del tiempo, la tradición perdura y el mariachi ha sabido evolucionar. Pasó de tocar en celebraciones populares y familiares, a tener una representación en el cine, la televisión y ser un símbolo de México en el mundo.
Hoy el mariachi no solo se escucha en el extranjero, sino que han nacido agrupaciones en diferentes países, desde Latinoamérica, hasta Europa, Asia y Medio Oriente.
Esto resume su valor musical y cultural, y reafirma la importancia de mantener viva la tradición. Transmitirlo de generación en generación va más allá de seguir cantando sus canciones, se necesita buscar nuevas voces y músicos dispuestos a interpretarlas.
Un arte que necesita nuevas voces
“El mariachi es esencia de México en el mundo, presencia de Jalisco en México”, así describe la importancia de este género musical Don Ángel Martínez, representante del Mariachi Nuevo Tecalitlán.
Por eso es importante conservar la tradición, algo que se ha buscado impulsar en Jalisco, la meca del mariachi, con el objetivo de que los jóvenes mantengan el cariño hacia esta música y la transmitan con dignidad y orgullo.
Y los frutos se ven en los mariachis infantiles que tienen muchas agrupaciones, incluyendo el Mariachi Nuevo Tecatitlán, que también tiene su rama femenil. De esta forma, se vuelven semilleros de las próximas generaciones.
Pero, aunque no todos se conviertan en músicos profesionales, “el hecho de tener un contacto con el arte y la cultura de México, los hace ciudadanos más sensibles y empáticos con la sociedad”, explica Don Ángel.
Ser mariachi no es algo improvisado. En México existen escuelas de mariachi que permiten estudiar esta carrera de forma profesional, algo que puede llevar alrededor de cuatro años.
Sin embargo, como señala el músico, lo más importante es la práctica. Un mariachi profesional tiene ensayos múltiples días de la semana, con varias horas cada uno, pues la técnica para tocar los instrumentos, incluyendo la voz, debe trabajarse continuamente.
De esta forma se logra lo más importante para este género: transmitir diferentes emociones al público, pues “la música de mariachi no solo se escucha, se siente”, apunta Don Ángel.
Esto es lo que ha permitido romper las barreras del idioma y llevarlo a diferentes partes del mundo, pues, aunque las personas no entiendan lo que dicen las letras, sí sienten lo que expresan.
El traje, la identidad del mariachi
Si hay algo que identifica a estos músicos es su traje. Su inspiración es la ropa que usaban los campesinos con adornos de vestimenta española.
Como explica Don Ángel, se compone por el moño, la chaquetilla, la botonadura, botines charros especiales con fuelle, el fajo de vaqueta y la hebilla de plata, todo esto como parte del traje clásico de los charros hacendados.
Aunque hoy el mariachi se encuentra en casi cualquier rincón de México, la experiencia completa se vive en Jalisco. Desde la Plaza de los Mariachis en Guadalajara, donde se reúnen diferentes grupos, hasta los diferentes pueblos mágicos.
Un fin de semana en Cocula te acercará a las raíces de esta tradición, donde las presentaciones en vivo se unen al Museo de la Cuna Mundial del Mariachi, mientras en Tecatitlán te espera el Museo Silvestre Vargas con la historia del Mariachi Vargas.

title: Culiacán marcha por la paz: ciudadanos exigen un alto a la violencia y buscan a sus desaparecidos
content:
Culiacán marcha por la paz: ciudadanos exigen un alto a la violencia y buscan a sus desaparecidos
Vestidos de blanco, con globos y pancartas, cientos de ciudadanos salieron este domingo a las calles de Culiacán para participar en la “Marcha de la Paz”.
Vestidos de blanco, con globos y pancartas, cientos de ciudadanos salieron este domingo a las calles de Culiacán para participar en la “Marcha de la Paz”, a dos años del inicio de una ola de violencia que ha dejado una estela de homicidios, desapariciones e inseguridad en Sinaloa.
La movilización comenzó en La Lomita, luego de una misa encabezada por el obispo de Culiacán, Jesús José Herrera Quiñónez. Al finalizar la ceremonia, los participantes soltaron decenas de globos blancos y emprendieron su recorrido rumbo a la Catedral de Culiacán.
Durante la marcha, las familias y ciudadanos mostraron pancartas con mensajes como “Sinaloa ponte de pie”, “No más inocentes”, “SOS, salven al campo sinaloense”, “Queremos paz en Sinaloa” y “Prometieron paz, nos entregaron miedo”.
Uno de los momentos más sensibles de la movilización fue la presencia de familiares de personas desaparecidas, quienes llevaron fichas con sus fotografías y datos para exigir a las autoridades que intensifiquen su búsqueda.
Entre los casos recordados se encuentran los de David Antonio Ruelas y José Isaías Ibarra, quienes fueron vistos por última vez en marzo del año pasado cuando se dirigían al Colegio del Aire de Sinaloa.
En su mensaje, el obispo Jesús José Herrera Quiñónez llamó a la ciudadanía a mantener la unidad y buscar la reconciliación para hacer frente a las condiciones de inseguridad que atraviesa el estado.
Mientras el contingente avanzaba hacia el centro de la ciudad, se observó la presencia de elementos de la Guardia Nacional, al tiempo que más ciudadanos se sumaban a la protesta.
La marcha se convirtió así en un llamado colectivo de las familias sinaloenses: paz, seguridad y respuestas para quienes aún esperan el regreso de sus seres queridos.

title: Rarámuris de Norogachi piden respeto a su autodeterminación
content:
Funcionarios locales intentan imponerles proyectos
Domingo 13 de septiembre de 2026, p. 22
Integrantes de los gobiernos indígenas rarámuri de la región de Norogachi, de la sierra Tarahumara en Chihuahua, exigieron respeto a su derecho a la libre autodeterminación, pues señalaron que a través del Fondo Federal de Aportaciones para la Infraestructura Social para Pueblos y Comunidades Indígenas y Afromexicanas (Faispiam), funcionarios locales intentan imponerles los proyectos, proveedores y prestadores de servicios, cuando éstos necesitan ser decididos en asambleas comunitarias.
Ejemplificaron que en el presente año se les planteó invertir en letrinas, pero muchos pobladores prefieren que el recurso sea para otras obras, además han detectado que las personas quienes les recomiendan los servidores públicos para ejecutar los proyectos son familiares o gente cercana a ellos.
En un escrito dirigido a la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum y al Instituto Nacional de Pueblos Indígenas (Inpi), rechazaron “cualquier forma de tutelaje sobre nuestros derechos comunitarios, los cuales se encuentran plenamente reconocidos tanto en instrumentos jurídicos internacionales como nacionales y locales”.
Isidro Gardea García, primer siríami de Norogachi; Jesús Raúl Naba Peña, primer siríami de Pawichíki, Juan Espino Hernández, comisario policial de Siquirichi, Guachochi, entre otros, resaltaron que actualmente el pueblo rarámuri está en proceso de adquisición y desarrollo de habilidades, las cuales “nos permiten organizar y administrar nuestro capital social, humano, económico y político”.
Frenan empoderamiento técnico y operativo
Por ello, afirmaron, “la imposición de una tutela gubernamental frena nuestro empoderamiento técnico y operativo, reduciendo con ello nuestra autonomía a una simulación burocrática”.
Así, rechazaron la imposición de proveedores, prestadores de servicios y logística externos para la ejecución de sus proyectos comunitarios. “Somos nosotros quienes poseemos la capacidad y el derecho legítimo de decidir con qué constructores trabajar, a qué fleteros locales contratar y dónde adquirir materiales a implementar para materializar infraestructura comunitaria, de modo que el beneficio económico se quede y circule dentro de nuestra propia región indígena”.
Defendieron que sus asambleas comunitarias, en las cuales se planea, proyecta y deciden las obras, cuentan con los mecanismos internos de control, consenso y transparencia para administrar los recursos entregados a través del Faispiam, a cargo de la Secretaría del Bienestar.
Asimismo, los integrantes de los gobiernos indígenas rarámuri señalaron que el hecho de limitar los rubros de inversión a obras preestablecidas “anula las prioridades reales de nuestras comunidades”.

title: ‘It’ll never be the same’: Regina family seeks justice for Rebecca Wilson
content:
Friends, family and loved ones of 37-year-old Rebecca Wilson gathered outside Regina’s Legislative Building Friday evening to remember and honour her life.
Wilson, referred to as ‘Becca’ or ‘Becky’ by those who knew her, was described by family as a devoted older sister, a woman of faith and someone of strong character. Her sister, Katie Wilson, said Rebecca was a creative person who spent a lot of time painting and writing.
“As her sister, there’s a huge gap now and I’ll never be able to fill it the same way,” said Katie Wilson. “It’ll never be the same.”
The family took turns speaking about Rebecca Wilson, describing her as funny, loyal and a huge loss for the family. Wilson said the circumstances around the death make the loss that much more difficult.
Get daily National news
“She didn’t just die. She didn’t just pass away from some sickness or anything or some freak accident. She was murdered,” said Wilson.
Police are investigating.
Rebecca Wilson’s mother, Wendy Lerat Lynn said Wilson, who was the oldest of five, always embodied the trait of advocating for others.
“She took on being the big sister,” she said. “She did that on the playground too with other kids. She kind of was like that.”
Lerat said her daughter’s laugh was contagious and wanted people to remember Wilson as faithful, funny and an amazing human being.
“The way she ended, it didn’t do her any justice at all,” said Lerat.
Signs at the vigil called for justice for missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls. Lerat said what happened to her daughter is not an isolated incident.
“I understand there’s different degrees and understanding of murdered and missing Indigenous women,” said Lerat. “The more that people start to talk about it maybe it’ll become something that people will actually see.”
Rebecca Wilson was the victim of an aggravated assault on Aug. 14. She was found in an alley in the 1400 block of Wascana Street and died from her injuries on Aug. 30.
“There needs to be something more that is addressing why these women are being murdered,” said Lerat.
No arrests have been made in Wilson’s death.
“Our family will not stop, I will not stop. It is my mission to find truth for my sister, we will know the truth. The truth will come to light, it’s just a matter of when,” said Wilson.

title: Family of murdered teen pleads for action to solve 36-year cold case
content:
Colleen Walker-Craig's family demands action in Bowraville cold case
In short:
The families of Colleen Walker-Craig, Evelyn Greenup and Clinton Speedy-Duroux are calling for more action from police to find their children's killer.
Homicide detectives are in northern NSW engaging with locals in Macksville, who they hope may have information regarding Ms Walker-Craig's remains.
What's next?
Police say they have not previously targeted the Macksville community, north of Bowraville, and anyone with information is urged to come forward.
WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised this article contains the names and images of people who have died.
After grieving for more than three decades, an Indigenous family is demanding police "stop appealing and just go out" as homicide detectives return to northern NSW in a bid to find the body of murdered teenager Colleen Walker-Craig.
The 16-year-old was last seen at Bowraville, north of Coffs Harbour, on September 13, 1990.
Her mother, Muriel Craig, has renewed her pleas for police to solve the 36-year-old cold case.
"I know that there's people who live in the Bowraville community who know what happened to Colleen," she said.
"Sometimes I think the police don't believe me.
"I know they haven't questioned these people. I can't wait any longer."
The teenager’s weighted-down clothes were discovered in the Nambucca River months after her disappearance, but her body has never been found.
In an inquest, a state coroner declared her dead and most likely murdered.
A $1 million reward has been offered for information leading to the recovery of her remains.
Today, detectives arrived in Macksville, just south-east of Bowraville, for a week of community engagement, appealing for new information.
Four-year-old Evelyn Greenup and 16-year-old Clinton Speedy-Duroux, who were also First Nations children, disappeared in the area about the same time.
Their remains were discovered in 1991, but no-one has ever been convicted of their murders.
Separate $1 million rewards have also been offered for information that leads to police solving their cases as well.
Asking for answers
Detective Superintendent Joe Doueihi did not directly respond when asked about the family's concerns but said this week's community engagement could help the investigation.
He said officers would be stationed at Macksville's Phillip Hughes Pavillion to speak with locals until Friday afternoon, after a similar operation in Bowraville in 2024.
"It's not just an exercise to keep people happy," Detective Superintendent Doueihi said.
"In 2024, a lot of valuable information was obtained through that.
"What we learned is that we didn't target that community here and we've taken those lessons on board."
Detective Superintendent Doueihi said loyalties could change over the course of 36 years.
"We believe that people in this community didn't present in 2024, and we're giving them that opportunity now," he said.
Colleen Walker-Craig's brother Lucas Craig urged those with information to contact police.
"Think about the families, how long we've been suffering with this," he said.
"This was three quarters of my life that I've had to deal with this.
"Going to work and coming home to your family and seeing your parents upset every day because there's nothing they can do."
Mr Craig said the family's relationship with police was "not as strong as we'd like it to be".
Elijah Duroux, the nephew of Clinton Speedy-Duroux, said his family felt like the investigation had stagnated.
He said they were not informed police would be in Macksville until this morning and were not informed when police divers led new searches of the Nambucca River late last year.
"Don't you think my grandfather and grandmother deserve to know when there's stuff going on in regards to their son's murder?" Mr Duroux said.
Evelyn Greenup's mother, Rebecca Stadhams, released a statement through NSW Police, calling on people to come forward.
"Maybe you have carried this information for years. Maybe you were afraid to speak. Maybe you think what you know is too small or doesn't matter," she said.
"But it might matter. It might be the piece of information that finally helps us find the truth about what happened to Evelyn.
"After all these years, I am asking you to think about my little girl."

title: Mafalala pede mais homenagens a Noémia de Sousa
content:
No coração da Mafalala, bairro de Maputo onde Noémia de Sousa cresceu, jovens poetas apelam a iniciativas para preservar o legado da escritora no ano do seu centenário, incluindo bibliotecas, escolas e até ruas com o seu nome.
“É preciso falar da Noémia e como é que se fala dela? Fazendo o livro da Noémia circular. Já se publicou com muito custo “Sangue Negro”, o seu livro de estreia, mas há muito mais coisas que podem ser feitas”, disse à Lusa o jovem poeta e escritor Álvaro Taruma.
No bairro da Mafalala, onde a poeta e jornalista Carolina Noémia Abranches de Sousa cresceu, Taruma considera que a celebração do centenário da autora é importante por representar a génese da poesia moçambicana e a persistência do seu legado.
Por isso, entende que o nome de Noémia de Sousa deve ser mais exaltado, numa altura em que continua menos celebrada e conhecida do que alguns contemporâneos, como José Craveirinha ou Rui Nogar.
Taruma defende igualmente a divulgação das cartas e correspondências da escritora como forma de aprofundar o conhecimento sobre o seu pensamento e a forma como refletia o país.
O poeta considera ainda importante que as editoras resgatem textos dispersos de Noémia de Sousa e os publiquem em novas edições.
“Estamos num centenário, mas sinto pouco barulho (…) mas é preciso muito mais, até sair destes espaços privados e ir à escola, porque são figuras fundamentais na criação do pensamento da direção ideológica do nosso país e é preciso revisitar estas figuras e compreender com mais profundidade como essas pessoas viam o país”, defendeu.
“Se o nome estiver lá, se as ruas levarem o nome da nossa poeta, as avenidas, as escolas, as bibliotecas, os centros de formação, as pessoas terão curiosidade de procurar saber quem é essa figura que está patente na avenida ou rua”, acrescentou.
Taruma lembra que o primeiro contacto com a escrita da poeta aconteceu no ensino primário, afirmando que essa leitura continua a influenciar a forma como olha o mundo.
“Noémia foi uma poetisa que sempre se preocupou pela condição humana, o trabalhador migrante moçambicano para com o trabalho assim escravo nas minas da África do Sul, preocupou-se com o trabalho e a condição da mulher, por isso temos aqueles poemas como ‘As meninas das docas’. Preocupou-se com a questão da raça, da negritude, da afirmação de todas as pessoas africanas, moçambicanas, independentemente da sua cor”, afirmou, referindo que são temas que também fazem parte do seu labor literário.
Também o jovem poeta Nick de Rosário disse à Lusa que o nome de Noémia de Sousa deve ocupar o mesmo espaço de destaque que os seus contemporâneos, defendendo a criação de iniciativas permanentes para garantir maior visibilidade à escritora.
“Temos várias casas que acolhem a literatura e um evento que pudesse ser feito em dois dias, mas [queremos] que a gente só fale da Noémia, que a gente declame textos da Noémia e que se façam mais antologias, que se chamem mais mulheres a escreverem poesia, porque neste momento temos poucas mulheres na poesia”, sugeriu.
Nick conheceu a escrita de Noémia de Sousa no ensino primário, mas foi na universidade que aprofundou o estudo da autora, descrevendo a sua poesia como uma escrita “com muita força”.
“Ela tem aquela literatura da geração dela com muita força, muita vontade e que de certa maneira posso dizer que transformou algumas mentes e a maneira como se encara a poesia moçambicana, então acredito que para ela tem que ser feita uma homenagem à altura”, anotou.
O Museu Mafalala, localizado no bairro onde Noémia de Sousa cresceu, dispõe atualmente de uma biblioteca com o nome da escritora e de uma coleção dedicada à literatura moçambicana. O responsável pelo espaço, Ivan Laranjeira, explicou que a iniciativa procura estimular o gosto pela leitura entre crianças.
“Nós sentimos que de facto a Noémia é muito pouco divulgada, se calhar o facto de ter passado a maior parte da sua vida no exílio contribuiu para que não se soubesse mais sobre ela, entretanto, o impacto da sua obra é tremendo e é uma obra rica, tendo em consideração que só publicou um único livro, mas, mesmo assim, aquilo que ela aborda, a sua poesia, é tremendo e continua a ser bastante atual”, disse à Lusa Ivan Laranjeira.
O Museu Mafalala trabalha igualmente num programa para assinalar o centenário da poeta, ao mesmo tempo que, desde o início do ano, promove palestras em escolas do bairro e de outros pontos de Maputo para divulgar a vida e obra de Noémia de Sousa.
Nascida no dia 20 de setembro de 1926, na Catembe, atual Maputo, Carolina Noémia Abranches de Sousa Soares, mais conhecida por Noémia de Sousa, foi a primeira mulher negra a publicar poesia em Moçambique, fazendo da escrita uma forma de resistência ao colonialismo e à repressão da Polícia Internacional de Defesa do Estado (PIDE).
Apesar de ter produzido a maior parte da sua obra entre 1948 e 1951, os seus textos permaneceram dispersos por jornais e revistas, sendo reunidos apenas em 2001 no livro Sangue Negro, por iniciativa da Associação dos Escritores Moçambicanos.
Noémia de Sousa morreu a 4 de dezembro de 2002, em Cascais, Portugal.

title: Alice Duncan-Kemp was an empathetic observer of Mithaka culture, but her legacy is complicated
content:
Alice’s dreaming is centrally about the childhood, memories and writings of Alice Duncan-Kemp (1901-1988), who grew up on a pastoral property named Mooraberrie in the first decades of the 20th century.
Mooraberrie was a vast sheep and cattle station located in the Channel Country between Birdsville and Windorah in inland south-western Queensland. A 2015 native title determination recognised Mithaka people as the traditional owners of the region.
Duncan-Kemp published four books in her lifetime and another was published posthumously. All of these works drew on a childhood spent in intimate contact with Mithaka people. Her extraordinarily detailed and empathetic observations formed part of the documentary basis for the 2015 native title determination.
Review: Alice’s dreaming – Tom Griffiths (Black Inc.)
What then of the word “dreaming” in Tom Griffiths’ title?
According to the historian Patrick Wolfe, the word “dreamtime” entered the Australian lexicon via the early anthropological research collaboration between Frank Gillen, the postmaster at Mparntwe (Alice Springs), and Baldwin Spencer, a professor of biology at the University of Melbourne. Their famed partnership resulted in a huge collection of objects, images and films, which has been digitised.
The Arrernte term “alcheringa” was translated by Gillen as the “dream-times”: a long-distant epoch in which the world was created and rules of conduct were laid down.
Wolfe was critical of the generalisation of Spencer and Gillen’s notion of the “dream-times”. He showed that dreams were a counterpoint to European scientific rationalism; the connection between “dreaminess” and Aboriginal people reinforced some of the racist presumptions of both 19th-century anthropology and the popular imagination.
The mid-20th century anthropologist W.E.H. Stanner preferred the term “Dreaming”, which better captured the complexity of an “impalpable and subtle” concept that refers to cosmogony as well as institutions, totemic affiliations and ever-present responsibilities to Country.
