The recent findings marked the culmination of several years worth of hard work, titled Project Eisirean.
It is a collaboration between ecology and environment researchers, Gaelic and education experts at the University of Glasgow and local community organisations on the west coast of Scotland.
Dr Anna McGregor, an expert in coastal ecology and a lecturer at the University of Glasgow , had the original idea of locating oysters through traditional place-names, then applying scientific techniques to confirm oyster presence within them.
She explained: "This is a really exciting outcome, for a project that started off looking for the historic distribution of oysters along the West Coast.
"We thought that as native oysters are now really rare throughout Europe, is there a way to look where they used to be, using people's memory and understanding - that can come through place names.
"We found two areas with oyster in the name, both on Mull, and after about two years we found another one on Lewis. Then we broadened the search to look for habitat related names, like sand banks."
The group then examined those locations for factors like the sea bed and the level of the water flow.
Dr McGregor hopes the team can build on their findings through continued work with local communities in Islay and Mull, alongside oyster bed restoration and protection work in key areas.
The research team will now trial the feasibility of a mobile oyster hatchery, in the hope it could both supply oyster larvae to coastal communities and help rebuild oyster beds in various areas.
The first mobile hatchery is being trialled in Millport, with plans to trial more in the future.
Dr McGregor said: "What we are hopping is to connect knowledge of the past, where shellfish was an important part of people's diets, to future improvement.
"We want to look where shellfish used to be, where communities had a connection with them, and develop that again.
"A small scale hatchery like this [on Millport] can be sustainable on an island, and really help people to connect with them.
"Seeing oysters life cycle can help people understand why it's important to keep them in the wild, and then get the numbers back up to levels where we can harvest them for lots of purposes."
The Native Oyster Restoration Alliance – NORA – coordinates projects across Europe to enhance the restoration of flat oyster reefs.
Hein Sas, the secretary of NORA, said: "The Eisirean project can serve as an example for other projects on how cultural heritage can help to identify suitable restoration sites."

title: The Amandelboom Basters’ forgotten Northern Frontier story: A 19th-century tragedy
content:
During one of my first visits to the small Karoo town of Williston, Elsa van Schalkwyk, the local town historian, alerted me to a forgotten history of the Northern Cape frontier involving the “Basters” of mixed Khoi and European ancestry who lived at the German Rhenish mission in Amandelboom (renamed Williston in 1883) for much of the 19th century. The Amandelboom Basters were a prosperous and independent livestock-owning community who were pushed off their land in the late 1860s and decided to trek more than 1,000km northwards to Rehoboth in what is now Namibia.
While doing research for my book Letters of Stone I made the startling discovery that in 1908, the year the Nama and Herero genocide ended, the Rehoboth Baster community had been measured and photographed by the German physical anthropologist Eugen Fischer, who later became Hitler’s most senior racial scientist. Fischer’s career as a leading international eugenics scientist soared after he published his ethnography on the Rehoboth Basters in 1913. From 1928 to 1942, Fischer was the director of Berlin’s notorious Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Anthropology, Human Heredity and Eugenics. During World War 2 the Institute had received eye specimens and blood samples from Auschwitz from one of its postdoctoral researchers, Dr Josef Mengele. These strange and disturbing historical entanglements had made me even more curious about the little-known history of this forgotten frontier town.
Reclaiming the past
There are, of course, many forgotten histories in South Africa. There are also many attempts to reclaim buried pasts through grassroots heritage initiatives. One such initiative is taking place on Heritage Day in Williston and includes activities such as indigenous games, potjiekos, dermbraai and a roosterbrood competition. Those who attend will also be able to see 19th-century rock engravings on a nearby farm where the Amandelboom pastoralists once lived. Not much is known in the town about these rock engravings or the herders who inscribed the landscape with these impressive images.
ROCS, a local NGO based in Williston’s Coloured township of Amandelboom, is using this year’s Heritage Day to engage with this forgotten history. As Reggie Nutt, the founder of ROCS, told me: “Knowing where your people come from is vital in a community like Amandelboom, which has massive unemployment, poverty, substance abuse and a sense of hopelessness and despair amongst many youth.” But the history of Amandelboom does not easily lend itself to a straightforward heritage narrative of victims and villains. Instead, it is a complicated story that raises all sorts of troubling questions and ethical challenges.
In the early decades of the 19th century, increasing pressure of overgrazing and drought in the Cape Colony resulted in Baster and Boer pastoralists moving into this area beyond the colonial border. By the 1860s the Basters’ access to their communal pastures was increasingly threatened by trekboers and colonial land policies that ultimately resulted in their displacement. Crown Land laws of this period required Amandelboom Basters to pay for land surveying and registration, which they could not afford. Rather than be turned into landless farmworkers, they trekked to Rehoboth where they established their own Christian settlement.
You will not find anything about this Great Trek from Amandelboom to Rehoboth in school history books, museums or tourist brochures. For that history you will need to consult Dr Herbst’s (2004) Stellenbosch University PhD thesis. Herbst begins his account in 1845 with the establishment of the Rhenish mission in Amandelboom (now Williston) and ends in 1868 with the abandonment of the mission, and the trek of its Baster congregants to German South West Africa. Herbst, who grew up in Williston, wrote his thesis in Afrikaans and never published it. As a result, his dissertation has had minimal public exposure. Although historians Nigel Penn (1995) and Martin Legassick (2010) have written extensively about the Northern Frontier as a culturally diverse, contested and interstitial space where friends and foes were not always defined by “race”, the history of Amandelboom is far less written about or known.
Another source for this forgotten history is the landscape itself. You can find material traces of this buried past inscribed in the stone-domed corbelled houses and 19th-century rock engravings at Grootfontein farm some 40km northeast of Williston. Grootfontein, the original site of the Rhenish Mission Station, has been studied by University of Cape Town archaeologists Vuyiswa Lupuwana and Simon Hall (2019). They interpret these stone corbelled houses and rock engravings as evidence that Baster pastoralists inhabited both Victorian Christian and Khoi identities. The engravings include depictions of ox wagons, Victorian dress, European-style domestic architecture and images of Khoi initiation rituals and rainbulls. What these images of Victorian dress and corbelled houses suggest is that these nomadic pastoralists aspired to a modern Christian lifestyle of dignity, respectability and acceptance as subjects of the British Crown. But this was not to be because of the rigid racial hierarchies and discrimination of colonial rule.
Understanding a tragedy
The story of the two-decade-long Amandelboom mission can be understood as a tragedy of ambiguous belonging that culminated in Baster exclusion and displacement. From this perspective, the tragedy was that Basters had voluntarily assimilated into a modern Christian identity with the belief that this would help them secure protection from the British Crown. Taking on this identity involved wearing modern dress, bible reading, paying tax, carrying firearms and participating in Boer Commando massacres against the San. In their strivings to secure a better position within the racial hierarchy of the white colonial order, the Basters participated in acts of colonial collaboration and Commando violence that failed them in the end. Ultimately, they came no closer to being accepted within the white colonial social order. A similar situation unfolded in German South West Africa in the early 1900s when the Rehoboth Basters sided with the genocidal German forces against the Nama and Herero.
The other aspect of this tragedy concerns the institutional blind spots and shortcomings of the Rhenish missionaries that the Amandelboom Basters enlisted. Based on four months of intensive research in the Rhenish Mission Society Archives in Barmen, Germany, Herbst concluded that the Basters did not invite the missionaries to Amandelboom in 1845 solely for their spiritual teachings. Instead, the invitation was part of a pragmatic strategy aimed at navigating a violent and hostile colonial frontier where Afrikaner trekboers with the large herds were increasingly intruding onto the Basters’ vital water fountains and communal pastures. It was hoped that the missionaries would be effective mediators, brokers and advocates on their behalf and help them acquire protection from the British Crown. As it turned out, the Rhenish missionaries were ill-equipped for this task.
Herbst writes that by privileging spiritual concerns, the missionaries totally underestimated the impact of local ecological and political circumstances on the mission. Instead, the missionaries were bent on turning the Amandelboom pastoralists into a sedentary Christian community of cultivators and artisans along the lines of the Rhenish model of Christian settlement in the Wupper Valley of Germany. This determination was reinforced by the successful establishment in the 1830s of small-scale agricultural and shoe and tannery industries at the Rhenish mission at Wuppertal in the Western Cape. However, the Amandelboom missionaries failed to grasp the influence of the agroecological conditions of the Karoo drylands. Their German model of sedentary settlements of cultivators and small-scale industry was unworkable in the drought-prone Karoo. By contrast, the indigenous practice of nomadic pastoralism that they denigrated as “aimless wandering” was ecologically appropriate for this arid region.
The missionaries’ fixation on spiritual matters also meant that they did not have the political and strategic savviness to negotiate the escalating conflicts between white trekboer and Baster pastoralists over water points and communal pastures. They were also unable to address another sharp line of division that had begun to surface. Since the early decades of the 19th century, a class of merino wool farmers from the Beaufort West district were increasingly competing with pastoralists over access to water and land. These commercial wool farmers, and those within the colonial state who represented the interests of a growing wool export industry, lobbied for the introduction of private property laws and the enclosure of the communal rangelands. The culmination of this pressure was the passing of the 1865 Crown Lands Act. Later, the Fencing Act of 1883, and the introduction of technologies of fencing, windmills and boreholes ensured that modern livestock and wool farming would replace nomadic pastoralism (Archer 2000; Beinart 2003; Van Siddert 2002).
In the mid-1860s, the missionaries had stood by helplessly as the Basters lost access to their water points and grazing lands due to competition with other pastoralists as well as colonial land laws. It was this that led the Basters to decide to defend their autonomy by trekking to Rehoboth where, in 1872, they established a modern Christian ethno-state with a representative Baster council and constitution.
Herbst concludes in his doctoral thesis that the Basters were both devout Christians and astute pragmatists. They had invited the Rhenish missionaries because they believed they could help them negotiate inclusion and belonging as subjects of the British Crown. In many respects, the relationship between the Basters and the Rhenish missionaries mirrors the historical experiences of the Griquas, the Basotho under Moshoeshoe and the Batswana under Khama III. In each of these cases, missionaries were enlisted by indigenous communities as part of what the historian Paul Landau (2010) analyses as a pragmatic politics of belonging, inclusion and protection. Landau notes that precolonial and 19th-century southern African politics was not defined by fixed ethnic or tribal affiliations, but instead was shaped and mediated by shifting traditions of strategic and pragmatic mobilisation, alliance and amalgamation.
The tragedy of this story is that even though these nomadic pastoralists aspired to modern Christian respectability and acceptance as subjects of the British Crown, and even though they collaborated with Boer Commandos in San massacres, they were abandoned by both the missionaries and colonial authorities who failed to protect them. This 19th-century Northern Frontier history, which blurs the lines between victims and perpetrators, is important to engage with precisely because of the challenges it poses for reclaiming cultural heritage. DM

title: Governance Rooted in the Land: Maasai Models of Collective Leadership and Community Responsibility
content: Governance Rooted in the Land: Maasai Models of Collective Leadership and Community Responsibility tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 14:02 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe By Alice Tipap (Maasai) For countless generations, the Maasai have governed their communities without separating leadership from land, culture, spirituality, livestock, and collective responsibility. Our governance system is not built around one powerful individual. It is a living network of Elders, women, spiritual leaders, family heads, and community assemblies, each carrying different responsibilities. Authority is earned through service, wisdom, integrity, experience, and the ability to protect the well being of the whole community. These structures continue to guide communities through drought, land conflicts, social change, and increasing pressure from conservation, tourism, and investment projects. Although State institutions now exercise formal administrative power, Maasai customary governance remains central to community identity and decision-making. Governance as a Collective Responsibility The Maasai understanding of leadership is based on the principle that no person exists alone. An individual belongs to a family, a clan, a neighborhood, an age-set, a territory, and the wider community. Decisions affecting grazing land, water, livestock, ceremonies, peace, and community relations are therefore not expected to be made privately. Traditionally, important matters are discussed through community gatherings where traditional leaders (spiritual, clan, and age-set), Elders, and other respected members contribute their knowledge. Discussion continues until there is broad consensus and a decision that protects the collective interest. The Maasai age-set system is one of the most recognizable foundations of our social and political organization. Men pass through age-related stages with different responsibilities, moving from boyhood to warriorhood and into adulthood. Each age-set develops its own identity, solidarity, duties, and leadership, playing important political and representative roles. The Olaigwanani is an age-set or a clan leader and spokesperson. His responsibility is not to rule as an individual, but to represent, coordinate, advise, and guide. A respected Olaigwanani must listen carefully, communicate clearly, maintain unity, and act in accordance with community values. He is supported by Elders and cannot legitimately make major decisions without consultation. Elders hold authority because they carry historical knowledge, experience, customary law, memory of relationships among clans, territories, and generations. They mediate disputes, advise families, guide ceremonies, negotiate peace, and interpret community responsibilities. Their legitimacy depends on fairness and trust. An Elder who repeatedly acts selfishly or dishonestly may lose moral authority, even if he retains social status. Customary dispute resolution is intended to restore relationships rather than merely punish the offender. When conflict occurs over livestock, marriage, grazing areas, or family responsibilities, Elders bring the parties together to hear both sides and seek an agreement that allows the community to continue living together. Maasai self-governance is inseparable from pastoral land management. Rangelands are not empty spaces waiting for investment. They are collectively used landscapes that contain wet-season and dry-season grazing areas, livestock routes, salt licks, water points, medicinal plants, sacred sites, wildlife habitats, and areas reserved for calves or vulnerable animals. Community members have traditionally used detailed ecological knowledge to decide when different areas should be grazed or rested. Pasture quality is assessed through the presence of particular grasses and plants, soil conditions, water availability, livestock health, and seasonal patterns. This system depends on mobility. During drought, livestock may need to move across large areas to reach water and pasture. Community leaders negotiate access, coordinate use, prevent premature grazing of reserved areas, and address conflicts between neighboring groups. These practices have allowed people, livestock, and wildlife to coexist across variable dryland environments. The modern fragmentation of rangelands by conservation boundaries, farms, tourism concessions, roads, trophy-hunting areas, and private investments has weakened these governance systems. When communities lose access to dry season grazing areas or livestock routes, they also lose the ability to apply their knowledge responsibly. The result is overcrowding, pasture degradation, conflict, livestock deaths, and poverty. Women’s Leadership and Authority The Maasai governance system often focuses only on males. However, Maasai women have always exercised important forms of social, cultural, spiritual, and household authority, even when they are excluded from formal public leadership. Women manage households, food and water distribution, water, housing, and much of the daily knowledge connecting family well being to livestock and the environment. They preserve and transmit songs, oral histories, medicinal knowledge, ceremonies, and values to the children. Women also observe changes in water availability, nutrition, livestock productivity, disease, and household vulnerability. This knowledge is essential to community decision-making. Women may collectively express approval, concern, blessing, or protest through gatherings, songs, ceremonies, and direct engagement with elders. Their moral voice can influence family and community decisions. Patriarchal practices have limited women’s participation in land allocation, village leadership, and formal negotiations with government or investors, but today, Maasai women are demanding fuller recognition by strengthening governance so that it reflects the knowledge and rights of the whole community. Indigenous Women Development Affairs supports women to participate in village councils, land discussions, environmental governance, and advocacy. Maasai women are also beginning to serve on leadership bodies responsible for grazing, conservation, and finance. Self-Governance Under Pressure In Tanzania, customary Maasai governance now operates alongside village governments, district authorities, courts, conservation agencies, and national laws. This creates both opportunities and tensions. Some traditional leaders work closely with elected/appointed leaders, while others are consulted only after decisions have already been made. In many cases, communities receive information about our land use plans, restrictions, conservation/tourism investments, or carbon projects after negotiations have advanced. When outsiders/negotiators identify only a few individuals as community representatives and bypass broader assemblies, they create division. Meaningful self-governance requires Free, Prior and Informed Consent. Communities must receive information in languages they understand, have sufficient time to discuss it through their own institutions, and include women and youth. They must be free to accept, reject, or reshape proposed activities. Consultation cannot be reduced to attendance sheets or meetings called after decisions have been made. Current pressures in Ngorongoro and Loliondo demonstrate why Indigenous governance remains essential. Restrictions on land access, livestock confiscation, reduced services, and displacement threaten not only livelihoods but also the institutions through which Maasai communities govern themselves. Reports have documented serious concerns regarding access to health services, pressure to relocate, and interference with pastoral life in Ngorongoro. Preserving Maasai governance does not mean freezing it in the past. It means strengthening its core principles of collective responsibility, accountability, consensus, respect for Elders, protection of land, intergenerational learning, and service to the community while ensuring equality and responding to new realities. We need stronger collaboration among customary leaders, women’s groups, youth, local government structures, civil society, and legal advocates. We need documentation of customary laws, grazing institutions, oral histories, and ecological knowledge, while protecting sacred and confidential information. Young people should learn not only the names of leadership structures, but also the values that make them legitimate. Digital tools can help record community decisions, map resources, preserve oral knowledge, and communicate threats. However, technology must remain under community control. Knowledge should not be extracted, commercialized, or published without consent. For the Maasai, self-governance is ultimately about maintaining a living relationship with people, territory, livestock, wildlife, ancestors, and future generations. As environmental and political pressures increase, the survival of Maasai governance will depend on recognition of our collective land rights and our authority to determine our own futures. Our governance systems are not obstacles to development. They are proven models of resilience, stewardship, peacebuilding, and belonging. Protecting them is essential not only for Maasai cultural survival, but for the dryland ecosystems that our communities have sustained for generations. A strong Indigenous governance system must be honest about internal inequalities. Culture should protect dignity: it should not be used to silence women, youth, persons with disabilities, or poorer households. Our traditions are living systems capable of reflection and change. Alice Tipap (Maasai) is Climate Change Action Coordinator at Indigenous Women Development Affairs (IWDA). Top photo: Olamal loo ndomonok, a women’s ceremony guided by Elders and traditional leaders at Maaloni village, Loliondo division, Tanzania. Main Image

title: Chasing la dolce vita
content:
When he was a child growing up in Emilia-Romagna, my great-grandfather Marco once found an eagle fledgling that had fallen from its nest. He kept it warm in the folds of his shirt and ran home, only to discover as he undressed that the bird had eaten strips of his flesh, its beak tinged red with blood. The rescued eagle thrived in my great-grandfather’s care, its wingspan soon a remarkable length. And all the while, Marco himself grew immensely tall. Then, one day, without warning, the eagle flew away.
The moment my father told me this story when I was a boy, it lodged itself deep in my imagination. I pictured young Marco as a giant striding through the forests of north-central Italy, calling to the bird of prey, waiting in vain for it to land on his outstretched hand. Marco merged with the heroes of my illustrated classical civilisation books, earning his place between the busts of Roman emperors and the chapters on Greek mythology.
What I never realised was that this family legend held clues to who I am and to my relationship to Italy.
Lina Stores deli in Soho, London, has been a pillar of Italian life in England for decades. It’s where we’d sometimes meet our paternal grandparents when visiting London from our home in France. My brothers and I would line up in front of the refrigerated counter and ask for our favourite ravioli, doing our utmost to avoid any slip-ups in Italian that would make the staff wince: ‘ricotta e spinaci’, ‘zucca’, ‘funghi porcini’. Back at our grandparents’ flat, Nonna served the ravioli on an elaborately laid table, and my grandfather appeared with freshly grated Parmigiano. He’d sprinkle the cheese evenly over our pasta; never too much, nor too little. How he did this, and with such speed, we didn’t know. If we had spaghetti, Nonna would wrap her right hand around ours and twirl the fork with us so we held just the right amount, the bespattered tablecloth damning proof of our slapdash habits at home.
My grandparents trusted that these rituals of the table (they saw them as basic codes of Italianness, connecting displaced Italians everywhere) would allow us to paper over the differences in our ethnically blended and peripatetic family. In this way, we’d be able to claim Italian identity for ourselves, despite its competition in our lives with Englishness and Frenchness. It would anchor us, or so they believed, and prevent us being bullied and singled out.
Revving their Vespas and wearing clothes I’d have avoided, they couldn’t make head nor tail of me
Every summer, on car journeys to Italy we’d listen and re-listen to Italian songs and fairytales to drum the language into us. Once we’d crossed the Alps, any stopover became an opportunity for my father to immerse us in further knowledge. He kept a torch in his pocket, and in the stillness of churches he’d let the beam scurry over frescoes until it hovered, halo-like, above a painted face or a feature in the background. ‘Such bellezza,’ he’d whisper, ‘look at the beauty of that.’ In explaining Masaccio’s brushstrokes, or playing Verdi and Puccini arias at car-shaking volume, we sensed my father was offering us, his sons, yardsticks by which to measure life. He needed us to see ourselves as the inheritors of a civilisation unlike any other. Italianness was his gift to us.
In my teens, I spent a month in Florence looking after the child of a couple of scientists, colleagues of my father. My role was to speak to the boy in English; his parents’ job was to improve my Italian. The moment I was alone with the seven-year-old, he locked himself in his room and refused to come out. As a consolation, one evening, I was entrusted to a 16-year-old nephew who took me to join his friends in a packed central piazza. Within minutes, the assembled youngsters were trying to identify my hybrid accent, crowding round with questions, trying out their English: ‘Are you French or British?’ ‘Which football team do you support?’ ‘Have you got a girlfriend?’ Revving their Vespas, blasting music I didn’t recognise, and wearing clothes I’d have avoided, they couldn’t make head nor tail of me. I escaped into Florence, only vaguely aware of where I was going. Leaning against a wall on the banks of the Arno, the Ponte Vecchio in the distance, I tried to convince myself that the surrounding ‘bellezza’ vaunted by my father was mine, that I fitted into the circus of Italian life I’d seen in Fellini films, but I felt I was a baffling anomaly, an impostor. The chameleon skills I’d always employed to fudge my way through existence had let me down. My hosts were in a state of panic on my return. Where had I been? I wasn’t going to be allowed out again. I’d failed as a childminder. And as an Italian.
A cousin recently emailed me photographs of my great-grandfather Marco, the first to set the family’s migrations in motion. I was surprised to see that he was as tall as the family legend of the eagle would have it, towering over others, but also that he was standing in front of what was the Italian Hospital in Queen Square, Bloomsbury, the place he’d apparently helped to run. This was the very spot in London I’d sat on many occasions when, as a student at King’s College, I’d search for quiet garden squares in which to read and revise for exams. I’d always believed I was drawn to the Italian Hospital because of its name. But I remember how, more than once, I’d had to get up and leave, overwhelmed by an inexplicable sadness. In another photograph, Marco was posing with my great-grandmother Delfina, also from Emilia-Romagna, on a patch of grass in Hyde Park. I recognised it immediately as the hidden slope leading down to the Serpentine lake where I often go.
After an online census revealed my great-grandparents’ old address on Highbury Fields, the sorrow I experienced outside the Italian Hospital returns. But this time its source is evident: we used to take our children to the playground by that house, parking right by my great-grandparents’ front door, our shouts and chatting rebounding off the windows. All these coincidences can doubtless be rationally explained, yet they leave me feeling that I live in the wake of tumultuous decisions made long before I was born, that I’m in a web of unseen connections, in friction with the mysteries of an uprooted Italian past.
Dressed in British suits, all the more impeccable to hide his suffering, Marco would declare that he was finally home
In 1940, when Mussolini declared war on Britain and France, all the ‘enemy aliens’ living in Britain had to be imprisoned, or as Winston Churchill put it: ‘Collar the lot!’ Marco, along with thousands of other Italians, and Germans, was rounded up and interned on the Isle of Man. As Rachel Pistol writes in ‘Enemy Aliens’ (2024), many Italian shops and businesses across the country were broken into and smashed by mobs. Marco was lucky not to be placed on the SS Arandora Star, a prisoner-of-war ship heading to Canada. More than 800 of these internees, including 442 Italians, died when the boat was torpedoed off the coast of Ireland. Just under a quarter were from different corners of Emilia-Romagna – some of them friends of Marco. The Italian Hospital scraped through the war and Marco returned to assist them. Researching this essay, I discovered that the building was broken into in 1947 and my great-grandmother, who was with her husband that day, died while confronting the intruders.
On a visit to Emilia-Romagna some years ago, I met old people who recalled widowed Marco’s long stays every summer. Dressed in British suits, all the more impeccable to hide his suffering, he would declare that he was finally home. Then he would leave for London again, returning the summer following, then again setting off, over and over. Just like us, his descendants.
Between the unification of Italy, in 1861, and 1985, around 29 million Italians left the peninsula. Political instability, high birth rates, natural disasters, unprofitable sharecropping (especially in the South), deprivation and overpopulation were major drivers for this exodus. And the more people left en masse, the more they encouraged others to join them. Today, about 80 million people outside Italy claim full or partial Italian ancestry. This diaspora has generated Little Italys across the world: in New York’s Manhattan, in La Boca, Buenos Aires, and in Clerkenwell, London. Once oases of solidarity, home-away-from-home citadels, where you could find anything – from the Italy football kit to keyrings with Leonardo da Vinci’s Vitruvian Man – they now mostly feel like places of historic, even faded, hyper-Italianness. By 1920, São Paulo alone was home to 70 per cent of the Italians who emigrated to Brazil; as many as 60 per cent of Argentinians have a link to Italy, and Italian is still one of the main mother tongues spoken in Toronto, Canada. In Australia, 4.4 per cent of the population is of Italian heritage. In America, around 17 million people identify as Italian.
Descendants of Italian migrants generally express an intense pride in their heritage, and many continue to live by its sociocultural tenets in spite of decades, or more, of absence. It is as if time away from Italy, and geographical distance, only amplify a yearning for it. Stanley Tucci, to cite but one well-known example (the same could probably be said of Lady Gaga or Francis Ford Coppola) begins his TV food series Searching for Italy (2021-22) by stating in his broad American accent: ‘I’m Italian on both sides.’
Every summer, as per my own family’s tradition, members of this diaspora return to Italy. They enjoy the peninsula in the heat-filled months: sea, mountains, food, art and music, and its dolce vita. Where Italians living in Italy might imbue their identity with more intrinsically regional elements, the diaspora, in its dissemination around the globe, carries with it a more all-encompassing interpretation of the country. Their version of Italy, like the one I grew up with, is capable of brushing over fractures and complications, and the darker sides of the nation, articulated as it is by ideals that extoll the peninsula as a connected whole.
For bona-fide Italians, a tomato sauce is never just a sauce, but a form of alchemy
By upholding and publicising the symbols of Italy – fashion, art, food, football – the diaspora has helped turn them into a recognisable shorthand for the country abroad. Visiting London’s Italian restaurants with my family, I’m struck by how many still have straw-clad Chianti bottles on the tables, and a packet of grissini tucked next to the plates, not to mention waiters who make a show of noisily grinding pepper onto our food. The performative nature of this overseas Italianness, its theatricality, is reinforced by walls decorated with photos of the owners posing with Italian American celebrities like Al Pacino, Robert De Niro or Sylvester Stallone. It is as if we’ve all been given roles, customers and waiters alike, in a Pirandello play that challenges distinctions between illusion and reality.
My kids love YouTube and TikTok videos in which a nonna or nonno, from a well-ordered kitchen in Italy, reveals how to make the creamiest cacio e pepe or the tastiest tomato sauce. These elderly cooks appear to embody an authentic art to being Italian that cuts through the mimicry and stagecraft. The children laugh loudest when these elderly home chefs from Italy screw up their faces in disgust when asked to taste American shop-bought pizza or frozen lasagne. ‘Do you know what merda means in English?’ one asks.
For bona-fide Italians, a tomato sauce is never just a sauce, but a form of alchemy. In an ideal world, it is seasoned with herbs once grown by the Romans, made with San Marzano tomatoes nourished by volcanic soil, and olive oil from Puglia’s ancient groves. This level of culinary precision largely explains why Italians are baffled, outraged even, by foreigners committing offences with their cuisine – snapping dry spaghetti in two before cooking it, grating parmesan onto seafood risotto, or mixing garlic and onion as a base for the same sauce. It might seem precious to outsiders, but a belief in excellence and the purity of traditions underpins Italianness. Indeed, something akin to the formula for tomato sauce can be applied to all areas of Italian production, from coffee machines and scooters to architecture. For my father and grandparents, Italian ingenuity stemmed from the peninsula’s endemic flair. A Lamborghini or a Gio Ponti chair was simply the latest layer of sediment in an accretion of refinement that had already given rise to Brunelleschi’s Dome and Scarlatti’s sonatas.
Despite endorsing the country as the paragon of human advancement, my father routinely turned down job offers at Italian universities and research centres, choosing instead to work in France. The resulting tension, played out in frequently announced but endlessly postponed homecomings, threw us into ever more convoluted cycles of l’eterno ritorno that had already tormented my family for two generations with their toing and froing between the peninsula and Britain. Now, with a family of my own, and living and working in London, I’m aware of how I’m resuscitating the dilemmas my parents and grandparents faced.
Increasingly, I’m hankering after Italy, wanting to pass on its rituals. I’ve made sure my children have Italian first names and a basic knowledge of Italy’s geography and history, and they seem to accept this as a given. I’ve fed them stories about eagles and ancestors, accounts of my childhood holidays in Emilia-Romagna and Tuscany, snippets of my time studying in Padua and Florence. I refer back to weddings and family gatherings we’ve all been to, seeding these memories in them, tincturing them with the aura of official history. I tell them about films they should watch one day, by Antonioni and Visconti, of the writings of Boccaccio and Dante. This visceral attachment to Italy is something I feel compelled to pass on. All the while, in parallel, I know I must value the family environment my wife and I have built in England – which is their home. It is an acknowledgement, too, of the sacrifices my ancestors made.
At times, the trap snaps shut. I sense I’m merely living out the choices of the dead, unable to escape their restlessness. Visits to Italy only temporarily assuage the feelings of unsettledness, while leaving again stirs it up. I’m losing something I’ve never owned, just as I’ve been defined by a homeland I don’t inhabit, a past I cannot alter.
Italian Americans were at times deemed ethnically ambiguous, their whiteness questioned
Perhaps, like my diasporic peers who return every summer, I find it easier to fall back on wistful memories and fantasy. I revert all too conveniently, obsessively, to the house we stayed in every year during my youth. As if in a vision, I hold on to the hoopoes in the Tuscan grassland, their heads bobbing up and down in search of insects; my parents arriving with fresh focaccia from the village; the lizards darting across the stone walls; the steady strumming of the cicadas, and the sun tensing the vineyard wires until they buzzed and sang. Warm, moonlit evenings, too, with long tables under giant oaks, friends of our parents talking and singing Italian songs late into the night, knowing no one would tell us to go to bed. I want my children to experience all this, yet I know that I can’t recreate it.
I’ve hunted for echoes of these idyllic days in Italian literature and art, and added them to the building blocks of my emigrant longing. Reading Italo Calvino’s novel The Baron in the Trees (1957), I picture the specific branches and trunks I climbed in childhood. I smell and feel the remembered coolness of stone floors and shaded high-ceilinged rooms when immersed in Lampedusa’s novel The Leopard (1958). An Andrea Mantegna painting, like The Agony in the Garden (1455-56), sends me right back to horizons dotted with hilltop villages and fortified towers of crumbling stone. I’m conscious of the pull of Italy whenever I watch its films – and the irrational reverence this triggers. Recently, I found Alice Rohrwacher’s film La chimera (2023) almost too poignant to watch as it teemed with the details of Italian life.
I know that, for every idealised image of the country, there’s a darker insinuation that Italians have had to face abroad. Late 19th-century and early 20th-century migrants from the peninsula frequently encountered discrimination – accompanied by a range of slurs, from ‘wop’ and ‘eyetie’ in Britain and the US, to ‘rital’ in France. Italian Americans were at times deemed ethnically ambiguous, their whiteness questioned, particularly when they were from the south of the peninsula. Hate-mongers, such as the Ku Klux Klan, alleged that the dregs of Italy were being sent abroad to cleanse the peninsula of its undesirables. In Protestant and English-speaking countries, Italian immigrants became easy targets because of their Catholicism, or their associations with anarchism and organised crime.
Direct conflict regularly flared up. In 1891, in New Orleans in the US, 11 Italians were acquitted of the murder of the local police chief only to be seized by a mob of thousands and lynched. In France in 1893, locals turned on Italian immigrant workers in Aigues-Mortes, reportedly killing eight men, though the number is thought to be far higher. And in 1934, in Kalgoorlie, Australia, anti-Italian killings took place against a similar backdrop of resentment against foreigners allegedly taking jobs.
Even assimilated Italians had their loyalty to their newly adopted lands questioned. It wasn’t just more recently arrived Italians like my great-grandfather who were interned as ‘enemy aliens’ during the Second World War. Some of the 4,000 men who were rounded up had spent most of their lives in Britain. This suspicion was mirrored, to a lesser degree, in Australia and the US – and this while half a million Italian Americans served in the US army during the Second World War, and 7,000 Anglo-Italians served in the British army.
In today’s world of hardening borders and changing alliances, challenges lie ahead for diaspora Italians within Italy itself. Rules for claiming Italian citizenship through ancestry or ius sanguinis (‘right of blood’) have been tightened for descendants of emigrants. This route to citizenship is now granted only to people who have a parent or a grandparent with exclusive Italian nationality, or a parent who was a citizen for two years before their birth. A 160-year history of citizenship by descent has been undermined. The question, officially at least, of who is Italian or not will be thrown into further disarray. I know from experience how hard it will be to extricate Italy from the bodies, imaginations and feelings of these figli d’italiani, these sons and daughters dispersed and far away – people who often feel they have earned the right to call themselves Italian, or at least proudly Italo-something, not least because of the stigma and rejection they or their ancestors once encountered.
At the heart of this circling around identity lies a thorny and painful question. Why do so many Italians continue to leave, and stay away? Between 2023 and 2024, 270,000 Italians emigrated, a figure considerably higher than in the previous two years. And behind the statistics lurks another grave concern: Italy’s population has been declining and is set to lose about 7 million people of working age by 2050. In 2025, there were only 355,000 births – the lowest number since the unification of Italy. In this context, the question of impossible returns is all the more troubling.
I’d like to think that there exists a worldwide collective remembrance of all things Italian, even from the days before the Risorgimento, or the movement for unification. I want to believe the countless stories of regions, cities and villages, of injustices and glories, are being kept safe by millions of descendants of emigrants who have become fervent storytellers. They are the unsung chroniclers of the peninsula, the guardians of a rich repository of traditions and customs, precisely because they have had to work harder to preserve this heritage than natal Italians. In families everywhere, from Argentina, Brazil, Canada, the US, Uruguay and Australia to France and the UK, traces of Italy remain in photographs, books and art, in buildings and the rituals of food. It is one of the paradoxes of diasporas that it is those who leave who want their country of origin to be fixed in time and preserved a certain way.
My children and I have now visited most of the spots across London where my family lived and worked. Walking further from the former Italian Hospital in Queen Square, Bloomsbury, it doesn’t take us long to reach Clerkenwell’s once-vibrant Little Italy. Though many of the delis and ice-cream parlours have been changed by new waves of immigration and redevelopment, the plaque to Giuseppe Mazzini, a champion of Italian unification, on Laystall Street, reminds passersby of the area’s historic importance to Italianness. Mass is still celebrated in Italian at St Peter’s Church, and near the back of the church is a monument to the dead of the SS Arandora Star. We sit and read the list of surnames as they mingle with the priest’s prayers to form one long lament. I picture the churches of Emilia-Romagna, and the cemeteries where my ancestors are buried, and I see the roads that lead from there to London and back, worn down by constant travelling in both directions, a straddling between nations, where ghosts are as substantial as the living.
My brothers have now exited the cycle of deferred returns by establishing families with Italian women who grew up in Italy itself. One of them has moved to Italy. In his family, Italian is, once again, the language spoken. We’ve all had to play catch-up with Italianness, but I have focused too much on the uncertainty this elicits in me. Instead, I should turn to the strength of the diasporic experience. There is power in duality, in multiplicity, and restlessness. And reassurance, too, in knowing that in London, my home, the invisible figure of my great-grandfather walks ahead of me, an eagle from Emilia-Romagna circling the sky above us.

title: Reclaiming Indigenous Self-governance in Minahasa: Reviving Community Authority in a Modern Nation State
content: Reclaiming Indigenous Self-governance in Minahasa: Reviving Community Authority in a Modern Nation State tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 11:18 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe Long before the concept of modern democracy emerged in ancient Greek political thought, the Minahasan Peoples had already developed their own system of governance rooted in consensus-based deliberation, equality, division of responsibilities, and collective accountability. Unlike societies structured around rigid social stratification, Minahasan society embraced the principle of human equality. Individuals were seen primarily based on the roles and responsibilities they assumed within their communities, rather than social status. Minahasan people earned respect because of the duties they fulfilled, the knowledge they possessed, or the responsibilities entrusted to them, a principle reflected in a Tontémboan proverb: “Si tou peleng masuat, mapute waya. Cawana se pakuru’an, cawana se paruku’an,” which means, “All people are equal; no person is meant to be worshipped, and no person is meant to worship another.” This understanding of equality became one of the fundamental pillars of Minahasan governance. Leadership was understood as a social responsibility entrusted by the people, and important decisions were not made unilaterally. Instead, they emerged through collective deliberation involving the community. Located in Tontemboan Indigenous Territory, "Watu Tumotowa Wangko" (The Great Altar Stone) or also called "Watu Rurumeran Ni Empung" (The Stone Throne of the God) or commonly known as "Watu Pinawetengan" (The Stone Where Division Were Made) contains etchings or engravings that symbolizes a directive or decision. Architecture of Minahasan Governance At the most fundamental level, Minahasan governance was rooted in the taranak, a kinship group or family clan. Within each taranak were three key figures who carried different responsibilities: the pahéndon tu’a, a person recognized for their wisdom and ability to make decisions for the benefit of all members of the clan; the wali’an un taranak, the ritual leader responsible for maintaining the spiritual relationship between members of the taranak, their ancestors, and the natural world; and the si lumulukaz or tétérusan, responsible for the physical security and protection of clan members. From the taranak, several family groups formed a wanua. A wanua was the primary space where the social, political, economic, and spiritual life of the Minahasan Peoples took place. It was the most fundamental unit of community where important decisions concerning collective life were made and implemented. Each wanua had a leadership structure composed of figures who carried specific functions. The tona’as umbanuа served as the primary leader of the community, the wali’an wangko’ led rituals and maintained the spiritual relationship of the wider community, the tétérusan wangko’ was responsible for the security and defense of the community, and the gumigirot carried out functions related to dispute resolution and justice. Beyond the wanua, the walak was based on geographical proximity and relationships between communities, while the pakasa’an was primarily formed through shared language, history, and ritual connections. There were also various tona’as who possessed specialized knowledge and expertise in particular fields, respected for their abilities and the responsibilities they carried for the benefit of the community. Even a young person could become a tona’as if they fulfilled the criteria known in Minahasan philosophy as sigha, enté’, wo wuaya—someone possessing intelligence, conscience, physical capability, and courage. Together, these interconnected structures formed a system of self-governance that emerged from within the community itself, growing from social relationships, collective responsibility, and the community’s own needs. Restoring a waruga (Ancient Minahasan stone sarcophagi) in a housing area. Not only this is the act of honoring our ancestor, it is also an action to show that despite the land has been bought by the housing corporation, it will always belong to the indigenous people. Photo by Rinto Taroreh. Displacement and Survival of Indigenous Governance Minahasan governance was disrupted by colonialism. The Dutch implemented a centralized, hierarchical administrative system to monitor and control territories, frequently appointing the heads of the walak as district heads within the colonial administration—a strategy that allowed the Dutch to expand their influence through figures already recognized and trusted by local communities. As authority became controlled by the colonial government, the position of the wanua as the center of governance and community life gradually weakened, while the walak began to transform into an administrative unit more aligned with colonial interests. The end of Dutch colonial rule did not automatically restore Minahasa’s Indigenous governance system. After Indonesia emerged as a modern nation State, it developed a governance structure based on nationally standardized administrative divisions. These new administrative boundaries did not always correspond with the social, cultural, and ethnic territories that had previously existed. In Minahasa, Indigenous territories that had historically developed through shared histories, languages, and cultural identities were divided across several administrative regions. Although Minahasan governance structures are no longer formally recognized within the State administrative system, traditional Indigenous self-governance has not completely disappeared. In many parts of Minahasa, village leaders are known as Hukum Tua, a position that has a historical connection to Minahasan leadership traditions, as they are directly elected by the village community. When issues arise that affect the entire community, a sidang adat, or Indigenous council meeting, will be convened as a forum for communities to reach decisions through deliberation. An important element of the sidang adat is the role of the taranak as the community’s basic social unit. Each taranak is represented by a pahendon tu’a, who attends as a representative of all members of their clan. During the council, the pahendon tu’a each carry a piece of tawaang, symbolizing that they have received a full mandate from their community to speak, express views, and make decisions on behalf of the taranak they represent. Decisions produced through this process are outcomes of community representation. Indigenous councils are generally led by three, five, seven, or nine Indigenous leaders; the number nine holds profound meaning as it is regarded as a symbol of human completeness. The use of an odd number of leaders also reflects the importance of balance and wisdom in decision-making processes, while ensuring that deliberations can reach agreements accepted by the entire community. Equally important, decisions made by Indigenous councils are binding and must be respected by all community members. Indigenous sanctions may take the form of fines in accordance with the provisions applicable within each community. However, the most severe form of sanction is not a monetary fine, but social exclusion from community life. In societies where social relationships are built on kinship, mutual cooperation, and a sense of belonging, losing acceptance within the community is a far greater consequence than material punishment. Minahasan Elders and representatives during a meeting. Reclaiming Identity, Rebuilding Governance The active involvement of Indigenous youth in shaping regulations is providing the foundation for recognition of their existence, through involvement in historical documentation, Indigenous territory mapping, revitalization of Indigenous institutions, and development of public policies. The Tomohon city government recently invited Indigenous youth to participate in drafting the Regional Regulation on Indigenous Peoples. If enacted, the instrument is expected not only to provide legal certainty for the Tombulu community, but also will ensure that local government development respects Indigenous rights and decision-making systems. This experience shows that reclaiming Indigenous self-governance does not mean just rebuilding past Indigenous governance, rather, creating spaces where Indigenous governance principles, community participation, social legitimacy, deliberation, and respect for Indigenous institutions can coexist alongside modern governmental systems. If successful, Tomohon will offer a model of how Indigenous communities and local governments can build an equal relationship within a democratic nation State. History has taken the Minahasan Peoples through colonialism, centralized governance, and urbanization. This journey has not completely erased how Minahasan society understands leadership, deliberation, and collective responsibility. What needs to be reclaimed are not the exact past institutional structures, but the right of Indigenous communities to participate in determining their futures. Indigenous governance is a living, social practice that ensures that the values that have sustained Minahasan society for centuries will continue to shape the future. Gerard Tiwow is a journalist belonging to the Tombulu’ Tribe of the Minahasa Peoples in Tomohon, Sulawesi Utara, Indonesia, and a former CS Youth Fellow. Top photo: 1920s reenactment (colonized and processed) of 1679 Tombulu Elders meeting with the Dutch East India Company. All photos courtesy of Gerard Tiwow. Main Image

title: Indigenous Peoples Are Canada’s Political and Economic Future
content: Indigenous Peoples Are Canada’s Political and Economic Future tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 14:08 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe Indigenous Peoples in Canada, through diverse ways of organizing—whether traditional and hereditary Chiefs, Chiefs and Councils, or collectives and organizations—have a clear direction at the core of their existence: the protection and continuous relations with Mother Earth and all beings on the land for generations to come. “For us, knowing the land, knowing the plants and animals, knowing the health of the territory, conducting collective decision-making about how something is going to be impacted by the decisions that you are making—this is why our Peoples have been doing it for thousands of years,” says land defender Molly Wickham (Wet’suwet’en). Sleydo’ (Molly Wickman) at a campfire at Gidimt’en camp, British Columbia, Canada. Photo by Brandi Morin. A significant part of Indigenous identity stems from the fact that Indigenous Peoples live in relationship to the land. We are the Nations of the world that did not lose our earth-based spirituality, cosmovisions, and ways of life dependent on the land. Even when Indigenous communities were colonized by a religious order, we kept some of our traditional practices in parallel to those religions. Most First Nations continue to obtain their food from the land through hunting, fishing, and foraging. “It is our responsibility to take care of the land, and the land will take care of us,” explains Freda Huson (Wet’suwet’en), also a land defender. “Annually, we use the harvest as part of our governance; we give it away in our feasts. We hunt moose and deer, and we preserve them. We depend on the land for a food source. That is why we fight so hard to keep it intact—so that we can continue to teach the next generation how to live off the land.” This sense of responsibility is why Indigenous Peoples in Canada continue to oppose and resist major developments in their territories. They know how such projects will negatively impact the land, the animals, their own communities, and the entire ecosystem. In the last decade, Canada has seen ongoing resistance from Indigenous communities to large-scale resource extraction. The Wet’suwet’en Peoples’ resistance against a pipeline in northern British Columbia in 2018 and against sand extraction at Camp Morningstar near Winnipeg Lake in 2021 are only two examples. This resistance is usually met with repression and violence, rather than dialogue and protocols to address Indigenous inherent rights issues. Grand Chief Steward Phillip, Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs. Grand Chief Steward Phillip (Syilx Nation) of the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs describes some of the violence. “The Canadian government used the [Royal Canadian Mounted Police]. It was a paramilitary enforcement regime. It was impossible to differentiate the RCMP from the military because they used assault weapons, drones, and helicopters. People were arrested, injured, and there are still court cases about that abuse of power. That is the dynamic of colonialism and neocolonialism. It continues to be the same for many Indigenous Peoples around the world, where there is more brutality than before when Indigenous Peoples oppose hydroelectric dams, mining, and other extractive industries. This dynamic has not changed for hundreds of years,” he says. There is also the misuse of the justice system to criminalize Indigenous defenders. Amnesty International declared Chief Dsta’hyl, a Wet’suwet’en leader and defender, a prisoner of conscience in 2024 after he was sentenced to 60 days of house arrest for resisting the Coastal GasLink pipeline on his territory. This is the first time Amnesty International has given this designation in Canada, indicating that the right to Free, Prior and Informed Consent was not upheld by British Columbia or Canada. The Assembly of First Nations, a national organization representing 634 Chiefs and their communities across Canada, is currently opposing Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Liberal government’s plans to fast-forward the approvals of major development projects affecting the environment and Canada’s Indigenous Peoples without proper consultation. The right to Free, Prior and Informed Consent is enshrined in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, an international set of standards that Canada accepted and ratified in 2021. In addition to the Declaration, Section 35 of the Canadian Constitution affirms Aboriginal and Treaty rights for Indigenous Peoples, indicating that Canada has a legal obligation to respect First Nations, Inuit, and Métis land rights, self-determination, and self-governance. First Nations, Métis, and Inuit Peoples are the original occupants of what is now known as Canada. From the moment of colonial contact in the 1500s, the British and French governments entered into treaties as sovereign Nations and recognized Tribes as self-determined Nations. The British and the French who came to these territories saw Indigenous Peoples as enemies who could kill them or prevent them from settling in these lands peacefully. The Crown, through its representatives, and Indigenous Peoples, through their traditional leaders, sat together to negotiate and sign treaties. Many First Nations in Canada did not sign treaties, and therefore have not surrendered rights to their land and self-determination. These lands are known as unceded territories. In our current moment of history, Canadians need to see that at the point of contact with the Indigenous world, the colonizers treated Indigenous Peoples and Nations as equals. They knew that the so-called democracies that they proclaimed would not be fulfilled unless Indigenous Peoples were part of the decision-making powers. Today, Canada doesn’t regard Indigenous Peoples and their governments as equals. “The Canadian government wants Indigenous Peoples to be a delegation of their power, like a municipality,” Grand Chief Phillip says. “And [that] doesn’t come close to the sovereign political rights they deserve as the First Peoples of Canada.” Among the most important rights that Indigenous Peoples in Canada are asserting is the right to self-determination and self-government, as written in Articles 3 and 4 of the Declaration. Article 3 refers to the right of a People to determine their political status and to be the decision-makers in their economic, social, and cultural development. The right to self-government (Article 4) refers to First Nations having their own governance structures, in accordance with their cultures and traditions. “Self-government is based on Indigenous history, traditional laws, and cultural values in taking care of the land and people. There are groups that are incredibly powerful in terms of their culture, language, traditions, and governance. They are directed by Elders, knowledge keepers, and people who actually depend on the land for sustenance and as part of their cultural heritage. They have their own decision-making mechanisms, and everything is done according to Indigenous law and ceremony,” Grand Chief Phillip explains. In Canada, most of the current Indigenous governance systems were imposed by the Indian Act, commonly known as the Chief and Council system, which follows Canadian government rules. However, there are also hereditary and traditional governance systems that survived colonization. These systems do not involve monetary compensation, as they are based on service and follow the cultural laws of those Peoples. Traditional leadership is an expected and recognized role in the community. While traditional and hereditary governance systems exist in many Indigenous communities, they are not recognized by the Canadian government when federal and provincial economic and political interests have priority. Recent legislation, such as Federal Bill C5, Ontario Bill 5, and British Columbia Bill 14, which allow the federal and provincial levels of government to expedite large development projects, will bring another wave of large-scale resource extraction across the country without proper consultation, consent, or adequate participation from Indigenous Peoples. One option is to continue labeling Indigenous Peoples who resist these projects in defense of the land as being against the country’s prosperity; to continue violently persecuting them while also creating an image of an anti-democratic government that misuses power and loses significant money in the process. A better option is to act in historical justice and involve Indigenous Peoples and their governments, including traditional forms of governance, as equal partners at the federal and provincial levels in decision-making about the future of Canada. Such a change will benefit all Canadians by bringing leadership to the table that aims to balance prosperity with the sustainability of natural resources for generations to come. Avexnim Coiti Ren (Maya K’iche’) is Cultural Survival Director of Programs. Top photo: Members of Camp Morning Star, Winnipeg Lake, Manitoba, Canada. Main Image

title: Indigenous 'turtle women' help save endangered freshwater turtles in the Amazon
content:
On the banks of the Aguarico River in the Ecuadorian Amazon, a group of Indigenous Siekopai women are combining traditional knowledge and modern technology to help a threatened native turtle recover.
Their efforts center around charapa turtles (Podocnemis unifilis), also known as the yellow-spotted Amazon River turtle, Mongabay Latam’s Astrid Arellano reported. The animal’s populations have declined due to hunting adult turtles, harvesting eggs from nests, and pollution from garbage, oil, and gasoline.
“Sometimes we see plastic, garbage bags,” Janeth Piaguaje, a Siekopai community leader of the project, told Mongabay Latam. “We also see dead animals floating down the river. We can’t control all of that, but we do make a significant effort to clean the beaches where we work.”
Boat traffic is also eroding riverbanks, and climate change has caused water levels to rise, flooding the flats where turtles make their nests. Charapa turtles are listed as vulnerable by the IUCN, the global conservation authority.
To help the turtles recover, a group of seven Siekopai women, who call themselves Tari Nomiowa’i, or “turtle women,” patrol the riverbanks looking for turtle tracks and nests. When they find nests, the women carefully collect the eggs, a skill Piaguaje said she learned from her father.
“He taught me how to handle the eggs, how to see on what dates and in what months the turtles lay their nests,” she said.
The women document the date, time, location, and number of eggs in each nest using the Epicollect5 app, a field data collection tool.
Then they take the eggs to an incubation facility where they are protected from predators, flooding, and pollution. Once the eggs hatch, the women continue to care for the baby turtles for another month, feeding them cassava, sweet potato, and taro leaves.
Their painstaking work has paid off.
Over the 2025-26 nesting season, the women collected 235 eggs and successfully hatched and released 208 hatchlings into the Aguarico River over March and April this year. The group invited the local community, including schoolchildren, to participate in the turtle release and attend workshops.
“A little girl said, ‘I’m going to take care of them, I’m going to tell them not to touch the eggs,’” Piaguaje recalled.
A driving force behind the work of the Tari Nomiowa’i is their culture and the ancestral belief that the turtles are a link between the visible and spiritual worlds, each swimming with protection from Koouwajëo, the spiritual chief, mother, and ancestral guardian of the turtles.
“I want Koouwajëo to be proud,” said Piaguaje. “When we protect turtles, we don’t just care for a species; we honor the spirits of the river, strengthen our culture, and maintain the sacred pact between our community and nature.”
Read the full story by Astrid Arellano in Spanish here. This article was originally published on Mongabay.
Featured Image: Amalavida.tv/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)
