content: Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 12:42 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe Halito akana (Hello friends), Indigenous governance models, practiced for millennia and rooted in our cosmovisions, traditions, laws, and cultural values, are systems of cultural sovereignty through which our Peoples enact self-determination and ensure balanced relationships within communities and with our more-than-human-relatives in the lands and waters we call home. Our traditional models of governance often center collective decision-making, community responsibility, and respect for ancestral knowledge, which is intertwined with the natural laws of Mother Earth. By maintaining self-governance, Indigenous communities protect their cultural identity, strengthen local leadership, and address social, economic, and environmental issues in ways that reflect their Peoples’ values, needs, and perspectives. International bodies like the United Nations recognize the effectiveness and global importance of Indigenous governance in managing land, water, and biodiversity, improving well being, and addressing inequities, and the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples affirms rights to self-determination and self-government. In this issue of the CSQ, we share examples of cultural sovereignty in practice from the regions where we work. Some lessons that arise include: Indigenous governance systems have endured for centuries, surviving colonialism, State pressures, and modern challenges. They are living systems rooted in ancestral knowledge and adaptable to community needs. Leadership is based on service to the community, not personal power. Authority is earned through demonstrated responsibility, wisdom, and integrity. Decision-making is collective. Governance is inseparable from stewardship of land, water, plants, and animals. The land and all beings, flows, and entities are seen as living relatives with whom we have reciprocal relationships and responsibilities to protect. They are not treated merely as resources. Political, spiritual, and cultural life are intertwined. Elders and knowledge keepers guide decisions and maintain traditions. Women and youth are recognized as vital to governance, carrying knowledge of food systems, environmental stewardship, cultural continuity, and more. Indigenous governance systems face ongoing threats from State policies, extractive industries, and legal frameworks that often undermine autonomy. Recognition of Indigenous governance by States is often partial or conditional, leading to tensions and manufactured dependency. Despite these pressures, communities continue to assert their rights, resist dispossession, and adapt their governance to new realities. Indigenous governance is not static, but incorporates new tools, technologies, and organizational forms to address modern challenges such as climate change and legal advocacy. The most important message is perhaps one that Irma Velásquez Nimatuj (Maya K’iche’) points out: “The challenge, according to those consulted in the regions where Cultural Survival operates, is not proving that Indigenous self-governance works, but rather getting nation States to stop sabotaging it.” Our systems have governed our Peoples from the beginning. Our greatest challenges are the outside threats that hinder our self-determination. As a supporter of Cultural Survival, you contribute to the efforts of Indigenous Peoples who are safeguarding knowledge systems, languages, and lifeways for future generations. Please give generously at www.cs.org/donate. Hóchi yakoke li hoke (I thank you all so much), Aimee Roberson (Choctaw and Chickasaw), Executive Director Main Image

title: More than a Leader, More than a Town: How Indigenous Self-governance Continues to Shape the Identity of the Rehoboth Baster Community
content: More than a Leader, More than a Town: How Indigenous Self-governance Continues to Shape the Identity of the Rehoboth Baster Community tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 14:10 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe People who know where they come from will always know where they are going.” Those are words I often heard while growing up in Rehoboth. Whether it was around the family dinner table, during church gatherings, or listening to our grandparents’ stories under an old camelthorn tree, one lesson remained constant: our community exists today because our ancestors chose to govern themselves according to their own values. Rehoboth is located about 90 kilometers south of Windhoek, Namibia’s capital. For those who call it home, it tells the story of a Peoples who traveled hundreds of kilometers in search of freedom, built a community from the ground up, and created a system of governance that reflected their beliefs, traditions, and shared responsibilities, long before modern Namibia came into existence. Conversations about Indigenous self-governance are becoming increasingly important worldwide. Indigenous communities are reclaiming their voices and demonstrating that traditional governance systems are not outdated institutions, but living structures capable of addressing modern challenges while protecting cultural identity. The Rehoboth Basters are no exception. Our history illustrates how Indigenous governance has allowed a small community to safeguard its identity, maintain social order, and remain connected to its heritage despite colonial rule, political change, and globalization. To understand Indigenous self-governance of the Rehoboth Baster community, one must first understand the people. We trace our origins to the Cape Colony of present-day South Africa during the 18th and 19th centuries. Descended primarily from European settlers and Indigenous Khoikhoi women, we gradually developed a unique cultural identity distinguished by our language, Christian faith, customs, and strong sense of community. During the 19th century, increasing political uncertainty, discrimination, and land disputes in the Cape motivated many Baster families to migrate northwards in search of a place where they could determine their own futures. Their journey eventually brought them to central Namibia. In 1870, under the leadership of Kaptein Hermanus van Wyk, the Basters settled in what is today Rehoboth after concluding a Peace and Friendship Treaty with neighboring Nama communities. This agreement was among the earliest examples of diplomacy between Indigenous communities in southern Africa and demonstrated the Basters’ commitment to peaceful coexistence. Settling on the land was only the beginning. The community understood that survival required more than fertile grazing land. It required rules, accountability, leadership, and unity. Only two years after settling in Rehoboth, the Basters formally adopted what became known as the Vaderlike Wette (Paternal Laws) in 1872. For outsiders, these laws are simply an old historical document. For Basters, they represent something much greater. The Vaderlike Wette became the constitutional foundation upon which the community governed itself. They outlined responsibilities regarding land ownership, justice, public administration, leadership, and community conduct. Most importantly, they reflected the values that the Basters believed were essential for maintaining peace and unity. Unlike imposed colonial legal systems, these laws were created by the people, for the people. This is precisely what Indigenous self-governance means. Rather than relying solely on external political systems, Indigenous communities govern according to their own customs, traditions, knowledge systems, and cultural values. Decisions are made with the collective well being of the community in mind, recognizing that leadership exists to serve the people rather than rule over them. This philosophy remains one of the defining characteristics of Rehoboth’s traditional governance. When people hear the title Kaptein, many immediately think of a chief. While there are similarities, the role of the Baster Kaptein carries its own unique history and responsibilities. Kaptein was never spoken about merely as a political figure. Older generations viewed the Kaptein as the custodian of our history, traditions, and identity. The office symbolized unity more than authority. The Kaptein served as the highest traditional leader of the Baster community, representing the people in negotiations, safeguarding communal land, overseeing customary law, promoting peace within the community, and ensuring that the principles of the Vaderlike Wette were respected. Today, although Namibia functions under a democratic constitutional government, the institution of the Kaptein continues to hold profound cultural significance for many Basters. The first, and perhaps most influential, Kaptein was Hermanus van Wyk, whose leadership guided the Basters through migration, settlement, and the establishment of Rehoboth. The Kaptein never governed in isolation, working alongside elected councils and respected community advisers. Decisions were reached through consultation rather than command. This collective leadership style reflects one of the core principles of Indigenous governance: authority is strengthened through participation rather than domination. One lesson many of us learned from our parents and grandparents is that nobody succeeds alone. This philosophy lies at the heart of Indigenous governance. Unlike many modern political systems that emphasize individual rights above all else, Indigenous governance often begins with collective responsibility. Every person’s well being depends upon the well being of the community. This was especially evident in the management of communal farms around Rehoboth. Land was never viewed merely as private property or economic capital. It was regarded as an inheritance entrusted to each generation. Responsible grazing, water conservation, and mutual assistance ensured that future generations would benefit from the same natural resources. Similarly, disputes were resolved through dialogue, mediation, and reconciliation rather than punishment alone. Restoring relationships was considered just as important as enforcing rules. These practices strengthened social cohesion and helped preserve peace within the community. Baster community members in Baster traditional wear and the former late Rehoboth Baster Kaptein John McNab (in tie) with the official photograph of the former late Kaptein Hans Diergaardt. Self-Governance as a Guardian of Culture Perhaps the greatest achievement of Indigenous self-governance is not political independence, but cultural survival. Despite German colonial rule, South African administration, and Namibia’s transition to independence in 1990, the Rehoboth Baster community has maintained a distinct cultural identity. Church traditions remain central to community life. Family gatherings continue to safeguard oral history. The Afrikaans language remains widely spoken. Annual commemorations honor our ancestors. Above all, the stories passed down from generation to generation continue to remind young Basters where they come from. Without self-governance, many of these traditions might have disappeared. Traditional institutions have served as guardians of our identity, ensuring that culture is not forgotten amid social and political change. The Rehoboth Basters face modern challenges. Youth unemployment, migration, economic inequality, climate change, and debates surrounding communal land all require thoughtful leadership. These challenges also demonstrate why Indigenous governance remains relevant. The values of consultation, accountability, environmental stewardship, and community responsibility offer practical lessons for addressing contemporary problems. Our ancestors did not create the Vaderlike Wette simply to govern 19th-century settlers. They created a philosophy of leadership built upon service, unity, and responsibility—principles that remain just as important today as they were more than 150 years ago. Growing up in Rehoboth, I do not see the Kaptein or our traditional governance as relics displayed in history books. I see them every time an Elder reminds young people to respect their community. I see them whenever neighbors help one another during difficult times. I hear them in the stories told around family tables and church gatherings. Indigenous self-governance is not merely about who leads us. It is about remembering who we are. As long as we continue to value our history, honor our traditions, and teach future generations where they come from, the spirit of Rehoboth’s self-governance will continue to live—not only in our institutions, but in the hearts of our people. Marcus Gentz (Rehoboth Baster) is a radio presenter and reporter for the Rehoboth-based radio station Infinity Live 102.3 FM. All photos courtesy of Rehoboth Baster Kaptein’s Office. Top photo: Members of the Rehoboth Baster community at the recently inaugurated “I love Rehoboth” sign. Main Image

title: Luo Yang’s Diaspora Birds Lands in NYC Chinatown
content:
Karen Wong steps into Manhattan’s Chinatown with Luo Yang, meeting the seven women behind her latest Diaspora Birds series
When Luo Yang was in her twenties, she began capturing a new generation of young women, her generation, of lived experience in China. Traveling across the continent, she sought out communities where young people were discovering their voices and individuality. Following the visual diaristic lineage of Nan Goldin and Ryan McGinley, Luo establishes trust and elicits an intimate connection with her subjects; many became friends, whom she documented over two decades in her best-known series, Girls.
In 2012, artist and dissident Ai Weiwei praised Yang as one of the “rising stars of Chinese photography”. He included her in his group exhibition of 37 contemporary Chinese artists, “Fuck Off 2,” presented in 2013 at the Groningen Museum in the Netherlands. As her profile grew in Europe, she was accepted to the Cité internationale des Arts 2022 artistic residency program in Paris. While in the city of lights, she encountered her first Chinatown. She shares, “Chinatown was familiar, but it felt like China from a different era, frozen in time; immigrants from an older generation brought an aesthetic that China has moved on from.” Visiting various European cities, Yang met Asian women who resettled in the West and whose stories of shifting cultural identities spurred her latest ongoing portrait series, Diaspora Birds.
In May this year, Yang was on assignment in New York City and was commissioned to extend her Diaspora Birds project to include a group of New Yorkers born in Asia. While scouting for locations, she chose Manhattan’s Chinatown as the obvious backdrop and shot all seven women in one long day. It’s no coincidence that, having recently turned 40, Yang is capturing the stories of accomplished, creative women in the prime of their lives.
With a sensitive eye and calm demeanour, Yang read the energy of each woman and set them up in a restaurant, barbershop, gift shop, or next to a fruit vendor. She was looking for that elevated moment, where there was a bit more drama, possibility, and imagination. After wrapping up the photoshoot, Yang, besotted with her new friends, whom she described as “so beautiful,” felt more connected than ever to the city of New York.
Presented as an Elephant exclusive:
LUO YANG
Diaspora Birds (Manhattan Chinatown), 2026.
FiFi Zhang is a Shanghai-born, NYC-based electronic producer, vocalist, DJ, and visual artist. Signed songwriter at 88rising, her self-produced debut album, FLEETING HEARTS, earned Best Electronic Album at the 2025 HMA Awards.
“Chinatown feels like a time capsule of my homeland, China, with its traditional Cantonese restaurants, newly opened bubble tea shops, fashion boutiques, and the lingering scent of the fish markets. I love playing table tennis in Chinatown, walking along Allen Street, and ending my day with a great meal at August Gatherings.”
Yuhee Yang is a dancer, choreographer, and movement director originally from Jeju Island, South Korea.
“Chinatown is where I go to ground myself and recharge. The chaotic, vibrant energy of the neighbourhood always makes me feel inspired and connected to New York.”
Shien Lee was born in Taiwan and currently resides in Brooklyn. She is the founder of the Red Pavilion in Bushwick, a beacon of AAPI culture and resilience.
“I surround myself with incredible Asian female artists through my club, and I was actually brought on to the project through another Chinese female photographer that shot our opening party – so being chosen by Luo Yang to work on this project felt especially special.”
Ruoyi Jiang is the founder of NYC Chinatown boutique Chop Suey Club. Born in Beijing, she was a professional golfer and scuba diving instructor before earning her BFA in photography from NYU. She is a leading voice in Mahjong culture and the author of Mahjong For Dummies.
“I was a fan of Luo Yang already, so I was really excited to meet her and be photographed by her! Our store actually carried her photo book, Girls, when it first came out. I love her perspective on Asian femininity, she understands how strength and individuality manifest in Asian women.”
Natasha Jen is an award-winning designer, educator, and partner at Pentagram.
“NYC’s Chinatown is messy, crowded, imperfect, and comforting. It reminds me of Taipei. They share a certain density, directness, and sense of everyday life happening all at once. I go there when I want something specific to eat, but also when I want to feel briefly closer to home.”
Jacky Lee was born in South Korea in 1957, she was relinquished by her Korean mother at age five alongside her younger sister and adopted by a Black military family.
“As a biracial adoptee, being photographed by an Asian woman was really meaningful. I felt embraced.”
Bea was raised in Flushing, Queens. Ever since she was little, she was interested in creating, from drawing to crafting to gardening with her grandparents.
“I worked at a boutique in Chinatown for almost 10 years, and it’s how I met and made most of my best friends today.”

title: When the Land Speaks, the Community Listens: How Indigenous Self-governance Protects Climate Knowledge and Food Systems in Abim, Karamoja, Uganda
content: When the Land Speaks, the Community Listens: How Indigenous Self-governance Protects Climate Knowledge and Food Systems in Abim, Karamoja, Uganda tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 14:27 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe For generations, Indigenous communities in Abim District, Karamoja, in northeastern Uganda, have depended on a deep relationship with their land, water, animals, forests, and natural environment. This relationship has guided how communities make decisions, resolve challenges, protect resources, and prepare for uncertain times. Long before climate change became a global concern, communities had their own ways of understanding environmental changes. Cattle and goats became unusually restless or vocal, signaling upcoming heavy winds or rainfall. Elders observed birds’ behavior and the flowering of trees. They used the alignment and brightness of specific stars and the moon to gauge seasonal timing and predict long dry cycles. Haruspicy (reading goat intestines) was used to forecast weather patterns, seasonal rainfall quality, and impending environmental or social shocks. These observations helped communities decide when to plant crops, how to prepare for drought, and how to protect needed resources. This knowledge was not written but was carried through stories, community gatherings, cultural practices, family teachings, and intergenerational relationships. In Abim, governance has never been only about leaders and decision-making structures but foremost about responsibility to the community, the land, and future generations. Today, this relationship faces increasing pressure. Climate change has brought longer drought periods and unpredictable rainfall, leading to declining pastures and crop failures and increasing challenges to food security, famine, and death. Many Indigenous practices and knowledge systems are at risk of disappearing as younger generations have fewer opportunities to learn from Elders. Indigenous self-governance in Abim is built on collective responsibility. Important decisions affecting land, natural resources, community well being, and social relationships have traditionally been discussed through community consultation involving Elders, women, clan representatives, and other members. Leadership is understood not simply as authority over others, but as a responsibility to serve and protect community interests. Elders play an important role as custodians of history, cultural values, and environmental knowledge, carrying memories of droughts, food shortages, traditional farming practices, and emergency management. When disagreements arise, Indigenous approaches focus on dialogue, mediation, and restoring relationships. The purpose is not only to determine who is right or wrong, but to rebuild trust because community survival depends on cooperation. A reflection shared during community knowledge discussions highlights this understanding: “Our Elders taught us that the land is not something we own alone. We are only caretakers for those who will come after us. When we sit together and listen to each other, we find solutions that protect both people and nature. The knowledge of our ancestors helped our communities survive difficult seasons. Protecting this knowledge means protecting who we are.” Women as Keepers of Knowledge In Abim, women have always played a central role in sustaining communities, carrying essential knowledge of seeds, traditional crops, food preservation, medicinal plants, and wild foods that provide nutrition during difficult periods and support family and community survival. As custodians of this knowledge, women have relied on passed-down teachings about which foods can support families and which Indigenous crops can withstand harsh environmental conditions. Traditional crops such as millet, sorghum, and other Indigenous varieties have provided resilience because they are adapted to local conditions and have survived through generations of careful selection. These knowledge systems face increasing challenges. Changing lifestyles, climate pressures, and reduced opportunities for intergenerational learning are contributing to the loss of Indigenous practices. Strengthening women’s participation in community decision-making helps ensure that climate adaptation strategies include the experiences of those who have long protected household food systems. A reflection from women leaders during community dialogues expressed this connection: “Women have always carried important knowledge in our homes and communities. We know the seeds that survive, the foods that help families during difficult times, and the ways our mothers protected the environment. When women participate in decisions about land and resources, the whole community benefits because our experiences are included.” Restoring the Relationship with Nature One of the greatest strengths of Indigenous communities is the ability to understand environmental changes through generations of observation. Elders have traditionally used signs from nature as early warning systems. Changes in plants, animals, insects, and weather patterns provided important information about potential droughts, changes in rainfall, or challenges affecting crops and livestock. The flowering of certain trees, changes in bird behavior, the appearance of insects, and the availability of specific wild foods were carefully observed and discussed within communities. This knowledge, based on experience, careful observation, and adaptation, represents generations of relationships with the environment. As climate change grows more unpredictable and Elders become fewer in number, there is a growing need to document and strengthen these knowledge systems. Food security in Abim has always depended on Indigenous Knowledge of crops that can withstand challenging environmental conditions. For generations, communities have preserved crop varieties that withstand drought, require fewer external inputs, and provide important food sources during difficult seasons. Many Indigenous seeds are becoming less common due to changing agricultural practices and reduced transmission of Traditional Knowledge. Community efforts to preserve Indigenous seeds are helping restore local food systems. Women, Elders, and young people are working together to document traditional crops, share planting knowledge, and encourage the continued use of climate-resilient varieties. Protecting Indigenous seeds is more than protecting agriculture. It is protecting identity, independence, and the ability of future generations to sustain themselves. Indigenous Governance as a Pathway Forward Indigenous governance also guides how communities relate to natural resources. Land is not viewed only as an economic resource. It is connected to culture, history, spirituality, and community identity. Community members have recognized their responsibilities to protect important trees, water sources, grazing areas, and culturally significant places. Through collective action, communities are strengthening environmental protection practices, including restoring degraded areas, protecting water sources, and responsibly managing communal resources. These actions are based on the understanding that humans are part of nature and have responsibilities to maintain ecological balance. The survival of Indigenous governance depends on whether knowledge can continue moving from one generation to another. Young people in Abim are becoming increasingly involved in learning from Elders, participating in environmental activities, and understanding their responsibilities as community members. Intergenerational learning creates a connection between the wisdom of Elders and the energy and creativity of young people. Youth who understand the importance of Indigenous knowledge can become future custodians of culture, land, and community resilience. Indigenous self-governance remains highly relevant in today’s world. As communities globally face climate change, environmental degradation, and social challenges, Indigenous governance systems offer important lessons. Communities create stronger solutions when they participate in decisions affecting their lives. Environmental protection becomes stronger when people maintain relationships with the land. Women’s knowledge and leadership are essential for resilience. Elders carry valuable knowledge that complements modern approaches. Culture and identity are sources of strength during times of uncertainty. In Abim, Indigenous self-governance continues to guide communities in understanding their environment, protecting resources, strengthening food systems, and preparing for the future. The knowledge held by Elders, women, and community leaders is not simply cultural heritage, but a living resource that contributes to climate resilience, food security, and community well being. As the world searches for solutions to environmental challenges, Indigenous communities remind us of the importance of listening to the land, Elders, and communities that have cared for their environments for generations. Oscar Ogole (Karamojong) is Executive Director of Community Development Shield Uganda. Main photo: Bridging generations in Karamoja. Community members in Abim gather to discuss traditional weather forecasting methods and the preservation of climate-resilient Indigenous seeds. Photo by Community Development Shield Uganda. title: Indigenous Futurism: Kichwa Art as Memory in Motion
content: Indigenous Futurism: Kichwa Art as Memory in Motion tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 16:12 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe For as long as I can remember, art and story-telling have surrounded every corner of my life. Embraced through every detail, showing up in music, songs, textiles, food, and celebration, for me, art, culture, and identity are inseparable. They are roots that expand from my body to my homelands, grounding me to my community no matter what territory I find myself in, always strong, always present. The love I have for my culture and for the people I come from has always been the reason to channel that collective memory, that collective love of our community. I come from a culture where people carry art into all aspects of their lives. I am the daughter and granddaughter of artisans, musicians, textile weavers, and mindalaes, who are artists, merchants, musicians, dancers, and cultural carriers. They have built systems of commerce across territories, creating paths that allowed Kichwa Otavalo communities to sustain themselves economically around the world. I was never formally taught how to draw or paint. Our art is intergenerational, influenced and guided by the love of all those who came before us. Today, I call myself an artist through digital illustration, photo embroidery, murals, and wearable art. Wherever I go, I am proudly Kichwa Otavalo, carrying the Imbabura mountain in my body and the love, knowledge, and memory of my grandparents and ancestors; a whole universe of generations compacted in my heart. “water yourself” (2024). Wherever Kichwa Otavalo people migrate out of necessity, we carry our culture with us. There is no way to separate our bodies from our territory. It is so deeply embedded in our memory that it traverses colonial borders and generations. Our art has always been a way to sustain ourselves, creating those spaces while being away from home. At the root, it has been the beating heart of the Kichwa Otavalo Peoples. Drawing and illustration entered my life during college. What began as something fun and grounding became a way of processing identity, memory, and belonging. As I continued creating, I noticed I was constantly drawing variations of the same image: myself wearing my traditional clothing, the anaco. Over time, I realized that every drawing held something deeper than a woman in traditional clothing. When I wear my anaco, I feel the most elegant and the most beautiful. Those drawings transported me back to being a little girl, my mom helping me get dressed, placing each piece, teaching me how to wear it. My mother, my first teacher, the first storyteller I met, the first artist I knew. Through drawing, I was bringing those memories, those relationships, those raw feelings, pieces of home, into every space I occupied. It took me years to confidently call myself an artist, despite coming from a culture that lives and breathes art. Yet the more I created, the more intention it carried, and I began to find language to describe why creating Kichwa art in the present matters. For me, art has always been political and never separate from resistance. Every illustration, every mural, every piece of wearable art is a way to assert our presence. That same force moved me to create work in response to the violence my community was facing—artwork that took direct action and broke into the news cycle, making the message land. That is what brought me to Kichwa Futurism. “Pawkar Szn” (2025). Indigenous Futurism as a term has always resonated with me, but Kichwa Futurism is how I name it from where I stand, explicitly centering my people, our territory, and the Global South in a conversation that often looks only northward. It is the belief that Kichwa people belong in the future just as much as we belong in the past and present. Too often, Indigenous people are imagined only through books, museums, or tokenized narratives. Yet our communities are living and continuously creating new ways of expressing our existence in the world. Kichwa Futurism is alive across every creative form our people are working in, bringing our identity into spaces where Indigenous music, visual art, film, photography, and fashion haven’t always been centered. I am equally inspired by Kichwa artists and creatives in the diaspora, those of us creating from distance, holding our culture with the love that comes from knowing what it means to be far. Indigenous Futurism creates space to imagine ourselves beyond settler colonialism, asking what is possible when Indigenous people can visualize and manifest our own futures. Our art and our futures are an extension of our bodies, universes, galaxies, the manifestation of the dreams of all our relatives. Every time I create, I am pushing back against the idea that we can only be seen through a settler colonial gaze. Art has allowed me to contribute to representation that goes beyond visibility. It has become a way to reclaim narratives and ensure that our voices actually take up space. When people from my community see themselves in my work, I am always reminded of how powerful that is, not only for newer generations, but for little me, who never saw herself reflected anywhere. Sharing my work online opened something I didn’t expect. It brought me to other Kichwa youth in the diaspora, people who saw my work and recognized themselves in it, and from those connections grew some of my deepest friendships. Creating art has allowed me to contribute a part of myself to the collective history of our community, a way to show up as a Kichwa Otavalo warmi (woman) from the diaspora, raw and unromanticized, outside of any tokenized frame. “Ñuka Adina” (2021). Within Ecuador, Indigenous identities are constantly co-opted by nationalist narratives, the idea that our culture belongs to everyone, that it is simply part of being Ecuadorian. Yet, Indigenous communities continue to face discrimination, exclusion, and racism, celebrating Indigenous aesthetics while actively erasing Indigenous people. Every year when I go back home for Inti Raymi, I see it firsthand: Ecuadorians and tourists wearing our clothing, playing dress-up in the name of celebration, as if our identity were a costume available to anyone who wants to try it on. But this is not only a phenomenon of Inti Raymi. Brands use the Kichwa language for business names, our symbols for marketing, our people as props, and call it appreciation. Politicians wear our clothing to get votes. Folklore dance groups perform our dances outside any cultural context. Even in the diaspora, the appropriation of our identity continues, people claiming identity without community attachment, while the extraction of our culture and bodies goes unnamed. I see this most visibly in the anaco. For Kichwa women, our traditional clothing is not simply an outfit or a symbol of Ecuadorian heritage. It is a political act of resistance. Every time someone treats it as a costume, they are not just borrowing an aesthetic. They are participating in the erasure of what it actually means to wear it, to carry it, and everything it took to still be able to wear it till this day. This is why it is so important for Indigenous people to create from our own eyes and experience. To tell our own stories from memory, responsibility, and lived experience that cannot be replicated from the outside. To move away from stereotypes and create space for how we want to be seen. “Ñuka" (2021). For me, art is both self-expression and responsibility. It is a way of honoring the people who came before me and honoring the futures that will come after me. Every work I create becomes part of the collective memory of who we are. It is my little seed for the future generation of Kichwa youth, artists, and creatives. Kichwa art lives in our bodies, and we carry our homelands wherever we go. The most radical act of love we can do is to speak from our experiences into every space we walk into. Adina Farinango is an Indigenous Kichwa Otavalo artist and designer based between Lenapehoking/New York City and Ecuador. Learn more about her work at adinafarinango.com and follow her Instagram account @adinasdoodles. Top image: “Sapi” (2021). All art by Adina Farinango. Main Image

title: Heal the Land, Heal Our People: Still Fighting to Free the Klamath River
content: Heal the Land, Heal Our People: Still Fighting to Free the Klamath River tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 17:06 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe Many believe the Klamath River is free, but it’s not—not yet. Four of the six dams on the Klamath River were removed in 2023-2024, prompting major media outlets, prominent environmental organizations, and even other Indigenous people to proclaim that the river is free. The fight is not over—we still need to remove the Keno and Link Dams and heal our watershed. The misinformation about our sacred ambo (water in Klamath/Modoc) has made many Klamath Tribal members feel like we are experiencing termination all over again. The Termination Era was a period where the U.S. government targeted Tribal Nations whose land they wanted to steal, like the Klamath Tribes, with lands rich in natural resources. They “terminated” our status as a federally recognized sovereign Indigenous Nation in 1954. Our home was once a massive watershed filled with lakes, rivers, wetlands, and marshes, historically known as ancient Lake Modoc. A biodiverse ecosystem, once the third-largest salmon run on the Pacific coast. The Klamath River starts in our homelands and ends in the Pacific Ocean, in Yurok territory. The Klamath watershed historically connected many Tribal Nations: the Klamath, Modoc, Pit River, Karuk, Hupa, Yurok, and other Tribes. Photo taken July 2026. The start of the Klamath River flows out of the Upper Klamath Lake. The Link Dam is shown below, and in the photo, the remains of two natural reefs that were nearly destroyed during its construction. The rocky area before the dam and the green area near the dam. The Klamath Tribes are three Tribes—Klamath, Modoc, and Yahooskin Paiute—all forced onto a single reservation. We are the maqlaq and neme, located at the heart and lung of the Klamath watershed. We ceded over 22 million acres of land to the U.S. government via the Treaty of 1864 in exchange for a 2-million-acre reservation and reserved treaty rights to hunt, fish, gather, and trap, including water rights. We are the only Tribal Nation along the Klamath River with a ratified treaty, and hold the most senior water rights. We did what we could to survive colonization and sold timber to support our people. Our sales made us one of the wealthiest Tribes in the U.S., which gave us the financial ability to advocate. We stewarded our land with fire until the government outlawed its use in 1911. We were an impediment to the government, which wanted to log our forests, steal water for irrigation to farm cattle, mass produce non-native agriculture, construct railroad lines, and create hydroelectric energy with dams. Sadly, all was accomplished throughout the 1860s,1870s, and continues. In 1905, the Klamath Project was authorized under the 1902 Reclamation Act, allowing irrigation development for 200,000 acres in the Klamath Basin. Construction of the first of six dams began in 1909, marking the beginning of our severance from our c’iyaals (salmon). The government wanted full control over our home, so they broke our treaty. In 1954, the U.S. ceased to recognize us as a sovereign Indigenous Nation. Our delegates traveled to the termination hearings in Washington, D.C., to tell Congress we would never give up our rights, but it did not matter. We were terminated, and so were our c’iyaals— a near genocide of our culture. Aerial drone image post 2021 Bootleg Fire. The areas not burned were stewarded with fire by the Klamath Tribes. After termination, we could no longer hunt, fish, gather, or steward our lands until we successfully advocated to restore our treaty rights in 1974, which helped lead to recognition as a sovereign Nation again in 1986. Our recognition was restored, but with no land. We are salmon Peoples who have been without our c’iyaals for over 100 years; the only Tribe along the Klamath River that was, and remains blocked from our salmon relatives. Colonization and termination had catastrophic impacts on the Klamath River. We are the namesake, being located at the headwaters. What happens in our headwaters impacts all downstream. Today, toxic water continues to flow from our headwaters. Our sacred watershed is sick, crying for help, and our aquatic relatives are on the brink of extinction. When we hear others say the Klamath River is free, it feels like colonial erasure, the termination of our Peoples and animal relatives all over again. We are still healing from termination. The government was almost successful in their genocide, but, like our c’iyaals, we are finding our way back home. After the removal of four dams, c’iyaals were spotted in our upper watershed in October 2025. We do not know how they made it over the remaining two dams, as the fish ladders are not designed for salmon. Miraculously, our c’iyaals are coming home, but return to deadly, toxic waters. Lighting a prescribed fire in a culture and fire workshop. Using Fire to Restore Our Sacred Watershed Indigenous Peoples’ use of loloqs (fire) has shaped landscapes and cleaned water for thousands of years. Our homeland is a volcanic plateau, a fire-dependent ecosystem that provides pristine water to the Klamath watershed and is interconnected throughout the upper and lower basins. Fire acts as a natural selection process, creating resilience and resistance to future disturbance by favoring fire-dependent and adapted species, while reducing accumulated fuels, disease, and invasive species. It renews soils, stimulates the growth of culturally important plants, enhances wildlife habitat, reduces hazardous fuels, and increases an ecosystem’s resistance to severe wildfire, pests, and climate stress. Fire is the solution to fighting mega fires, but also the medicine to heal our watershed and people. Without intentional burns on our landscape, we get massive wildfires. In 2021, Oregon’s Bootleg Fire obliterated over 400,000 acres. It ravaged through the canopy and when it reached the areas treated by the Klamath Tribes, it dropped to the understory and walked across the forest floor. Drone footage captured the effectiveness of our stewarding. We co-steward with the U.S. Forest Service since 1999, but have limited capacity to fully steward all of our homelands. The portions we managed were the proof needed to change the national perspective on fire in the U.S. What happened in our homeland during the Bootleg was what we have known about fire since time immemorial. Post Bootleg Fire meadow portion of the burn, 2021. Our lands would burn on average, every 10-13 years, anywhere from 300,000–500,000 acres at a time; smaller fires would burn more frequently. Our ancestors spread fire for many reasons; managing the watershed was one of them. Over the past decade, fire suppression has created a fuel load of dense, down woody fuels and layers of duff. To relieve an overloaded fire suppressed forest from mega fires, cattle are being introduced to steward the land and reduce fuels, replacing Indigenous Traditional Ecological Knowledge in the system and destroying the once-pristine waterways. Fire is essential for our culture, spiritual practice, land, water, and has been the primary tool for thousands of years. The government severed our ability to steward the land with fire and created pollution with cattle, pesticides, plastics, and dams, sickening our homelands. The majority of our watershed is toxic. Upper Klamath Lake is choking with algae blooms. Because the connection between Lower Klamath Lake and the Lost River has been fragmented, dammed, and poisoned, our sacred fish are unable to reproduce or reach their original spawning grounds. Traditionally, we would cremate our loved ones and place them back into the water, something we can no longer do with the fracturing of our watershed. Post Bootleg thicket burn 2021, photo taken Spring 2022. Our creation story is tied to our sacred c’waam (lost river sucker) and koptu (short-nose sucker), who are found nowhere else in the world except in our ambo. We are spiritually tied to these fish, and if they suffer, we do. In our stories, animals came first, and then later our Peoples. The most powerful bird that worked alongside Creator is Ka-ak (Old Raven), the supreme ally to Creator, who watches over the people and has oracular powers. Ka-ak is guiding us back to our old ways. As our Elders have told us, we must build it as it was before. This is why, as Co-executive Directors of tonip ka-ak (5 Raven) Alliance, we are working together to advocate for the change needed to heal our lands. We have the solutions to healing the Klamath watershed; remove the dams and use fire to heal our watershed and Peoples. Juliette A. Jackson and Anna Merritt are enrolled members of the Klamath Tribes and Co-directors and Co-founders of tonip ka-ak (5 Raven) Alliance, a Native women-led nonprofit in Chiloquin, Oregon, whose core mission is to “heal the land, heal the people.” Top photo: Culture and fire workshop on the Sprague River, Oregon. All photos courtesy of Tonip Ka-ak (5 Raven) Alliance. Main Image

title: Lalbaugcha Raja: How a broken market and a vow created Mumbai’s iconic Ganpati
content:
Mumbai’s most famous Ganpati did not begin with a grand pandal or celebrity crowds. Its story began with a market that had shut down, families worried about their livelihood and a promise made to Lord Ganesha. In 1934, that promise took the form of an idol. More than nine decades later, Lalbaugcha Raja remains one of Mumbai’s most powerful symbols of faith and community.
When a market disappeared, so did livelihoods
In 1932, a market near Peru Chawl in Lalbaug was shut down. The closure affected vendors, traders and fishermen, including members of the local Koli community who depended on the area for their livelihood.
The community wanted a permanent marketplace. They prayed for a place where they could continue their trade. Their wish was eventually fulfilled when land was made available for a permanent market, which became the present Lalbaug Market.
A vow became Lalbaugcha Raja
The community’s gratitude became a religious promise, or navas. In September 1934, the traders and fishermen installed a public
Ganesha idol dressed in the traditional attire of a fisherman.
The Lalbaugcha Raja Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav Mandal was established in 1934. The idol soon became associated with the idea of a Navsacha Ganpati, or Ganesha believed to fulfil devotees’ wishes.
That origin gives the festival a meaning that goes beyond spectacle. At its heart is a very ordinary human hope: finding work, stability and a place to belong.
The Kambli family gave the Raja his familiar face
The idol’s distinctive form has another remarkable story. The Kambli family has been making the Lalbaugcha Raja idol since 1935, when Madhusudan Donduji Kambli began the tradition. Three generations of the family have since carried the work forward.
In 2011, Kambli Arts secured intellectual-property protection for the traditional design, after replicas of the famous idol became increasingly common.
So the Raja seen today is not simply a yearly sculpture. It carries a recognisable artistic tradition that has been carefully passed down.
Why millions still stand in line
The scale of Lalbaugcha Raja today is almost difficult to imagine. The idol is widely reported to attract around 1.5 million devotees a day during the festival.
There are separate arrangements for Mukh Darshan and Charan Sparsh or Navsachi darshan. Long queues, sometimes stretching for many hours, have become part of the Lalbaug experience.
The Maharashtra Tourism Department describes
Ganesh Chaturthi as a festival that brings together devotion, culture and community life. Lalbaugcha Raja is perhaps one of Mumbai’s clearest examples of that idea.
92 years completed, 93rd year begins
The mandal is celebrating its 93rd year in 2026, with the festival running from September 14 to September 25.
There is, however, one detail often missed in retellings of the story. The annual celebration was not literally held without interruption. In 2020, the mandal cancelled its traditional festivities during the COVID-19 pandemic and instead focused on awareness activities.
That interruption does not weaken the story. If anything, it makes the history more human. Lalbaugcha Raja began with people asking for a livelihood, survived generations of change and continues to bring strangers together every Ganesh Chaturthi.
Disclaimer: Historical accounts of Lalbaugcha Raja contain traditional narratives alongside documented records. Details such as the navas and its wish-fulfilling reputation reflect community belief and should not be treated as independently verifiable supernatural claims.

title: The Enduring Life of Indigenous Self-governance Systems
content: The Enduring Life of Indigenous Self-governance Systems tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 12:53 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe In Santiago Atitlán, a Tz’utujil town located on the southern shore of Lake Atitlán, Guatemala, there are two mayors. One operates from the municipal building; he assumed office through the political party system and answers to the State’s ordinary laws. The other does not appear on any ballot. He is the Cabecera del Pueblo (Head of the Town)—the community’s highest ancestral Indigenous authority. He is chosen from among the principales (individuals who have served their community for decades), with the participation of the town’s assembly and the cofradía (religious brotherhood) system. The Cabecera del Pueblo is responsible for upholding local norms and leading the municipality’s significant ceremonies. To an unknowing visitor, this second mayor might go unnoticed. But to the community, he represents an institution that has survived three centuries of colonialism and the 200-year-old republic, the Liberal dictatorships of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, military dictatorships from 1954 to 1985, and the more recent genocide committed by state forces between 1978 and 1986. This institution is known as the sistema de cargos (cargo system). It is simultaneously a structure of self-governance, a school for political training, and a way of understanding and exercising power from within the community. Its logic is simple, but demanding: in the cargo system, one does not rise by accumulating wealth or votes, but by serving the community. Members ascend step by step up a ladder of responsibilities—almost always without remuneration—because service is both a duty and an honor. Positions generally last for one year before rotating, ensuring that authority circulates and no one becomes entrenched in power. Those who fulfill their responsibilities earn the prestige, respect, and trust of their people—assets that will become a legacy for future generations. In Santiago Atitlán, young men begin as alguaciles (Aj Ch’ami’ in Tz’utujil), serving as messengers and aides who summon meetings and assist senior authorities with assigned tasks. Over the years, they may join the cofradías, taking responsibility for the care of patron saints and the organization of festivals—events where the civic and the spiritual intertwine. Those who complete this journey become principales and eventually Elders, possessing the moral authority to offer counsel and resolve community conflicts. From among these principales emerges the alcalde Indígena, or Cabecera del Pueblo. It is, in essence, a school of exemplary living; no one reaches the top without having started at the bottom. In other words, political and representative leadership is learned and forged by sweeping the town square, carrying the saint, and listening to the Elders. Though the roots of this hierarchy are pre-Hispanic, the structure we see today was shaped during the colonial era, when surviving Maya communities reorganized their political and religious hierarchies despite Spanish rule. The result is a hybrid model that has endured to the present day. But this persistence has come at a high price. During the Guatemalan internal armed conflict (1960–1996), specifically in the 1980s and 1990s, several Indigenous mayors of Santiago Atitlán were assassinated, and the traditional structure was severely damaged. Remarkably, in recent decades, the community has revitalized its traditional offices, adapting to new challenges—a process mirrored across the Guatemalan central highlands and the Altiplano, ranging from the reactivation of Indigenous mayoralties to the renowned “48 Cantones” of Totonicapán department. Santiago Atitlán is no exception. Cultural Survival, through its consultancy on self-governance, has engaged in dialogue with Indigenous partners and leaders around the world about which forms of self-governance have endured over time, and why. The responses, gathered via focus groups held between March and May 2026, reveal a striking map showing that across different continents, names, and landscapes, the same grammar of self-governance practiced on the shores of Lake Atitlán emerges. In Mesoamerica, the Guna Yala territory in Panama was cited as a key reference point. Comprising 52 communities, each village elects its own sagla (leader), with most of them converging at a general congress to make collective decisions. The Guna, it was explained, resolved one of self-governance’s most complex dilemmas—financial dependence on the State—by generating their own revenue through self-managed tourism. In Mexico, one participant described her village’s cabildo (council) and comisariado de bienes comunales (communal land commission)—roles that are rotational, mostly unpaid, and short-term. She explained that this design hinders corruption and capture by external interests, as no one holds office long enough to be bought off. She also mentioned the mayordomías—sister institutions to the Guatemalan cofradías—which still divide the territory into neighborhoods; urban boundaries that no longer appear on official maps, but remain alive in the memory and self-governance practices of the communities. In South America, discussions revealed that Indigenous organizations in the Colombian Amazon successfully secured State recognition for the first Indigenous territorial entities, entrusting them with the administration of their own lands, including certain reserves. In Ecuador, decades of community leadership have emphasized that strengthening these systems “springs from the heart of the communities” and entails safeguarding the language, defending the territory, and instilling in children the sense of pride that sustains the community. In Chile, the focus was on reconstruction: the Mapuche people assert the autonomy of each lof (grassroots community) by rebuilding their own governance structures, even without constitutional recognition. Seykún community members in Colombia. Photo by Joshua Dautoff. Brazil contributed a lesson to the dialogue that was striking in its clarity: without land, there is no self-governance. It was explained that Peoples living on State-demarcated lands can exercise and defend their own governance, whereas those still awaiting demarcation—sometimes for 20 years or more—govern in a state of extreme vulnerability, exposed daily to mining, dispossession, and death. The highlighted examples of remarkable persistence: the Xingu territory, where diverse Peoples with their own organizational structures coexist, and the more than 100 Peoples living in voluntary isolation who, without asking for permission, have kept their systems of self-governance—among the most autonomous on the planet—intact. Dogon cultural festival, Mali. Photo by Georges Dougon (Dougon). Across the Atlantic, Mali possesses an architecture of authority that a Tz’utujil person would instantly recognize: every family has a head, every village has its authorities, and rising above disputes is the hogon—the supreme mediator whose word is considered the final authority. Important matters are deliberated in the togu na (House of the Word), and the ceremonial calendar structures political life. When a wedding is celebrated, or a conflict arises, the community turns first to traditional authority and only later to the State. Among the Kel Tamasheq in the north, there are communities in which women exercise supreme leadership and serve as custodians of the cosmology. From Namibia and South Africa, other voices described the contrast between Peoples like the Nama, who possess recognized traditional councils of authority, and the San, whose authorities largely lack State recognition. This distinction carries significant implications, for without recognition of authority or self-governance, there is no recognition of land rights, either. Nama people in Namibia recognize traditional councils of authority. Photo by Nichodimas Cooper. In Asia, home to the majority of the world’s Indigenous Peoples, this pattern repeats with particular intensity. Nepal has legally recognized only 59 Peoples, and its 2015 Constitution promised autonomous zones that have yet to materialize. Still, the systems function. The Tharu elect a barghar in each village to resolve problems and make community decisions, while the Thakali administer justice through the mukhiya system, deliberating democratically before consulting the chief. This collective voice guides the community, often without regard for government dictates. Their central warning aligned with the Brazilian position: self-determination is inextricably linked to the land, and those displaced from their territory lose the very possibility of self-governance, of creating and recreating their own forms of government. March in Nepal, where 60 Indigenous Peoples are officially recognized. Photo by Dev Kumar Sunuwar (Sunuwar). North America introduced the most complex scenario to the dialogue: Peoples governed by structures they did not choose. Several participants from the United States and Canada described Tribal councils shaped by the State, while noting their sustained efforts to reclaim their own traditional systems. Examples include Canadian First Nations that supplement the imposed structure with a traditional council and a council of matriarchs for decision-making; communities that maintain a “big house” as a ceremonial heart; councils of Elders working alongside youth programs; and a conviction voiced by many that reclaiming self-governance requires unlearning colonial concepts of power and restoring women to the status they held in matrilineal societies. These experiences of governance reveal not so much differences as variations on a common theme. Everywhere, self-governance is rooted in service rather than power; a position of leadership exists to serve, not for personal gratification. In all these contexts, Indigenous authority is exercised through collective deliberation. Elders embody memory and counsel, while the spiritual dimension permeates political life, with no attempt to separate the two. Everywhere, too, the land appears as the condition of possibility, because the territory is not a resource to be managed, but the very body of the community. Differences arise from the outside, sustained by nation States through the degree of recognition each grants, the access to funding they permit, the pressure imposed by extractive economies, or the criminalization faced by ancestral authorities defending their territories. International bodies are finally reaching the same conclusion as Indigenous Peoples. UN reports document that Indigenous governance systems often manage services for their communities more effectively than external agents, and that where Indigenous Nations govern themselves, indicators such as education and employment actually improve. The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, which will mark its 20th anniversary in 2027, recognizes the rights to self-determination and to maintain one’s own governing institutions. The challenge, according to those consulted in the regions where Cultural Survival operates, is not proving that Indigenous self-governance works, but rather getting nation States to stop sabotaging it. The former UN Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, Victoria Tauli-Corpuz (Kankanaey Igorot), in her 2018 report on self-government, explained that long before colonization and the rise of nation States, Indigenous Peoples around the world had developed complex forms of self-governance—systems that regulated relationships among themselves, with their neighbors, and with the natural world, while incorporating their worldviews, values, and unique understandings of authority. Colonizers dismissed these systems as inferior and attempted to eradicate them; today, post-colonial States often continue that same effort. Yet, Indigenous forms of self-government endure. The work of the Indigenous mayor of Santiago Atitlán stands as proof of the continued vitality of Indigenous self-governance. These systems have survived for centuries because they predate the colonial era and possess roots far deeper than the nation States that seek to stifle them by every possible means. They endure because they meet a daily need within their communities: a form of governance in which authority is earned through service, decisions are made collectively, and the territory is not owned, but cared for. Each year on the shores of Lake Atitlán, with the quiet, deliberate gesture of a young Tz’utujil man accepting his first leadership role, a millennia-old institution begins its cycle anew. --Irma A. Velásquez Nimatuj (Maya K’iche’) is a journalist, activist, and social anthropologist. Top photo: People gathered in Santiago Atitlán, Guatemala, for a public assembly. Photo by Kerstin Sabene.
