Por tanto, la expansión de ferrocarriles, carreteras, proyectos hidroeléctricos, monocultivos y otros proyectos a gran escala no se entiende meramente como una transformación física del entorno, sino como una amenaza a las relaciones que hacen posible recibir, transmitir y aplicar este conocimiento.
Entonces, defender el derecho a soñar es defender las condiciones territoriales que hacen que soñar sea posible.
Ró: Cerrado, mundo, territorio y vida
La palabra «ró» no tiene un equivalente completo en la traducción convencional de “territorio”. La geógrafa Maria Lucia Cereda Gomide explica que ró puede significar simultáneamente “cerrado, mundo, nuestra tierra, todo”. Se refiere a una complejo territorial y cosmológico que se extiende desde el espacio de la aldea al cerrado [bioma en el centro de Brasil], y comprende sus aguas, animales, plantas y los espíritus que viven en este mundo. Ró es una red viviente de relaciones. Abarca cazar, recolectar y pescar; aldeas antiguas, tierras de sepultura, ríos y caminos, plantas medicinales; lugares ceremoniales y presencias ancestrales que sostienen la vida colectiva.
Una nota técnica de la Asociación Antropológica brasileña, publicada en 2025, enfatiza que la territorialidad a’uwẽ-xavante depende de prácticas como recorrer el cerrado, recolectar raíces, frutas y fibras, pescar, cazar y circuitos de reciprocidad que conecta familias, clanes, grupos etarios y diferentes tierras indígenas. Por tanto, la fragmentación territorial compromete el acceso a recursos naturales y la capacidad de realizar ceremonias, transmitir conocimiento y mantener las relaciones sociales y cosmológicas a través de las cuales los a’uwẽ se constituyen como pueblo. También va más allá de relaciones que no se pueden contener dentro de los límites administrativos trazados por el Estado.
Entonces, el mensaje proyectado en Ginebra –“Dejen que los a’uwẽ-xavante sigan soñando”– es un pedido para proteger la integridad de ró y por la continuidad de su propia existencia. Hiparidi Top’tiro, líder a’uwẽ-xavante, dice en el documento de la campaña: “Cualquier proyecto que afecta a uno de nuestros territorios es un problema para todo el pueblo a’uwẽ-xavante”.
Territorios, vidas y sueños cortados por pistas
El pedido central de la campaña es proteger los derechos del pueblo a’uwẽ-xavante ante la construcción del Ferrocarril de Integración Centro Oeste (FICO), también conocido como EF-354. El Gobierno brasileño lo ha presentado como un proyecto estratégico para reducir costos logísticos y expandir el transporte ferroviario de carga, y es parte de un corredor más amplio diseñado principalmente para trasladar soya, maíz y otros productos de la región. Al avanzar el proyecto sin garantizar una consulta adecuada, libre, previa e informada, el Estado brasileño no ha logrado proteger los derechos de los pueblos indígenas.
La vía de FICO es un proyecto federal de aproximadamente 1641 kilómetros (1020 millas) bajo la responsabilidad de Infra S.A. La empresa minera Vale está construyendo la primera sección, que recorre 363 kilómetros (226 millas), entre Mara Rosa, en el estado de Goiás, y Água Boa, en el estado de Mato Grosso, como compensación por la renovación prematura de otra concesión. Estudios y procesos administrativos relacionados con la ruta han identificado los territorios xavante dentro de su zona de influencia, lo que plantea serias preocupaciones sobre el impacto territorial, ambiental, social y cultural.
En mayo de 2026, la propia Infra S.A. informó que aproximadamente 80 kilómetros (50 millas) de la parte final de la porción de la sección que actualmente está en construcción dependía de que se completara el Plan Ambiental Básico – Componente Indígena (PBA-CI) y de negociaciones con las comunidades xavante. Esto deja en claro que la relación entre el ferrocarril y los territorios indígenas no es meramente indirecta, sino un asunto central que afecta la implementación del proyecto.
La nota técnica emitida por la Asociación Antropológica brasileña establece que el ferrocarril afecta zonas de ocupación tradicional, tierras reclamadas que aún no se han demarcado, ha juntado zonas, aldeas antiguas, tierras de sepulturas, ríos navegables y sitios sagrados. El documento recomienda suspender la construcción y la licencia de instalación hasta que se haya hecho una consulta adecuada, y alterar la ruta para que el ferrocarril no cruce territorio a’uwẽ-xavante.
El informe de defensa de la campaña Dejen que los a’uwẽ-xavante sigan soñando, iniciada en Ginebra, sostiene que FICO no puede evaluarse meramente como una línea ferroviaria aislada. Es parte de una arquitectura más amplia de carreteras, ferrocarriles, cursos de agua, y exporta corredores que probablemente intensifique los flujos de mercadería, ocupación no indígena y presión económica en territorios ya fragmentados.
Consulta en disputa
En febrero de 2026, la Coordinación de Organizaciones Indígenas de la Amazonía Brasileña (COIAB) denunció irregularidades en el proceso de consulta relacionado con FICO. Según la organización, las reuniones programadas para algunas tierras indígenas se hicieron a intervalos muy cortos, lo que dejó a las comunidades con poco tiempo para tener debates internos de acuerdo con sus propios procesos de toma de decisiones. También hay documentadas denuncias de presiones a líderes indígenas, falta de asistencia técnica independiente y dificultades de comunicación entre comunidades distribuidas entre territorios que históricamente han estado fragmentados. El Ministerio Público Federal inició un procedimiento administrativo para dar seguimiento al proceso de consulta.
La Organización Internacional del Trabajo (OIT) y la Declaración de Naciones Unidas sobre Derechos de los Pueblos Indígenas establece que los Estados deben consultar y cooperar de buena fe con los pueblos indígenas después de aprobar proyectos que afectan a sus tierras, territorios o recursos, para obtener su consentimiento libre, previo e informado.
La consulta no solo significa informar a una comunidad que un proyecto procederá, sino también respetará sus cronogramas de toma de decisiones, sin coerción y su capacidad de retener el consentimiento de medidas que pudieran comprometer su futuro.
A Europa: el colonialismo solo viaja por tren y autos eléctricos
La intervención en Ginebra tiene un peso simbólico particular. La ciudad es sede de la Oficina de Naciones Unidas y de numerosas instituciones relacionadas con el sistema internacional de derechos humanos. A los representantes indígenas se les da poco minutos para presentar conflictos territoriales delineados por décadas de violaciones.
La campaña también desafía las contradicciones de la llamada transición ecológica. Ferrocarriles, corredores logísticos, operaciones mineras y proyectos de infraestructura a gran escala se presentan frecuentemente como instrumentos necesarios para construir una economía con bajo carbono. Pero cuando avanzan sin la participación efectiva de los pueblos afectados, pueden reproducir mecanismos coloniales que perduran: apropiación territorial, concentración de beneficios económicos y transferencia de costos ambientales y sociales a pueblos indígenas y comunidades tradicionales.
La proyección delante de Jet d’Eau confronta esta paradoja. Europa, históricamente implicada en la colonización de territorios indígenas, sigue conectadas con estas regiones por medio de redes de finanzas, consumo, minería, agroindustria e infraestructura de exportaciones. Cambiar la fuente de energía sin transformar estas relaciones no es suficiente. Una transición que sigue amenazando territorios indígenas como zonas de sacrificio puede ser tecnológicamente nuevo, pero sigue siendo políticamente colonial.
Para los a’uwẽ-xavante, un territorio fragmentado no significa simplemente reducir el espacio físico. Significa interrumpir caminos, canciones, ceremonias y recuerdos, y relaciones ancestrales. Ningún megaproyecto puede decir que representa el futuro si su existencia depende de destruir los sueños de quienes siempre han cuidado la tierra.

title: Antes dos farroupilhas pelearam os guarani
content:
Vicente Rauber*
Claudio Knierim**
Precisamos falar mais sobre as principais conquistas dos Guarani e da Revolução Farroupilha incorporadas como qualidades, conhecimentos e costumes do(a) gaúcho(a), complementando nosso artigo anterior “O gaúcho vem dos Guaranis”. As qualidades de dignidade, justiça, bravura, resistência, altivez e pertencimento ao solo habitado pelos(as) gaúchos(as) como legado fundamental de um longo processo histórico que principia com a chegada de indígenas Guarani e Charrua nesse território pampeano, com a chegada de negros juntamente com espanhóis e portugueses, além do episódio da Revolução Farroupilha.
O Acampamento Farroupilha de Porto Alegre deste ano, muito justificadamente, adotou o tema: “Herança Jesuítica e Guarani no RS: 400 anos de cultura e tradição”, tendo como referência o ano de 1626, quando foi constituída a primeira redução Guarani chamada de São Nicolau.
As Missões Jesuíticas foi a única tentativa relevante de desenvolvimento conjunto entre europeus e povos originários.
Essa foi a única tentativa relevante de desenvolvimento conjunto entre europeus e povos originários. Poderia ter construído uma sociedade justa e evoluída para sempre. Era um sistema avançado de saberes milenares indígenas e técnicas trazidas pelos padres jesuítas, com uma gestão organizada coletivamente. As Aldeias ou Tekoas foram unificadas e “reduzidas” a um espaço delimitado, adotando um modelo de gestão que unificava as práticas Guarani a um modelo de governo espanhol chamado de “Cabildo”. O seu desenvolvimento era muito superior ao de outras regiões ocupadas por portugueses e espanhóis.
O Brasil não foi descoberto, foi ocupado para ser explorado
O Brasil não foi descoberto; foi ocupado para ser explorado. Os povos indígenas, que já habitavam esta terra com seus conhecimentos milenares, vivendo em na natureza, foram estupidamente destruídos.
Os Guarani, vindos inicialmente da Amazônia, há milhares de anos já cultivavam vegetais que hoje fazem parte da alimentação do povo brasileiro. Entre esses estão o milho (avati), batata doce (jeti), mandioca ou aipim, abóbora ou jerimum, feijão e batata. Já usavam o plantio direto (saraquá) ou coivara. Cozinhavam em panelas de pedra ou cerâmica, além de fazer assados. Colocavam a carne ou pescado num “jirau”, uma armação feita de taquara, colocando-a sob brasas, técnica chamada de “barbaquá”, que originou o churrasco.
Além das qualidades pessoais, os Guarani das Missões nos legaram a gestão coletiva, a agricultura, a pecuária, a cozinha, construções, oficinas, a estocagem, o comércio, churrasco e chimarrão.
Também usavam o pilão (monjolo) para triturar alimentos e facilitar o cozimento. Usavam-no também para produzir farinha e fazer o mingau para os idosos e crianças (curumins). Já tomavam o mate ou chimarrão, feito com a erva “ilex paraguaienses”, hoje identidade do gaúcho brasileiro, uruguaio, argentino e paraguaio.
Há muito tempo, os Guarani faziam panelas e outros objetos com argila, técnica que dominavam. Nas reduções, tijolos, lajotas e telhas em olarias.
Os jesuítas descobriram jazidas de cal e, com os Guarani, fizeram a argamassa. Assim, os missioneiros construíram residências, colégios, igrejas, ruas e calçamentos. Instalaram sistemas de captação de água, canaletas, esgotos e moinhos hidráulicos.
Desenvolveram oficinas para carpintaria, tecelagem e metalurgia, entre outras. Produziam instrumentos musicais, esculturas de madeira e pedra, roupas, instrumentos de trabalho como enxadas, martelos, foices, pregos e, inclusive, armas rudimentares.
Plantavam trigo, algodão, videiras e pomares de frutas até então inexistentes na América. O trabalho era dividido em Abambaé, para o cultivo das famílias, e Tupambaé, um mutirão para a produção coletiva com o objetivo de sustentar órfãos e viúvas. Essa produção servia ainda para trocas e comércio.
Fora do espaço urbano das Reduções Missioneiras, existiam as estâncias de criação de gado bovino, ovino e equino para tração de carretas, arados e moinhos, bem como produção de carne e couro.
As Reduções Guarani tinham autossustentação e possuíam depósitos em paióis para os excedentes, os quais eram trocados (escambo) com outros povoados. Também eram realizadas vendas para outras províncias e, até, para Buenos Aires.
Os Charrua nos legaram vestimentas, boleadeiras, a doma dócil do cavalo. Também foram chacinados.
Outro grupo indígena importante em nosso legado foram os Charrua, possivelmente originários dos Andes. Eram nômades e viviam da caça, pesca e coleta de frutas, fundamentalmente. Não aceitaram ser catequizados pelos padres jesuítas e nem serem reduzidos dentro de um espaço urbano. No vestuário, herdamos deles o chiripá – antecessor da bombacha –, a vincha – fita de tecido ou couro amarrada no cabelo – e do toropi, uma manta de lã ou couro para proteger as costas do frio.
Das lides campeiras, recebemos as boleadeiras, usadas para caçar avestruzes (inhandu). Hoje, são encontradas em museus e na dança folclórica do RS e da Argentina, o Malambo.
Enquanto outros realizavam a doma dos cavalos com brutalidade, os Charrua tratavam os animais com estima. Com o filhote (potrilho), desenvolviam uma doma dócil, método que vem sendo reaprendido atualmente. Sequer usavam o freio (peça de metal colocada na boca do cavalo para guiá-lo).
Vestem calças de crivo e chiripá-saia e mostram guasca de couro e boleadeiras
Em 1831, o Presidente do Uruguai, Frutuoso Rivera, pressionado por estancieiros brasileiros e uruguaios, atacou os Charruas. Eles foram massacrados numa emboscada junto ao Arroio Salsipuedes (Uruguai), dando início ao seu extermínio enquanto grupo étnico.
Em terras sul-americanas as línguas portuguesa e espanhola incorporaram 6000 palavras indígenas.
As línguas portuguesa e espanhola, em terras gaúchas, incorporaram cerca de 6000 palavras indígenas do tupi, guarani, quíchua e de outros povos, incluindo nomes de rios, lagoas, montes e outros lugares, das quais destacamos:
– Gua-hi-ba – Gua: encontro; hi: água; ou seja, o encontro das águas; neste caso, dos dos Rios Jacuí, Caí, Sinos e Gravataí;
– Guri – Menino ou criança;
– Tapejara – o que conhece bem os caminhos, habilidoso;
– Chácara – Espaço de terra para criação de animais;
– China, chinoca – mulher indígena, moça, mulher jovem;
– Chiru – Caboclo ou indígena com a pele morena;
– Guasca – gaúcho, homem caipira. Tira feita de couro cru;
– Guampa – corno, chifre ou vasilha feita com este material;
– Guaiaca – cinto largo de couro com bolsos;
– Cuia – Recipiente feito com o fruto da cuieira utilizado para tomar chimarrão;
– chucro – não domado, bravio, esquivo.
As Reduções Guaraníticas eram uma afronta às metrópoles europeias. Foram chacinadas.
O exemplo das Reduções Guaraníticas era uma afronta às metrópoles europeias. Em 1750, as duas maiores potências mundiais da época, Portugal e Espanha, que disputavam as terras da América do Sul, acordaram o Tratado de Madri, estabelecendo que a Colônia de Sacramento ficaria com a Espanha e o território das Reduções Jesuíticas, com Portugal. Mais: que todos os indígenas e os padres jesuítas deveriam abandonar as reduções e cruzar o Rio Uruguai para as terras da atual Argentina.
Parte dos indígenas, aconselhados por padres jesuítas, obedeceram às ordens. No entanto, outra parte dos Guarani, liderados por Sepé Tiaraju as ordens vindas da Espanha através do Tratado de Madri e se opuseram à demarcação das terras. Para fazer cumprir o Tratado, Portugal e Espanha enviaram seus maiores exércitos, o português comandado por Gomes Freire de Andrade e o espanhol pelo Governador de Buenos Aires José de Andonaegui.
Sepé Tiaraju manda o exército português parar em Santa Tecla (atual Bagé), onde teria exclamado: “Esta terra tem dono”. Depois de muitas tentativas de negociação, todas frustradas, em 1756 – os exércitos de Espanha e Portugal, avançam sobre a região e Inicia a Guerra Guaranítica, não resolvida em negociações. Em 7 de fevereiro de 1756, os exércitos matam Sepé Tiaraju. Em 10 de fevereiro, na Batalha da Caiboaté, eliminam mais de 1500 indígenas. Na sequência, tanto Portugal como Espanha expulsam todos os padres jesuítas e confiscam seus bens. Desse modo, liquidam em definitivo com a excepcional experiência missioneira, ocorrendo a dispersão dos Guaranis sobreviventes.
O gado das estâncias missioneiras ficou vagando. Foi caçado pelos gaúchos para a sua sobrevivência, sendo considerados ladrões de gado, malfeitores. A Revolução Farroupilha recuperou a sua dignidade.
O gado das estâncias missioneiras ficou vagando livremente e se reproduzindo pelos campos. Esses rebanhos passaram a ser caçados pelos gaúchos ou gauchos, um bando de homens constituído por indígenas, negros, mestiços, soldados espanhóis e portugueses desertores dos seus exércitos. Esse gaúcho ou gaudério que vivia na pampa do sul do Brasil, Uruguai e Argentina, era tido como malfeitor, “ladrão de gado”. Após a ocupação desse território pelas estâncias ou haciendas e após o cercamento dos campos, os gaúchos acabam sendo incorporados às estâncias como peões e desaparecem enquanto um grupo social que caçava o gado para retirar e vender o couro, assegurando assim sua sobrevivência.
Através de pesquisas e compilações históricas, os saberes e as técnicas dos indígenas, e em especial das Reduções Missioneiras, felizmente foram recuperados e hoje possuem amplo uso entre o povo gaúcho da região platina.
Os negros, mesmo escravizados e discriminados, somaram costumes e valores fundamentais.
Ainda na formação do gaúcho cabe citar o importante legado dos negros. Mesmo trazidos como escravos, e ainda discriminados depois de libertos, deixaram contribuições no trabalho, na culinária e em diversos costumes gaúchos. A sua valentia e resistência fazem parte da História, como ocorreu com o Corpo de Lanceiros Negros da Revolução Farroupilha.
Os imigrantes europeus e asiáticos trouxeram mais conhecimentos e técnicas e incorporaram as experiências indígenas e negras.
Com a vinda ao Brasil de outros povos europeus e asiáticos, chegaram mais conhecimentos e técnicas, que foram agregados ao que indígenas e negros nos legaram. Acaso existe alguma região onde o chimarrão não é sorvido e a carne assada para um bom churrasco? E, no dia seguinte, aparece um carreteiro com a carne que sobrou do churrasco!
Este é um momento fundamental de recuperar as qualidades do gaúcho no RS e avançá-las no Brasil.
Mas há o que se recuperar e há o que avançar! A construção de uma sociedade mais digna e justa, com evolução permanente, precisa ser retomada em nosso Estado. Um país que busca a sua soberania, com justiça social e reconhecimento internacional, precisa dar continuidade às conquistas herdadas e àquelas construídas no tempo presente. Que em 4 de outubro saibamos honrar as qualidades de dignidade, justiça, altivez e resistência, praticadas nas Reduções Guaraníticas Missioneiras e na Revolução Farroupilha, acrescidas do mais que nunca necessário desenvolvimento com sustentabilidade ambiental!
*Vicente Rauber é engenheiro Especialista em Planejamento Energético e Ambiental.
**Claudio Knierim é historiador.
**Este é um artigo de opinião e não necessariamente expressa a linha editorial do jornal Brasil de Fato.

title: Support Emergency Relief in Nepal
content: Support Emergency Relief in Nepal Country Nepal agnes Thu, 09/17/2026 - 12:13 Issues Human Rights Program 5 Main Image Give Now to Double Your Impact! The devastating impacts of the sudden flash flood on August 26 that occurred in Nepal continue to be felt, and Cultural Survival continues to work to support our Indigenous community partners who are on their journey towards recovery. As we work to channel funds toward humanitarian aid that is Indigenous-led and locally determined, your gift continues to be matched dollar-for-dollar up to $10,000 through a grant from The Fund for Nonviolence. We express our deepest gratitude and appreciation to those who have already supported this cause - your contribution has helped ensure that urgent assistance reaches Indigenous communities whose livelihoods, territories, and cultural systems are under threat. Destruction from the flooding has been devastating, impacting all aspects of daily life, and getting assistance and information to the people who need it most has become one of the greatest challenges. Dipak Lama, a station manager based in the Dhunche district headquarters of Rasuwa, described how even local radio stations struggled to continue communicating with communities when the disaster struck. “On the very same morning, we had information from the police about the flood, and we were in the middle of sharing information through the radio, but the electricity went off, as the electricity office was destroyed by then,” Lama told Cultural Survival. Local FM radio is a vital source of information for communities cut off from conventional communication systems. Yet, even radio operations face challenges due to a lack of battery backup and solar power. In remote settlements, residents need information about rescue operations, safe routes, food distribution, and emergency services, but damaged infrastructure makes communication increasingly difficult. The disaster has also intensified debate over climate change and state responsibility. Environmentalists have classified the Bhotekoshi disaster as climate-induced, and Dr. Maheshwar Dhakal, Head of the Climate Change Management Division under the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Environment, said the catastrophic loss of life and property resulted from forces to which Nepal has contributed very little. “The loss of life and property we suffered in the Bhote Koshi flood is purely a climate-induced disaster,” Dhakal said, arguing that developed and industrialized countries have emitted vast quantities of carbon while Nepal’s contributions remain less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Indigenous Peoples’ rights activists are calling for disaster response and climate adaptation strategies to incorporate Indigenous knowledge and values. As development projects, including dams and hydropower facilities, make lands fragile, Indigenous Peoples are calling for Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC), protection of traditional ecological knowledge, and greater attention to forests, biodiversity, soil conservation, and traditional practices that can reduce vulnerability to landslides and erosion. We continue to stand beside our partners in Nepal, channeling funds toward humanitarian aid that is Indigenous-led and locally determined, but we need your help to reach our $10,000 goal. Your gift will be matched dollar-for-dollar up to $10,000 through a grant from The Fund for Nonviolence, helping us respond to the needs of our partners. You can provide support and give Indigenous communities greater agency in determining their journey towards recovery. If you haven't already, please consider donating today – your contribution will help ensure that urgent assistance reaches Indigenous communities whose livelihoods, territories, and cultural systems are under threat. Thank you for standing with our Indigenous partners in Nepal. Support Indigenous communities in Nepal! Read more: "Deadly Flood, Dubbed “Himalayan Tsunami,” Leaves Over 1,300 Dead and Thousands Missing in Nepal" by Dev Kumar Sunuwar (Koĩts-Sunuwar, CS Staff)

title: When Pammal Sambanda Mudaliar took Tamil theatre to Ceylon
content:
Pammal Sambanda Mudaliar’s magnum opus Nataka Medai Ninaivugal is a fascinating study of Tamil theatre of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, as seen through the journey of the Suguna Vilasa Sabha. Written in excruciating detail in most parts, this work documents the important role played by the Sabha in creating a renaissance in theatre, nurturing several talents and troupes. Ahead of Sambanda Mudaliar’s 62nd death anniversary on September 24, a look at the Suguna Vilasa Sabha’s performances in Ceylon and how they inspired the formation of a theatre group in the island nation.
In 1909, Sambanda Mudaliar and a few friends went on a private tour to Ceylon and happened to visit the Public Hall in Colombo. They made enquiries about staging performances there and the costs involved. In 1911, the Suguna Vilasa Sabha decided to venture into something it had not attempted before — taking their plays to Ceylon. Sambanda Mudaliar had to deal with multiple challenges in the preparations. One of them stemmed from within the Sabha itself, as a group of Telugu-speaking members protested against the inclusion of a junior artiste, who had just joined, at the expense of seniors. Another challenge was obtaining leave from work for artistes going on the tour, with Sambanda Mudaliar himself intervening on behalf of a few of them to resolve the matter. Costs, too, posed a challenge. This was, however, taken care of, since a drama contractor agreed to take responsibility of the entire production, paying the Sabha a lump sum of Rs 2,500 towards the staging of five plays.
Finally, a nearly 50-member delegation travelled to Colombo, where it was welcomed by a group of prominent Tamils led by the eminent lawyer Sir A. Kanagasabai. Sambanda Mudaliar later wrote in his book Naan Kanda Naadaga Kalaignargal that the tour drew large crowds and began with the staging of Leelavathi Sulochana. Among the audience for the play was Warwick Major, who held a long lease on the Public Hall and regularly let it out for performances. This man would later etch himself in the history of Madras for giving it its first permanent cinema house, the Electric Theatre on Mount Road. Today, this building houses the Philatelic Bureau. The other plays staged included Manohara, Galava Charithram, Amaladityan and Sarangadhara. The Governor of Ceylon Sir Henry Edward McCallum, presided over the performance of Amaladityan (an adaptation of Hamlet). Such was the success of the plays that Sir Kanagasabai requested Sambanda Mudaliar to stage another play in aid of the Governor’s Tuberculosis Fund. The Sabha staged the comedy Kaadhalar Kangal and donated half the proceeds, net of expenses, to the fund.
Sambanda Mudaliar writes of the warm hospitality accorded to the Suguna Vilasa Sabha members by people from across all sections of the society.
The Sabha embarked on its second visit to Ceylon in May 1913, this time including Jaffna in their itinerary. After staging five plays at Colombo, the troupe travelled to Jaffna, where things ran into rough weather. Sambanda Mudaliar took ill (which he attributes to a severe bout of indigestion brought on by his inability to refuse the grand hospitality at various gatherings in Colombo!), and adding to the troupe’s discomfort were the less-than-satisfactory arrangements made by the contractor for the performing venue as well as their stay. It was decided by the Suguna Vilasa Sabha committee to refund the advance taken and cancel the tour.
The development led to rumours that the tour was being cancelled because the Sabha was dissatisfied with the reception it had received. The people of Jaffna took it to be an affront to their reputation as gracious hosts. Fortunately, the District Judge, MS Pinto happened to be Sambanda Mudaliar’s classmate at Madras Presidency College. At his behest took a group of lawyers took it upon themselves to ensure that the members were provided with better accommodation and facilities. The tour eventually continued and earned the sabha a surplus of Rs. 1,500, which went towards its building fund. As on its earlier visit, a benefit performance was staged at the request of a few prominent personalities, this time in aid of the Jaffna University.
During its silver jubilee year in 1916, the Suguna Vilasa Sabha undertook a final visit to Ceylon. According to Sambanda Mudaliar, it turned out to be a memorable occasion, since he was awarded the ‘Rao Sahib’ title as part of the king’s birthday honours. It was announced as part of a scene in their popular play Sabapathy. It was greeted with thunderous applause.
According to Kalaiarasu K. Sornalingam, a doyen of Tamil theatre in Ceylon, the Suguna Vilasa Sabha’s tours marked a turning point in the history of theatre in the island nation. Inspired by its performances, he founded the Lanka Subodha Vilasa Sabha in 1913, which in turn led to the formation of other troupes in places such as Jaffna. Sornalingam considered Sambanda Mudaliar his guru, and the latter, too, recognised him as an artiste of repute in his book Naan Kanda Naadaga Kalaignargal.
Sambanda Mudaliar’s influence as a theatre-personality truly transcended borders.

title: Ubulu-Uku INE Festival: A Celebration of Culture, Peace and Renewal
content:
UBULU-UKU, Delta State — The people of Ubulu-Uku celebrate with gratitude and deep respect His Royal Majesty, Obi Chukwuka Noah Akaeze, and commend his enduring reign and commitment to the growth, peace and development of the ancient kingdom. His support for initiatives that promote the preservation of Ubulu-Uku’s rich cultural heritage remains an important part of the community’s continuing journey.
It was in this spirit of support for the traditional institution and the cultural heritage of Ubulu-Uku that the community came together for the annual INE Festival, in a celebration marked by colour, tradition, unity and, most significantly, peace.
This year’s celebration was particularly remarkable as the festival was held within the palace in an atmosphere free from fighting, violence or disruption. The peaceful gathering represented an important moment for a festival deeply rooted in the history and traditions of the kingdom.
A central figure in the organisation and successful coordination of the celebration was the Traditional Prime Minister of Ubulu-Uku, Chief James Asika Onwordi, the Onishe of Ubulu-Uku, whose vision has consistently centred on fostering progress, unity and growth within the community.
The celebration brought together traditional groups, community stakeholders, youths, families and visitors, creating a vibrant display of the cultural identity of Ubulu-Uku.
Among the major highlights were the traditional displays by the revered Agana men, who performed their sacred rites as part of the festival. The appearance of the Eze Dibia, who had not surfaced publicly for a considerable period, was another notable moment, as he performed his traditional rites to the excitement of those gathered.
The younger generation also embraced the festival with enthusiasm. The major road became a colourful scene of music, dancing and traditional attire, giving the celebration the atmosphere of a cultural carnival while allowing the younger generation to participate actively in the traditions of their forebears.
The presence of major community stakeholders, including the Umuobi, Umu Ozim, Ani-Eke and others, further demonstrated the collective importance of INE to the people of Ubulu-Uku.
The celebration also attracted notable dignitaries, including Rt. Hon. Isaac Anwuzia, Member representing Aniocha South Constituency in the Delta State House of Assembly, Hon. Smart Ijeoma Ufoh, Commissioner for Technical Education, and other distinguished guests.
Beyond the festivities, the INE Festival continues to serve a deeper purpose. It provides an avenue for Ubulu-Uku indigenes at home and in the diaspora to reconnect with their roots, preserve indigenous traditions and strengthen the bonds that hold the community together.
The peaceful conduct of this year’s celebration was particularly significant. It offered a powerful demonstration that culture can be preserved and celebrated in an atmosphere of harmony, mutual respect and communal responsibility.
With the support of the traditional institution and the efforts of those committed to the advancement of the kingdom, the INE Festival continues to provide an opportunity for Ubulu-Uku to celebrate where it has come from while looking towards where it is going.
For Ubulu-Uku, the message from this year’s celebration was clear: culture remains alive, tradition remains relevant, and peace remains essential to the progress and development of the kingdom.

title: On Yom Kippur I was shot protecting my synagogue, now I carry the torch. - Sponsored Content
content:
One year ago on Yom Kippur, my life changed forever. I was shot while protecting the doors of Heaton Park Synagogue in Manchester during a terrorist attack. Badly injured, I underwent seven hours of surgery and spent the next ten days in hospital. I survived. Adrian Daulby and Melvin Cravitz, two remarkable men I think about every day, tragically did not.
Since the attack, I have looked for ways to honour life and remember those we lost. So, when I was invited to join the 2026 International March of the Living, I welcomed the opportunity to march alongside Holocaust survivors and fellow survivors of antisemitic attacks. Together, we set off on the march.
As the shofar was blown, we began the 3.5 km walk from Auschwitz to Birkenau. Israeli flags were waving and 8,000 people walked with us.
They did not beat us.
The March gives you the extraordinary opportunity to spend time with survivors who rebuilt their lives and now educate the next generation. As Elie Wiesel said, “When you listen to a witness, you become a witness.”
I wasn’t the only one there carrying scars of my own. I met Hannah Abesidon and Eva Wietzen, survivors of the Bondi Beach attack, and Abbie Talmoud and Catherine Szkop, who witnessed the murders of their friends Sarah Milgrim and Yaron Lischinsky in Washington, D.C. We were asked whether these experiences had made us afraid to be visibly Jewish. I was wearing a kippah, Abbie a Magen David, Hannah a Chai necklace. We all gave the same answer: we were proud to be Jewish, and our pride had only been strengthened.
Together, we lit the first torch at the March’s closing ceremony in Birkenau, dedicated to combating antisemitism, alongside Sylvan Adams, President of the World Jewish Congress–Israel, and Ambassador Yehuda Kaploun, the U.S. Special Envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism.
In a symbolic moment, the next torch was lit by the international law enforcement delegation, who had come to pledge their commitment to “Never Again – Not on Our Watch.” I was privileged to address the delegation, and I told them that members of my synagogue were killed and I was injured because hatred had moved from social media and marches into real life. Hate is not abstract. It has consequences, and I am living proof.
The community doesn’t feel any safer a year on from Heaton Park. There are more gates and more security than we have ever had. Any event we hold does not have the address displayed on the poster. Our kids go to schools that look like fortresses. Every Jewish building has to have security.
Combating antisemitism is not the responsibility of the Jewish community alone. As history has shown, when radicalisation or hate targets Jews first, it threatens the freedom, safety, and human rights of society as a whole. We all have a responsibility to speak up and challenge antisemitism wherever we see it.
We did not march only against antisemitism. We also marched for Jewish life and Jewish pride. In Tykocin, I experienced one of the most inspirational moments of the trip. In the synagogue there, built in 1642, we prayed Mincha, then danced, holding hands and singing V’hi She’amdah with survivors. A testament that Jewish life would not just survive but thrive.
This instinct to dance rather than surrender was already familiar to me from Yom Kippur. While I was undergoing surgery, our rabbi, Daniel Walker, made the decision that we would carry on and refuse to let the terrorists win. Not a single prayer was missed. The first time I was able to return to my synagogue was Simchat Torah, where we danced like we had never danced before, with defiance. Even in the darkness and the pain, we carry on, and we dance.
As the plane lifted off from Warsaw, I made a silent promise to myself: I will be back.
I invite you to join me.
Join the March of the Living or help someone else make the journey.
Yom Kippur will never be the same for me. But I know that, as a community, we will carry on. This Yom Kippur, we will return to our Shul. Yes, we are different, but we are still here and we are saying the same prayers that we carried on saying last year. On the March, we prayed, sang and danced in the very places where the Nazis tried to wipe us out, alongside the very people they tried to murder. And we are continuing a story that has endured in every generation, despite those who have tried to stop it.
May we all be inscribed in the Book of Life, and may the memory of all those murdered because of antisemitism be a blessing.

title: How fantasy fans are keeping a Turkish blacksmithing tradition alive
content:
Kemeralti Bazaar, Izmir, Turkiye – To the casual passer-by, the Akdemir family’s workshop could be any traditional blacksmith’s forge. Dozens of hammers and tongs hang from the walls; kebab skewers, knives and axes lie across the benches; a length of steel glows in the fire. But for those familiar with fantasy worlds and gaming, a second look may be required.
Just a few steps inside the workshop's shutter-style doors, an enormous forged fantasy sword rests across a countertop, similar to the one wielded by the Lich King in the popular video game World of Warcraft. Elsewhere are weapons inspired by TV series and video games, including Game of Thrones and League of Legends, rendered in steel.
At the forge, Suleyman Akdemir, a large man with a furrowed brow, grips a glowing length of metal with long tongs, draws it from the fire, and lays it across the anvil. A few metres away, his father, Omer, 54, reaches for a tool. Then the power hammer crashes down, its blows reverberating through the narrow workshop and out into the covered streets of Izmir’s Kemeralti bazaar, forcing conversation to wait.
Suleyman, 30, wears a brown leather apron over a black T-shirt, his hands encased in black gloves. His father rarely stops working while he talks; Suleyman often pauses, turning towards his customers before returning to the forge.
Between father and son, exchanges are calm, almost formal. Here, they seem less like family than two craftsmen who have spent years learning how to work around one another.
When the hammer falls silent, Suleyman turns from the forge.
“Ever since I was a child. I’d say since I first learned to walk, I've been working here with hot forging,” he says, breaking into a smile.
The surroundings bear that history. The fantasy weapons are newcomers to a workshop where Suleyman's family has practised blacksmithing for generations. Yet, incongruous as they look among the agricultural tools and barbecue skewers, they may be one reason the forge is still running.
“Thank God, we can make anything we see,” Suleyman says.
That conviction has taken the Akdemirs somewhere his predecessors could hardly have imagined. Customers from around the world now send Suleyman images and ideas inspired by weapons they have seen on screen, which he interprets as individually designed, hand-forged pieces.
Kemeralti has been a commercial centre of Izmir for centuries, with its dense network of streets and hans stretching inland from the city's waterfront.
For Suleyman, one of his earliest memories is of its power hammer at his father’s workshop. He was seven or eight, he says, when he became fascinated by the machine, which weighs about 1.5 tonnes.
He watched it rise and fall over the incandescent iron.
“I was spellbound when I saw it,” he says. “I knew right then that I would do this for a living."
By 12, he was using a hammer himself. The first object he forged was considerably less dramatic than the weapons now surrounding him: everyday cooking utensils.
After school, he returned to the workshop, learning to make hoes, billhooks, axes, skewers and other household objects.
Blacksmithing was not his only possible future. Suleyman trained in taekwondo and considered pursuing sport professionally. But the difficulty of building a sustainable career in sport eventually brought him back to the trade he had known since childhood.
By then, the business he was inheriting was beginning to change.
Two or three decades ago, the family says, agricultural tools and basic hardware accounted for nearly all its production. Their customers came largely from Izmir and the surrounding countryside, looking for practical objects made for work. Then some of that work began to disappear.
Factory production could make many everyday tools more cheaply, while changes in the work around them erased the need for others. As tobacco farming declined, so did orders for the needles the Akdemirs once made for growers. Shoemakers who had relied on their hand-forged sole-cutting blades turned instead to laser-cutting technology. Other agricultural tools increasingly faced competition from mass-produced alternatives.
One by one, some of the objects that had kept the forge busy were becoming obsolete.
Omer's generation had inherited a craft. Suleyman was confronting a different question: what happens when people no longer need the things that craft traditionally produces?
"The work my father and his generation do appeals to a specific demographic," he says. "They make general hardware products. But in truth, they craft them with such artistry that I felt it belonged somewhere far beyond."
In 2014, he decided to see how far and opened an Instagram account.
Initially, the internet brought relatively ordinary requests.
Suleyman's first online customer was a police officer in Erzurum who wanted a hand-forged machete for outdoor use. Making it was easier than sending it: the courier repeatedly refused to accept a parcel containing such a sharp blade.
"I went back and forth to the courier four times for a single product," he recalls.
Then, in 2016, an order came in that pointed to an entirely different market.
The Turkish historical drama Dirilis: Ertugrul (Resurrection: Ertugrul) was attracting a huge following at the time. The series would eventually be broadcast in more than 60 countries. One of its main characters, Turgut Alp, carried a distinctive axe.
A customer in Turkiye called the workshop and asked Suleyman to make one; it took him almost a week.
Then another request arrived, and another.
"We made that axe. After that, people started asking, 'Can you make this, can you make that?'” he says. “As we kept doing it, we grew to love it."
The commissions became progressively stranger. Instead of bringing Suleyman an object to copy or describing a familiar tool, customers began sending images from films and games.
A fictional weapon presents a peculiar problem for a blacksmith. On screen, it does not necessarily have to obey the rules of weight, balance or construction. In Suleyman's hands, it must.
When an unfamiliar commission arrives, he sits at a computer at the side of the working area, and rewatches film scenes, pauses gameplay footage to study details before sketching his own version and working out how its components might fit together
"This isn't something you can just 'strike, forge, and hand over.'” he says. “It's an entirely custom design. How will it fit together, how will I cast the mould ... I research every single detail."
For the most complex pieces, developing the first version can take two and a half to three months. Once Suleyman has solved the design, making another becomes easier.
He says he has never looked at a request and thought it impossible. For him, the challenge is simply figuring out how.
Omer has spent most of his life here. He describes a chain of blacksmiths stretching back generations.
"My father's master's master was an apprentice here during the Greek occupation,” he says, referring to the Greek occupation of Izmir between 1919 and 1922. “Then came my father's master, my father, myself, and now my son."
The workshop's history predates the Akdemir family. According to Omer, a man named Sabri Alim was an apprentice there during the Greek occupation, and later took over from his own master, Suleyman Acarlar. In 1955, Omer's father, Suleyman Akdemir, arrived from Konya and began working under Sabri as an apprentice. He eventually took over the workshop himself, before passing the craft to his son Omer.
The family cannot establish that every generation worked in this exact room; what has endured is the blacksmithing tradition within Kemeralti.
Omer studied blacksmithing at vocational high school and later trained in lathe operation, but says the workshop was his real education.
When he began, the workshop produced shoe-sole cutting blades, tobacco needles, and agricultural tools. Laser cutting eventually displaced the blades they made for shoemakers. Tobacco farming declined. Other products simply stopped being ordered.
If that disappearance bothers Omer, he shows little nostalgia for it.
"I am open to progress of any kind,” he says, continuing to work as he talks. “If you stay fixed in one place, you cannot grow. The work we used to do disappeared. What were we supposed to do, insist on making things no one needed?”
Nor does he see anything particularly radical in his son's use of the internet. To Omer, it has simply changed who can find them.
"Suppose someone in a village in Kastamonu wants something custom,” he says, referring to the province in northern Turkiye. “Under normal circumstances, that person could never reach me. But through the internet, they do."
He gestures towards the workshop. "And since we have no shortage of craft skill, we can make whatever anyone asks for."
Almost on cue, the automatic shutter opens. A man walks in carrying an old axe with a loose handle.
Omer takes it to his workbench and begins repairing it. The customer, meanwhile, looks around. His attention moves from the everyday tools towards the swords and oversized axes.
"Did you really make these here?" he asks.
A few minutes later, his axe repaired, he disappears back into Kemeralti.
The transition looks almost seamless now: old axe through the door, fantasy sword on the wall. But it wasn't.
For years, the family's daytime business still revolved around its conventional orders. If Suleyman wanted to experiment, he had to wait until everybody else had finished.
"I worked here at night for nine years."
When Kemeralti's shutters came down, he started again.
He relit the forge, tested quenching temperatures, experimented with moulds and worked through designs he had never attempted before. Some nights, he slept in a small room he had set aside inside the workshop. Then, he got up and returned to work.
As orders grew from one to two, three, five and then 10, the family's initial scepticism turned to curiosity. Suleyman says business volume more than doubled within a year of starting online sales.
Eventually, the experiments he had squeezed into the night became the larger part of the business.
Custom and specialised products now account for roughly 80 to 90 percent of revenue, he says. The workshop handles about 450 orders annually, with customers in countries including Germany, the Netherlands and Switzerland; exports generate about 35 percent of revenue.
A piece that might sell for 2,000 Turkish lira ($40) domestically can command considerably more overseas, Suleyman says.
But the story he enjoys telling most is not about financial success; it’s about a lost axe.
A customer had taken one of his hand-forged axes hiking in the Kaz Mountains, between Balikesir and Canakkale in western Turkiye, and lost it. Months later, someone else found it.
There was no brand or maker's stamp on the steel. Yet, Suleyman says, the finder recognised his workmanship.
"If anyone made this," Suleyman recalls with a laugh, "it has to be Suleyman."
The axe, he says, eventually found its way back to its owner.
At the back of the workshop, another craftsman is quietly working with his hands. But his route here was very different.
Away from the heaviest hammering, wood shavings cover a smaller bench. Yagiz Can Sonmez, 33, works at the sanding station in protective goggles, busily shaping a handle.
Unlike Suleyman, he wasn’t born into blacksmithing, but went looking for it.
Sonmez had previously worked as a sadekar, a goldsmith artisan, in Istanbul's Grand Bazaar. After studying at university, he moved to Izmir and opened a shoe boutique in Alsancak with his wife.
"One day, while sitting in the store, my fascination with hot metalwork resurfaced," he says. "I started researching online to see who was doing this in Izmir. That's how I found Suleyman."
At first, he came just to watch. Then he started returning on weekends, picked up the hammer, and began learning. Eventually, he closed the boutique and moved into blacksmithing full-time.
"What drew me here is the ability to project what's in your mind and soul onto a hard metal,” he says. “It comes from within. You start a project with nothing specific in mind, and as you progress, something takes shape. In the end, the final piece is something you couldn't have even envisioned at the start."
His background in goldsmithing gives him a different approach to the work.
"Suleyman leans toward classic designs. I focus more on intricate, detailed work. Blending those two approaches works well for us; it’s like two opposing poles coming together."
"Our styles are different," Suleyman says, smiling.
A neat symmetry seems to run through their journeys into the craft. Suleyman had turned to the internet to find people interested in what an old forge could make, while years later, Yagiz used the internet to find someone who could teach him how to forge.
Suleyman hopes eventually to establish a creative space locally where visitors could try blacksmithing and encounter woodworking and leathercraft alongside it.
There are not many places left in Kemeralti where someone like Yagiz could have done this.
According to Akin Oz, vice president of the Izmir Ironworkers Craftsmen and Artisans Chamber, Solomon Metal is now the only active hot-blacksmithing operation remaining in the historic bazaar.
The decline is visible in the objects Omer no longer makes: blades replaced by laser cutting, tobacco needles left behind by changes in farming, tools undercut by industrial production.
Traditional craftsmanship is one of five forms of “intangible cultural heritage” recognised under a UNESCO convention adopted in 2003 and ratified by Turkiye in 2006. The designation is concerned less with preserving the objects craftspeople produce than with safeguarding the knowledge and skills used to make them, and ensuring those skills are passed on.
Inside the Akdemir workshop, that distinction is easy to understand.
It is knowing how to judge the heat of iron by eye; how to bring the hammer down at the correct angle; how to temper the steel. It is knowledge acquired by standing beside somebody who already knows, says Suleyman.
By late afternoon, Kemeralti begins to empty. Tea sellers collect empty glasses. The crowds in the narrow alleys thin. Inside the workshop, the three men are still at their stations. After pounding through the workshop for much of the day, the power hammer finally falls silent.
Generations ago, the customers seeking out the family's blacksmiths needed tools for the work immediately around them. Today, some live thousands of kilometres away. They find Suleyman through a screen and send him images of objects that may never have existed outside one.
And despite everything that has changed, the request often comes down to something remarkably simple. Can you make this?
Suleyman has spent most of his life working out the answer. "I can."

title: Learning to Live With the Aral Sea’s Changed Landscape
content:
In February, participants from a new school in Nukus joined local foresters on the dried bed of the Aral Sea to plant saxaul. The shrubs can take root in salty ground and help hold down dust blowing across Karakalpakstan. Foresters from the Karauzyak State Forestry Department guided the work, drawing on years of experience in the region.
The planting exercise, organized with the United Nations Development Programme, offered an early indication of how the Aral School intends to teach. Its participants work alongside people already responding to the sea’s retreat, learning from the landscape and those who live with its consequences.
Now, the school is preparing for a second intake with a six-month residency in Nukus from January to June 2027. Architect and curator Joseph Grima will lead the program, which will focus on climate and landscape. Applications are open until October 25.
Based in the capital of Uzbekistan’s autonomous republic of Karakalpakstan, the school brings international practitioners together with participants from the region. The Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF), which established it, announced the new intake and Grima’s appointment during an assembly at the Savitsky Museum in Nukus. The museum owes its remarkable collection to Igor Savitsky, who rescued thousands of works rejected by the Soviet authorities, finding them a refuge in remote Nukus.
Gayane Umerova, chair of ACDF, and Grima spoke to The Times of Central Asia about the school’s long-term goals and how local people will help shape its work.
“The Aral School was never conceived as a single cohort or a single event. It’s a long-term commitment by the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF) in line with the Government’s plan for Karakalpakstan,” she told The Times of Central Asia. “The programme is designed from the ground up to avoid simply taking knowledge without giving anything back. The cohorts live in Nukus for half a year, not for a two-week field trip, precisely so that the landscape and the people in it are teachers, not subjects.”
“Participants would also work directly with local professional bodies and institutions,” Umerova said. “Local experts sit inside the programme’s design, not as guest lecturers brought in to validate conclusions already reached,” she said.
Once the world’s fourth-largest lake, the Aral Sea shrank as Soviet irrigation projects diverted water from the Amu Darya and Syr Darya to grow cotton and other crops. The retreat devastated fishing communities and exposed a seabed contaminated by agricultural chemicals. Wind carried salt and dust across the surrounding land.
In Moynaq, once a fishing port, fishermen dug channels through the sand to reach the retreating water. Eventually, they abandoned their grounded boats, leaving rusting hulls on what had been the seabed.
The consequences differ across the former sea. In Kazakhstan, the Kokaral Dam has helped the North Aral recover, raising water levels and supporting the return of fishing. The southern basin remains severely depleted.
For the school, that damaged environment is also a place where people continue to farm and build livelihoods. Its first course concentrated on food and water at a household level. The second will examine the land and river systems that sustain them, including the effects of irrigation and the movement of salt through the landscape.
For Gulnaz Abutova, founder of the Clean Water project, those pressures became tangible while picking cotton in Turtkul in 2014. She told The Times of Central Asia in 2025 about the experience. “I even saw people using water from irrigation channels (aryks) for cooking, boiling it and adding it to their food.”
Grima told TCA he had previously thought of design education as a formula that could be applied anywhere, but “Nukus has shifted that perception.”
“It has reframed a question for me: not ‘how do we bring good design here’ but ‘how does the landscape itself teach the discipline something it doesn’t already know.’”
His background includes leading Design Academy Eindhoven and research into architecture that uses fewer finite natural resources. In Nukus, the approach will bring design into contact with environmental research, asking how changes in land use shape everyday life.
Ahead of the assembly, Grima visited the International Innovation Centre for the Aral Sea Basin and the Amu Darya. He also toured the Academy of Sciences of Karakalpakstan and met specialists from the region.
Umerova outlined how the foundation would judge the school’s progress.
“In practical terms: growth in the number of regional participants in each cohort, deeper integration with local professional bodies, and projects that move from the classroom into implementation, whether that’s in agriculture, water systems, or landscape design,” she said.
“We are hosting the Aral School Assembly this month, which is a deliberate three-day knowledge transfer programme; alumni and mentors pass on the questions they leave behind, so local insight builds and develops across the new cohort instead of resetting,” she told TCA.
“We’re building in publication/presentation and exhibition as explicit next steps and deliverables, so the method and the findings travel beyond the school, and the whole programme community and region itself gets to keep and use them,” Grima said. “The 2027 cohort will deliberately sharpen its focus toward participants from the region itself.”
Recruiting people who already live with the consequences would help keep the work rooted there, he noted.
There is already work to build on. In April, ACDF presented twelve objects developed by the first cohort at Milan Design Week. The collection grew from research into the region’s food and water systems and explored the use of accessible, sustainable materials.
The broader water problems require decisions far beyond the school. A World Bank-backed cooperation project is intended to improve the management of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya basins, with shared data and coordination between countries central to that work. The residency in Nukus operates at a smaller scale, allowing researchers to examine how those pressures affect particular places and households.
“Culture here isn’t just decoration on top of environmental policy. We see it as a way of building relationships between landscape, heritage, and the people who live with the consequences of what happened to this sea,” Umerova said.
The school forms part of a wider series of ACDF initiatives in Karakalpakstan, including the Aral Culture Summit, first held in April 2025.
“We’ll also be watching whether the Aral Culture Summit and the School continue to reinforce and complement each other, research impacting exhibitions, exhibitions feeding the next round of questions,” she said.
Alongside the postgraduate program, ACDF has announced the first Aral Artistic Research Fellowship. The nine-month fellowship has been awarded to Uzbekistan-born artists Zukhra and Fotima Sharipova, whose work examines landscape, material culture, environmental transformation and locally embedded knowledge.
Their research will continue until June 2027, with ACDF providing production and logistical support. The resulting work is expected to be presented at the second Aral Culture Summit in spring 2027.
Zukhra plans to expose raw cotton canvas to the landscape across two seasons, allowing salt and wind to alter its surface. She will also work with local craftspeople to explore Karakalpak ornament and textile traditions. Cotton gives the project a particular resonance in a region whose water systems were reshaped to support its cultivation.
Fotima will make pigments from local minerals and plants. Her research will build visual and sound archives, incorporating recorded voices into an installation. According to the foundation, both artists begin their fieldwork in Karakalpakstan in September.
The school’s application page says there is no tuition fee. Accommodation and research costs are covered, and participants receive a monthly stipend. The call is aimed at postgraduate practitioners, including people working in design and environmental research. The selected cohort is due to be announced on December 1.
“If we succeed, in a few years’ time the Aral Sea will be spoken about internationally not only for what was lost, but for what is being learned and built here,” Umerova said.

title: What te reo Māori taught me about the Irish language I never learned
content: I was told that Gaeilge was a language of the past. Learning about te reo Māori showed me what had really been taken from us – and what it means to fight for a language’s future. Growing up in Ireland, I attended a rural school with fewer than 60 pupils. Every morning, we’d clasp our sticky hands together and thrum the Lord’s Prayer. When the teacher called the roll, each child would say “anseo”, which means here – the first Gaeilge, or traditional Irish, word I learned. My teachers and family told me Gaeilge was a dead language; not a vital part of our heritage, but an inconvenient hour stuffed between maths and the lunch break. It was something we only needed to learn enough of to pass our exams. I spent years matching the shapes of the words to each other, never truly understanding their meaning. It wasn’t until I was here in Aotearoa, on the other side of the world, that I realised I grew up less than an hour away from one of Ireland’s strongest Gaeltacht regions, in which the community speaks primarily in Gaeilge. My language was still very much alive and I could have been a part of it. When I feel the weight of this missed opportunity, it makes me want to scream loud enough to wake my younger self up. When I was contemplating learning te reo Māori, I was hesitant because of my lack of Gaeilge. How could I ask someone to teach me their reo and expect them to trust that I would honour their language when I hadn’t honoured my own? This week is the 51st Wiki o Te Reo Māori. Ireland has had Seachtain na Gaeilge (Irish Language Week) since 1902. September here, March there, both held at the beginning of spring, breathing in new life and uplifting the languages. Our cultures are both deeply embedded in language, land and whakapapa. We were both colonised by the same country and, in some situations, the same people played roles in the colonisation of both countries. Some of the legislation used by the British in Ireland was implemented here, and the same tools of oppression used on the Irish were employed against Māori, including by some Irish settlers. Our timelines weave across each other like bruised rushes. Te tiriti was signed only six years before the Irish famine began. We often only understand the colonisation of a country in the language of the coloniser, which prevents us from understanding the depth of grief, horror and significance of the pain caused. If we talk about a mountain or river being bought, sold or stolen in English, it means something entirely different to hearing the same story in te reo from a Māori person speaking of how their tipuna, their ancestor, was bought, sold or stolen. Just as it is impossible to represent in English what certain sacred Irish landmarks hold – the centuries of story, memories and meaning that are embedded in the language we use to speak about them cannot be replicated in the language of those who tried to rip it all away from us. Bilingual Gaelige road signs in Creggs, County Galway. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons) Irish Ogham inscriptions date back to the 4th century, while te reo Māori came from the Polynesian languages brought to Aotearoa from Hawaiki, arriving here around the 13th century. Our languages sustained us for centuries; they were how we expressed what we understood about the land, what to plant and when. As the late Manchán Magan wrote, the Irish have 32 words for a field, because we needed that many. Similarly in te reo, there are at least 30 names for different types of oneone or soils. Our languages thrived until the English got involved. In the 1700s, while the Crown dug its claws into Ireland – destroying our Brehon legal system and enforcing English as the main language – James Cook was arriving on the shores of Aotearoa. Systematically, the native languages were pushed to the peripheries and associated with being rural and uneducated, while English was associated with prosperity. Education was used as a weapon against both languages. Systematic physical and psychological abuse of indigenous children literally beat the language out of them and their homes. But it wasn’t violence that posed the biggest threat, it was shame. In Aotearoa, students were beaten for speaking Māori in front of their classes and whānau. In Ireland, children were made to wear a bata scóir or tally stick around their necks. Every time they spoke Gaeilge, a notch would be added to the stick – the number of notches determining their punishment. Shame like that lasts generations, and produces adults who protect their children by denying them their indigenous language. The history of both Ireland and Aotearoa is scarred from the words torn from our ancestors’ mouths. An aching gap remains inside us as we try to reclaim what should never have been taken. After the Republic of Ireland reclaimed its independence, Gaeilge was declared the country’s first official language in 1937. It became compulsory to learn it in school. However, the north of Ireland remains under British rule and people there continue to fight to keep the Gaeilge language alive. In 1987, te reo Māori became an official language of Aotearoa after the Waitangi Tribunal found te reo was a taonga protected under te tiriti. Both countries reached a turning point when citizens focused on ensuring children could learn the languages again. This began healing the fractures between generations that had been unable to pass down their language. Kōhanga reo and kura kaupapa in Aotearoa, and gaelscoileanna in Ireland, were started by groups of parents and activists. Conradh na Gaeilge or the Gaelic League, the Gaeltacht civil rights movement in Ireland, the Māori language petition and Te Reo Māori Society of Wellington played essential roles in uplifting and sustaining our languages. Ireland launched its first indigenous-language radio station, Raidió na Gaeltachta, in 1972, which was followed by iwi radio in 1987 in Aotearoa. TV stations came in the 1990s and 2000s: TG4 in Ireland and Whakaata Māori in Aotearoa. This helped bring the languages into present, daily life, beaming them into homes across the countries. Te reo Māori is ebbing and flowing like the tides. (Image: Getty; additional design: Archi Banal) Still, the fight continues. Beyond these key moments, there have been ongoing, constant threats to the languages, and millions of people who have fought and fight, daily against these threats. According to Unesco, the world loses a language every two weeks, with at least 40% of the world’s 7,000 languages considered endangered. Gaeilge and te reo Māori continue to stand. As time goes on, both languages have progressed into digital and mainstream media, with music providing one of the most significant revival efforts. Jordyn with a Why, Te Kahureremoa, Stan Walker and Marlon Williams in Aotearoa and Roís, Kneecap and Seo Linn in Ireland are all artists proudly uplifting their reo, laying a path for others to follow. Irish signage features place names in Gaeilge first with English second. It grounds you in place, reminding you that you’re on indigenous land that some asshole tried to rename. The current president of Ireland, Catherine Connolly, made Gaeilge a central feature of her election campaign and won by a landslide. The Irish government is targeting 20% of public sector recruits to be Gaeilge-competent by 2030 as part of its ambition to become a fully bilingual public service. Meanwhile in Aotearoa, the current government has aggressively stripped back reo in public institutions, with English being prioritised over Māori. Significant money and time has been spent securing English as an official language despite the move being widely criticised. This led to Green MP Tamatha Paul’s viral kōrero in which she called English a “bastard language” and questioned why the “snowflakes” in charge can’t cope with hearing a language outside of their own. While it’s easy to think te reo is only being bludgeoned, there are also people working hard to uplift it. Those teaching their mokopuna, joining kura reo, signing petitions, speaking te reo at home and work, supporting their whānau. Grassroots community groups continue their mahi. Maihi Karauna – the Crown’s Māori Language Strategy – has committed to working towards one million people being able to speak conversational Māori by 2040 and 85% of Aotearoa to value te reo as a key part of its national identity. It’s our responsibility asIrish here in Aotearoa to help provide Māori protection over their reo. We don’t get to be racist and Irish, and we don’t get to be Irish living on colonised land without honouring its history, people and language. To live as te tiriti partners, we need to understand each other, and that begins with language. We don’t need to learn te reo to do this, but we do need to show it our respect. More Reading

title: Tuku whenua: A day Aucklanders can come to know and share
content: As we celebrate Te Wiki o te Reo Māori, it feels right to remember an important moment for Ngāti Whātua and Auckland. These kaupapa meet this week. Both ask us to listen, learn and reconnect with the people, places and stories of Tāmaki Makaurau. I grew up in Auckland knowing I was Ngāti Whātua, but not all the kōrero about the whenua beneath my feet. I knew the streets, beaches and landmarks, but few of their original names or histories. I knew the city I could see, but not the story underneath it. The history was close. My father, Hapi Pihema, was one of many kaumātua and cultural leaders who worked to strengthen our people and rebuild our cultural estate. He helped protect and pass on the kōrero. As a boy, I did not understand that work. Sometimes the stories closest to us take the longest to hear. As I grew older, I learned more about Apihai Te Kawau and the tūpuna beside him. In 1840, Te Kawau sent people north to invite governor William Hobson to Tāmaki Makaurau. He saw that a new township could bring peace, trade, opportunity, and hoped Māori and Pākehā could build a relationship together. On 18 September 1840, Te Kawau and his people made 3,000 acres available to establish Auckland. This is often called a gift, but tuku whenua means much more. The land was not handed over and forgotten. It was an act of mana, leadership and manaakitanga, offered in the hope that people would care for one another and build a future together. Sadly, that is not how the story unfolded. Ngāti Whātua lost almost all its land. By the 1950s, our people at Ōkahu Bay were virtually landless, and homes were pulled down before a royal visit. Years later, Takaparawhau became an important fight for justice and the survival of our people. Joe Pihema (Photo: supplied, additional design: Tina Tiller) That hurt is part of the story, but not all of it. We also remember the courage and generosity of Te Kawau and our tūpuna. They looked ahead with hope. We must hold both sides: the future they offered and what happened when the promise was not kept. For me, learning this history has been about finding my place. It explains why some places carry so much feeling, why Māori names matter and why whenua can feel familiar even when its stories are unknown. It has shown me what I must pass on. Today, Ngāti Whātua will gather at Auckland’s viaduct to remember Te Kawau and his people. Through karanga, karakia, whaikōrero and mōteatea, we will honour 1840. Beside the Waitematā, we remember the hopes our tūpuna held for the city that would grow here. This remembrance is not only for Ngāti Whātua. It is an open invitation to Auckland. That spirit sits at the heart of the Poumatua Festival, finishing Saturday 19 September. For the first time on this scale, Te Kawau, tuku whenua and Auckland’s beginnings are being shared openly. Through kōrero, kapa haka, learning, creativity and whakawhanaungatanga, we welcome Aucklanders from every background. We invite people to get out and explore this whenua. Walk across the land. Learn the Māori names. Find out about the maunga, waterways, bays and old pathways beneath our roads. Reach into those connections. They help us understand where we live and build identity and belonging. Whether your family has been here for generations or recently arrived, there is a place for you in this story of our shared city. Then, in 1951-2, the residents of the papakāinga (village) were forcibly evicted, and Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei’s last settlement was burned down to ‘tidy’ the area for the visit of Queen Elizabeth II. (Photo: Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei) Perhaps 18 September can become a day Aucklanders come to know and share for themselves. A day to stop, look around and think about what made this city possible. If people pick it up in their own way, its meaning will grow. In time, Auckland may choose to recognise it officially as a day of importance. My hope is simple: I want our children to know that Tāmaki Makaurau has a story shaped by courage, generosity and hope. On 18 September, Ngāti Whātua invites Aucklanders to remember with us and reconnect with that beginning. It can be a day we share as proud Aucklanders, each of us searching for connection and identity. By knowing this story, we may come to know our city, and one another, a little better. More Reading

title: African-American Blacksmiths Forge a Lineage of Sankofa
content:
African-American Blacksmiths Forge a Lineage of Sankofa
Blacksmiths in the South have long embedded West African symbolism into gates, rails, and window bars, proof that the craft evolved with every hand that held the hammer.
This article is part of a series focusing on underrepresented craft histories, researched and written by the 2025 Craft Archive Fellows, and organized in collaboration with the Center for Craft.
Growing up between New Orleans and Savannah, I was aware of the ironwork around me, but I didn’t really see it. While visiting a friend in New York City last year, I stopped mid-sentence to photograph a window with two metal Sankofa symbols. New York immediately felt familiar through that one piece of ironwork. I’ve been paying particular attention to Sankofa symbols in ironwork on gates, stair rails, and window bars. They’re usually black, other times painted white, sometimes incorporating leaves, flowers, or, in New Orleans, the fleur-de-lis. But again and again, I noticed that familiar heart.
Having studied West African traditions, including Ghanaian Adinkra symbols, I was familiar with Sankofa. It translates roughly to “go back and fetch it” in Akan, an exhortation to revisit the past and retrieve what’s needed for the present. Sometimes it’s a bird turning backward to retrieve an egg from its back (its past). Other times, it resembles a conventional heart with inward-spiraling coils.
Because Adinkra symbols originate in West Africa, where most African Americans have ancestral roots, I wondered if our blacksmiths embedded reminders to not forget where we came from into the ironwork. Was the design more than decoration? If so, was it ever legible within the Black community?
Interviewing blacksmiths and scholars and digging through the archives shifted my focus. Instead, I wanted to investigate how cultural knowledge is transmitted and how we recognize cultural continuity when the evidence isn’t linear.
Dr. Earnestine Jenkins, a professor of art history who curated a 2022 exhibition on African-American blacksmithing at the Metal Museum in Memphis, Tennessee, helped me understand why that evidence rarely falls into a neat line. “Whenever people migrate,” Dr. Jenkins explained, “naturally, they don’t do the things the same way they did them in their homeland. They have to make adaptations.” Cultural continuity ain’t the absence of change, but what manages to travel through it.

title: An East Somerville laundromat transforms into an art gallery
content:
Support WBUR
An East Somerville laundromat transforms into an art gallery
Editor's note: This story is an excerpt from WBUR's weekly arts and culture newsletter, The ARTery. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox, sign up here.
Cambridge-based photographer Mario Quiroz has dreamed of seeing his work inside a laundromat.
At City Line Laundromat in East Somerville, locally known as “la lavandería de la Broadway,” his dream is now a reality.
“It’s a collective living room,” said Quiroz. “If you ask me to choose between showing this work at the laundromat or as a solo show at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, I definitely will choose the laundromat.”
Quiroz’s exhibit “Re UNIDOS: Pasado Presente y Futuro/Past, Present & Future” is a collection of photographs and audio interviews documenting Unidos, the K-8 dual language program at East Somerville Community School (ESCS) for English and Spanish learners. The photographs will be on view from Sept. 15 to Oct. 15, in honor of Hispanic Heritage Month.
Quiroz grew up in El Salvador and moved to the United States in 1999, and received his bachelor’s and MFA from Lesley University in 2015 and 2017.
For the past two decades, Quiroz has documented the lives of many New England immigrants. His 24 projects include collaborations with Fitchburg’s Latino communities, Massachusetts’ domestic workers and members of Padres Latinos in Somerville, a community support group for Spanish-speaking Latino parents in Somerville. He hopes to use his art as a vehicle for social change.
“My practice is for the people, by the people,” he said. “My practice is community-based, which means that I always work with a community partner.”
By day, Quiroz is a pre-K educator at ESCS, where he’s known as “Mr. Mario.” For the photography project, Quiroz worked closely with Analiese Reigstad, the dual-language program specialist at the school.
Reigstad realized there wasn’t much information on Unidos’ 26-year history available online. The program commissioned Quiroz to document “a day in the life” of the students and educators.
From May to June of this year, Quiroz photographed students, educators and staff at the school with his 35mm film camera and signature black-and-white film stock. He would capture photos during the day of student life, develop and scan the photos at home, then show them to the ESCS community in the following days.
“We went to some classrooms and would just unfurl it and tell students about the process and ask for their perspectives and how it made them feel or what they noticed about it,” said Reigstad.
East Somerville is one of the city's most racially diverse neighborhoods; 35% of its residents are immigrants, many of whom come from El Salvador and Central America. The Unidos program at ESCS currently enrolls 370 students, and 283 reported their home language as Spanish, according to Reigstad.
“When you look back at history, all the bad things happen to people that don't have access to money, access to power,” said Quiroz. “And it's even worse when you don't have language access.”
At the opening reception on Wednesday afternoon, ESCS staff, students and parents gathered with laundromat customers and Somerville Mayor Jake Wilson. Visitors rotated around the room to gaze at the six large fabric sheets hanging from the ceiling. Each sheet displayed a grid of 12 of Quiroz’s black-and-white photographs, alongside a QR code linking to audio interviews with the ESCS community.
Included in one of the photographs is Sonia Conde’s son, who is a sixth grader at ESCS. Conde works for the city’s Office of Housing Stability and is originally from Peru.
