There was no refrigeration then, she points out, and the logic was simple: use what you had before it went to waste.
Story continues below this ad
It is a logic that appears again and again across regions.
In Andhra Pradesh, Hyderabad-based chef Vignesh Ramachandran, chef-partner at Theta Theta Telugu and Coffee Sangam, describes Telugu food as a treasure trove of chutneys. “Virtually any vegetable can be turned into one,” he says. In Telugu, chutney is called pachadi, and there is pachadi made from aubergine, ridge gourd, bottle gourd, ivy gourd, raw mango, cabbage and tomato.
His grated raw mango chutney, made with fresh coconut, chilli powder, salt and finished with a tempering of mustard seeds, curry leaves and dried red chillies, is very different from the chopped or pickled mango preparations many are familiar with.
In Assam, the tools too were part of the process. Nath recalls the dheki, a foot-operated pounding device used when families lived jointly and larger batches were required. Hard fruits such as hog plum were pounded whole. Softer star fruit was chopped and roughly pounded on a silbata, then served with chilli, mustard oil, salt and coriander. Lentils also found their way into chutney.
Sour, sweet and seasonal
Story continues below this ad
Before chutney, Bengal had tok and ombol. Today, they sit in harmony with one another.
“Tok and ombol are largely used interchangeably depending on where you hail from, but the word tok literally translates to ‘sour’. It’s a sour palate cleanser and has a definite place in a Bengali meal,” says Kolkata-based Sujoy Chatterjee, co-founder of Amar Khamar, which brings Bengal’s indigenous produce from farms to tables.
An old tamarind tok, he says, works well between the protein course and dessert. Sometimes, tok is eaten with a little rice so that the rice absorbs the sourness better. It is usually runny, and fish can also be used — early autumn, for instance, is the time for tok/ombol made with the head of hilsa.
Chutney, in contrast, is fruitier, sweeter and thicker. “Papaya chutney with lime juice is a classic,” he says.
Story continues below this ad
Chutney takes Chatterjee back to another time: weddings in the 1980s, when cooks arrived with large utensils and made big batches of tomato chutney with dates, cashews and raisins. Seasonality still decides what appears on many plates — Jolphai chutney in Assam in winter, kul’er chutney during Saraswati Puja in Bengal, raw mango tok in summer.
The chutney pantry
Up north in Kashmir, chutney is not an occasional accompaniment either. “Chutneys are an integral part of Kashmiri food culture, whether it’s the Kashmiri Muslim Wazwan or Pandit cuisine,” says chef Prateek Sadhu, a Kashmiri who grew up in Delhi.
Three are considered essential: “Doon Chetin, made with walnuts; Mujj Chetin, made with radish and particularly integral to weddings; and Pudin Chetin, made with Kashmiri mint, which is notably peppery,” says chef-founder of award-winning restaurant, Naar.
The method matters as much as the ingredients. A Kashmiri stone mortar and pestle is used to crush radish with salt, green chillies and kala jeera before yoghurt is added. For the walnut version, walnuts, radish, onions and soaked dried Kashmiri red chillies are mashed together, with yoghurt acting as a binder. These are not seasonal, they are constants.
Story continues below this ad
Chef Thomas Zacharias, founder of The Locavore, remembers a similar insistence on method from his Kerala home, where what is broadly called chutney in English is usually chammanthi or chammandhi. His grandmother, Ammamma’s ulli chammandi, made with green chillies, coconut oil and shallots and eaten with boiled tapioca, was always made with a mortar and pestle. That chutney later inspired the version of Eggs Kejriwal when The Bombay Canteen opened in February 2015.
Zacharias says his work with The Locavore has only reinforced how astonishing the range is: chutneys can be made from cultivated or foraged leaves, flowers, fruit, seeds, vegetable scraps, wild herbs, dried fish, fermented ingredients and even ants.
For Shahu Patole, author of Dalit Kitchens of Marathwada, thecha and kharda (top right) — the roasted, pounded green or red chilli chutneys now familiar across Maharashtra — were almost daily food during his childhood.
When chutney is the meal
For Shahu Patole, who hails from the Mang community in Marathwada, chutney wasn’t an accompaniment. It was the meal.
Story continues below this ad
“Some of us still have to run to the fields to work and don’t have the luxury of buying and making vegetables, so what would we do? Take a bhakri, put on a little kharda or thecha and the meal is done,” says the 64-year-old, who chronicled the foodways of Dalit communities in his 2016 Marathi book Anna He Apoorna Brahma, translated into English as Dalit Kitchens of Marathwada in 2024.
Dry chutneys were common at his home because they lasted longer. They typically combined red chilli powder, salt and another ingredient — peanuts (Shengadanayachi chatni), flax seeds (Jawasachi chatni), roselle (Ambadaichi chatni), dry prawn (Zinge) or dry Bombay duck (Bombilachi chatani). The main ingredient was roasted on a tawa, then pounded by hand with chilli, salt and, when available, garlic and coriander. There was also tikhat, simply red chilli powder and salt.
Anuradha Joshi Medhora and chef Prateek Sadhu.
Wet chutneys included thecha, made by pounding green chillies with salt; roasted chillies turned it into kharda. Then there was ola yesur: onions placed directly on the hot chulha after the bhakris were cooked, allowed to soften and then pounded with roasted green chilli and salt.
“We wouldn’t have oil. So we would cook meat in salt and turmeric, if available garlic-ginger paste and coriander and once done, add this ola yesur to give it more flavour,” Patole says.
More than a condiment
Story continues below this ad
A chutney with fish or meat has been a staple in some parts of the country. In Assam, fish was dried and smoked above the wood-fire kitchen stove on a bamboo rack called a chunga. When little else was available, it was pounded with chilli, chopped onion, mustard oil and salt. In Madhya Pradesh, leftovers from fish and mutton could become chutney too — maas ki chutney from leftover mutton, fish from lunch becoming chutney for dinner.
“There’s a saying in Marathi, ‘tondala lawaicha’, which means just enough to touch your mouth, and that’s exactly how much chutney one needed. But what it did was add a little punch to every meal,” says Medhora, founder of Charoli Foods, which began in 2015 as a pop-up serving the royal kitchens of Malwa and has since grown into a catering company specialising in royal cuisine.
It was also, she believes, a quiet culinary strategy in a patriarchal household. “Men then would get upset if the food wasn’t up to the mark. But you can’t cook elaborate meals all the time! So what would the women do? Add a little chutney, and it would spice up the most boring meal, and nobody would complain.”
Perhaps this is why chutney is so emotional. It is not merely what sits beside the food; it is a record of what was available, what was affordable, what grew in a particular season, what a grandmother knew to do with a peel, and what a mother could put together without measuring anything.
Story continues below this ad
For Zacharias, chutney is also a way of understanding a place. “Its ingredients and techniques can reveal a great deal about the local ecology, seasons, preservation practices and the knowledge held within home kitchens,” he says. At The Locavore, they featured Futkal Chutney from Jharkhand, made from tender wild fig buds gathered in a short season, boiled, sun-dried and later ground with roasted tomato, ginger, garlic and chilli. From Ladakh came Tangthur, made with buttermilk, seasonal greens and skotse, a wild Himalayan herb foraged in summer, pounded into cakes, dried and stored for winter. There was also Sukhti Chutney from Alibag, made with roasted and pounded dried jawla, garlic and chilli — particularly useful during the monsoon, when fresh seawater fish is less readily available. “Each of these is delicious, of course, but they also tell us how people respond to their surroundings and circumstances.”
There is nutrition in that little spoonful too. Munshaw-Ghildiyal points out that chutney helped complete the shadrasa — the six tastes — even as the rest of the plate changed with the seasons.
Much of this knowledge, she says, lived in the heads of women. Tanisha Phanbu, a home chef and proponent of Meghalaya cuisine, told Munshaw-Ghildiyal that after chutney was ground on the mawjingshoh, a ball of rice was rolled over the stone to collect every last bit of juice, flavour and spice. “People actually wait for those balls to come out,” says Munshaw-Ghildiyal.
Each dash of a chutney brings back a memory. Munshaw-Ghildiyal’s husband’s grandmother, Mohini Raturi, made a til-tamatar wali chutney that was closer in texture to an aloo sabzi. She wrote down the recipe during one of her visits to Dehradun, not knowing that it would be the last time she would see her.
Years later, she found the old notes, made the chutney and brought it home. Her husband Shekhar, who has co-published the book, finished it with six rotis that had originally been meant for dinner.
Recently, when Raturi’s great-granddaughter got married in Delhi, Munshaw-Ghildiyal made the chutney again. Her daughters and grandchildren were there.
“They were thrilled,” she says.
The recipe in the book is credited to Mohini Raturi. And perhaps that is what chutney has always done best: carry something forward — a season, a place, a way of eating, a little thrift, a grandmother’s instinct, or simply the memory of a meal, one small spoonful at a time.

title: Massacre site concerns halt plans for regional Victorian dog park
content:
Robinvale's proposed dog park halted over Tati Tati massacre site concerns
In short:
Works on a proposed Robinvale dog park have been paused after Tati Tati traditional owners raised concerns about the site's cultural significance.
They say it is a ceremonial, massacre and repatriation site for the Tati Tati people.
What's next?
State cultural body First Peoples — State Relations is investigating the matter.
A proposed dog park at Robinvale's Centenary Park has been put on hold after traditional land owners said the area contains Aboriginal ancestral remains.
Brothers Uncle Brendan Kennedy and Uncle John Kennedy said the area, traditionally known as Bumbang, is a ceremonial, massacre and repatriation site for the Tati Tati people.
Uncle Brendan said the Tati Tati people have always known about its significance.
"It's not new knowledge, and it didn't spring up just because they wanted to build the dog park,"he said.
"It's obvious that the investigations weren't thorough by whoever investigated the cultural significance of the area."
According to the two men, the last recorded Tati Tati ceremony held at the site was in 1892 and was witnessed by Annie Carrington, a woman who lived at the Bumbang estate as a girl.
In the 1960s, Ms Carrington recounted what she had seen to local historian Kaye Gross, who later shared the account in a letter to Uncle John.
The Kennedy brothers provided the letter to Swan Hill Rural City Council more than 15 years ago as part of a submission opposing a proposed rezoning of Centenary Park.
The letter had stopped that project at the time, but has since gone missing.
"We gave that letter to former Swan Hill councillor, Bill McGinty," Uncle Brendan said.
"We had First Peoples — State Relations investigating the Swan Hill Council about where that letter is and … Swan Hill Council doesn't have that letter.
"But we do know that letter did exist."
Council unaware of history
At the request of the state cultural body First Peoples — State Relations, Swan Hill Rural City Council has paused works at Centenary Park while investigations are undertaken.
Mayor Stuart King said the council was not aware of the site's history before work began, and that council had followed the required process and had an approved cultural heritage management plan for the dog park.
"Going through the process … to get a cultural heritage management plan done, we would expect that those issues would be identified through that process,"he said.
"It came as a bit of a surprise to us."
Cr King said it was disappointing to have projects halted after going through the proper processes.
Heritage concerns investigated
First Peoples — State Relations has confirmed work in the area has been stopped until the matter is resolved.
A Department of Premier and Cabinet spokesperson said the government was working with the Swan Hill Rural City Council and traditional owners to investigate.
Uncle John and Uncle Brendan have also contacted Deputy Premier Gabrielle Williams to order a cultural heritage audit regarding the Cultural Heritage Management Plan submitted as part of the dog park proposal.
A decision regarding the audit is due in the coming weeks.
The Kennedy brothers said they do not want any further works happening at the site.
"We definitely don't want a dog park built right on our repatriation site or on this ceremonial site," Uncle Brendan said.
They would like to see the area preserved and revegetated with native food and medicine plants, alongside cultural information about its Tati Tati history.
Uncle Brendan said protecting the site was important for future generations.
"We're trying to protect our heritage here," he said.

title: Mariscal Cáceres: concurso del Pescado Pango se realizó en fiesta por Virgen de la Merced
content:
17:39 | San Martín, set. 20.



Con el colorido y el bullicio propios de las celebraciones patronales, se dio inicio oficial a las festividades en honor a la Virgen de la Merced, patrona de la provincia de Mariscal Cáceres, región San Martín. Una de las actividades más esperadas por la población local fue el tradicional concurso costumbrista del Pescado Pango, que año tras año congrega a un numeroso público en torno a una de las expresiones más genuinas de la identidad cultural de la zona.


El certamen, que se ha convertido en un emblema de las fiestas mercedinas, puso a prueba la rapidez, destreza manual y el conocimiento práctico de las participantes en una dinámica tan sencilla en apariencia como exigente en su ejecución: pelar plátanos y retirar las escamas de pescados propios de la zona en el menor tiempo posible.
Bajo la atenta mirada del jurado y entre el aliento constante de familiares, amigos y curiosos, cada concursante desplegó técnicas transmitidas de generación en generación, en una suerte de homenaje viviente a las labores cotidianas que durante décadas han definido la vida ribereña de la provincia.
Tras varios minutos de intensa competencia, resultó ganadora la participante que logró completar ambas tareas —el pelado del plátano y el descamado del pescado— en el tiempo más corto, sin que ello fuera en desmedro de la calidad del trabajo realizado, uno de los criterios que el jurado tuvo en cuenta al momento de definir a la vencedora. Su triunfo fue celebrado con aplausos y vítores por el público asistente, que no dejó de acompañar cada etapa del concurso con entusiasmo.
La actividad fue organizada e impulsada por el Sindicato de Trabajadores de la Municipalidad Provincial de Mariscal Cáceres, entidad que, a través de esta y otras iniciativas similares, busca contribuir a la revaloración y preservación de las costumbres locales.
Según los organizadores, el propósito central de este tipo de concursos es generar espacios en los que las tradiciones puedan ser conocidas, practicadas y, sobre todo, transmitidas a las nuevas generaciones, de modo que el vínculo entre la población y su patrimonio cultural inmaterial no se debilite con el paso del tiempo.
El concurso costumbrista del Pescado Pango se enmarca dentro de un calendario más amplio de actividades programadas con motivo de las festividades de la Virgen de la Merced, celebraciones que combinan la fe religiosa con expresiones culturales, gastronómicas y recreativas propias de la provincia.
En esta ocasión, el evento sirvió como punto de encuentro para la población, que además de disfrutar de la competencia, tuvo la oportunidad de compartir un ambiente de confraternidad en torno a la celebración de su identidad.
Con esta primera actividad, la Municipalidad Provincial de Mariscal Cáceres y las organizaciones locales dan inicio formal a una agenda festiva que se extenderá en los próximos días, y que continuará reuniendo a los pobladores en torno a la devoción mariana y a la reafirmación de las tradiciones que distinguen a esta provincia sanmartinense.

title: Alux Nahual recibe las Llaves de la Ciudad de Providence, Rhode Island, por su aporte a la cultura en la comunidad centroamericana
content:
Escenario
Alux Nahual recibe las Llaves de la Ciudad de Providence, Rhode Island, por su aporte a la cultura en la comunidad centroamericana
La banda guatemalteca Alux Nahual recibió una distinción en Providence, Rhode Island, EE. UU., por su aporte a la cultura en una ciudad donde guatemaltecos residen y contribuyen al desarrollo de su comunidad.
La banda guatemalteca Alux Nahual recibe distinción en Providence, Rhode Island, EE. UU. (Foto Prensa Libre: Cortesía Juan Pablo Mijangos)
Alux Nahual continúa cosechando éxitos en la escena nacional e internacional. En la actualidad, la banda celebra 47 años de carrera musical durante una gira de conciertos por Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Costa Rica, México y EE. UU.
Sus integrantes viajaron a EE. UU. y fueron honrados con una distinción que otorga la ciudad por su aporte a la cultura de la comunidad centroamericana.
Brett Smiley, alcalde de Providence, entregó las Llaves de la Ciudad de Providence, Rhode Island, a la banda guatemalteca de rock, un reconocimiento que otorga la ciudad estadounidense a ciudadanos destacados.
De acuerdo con autoridades locales, las Llaves de la Ciudad constituyen uno de los honores cívicos más antiguos que se otorgan en la ciudad. Además, representan confianza y gratitud y, de forma simbólica, dejan las puertas de la ciudad abiertas para los condecorados.
En el caso de Alux Nahual, sus integrantes recibieron el reconocimiento debido a la importancia que la comunidad guatemalteca y centroamericana tiene para la localidad, donde guatemaltecos residen y aportan al desarrollo.
“Este es un reconocimiento que celebra la importancia de Alux Nahual en la escena musical y se hace en atención a la comunidad guatemalteca que habita la ciudad y que aporta tanto a nuestra cultura. De mi parte me siento honrado de recibirlos y darles esta distinción simbólica”, dijo Smiley.
De acuerdo con los músicos guatemaltecos, viajaron a Providence, Rhode Island, EE. UU., durante una gira en la que celebraron la independencia de Guatemala y Centroamérica. El 12 de septiembre recibieron la distinción durante un evento en la ciudad, debido a las gestiones de la organización comunitaria Guatemalan Center de New England.
“Nos sentimos muy halagados y felices por este honor tan grande. Uno nunca se imagina los caminos que tomarán las canciones. Trataremos de contribuir con nuestra música para que adornen las calles y los corazones de Providence”, indicó Álvaro Aguilar, vocalista de la banda.

title: Tairāwhiti's beaches overrun with forestry slash
content:
Tairāwhiti's beaches overrun with forestry slash
Tairāwhiti's beaches are some of the most well-known and loved in New Zealand, only now they're covered in forestry slash. It's so normal that some children have never known the sandy shores in their rōhe without it. Teuila Fuatai reports.
Graeme Atkins lives about 30 minutes from Ruatoria, near the mouth of Waiapu River and Tikapa beach.
The hilly, gravel road to his house runs alongside the Waiapu, and on a clear day, you get a full view of the lower part of the expansive waterway. It's wide and shallow, with the riverbed showing in a lot of places. Steep, stony hillside where the road is cut into run along one side while farmland borders the other.
Atkin's house, like all the properties around him, is off the grid. That includes the local marae, which runs on solar and has a chest freezer whānau around the area use for meat.
Being self-sufficient, living off the land, and the moana, is part of life, and it's been that way for generations, Atkins says.
"You don't see any power lines here," he says with a grin.
One of his three mokopuna, one-year-old Te Ahupo, hangs out with us for the afternoon.
Atkins says he'll be the 22nd generation of his family to whakapapa to the area.
"So that's such a comforting thought."
Less hopeful, and infinitely more challenging is what's happening with forestry in the region.
We head a couple of hundred metres up the road to look at Tikapa beach.
Like all the beaches we've seen on our trip around the East Cape, it's covered in forestry waste.
The slash and woody debris are washed down from forestry blocks when it rains, and when there's a major weather event - like cyclones Gabrielle and Hale in 2023 - the waterways, rivers and coastline are choked with it.
Atkins shows us pictures and videos of the beach after the storm - at first glance, it looks like someone's emptied dozens of boxes of match sticks onto a surface and taken a photo.
That's what came down the river, he says.
Another video shows kōura and paua littered among the slash and logs.
They are another casualty of what's happening on the forestry blocks, Atkins says, because when there's a storm, along with the trees and waste, huge amounts of soil and sediment go into the waterways and sea.
"I think they just get choked," he says, "it's heartbreaking."
Atkins says they first started to notice the slash on the beaches about 10 years ago.
"Our childhood around here, and the access to the beach - we could go to the beach whenever we wanted to.
"Since about 2014, 2015, once they started harvesting inside those Cyclone Bola forests…we just started noticing more and more forest waste - slash, logs, whatever you want to call it - ending up on our beach."
Cyclone Bola, which devastated the region in 1988, is mentioned in every conversation I have about forestry impacts in Tairāwhiti.
Like Gabrielle and Hale, the weather event had significant and long-lasting impacts on the region.
For hundreds of mana whenua like Atkins, who are shareholders in land blocks across their rōhe through whakapapa, it also triggered a fundamental shift in the use of that land to pine forest plantations.
The pine planting frenzy post-Cyclone Bola
About 40 minutes up the cost from Atkin's place is the Whakaangiangi Valley, near Te Araroa.
We meet Roger Haerewa at his house, which looks out at several forestry blocks dominating the valley. He points to the Awatere block, which he used to be a trustee of, and talks about how things were in the area after Cyclone Bola.
"Bola left a lot of damage on our whenua - huge slips," he says, "and forestry at the time was the way to solve it.
"I was on Awatere and Tarere at the time when we planted it. We thought it was a good idea... for future work."
Haerewa is describing the push into pine plantations the government incentivised at the time.
The policies, implemented through the East Coast Forestry Project, sought to stem erosion across the region, particularly on steep hillsides through the planting of pine. The jobs and industry that would result were promoted as a twin-benefit.
Not only have the benefits not eventuated, but Māori landowners have also been disproportionately affected because of the kind of land that was targeted through incentives.
By the late 1980s, much of the land which remained in Māori ownership in Tairāwhiti was classified as marginal - essentially it was too steep to do much with like farming. Planting it with pine was seen as an investment, Haerewa says.
Now, it's not just the forestry waste and erosion that's causing harm and concern, there's serious questions over the financial viability of harvesting pine - with the price of logs down over the decades and the costs of transporting them to Gisborne climbing.
"At the moment, we've still got forests that should have been cut, but we can't cut it because the owners would get nothing," he says.
'The messaging I'm receiving now is that we are doing too much'
Gisborne District Council is the regulatory body for the forestry industry. It's trying to forge a path to more sustainable land use across the region with the tools it has under the Resource Management Act.
Mayor Rehette Stoltz admits it's a work-in-progress.
Since cyclones Gabrielle and Hale, the council's taken a tougher approach in its consenting and monitoring processes for the forestry industry. The shift followed a ministerial inquiry into the disasters and damage caused by forestry waste, woody debris and sediment in Tairāwhiti and Wairoa.
It's resulted in the council using enforcement orders - issued by the Environment Court against forestry companies - to target areas like poor harvesting practises and unmanaged slash.
But that hasn't come without setbacks.
It's been nearly a year since the council's land transition business case was shot down by the central government. The council was asking for a $359 million contribution or co-investment over a decade to help stabilise the region's most erosion-prone land.
More recently, Stoltz has been contacted by several government ministers over her council's approach to the forestry industry.
Chris Bishop, the minister responsible for reform of the Resource Manage Act, has also refused to grant the council an exemption to implement a plan change that would've enabled it to use more stringent rules to manage erosion-prone land through its consenting processes.
"It's tough," Stoltz says.
"After Cyclone Gabrielle, the [Ministerial inquiry] panel recommendations made it clear that we had to step up in the consenting, monitoring, and enforcement area.
"The messaging I'm receiving now is that we are doing too much in that space, and it is tough for us because we do want to do the right thing.
"What that that means for us is that the work that we've done in the last two to three years can't really get traction, because we need a plan change to do that."
The uncertainty looming over its regulatory work has led to the council commissioning an independent review into its own consenting, compliance and enforcement practices. Alongside that, Forestry Minister Todd McClay's appointed facilitator Doug Leeder to advise it on what's happening with forestry in the region.
Leeder's a month into his contract and has met with both Stoltz and the council's chief executive Nedine Thatcher Swann. He's also met with the council's consenting, compliance and enforcement teams.
He told Checkpoint there's been a breakdown in the relationship between the council and the forestry industry.
Diggers needed to clear forestry debris crowding
"Essentially, there's been a lack of trust. It has broken down between the regulator, being [Gisborne District Council] and the forestry companies.
"But that's just not forestry companies. It's those mum and dad businesses, those family businesses that operate harvesting operations throughout the Gisborne Tairāwhiti area."
Despite that, he doesn't believe the council are being overzealous in its approach, and says the use of enforcement orders have been justified.
"I think, on balance, enforcement orders have done their job, and it's really brought focus to the forest companies to get their act together and clean up some of the stuff."
Leeder says he's due to report to McClay on his progress by the end of the week.
'The nannies would be shocked at the condition the land's been left in'
Atkins, who's been working with the council on its land transition case, says change has to happen now.
He's a member of Mana Taiao Tairāwhiti, a group pushing for sustainable land use in the region that was established after Gabrielle.
"There's a responsibility on us as kaitiaki to leave it in a better state for the generations to come.
"That's the underlying principles and how it operates around here. Kaitiakitanga is to be able to practice that on your own whenua - it doesn't get any better than that."
He looks at his moko Te Ahupo and says the decisions made around the use of whenua by his predecessors were made with the best intentions. In hindsight, that just hasn't worked out.
"I reckon that the nannies that signed those blocks up, in good will and good faith - that they were going to provide employment and the whenua was going to be cared for - I reckon they'd be shocked if they saw the condition that the land has been left in.
"When you fly around here and see all the damage to our whenua, and a lot of it is permanent damage because the land has gone right down to the base rock. Nothing's going to grow on rock - we don't want that."
Now, it's about shifting away from the practises which shouldn't be happening so future generations have a chance to thrive on the land they belong to, Graeme says.
"You know, there's always going to be a place for forestry here, just not on that real steep land. And same with farming.
"But we just have to change how we do things. I want my tamariki and their tamariki to be staying here too."

title: 190 Days Without a Homicide
content:
Jenee Gragston dropped to the ground and held on to the grass as if it could save her life. She yelled to her family members to get down. She later told me that she didn’t know where the bullets were coming from, but she knew they were close. When the firing stopped, the cries began. She could hear her 4-year-old nephew howling: “Get it off me! Get it off me!” She wasn’t close enough to see what had happened, but it looked like he had blood on his chest. A teenage boy was lying near the child. The teenager “never screamed or anything,” she said. “I can still see all of it.”
It was a Saturday afternoon, mid-August in Lexington, Kentucky. Hundreds of people had gathered in Charles Young Park to celebrate what’s called East End Day—a combination of family reunions, live music, and lots of food. I grew up going to festivals in that park, though I lived on the west side of town, in the Charlotte Court housing projects.
Kentucky isn’t the most dangerous place in America, but it’s up there, with the 14th-highest rate of gun deaths. Twelve years ago, my uncle was murdered in Lexington. Three years ago, my sister’s husband was shot and killed there. I worry about my brother, who still lives there. He had gotten himself off the streets for a while, but is now back living in the city. Lexington had recently seen a hard-won drop in gun deaths—last year was the fourth straight year of declines in gun violence among young people. This spring and summer set a record of 190 straight days without a homicide. Then came the East End Day shooting, which killed that teenager, 16-year-old Di’Zhon Robertson, and wounded four others—including the 4-year-old, who was shot in the leg. The next weekend, another person was killed. The weekend after that, four separate shootings left two more dead.
Gragston was selling Polish sausages in the park. She’d paid more than $300 for the grill, $300 for the sausages, more than $1,000 in fees, $75 for the booth. Business was good; some people returned for seconds. Her husband, her kids, and other family members had come to help her set up her tent. Her 4-year-old nephew was handing customers sodas and water bottles. On the basketball court nearby, Devine Carama was talking with a group of young people. Carama is the director of ONE Lexington, a city-funded program that tries to prevent gun violence by mentoring at-risk boys. He, too, threw himself down when he heard gunfire. “I almost got shot that day,” he told me. Two people near him were hit—a man and his girlfriend. Carama and others tried to bandage the man’s leg; he told me he could see a glimmer of bullet or bone through the blood.
A day later, 18-year-old Jametrius Griffin turned himself in and was charged with murder. According to court testimony, Griffin’s younger brother had gotten into an argument; punches were thrown, and the younger brother fell or was pushed. When Griffin saw that, he yanked out a gun and started firing.
For the past three years, Robertson had participated in ONE Lexington’s summer youth program, which offers workshops on building emotional and social skills, as well as college-campus visits. “He wasn’t a street kid,” Carama said. Griffin’s younger brother was in ONE Lexington, too—in its school mentoring program. The organization had also helped Griffin get a job at UPS. The group’s work seemed to be making a difference. And then a fight left one young man dead, one wounded, and one in prison.
In many ways, Lexington feels like a small town, where everyone knows everyone. I went to middle school with Griffin’s lawyer, Daniel Whitley, who has a big reputation locally for representing people accused of murder—and for winning their cases. The week after the shooting, I spoke with Whitley and with Griffin’s mother, Jay-Me Baxter, on a video call.
“A bunch of bullshit” was how Baxter described the park shooting, “because everybody’s friends and everybody’s family.” She said her youngest son told her he had been bullied by Di’Zhon Robertson and others. The day after the shooting, she made the same argument in a video she posted on Facebook that outraged many in the community. She suggested that her older son had had no choice and said she didn’t care “who makes it home as long as mine do.” (I tried to reach Robertson’s mother through family members to see if she would talk with me about what happened to her son; her sister replied that the family didn’t want to relive it. But friends and family members described the teenager as quiet, observant, and “very respectful.”)
“I’m like, Shit, I know Di’Zhon’s mama,’” Baxter told me—the other mother was close friends with her own sister. Baxter said she had had a conversation with her about the beef between the boys, and assumed the issue had been settled. Griffin loved football, and he had started college at Kentucky State University. “But you know them kids,” she said. “They be doing stuff in silence.” Her son must have been simmering with fury.
I knew Baxter’s family growing up—she’s a year older than me, and they, too, lived in the Charlotte Court housing projects. She didn’t remember me, but she knew my brother. Her mother was white, and had nine children. Baxter, the third-oldest, is half Black, like her younger siblings. But the oldest two are white. Her mother used to cry, Baxter told me, because “the white kids didn’t ever live with us.” In our majority-Black neighborhood, a white mother with mixed-race kids stood out. Baxter remembers people throwing rocks through their windows and a lot of name-calling—“white bitch.” Her family was poorer than many others, but people in the neighborhood assumed that she was privileged, and tormented her for it. “That white mama, man,” she said. “You know what I’m saying?”
That kind of bullying is part of the pain of being impoverished. You feel so low, you desperately want to make someone else feel lower.
Baxter is a single mother, and Griffin is the oldest of her five children. Like my own mother, she lost custody of her kids because of drugs—she signed over her parental rights to her mom. She told me the story as if she was discussing a character in a book: “Jay-Me got in trouble. Jay-Me started using drugs, cocaine specifically.” Like my mother, Baxter was a victim of sexual abuse. She grew up watching her mother “get beat by men. I done been touched by men, and I never told my mama until a couple months before she died.”
It took Baxter seven years to stop using drugs and get her kids back. Those kids needed her, yet she kept choosing drugs over them, she said, as her voice cracked and tears hit her cheeks. “That hurts, because I can’t believe I did that.” I’ve heard those same words from my own mother and watched her cry for the same reason.
Before Baxter signed over her rights, she said, she asked her mother to promise that what she’d experienced as a little girl wouldn’t happen to her kids. She wanted to break the cycle of violence, poverty, and dysfunction that is the inheritance of so many children. “I’m not a gun mama,” Baxter told me, but she believes in “stepping in the street” to fight. “I’ve been fighting all my life,” she said.
Backgrounds like these are so common in Whitley’s line of work that he seemed to tune out our conversation. At one point on the video call, we heard the sound of snoring. Baxter joked about it: “Listen to him. My lawyer tiiiiiired.” We continued talking for a few more minutes and never heard from him again. “Night night, Daniel,” she said before we hung up. He called me back later, apologized for not saying goodbye, and said he hadn’t been asleep.
Despite the pity I felt for Baxter and her family, I felt more for those shot by her son, and their families.
Di’Zhon Robertson’s uncle Tyrone Johnson officiated his funeral, and told me that the church was full of people “struggling with their emotions.” I was told by attendees that the teenager’s grieving mother had to be pulled off the coffin. Damon Williams Jr., a 14-year-old wounded in the shooting, was hit in the thigh. He had been planning on joining his middle school’s football team this season. Lakeisha Martin was shot in the stomach and the sternum. East End Day, her older brother Isaiah Barron told me, “is a day for our community that we look forward to every year.” Martin was in the hospital for 21 days and will be unable to work for months.
The day of the shooting, Jenee Gragston rushed to the hospital as her nephew went into surgery. She told me the police said she should leave her tent, and could return later to retrieve everything. But when her husband went back to the park, almost everything was gone. The cooler with the meat. The grill, the propane tank, even her prescription eyeglasses. Other tents had been robbed as well. Gragston told me that she was grateful her nephew was okay, but that she would never go to one of the park festivals again.
Lexington is trying hard to reduce this kind of gun violence. Mayor Linda Gorton told me the city has handed out free gun locks and offered to buy back guns from residents, among other interventions. Through ONE Lexington, it offers groceries, hotel stays, and educational funds to people affected by gun violence. The city relocated a family whose house had been shot up, Gorton said. Still, she conceded, “there are times when we cannot control every human being’s behavior.”
It doesn’t help that Kentucky has such lax gun laws. Just this year, state legislators dropped the age required to carry a concealed firearm from 21 to 18. When I was growing up in Lexington, gun violence was even worse. Whenever you have a community of young men who feel powerless and disrespected, who have been raised to protect themselves and their families from perceived threats, and who believe words can’t save them but a gun might, then death will follow. The story of what happened in Lexington this summer is particularly tragic because so many had worked so long and so carefully to make a difference. But a gun changes everything in a moment.
Carama, of ONE Lexington, told me he has more friends who are dead than alive. He, too, said that “a lot of it is out of our control,” and that there’s only so much someone from outside a young person’s family can do. You can monitor a kid all you like, but if he has a gun, “you got a split second to react.” Ultimately, he said, “you can’t prevent everything. It’s just not possible.”
In Jay-Me Baxter’s account, she tried, in her way, to intervene. “The mamas grew up together,” she told me. “This could’ve been prevented.” But it wasn’t.

title: Robotic sign language interpreter for deaf Māori in development
content:
World's first indigenous language robot interpreter
New robotic interpreters built by experts at the University of Auckland will bring sign language underpinned by a Māori worldview to Turi Māori - Māori who are deaf.
Dr Tauwehe Tamati, who is leading the project alongside Dr Ho Seok Ahn told Morning Report, the signs have been developed in partnership with Turi Māori, whānau, Iwi and Hapū.
"I think that's why I got involved in the project in the first place. That would have been at least five years ago when I was approached by our colleagues.
"I had to think through how to connect the expertise of my colleagues in robotics, megatronics and so on. How do you connect it with a culture, with a people? And particularly with the most vulnerable of our own people."
Tamati is bilingual in Te Reo Māori and English. She used both languages and a whānau-based home sign with her father who was hard of hearing for most of his life, becoming profoundly deaf in his final 20 years.
"Our dad grew up in Te Ao Māori. He knew he was Māori and he was a hard worker at our pā. The cultural, social, and collective life on the marae continually reinforced his identity and sense of belonging.
"Over time, however, he stopped going to the pā and didn't like relatives coming around.
"We'd be making up excuses because he was deaf. We couldn't help him get through that. So when my engineering colleagues approached me about the project, I just thought of him and said, 'I'll do this for dad."'
Researchers used Māori sign-language models who were filmed and photographed, to capture the different elements of communication, including mannerisms and lip movement.
An advanced AI system called a weighted multimodal network was then used to develop the robots ability to interpret the signs.
The University of Auckland says the robots are now built and functioning within its research lab.
Models have been made at both adult and children's sizes.
Work on the project began more than five years ago as part of the Science for Technological Innovation National Science Challenge, with additional financial support coming from the Vision Mātauranga Fund and the Endeavour Fund in 2024.
"I think our project now has reached such a level of success that we do have all the people in the hapū excited and participating.
"They don't need to hear us. They just look around and they know they can feel they are the reason why we're all helping," Tamati said.

title: The commodification of Indigenous cultures and traditions
content:
This post is part of Global Voices’ August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights.” This series offers insight into the lives and experiences of Indigenous peoples to build connections across regions, center Indigenous experiences, and share the stories of leaders, activists, community members, and more. You can support this coverage by donating here.
For many Indigenous communities, the traditions, art, and ceremonies are the backbone of their shared identity, essential for marking important milestones, fostering a sense of community, and passing on histories to the younger generation. However, all too often, these traditions are extracted, repackaged, sold, or seized for someone else’s gain.
Spiritual ceremonies get restaged for tourists. Manufacterers co-opt Indigenous art without credit or payment. Governments annex Indigenous heritage to legitimize their own power. The mechanics differ across geography and culture, but the result is the same: Resources and meaning flow outward from the community that created them and enrich outsiders — often the same groups that have been oppressing them for centuries.
In Oaxaca, Mexico, wedding planners sell “Oaxacan weddings” as a commercial package, offering calenda processions, mezcal, and traditional dancing, stripped of the ceremonies and reciprocity that give the tradition its meaning.
Meanwhile, major international fashion houses shamelessly lift Indigenous textile patterns, profiting off their designs while failing to give credit or payment to those who conceived of them. But this story isn’t only about extraction: In Guatemala, Maya weavers are fighting back, pushing for legal recognition of their collective intellectual property rights.
In Southern Mexico, Oaxacan communities have a rich tradition of elaborate wedding ceremonies that are being commodified and monetized to reach outside audiences. Oaxacan weddings typically involve elements like calenda (a traditional Oaxacan procession), Guelaguetza (a traditional Oaxacan festival), as well as specific food, music, dance, drink, and rituals.
These “Oaxacan wedding packages” strip the events of all of their cultural significance and reduce them to a transaction. As Oaxacan author Kupijy Vargas explains:
El concepto de bodas oaxaqueñas está ofertado en un mercado comercial, ofrecido al público por paquetes, construidos a partir de la apropiación cultural de una calenda, incluyendo el mezcal, la música y las mujeres bailando.
Estos paquetes ofrecen ese concepto para después tener una fiesta en el jardín etnobotánico, en donde se sirve comida oaxaqueña gourmet, alimentos que se comen dentro de la región pero servidos de manera estilizada. Quienes los preparan y los sirven, es decir, los meseros, cocineras, etcétera, son quienes sostienen con sus atenciones a esa fiesta en donde no existe la Guelaguetza, ni el acto de dar y recibir, sino que existe una monetización por los servicios. Es allí cuando el colonialismo vuelve a triunfar, convirtiendo en trabajadores a todas esas personas de la cultura en la que crecieron y nacieron, en sus propias tierras.
The concept of Oaxacan weddings is marketed commercially, offered to the public in packages built upon the cultural appropriation of a calenda (a traditional Oaxacan procession), including mezcal, music, and women dancing.
These packages offer this concept followed by a party in the ethnobotanical garden, where gourmet Oaxacan food is served — foods eaten within the region but presented in a stylized manner. Those who prepare and serve the food — the waiters, cooks, and so on — are the ones who sustain this party with their attention to detail. There is no Guelaguetza (a traditional Oaxacan festival), no act of giving and receiving, but rather a monetization of services. It is here that colonialism triumphs once again, turning all those people of the culture in which they grew up and were born, in their own land, into mere laborers.
A similar dynamic unfolds with textiles in this region and other Indigenous communities. Oaxacan author Tajëëw B. Díaz Robles argues that extracting traditional textiles without acknowledging or compensating the communities that invented them is a form of appropriation.
…propongo que el plagio y/o apropiación de la blusa de Tlahui y de sus patrones gráficos por parte de Isabel Marant y Antik Batik (otra empresa de moda francesa que también incurrió en la copia del textil de Tlahui en su colección Bartra de 2014) es la conversión de formas diversas de derechos de propiedad colectiva-comunal a propiedad privada, puesto que hasta el momento del plagio los bordados eran considerados parte de la identidad cultural de un colectivo, un textil cuyos patrones gráficos identifican a una comunidad en específico y que se recrea comunitariamente. Esto no significa que no sean personas específicas las que las elaboran ni que no exista una comercialización local, pero estas personas crean y producen en un contexto comunitario delimitado y las prendas circulan en un mercado que identifica claramente su origen. De ahí que Marant y Antik Batik, en palabras de las autoridades comunitarias de Tlahuitoltepec en su pronunciamiento de junio de 2015, hayan cometido algo que enuncian como ‘la apropiación de un patrimonio cultural.’
I propose that the plagiarism and/or appropriation of the Tlahui blouse and its graphic patterns by Isabel Marant and Antik Batik (a French fashion company that also copied the Tlahui textile in its 2014 Bartra collection) constitutes the conversion of various forms of collective/communal property rights into private property. Until the plagiarism, the embroidery was considered part of a collective’s cultural identity, a textile whose graphic patterns identify a specific community and are recreated communally.
This does not mean that specific individuals do not create them, nor that local commerce does not exist, but these individuals create and produce within a defined community context, and the garments circulate in a market that clearly identifies their origin. Therefore, Marant and Antik Batik, in the words of the Tlahuitoltepec community authorities in their June 2015 statement, committed what they describe as ‘the appropriation of cultural heritage.’
Some Maya communities in Guatemala are fighting back against this phenomenon by pushing for legal protections for traditional crafts and textiles.
The fight has been going on for over a decade: In 2016, the Women’s Association for the Development of Sacatepéquez (AFEDES) and a coalition of weaving cooperatives filed a constitutional challenge arguing that Guatemala’s silence on Indigenous textile rights was itself unconstitutional. The Constitutional Court sided with them twice, ordering Congress to pass protective legislation. Thus far, Congress has failed to do so. Two bills have died in the legislature: Initiative 5247 in 2017, and Initiative 6136 in 2022.
In June 2026, the movement, now working under the name “Ru Chajixik ri Qana'ojb'äl” (“safeguarding our knowledge,” in the Kaqchikel language), delivered a third proposal, Initiative 6788.
Like its predecessors, the bill defines textile intellectual property as “collective, inalienable, and imprescriptible,” meaning it belongs to the community rather than any individual, can’t be sold or signed away, and can’t expire.
If passed, it would formally recognize Indigenous peoples as the legal authors of their weavings, designs, and techniques — including specific motifs, patterns, symbols, colors, glyphs, and petroglyphs passed down through generations — and create a National Council on Textile and Indigenous Clothing Intellectual Property to enforce those rights. The weavers have also asked Congress for three concrete commitments alongside the bill itself: A favorable ruling affirming the constitutional and international legal basis for collective Indigenous intellectual property, expedited legislative handling, and a standing dialogue between Congress and the movement to track the bill’s progress.
Regardless of how the bill fares in Guatemala’s legislature, the proposal presents a model for other Indigenous groups around the world looking to safeguard their own intellectual property rights.

title: Ganjasar Monastery reflects legacy of Albanian Church — chairman
content:
AGHDARA, Azerbaijan, September 21. The Ganjasar Monastery is part of the heritage of the Albanian Church, Robert Mobili, chairman of the Albanian-Udi religious community, told reporters during a visit to the Ganjasar monastery complex, Trend's Karabakh bureau reports.
He noted that members of the community recited prayers in Ganjasar and honored the memory of the martyrs.
“Today is the Nativity of the Most Holy Mother of God. Yesterday was State Sovereignty Day, and today is World Peace Day. It is especially important for us to visit the Ganjasar monastery complex on such significant days,” said R. Mobili.
According to him, the Ganjasar monastery complex is one of the most important examples of the Christian heritage of Caucasian Albania.
“This is our first visit to Ganjasar. We have visited many churches in the liberated territories, prayed, and lit candles. The Ganjasar Monastery is an important example of the surviving Albanian ecclesiastical heritage of Caucasian Albania,” noted the community chairman.
Mobili said that the ancient Christian churches in Azerbaijan are part of the heritage of the Albanian Church.
“The legacy of the ancient Albanian churches that exist today in Azerbaijan is the legacy of the independent Apostolic Albanian Autocephalous Church. It is a very rich legacy. These churches have no connection whatsoever to the Armenian Church,” he emphasized.
The community chairman said that after Christianity was adopted as the state religion in Caucasian Albania, many churches were built in the region.
According to him, the cessation of the Albanian Church’s activities in 1836 and its subordination to the Armenian Church had a serious impact on the Albanian Christian heritage.
“The decree-statute of March 11, 1836, put an end to the activities of the Albanian Church. The center of the Albanian Church was located in Ganja. After that, the heritage of the Albanian Church was Armenianized. Part of the Albanian community left for Georgia, including the Udis. Some converted to Islam. “We, the Udis living in Gabala, have preserved our native heritage,” Mobili said.
He noted that the opportunity to visit Christian churches in the region following the liberation of Karabakh from occupation is a significant event for the Alban-Udi community.
“Today, the doors of the churches are open, and services are being held there. We can pray in our native churches. This is a great blessing bestowed upon us by God,” the community chairman said.
Mobili also emphasized that the sphere of influence of the Albanian Church is not limited to the current territory of Azerbaijan. He cited the ancient churches in Eastern and Western Zangazur, including the Tatev Monastery, as well as those in the Derbent region, as part of the historical heritage of the Albanian Church.
The community chairman also drew attention to the existence of the Albanian alphabet and religious texts in the Albanian language.
“Caucasian Albania had its own centers of scholarship. Religious books were translated into Albanian. In this regard, ancient sources have also been preserved at the Monastery of St. Catherine on Mount Sinai,” R. Mobili said.
He noted that the ancient church located in the village of Sheki Kish is also an example of Albanian Christian heritage.
R. Mobili also noted that depictions of crosses and other religious symbols in Azerbaijan are part of the heritage of the Albanian Church.
“At a UNESCO event held in Geneva in 2010, we expressed our position regarding the affiliation of cross-shaped elements and symbols found in Azerbaijan to the Albanian Church,” he added.
The community leader emphasized that the atmosphere of tolerance prevailing in Azerbaijan allows the Alban-Udi community to preserve its religious heritage.
“One of the most heartwarming moments for us is the tremendous support we receive in Azerbaijan, where the overwhelming majority of the population is Muslim. The tolerance of the Azerbaijani people and the atmosphere in the country allow us to attend our own churches. This is our heritage,” Mobili said.

title: Buipe Hausa Festival: National President Tafida calls for vigilance, unity, and youth reform
content:
Audio By Carbonatix
The ancient town of Buipe in the Savannah Region came alive over the weekend as the Hausa community gathered for their annual cultural festival, a vibrant celebration of language, tradition, and economic heritage that drew chiefs, community leaders, and diaspora members from across Ghana and beyond.
But beneath the colorful display of horsemanship, traditional attire, and kalangu drumming, the festival carried a powerful message: the Hausa people are not peripheral to Ghana's story—they are foundational to it.
A Call to Order: Tafida's Charge
Alhaji Ahmed Tijani Abubakari Ali, National President of the Hadinkan Hausa da Hausawa, known widely as Tafida, used the occasion to deliver a frank and wide-ranging address that touched on security, citizenship, and the future of Zongo youth.
His first concern was vigilance. Tafida cautioned Zongo communities across Ghana to be careful about the strangers they welcome—particularly those arriving from neighboring countries without proper vetting.
"We are a people of trade, of faith, of hospitality," he said. "But hospitality without wisdom is a door left open to danger. We must not be naive. Not everyone who speaks our language shares our values. Do your due diligence. Know who you are harboring. The safety of our communities—and of Ghana—depends on it."
It was a delicate balance—honoring the Hausa tradition of hospitality while acknowledging the realities of modern security threats.
The Passport Struggle: "A Right, Not a Favor"
Tafida also took aim at what he described as a "quiet injustice" at home: the struggles Hausa people face in obtaining Ghanaian passports despite generations of citizenship.
"We are Ghanaians. Our fathers were born here. Our children were born here. Why then must we prove what is already written in our blood? A passport is not a favor—it is a right."
His words resonated with many in the crowd—families who have lived in Ghana for generations yet still face bureaucratic hurdles that question their belonging.
Drug Abuse: A Community Emergency
Perhaps the most urgent warning came on the issue of drug abuse among Zongo youth as the Zongo Chief of Buipe, Sarki Abdullahi Mohammed noted.
"Our youth are being consumed," Sarki Abdullahi said. "And we—parents, chiefs, elders—are we not the ones who looked away? The time for silence is over. The time for action is now."
He called on parents to reclaim their role as first teachers, on chiefs to enforce accountability, and on the community to build alternatives—skills training, education, and economic opportunities that can pull young people away from addiction.
The Zongo Chief of Buipe, Mei Martaba Abdullahi, raised these concerns, urging parents to step up and change the narrative.
The Economic Case: Hausa as Infrastructure
Earlier, General Secretary Suhail Abdul Mumin delivered a keynote address that reframed the Hausa narrative—from marginalized migrants to economic architects.
He argued that the historic Zongo settlements were, in fact, Ghana's earliest Special Economic Zones. Centuries before formal regional blocs, Hausa trading networks linked the Sahel to the coast—pioneering livestock supply chains, textile trade, and leather craftsmanship that sustained cities like Kumasi, Salaga, Tamale, and Accra.
"To study the economic history of Ghana without centralizing the Hausa commercial framework is to read a book with its foundational chapters torn out," he said.
Suhail also highlighted the strategic value of the Hausa language in contemporary trade. In markets from Techiman to Makola, Hausa serves as the transaction language that bridges ethnic lines—allowing a Ga woman, an Akan man, an Ewe trader, and a Dagomba merchant to bargain, agree, and prosper together.
With over 150 million speakers across West and Central Africa, he argued, Hausa is Ghana's organic diplomatic and commercial bridgehead into the largest markets in Africa—an untapped asset for economic diplomacy under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
A People of Builders
As the festival drew to a close, Tafida reminded his people of their strength.
"We are not beggars at Ghana's table. We are builders. We built the markets. We built the trade routes. We will build the future—but only if we first build ourselves."
It was a message that resonated long after the drums fell silent—a call to order, a call to unity, and a call to pride.
About the Hadinkan Hausa da Hausawa
The Hadinkan Hausa da Hausawa is a worldwide organization dedicated to the promotion of Hausa language, culture, and socio-economic development in Ghana and around the globe.
The annual Hausa Festival serves as a platform for cultural celebration, community dialogue, and economic empowerment.

title: Tribes hit hard by wildfires face health effects, cultural losses
content:
Nada Hassanein
Stateline
Neighbors across the Colville Tribes communities in Washington state knew Matilda Bob’s log home as the “rainbow house,” for its brightly painted exterior.
Now it’s gone.
Sparked by a lightning strike in mid-July, the Kaiser Canyon Fire destroyed Bob’s home and 42 other houses on the Colville Reservation, along with 100 outbuildings such as sheds and barns, tribal leaders said.
“I couldn’t believe that it had happened,” said Bob. “It went so fast.”
Tribal leaders across Washington and Oregon told Stateline that this year’s record-breaking wildfires burned timber that they rely on for income, threatened food sources and waterways, and harmed the health of their communities. Power outages left families without food they’ve hunted or gathered and frozen.
Hotter, drier conditions driven by climate change already have made wildfires nationwide more frequent and intense, a trend that is expected to accelerate. Substandard housing and higher rates of acute and chronic underlying health conditions, including respiratory illnesses, make tribal communities more vulnerable during and after the fires.
“What typically used to be like a two-month fire season for us when I first started fighting fire about 25 years ago — now that’s at least three months and sometimes longer, depending on the year,” said Cody Desautel, executive director of the Colville Tribes, who is also a forester and wildland fire expert.
An especially warm winter also left Washington state with about half its usual snowpack, raising drought concerns and wildfire risks.
This year saw particularly devastating fires in eastern Washington, including arson-instigated fires that destroyed over 700 homes in Spokane. The conditions prompted Washington state Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson to declare a statewide state of emergency on Aug. 1, citing an “unprecedented” red flag alert of extreme fire danger from the National Weather Service.
The Colville Reservation includes the southern portion of Ferry County, which has the second-lowest median household income of all counties in the state. The tribe lost a significant amount of timber, a main source of income, during the fires.
Many residents didn’t have home insurance because the housing didn’t qualify or they couldn’t afford it, said Cindy Marchand, chairwoman of the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation, adding that about half of homes destroyed in the fires weren’t insured. Other residents couldn’t afford to upgrade to more fire-resistant material, she said.
“The rates are just astronomical in the sense that a lot of people in our area are not able to afford this,” Marchand said. “We have elders living on a single income, they’re on a fixed income, and so they’re having a hard time making it as it is.”
By mid-September, the total acres burned across the state reached roughly 900,000 acres, the worst since 2015.
Since July, about 200,000 acres burned across the Colville Reservation alone, with the Kaiser Canyon Fire scorching over 138,000 acres and the Modrite fire burning more than 57,000 acres.
In Oregon, over 60,000 acres burned across the reservation of the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs, where at least six homes were destroyed.
The Wrights Spring Fire in Oregon burned through 55,000 acres across Klamath County, national forest and tribal lands.
Health effects
Faith Zacherle-Tonasket has seen how the wildfires have affected perinatal health. Founder of xa?xa? Indigenous Birth Justice, which offers perinatal and doula support across the Colville Reservation, Zacherle-Tonasket said three of her clients went into early labor during this year’s fires. She and her team believe stress amid displacement due to evacuations contributed to the early labor. Emerging research is also showing how wildfire smoke is a primary pollutant affecting pregnancy.
Zacherle-Tonasket also helps lead the River Warrior Society, a nonprofit offering wildfire relief for tribal and non-tribal members. The group has been coordinating shelter placements for elders, donations and food assistance.
“This is one of the biggest fires our reservation has had,” she said. “The biggest need we have on our reservation is air purifiers.”
Respiratory health has been a major concern post-wildfires amid smoke and poor air quality. American Indian and Alaska Native people disproportionately have chronic respiratory health conditions exacerbated by wildfire smoke, including asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Matilda Bob’s father, a veteran who is now displaced with her, has COPD.
Along with respiratory distress, there’s been “tremendous stress, anxiety, grief, trauma — and we expect and know that those behavioral health needs are going to continue beyond this current emergency. Post-fire recovery creates additional health concerns,” said Dayna Seymour, the Colville Tribes’ health and human services chair. “Our members are going in now to clean up the ash and debris, and aren’t really always sure what’s in that ash and debris, whether there’s hazardous materials, heavy metals, asbestos or other contaminants.”
Seymour added that community members helped deliver medications to their displaced neighbors and helped each other dig fire lines.
Research shows disproportionate smoke exposure among tribes in California, noted University of Kansas Assistant Professor Melinda Adams, a cultural fire practitioner and scholar who teaches in the Department of Earth, Energy, and Environment.
“Because wildfire is increasing in frequency and intensity,” said Adams, a member of the N’dee San Carlos Apache Tribe of Arizona, “we must look at cumulative effects and identify patterns in human and environmental health while investing in climate and wildfire mitigation strategies that include Indigenous knowledge.”
Prescribed burns, carefully controlled fires to reduce brush that could fuel megablazes, are crucial tools in preventing dangerous wildfires and preserving ecosystem health. But regulatory barriers have made implementing traditional Indigenous burn practices difficult, Desautel and Adams said.
This week, the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee advanced legislation that would streamline approval of prescribed burns, while the EPA issued guidance last year.
Funding and staffing limitations are also a barrier, Desautel added. The Indian Forest Management Assessment Team found that Indian trust forest lands are funded at about a third per acre of comparable federal forests.
Waterway pollution, cultural art lost
Seymour added that traditional foods including huckleberries and herbs and roots, such as bitterroot and camas, that the tribes rely on were scorched across the land.
“Those are things that we utilize to help us in ceremony, that we utilize to eat for subsistence. So that was a huge loss for our people,” Seymour said.
In Oregon, while no homes were lost on the Klamath Tribes’ lands, leaders still have concerns and uncertainty around environmental aftereffects, particularly on traditional food systems the tribes were finally in the process of regenerating.
The tribes had just started restoring their ancestral salmon after removal of four dams two years ago. Last year, the tribes documented the first adult Chinook salmon in the Williamson River, and earlier this year detected the first salmon hatch in over a century in the tributaries of the Upper Klamath Lake.
“The biggest (wildfire) impact is the effects on hunting and gathering that may be felt in the future. …With this high-intensity, high-severity wildfire, there’s likelihood of sedimentation into the streams that could serve as spawning grounds for that new salmon,” said Tim Sexton, Wildland Fire Program Manager at the Klamath Tribes. Research is showing how wildfires affect fish habitats.
Klamath Tribes Chairman William Ray Jr., a former firefighter of 40 years, said he’s been advocating for tribal control of the waterways amid pollution that already existed before this year’s wildfires.
“We have ecological collapse going on. Our water quality in our lake and rivers isn’t very good,” he said.
At the Colville Reservation, Zacherle-Tonasket said many of her community members are holding off on traditional hunting and instead her nonprofit has gotten discounts from local butchers to help families.
“We don’t want to hunt this year,” she told Stateline. “It’s just ethically not right to hunt when our own animals are suffering the way we are.”
Bob said that many cultural heirlooms burned — her own traditional beadwork, a 100-year-old berry basket passed down from her great grandmother, and her nephew’s handmade attire worn during special dances at powwows.
But her family will continue to dance as they do “for the people who can’t,” she said, on their ancestral land.
“Every time your foot hits the floor’s a prayer,” she said. “We were raised to respect the land. … We’re still standing in the fact that we’re all OK, that we all made it, that we didn’t lose anybody.”
Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org.

title: Alban-Udi community representative shares impressions of Ganjasar Monastery visit
content:
Alban-Udi community representative shares impressions of Ganjasar Monastery visit
- 21 September, 2026
- 18:16
Rafig Danakari, Deputy Chairman of the Alban-Udi Christian Religious Community, who visited the Ganjasar Monastery in Vangli village of the Aghdara district, shared his impressions of the visit.
According to the Public Relations Department of the Reconstruction, Construction and Management Service in Khankandi city, Aghdara and Khojaly districts, Danakari told Report that the visit of members of the Alban-Udi community to the Ganjasar Monastery after many years was of particular significance.
"We are very happy to be here today. As a result of the liberation of our lands, we can now come to this sacred place freely. For many years, for 100-200 years, we could not come here. Today, we prayed for the souls of our martyrs, commemorated their memory, and lit candles. May God rest the souls of all our martyrs.
Today is also significant for us from another perspective. It is the birthday of the Virgin Mary. Being at the Ganjasar Monastery on this special day has a special meaning for us. We want to continue regularly visiting Ganjasar Monastery, as well as churches and monasteries located in other regions of Azerbaijan, pray here, and light candles," he said.
Danakari stressed that it is also important to introduce these historical sites to the international community:
"Because these are our history and our cultural and religious heritage. We want the whole world to see that the historical heritage of Caucasian Albania is still being preserved today."

title: Sportromantiek in Turkse voetbalcompetitie: club met Koerdische identiteit nu bovenaan
content: Voetbalclub Amedspor uit Diyarbakir heeft opnieuw voor een grote verrassing gezorgd in Turkije. De club met een Koerdische identiteit won gisteravond van Besiktas met 3-2 en staat nu zelfs bovenaan in de Turkse competitie. In Diyarbakir en in de regio, in het zuidoosten van het land, werd dat groots gevierd. "Dit is iets om heel trots op te zijn", zegt een fan vlak na de wedstrijd. "Niet alleen voor de inwoners van Diyarbakir, maar voor alle Koerden. Uit Van, Batman, het maakt niet uit. Alle Koerden zijn op dit moment trots op Amedspor." Dat de club nu bovenaan staat is opvallend. In het verleden heeft de club met tegenwerking te maken gehad. Zo werden de fans soms niet toegelaten bij uitwedstrijden. Ook beschikt de club over aanzienlijk minder financiële middelen dan de traditionele topclubs. Ter vergelijking: het budget van Besiktas ligt tien keer hoger. "We zijn in tegenstelling tot andere clubs geen bedrijf, we blijven overeind dankzij de steun van het volk, dankzij de shirts die mensen kopen en dankzij de kaartverkoop", zegt voorzitter Nahit Eren tegen de NOS. Het is volgens velen dan ook een bijzondere prestatie dat deze club als debutant na zes wedstrijden de leiding neemt. Voor sommige fans voelt het alsof ze de competitie hebben gewonnen. Koerdische identiteit Amedspor is nauw verbonden met de Koerdische identiteit, maar supporters benadrukken dat de club voor hen ook staat voor gelijke rechten en vrouwenrechten. Veel Koerden strijden al decennialang lang voor politieke en culturele rechten in Turkije. Winst op het voetbalveld draait dan ook om veel meer dan alleen voetbal. Dat is ook zichtbaar op de tribunes. Twee 22-jarige vrouwen, Berfin Ayder en Evindar Tan van de supportersgroep voor vrouwen Mor Tribun, proberen via de wedstrijden aandacht te vragen voor vrouwenrechten. "Vrouwen worden gedood en lastiggevallen. Als we hier een spandoek ophangen, heeft het een grotere kans internationaal zichtbaar te worden." Volgens Berfin verbroedert sport ook. "We kunnen ook zeggen dat we Koerden zijn, we kunnen Koerdisch spreken. Steeds meer vrouwen sluiten zich bij ons aan, er zijn veel mensen in de omliggende gebieden die betrokken zijn. Er zijn niet alleen Koerdische vrouwen, maar ook Turkse vrouwen die zich aansluiten." Gele zakken Toch zie je soms op de tribunes de spanningen hoog oplopen. Er zijn fans van andere teams met nationalistische opvattingen. Zo is onlangs een supporter in het noordoosten van Turkije op straat aangevallen en liep hij een gebroken neus op omdat hij een tenue van Amedspor aanhad. Ook zijn er de gele plastic zakken op sociale media of op de tribunes. Het is een verwijzing naar de gele zakken waarin lichamen van Koerdische militanten werden vervoerd. Turkije voerde jarenlang een bloedige strijd met de Koerdische PKK waarbij meer dan 40.000 mensen om het leven kwamen. Inmiddels zijn er gesprekken over vrede en ontwapening. Zo houden sommige uitwedstrijden veel meer lading dan een gewone voetbalwedstrijd. De veiligheidsmaatregelen rond wedstrijden zijn daarom ook zwaar. Volgens de voorzitter van Amedspor worden bij een thuiswedstrijd ongeveer 1500 politieagenten en 500 particuliere beveiligers ingezet. Vooroordelen verbroken Tegelijkertijd weet de club ook de harten te raken buiten het overwegend Koerdische Diyarbakir. Mensen uit andere delen van Turkije volgen Amedspor en ook vanuit Europa reizen fans naar de stad. Tijdens de wedstrijd gisteren waren er fans vanuit Nederland en Duitsland. Volgens Eren helpt het sportieve succes in de manier hoe er naar de club wordt gekeken. Het succes van het team leidt ook tot saamhorigheid onder Koerden met uiteenlopende opvattingen. "Eigenlijk worden daardoor bepaalde vooroordelen weggenomen", zegt voorzitter Eren. Op de tribunes zie je soms zelfs Turkse vlaggen wapperen. "Mensen uit de Zwarte Zee-regio, de Egeïsche regio en de Marmara regio volgen Amedspor ook met belangstelling." Een team dat eerder vooral werd gezien als een Koerdisch nationalistische of politiek beladen club, krijgt zo door het succes steeds meer nationale aandacht. En daar ziet de club ook kansen. Eren wil vooral een duurzame club bouwen, gedragen door de gemeenschap. Volgens de 22-jarige Berfin zijn ze er nog lang niet: "Je denkt dat bepaalde vooroordelen zijn weggenomen, maar blijft een een lange weg met obstakels, maar geen onmogelijke."

title: Sandbondtenga/Culture: la communauté soninké se mobilise pour préserver sa langue
content:
BURKINA-SANDBONDTENGA-CULTURE-SONINKÉ-PRÉSERVATION
Sandbondtenga/Culture: la communauté soninké se mobilise pour préserver sa langue
Kaya, 20 sept. 2026 (AIB)-La communauté soninké de la région des Koulsé se mobilise pour la préservation et la transmission de sa langue et de son patrimoine culturel, à l’occasion de la Journée internationale de la langue soninké, prévue les 24 et 25 septembre 2026 à Kaya.
L’annonce a été faite dimanche à Kaya au cours d’une conférence de presse organisée par le comité d’organisation.
Placée sous le thème « La langue soninké, un patrimoine culturel à préserver et à transmettre aux générations futures », la célébration se tiendra notamment à la Place de la Nation et à la Salle polyvalente de Kaya avec la participation de membres de la communauté du Mali.
Selon le président de l’association provinciale « Qiite quitte », qui signifie « main dans la main », Zida Issa, l’initiative vise à mieux faire connaître la communauté soninké, son histoire, sa langue et ses traditions, tout en renforçant les liens entre ses membres.
Il a expliqué que cette communauté, venue du Mali et installée dans la localité de Pensa depuis plusieurs siècles, demeure aujourd’hui fortement attachée à la préservation de sa langue.
« Notre objectif est de faire connaître davantage la langue et la culture soninké et surtout de faire en sorte que les jeunes puissent les transmettre aux générations futures », a indiqué le président du comité d’organisation.
Les organisateurs ont également relevé que les Soninké sont parfois confondus avec d’autres communautés, notamment les Peuls, alors que leur identité culturelle et linguistique possède ses propres caractéristiques.
Plusieurs patronymes sont associés à cette communauté, dont Zida, Silla, Doukouré, Diawara, Soudré et Gassama, ont-ils précisé.
Le programme de la célébration prévoit notamment un panel-débat, des contes et légendes, des chants traditionnels ainsi que des activités de valorisation culturelle. La communauté soninké entend également participer aux activités de Faso Mēbo.
Pour Amado Zida, trésorier adjoint de l’association, cette célébration constitue surtout une occasion de « mobiliser davantage les membres d’une même famille dispersée » et de renforcer les liens entre les différentes composantes d’une même communauté.
Agence d’Information du Burkina
AIO/bak

title: Edward Colston’s remains likely to stay at Bristol church that could become community space
content:
Bones of the enslaver Edward Colston are likely to remain interred in a church in Bristol if and when the currently unused building is given a new lease of life as a community resource, it has emerged.
The dean of Bristol, the Very Rev Mandy Ford, said Colston’s remains would probably stay where they were in All Saints church on one of Bristol’s busiest streets.
Colston, who died in 1721, made headlines around the world in 2020 when his statue in the city centre was toppled during a Black Lives Matter protest and thrown into the harbour.
The diocese of Bristol has been consulting with Bristolians over what to do with All Saints on Corn Street, which has been closed since 1984.
While no final decision has yet been made, it seems likely it will be used as a space to reflect on the port’s connections with the slave trade – and Colston’s remains will stay where they are.
Ford said: “There is very, very clear guidance which assumes that you don’t disturb remains that have been given Christian burial, except in exceptional circumstances and so the presumption is that they will stay where they are.”
The dean said that if there was to be a radical rebuilding of the space there could be an argument to inter the remains elsewhere. “Otherwise the assumption is that Christian burial is permanent and that’s where they stay.”
Ford brings deep expertise to the job of helping decide what happens to Colston’s bones, as when she worked in Leicester she was closely involved in the reinterment of Richard III’s remains after they were found in a car park there.
She acknowledged people had different understandings of the theological or spiritual significance of human remains. “But it’s a Christian place of burial and we are a Christian church trying to do the right thing. This is the burial place of a human being who was involved in a practice which we recognise to be utterly sinful and wrong.”
The question of what to do about sites connected to Colston in Bristol is a thorny one.
After the Colston statue was thrown into the harbour, windows celebrating him were removed from two Bristol churches as the diocese declared the fall of the statue was a “signal” for it to take action.
