In the same year, Bristol’s concert hall was renamed Bristol Beacon, having previously been called Colston Hall.
It is likely to be many months before a final decision is made over the fate of All Saints.
But the dean said: “I think people do see that it has potential as a place of learning and also a place of reconciliation. From the work that we’ve been doing in the cathedral and the relationships and the conversations that we have, I think there’s a strong sense that there’s huge potential in Bristol to have difficult conversations and to build a better future on the basis of truth-telling about the past.”
She added that work carried out at a new All Saints had the potential to sit alongside projects on Bristol’s history being done by institutions including the University of Bristol and Bristol Old Vic.
Ford said: “I think one can see it as part of a much bigger picture, which I think is really important if Bristol’s going to have a peaceful and flourishing future as a civic space and as a city.”
The Rev Anjali Kanagaratnam, who is leading the All Saints consultation, has been taking groups into the church.
She said there had been a huge range of views. “Each extreme was covered from: ‘I never want to come back into this building’ to ‘Why haven’t I been told that this building is here? I need to bring my children.’ Some people find it a hard space to be in. Some were annoyed by the fact that they didn’t know it was there.”
Kanagaratnam said it had been vital to hear the voices of people in Bristol that had been affected by transatlantic slavery but the church had also made sure it heard what people from other communities, such as white working-class areas in south Bristol.
Kanagaratnam said there was great potential for All Saints to be a place of “truth-telling”. She added: “I think people do see that it has potential as a place of learning and also a place of reconciliation.”

title: How fake Naxos potatoes and modern ambitions are threatening the future of a world-renowned crop
content:
Historic Naxos potatoes hold protected status, but young people on the island no longer want to be farmers.
Naxos is the largest island in the Cyclades and its eponymous variety of potatoes has been grown here since the late 18th century. Sold all over Europe, the crop is an important part of the local economy. Sowing and harvesting takes place twice a year with the second time happening every September. Euronews went to meet Naxos potato farmers and learn more about a crop under threat.
We meet Stelios Vathrakokoilis, one of the biggest potato growers on Naxos and President of the Galanado Agricultural Cooperative, and ask him what makes the island’s potatoes so special. "First of all, we have abundant sunshine almost all year round," he says. "Second, we have the sea all around us, at a distance of three to four kilometres. Third, we use cow manure on our fields, as much as we judge necessary, and the fourth and most important factor is that our subsoil lacks certain elements. That element is calcium. If, in these areas, you grow tomatoes or vegetables without adding fertilisers, they will start rotting on the back side of the fruit. That means a lack of calcium. Potatoes are not bothered by this. So it is the absence of calcium from our soils that gives the potato about 80 per cent of its distinctive flavour."
Young people don't want to farm potatoes anymore
In the 1980s, annual production of Naxos potatoes reached 15,000 tonnes. Every member of a family worked on the crop. Families today are smaller and children follow other career paths. Some 300 families on the Cycladic island are involved in potato farming today and production has dropped to a mere 5,000 tonnes.
What is a fake Naxos potato?
In 2010, the Naxos potato was granted protected status. This means that potatoes must be given the seal of approval before being able to be sold under the Naxos potato label.
Farmer Stelios Vathrakokoilis explains that some package up potatoes as Naxos when they are, in fact, inferior varieties.
"We started marketing Naxos potatoes first through the AB Vassilopoulos supermarket chain. A year later, Sklavenitis came in very strongly, followed by all the chains, so that all this product was going straight onto supermarket shelves."
"But even there, some fraud takes place. I don’t know who, but certain people buy potatoes from other regions, even other continents, especially Egypt. They take them into their packing plants, package them and sell them as Naxos potatoes."
"This happens even more in the street markets. If you walk into a market with 20 or 30 stalls, you will see all of them claiming to sell Naxos potatoes. They are not from Naxos. Out of forty stalls, perhaps one or two sell the real thing. Everyone calls their potatoes Naxos because the price is higher and the taste better. The upshot is that consumers can find genuine Naxos potatoes in 99 per cent of cases only on supermarket shelves. Only there will they find them."
Water and labour shortages threaten the future of Naxos potatoes
The shortage of labour has become acute in recent years and is a serious concern for farmers - it is very difficult to find workers with the legal right to work.
Water shortages are also an issue. More residents and tourists on the island along with prolonged drought means water resources are spread much more thin.
Farmers have to buy expensive water from the municipality, supplied from desalination plants.
Farmer Stelios Vathrakokoilis is sounding the alarm for the future, seeing production shrink and problems multiply:
"The basic precondition for having production is manpower. A second point, and what I see when I look ahead over the next five to ten years, is that we will be searching with binoculars to find a farmer, not only on Naxos but across Greece."
"It makes no sense for one 'stremma' of land to leave €1,500 in a Dutch farmer’s pocket, €1,200 for an Israeli farmer and €50 for a Greek farmer. It can not go on like this! Clearly we are doing something wrong. We are still using traditional methods, techniques from decades ago, and we are not moving towards something different, such as hydroponics or similar systems, with smaller areas, better working conditions and more income."
"What I see is that in 5–10 years there will be no Greek farmers left anywhere in the country. And I think this is broadly a European issue as well, as we can see from the protests farmers are staging in France and Germany."
"It is not sustainable to pay €2.5 per litre for diesel fuel, to have fertiliser prices through the roof, seed prices through the roof and monthly wages of around €2,500. If you try to farm under these conditions, you will end up completely in the red," stresses Stelios Vathrakokoilis.
The local farmers union is trying to help
This year the Union of Agricultural Cooperatives of Naxos marks a century of activity. It stands by the producers and works to solve the many challenges facing the island’s agricultural and livestock sectors. The Union’s goal is to support both the product and the people who grow it:
"Naxos potatoes are not just another product. They are the history of the place, its production, its economy. They are the wealth of the farmer and the livestock breeder," Dimitris Kapounis, President of the Union of Agricultural Cooperatives of Naxos, tells Euronews.
"Potatoes arrived on Naxos before the time of Kapodistrias, so you can see the passion, the love, the genuine cultivation of the land in this chapter we call Naxos potatoes," he says.
Every year the island hosts a major festival celebrating the potato. The 17th Potato Festival was held on 12 September at the port of Naxos. The centenary of the founding of the Union of Agricultural Cooperatives of Naxos was celebrated at the same time.
More than 3,000 people took part in the event in Nikiforos Mandilaras Square, alongside local organisations and representatives of the farming community. Residents and visitors sampled different recipes in which Naxos potatoes took centre stage, and enjoyed performances by musicians and dance groups.

title: In Chicago, Mexican-American Altars Reimagine Home
content:
In Chicago, Mexican-American Altars Reimagine Home
As ICE increasingly targets migrant neighborhoods, carefully crafted altars to La Virgen de Guadalupe outside homes transform sidewalks into sites of community and protection.
This article is part of a series focusing on underrepresented craft histories, researched and written by the 2025 Craft Archive Fellows, and organized in collaboration with the Center for Craft.
I come from a family of both tradition and the trades. Work, even something as simple as mopping, was often coupled with the saying échale arte — to add art to the utilitarian. Craft, artesanía in Mexico, was never entirely separate from work, necessity, or the everyday. It is a knowledge embedded in the hands.
Hands are central themes in my research on Mexican-American altars as craftwork. These altar-makers’ hands — often just as accustomed to labor as to craft — are capable of transforming displacement and recreating home. Craft attempts to abarcar, or encompass, something more than the aesthetic. It grasps the symbols, skills, histories, and inherited knowledge that make handiwork dense with meaning. A crafted object evidences not only the hands that made it, but generations of repeated gestures carried forward through those hands.
Much of folk craft begins with the home: made in the home, for the home, and essential to constituting what a home is. This becomes particularly meaningful in migration, when home must be remade. Among Mexican migrants in the United States, part of that remaking is altar-raising (levantar un altar) to La Virgen de Guadalupe. Collectively, these altars form their own archive of an overlooked American craft tradition — one rooted in the migrant and homesteading experiences of recreating home in new, even hostile environments.
Mexican altar-making is not entirely absent from institutional spaces. Chicago’s National Museum of Mexican Art, for example, has presented an annual Día de Muertos exhibition for four decades, placing ofrendas from Mexico and the United States alongside folk and other forms of visual art. Yet the everyday devotional altars raised to La Virgen de Guadalupe on porches, in gardens, storefronts, windows, and along streets in Mexican neighborhoods have received far less institutional attention.
I turn first to my personal archive of photography. For nearly 15 years, I have been documenting public altars, often without thinking of the photographs as an archive at all. I was simply drawn to altars and their frequency. For this project, I returned to those images while also refreshing my collection, walking through South Chicago and Pilsen, Illinois, both historically Mexican neighborhoods, to document the altars that exist today.

title: 13yo Mount Isa bull rider sets sights on Texas
content:
Mount Isa Rodeo backs next generation of outback stars
In short:
The Mount Isa Rodeo is backing the next generation of outback riders, committing $10,000 to help 13-year-old Lareece Daley-Kennedy compete at two youth world finals in the United States.
The Kalkadoon and Pitta Pitta cowgirl is among several young North West riders making their mark as the revived rodeo puts greater focus on developing local talent.
What's next?
Lareece will travel to the United States to compete in youth world finals in Oklahoma and Texas.
Inside the Kalkadoon Arena, in the heart of Queensland's wild north-west, courage can be measured in eight seconds.
The Mount Isa Rodeo is the biggest in the Southern Hemisphere and this year some of its youngest riders made the biggest impression.
Kalkadoon and Pitta Pitta cowgirl Lareece Daley-Kennedy, 13, is preparing to step onto the international stage after receiving invitations to two youth world finals in the United States.
She has been invited to compete at the Professional Youth Roughstock Association World Finals in Oklahoma and the World Championship Mini Bulls World Finals in Texas.
The invitations follow a string of strong performances across the North West, including a second-place finish on her first steer ride earlier this year.
At this year's Mount Isa Rodeo she came just short of the buzzer in the Mount Isa round before returning to place third in the Indigenous mini bulls.
Now the Mount Isa Rodeo is putting real weight behind that next generation, committing $10,000 to help get Lareece to the United States.
It is the first time the incumbent board has directly backed a young rider in this way.
For Lareece, the secret to lasting eight seconds is simple.
"Just lock your knees in and your legs and just hold on," she said.
Lareece was not the only young rider to impress.
Cloncurry brothers Dallas and Ashley Murphy, aged 10 and 14, swept the mini bull titles.
Cade Ferguson, 19, was crowned the rodeo's all-round cowboy, just weeks after becoming world champion in bull riding and reserve world champion in saddle bronc at the Cinch World Championship Junior Rodeo in Oklahoma.
In her father's footsteps
Lareece took up riding after hearing stories about her father Nathan Kennedy's own days in the sport.
"I just wanted to follow my dad's footsteps," she said.
The sport has taught her how to take a hard landing and get back up.
Earlier this year she was winded on her first steer ride and last year at Cloncurry she was thrown and landed on her neck.
"I'd heard people say, 'Oh, she came second', and I just got up like nothing happened," she said.
Her family initially set out to raise about $15,000 to make the trip to the US possible, with supporters across the north-west chipping in through raffles and donations.
Then came the call from the Mount Isa Rodeo to the shock and delight of her family.
"Blew me away, made me cry actually," Mr Kennedy said.
"It's got us there. It's got us over the line."
Backing the young ones
The Mount Isa Rodeo has already had to fight for its own future.
The event fell into voluntary administration in September 2024, before a group of residents rallied to revive it for last year, bringing it back before a record crowd.
Now the board is turning its attention to the riders coming through.
Mount Isa Rodeo vice-chair Marcus Curr said developing young riders was becoming an important part of the organisation's future.
"A lot of kids in the bush … don't get to play cricket and football as much as city kids do," he said.
"So rodeo is a big part of their life and their culture."
The board runs an annual junior clinic where young people including children from remote communities learn about safety, technique and competition.
Mr Curr estimated about 50 children attended this year.
Smaller rodeos across the region also give young competitors somewhere to build their skills before stepping into the Kalkadoon Arena.
Mr Curr said the Murphy brothers and Cade Ferguson were examples of what can happen when talent was matched with family support and opportunities to compete.
"If there's talent around, we've got to support them and encourage them and give them opportunities," he said.
Beyond the Kalkadoon Arena
Mr Curr said he wanted the Mount Isa Rodeo to become "more than just running a rodeo for the weekend".
"It's about investing in opportunities for kids and having Mount Isa Rodeo being a part of Australia developing some of the best cowboys and cowgirls in the world," he said.
For Lareece, one of those opportunities is already waiting in the United States, with plenty of pressure and expectation.
But ask what she loves most about bull riding and the answer is much simpler.
"Winning and holding on."

title: Mulheres no coco de roda: Mestra Beba Lima
content:
Por Camila da Conceição Magalhães*
Pisei no cantinho que vovô pisou para dançar coco de roda, pode me chamar que eu vou… (Trecho de Coco de Roda, composição de Mestra Beba).
É pedindo licença para pisar que vamos adentrar o terreiro da comunidade quilombola Caiana dos Crioulos, localizada no município de Alagoa Grande (PB). É lá, pertinho do Reino Encantado, que reside Josefa Maria, mais conhecida como Beba, ou Beba Lima ou Mestra Beba. Atuante no movimento de mulheres negras, cuidadora do Museu Vivo da comunidade de Caiana que carrega a história do coco de roda e da ciranda, agricultora, mãe, zabumbeira e compositora.
Sua trajetória com o coco de roda inicia muito cedo, aos sete anos, acompanhando seu avô que tocava triângulo nas brincadeiras tradicionais do quilombo. A partir daí surge o interesse pela cultura. Começa tocando triângulo assim como seu avô. Ensaiando com um “estribo” dos cavalos e uma colher. Como ela conta:
“Na época, quando eu era pequena, ainda caminhava com meu avô. E eu fui tomando gosto pelo pela cultura. Desde que eu comecei a tomar gosto e quando chegava em casa eu começava a tocar nas bacias, cadeirão, balde, né? O triângulo eu fazia com estribo, aquele estribo de cela de burro onde a gente coloca os pés. Eu pegava uma colher e ficava treinando em casa. Foi assim que eu aprendi. Aí fui crescendo e tomando gosto pela cultura, pelo coco de roda”, relata Mestra Beba, em entrevista concedida ao projeto de extensão Comunidade Colaborativa de Mulheres Afro-brasileiras e Ameríndias (Cocam), ligado à Universidade Federal da Paraíba (UFPB).
Por amor à cultura, Mestra Beba participou por muito tempo de forma voluntária, sem compor nenhum grupo. Recebendo posteriormente os convites para integrar os grupos: As Caianas e Brilho do Coco.
Sobre o grupo As Caianas ela conta:
“Eu comecei com as Caianas. Inclusive que a gente foi para Goiás. Criamos as caianas, que é um grupo de mulheres, de sete mulheres. Fomos para Goiás, que na época eu tinha um medo danado de participar porque eu não tinha saído para cantar. Eu não me sentia segura de ser zabumbeira, né? E na época a gente subiu no palco lá em Goiás com aquela multidão de gente e eu insegura. Mas depois que eu cheguei lá em cima e comecei a tocar e o povo começou a dançar, eu esqueci que tava lá em Goiás e comecei a bater zabumba. E aí ficou a zabumbeira aqui do Quilombo Caiana dos Crioulos. Eu amo tocar zabumba!”.
É muito bonito ver o amor com que a Mestra fala sobre a brincadeira do coco de roda e da ciranda. Trazendo sempre a importância de manter viva a tradição. Nesse intuito, faz questão de transmitir seus conhecimentos para a juventude. Participando de forma ativa em projetos voltados ao compartilhamento de saberes. Apesar das dificuldades enfrentadas por conta do racismo, do machismo e dos preconceitos atribuídos à tradição, Mestra Beba tem na brincadeira um momento de celebração e agradecimento às conquistas comunitárias.
Perguntada sobre as inspirações para a composição das toadas de coco de roda, Mestra Beba nos diz:
“A composição vem também trazendo uma raiz das nossas ancestralidades, que as nossas composições antigas dos nossos cocos foi tudo feita daqui da comunidade de fatos reais, né? Por exemplo, o meu avô, ele contava um coco que ele ficou viúvo, aí pegou e se apaixonou de novo. Na hora da roda do coco, ele olhou para uma moça lá. Ele disse: ‘Eu caso com você, ô morena’. Aí pronto, saiu a palavra chave e saiu a composição. Eu tô aqui seguindo os passos, né? Os passos do meu avô. Uma das primeiras composições minhas foi inspirada no meu avô, que eu canto que é essa que diz assim: ‘Pisei no cantinho que vovô pisou para dançar coco de roda, pode me chamar que eu vou’ e aí vai.”
Mestra Beba ainda fala sobre o desejo de reavivar a tradição das bandinhas de pífanos que acompanhavam as novenas e faziam a abertura da brincadeira do coco, tocando em conjunto. Já está empenhada em aprender a tocar o “pife”, podemos aguardar novidades vindo por aí, muito em breve.
*Camila da Conceição Magalhães é brincante e pesquisadora da cultura popular, graduanda do curso de antropologia com habilitação em antropologia visual na Universidade Federal da Paraíba (UFPB). Atualmente é extensionista bolsista no projeto Cocam.
**Este texto faz parte de uma série de artigos que terão como protagonistas mestras do coco Potiguara. Leia o primeiro artigo aqui.
***A opinião contida neste texto não necessariamente representa a linha editorial do Brasil de Fato.

title: Outback town marks 60th anniversary of plane crash that claimed 24 lives
content:
Winton remembers deadly Ansett-ANA Flight 149 crash 60 years on
In short:
Ansett-ANA Flight 149 crashed near the outback Queensland town of Winton on September 22nd 1966, killing all 24 people aboard.
The crash triggered one of the largest aviation investigations in Australia's history.
As the Winton community and loved ones of those who died pay their respects, the daughter of one of the pilots continues to work on an oral history project to document the crash and its fallout.
Sixty years ago, what was meant to be a short flight between two Western Queensland towns ended in one of Australia's deadliest aviation crashes.
Conditions were favourable when Ansett-ANA Flight 149 took off from Mount Isa, bound for Brisbane via Longreach, on September 22, 1966.
But 30 minutes into the flight an engine was on fire and the aircraft was put into an emergency descent before breaking apart in the air and crashing onto a cattle property 19 kilometres west of Winton.
All 24 people on board died.
As the small outback community nearly 200 kilometres north-west of Longreach gathered to mark the 60th anniversary, they remembered the lives that were lost and the impact the tragedy had on the aviation industry.
Community mourns
Winton Mayor Cathy White said the crash greatly affected the community.
"Sixty years on, there are people here that remember it like it happened yesterday," she said.
"I think we should always come and remember [together]."
At the ceremony on Tuesday locals and the families of those who died paid their respects.
Elizabeth Gillam, the daughter of co-pilot John Gillam, was 18 months old when her father died.
"It was a defining feature of my life," she said.
"When the crash happened, my mum went from being a stay-at-home mum to being the breadwinner, so everything changed."
Dr Gillam said it was important to hear the stories of other people affected.
"All of these families, all of these people in the Winton community were brought together by this one singular event," she said.
"So many lives were changed."
Anne O'Leary's father, Ken Cooper, piloted the plane.
She said his loss significantly changed the dynamic of her family's life. Her mum had no choice but to go to work and the family home was sold to make ends meet.
Ms O'Leary said her two younger brothers followed in their dad's footsteps and became pilots themselves.
"I became a teacher. My older brother and I do not like to fly, but we do manage that," she said.
Ms O'Leary attended the 25th anniversary, which she said was "cathartic and gave them closure".
"After 60 years it's more about meeting other people, sharing stories and dedicating the memory to them," she said.
Extensive investigation
The tragedy led to one of the largest aviation crash investigation in Australian history.
State Library of New South Wales historian Peter Hobbins said the Air Safety Investigation Branch (the predecessor to the Australian Transport Safety Bureau) launched an investigation and the federal government ordered an independent inquiry.
"[It] ended up costing the Commonwealth an estimated $1.12 million, in 1967 terms," he said.
Dr Hobbins said the investigation and the following independent inquiry concluded that a small "blower" motor that helped deliver air into the cabin had worn out and caught fire, also igniting one of the engines.
That caused parts of the plane to melt before the wing broke off, tearing the roof open on descent.
Dr Hobbins said the crash attracted the attention it did because there had been two other similar crashes in Australia that decade.
"I think to have an accident as severe as the one at Winton pushed hard against that sense of comfort that Australians were starting to assume about airline travel," he said.
Dr Hobbins said the inquiry drove home the need for better monitoring and servicing intervals, and that the investigation reinforced Australia's dedication to becoming a world leader in aviation safety.
"For the last nearly 60 years, it actually has been incredibly safe," he said.
"I think a lot of the roots of that [safety] culture were set in the 1950s and the 1960s."
Documenting oral history
Dr Gillam believes there are lessons to be learned from the crash and has spent the last decade working to document them.
After the 50th anniversary she started an oral history project to collect testimonies from anyone who remembered the days and weeks following the tragedy.
As part of that research Dr Gillam spoke with investigator Don Wally.
"He was able to explain in great detail what had happened," she said.
Dr Gillam's project is ongoing and she is keen to speak with other people who have been affected, not just to capture what happened on that day in 1966, but to learn more about the wider ramifications, including how the families were compensated in the aftermath.
"All of these are important to capture, for history, to work out how we can do things better."

title: Murió Ismael Querales, pilar de la bandola y la canción venezolana
content:
Falleció Ismael Querales, el bandolista, uno de los fundadores de Un Solo Pueblo, la agrupación que en los años setenta y ochenta despuntó en los medios para mostrar su revisión de las tradiciones venezolanas, una propuesta que se volvió fija para las generaciones de entonces, que vieron en las canciones del grupo una búsqueda que encontró asidero para hacer su obra parte de la cultura del país.
En 1986, en una entrevista con Judith Castillo en el programa Cita con…, dejó muy claros los objetivos: “Cuando aparece Un Solo Pueblo, ahorita no tanto porque ya hay mucha gente preocupada por la música venezolana y el trabajo a nivel de grupos, pero en esa época era muy fuerte la penetración de otros países, sobre todo la música gringa y la salsa. Nuestros objetivos principales eran, y todavía son, la difusión y promoción de nuestros valores y nuestra identidad. Un país sin identidad es igual que una persona sin personalidad”, indicó el músico entonces, que fue parte de la agrupación junto con sus hermanos Jesús y Florentino.
Ismael Querales nació en Caracas el 17 de junio de 1953. Se crió en Chapellín, ahí, cerca del Ávila, entre La Florida y el Country Club. Era hijo de Teo Capriles, sí, el de la academia de natación, un atleta que también destacó en la música como tenor solista; pupilo de Vicente Emilio Sojo que formó parte del Orfeón Lamas y que interpretó a Florentino en 1954 en la Cantata criolla de Antonio Estévez.
De acuerdo con la biografía oficial de Ismael Querales, por ese contexto familiar desde niño estuvo rodeado de grandes músicos. “Su padre le heredó, además del oído superdotado y del amor por lo autóctono, la tarea de adquirir conciencia sobre el arduo trabajo de investigación que requería conocer la cultura popular”, indica el portal web del artista.
Con Un Solo Pueblo grabó 25 discos, pero hizo vida más allá de la agrupación con trabajos en solitario como Bandolas, publicado en 2002 por la Fundación Bigott, institución clave también para la conformación de Pasacalle, otra de las agrupaciones de la que formó parte y con la que grabó cinco discos. Además, estaba enfocado en los años recientes en Venezuela Un Solo Pueblo.
“Ismael Querales fue y seguirá siendo siempre uno de los grandes bandolistas de este país. No solo por su notable virtuosismo en la ejecución de la bandola, su velocidad, su temple, su fortaleza a la hora de ejecutar el instrumento, que es una cosa innegable, sino que también es importante decir que fue muy virtuoso a la hora de poder tocar los diferentes tipos de bandolas que tenemos en el país con solvencia y respetando los estilos de cada una de las músicas de las regiones en donde él se quería ubicar”, indica el mandolinista y compositor Jorge Torres.
Subraya cómo el músico caraqueño podía tocar un joropo llanero con toda la reciedumbre que exige para pasar a un joropo oriental perfectamente dentro de la estética de esa música, y lo mismo cuando iba al joropo tuyero. “Esto es muy difícil. Ismael Querales podía hacerlo sin ningún problema porque fue una persona que se dedicó a estudiar muy bien la música venezolana. Era un gran conocedor de la música de toda nuestra geografía”.
Jorge Torres resalta que su legado no solo se mide por su virtuosismo, sino por una labor pedagógica caracterizada por la generosidad. Recuerda que el músico nunca dudó en compartir sus conocimientos con amigos, seguidores y colegas. “Por otro lado, deja un legado como compositor también muy interesante. Estoy seguro de que las nuevas generaciones lo van a asumir para seguir proyectándolo. Porque Ismael Querales, aparte de todo lo dicho anteriormente, fue una persona muy creativa. Y como compositor dijo mucho, y de una manera muy interesante, por supuesto, pegado a la tradición venezolana, pero con un enfoque muy personal”.
Caracas y legado
Para el cronista musical y gestor cultural Xariell Sarabia es importante destacar que Ismael Querales fue también un gran cultor de la música caraqueña, del merengue, de la guasa. Un interés que asegura viene de su papá, Teo Capriles, que grabó discos como Teo le canta a Caracas junto con el pianista Evencio Castellanos.
“Ismael toma el testigo de su papá y todo el tiempo él va a estar tratando de hacer música caraqueña con El Rucaneo de Mabil, con Daniel Gil y otros tantos. Va a estar siempre diciendo que la canción caraqueña debe cantarse de cierta manera, como si fuese un caraqueño antiguo, no solamente por el swing que tiene que tener esa voz, sino incluso en lo que se dice, en la construcción de las frases. Hablamos de un gran cantante de música caraqueña, de música cañonera”.
Para la joven Constanza Cegarra, Ismael Querales es un pilar de la identidad venezolana. Reconoce que no fue tan cercana al músico. “Lo fui descubriendo poco a poco en los años recientes. Yo vengo de un background donde hay mucha más fusión, una música venezolana más estilizada. Entonces, descubrir y conocer a Ismael Querales es saber de dónde viene toda esa fusión”, indica la integrante del dúo Constanza y Fernanda, uno de los más prometedores de la música en Venezuela de años recientes.
“Uno se queda corto si habla de él como músico, como el gran bandolista que fue. No solo fue un intérprete y un compositor de música tradicional, sino que fue un investigador, una persona que fue a cada uno de los pueblos en Venezuela a recoger y recopilar la tradición. Eso fue algo que le inculcó incluso a sus hijas, a las que también admiro muchísimo porque continuaron con el legado de su padre, con ese fervor investigativo”.
La también estudiante de Comunicación Social recalca que tal vez muchos conocen de él sin saber que lo conocen, por canciones como “Caracas, Caracas” o “Viva Venezuela”. “Es muy difícil empezar a despedir maestros, es muy difícil ver cómo se van cuando uno siente que tienen muchísimo más por dar. La huella de Ismael es muy grande. Creo que en este momento se va a empezar a esparcir mucho más. Una de mis composiciones favoritas es una fulía que se llama 'Juro por la clara luna'. Cada vez que la oigo me para los pelos. Hablamos de un coloso de la música tradicional al cual uno va a referenciar, al que uno le debe mucho”.

title: A Queen Ruled Warangal As A King. Centuries Later, Her Kakatiya Legacy Lives On In Telangana’s Flower Festival
content: Every year, as the monsoon retreats from Telangana's parched plains, women wake before sunrise to gather wildflowers that bloom nowhere else in quite the same way, stacking them into towers shaped like temple gopurams. The ritual is called Bathukamma, and while it now draws crowds from Los Angeles to London, its earliest echoes lead back roughly 800 years, to the fort city of Warangal and a queen who governed disguised as a king. A queen's devotion becomes a kingdom's memory The Kakatiya dynasty ruled large parts of present-day Telangana through the 12th and 13th centuries, with their capital at Orugallu, known today as Warangal. Their reign left behind some of the Deccan's finest architecture, including the Thousand Pillar Temple, built in 1163 under King Rudradeva, and the Ramappa Temple, completed in 1213 and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It was Rudradeva's descendant, Rani Rudramadevi, who became part of one of the enduring stories associated with Bathukamma. Ganapatideva, her father, had no son, so he formally designated her as his male heir through the putrika ceremony and gave her the name Rudradeva. She took the throne around 1262, ruled in male attire, put down rebellions from nobles who resisted a woman's authority, and strengthened the Warangal Fort her father had begun. Historical tradition credits her with promoting the worship of Kakatamma, a regional mother goddess, particularly around Mogilicharla, where grand processions were held on Durga Ashtami, complete with music, dance, and the ceremonial immersion of the deity in nearby water. Wildflowers including tangedu and gunuka form the vibrant base of Telangana's annual Bathukamma celebrations. Photograph: (The Hindu) That closing ritual has often been cited as one thread in the long history of Bathukamma: flowers offered to water and a prayer for their return the following year echo the symbolism of what is now Saddula Bathukamma, the grand finale of the nine-day festival. But Rudramadevi's story is not an uncontested founding account of Bathukamma. Historians and scholars have also traced the festival to older local agricultural, seasonal and feminine fertility traditions, some of which may predate the Kakatiyas. The Kakatiya-Rudramadevi connection is therefore one of the historical memories woven into the festival's story, rather than a definitive origin. Historians admit the precise origin remains genuinely contested, but the Kakatiya connection is the version sung most often in Bathukamma's own folk songs. It is this layered history that leads many in Telangana to call Warangal the symbolic birthplace of Bathukamma, even as other folk traditions, including stories involving a Chola king's daughter and goddess Parvati, circulate alongside it. Flowers that follow the rains Whatever its exact origin, Bathukamma is unmistakably a festival of the land. It begins on ‘Mahalaya Amavasya’ and runs for nine days until Durga Ashtami, tracking the seasonal shift from Varsha Ruthu, the monsoon, to Sharad Ruthu, autumn. Bathukamma's flower towers are traditionally built in concentric layers, often resembling the shape of a temple gopuram. Photograph: (The Hindu) As the rains recede, wild and largely medicinal flowers bloom across Telangana's uncultivated plains, chiefly gunuka and tangedu, alongside banti and chamanti. Men and boys gather these blooms each morning, and women arrange them into seven concentric layers resembling a temple gopuram, crowned with a small turmeric idol called Gauramma. Each of the nine days carries its own food offering, from sesame and rice on the first day to a rich, sweetened rice preparation on the last, and every evening the flower stack is carried in procession, sung to in call-and-response folk verses, and finally immersed in a pond or lake. This closing act depends entirely on Telangana's older water culture: the region's dense network of tanks and lakes was originally built to trap monsoon runoff for farming, a legacy so tied to local memory that a lake in Hyderabad's Amberpet still carries the festival's name. Many of these water bodies, strained by decades of urban growth, are now being nursed back to life by community-led efforts that echo the same ecological instinct Bathukamma has carried for centuries: give back to the water what it once gave you. From village courtyards to a state's identity When Telangana became India's 29th state in 2014, its government declared Bathukamma, alongside Bonalu, an official state festival on 26 June, 2014. Since then, the state has funded free sarees and large public celebrations, and Bathukamma has grown into an emblem of Telangana identity celebrated well beyond its borders, among diaspora communities in Dubai, Qatar, the United Kingdom, the United States and Australia. That instinct to keep an old practice alive through new hands runs through much of Telangana's culture. In Cheriyal, a handful of Nakashi artist families still hand-paint the scroll paintings that once accompanied travelling storytellers narrating exactly the kind of oral folklore Bathukamma's songs preserve. From village courtyards to celebrations around the world, Bathukamma has become a vibrant symbol of Telangana's cultural identity. Photograph: (Dakshinapatha) Around Pochampally, weavers whose craft was transformed by the Laxmi Asu Machine, invented by a school dropout to spare his mother's aching joints, show how tradition survives by adapting rather than standing still. And as concerns grow nationally over flowers dumped into rivers after festivals, entrepreneurs elsewhere are already turning discarded blooms into incense and dye rather than letting them pollute the water, a shift Bathukamma's own communities are beginning to consider for their post-immersion flowers too. This year, Bathukamma runs from 11 October to 18 October. As it has for generations, the festival will unfold as women's private history made public: songs never written down, carried instead from mother to daughter, filling Telangana's streets, courtyards and lakesides with colour that, if the Kakatiya-era memory holds, has been blooming there for the better part of a millennium. Sources 'Historical traditions link Bathukamma to Kakatiya-era worship of goddess Kakatamma at Mogilicharla': Orugallu Andhalu, Published 18 March, 2026 'About Bathukamma': Government of Telangana, Official Bathukamma portal 'How Bonalu festival has become an empowering space for trans women in Telangana’: Written by Jagadish Babu for The News Minute, on Bonalu and Bathukamma being awarded state festival status on 26 June, 2014

title: Group to showcase Domboshava heritage at Bira reMbira
content:
Herald Reporter
DOMBOSHAVA’S Mbira Dzepadombo Ensemble will be among featured groups at this year’s Bira reMbira National Festival, bringing the area’s rich mbira traditions to the national cultural showcase at the Glamis Arena on Friday.
The third edition of Bira reMbira, which starts at 10am on September 25 and runs through to the morning of September 26, will bring together leading “gwenyambiras” master mbira players in a celebration of traditional acoustic music, spiritual heritage and the country’s mbira value chain.
The festival is being held under the theme “Roots to Markets – Empowering Makers, Players and Markets”, according to the Ministry of Sport, Recreation, Arts and Culture’s official festival brief.
The festival is being held with support from the Ministry of Sport, Recreation, Arts and Culture and the Ministry of Tourism and Hospitality Industry.
For Mbira Dzepadombo, the festival provides an important national platform to showcase the cultural traditions of Domboshava while highlighting ongoing efforts to preserve and pass on mbira knowledge to younger generations.
The ensemble was initiated by Dr Pearson Pfavayi, a tourism and cultural heritage advocate who recognised the deep cultural and spiritual connection between mbira music and the Domboshava community.
The group has been selected as one of the featured ensembles at Bira reMbira 2026 in recognition of its artistry, cultural preservation work and performance standards.
It will be led by master “gwenyambira,” Sekuru Thomas Chiombera, alongside Percy Dandiro, David Matiza and Nokutenda Kadzima.
Dr Pfavayi said the group’s participation was part of a broader effort to ensure that mbira remains a living cultural tradition rather than merely a historical artefact.
“Mbira is a sacred art form and a foundational pillar of our Zimbabwean cultural heritage that we must actively honour, preserve and identify with. Through Mbira Dzepadombo, we seek to safeguard these ancient rhythms while creating opportunities for people to learn, experience and appreciate their cultural significance,” he said.
The group’s activities are closely linked to Basecamp Domboshava, which serves as the home of Mbira Dzepadombo.
Situated at the foot of the historic Domboshava Caves and granite mountain, Basecamp Domboshava brings together cultural heritage preservation, community arts and adventure tourism.
A Mbira Training Centre is set to commence training on October 10, offering structured lessons to local youths, national students and international visitors in traditional mbira tuning, crafting and playing techniques.
The training centre forms part of the broader cultural activities being developed at Basecamp Domboshava, which also operates alongside Domboview Adventures, providing a base for guided cave hikes, team-building activities, art gallery sales and traditional food experiences.
Dr Pfavayi said the forthcoming training programme would help strengthen the inter-generational transmission of mbira knowledge.
“By establishing Mbira Dzepadombo and our dedicated Mbira Training Centre at Basecamp Domboshava, our mission is to preserve traditional knowledge and skills while opening the mbira experience to young Zimbabweans, visitors and international audiences,” he said.
The 2026 Bira reMbira festival will feature a wide range of artistes and mbira groups, including Victor Kunonga, Feli Nandi, Andy Muridzo, Duramazwi, Nyamasvisva Nemaungira Enharira, Amadhuve, Sasha, Kurai Makore, Mangwenya, Diana Samkange, Vee Mhofu, Texas Tekenya, Jah Lemmy, Gushungo, Jaka Band, Lioness Shumbakadzi, Ntswai Ntswai Arts, Brity Yonly, NzombeHuru Mbira Ensemble, Pauline Mafriq, Tatu Maluba, Dzambira, Mbira Dzenharo, Ambuya Mavhu Mbira Group, Chikwata 263, Batroy Movement, Nemachinda Ehondo Crew, Nina X and Zariyah Roots Band, Professor Muzvinafundo, Sekuru Gore and Mazana Movement, Ruyamuro Mbira Crew, Rose Wembira, Madzimambo Edu Mbira Family, Culture Livingstone, Dzimbanwe Mbira Crew, Pastoral Entertainment Group, Masimba Evanhu Mbira Group, Madzinza Embira, Dzamawuruka Mbira Band, Sekuru Mushore Mbira Custodians, Chishawasha Nhare Mbira Group, Izwi Remhondoro Mbira Group, Mbira Dzepadombo, Jangu Wiriranai Arts and Mbira Group and Nelson Tswatswa.
The extensive line-up reflects the organisers’ intention to bring together established musicians, emerging performers and traditional mbira ensembles under one platform.
Festival organiser Benjamin “Benjie” Nyandoro said Bira reMbira was designed to create a meeting point for musicians, cultural practitioners, audiences and the wider creative economy.
“Bira reMbira is more than a music event. It is a platform for Zimbabweans to celebrate their heritage while creating opportunities for musicians, instrument makers, cultural practitioners and young creatives. Our intention is to connect the roots of mbira with markets so that those who preserve and promote this heritage can also find sustainable opportunities within the creative economy,” he said.
The festival will provide a free-to-the-public cultural experience and will feature established and emerging mbira musicians, school ensembles and young creative collectives.
There will also be exhibitions showcasing mbira instruments, national fabric, herbs and medicinal plants, indigenous foods and other expressions of Zimbabwe’s diverse cultural heritage.
A major feature of this year’s festival will be a special tribute honouring the late Mbuya Stella Chiweshe, one of Zimbabwe’s foremost mbira practitioners and cultural ambassadors.
The Ministry’s official brief states that the festival will honour her through dedicated performances of her songs in a commemorative segment highlighting her influence on contemporary mbira practice.
Her artistic journey, leadership and longstanding commitment to the mbira tradition inspired generations of musicians, cultural practitioners and mbira custodians.
The tribute will form part of a broader celebration of Zimbabwe’s living heritage, with performers using the festival to demonstrate how the mbira continues to evolve while remaining rooted in traditional practice.
For Mbira Dzepadombo, the Bira reMbira appearance will be followed by another community-focused engagement when the ensemble is scheduled to perform at the Pinktober Breast Cancer Awareness Event on October 31.
The performance will form part of activities supporting cancer survivors and breast cancer awareness.
The continued involvement of Mbira Dzepadombo in cultural, tourism and community initiatives reflects the group’s broader objective of using mbira as a vehicle for cultural education, heritage preservation and community engagement.
The Ministry of Sport, Recreation, Arts and Culture has said Bira reMbira complements the Government’s broader cultural development agenda by creating platforms for heritage preservation, youth participation, creative enterprise, skills development, market access and cultural diplomacy.
As Glamis Arena prepares to host the overnight cultural gathering, Mbira Dzepadombo will carry with it the sounds and traditions of Domboshava, giving audiences an opportunity to experience a living heritage that continues to evolve while remaining rooted in Zimbabwean cultural identity.

title: La mercantilización de culturas y tradiciones indígenas
content:
Este artículo es parte de la serie «Spotlight» de Global Voices de agosto de 2026, «Derechos indígenas«. Esta serie ofrece una visión de las vidas y experiencias de los pueblos indígenas con el fin de establecer vínculos entre regiones, destacar las experiencias indígenas y contar historias de líderes, activistas, miembros de la comunidad y otras personas. Puedes apoyar esta cobertura con una donación.
Las tradiciones, el arte y las ceremonias son el eje de la identidad colectiva de muchas comunidades indígenas, fundamentales para conmemorar acontecimientos importantes, fomentar un sentido de comunidad y transmitir la historia a las generaciones más jóvenes. Sin embargo, con demasiada frecuencia, estas tradiciones se extraen, reformulan, comercializan o se las apropia alguien para beneficio ajeno.
Las ceremonias espirituales se recrean para los turistas. Los fabricantes se apropian de expresiones artísticas indígenas sin reconocer a sus creadores ni remunerarlos. Los Gobiernos incorporan el patrimonio indígena para legitimar su propio poder. Los mecanismos varían según la región y la cultura, pero el resultado es el mismo: los recursos y el significado se alejan de la comunidad que los creó y enriquecen a personas que les ajenas, a menudo pertenecientes a los mismos grupos que han oprimido a esa comunidad durante siglos.
En Oaxaca, México, los organizadores de bodas comercializan las llamadas “bodas oaxaqueñas” como paquetes turísticos que incluyen calendas, procesiones festivas tradicionales, mezcal y bailes, pero que despojan estos elementos de las ceremonias y la reciprocidad que les confieren su significado.
Mientras tanto, importantes casas internacionales de moda se apropian de diseños textiles indígenas, se benefician de sus creaciones y no reconocen ni remuneran a quienes las idearon. Pero la apropiación no termina allí: en Guatemala, las tejedoras mayas luchan por el reconocimiento jurídico de sus derechos colectivos de propiedad intelectual.
En el sur de México, las comunidades oaxaqueñas tienen una rica tradición de elaboradas ceremonias matrimoniales que se están convirtiendo en productos comerciales para atraer a públicos externos. Las bodas oaxaqueñas suelen incluir elementos como la calenda —una procesión tradicional de Oaxaca—, la guelaguetza —celebración tradicional oaxaqueña—, además de comidas, música, danzas, bebidas y rituales propios.
Estos “paquetes de bodas oaxaqueñas” despojan a las celebraciones de todo su significado cultural y las reducen a una transacción. Como explica la escritora oaxaqueña Kupijy Vargas:
El concepto de bodas oaxaqueñas está ofertado en un mercado comercial, ofrecido al público por paquetes, construidos a partir de la apropiación cultural de una calenda, incluyendo el mezcal, la música y las mujeres bailando.
Estos paquetes ofrecen ese concepto para después tener una fiesta en el jardín etnobotánico, en donde se sirve comida oaxaqueña gourmet, alimentos que se comen dentro de la región pero servidos de manera estilizada. Quienes los preparan y los sirven, es decir, los meseros, cocineras, etcétera, son quienes sostienen con sus atenciones a esa fiesta en donde no existe la Guelaguetza, ni el acto de dar y recibir, sino que existe una monetización por los servicios. Es allí cuando el colonialismo vuelve a triunfar, convirtiendo en trabajadores a todas esas personas de la cultura en la que crecieron y nacieron, en sus propias tierras.
Una dinámica similar se observa con los textiles de esta región y de otras comunidades indígenas. La escritora oaxaqueña Tajëëw B. Díaz Robles sostiene que extraer textiles tradicionales sin reconocer ni compensar a las comunidades que los crearon constituye una forma de apropiación.
…propongo que el plagio y/o apropiación de la blusa de Tlahui y de sus patrones gráficos por parte de Isabel Marant y Antik Batik (otra empresa de moda francesa que también incurrió en la copia del textil de Tlahui en su colección Bartra de 2014) es la conversión de formas diversas de derechos de propiedad colectiva-comunal a propiedad privada, puesto que hasta el momento del plagio los bordados eran considerados parte de la identidad cultural de un colectivo, un textil cuyos patrones gráficos identifican a una comunidad en específico y que se recrea comunitariamente. Esto no significa que no sean personas específicas las que las elaboran ni que no exista una comercialización local, pero estas personas crean y producen en un contexto comunitario delimitado y las prendas circulan en un mercado que identifica claramente su origen. De ahí que Marant y Antik Batik, en palabras de las autoridades comunitarias de Tlahuitoltepec en su pronunciamiento de junio de 2015, hayan cometido algo que enuncian como ‘la apropiación de un patrimonio cultural.’
Algunas comunidades mayas de Guatemala están dando batalla a esta situación con promoción de medidas legales que protejan las artesanías y los textiles tradicionales.
La lucha lleva más de diez años. En 2016, la Asociación Femenina para el Desarrollo de Sacatepéquez (AFEDES) y una coalición de cooperativas de tejedoras presentaron una acción de inconstitucionalidad en la que argumentaron que el silencio de Guatemala respecto de los derechos sobre los textiles indígenas también era inconstitucional. La Corte de Constitucionalidad falló dos veces a su favor y ordenó al Congreso aprobar una legislación de protección. Hasta ahora, el Congreso no ha cumplido. Dos proyectos quedaron truncos en el proceso legislativo: la iniciativa 5247 en 2017, y la iniciativa 6136 en 2022.
En junio de 2026, el movimiento, que ahora trabaja con el nombre “Ru Chajixik ri Qana'ojb'äl” (“salvaguardar nuestros conocimientos”, en kaqchikel), presentó una tercera propuesta: la iniciativa 6788.
Al igual que sus antecesoras, la iniciativa define la propiedad intelectual sobre los textiles como «colectiva, inalienable e imprescriptible». Esto significa que pertenece a la comunidad y no a una persona en particular, que no puede venderse ni cederse y que no está sujeta a caducidad.
Si se aprobara, reconocería formalmente a los pueblos indígenas como titulares de los derechos de autor sobre sus tejidos, diseños y técnicas, incluidos los motivos, patrones, símbolos, colores, glifos y petroglifos específicos transmitidos de generación en generación. También crearía un Consejo Nacional de Propiedad Intelectual sobre Textiles y Vestimenta Indígena a cargo de hacer cumplir esos derechos. Las tejedoras también han solicitado al Congreso tres compromisos concretos junto con la iniciativa: un fallo favorable que reafirme el fundamento constitucional y jurídico internacional de la propiedad intelectual colectiva indígena; un tratamiento legislativo acelerado; y un diálogo permanente entre el Congreso y el movimiento para hacer un seguimiento de los avances del proyecto.
Independientemente de lo que ocurra con la iniciativa en el Congreso de Guatemala, la propuesta constituye un modelo para otros pueblos indígenas de todo el mundo que buscan proteger sus derechos de propiedad intelectual.

title: A cowboy act: Photographer Ivan McClellan on capturing the world of Black rodeo culture
content:
A cowboy act: Photographer Ivan McClellan on capturing the world of Black rodeo culture
Photographer Ivan McClellan has a new edition of his Eight Seconds project, featuring 91 unseen photographs capturing Black cowboy and rodeo culture in the United States.
Few figures are more deeply woven into the American imagination than the cowboy. The rugged embodiment of independence, freedom and self-reliance - a national icon immortalised by films like The Searchers and The Good, the Bad and the Ugly.
But for generations, that image been overwhelmingly white.
Growing up in Kansas City, photographer Ivan McClellan knew a man down the street, Mr Wills, who raised cattle. But he was Black, wore a ball cap and overalls and looked nothing like John Wayne or Val Kilmer in Tombstone. So he never thought to call him a cowboy. The image on screen and the life around him simply didn't connect.
But in 2015 McClellan travelled four hours to a rodeo in Oklahoma and saw thousands of Black cowboys and cowgirls who looked far more like the people he had grown up around than anything Hollywood had shown him: men in gold chains and Jordans, women with long braids and acrylic nails riding horses at 50mph, with gospel, R&B and hip-hop filling the air.
That moment became the beginning of a decade-long obsession. McClellan began travelling across the US, photographing Black cowboy and cowgirl culture at rodeos, ranches, homes and events. His 2024 project, Eight Seconds, named after the time a bull rider must stay mounted to achieve a qualified ride, eventually became a much-loved book.
McClellan has since organised his own rodeo under his Eight Second project, putting significant prize money into the hands of Black competitors, while continuing to photograph and document a culture he believes has been overlooked.
Now he is releasing a new edition of his book titled Eight Seconds: Legacy in Motion, featuring 91 additional images, which he describes as more "precious" and "urgent".
Euronews Culture sat down with McClellan to discuss his latest book, his journey into Black cowboy culture, and why he has gone from photographing the rodeo to building one of his own.
So, the first edition came out in 2024, and this new edition of Eight Seconds has 91 new images. What made you want to revisit the book so soon?
It felt like a nice bow on nearly a decade of work, hanging on fences and chasing down cowboys and dodging bulls, and just really getting fully observed, absorbed and immersed in a culture that I just got obsessed with and completely loved.
That book came out, and my assumption was that the project was over, that I was going to go on and shoot something else. But it kept going, and it intensified, really. I started doing my own rodeo and photographing there, and spending time at more rodeos at a velocity like I had never done in any other previous years.
So two years later, I looked up and I had accumulated thousands of photos at people's ranches and homes and at events - mine and other events. And the portraiture had gotten a lot more intimate and a lot closer to the subject. And I felt like this work deserves a place in the world as well.
So I started to compile it into a book, and it felt similar. It felt like an extension or a sequel to the first book, but very different, and a lot more precious and a lot more urgent than the first one.
Growing up in Kansas City were you surprised by what you discovered about cowboy culture?
I grew up in Kansas. We would pick blackberries, we would climb trees, we would chase down fireflies, and all of the things that you would imagine. There were tornadoes, you know. There were a lot of things in Kansas that felt very country, but it didn't seem like anything familiar, like the films that I had seen on TV about cowboys. It didn't relate to that or connect to that in any way, mostly because everyone around me was Black.
You know, there was a man down the street, Mr. Wills, who raised cattle, but he was a Black man. So I never assumed that he was a cowboy because he didn't look a thing like John Wayne. He didn't look a thing like Val Kilmer in Tombstone. He was just out there in a ball cap and overalls, pushing cattle. And Junebug next door raised dogs and chickens, and was in a street gang. And he didn't seem like a cowboy either.
So it wasn't until 2015 that I went to a rodeo four hours away from the home that I grew up in, and I saw thousands of Black cowboys that looked a lot more like the people that I grew up with and the people in film that I realised that image in the film is the thing that's inaccurate. It's not the environment that I'm in. It's not the culture that I'm in. It's the movie that is, you know, an exaggeration or a falsehood of this culture.
I saw Black folks in cowboy hats and no shirt and gold chains, riding horses and basketball shorts. I saw women with long braids and acrylic nails riding horses 50 miles an hour. It felt very familiar. It felt a lot like home. And it had a hint of that movie, but not enough for me to feel so comfortable with the representations that I had seen in movies and TV.
What do you find so captivating and compelling about Black cowboy and cowgirl culture?
The cowboy thing in America is more than just entertainment. It's more than storytelling. It's myth-building. It's essential to our identity as Americans. These things that we attribute to cowboys - resilience, grit, independence - are core to our definition of self.
But that Black people have been excluded from that icon, that Black people have been excluded from that story, keeps us from attributing those things to ourselves. It says, yes, Americans are gritty and resilient and independent, but Black people aren't those things because they're not included in this image.
And realising that that wasn't true, I decided to bust up that myth and to put out imagery and to put out film and to tell stories and do live events in arenas that made it so the next generation of Black folks in this country will have no doubt that they're absolutely under the umbrella of all of those noble traits that we attribute to ourselves.
Women are really essential to this world. Women are in charge in cowboy culture for the most part. Like, the big rodeos, the big events that you go to, most of the presidents are women, and most of their teams are women. So if you're going to get money as a cowboy, that check is going to have a female name on the front of it.
Now, we're talking at a time when perhaps the United States, some might say, has never been so divided. What kind of feedback and reception did you get to the first edition?
The first edition, and this wasn't on purpose, came out on the same day as Beyoncé's Cowboy Carter. It came out on the exact same day, at the exact same time, as that album. And so the book just caught on fire, and people were searching for side stories to tell, or digging for the culture or the sources that she was pulling from. And the book was right underneath every single story about Beyoncé, around the world. So it was a gift of coincidence. I think it was, you know, fate in a lot of ways. It was kismet that that aligned in that way. I think it's the only thing that I have in common with Beyoncé, but it's the thing that I'm incredibly proud of.
People keep it on their dining room tables to this day, and people keep it on their shelves. I think a lot of Black folks and white folks viewed it as a point of pride. You know, white folks looked at it as, "This is a part of the country that I live in. This is something that I can be proud of as well." And Black folks looked at it as a definition, as proof of an identity that they hold within themselves.
There was some negativity, but I don't pay a ton of attention to that stuff. I would get calls on the phone from people that said, "Hey, I'm looking for tickets to that monkey rodeo." And I would just hang up the phone and go on about my day. I just don't dwell on that stuff. I don't let it take over because there's thousands and thousands and thousands more people that receive it positively and don't take offense to someone just celebrating their own culture.
The title of the book is “Eight Seconds” refers to the time that you have to hold on to a bull or horse. Have you tried it yourself? Now that you've got your own rodeo...
I have not tried to ride a bull or a bucking bronco. It's not anything that I have any interest in. I've been pressured to. We throw training camps now for the cowboys because it's bull riding, not bull hanging on. Like there's a technique to it, and there's a way to give yourself a better chance of hanging on.
So I throw camps. I have coaches come in and teach the athletes how to do their skill better. But every single time we have one, and the cowboys say, "Ivan, it's your turn. Put on a vest. Get on this bull." And I say, "My name is on the front of the check, not the back. I don't do that. I'm not performing for you all."
So I'm old, I'm big. That time is past. It's not anything that I'm going to be doing anytime soon.
You've gone beyond photographing the culture and set up your own rodeo. Why was that important to you?
You know, I saw a lot of inequality in this world. There were Black cowboys competing for a few hundred dollars that were doing the exact same events as white folks that were making tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of dollars to ride the same bulls and do the exact same event. So I decided that the best thing I could do to close that gap was to put on my own event and to give away $60,000 in prize money, which was money that these Black athletes had never seen before.
And I wanted to do it artfully. I wanted it to be lit like a photo studio in there. I wanted it to be spiritually powerful and physically moving. I wanted it to be like a live event like no one had ever seen. But me, personally, I had never thrown a birthday party. I had no reason to think that I could fill an arena with thousands of people, but I just stepped out on faith and did it anyway, and it was a resounding success.
Our first year, we had 2,000 people there. We gave out $60,000 in prize money. I saw athletes get new trucks, new trailers, get their pro cards and stay on the road all summer doing what they love. The next year, we were in a hockey arena and we sold 7,200 tickets. And it was packed, and people were dancing and just having a wonderful time experiencing the culture for the first time, like I did, in a place that was culturally rich and familiar to them.
And in a lot of ways, the third year we went to Portland, Oregon, where we started, and we went to Philadelphia on the East Coast. So we did two events, and we just continue to grow and refine the rodeo and touch more lives and bring people under this umbrella, which I think is wildly important, especially now with the discourse in America.
It's like, "You're not going to tell us who we are, and you're not going to limit where we go." What if there were 7,000 of us in an arena? It's wildly powerful. So we're going to continue to gather, we're going to continue to collect and tell this story to as many people as possible.
Do you hope to see a future where the distinction between Black and white rodeos disappears?
That would be the dream.
I mean, everything Western and everything to do with agriculture, everything to do with rodeo in America is incredibly tribal. The Mexicans are doing one thing, and they do it in their own cultural way. There are Indian rodeos, there are white rodeos, there are gay rodeos, there are female rodeos. It's all very segmented, and it's all very culturally rich.
But under the identity of whatever group you're going to - I love Mexican rodeos. They're incredibly fun. People are dancing in the dirt while people are riding bulls. There's a 32-person band playing music. It's a phenomenal time. But it's not a place that I feel like I necessarily fit in or belong. It's not the same as when I go to a Black rodeo.
So I would love for these events to maintain their identity and their cultural richness, but I would like for us to also recognise, "Hey, we're all doing the same thing," and we're doing it in a place and in a time where cowboys are becoming rarer and rarer. They're in rapid decline. Less people are getting into agriculture, less people are living in rural communities. A lot of farmland is becoming data centres in the United States.
And so, across the board, across all of these racial groups, this thing that they love, this heritage that's been passed down for generations, could not exist in the next ten years at all. You know, it could go away completely.
So I think that there might necessarily -it might be a necessity - for all of us to gather, and for all of us to depend on each other a little bit more, just to keep it going, so that, you know, we can continue to have livestock and we can continue to have people that know the skill of horsemanship, and we can continue to, you know, have food that's somewhat local.
Eight Seconds: Legacy in Motion by Ivan McClellan is published by Damiani Books.

title: He spent years reconciling his identity. Now he’s the first Arab bishop in Episcopal history.
content:
He spent years reconciling his identity. Now he’s the first Arab bishop in Episcopal history.
Get RNS’ thoughtful, essential religion reporting every morning. Sign up for free!
BROOKVILLE, N.Y. (RNS) — When Adam J. Shoemaker became the first bishop of Arab and North African descent in the Episcopal Church’s 237-year history this past weekend, many of his colleagues saw it as a glass-ceiling smashing.
Donning vestments with a Turkish blue tulip and North African pattern, Shoemaker greeted families, clergy and laypeople alike after his ordination and consecration as the ninth bishop of the Episcopal Diocese of Long Island on Saturday (Sept. 19). Nearly 2,000 people attended the ceremony at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts in Brookville, New York. The line to meet him stretched for more than 90 minutes.
“He embodies what it means to be the church in the world, and in particular, in New York City and the suburbs,” said the Rev. Lindsay Lunnum, rector of Zion Episcopal Church in Queens, which is part of Shoemaker’s diocese alongside Brooklyn.
Shoemaker, 47, told RNS he sees himself as an “imperfect vessel” for serving the church. But his background is almost tailor-made for leading one of the Episcopal Church’s most ethnically diverse dioceses: he was baptized in the diocese; he’s lived in Latin America and speaks advanced Portuguese and basic Spanish; and he is the son of a Muslim Egyptian and a New Yorker with Jewish roots. His background covers the trifecta of the Abrahamic faiths.
But accepting his heritage hasn’t always come easily for him, he said.
Prior to his election as bishop in April, Shoemaker served as rector of St. Stephen’s Episcopal Church in Charleston, South Carolina, for nine years. His ministry assignments have also taken him to North Carolina, Massachusetts and Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. He holds degrees from the General Theological Seminary in New York City, Harvard Divinity School, Boston University and a Doctor of Ministry from Duke Divinity School.
“The first time someone breaks that glass ceiling is really meaningful and really powerful, to be able to see yourself represented in the positions of high power in the church that you have served,” said the Rev. Leyla King, canon for Mission in Small Congregations in the Episcopal Diocese of West Texas and co-founder of Palestinian Anglicans and Clergy Allies. His ordination means a great deal to her and other Southwest Asia and North Africa (SWANA) Episcopalians and clergy from other traditions, particularly in an era of increasing anti-Arab and anti-Muslim rhetoric, she noted.
Shoemaker, born Adam James Haggagi, was raised in New York, where his parents moved just before he was born. They had met at a train station in Luxor, Egypt, while his mother — a New York native, secular Jew and Egyptologist — was on vacation. His father struck up a conversation, and romance ensued. His mother didn’t come back from that vacation until just before he was born, he said.
While he was still a young child, his parents separated, and his father returned to Egypt. Shoemaker would see him only periodically when he had business trips to New York. Upon advice from the State Department, his mother never allowed him to travel to Egypt to visit his father’s family.
Eventually, his mother remarried, and he was enrolled in school with his stepfather’s name, Shoemaker.
Without much contact with other Arabs, Shoemaker described internalizing a sense of racism around his heritage growing up.
“There were times in my life when I would blame everything I didn’t like about myself on my Arabness,” he said. “It had a really corrosive effect on my personhood.”
By the time he was 18, he legally changed his name to Shoemaker. He estranged himself from his father after his mother died a few years later, he said.
The 9/11 terrorist attacks, which happened during his senior year of college, began to change things for him, however. “I remember 9/12, 9/13, 9/14 very differently because of my background,” he said.
While he said he was largely shielded from racism because of his lighter skin tone, he saw the accelerating racism toward Southwest Asian and North African Americans and Muslims in the U.S. He remembered seeing Arabs and Muslims pinning American flags to their clothes, in efforts to shield themselves from a pervasive feeling of retribution.
Between seeking therapy and serving as a missionary in his early 20s in Brazil — where his mixed ethnic background was both normal and celebrated — he began learning to cherish his ethnic identity, he said. At the same time, he had begun discerning a call to the priesthood in the Episcopal Church, in which he was raised.
He was ordained as a deacon in 2007, and as a priest in 2008.
Around that time, in his mid to late 20s, he reconciled with his father in Egypt. When he visited in 2020, just before the COVID-19 pandemic, he wasn’t sure if his Muslim family would accept their half-American relative who was a Christian priest.
But when one of his aunts saw him for the first time, she approached him with tears in her eyes and immediately embraced him “the way you hug something that’s been lost for so long, and you’ve found it,” he recalled. His father drove him around Luxor honking and exclaiming to neighbors that his long lost son had returned. It was a deeply meaningful experience for the bishop.
“The journey that I’ve been on my whole life to reconcile the disparate parts of my personhood and certainly my Arabness … it’s been liberating,” he said. “It’s helped me to become more fully the beloved child of God that I believe I’ve been called to be, and the priest and hopefully the bishop that I’ve been called to be.”
He hopes to use his new role to help elevate the voices and experiences of SWANA peoples within the Episcopal Church, he added.
The Rev. Julie Hoplamazian, the Armenian-American rector of St. Michael’s Episcopal Church on the Upper West Side of Manhattan, said Shoemaker is the perfect person to help bring that perspective.
“The perspective of folks who live in that region of the world is a perspective that the church has conventionally tried to colonize,” she said. “And now we have a person from that part of the world who is a voice and a leader in the church to remind us and be a voice for the people who are the original Christians, the oldest Christians.”
The Rev. Halim Shukair, a Lebanese Episcopal priest who serves as priest-in-charge of Christ Episcopal Church and Mother of the Savior, an Arabic-speaking Episcopal-Lutheran mission congregation in Dearborn, Michigan, said the lack of awareness of SWANA peoples and cultures has led to frustrating, and at times, comical experiences in the church. While at Virginia Theological Seminary, he said he was regularly asked when he converted to Christianity, before reminding his classmates that Christianity, in fact, started in the Middle East.
But for King, the challenges go beyond ignorance. She pointed to a failed Episcopal House of Bishops resolution to acknowledge Palestinians as “among the indigenous people of the lands of Palestine and Israel lying between the Mediterranean Sea and the Jordan River.” Shoemaker’s election demonstrates the possibility of change, she said.
“There’s far more to come, and it doesn’t erase the hurt and sense of betrayal … but there is hope,” she said. “Adam is representative of that hope.”
Shoemaker also said he sees his leadership as an opportunity for change within the church, including in its relationship to the realities of violence in Israel and the Palestinian territories.
“I would hope to find ways to share my (Arab-American) perspective in Christian love, not only as bishop of the diocese, but as a bishop writ large in the wider church, and to be compassionate for the suffering that goes on in Gaza, in the West Bank,” he said.
As bishop, he believes part of his job is to serve as a public theologian. This compels him “to speak for fundamental Christian values, baptismal covenant values — dignity, respect, the inherent dignity and worth of all,” he said.
A large contingent from South Carolina, where he previously served, attended the ceremony on Saturday.
“I think the people of Long Island will not only embrace him, but be energized by the passion which he speaks to the issues that are so prevalent in our society today,” said Michael Shaffer, rector of St. Mark’s Episcopal Church in Charleston, South Carolina, and a former colleague of Shoemaker.
Donna Landers-George, a parishioner at Church of the Advent, an Episcopal church in Westbury, New York, said the overwhelming feeling across the diocese is one of excitement. “He’s the bishop for what is yet to come, a bishop for the future,” she said.

title: Fasting, prayer and a call for unity: Jewish community marks Yom Kippur in Casablanca
content: They turned out in large numbers on Monday, September 21, to observe the holiest day of the Jewish year. Addressing worshippers gathered in Casablanca, Serge Berdugo, secretary-general of the Council of Jewish Communities of Morocco, began by reflecting on the meaning of this day of fasting and prayer. “During this month of Elul [the sixth month of the Jewish civil calendar, Editor’s note], the gates of heaven are open to receive our prayers and supplications, so that the Eternal may forgive us all our sins,” he said.Yom Kippur, he recalled, is “one of the most solemn and sacred days in the Jewish calendar, when each person takes account of their actions and asks forgiveness from those they may have wronged.” Divine forgiveness, however, follows a particular order. Before turning to heaven, worshippers must first turn to one another. “Before asking for and receiving Hashem’s forgiveness, we must ask forgiveness from our fellow human beings for any wrong we may have done,” Berdugo stressed.The day brings a particularly significant period in the Hebrew calendar to a close. Yom Kippur is “the culmination of the period known as the ‘Days of Awe,’ which lead us towards repentance as we stand in judgment before God,” he explained.The door to forgiveness is open to all, on one condition. “All people have access to divine forgiveness if they acknowledge their faults and make amends for the injustices they have committed,” the community leader said, before returning to the central principle: “God can forgive sins committed against Him, but before that, we must obtain forgiveness for those we have committed against our fellow human beings.”Putting those words into practice, Berdugo himself asked for forgiveness. “For my part, I humbly ask forgiveness, Mehila, from all those whom I may inadvertently have offended,” he told the congregation.Berdugo said Yom Kippur also carries a message of hope. It is “a day of soul-searching, humility and repentance, when a person looks inward and deeply examines their actions,” but also “a day of love for those who hold on to the hope that people can live in peace and harmony,” he said. He extended that hope to the wider region. “We hope that the year now beginning will finally bring a peaceful and just resolution to the fratricidal conflicts that are bringing grief to the Middle East,” he said.This year’s observance took on added significance as it coincided with the 28th anniversary of the death of King Hassan II. Rabbi Hazout was invited to offer prayers for the repose of the late Sovereign’s soul, describing him as “forever present in our hearts.” He also prayed for the soul of “our revered Sultan, the late Mohammed V,” whom the community commended to God’s “holy mercy.”Casablanca’s Chief Rabbi Yossef Israël then offered solemn blessings for King Mohammed VI. Worshippers prayed that the Almighty would protect the Sovereign and grant him “health, joy and success in all his endeavors for the glory of eternal Morocco.”Prayers were also offered for the happiness, health and success of Crown Prince Moulay El Hassan, Princess Lalla Khadija, Prince Moulay Rachid and the entire Royal Family. “May God bless this honorable gathering and the Moroccan people,” Berdugo said, followed by an Amen from the congregation.Preserve, defend and pass onThe secretary-general of the Council of Jewish Communities of Morocco then addressed members of the Kahal, the congregation, directly with a message focused on the future. “At this time of profound change, it is the duty of each and every one of us to rally around the Community to safeguard and ensure the continuity of the tangible and intangible heritage of Moroccan Judaism,” he said. That effort, he added, requires “defending its ancestral values, preserving the achievements of our Community and ensuring its place within the social fabric of our country.”For Berdugo, history has already shown the way forward. “As recent history demonstrates, anything is possible if we return to the community spirit that prevailed for centuries,” he said. Two words, in his view, sum up that spirit: “unity and solidarity,” which he described as “the keys to the future of our community.”The address ended with wishes for the Jewish New Year. “May Hashem guide your steps. May this year 5787 bring health, joy and serenity to our homes, and peace to hearts and peoples throughout the world,” Berdugo said.The ceremony was attended by the wali, governors, city officials and rabbis, alongside members of Casablanca’s Jewish community.

title: Podcast Vozes e Territórios estreia nesta quinta-feira (24) com o tema da economia solidária no RS
content:
Nesta quinta-feira (24), às 19h, estreia no Youtube do ICPJ, do Brasil de Fato RS e nacional, o podcast Igualdade e Cultura Negra: Vozes e Territórios, com apresentação de Iyá Vera Soares, que conduz encontros com lideranças religiosas, pesquisadoras, educadoras e militantes do movimento negro ao longo de todo o programa.
