A data da estreia marca os 50 anos de assentamento da vasilha da orisà Oiá Laja da bacia de Pai Ivo de Ogum Onira D’oby da Nação Oyò de Iya Vera Soares.
O projeto é uma realização do Instituto Cultural Padre Josimo (ICPJ), por meio do Termo de Fomento nº 973281 do Ministério da Igualdade Racial do Governo Federal, com correalização do Brasil de Fato RS. E percorre temas como visão de mundo africana, saúde pública, ervas medicinais, economia solidária, cooperativismo negro, cultura ancestral e educação de matriz africana. Cada episódio parte de uma conversa com uma convidada ou convidado que atua diretamente com o tema abordado, unindo vivência de terreiro, produção acadêmica e militância política.
O primeiro episódio debaterá a relação entre os povos de terreiro e a economia solidária. A convidada Gil Neves, educadora popular com atuação junto às comunidades de matriz africana no Rio Grande do Sul, fala sobre organização comunitária, segurança alimentar e estratégias de enfrentamento à fome, à desigualdade social e ao racismo estrutural.
Gil conta que seu contato com a economia solidária começou a partir de experiências familiares e comunitárias na vila Cruzeiro, onde sua avó já praticava formas de troca e solidariedade entre vizinhos para enfrentar a fome. Posteriormente, em 2008, ao ingressar na organização Maria Mulher, começou a trabalhar com alimentação, feiras e organização comunitária. Em 2012, aproximou-se ainda mais das comunidades de matriz africana e passou a atuar como educadora na área, através do Centro de Assessoria Multiprofissional (CAMP) – Escola do Bem Viver.
A convidada também destaca o papel das mulheres negras na construção da economia solidária. Segundo Gil, ocupar espaços historicamente negados às mulheres negras foi um processo desafiador, mas a organização coletiva contribuiu para fortalecer a autonomia e o empoderamento econômico dessas mulheres. Para ela, combater a desigualdade não significa apenas distribuir cestas básicas, mas garantir trabalho, renda, água, saúde, segurança e reconhecimento.
Entre os temas centrais do episódio está a ocupação de territórios. Gil relata as dificuldades enfrentadas para acessar espaços públicos e comerciais e denuncia processos de deslegitimação e apropriação da história construída por mulheres negras e comunidades de matriz africana. Diante disso, ela considera fundamental registrar e preservar essas histórias.
O episódio também aborda os quilombos, a agricultura familiar e o etnodesenvolvimento. Gil defende políticas que considerem a realidade e a ancestralidade desses territórios, com investimentos em máquinas, infraestrutura, cooperativas e formas de comercialização. Segundo ela, essas medidas podem contribuir para ampliar a produção dos quilombos e fortalecer a circulação de recursos dentro das próprias comunidades.
Por fim, Gil destaca que as comunidades já vêm se organizando por meio de cooperativas, associações e projetos, mas ainda enfrentam dificuldades para acessar financiamentos devido à burocracia. A entrevistada defende maior articulação entre as comunidades de matriz africana e quilombolas, além da criação de políticas públicas voltadas à segurança alimentar, ao financiamento e ao desenvolvimento econômico.
A série reúne 12 episódios dedicados à história, aos saberes, à espiritualidade, à cultura e às lutas da população negra no Rio Grande do Sul. Os episódios irão ao ar toda quinta-feira, às 19h, até dezembro. O podcast também será exibido nas sextas-feiras, às 11h, na TV Mais.

title: THÉÂTRE - Tropy Ilo croise amour et rancœur dans Voamaintilany
content: Le Tropy Ilo présente ce dimanche, à l’Ivokolo Analakely, « Voamaintilany », une pièce de théâtre malgache qui mêle amour, trahison et vengeance.Les membres de la Tropy Ilo réunis autour de « Voamaintilany ».Certaines blessures du passé peuvent se transmettre d’une génération à l’autre. C’est autour de cette idée que le Tropy Ilo présente « Voamaintilany », une pièce écrite par Nivo Hary, ce dimanche à l’Ivokolo Analakely.L’histoire met en scène trois amis dont la relation bascule après une trahison, un détournement d’argent et des manœuvres dirigées contre l’un d’eux. Des années plus tard, la victime revient animée par un désir de vengeance. Entre-temps, leurs enfants, qui ignorent les conflits du passé, tombent amoureux. « Le passé peut avoir des conséquences sur la vie et l’avenir des enfants », souligne un membre de la troupe.Le titre de la pièce fait référence à une plante aux couleurs rouge et noire, qui symbolise les contrastes de l’existence, entre joie et tristesse, espoir et déception. La représentation débutera à 14h 30, après l’ouverture des portes à 13h 30. Elle durera environ une heure et demie, sans entracte, et sera divisée en trois parties. Des chansons malgaches spécialement composées pour la pièce accompagneront l’histoire jusqu’au morceau final, « Voamaintilany ».Dix-huit ans de théâtre malgacheLa troupe a également porté une attention particulière aux aspects techniques du spectacle, notamment à l’audibilité des comédiens, à la sonorisation et aux éclairages.Le Tropy Ilo célèbre cette année ses 18 ans d’existence. La troupe a intégré officiellement la FMTM (Fikambanan’ny Mpanao Teatra Malagasy) en 2007. Elle œuvre à la revalorisation de la culture et du théâtre malgaches à travers des créations mêlant satire politique, humour et drame social. Ses représentations cherchent notamment à sensibiliser le public, à transmettre des leçons de vie et à contribuer à l’éducation des jeunes générations dans le respect des « fomba malagasy ».La mise en scène de « Voamaintilany » est assurée par Haja Ravaloson, actif depuis plusieurs années dans le théâtre et formateur de plusieurs troupes. La pièce a été préparée pendant près de 1 an, avec un travail consacré aux dialogues, aux mouvements, aux chants et aux aspects techniques du spectacle.Cassie Ramiandrasoa

title: This Sicilian community has endured for centuries. Can it survive a changing climate?
content: Giorgia Caruso always imagined her children one day inheriting the farm her family has tended for three generations. Her daughters would do more than produce organic meat and dairy. They would continue a way of life central to Piana degli Albanesi, a community founded 500 years ago by Albanian refugees fleeing the Ottoman conquest. Perched on a fertile plateau in the mountains south of Palermo, the town has long provided much of the wheat and dairy central to Sicily’s agricultural traditions. Caruso hoped to see her children carry those traditions on. “I have two daughters I wished could take over our farming business one day, which is like our third child,” Caruso said with teary eyes as she tended the last of the family’s livestock. Now she’d like to see them build their lives somewhere safer. A flock of sheep graze in a vineyard near Piana degli Albanesi, Sicily, Italy, in October 2017. De Agostini Picture Library / Getty Images One day in late July three years ago, flames as high as a three-story building engulfed the family’s fields and threatened their home. Caruso and her husband Vito lost several acres of land and almost two dozen sheep, making it difficult to imagine their daughters taking over a business that may no longer exist in a few years. “Many times we’ve thought of resettling to a safer area, even abroad,” she said. “But it’s just so hard to pack up and leave our homeland.” Caruso’s family is not alone in facing that decision. A growing number of residents are questioning whether they can continue working the land that has sustained the Arbëreshë, as Italy’s Albanian ethnic minority is known, for five centuries. Piana is subject to a microclimate marked by extremes even for the Mediterranean basin, which is warming 20 percent faster than the global average. Summertime temperatures have averaged 85 degrees Fahrenheit over the past decade, with little to no rain. Sicily accounts for nearly half of Italy’s wildfires, and blazes struck in or around Piana in four of the last six years, displacing more than 100 people in 2021 and damaging several homes this past summer. Firefighting operations took place on the ground and from the air after a wildfire broke out in the town of Piana degli Albanesi, near the city of Palermo in Sicily, Italy, in August 2025. Alberto Lo Bianco / Anadolu via Getty Images​​ As farming — the town’s main source of income — grows more precarious, people are leaving. Piana has lost nearly 17 percent of its population since 2015. That is almost three times the rate of decline across Sicily as a whole, raising fears that climate change is accelerating the erosion of one of southern Europe’s oldest ethnic minority communities. “If our lands burn, there are no jobs for us, no more homes,” Giovanni Scalora said in Italian. He is a fourth-generation Arbëreshë farmer who owns land overlooking a lake — once Sicily’s largest reservoir — that almost dried up in 2024. “It’s a pity because if we disappear a part of Sicily’s and Albania’s and Europe’s cultural history disappears.” Arbëreshë elderly talk in front of a cafe before the Easter Sunday Holy Mass in April 2004 in Piana degli Albanesi, Sicily, Italy. Marco Di Lauro / Getty Images Piana degli Albanesi and much of Sicily’s interior have long been considered the island’s breadbasket. When the Arbëreshë settled there in the 15th century, they integrated through farm work. Beyond cultivating wheat and raising sheep and cattle, they specialized in making ricotta, a cheese used, among other things, as the filling in the globally-renowned Sicilian cannoli. “Legends say we invented it,” Scalora said of the pastry. Each May, the town hosts an international cannolo festival, and for many years those made in Piana have been deemed the best in all of Sicily. “But it’s hard to keep making it if there are no sheep left,” Scalora added. A strong relationship with the land has shaped the community’s identity for generations, a bond that was tested long before climate change. In 1947, armed bandits killed 11 farmers and injured 30 others during a May Day celebration near the mountain pass of Portella della Ginestra. The massacre became an enduring symbol of the sacrifices Sicilians made for the right to work the land, and it shaped the spiritual connection the Arbëreshë have with it. A photo from the 1950s shows a member of the Arbëreshë community with a donkey carrying hay. Mondadori via Getty Images That link, however, is growing increasingly tenuous. An unprecedented drought has decimated fields and livestock across Sicily over the past five years. This summer, entire towns were left without running water or electricity for days as Europe endured one of its worst heat waves in decades. In extreme conditions, particularly when hot, dry scirocco winds blow in from Africa, temperatures can top 100 degrees Fahrenheit. On August 11, 2021, they reached a European record of 119.8 F, and the island is increasingly at risk of desertification. “Extreme droughts as well as sudden, temporary extreme rainfall are severely damaging agricultural fields,” said Christian Mulder, an ecologist and professor at the University of Catania. “Climate [change] is aggravating the emptying of inner rural areas of the island and forcing emigration.” The European Environment Agency reports that the impacts of a warming world are increasingly concentrated among already vulnerable groups, including ethnic minorities like the Arbëreshë — a point Mulder emphasized. “Ancient populations, as well as ancient grains, are at risk of disappearing forever,” he said. Piana degli Albanesi sits amid mountains and farmland in Sicily’s tranquil rural interior, about 40 miles south of bustling Palermo. Flanked by two smaller Arbëreshë towns, it is the social and cultural hub of the entire community. Cobblestone alleys lead to the Church of San Giorgio Megalomartire, named for the town’s most revered saint. It is Piana’s North Star, a point of reference for locals and tourists alike. People have gathered there for centuries, most visibly during Easter Week, when residents past and present come together once again, and the town comes alive. An Arbëreshë priest celebrates the Easter Sunday Holy Mass in April 2004 in Piana degli Albanesi, Sicily, Italy. Marco Di Lauro / Getty Images When the celebrations end, the streets grow quiet once again. In Sheshi, Piana’s oldest neighborhood, colorful murals of Arbëreshë women in traditional attire offer a reminder of a vibrant culture that endures even as there are fewer people around to sustain it. Piana’s population has fallen from 6,293 residents in 2015 to 5,245 in 2024, with some of the steepest losses coming in recent years. (The true number is almost certainly lower, because many Sicilian expatriates do not change their residency status.) Although no data explicitly links the exodus to the changing conditions reshaping Sicily, residents say high unemployment and the resignation that has settled over the town are intertwined with the loss of farmland. Mulder believes what is unfolding there may represent the first case of climate migration leading to the potential loss of an entire ethnic minority in southern Europe. Sicilian emigration from rural areas, often prompted by crushing poverty and political strife, dates to the late 19th century. Many sailed for the United States, including a small number of Arbëreshë who, attracted by the similar climate, settled in California. For some leaving Piana today, California remains a key destination. Many of the people moving on are young, and their elders are coming to terms with the fact that they may be the last to work the land. “We adults don’t want to go away,” Caruso said. “But the new generation, the one of my daughters, I’m sure will not grow up here. I’ve told them, ‘America awaits you.’ I want a better life than this for them.” Farms dot the landscape near Piana degli Albanesi, Sicily, Italy, in September 2015. DeAgostini / Getty Images Those who choose to stay find hope in the possibility of adaptation. Scalora has seen members of his own family, mainly uncles and cousins, leave for the United States. But he is trying to find a way to remain, and has begun breeding cattle better suited to Sicily’s changing climate after failing to find a breed of sheep that can adapt as well. The tradeoff is that the ricotta Piana has made for centuries with sheep’s milk may one day have to be made with cow’s milk. “Our cheese will not be the same, but one can leave, or adapt to survive,” he said. Piana’s city council is trying to adapt, too. Rosario Petta, who has been mayor since 2022, has made slowing the exodus and preventing Piana from becoming a ghost town a goal of his administration. “One thousand people who leave is an extra 1,000 people who will no longer speak Arbëresh, which can put at risk language and identity preservation,” he said. Mayor Rosario Petta (on the right) sits in his office at one of the weekly city council’s meetings in Piana degli Albanesi. Courtesy of Rosario Petta To counter the population loss and wildfires, which often start on abandoned land, Petta has strengthened collaboration with the local committee of the Civil Protection unit and encouraged more residents to volunteer in wildfire prevention to protect their land. But the town is also looking beyond agriculture. “We are also trying to diversify our economic strategy by encouraging tourism,” Petta said. He is part of an international diaspora committee that is giving Piana opportunities to build ties with the United States, Albania and Kosovo, hoping their shared cultural connections will attract more visitors. Petta said Piana has seen an increase in tourists from the Balkans over the past three years, and he is now lobbying for direct flights between Palermo and Tirana. But tourism presents its own challenges. Across Sicily, its growth has offered an alternative to agriculture even as development takes over farmland and increasing numbers of visitors place additional pressure on already strained water and energy supplies. The San Nicola church or sanctuary, built by the Albanians in the 15th century, is the oldest church in Palazzo Adriano in western Sicily, Italy. elifranssens / Getty Images Not everyone believes adaptation is enough. Anna Liscari comes from a family of Arbëreshë tailors that has lived between California and Piana for the past 50 years. She permanently relocated to Newport Beach after developing what she called “a love-hate relationship” with Piana because it “seems to be stuck in time in the way it is managing its disappearance.” Liscari has seen how Piana’s environmental challenges can ripple through the local economy and traditions. Her great-aunt once owned one of the town’s most famous bars, known for selling some of its best cannoli. She eventually closed the business after the organic suppliers she relied on shut down because of constant livestock and land losses to droughts and wildfires. “We have survived wars, displacement, and poverty over the course of 500 years,” she said. “It’s crazy to think that climate and the inability to manage its effects is what might wipe us out,” Liscari said from her office in Newport Beach, where she works as a tourist agent for American tourists traveling to southern Italy. The lake of Piana this past spring, after unusually heavier rainfalls in early 2026 briefly reinvigorated it, sits between mountain plateaus in the Palermo countryside. Stefania D’Ignoti Whether that fate can be avoided depends on decisions made beyond Piana. Salvatore Cona, who leads Sicily’s Civil Protection Unit, said the Italian government must lead the response needed to develop an adaptation strategy that can prevent further population loss. Towns like Piana, he said, simply do not have the resources available at the national level and are, in practice, being left to find their own solutions. Officials in Rome, however, maintain that the national government is providing resilience funding and that regional governments are responsible for tailoring the response to local needs. Sicilian officials say they lack the resources to meet the crisis. Mulder argues that the island’s climate crisis has been aggravated by poor governance at both the regional and national level, worsening its effects. In 2023, wildfires scorched 142,150 acres across Sicily, while extreme heat caused more than 200 million euros in damage to agriculture and infrastructure. The following year, after prolonged drought depleted reservoirs and groundwater supplies, Rome declared a national state of emergency and initially allocated 20 million euros to mitigate water shortages. More national funding followed while Sicily committed 100 million euros to help farmers combat and prevent drought damage. But adaptation is not simply a matter of resources. Like the Arbëreshë, many of Europe’s linguistic minorities live in rural regions particularly vulnerable to climate change. The European Environment Agency says vulnerable groups, including ethnic minorities, must be considered in adaptation planning to ensure their specific risks and needs are addressed. Petta said that has not happened for his community, which he believes receives far less attention than other ethnolinguistic minorities in Italy. Anthony Plescia remembers his elders speaking with great reverence about their ancestral home of Piana degli Albanesi, which they referred to fondly by its Arbëreshë name “Hora” even though most of them knew it only from stories told by their parents and grandparents. Plescia, the president of the Arbëreshë of Sacramento association and a descendant of immigrants who left Piana more than 100 years ago to settle in that California city, grew up surrounded by such stories. “I also remember the large Arbëreshë picnics in McKinley Park and the strong sense of cultural pride that pervaded the events,” he said, referring to the park that has long been a gathering place for the Arbëreshë of Sacramento. “The picnics continue to this day, though many of the old family members are now gone.” Anthony Plescia (on the right) poses next to a painting of a Sicilian chariot, one of the island’s most famous cultural symbols, at a gathering of the Arbereshe of Sacramento. community Courtesy of Anthony Plescia Several Arbëreshë families arrived in California as early as 1910. Many chose Southern California for its plentiful agricultural jobs and nascent wine industry; some even established wineries in Etiwanda and Rancho Cucamonga, continuing their heritage of tending the land. Others favored Northern California and the Central Valley, including Sacramento, because its climate and fertile land mirrored that of Sicily. Some of Plescia’s relatives worked in tomato canneries, while his great-grandfather eked out a living gathering corn husks and selling them to local tamale makers. Language and culture can fade after families leave Piana, a loss that compounds across generations. Plescia was an adult before he learned of his Arbëreshë heritage; he grew up knowing only that his parents were from Sicily. Losing touch with one’s past is, he says, often the price of safety and stability. Still, he’s found that, nostalgia aside, he hasn’t met anyone who regrets coming to America, as it invariably improved their lives. Even though California also regularly endures devastating wildfires, Plescia believes it isn’t experiencing the same pressures he sees in Piana. He also believes the state and federal governments are taking the threat more seriously. In October, Plescia traveled to Piana, where he met Petta. They agreed to explore creating a confederation of the Arbëresh organizations in the U.S. to establish a formal relationship with the town and strengthen cultural ties and exchanges between the communities. As more young Arbëreshë leave Sicily, those ties could help preserve a culture that has survived so much over the past 500 years, even if fewer and fewer people remain in the town where it first took root. This story was originally published by Grist with the headline This Sicilian community has endured for centuries. Can it survive a changing climate? on Sep 23, 2026.

title: For Years, the Smithsonian Strove to Bring the African American History and Culture Museum to the National Mall. Now, It Celebrates a Decade as a Beacon of Understanding, Community and Resilience
content:
For Years, the Smithsonian Strove to Bring the African American History and Culture Museum to the National Mall. Now, It Celebrates a Decade as a Beacon of Understanding, Community and Resilience
The museum lovingly called the “Blacksonian” chronicles the past and present and envisions the future to tell the stories of Black life in America
On a visit to the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American History and Culture, Elizabeth Beckett stands proudly in front of a uniform worn by one of the thousands of Black men who worked aboard segregated trains, in palace cars built by industrialist George Pullman. They were called Pullman porters, and Beckett’s grandfather was among them.
“His name was James Syres. He died when he was 90 or 91,” Beckett recalls.
The first porters were recently emancipated men hired by Pullman starting around 1867 to staff the luxury sleeping cars. They did everything from serving gourmet meals to shining shoes to carrying baggage. Some were even forced to sing and dance.
The porters formed the backbone of the Black middle class, following the path of their wealthier white passengers to save money to send their children and grandchildren to college. That opened the door to opportunities they never had, and many descendants of porters went on to become influential figures in American society, including Supreme Court Justice Thurgood Marshall.
Just around the corner in the “Defending Freedom, Defining Freedom” exhibition is a gorgeous pump organ bought by Pullman porter Henry L. Long in 1911. Museum curator Mary Elliott, whose uncle was a Pullman porter based in Denver, says the organ is a symbol of the importance of the men who formed the first predominantly Black labor union, which was later crucial to the civil rights movement.
“Let’s think about these men as Pullman porters just like we think about people who held prestige in their communities—a teacher, a doctor, a lawyer,” Elliott says.
In their everyday lives, Elliott notes, the job allowed porters like Long “to celebrate their being a community, being Black, being middle-class, even to acknowledge how far they had come, just gathering around an organ and singing.”
Elliott says these are the connections she hopes visitors consider when they peruse the thousands of objects on view at the museum as it celebrates its tenth anniversary.
“I want you to go home and look at something in your own home that has that same impact,” Elliott says. “How does that bring us together in these everyday, mundane moments?”
The museum opened on September 24, 2016, with a staff of about 200 people. It would serve as a living symbol of the importance of the nation’s shared history and the joy of celebrating a journey begun by African American Civil War veterans in 1915 who sought to get a museum built on the National Mall.
The decades-long effort got its final push with the bipartisan efforts of Congressman John Lewis of Georgia, a stalwart of the civil rights movement, and Senator Sam Brownback of Kansas; the bill establishing the museum was signed by President George W. Bush in 2003.
During a recent visit, throngs of visitors wandered transfixed through the galleries at the museum known colloquially to some as the “Blacksonian,” a few crouching down to read the dense signage and panels that crowd the walls and exhibitions. Carolyn Harris came with her husband, Shawn, from Mount Vernon, New York, and says this museum is crucial to teaching young Black people about their history.
“They need to know what we went through to get where we are now,” Harris says. She also thinks the museum is important for those who aren’t African American, to understand “where we came from.”
Quick facts: Celebrating ten years
Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie G. Bunch III, the founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, will commemorate the tenth anniversary on September 25 with a conversation moderated by the journalist Laura Coates.
Founding deputy museum director Kinshasha Holman Conwill feels the occasion is more like the museum’s 20th anniversary because of all the longtime legwork the staff put in. Celebrities—Oprah Winfrey and Michael Jordan, among others—donated millions of dollars to the museum prior to its opening, and $4 million alone came in gifts of less than $1,000 from average Americans.
At the opening dedication, President Barack Obama reminded the crowd how many historians, civil rights leaders, lawmakers and others in the nation came together, across parties and politics, to make this happen. Those gathered at the event were serenaded by the likes of Stevie Wonder and Patti LaBelle.
Conwill says the museum’s founding director, Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie G. Bunch III, had a wish list of major objects, including a slave ship remnant and a cabin that housed enslaved people. Today, the collection has searing artifacts, such as a prison guard tower from the infamous Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola, which was built on land that formerly held a plantation. Conwill notes that the museum was constructed around that guard tower and a segregation-era railway car, because of their size. Another haunting artifact at the museum is the casket of Emmett Till, the Black 14-year-old who, in 1955, was kidnapped and murdered in Mississippi. The killing of Till became a rallying point for the civil rights movement.
“At the core of some of the questions were: What is appropriate for a Black museum to collect?” Conwill says, referencing Till’s casket and the prison tower. “Should we collect it? And if we do, how do we display it? And that’s why, from the beginning, it has been displayed in a very respectful way.”
A silk lace and linen shawl given to Harriet Tubman by Queen Victoria around 1897 was a gift to the museum from scholar and collector Charles L. Blockson, who also donated Tubman’s hymnal. She was nicknamed “Moses” because she repeatedly returned to the South to rescue enslaved people.
“It’s such an extraordinary thing to know that you are literally touching history, that you are in the presence of an object that was owned by a woman who helped you become free,” Conwill says. “There’s something about Harriet Tubman that is quintessential of the struggle of Black people, and having those objects made all the difference.”
Standing with her daughter between Tubman’s shawl and the slave cabin, visitor Maureen Bobo says she wanted to stop at every exhibit “just to inhale it.”
“I’m trying not to cry, but it is hard not to, because our ancestors endured so much so that we can have what we have,” she says. “Everyone who is American in the world should know this, because they view us in a certain way without knowing, and there’s been a narrative going on in this nation since we set foot in this land about who we are and the way we are that just isn’t true.”
Beyond the high-profile objects, donated images help define the meaning of African American history and culture. Conwill points to the Henry Clay Anderson collection of photographs and the Johnson Publishing photo archives, in which the lives of both well-known and ordinary Black people are captured for posterity.
“Everybody was not Benjamin O. Davis Sr., the first African American general officer in the U.S. armed forces, or Benjamin O. Davis Jr., right? Not everybody was Joe Louis, the great boxer who was also in the service,” Conwill says. Black people “were the heroes and the marquee names, but they were also everyday people.”
Elliott says part of the museum’s mission, and legacy, is giving the American public credit for being able to look at this history in its fullness. “This is a shared history,” Elliott says. “We’re still all in this together. We’re talking to each other, right? … It’s a cacophony of all of these voices. And what does that tell us about the development of this nation in its many aspects?”
Bunch, who recently announced he would retire at the end of the year, put his soul into this museum, and he persuaded others to do the same. He “felt the weight of history” in this endeavor, he says, and realized that he “wanted it to be a museum that both celebrated African American culture and made this the quintessential American story.”
He says he kept “a huge chart” that questioned what each exhibition says about African American culture and American culture in general, and he “sat in every design meeting.” Bunch and the staff fine-tuned every detail. Shortly before the museum opened, those who worked to create it visited and brought their families, to see how their achievement could help transform a nation.
As Bunch says, “I guess the best way I can describe it is a sense that we gave a gift to America.”

title: ¿Cómo aprender las primeras sesenta palabras?
content:
Meta humanos
¿Cómo aprender las primeras sesenta palabras?
Todavía podemos agregar una meta a nuestra lista para 2026: aprender 60 palabras del idioma indígena del territorio que habitamos.
En una columna anterior se habló de una alegría difícil de medir: la de una persona indígena que reconoce un interés verdadero cuando alguien se acerca respetuosamente a su idioma. La alegría se vuelve una experiencia compartida. Quien adquiere un conocimiento inicial del idioma indígena de su territorio descubre otra manera de pensar, nombrar el mundo y navegar la cotidianidad. Los prejuicios mantuvieron cerrada esa puerta durante mucho tiempo y dejaron la curiosidad dormida, sin salir a luz.
Mucho se habla de amar a Guatemala en septiembre. ¿Qué hay de amar también a quienes la conformamos?
Esta columna quiere contribuir a que muchas personas ladinas despierten esa curiosidad: ¿cómo se saluda en el idioma indígena de mi territorio?, ¿cómo se expresan las emociones?, ¿cuánto desconozco todavía de quienes viven a mi lado?, ¿de qué manera se enriquecería mi vida si conociera su idioma? Son preguntas sencillas capaces de alimentar la empatía.
Todavía podemos agregar una meta a nuestra lista para 2026: aprender 60 palabras del idioma indígena del territorio que habitamos. No se trata de memorizar vocablos aislados con su traducción al castellano. La propuesta consiste en aprender expresiones completas para saludar, presentarse, preguntar cómo está alguien y despedirse. Al contar las palabras que forman esas expresiones, podemos observar nuestro avance.
Un ejemplo se encuentra en Maja’il Kaqchikel–Kaqchikel Autoaprendido. Su primera lección está dedicada al saludo y la presentación. La persona aprende a saludar por la mañana y por la tarde, preguntar cómo se encuentra alguien, decir su nombre y despedirse. Al completarla puede haber aprendido aproximadamente 20 palabras con significado y uso cotidiano. Son expresiones que pueden utilizarse desde el primer encuentro.
También podemos aprender en las relaciones cotidianas. Podemos preguntarle respetuosamente a una persona hablante, cómo se dice “feliz día”, “delicioso” o “hasta pronto”. Las herramientas de inteligencia artificial pueden ayudar a iniciar la práctica, pero sus respuestas en idiomas mayas deben verificarse con personas hablantes o materiales confiables, especialmente cuando se trata de la escritura y la pronunciación.
El sistema educativo abre otro camino. El acuerdo gubernativo 22-2004 establece la obligatoriedad del bilingüismo en idiomas nacionales para el estudiantado de los sectores público y privado. El CNB desarrolla este mandato en preprimaria y primaria. En el ciclo básico asigna cinco períodos semanales a culturas e idiomas mayas, garífuna o xinka. Las madres y padres pueden preguntar si sus hijas e hijos están aprendiendo el idioma indígena correspondiente al municipio, verificar si cuentan con libros y audios, y practicar con ellas y ellos en casa. La Digebi dispone de aplicaciones en Google Play, entre ellas Nutzij: Kaqchikel.
También existen recursos fuera de la escuela. Las personas interesadas pueden acudir a las 22 comunidades lingüísticas de la Academia de Lenguas Mayas de Guatemala. La Academia acumula más de tres décadas de elaboración de materiales, asesoría y enseñanza presencial.
En Editorial Maya’ Wuj contamos con series de tres libros de autoaprendizaje para k’iche’, mam, q’anjob’al, kaqchikel, tz’utujil, poqomchi’ y q’eqchi’, con audios mediante códigos QR y videos de apoyo en YouTube.
Mucho se habla de amar a Guatemala en septiembre. Esta columna pregunta: ¿qué hay de amar también a quienes la conformamos? Podemos comenzar por aprender 60 palabras del idioma indígena del territorio que habitamos. Un gesto de amor nacido de la curiosidad que diga: “Quiero acercarme, quiero conocerle, quiero aprender de usted”.

title: Documentário sobre cotidiano de feirantes agroecológicos do RS está disponível no YouTube
content:
O documentário “Vida Feirante”, desenvolvido pelo coletivo Vozes em Movimento e dirigido por Pedro Henrique Farina Soares, está disponível gratuitamente no YouTube. A obra registra, ao longo de um ano, a rotina dos feirantes Luciano e Roni Mühlenberg, integrantes de uma família pioneira no cultivo de alimentos sem o uso de agrotóxicos em São Lourenço do Sul (RS).
Os agricultores também foram responsáveis pela criação da primeira banca agroecológica da feira, que funciona na cidade há 32 anos. Entre o cultivo, a colheita e a comercialização, o filme percorre o caminho dos alimentos até os consumidores, enquanto aborda os saberes, as práticas e os desafios enfrentados pelos agricultores.
A partir dos relatos e das experiências dos próprios feirantes, o documentário também registra e valoriza a história da Feira Livre no município gaúcho, contextualizando o papel da atividade na economia local e na subsistência das famílias que dela dependem.
A produção também propõe discussões sobre o cultivo de Plantas Alimentícias Não Convencionais (Pancs) e a inserção desses alimentos na rotina da comunidade. As mudanças climáticas e a necessidade de políticas públicas voltadas ao setor também estão entre os temas abordados pelo filme.
Documentário evidencia trajetória de agricultores e importância da agroecologia
A pré-estreia ocorreu na última quinta-feira (17), em sessão realizada no campus da Universidade Federal do Rio Grande (FURG), em São Lourenço do Sul. Cerca de 50 pessoas participaram da atividade, entre os protagonistas Luciano e Roni Mühlenberg, agricultores feirantes, integrantes da comunidade universitária e público em geral.
Durante a sessão, os protagonistas ressaltaram a importância da obra para a compreensão do cotidiano e das dificuldades da produção agroecológica, entre elas a falta de subsídios governamentais. Apesar dos desafios, destacaram que o trabalho também representa uma missão de vida, que ultrapassa a dimensão financeira. “Para ser feliz, não basta ter sucesso, dinheiro, é preciso ter alma”, destacou Luciano.
O diretor, Pedro Henrique Farina Soares, contou um pouco sobre o processo de construção do audiovisual. “O seu Roni e o Luciano são personagens incríveis. O documentário apenas tenta transmitir aquilo que já é inerente deles. Pessoas que possuem uma grande convicção naquilo que fazem. Mesmo com todas as adversidades mantém em si um encantamento pela vida simples, sem abandonar seus ideais que ainda hoje são considerados utópicos para muitas pessoas”.
Produção independente
Em atividade em São Lourenço do Sul desde 2015, o coletivo Vozes em Movimento produz e divulga conteúdos independentes, além de promover atividades culturais, como cine-debates, rodas de conversa e saraus temáticos.
“Vida Feirante” foi viabilizado pela Política Nacional Aldir Blanc, por meio de edital aprovado pela Coordenadoria de Cultura da Prefeitura de São Lourenço do Sul. A produção também conta com o apoio do Pancpop, projeto vinculado ao Núcleo de Estudos em Agroecologia da FURG — Campus São Lourenço do Sul.
Além do documentário, o coletivo possui outras quatro produções audiovisuais, todas financiadas por editais culturais e disponibilizadas gratuitamente no YouTube.
Assista ao documentário “Vida Feirante” no YouTube.

title: Residents say Philippines’ Pax Silica Hub will force them off their ancestral land
content:
CAPAS, Philippines - Children’s laughter and the gentle sound of a flowing river are the daily accompaniment to life in a hamlet of about 200 indigenous Aeta families, but members of the community told Radio Free Asia they are in danger of losing their idyllic way of life because a planned U.S.-led tech hub will force them to relocate.
The majority of the residents of Sapang Kawayan, about 47 miles (75 kilometers) north of Manila, are not formally schooled, but they are educated by the ways of nature. Farming cycles are dictated by the monsoon season, and at all times, they are at the whims of a nearby volcano, Mount Pinatubo.
The Philippine government has approved the construction of the Pax Silica hub on a 4,000-acre (1,619 hectare) area inside New Clark City, on land that was part of the U.S. military reservation that included Clark Air Base until the area was returned to the Philippines government in 1991.
Families in the village have already received a letter from the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) informing them they must relocate from the village because it is included in the development plan, Casamira Capiz Maniego, a 72-year-old Aeta resident of Sapang Kawayan, told RFA.
“They should just have us killed because we will fight for our land,” Maniego said. “We have lived for generations in the mountains long before the Americans came. What will happen to us if they take our land?”
Economic and strategic boon
Defense analysts view the 14-country Pax Silica initiative as a symbolic return of the Americans to their former base in the Philippines, Washington’s staunchest ally in the region. But more than that, it is viewed as a plan to keep semiconductor and AI facilities under one U.S.-controlled roof as Beijing rolls out its own, similar initiative.
The larger geopolitical context, however, is not lost on observers, with Manila needing the support of Washington as it faces territorial threats from China, America’s chief rival in the region.
Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has touted the project as one that would “revitalize” the country’s economy and create “quality jobs” for the people. Marcos and top officials have downplayed concerns over potential impacts to the water table and the environment, and fears that the hub would hand too much control to Washington.
“I cannot see how another country can come into the Philippines and, for example, exploit our minerals without the agreement of our Philippine government,” Marcos said in August at a forum organized by the Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines.
The Pax Silica hub will enable the Philippines to process minerals locally instead of exporting ore, Marcos said, adding that once realized, it would be “the Philippines fully exploiting our own treasure, our own national treasure, our own natural resources.”
Many people concerned over the environmental and social impact of the project have organized protests, including one earlier this month, where five paralegals were arrested and nearly 30 others were detained while rallying outside a hotel that had been hosting a business forum about Pax Silica.
Regarding the displacement of the Aetas, the affected area sits roughly within 10 hectares (24 acres) of the 1,600-hectare site, BCDA President and CEO Joshua M. Bingcang told media, including Philippine outlet ABS-CBN, on Monday. He said any relocations would affect an estimated 200 people in 40 households, and they would stay within the same jurisdiction.
“They will not be displaced,” Bingcang said. “They will just be pushed a little bit but they will still be in the same barangay, the same community, the same BCDA land.”
Historical rights?
The Aetas have lived in the rough hinterlands as far back as they can remember, but it was in the 1850s during the Spanish colonial era that authorities formally recognized their presence in decrees, which the Aetas now view as historical proof of their occupation of the land.
Tribal elders believe that even without any piece of paper, the government should recognize their “ancestral domain.”
Spain later ceded the islands to the U.S. and during the time that the Philippines was a U.S. territory, Washington considered the Aetas to be nomadic peoples, displacing many to build Clark Air Base.
The Aetas are gentle hunter-gatherers and crop farmers who generally avoid conflict, Maniego said. They have learned over many years how to co-exist with the “lowlanders,” – what they call Filipinos who live in nearby cities and towns – with some Aeta even working outside of their tiny mountain communities alongside the lowlanders.
Visiting the tribal area is like being transported to an entirely different world, where the trappings of modern-day life are absent. Barefoot children walked on the dirt, while a herd of swamp water buffaloes grazed in the distance. The occasional hum of a motorcycle buzzed nearby as an Aeta caravan carrying wood charcoal slowly negotiated the muddy trail.
Private security guards hired by the BCDA blocked the dirt roads to Maniego’s village, however. RFA managed to reach one remote area by passing through small dirt roads accompanied by three social workers.
Tribal leader Petronila Capiz, 63, argued that their ancestral land was crucial to their story as a people, their heritage and the continued survival of the Aetas. The land, she said, has been passed down from one generation to the next.
People, water, and land
Allowing the government to erect a facility here would be a death knell to their way of life, Capiz said, adding that government surveyors have already been spotted measuring the land and studying the Bangot River, the community’s primary source of water and sustenance.
“It will destroy the environment and our source of water, the Bangot River, where we also fish,” she said. “Water and land, without these we will die. Nature has given us these, and they will just destroy it for the sake of Pax Silica.”
Capiz’ cousin, Nelson de Guzman, 57, was emotional. His weather-beaten face was covered in sweat as he called on fellow Filipinos for support against the multimillion project.
Pax Silica, he said, is like “a gigantic leech that will suck the life out of the soil and mountain.” De Guzman is volunteering to organize tribal communities in other areas to express solidarity with their cause.
“We will resist and fight for our rights,” he stressed. “We are not just fighting for ourselves individually, but for the entire tribe.”
Edited by Eugene Whong. Jojo Riñoza contributed to this report from Capas.

title: Keeping Indigenous Memory Alive Through Music, Language, and Storytelling
content: Keeping Indigenous Memory Alive Through Music, Language, and Storytelling Country South Africa agnes Wed, 09/23/2026 - 10:02 Issues Languages and Cultures Program 5 Main Image By Byron Tenesaca (Kichwa Kañari, CS Staff) Across Indigenous communities, culture is not something preserved only in museums or history books. It lives in songs, languages, instruments, stories, dances, and the knowledge carried from one generation to the next. But as globalization, displacement, and other pressures reshape Indigenous communities, many of these traditions are at risk of being lost. Indigenous youth are using their own voices and creative practices to keep their cultures alive. Through Cultural Survival’s Indigenous Youth Fellowship Program, young Indigenous leaders are developing projects that strengthen cultural identity and create new ways for their communities to share and transmit ancestral knowledge. In South Africa, musician, educator, and composer Asakhe Cuntsulana is using music, research, storytelling, and community engagement to help ensure that Indigenous musical traditions remain living practices passed on to future generations. Reviving the Sound and Story of the uHadi For South African musician, educator, and composer Asakhe Cuntsulana, music is a way of remembering, healing, and reconnecting with community. As a member of the amaXhosa community, Asakhe has built his work around Indigenous music and the stories it carries. His studies in music at Rhodes University, combined with his work with artists and cultural historians, have enabled him to explore how traditional African sounds can speak to contemporary audiences. Through his work as founder of IThala leAfrika, he promotes Ubuntu, arts, and literature while creating spaces for people to reflect on and celebrate Africa’s diverse cultural heritage. At the heart of Asakhe’s work is the uHadi, the traditional Xhosa bow harp. For generations, Indigenous instruments and the music surrounding them have carried histories, spiritual knowledge, relationships with nature, and ways of understanding the world. Yet much of this knowledge is increasingly vulnerable as younger generations are influenced by globalization and changing cultural practices. For Asakhe, preserving the uHadi is therefore about much more than saving an instrument. It is about protecting the stories, techniques, meanings, and relationships that give the instrument its cultural significance. His project also brings the uHadi into dialogue with the Adungu, a traditional harp from Uganda, creating a pan-African exchange around Indigenous musical traditions. By connecting musical practices across African communities, Asakhe’s work explores how traditional instruments can serve as bridges between histories, cultures, and generations. This vision is at the center of Ingoma yoHadi (Song of the Harp), a project that brings together music, research, storytelling, and publication. Asakhe is developing a music album featuring compositions that blend the sounds of the uHadi, Adungu, and other traditional instruments, while a companion book will document the instruments’ histories, oral narratives, playing techniques, and roles in traditional and contemporary music. The project builds on preliminary work that began in 2024 through live performances and the development of the concept. By bringing together musicians, cultural historians, and visual artists, Asakhe hopes to create a living archive that can reach both community members and wider audiences. Rather than treating Indigenous music as something fixed in the past, the project recognizes tradition as something that can continue to evolve while remaining connected to its cultural roots. The project will also create opportunities for knowledge to be shared directly within communities. Through local workshops, participants will learn how to play the uHadi and Adungu while exploring their cultural significance. Multimedia materials, exhibitions, online platforms, and public engagements will further extend these stories beyond the performance space. For Asakhe, this is a way of ensuring that Indigenous music remains a living practice rather than becoming something remembered only through historical records. By combining performance with documentation, education, and storytelling, he is creating opportunities for younger generations to encounter traditional music not simply as an artifact of the past, but as a source of creativity and connection in the present. Ingoma yoHadi is ultimately an invitation to hear the voices of the ancestors in traditional instruments while making space for younger generations to create their own songs.

title: Pearce ready to carve place in AFL history with Freo
content:
Fremantle captain and Tasmanian export Alex Pearce leads team into AFL grand final
In short:
Tasmanian footballer Alex Pearce can create history on Saturday by becoming the Fremantle Football Club's first-ever AFL premiership captain.
Pearce was born and raised on Tasmania's north-west coast, where resilience is bred, and sport reigns supreme.
What's next?
On Saturday, Fremantle face the Brisbane Lions, who are chasing a three-peat, having won the previous two years in a row.
If Fremantle wins the AFL premiership, the year 1995 will not only be known as the year the Dockers entered the AFL.
It'll be known as the birth year of the club's first-ever premiership captain.
Ruth Forrest was not only there on June 9, 1995, at the North West Regional Hospital in Burnie — she was the midwife who delivered Alex Pearce into the world.
"He was a beautiful, big baby," she says.
"And when you hold these babies in your hand after they're born, there's just this unlimited potential in every child."
Thirty-one years later, Pearce stands on the doorstep of football immortality.
Ms Forrest, who Tasmanians know as the independent member for Murchison in the state's upper house, has kept tabs on Pearce since he was a newborn.
"He's just this genuine, inspirational leader. That's what he is," she said.
"To see him grow up into that, it must be huge pride for his family, and I share a tiny bit of that."
Young Alex wanted to play cricket at the MCG
Forrest may have delivered Pearce, but it was parents Scott and Karen who raised him on the coast, in the cradle of Tasmanian sport.
Mum and sister Georgia were star equestrian riders, while Dad was a gun cricketer for Ulverstone.
He still umpires and administers the regional competition, while Uncle Jason remains as president of the Ulverstone Cricket Club.
For young Alex, cricket was the great constant.
"I played my last game of cricket ever with Alex, in a second grade grand final," Scott said.
But footy was in the blood too.
Grandfather Wayne Pearce was a goal machine for the Ulverstone Robins in the 1960s.
"As a kid growing up, his main aim was to play in a Boxing Day Test at the MCG in cricket,"Scott said.
"It's funny how things work out. He's now going to play at the MCG in a grand final as captain of an AFL team, so he got there in the end."
Scott still has to remind himself that his son is indeed on the brink of becoming an AFL premiership captain — a title he never thought Alex would hold.
"Christ, no," he said.
"We knew he had some ability as a junior; he had a growth spurt, played one year with the Tassie Mariners. He didn't play too bad."
"But he wasn't a stand-out player. He was okay," he said.
Out of nowhere, Pearce, who stands 200 centimetres, was drafted to the Dockers at pick 37 in 2013.
From there, he flourished, and the traits that would see him named Dockers captain began to blossom — loyalty, justice and trademark north-west coast resilience that was tested when he fractured his leg twice and didn't play for almost two years.
He forged a connection with a number of Fremantle's First Nations players and began to explore and celebrate his own identity as a Palawa man.
It's a pursuit that his dad is particularly proud of, and that inspired him to delve into his own ancestry.
"It's something I need to do more of, but I'm glad that I've looked into a little bit of it so far," he said.
"As a rule, you didn't look too much into that in years gone by, when I was a kid and in early adulthood.
"But we're very proud of the way he represents the Indigenous people of Tasmania, and it's something he's very proud of as well"
Ulverstone painting the town purple
Then came the confidence, and the individuality.
During COVID, Pearce decided to grow his hair out and pierce his own nose.
Scott said he "doesn't care much about that stuff" — but that he took the news of the piercing "better than his mother did".
Scott's job requires him to be on the road, hopping between Ulverstone, Devonport and Burnie.
His shifts run a little longer, due to locals bailing him up to talk footy, cricket and Alex.
It's indicative of a region where town rivalries are put aside when a coastal son or daughter succeeds.
"We're a footy family and we know Alex personally," Kim Smith, owner of Urban Surf and Co in Ulverstone, said.
"When they won the other night, his mum said to paint the town purple, so we thought why not."
Local real estate agent Jakub Lehman is on board too.
"That's what small communities are there for," he said.
The entire coast is aware of the history that Pearce stands to create if the Dockers defeat Brisbane.
He'd become the third-ever Tasmanian premiership captain, behind the iconic Darrel Baldock and Royce Hart.
And he'd also become the first-ever First Nations-identifying premiership captain.
But to his family, he will still just be Alex — or "Moose".
"That's probably one of the great traits," his dad said.
"He hasn't changed. He hasn't got ahead of himself or anything like that"
"He's just a boy from Ulverstone."

title: When the Páramo Becomes a River: Indigenous Communities Defend Water in Guapondelig, Ecuador
content: When the Páramo Becomes a River: Indigenous Communities Defend Water in Guapondelig, Ecuador Country Ecuador agnes Wed, 09/23/2026 - 09:11 Issues Languages and Cultures Lands, Resources, and Environments Program 5 Main Image By Byron Tenesaca (Kichwa Kañari, CS Staff) In the Andes of southern Ecuador, Indigenous women, youth, and community organizations once again took their territorial defense to the streets of Guapondelig (Cuenca) with their flags, signs, voices, and bodies and with a clear message: water must be protected. On September 16, 2026, hundreds of community members, Indigenous and campesino organizations, students, environmental groups, and residents gathered in Cuenca for the second Quinto Río (“Fifth River”) March in defense of water and the páramos. The mobilization came one year after the first Quinto Río, which brought an estimated 100,000 people into the streets, drawing national attention to concerns about mining in the Kimsakocha páramo and the Loma Larga Project. Cuenca is known as the city of four rivers. But for the people who came from the surrounding mountains, the name Quinto Río carries another meaning: when rural communities come together to defend water, people themselves become a river. Where the Water Begins To understand why people continue to march, it is necessary to travel beyond the city and into the rural communities close to the paramos, where the water gathers to flow downstream. Kimsakocha (whose name in Kichwa refers to three lakes) is a high-altitude páramo landscape and an important water-producing area in the region. Its wetlands and lakes form part of the headwaters of watersheds that sustain communities, agriculture, livestock, and ecosystems farther downstream. For communities, these waters are not simply resources. They are part of a living territory connecting the mountains to everyday life below. The defense of these waters extends into the Yanuncay River Valley, where part of the river’s water also descends from the Kimsakocha landscape in the Andes and flows toward Cuenca. Along its banks, Kañari Kichwa communities are confronting another form of pressure: the proposed Soldados–Yanuncay Hydroelectric Project. Youth Restoring the Territory For Kañari Kichwa youth living in communities along the Yanuncay River, the hydroelectric project is not an abstract infrastructure proposal. It is connected to the places where they live, farm, gather, and maintain relationships with their territory. Young people have joined community efforts to oppose the hydroelectric project, raising concerns about the potential impacts of large-scale infrastructure on the river, páramo ecosystems, agriculture, the local economy, and community life. During Cultural Survival's visit to the Yanuncay River Valley in August, we met a collective of young women, led by Patricia Pulla (Kañari Kichwa), working to restore native plants and páramo water-recharge areas affected by wildfires and climate change. Their project, supported through a Cultural Survival Indigenous Youth Fellowship, offers another way of understanding their relationship with the river: while organizing to defend the territory from threats, they are also actively restoring and caring for it. At the center of their work is a small native plant nursery, which they use to restore sections of the Yanuncay riverbanks and surrounding ecosystems while strengthening ancestral knowledge and creating opportunities for youth to participate in caring for their territory. Patricia Youth Collective During our visit, the young women welcomed us beside their nursery before leading us along the river. Later, we shared traditional food, music, dancing, and stories around a fire. These moments revealed something that is easy to miss when territorial defense is viewed only through protests and political campaigns: protecting territory is also about maintaining the cultural and social fabric that makes a community a community. Their work shows that territorial defense does not begin or end with a march. It happens through planting native species, restoring waterways, sharing knowledge, organizing community activities, and ensuring that younger generations remain connected to the land. Women at the Heart of Territorial Defense The leadership of women is particularly visible in many of the community projects Cultural Survival has been able to support in Ecuador. With many men working outside the community all day or migrating abroad, women have taken on central responsibilities in maintaining everyday community life, organizing, and caring for the territory. Across our visits, women shared a similar understanding: the páramo and rivers are not simply ecosystems to be protected. They are part of a living territory connected to culture, food, livelihoods, memory, and future generations. 30 Years of Organizing for Water Further south, in Tarqui, the Federación de Organizaciones Indígenas y Campesinas del Azuay (FOA), a Cultural Survival community media partner, has spent approximately three decades organizing around the protection of Kimsakocha and the defense of water. Their work has included community organizing, advocacy, legal action, communication, and mobilization. Its community radio station also provides a space for local voices and information, showing how media can become another form of territorial defense. For FOA (led by current president Lauro Sigcha) and the communities it represents, the páramo cannot be separated from the people who depend on its waters. Its wetlands and high-altitude ecosystems help sustain agriculture, livestock, families, and communities throughout the region. Lauro Sigcha The organization has been at the forefront of the long-standing defense of Kimsakocha and opposition to the Loma Larga mining project, a struggle that eventually helped give rise to the formation of Quinto Río. On September 16, that movement once again flowed into the streets of Cuenca, as communities carried banners and signs alongside families and community organizations from the surrounding highlands. Music, dancing, and calls to protect water transformed the historic center into a powerful public expression of a struggle that has been carried forward by generations in the mountains surrounding the city. Youth Imagining a Future in their Territories In Loja, Cultural Survival Indigenous Youth Fellow Tamia Contento, a Saraguro Kichwa youth leader, is working with young people to strengthen self-knowledge, entrepreneurship, livelihoods, and their ability to imagine a future connected to their communities. Her work is unfolding in the Fierro Urco region, where Indigenous and campesino communities are also organizing to protect páramos and water sources from mining pressures. Tamia Contento During our visit, young people spoke about communications, cinema, entrepreneurship, culture, and community life. One young community member imagined bringing films to rural communities as a way of creating spaces for storytelling, communication, and cultural expression. These initiatives show that Indigenous youth are not only defending what already exists. They are creating new possibilities for their communities to remain vibrant and connected to their territories. More Than One River The Quinto Río is one expression of a much broader reality across Ecuador. From the páramos of Azuay and Loja to Indigenous territories elsewhere in the country, communities continue organizing around water, land, forests, and the right to determine what happens in their territories. These struggles take different forms, like community assemblies, legal actions, cultural gatherings, media projects, ecological restoration, youth organizing, and marches, all carrying the message that territory is not simply a source of resources. It is where life is held. For Indigenous communities, protecting water also means protecting culture, food sovereignty, livelihoods, local economies, and the possibility of remaining on and caring for ancestral lands. As the second Quinto Río moved through Cuenca, the people walking its streets carried more than signs and banners. They carried the memory of the mountains, the work of generations, and the voices of communities that continue to organize for the future of their territories. The river begins in the páramo. And on September 16, the people became the river once again. All photos by Byron Tenesaca.

title: HERITAGE & RESTITUTION OP-ED: We walk to remember what apartheid erased of Newlands and Claremont
content:
There is a temptation, on Heritage Day, to reduce our history to braais and bunting, a comfortable, sanitised celebration that costs us nothing and demands nothing. But for the families dispersed from Newlands and Claremont across the wind-blown expanse of the Cape Flats, heritage is neither comfortable nor abstract. It is the memory of a home from which they were torn, an ancestral landscape closer to the mountain that was declared, by the stroke of an apartheid bureaucrat’s pen, to be no longer theirs.
On Thursday, 24 September, the Newlands/Claremont Heritage, Environmental Justice and Restitution Society (NCHERS) will convene its fifth annual Walk of Remembrance through these streets. We walk because remembering is itself a form of resistance. The dispossession of Newlands and Claremont did not begin with the Group Areas Act; it reaches back to the 17th century, to the very foundations of colonial conquest at the Cape. But it was the apartheid forced removals of the 1960s that completed the work, emptying vibrant, mixed neighbourhoods of their people and scattering them to the periphery, out of sight of the leafy suburbs that rose in their place.
What was lost was not merely property. It was a way of living together. NCHERS was founded by two neighbouring houses of worship, St Saviour’s Anglican Church and the Claremont Main Road Masjid, precisely because they stand as living testimony to a community in which Christian and Muslim, and many others besides, lived in mutual coexistence. These sacred spaces are among the few remaining threads connecting the exiled to the homes they were forced to abandon. To this day, many who can no longer live in the area still travel back to worship here, drawn to the last tangible fragment of a stolen belonging.
In the Qur’an we are taught that God made us into nations and tribes that we might come to recognise and know one another (49:13), that diversity is a divine intention, not a problem to be engineered away. Apartheid’s spatial planning was, at its core, a theological heresy as much as a political crime: it declared that people created to know one another must instead be separated, ranked and removed. Our walk is a quiet repudiation of that lie.
This year we begin at the Newlands Cricket Ground and follow a route marked by three stops, each a wound and each a testimony. At Draper Square, off Main Road, former residents will recall the families and institutions that once filled that space, Talfalah Primary School, the Orpheum Bioscope, the ordinary infrastructure of a community that dared to flourish. Passing under the subway, we will pause outside the Stegman Road Masjid to honour the towering witness of Imam Abdullah Haron, who resisted the forced removals and the wider machinery of apartheid, and who was killed in an apartheid detention cell on 27 September 1969.
Our walk falls within days of that date, which this year marks the 57th anniversary of his martyrdom, and that his youngest daughter, Fatima Haron-Masoet, walks with us is a reminder that this history is not distant: it lives and breathes among us still.
Our third stop, at the Cape Town Athenaeum in Mariendahl Lane, honours the life of the mind. This was an intellectual hub, a meeting place for the Teachers’ League of South Africa and the broader Non-European Unity Movement, who understood that liberation begins in the mind long before it is won in the streets. Here teachers turned the instrument of their own subjugation against the regime, refusing to collaborate with tyranny and forging in their pupils a political consciousness that would accept nothing less than full liberation. The Unity Movement’s disciplined philosophy of non-collaboration and boycott, and its refusal of the very racial categories apartheid sought to impose, were among the most rigorous intellectual challenges the system ever faced. Among its foremost teachers was RO Dudley, a towering figure of the Teachers’ League; it is fitting that his son, Russell Dudley, today chairs NCHERS, with Fatima Haron-Masoet as his deputy, standing together to reclaim what was taken.
That this tradition has been all but written out of the popular story of our liberation is itself a form of erasure, a reminder that history is not only made in the places we destroy but in the memories we are permitted to keep. To stand here is to restore the Unity Movement to its rightful place in that history. Then we return, along the railway line and under the bridge, to where we began.
Make the invisible visible again
There is a deliberate lesson in walking these streets on foot. Injustice, when it is spatial, is designed to be invisible to those who benefit from it. One drives past Draper Street without a thought for the school that once stood there; one passes the mosque without knowing an imam was martyred defending his people. To walk slowly, to stop and to name what was taken, is to make the invisible visible again. It is to insist that these places have not always been what they are now, and need not remain so.
This is why NCHERS speaks not only of remembrance, but of restitution. Memory that does not reach towards justice is sentimentality. The families on the Cape Flats remain disconnected from their ancestral land, and the areas from which they were removed retain almost no markers of the lives that once thrived there. The slow, incremental erasure of this history is not accidental; it serves those who would prefer that the moral debt of dispossession quietly expire. Our task is to refuse that expiry, to keep the account open until it is honourably settled.
After the walk, we will gather at the Newlands Cricket Experience Museum to hear the journalist and author Dougie Oakes reflect on the history of anti-apartheid resistance through sport, and on the extraordinary role played by the non-racial South African Council on Sport and its founder, Hassan Howa, whose principle, “no normal sport in an abnormal society”, captured a moral clarity we would do well to recover. That we hold this gathering at a cricket ground, a place where the politics of race and belonging were once fiercely contested, is fitting. It reminds us that the struggle for a just society was waged on every terrain, including the playing field.
We invite Capetonians of every faith and none to join us. Come and walk. Come and remember the sons and daughters of Claremont and Newlands. Come and honour the legacy of Imam Abdullah Haron. And come to affirm, with your feet, a simple and stubborn conviction: that what was unjustly taken must be remembered, named, and one day, God willing, restored.
Heritage, rightly understood, is not a monument to the past. It is a demand upon the present.
The Walk of Remembrance takes place on Thursday, 24 September 2026. The NCHERS AGM begins at 9am at the Newlands Cricket Experience Museum (the Snakepit Building), with the walk departing the Newlands Cricket Ground at 9.30am, followed by Dougie Oakes at 11am. Refreshments and exhibitions will be available. DM
Dr A Rashied Omar is Imam of the Claremont Main Road Masjid and a steering committee member of the Newlands/Claremont Heritage, Environmental Justice and Restitution Society (NCHERS), and teaching professor of Islamic studies and peacebuilding at the Keough School of Global Affairs, University of Notre Dame.

title: 100-year-old seaside church is Vietnam's first climate change heritage site
content:
The century-old structure, which stands outside the current sea dike, is the Church of the Sacred Heart, which is associated with the birth and development of the former fishing village of Xuong Dien, now part of Hai Tien Commune.
It is known more commonly as Hai Ly church.
Xuong Dien was a coastal settlement in the late 17th and early 18th centuries. As people came to settle in the area, they built dikes and reclaimed land from the sea for agriculture and protecting their homes.
In 1885, the Ngo Ham Dike was built to a length of nearly 12 km, helping protect the reclaimed land.
But the place has been constantly affected by storms, waves, and coastal erosion. In 1925, the dike in Hai Ly Beach was breached for three kilometers. In 1990, around 1.5 km was destroyed and a new one had to be built 150 m inland.
By 2005, a 700 m section of the coastline in Xuong Dien was eroded.
Over the last century or so, the sea has swallowed almost a kilometer of coastal land in the area.
The Xuong Dien shoreline has retreated inland due to the combined effects of waves, currents, winds, and storms, with climate change being a contributing factor.
Managing tourism site
Now, authorities in Hai Tien Commune have been tasked with developing and managing the tourism site.
Associate Professor and Doctor of Science Vu Cao Minh, former deputy director of the Institute of Geological Sciences at the Vietnam Academy of Science and Technology, said the current location of the bell tower provides visible evidence of changes in the shoreline and the process by which people reclaimed and protected coastal land.
"The fact that a structure built about 100 years ago now stands on the beach, outside the dike, provides valuable material for studying the history of shoreline changes. It also shows how people have had to continuously reinforce dikes and protect land and production from the forces of nature."
He said the church is not just a relic but also important for its connection with the shoreline, dike, and history of human settlement.
He called it "a special type of heritage in Vietnam and rare in the world."
Internationally, structures affected by erosion, rising sea levels, and natural disasters are preserved for research, community education, and tourism.
In the U.K., for instance, the twin towers of the St Mary's Church in Kent have been preserved as a navigation landmark, and the surrounding ruins illustrate the effects of centuries of coastal erosion.
Minh said these models show that disaster heritage can become a valuable visual record if it is preserved, documented and appropriately developed.
"The value of a heritage site is not simply about preserving a structure, but about helping people understand why the structure is there, how the shoreline has changed and how people have responded. When this is achieved, the site can provide scientific, educational, and tourism benefits."
The area around the Hai Ly church includes Thinh Long Beach with its distinctive culture, cuisine, and fishing life.
Recognition as a tourism site will enable its development as a heritage site and the protection of the remaining structure, landscape, and records documenting changes to the shoreline.

title: After two failed bids, Ipswich remains hopeful of becoming an NRL side
content:
Rugby league has a storied history in Ipswich, and local clubs are pushing for it to become home to the next NRL side.
The Ipswich Jets first made a bid to join the league 16 years ago.
The city's bid is facing strong competition from the Christchurch-based Southern Orcas.
After almost two decades and two failed bids, rugby league diehards in Ipswich are once again dreaming of a place in the NRL.
The league's 20th team is expected to be announced by the end of the year, with the Queensland city's bid facing strong competition from the Christchurch-based Southern Orcas.
"We don't underestimate the fight on our hands," Rugby League Ipswich Chairman David Nugent said.
"[But] don't underestimate an Ipswich person in a fight, we'll give it our all."
Rugby league has been inseparable from the cultural identity of the former coal-mining city since the early 20th century.
It takes hold of people early, often passed down through generations.
David Haug is a perfect example. At the North Ipswich Tigers clubhouse, it's easier to name what he hasn't done at the club.
"I've played since I was under nines … coached everything from under sevens through to A-grade, been on the committee and done everything from committee member to president," he said.
That tends to be how it goes in the former industrial city west of Brisbane.
Here the game takes hold early, often carried through generations.
Ipswich's community sports fields have been a consistent breeding ground of rugby league players.
From Dud Beattie in the 1950s, to Allan "Alfie" Langer in the 1990s, and Broncos NRLW captain Ali Brigginshaw today.
But none have been able to represent their home city at the top level.
"[Ipswich players] get to a certain age … and then get picked up by other Sydney clubs and they don't get a chance to actually come back and play for their city," Mr Haug said.
Player factory
It was this exodus of talent that sparked the first Western Corridor bid in 2010, which also included the Darling Downs city of Toowoomba.
"Our young kids were leaving home at 16 to live their rugby league dreams … and for every 10 that went down the Pacific Highway, nine came back with broken hearts," Ipswich Jets chair Steve Johnson said.
But Mr Johnson, who is spearheading the bid, believes the benefits of the Jets becoming the league's 20th team would spread far beyond Ipswich.
"With the expansion at the moment with PNG and Western Australia, [the NRL] needs more players and we will surely generate more players than we need."
"We'll become a player factory for the entire NRL."
University of Technology Sydney Sports Economics Professor Tim Harcourt said new clubs generally had to bring two things to the NRL: spectators and TV viewers.
"It's definitely rugby league heartland," Mr Harcourt said.
"And secondly, it's attractive economically to have more Brisbane derbies in a sense, because you'll have the Dolphins and Broncos, and then I guess the Jets."
But he believed the Ipswich bid's biggest competitor, the Christchurch-based Southern Orcas, was in a better position to become the NRL's 20th team.
He said Christchurch would be a more attractive destination for travelling fans, which the NRL would likely take into consideration.
"There's a lot of tourism to the South Island of New Zealand already, with Lord of the Rings and all the beautiful landscape."
"They've also got this brand new stadium which is fantastic for all sorts of sports and events, so they're kind of ready to go," Mr Harcourt said.
With no suitable stadium in Ipswich, the Jets would have to play at Brisbane's Lang Park.
The Jets are hoping to turn North Ipswich Reserve into a 12,000-seat rectangular stadium, but are yet to secure all necessary funding.
Eyes turn to next generation
Far removed from the boardroom machinations at Rugby League Central in Sydney, those who have spent decades working at the grassroots level consider an Ipswich NRL team through the eyes of local under-18s players.
"For me, the driving force is every kid involved in sport is one less kid on the street," Redbank Plains Bears President Jodie Elder said.
"For some kids it just means everything. It could be the highlight of their week to come to training."
Rory Morley-Davies plays for the North Ipswich Tigers under-15s side and started playing football at a young age.
"I don't think any other sport fulfils me like rugby does," he said.
"When [people in Ipswich] think of a sport, they don't think of anything other than rugby league."
"Everyone wouldn't want anything else, except for Ipswich to have a rugby league team, and I think it's a long time coming."

title: Ramaphosa lists and praises SA’s heritage traits
content:
Story audio is generated using AI
“Heritage is more than just a celebration of the past, it is the knowledge, traditions and values South Africans pass from one generation to the next,” said President Cyril Ramaphosa during a National Heritage Day celebration keynote address at Bongolethu Sports Stadium in Oudtshoorn, Western Cape, on Thursday.
Ramaphosa said the country’s languages, songs, food, clothing, stories and customs formed part of the heritage that South Africans celebrate.
But, he said, heritage should not remain something remembered only once a year. “Our heritage is living because it resides in people. It lives in our homes and our communities.”
He pointed to grandmothers telling stories to their grandchildren, traditional healers, craftspeople, musicians and dancers as examples of people keeping SA’s heritage alive.
