Ramaphosa also highlighted the importance of ceremonies, faith, rituals and the languages spoken by South Africans every day.
The theme for this year’s Heritage Day is “Celebrating Our Living Heritage: Strengthening the Ties That Bind Us”.
Ramaphosa said the country has a responsibility to make sure indigenous knowledge and traditions were not lost as older generations passed away. “We must record it. We must teach it. We must practise it. And above all, we must pass it on.”
Our constitution is our heritage. It is the tie that binds us together
— President Cyril Ramaphosa
He warned that heritage could disappear if it is not passed from one generation to another, “because a heritage that is not passed from one generation to another eventually ceases to be a living heritage”.
Ramaphosa also spoke about SA’s difficult history, including dispossession, slavery, colonialism, apartheid and forced removals. “South Africans should also remember the resistance, courage and solidarity that helped bring about democracy.”
The decision by South Africans to build one country together after generations of conflict was itself part of the country’s heritage, he said. “Our constitution is our heritage. It is the tie that binds us together.”
The country’s diversity should not be viewed as something that divides the country but rather that the many cultures, languages, religions and histories make South Africa what it is, he said. Heritage should shape the country South Africans want to build — a country where people have opportunities, talent matters more than connections, public office is a responsibility and young people can dream and succeed.
South Africans should be confident about the future without forgetting where they came from, he said. “A nation cannot grow stronger unless its roots are nourished every day by its people.”
Ramaphosa called on South Africans to protect the values of unity, ubuntu and human dignity. “These three — not race, culture, language or geography — truly make us who we are.”

title: Sites of memory in Western Azerbaijan: History of Abilkend village
content:
Sites of memory in Western Azerbaijan: History of Abilkend village
- 24 September, 2026
- 14:40
Western Azerbaijan is a geographical region where hundreds of thousands of Azerbaijanis historically lived. Despite attempts to erase the traces of compatriots in these territories today, it is considered a duty to remember their ancient places of residence in Western Azerbaijan and to stay informed about them.
The purpose of the Sites of Memory of Western Azerbaijan project is precisely to convey information to the younger generation about the native lands of compatriots expelled from their historical homeland.
Sites of Memory of Western Azerbaijan is a joint project by AZfront and a Ukrainian historian working under the pseudonym Kuzari. The project is based on the historical research titled "The Perished Civilization."
During field research conducted between 2021 and 2024 on the territory of modern Armenia, photo and video materials were collected about nearly 600 villages where the ancestors of modern Azerbaijanis originally lived. Information regarding the history of these settlements, their population, and surviving objects of Turkic cultural and historical heritage - such as cemeteries, shrines, mosques, and other monuments - has been systematized.
As part of the project, video materials in Azerbaijani, Russian, and English have been prepared for each village, along with a separate text based on historical sources. The materials will be presented in stages for each settlement.
The authors of the project first presented the history of the Azerbaijani village of Sheki (now Shaki), located in the territory of Armenia.
The new episode recounts the history of the Azerbaijani village of Abilkend (now Noramarg) in Armenia, whose population was subjected to expulsion and deportation on three occasions.
In documents of the Russian Empire and other written sources from the 19th century through the first third of the 20th century, the ancestors of present-day Azerbaijanis were referred to as "Tatars," "Caucasian Tatars," "Tiurks," or "Muslims," Report informs.
Some of the sources referenced in this project also use the terms "Turks," "Tiurko-Tatars," "Islams," or "Myugammedans." Hereafter, "ancestors of the Azerbaijanis" will be used when referring to the period before 1920, while "Azerbaijanis" will be used for the subsequent period.
The names of Abilkend in historical documents:
● during the Tsarist period – Abil-kend, Abul-kend, Abyul-kend
● during the Soviet period – Abilkend, Ablkend, Bulakhly, Bulagli, Bulakhlar, Kalinin Settlement, Kalinin.
In Russian imperial-era sources, the village appeared under the name Abilkend. It was renamed Bulakhly in April 1946 and Kalinin Settlement in the early 1960s. In April 1991, the village was renamed Noramarg as part of a policy of Armenianization and the erasure of Azerbaijani heritage in Armenia.
Since 1995, the village has been part of the Ararat Province of the Republic of Armenia.
From the mid-18th century until the Russian conquest, the territory of the village formed part of the Zangibasar mahal of the Iravan Khanate.
Russia occupied the territory of the Iravan Khanate in 1827, and its incorporation into the Russian Empire was formalized by the 1828 Treaty of Turkmenchay. During the Tsarist period, the village formed part of the Erivan Uyezd of the Erivan Governorate.
Historical population statistics
Between 1829 and 1832, an administrative census of the territories of the former Iravan and Nakhchivan khanates was conducted at the direction of the Russian authorities. According to the census, Abilkend had 85 inhabitants, all of whom were ancestors of the Azerbaijanis.
Tsarist-era statistical records, also cited in Armenian sources, indicate that at various times before 1914 the village was inhabited exclusively or predominantly by ancestors of the Azerbaijanis.
According to the collection of Information about the Caucasus, in 1873, the village had 183 inhabitants, all of whom were ancestors of the Azerbaijanis. Also, according to the Summary of Statistical Data on the Population of the Transcaucasian Krai, Extracted from the 1886 Family Lists, in 1886, the village had 222 inhabitants, all of whom were ancestors of the Azerbaijanis.
Z. Korkotyan, in his book "The Population of Soviet Armenia over the Last Hundred Years (1831–1931)," writes that in 1897, the village had 234 inhabitants, all of whom were ancestors of the Azerbaijanis.
Caucasian Calendar for 1909 says that in 1906, the village had 256 inhabitants, who were predominantly ancestors of the Azerbaijanis. Memorial Book of the Erivan Governorate for 1908 says that in 1908, the village had 256 inhabitants, all of whom were ancestors of the Azerbaijanis.
Caucasian Calendar for 1912 notes that in 1911, the village had 272 inhabitants, who were predominantly ancestors of the Azerbaijanis. Caucasian Calendar for 1915 says that in 1914, the village had 376 inhabitants, who were predominantly ancestors of the Azerbaijanis.
Events of 1918
On May 29, 1918, the government of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic (ADR) ceded Erivan, present-day Yerevan, and several surrounding territories to the Armenians. The First Republic of Armenia was thereby established on territory that had historically been inhabited by ancestors of present-day Azerbaijanis. Within the first few months of its existence, it began to make territorial claims against its neighbors: Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Türkiye (the Ottoman Empire at the time).
Between 1918 and 1920, Dashnaktsutyun, the nationalist party that held power in the Republic of Armenia, carried out ethnic cleansing of the Turkic population in the Erivan Governorate and in other areas, particularly in Zangezur, Karabakh, and Nakhchivan.
On October 20, 1919, the residents of Abilkend appealed to the government of the ADR in a letter in which they reported atrocities committed by the Dashnaks against the Muslim population and asked the government to take them under its protection and accept them as its subjects.
The consequences of the ethnic cleansing are reflected in the 1922 Soviet Armenian census, which recorded the village as destroyed.
Following the proclamation of Soviet rule in Armenia in late 1920, the communist regime fully consolidated its power over the country in 1921. The Azerbaijani population then began returning to the village.
During different periods, the village formed part of the Gamarli and Zangibasar districts (later the Artashat and Masis districts, respectively). During the Soviet period, the territories of the abolished Azerbaijani villages of Reyhanli, Seyidkend, and Gulujan were incorporated into Abilkend.
Azerbaijanis continued to live in Abilkend during the Soviet period as well.
Armenian sources indicate that Azerbaijanis inhabited the village until the late 1980s.
Z. Korkotyan, in his book "The Population of Soviet Armenia over the Last Hundred Years (1831–1931)," writes that in 1926, the village had 40 inhabitants, 36 of whom were Azerbaijanis.
In 1931, the village had 75 inhabitants, all of whom were Azerbaijanis.
Between 1948 and 1953, the Soviet authorities carried out the deportation of Azerbaijanis from the Armenian SSR to the Azerbaijan SSR. As a result, part of Abilkend's population was forcibly resettled to the territory of Azerbaijan.
A. P. Manvelyan and G. M. Martirosyan, in their book "Settlements and Population of the Armenian SSR over the Period 1831–1959," note that in 1959, the village had 413 inhabitants, who were predominantly Azerbaijanis.
T. Kh. Hakobyan, St. T. Melik-Bakhshyan and H. Kh. Barsegyan, in their "Dictionary of Toponymy of Armenia and Adjacent Territories," say that in 1970, the settlement had 741 inhabitants. In 1979, the settlement had 1690 inhabitants.
During the Soviet period, the organized resettlement of Armenians from abroad to Armenia took place. This is also confirmed by former residents of the village.
Sulduz Khalilov, who was born in Abilkend in 1965 and lived there until November 1988, recalls: "Armenians accounted for 38 percent of the population of Masis, and the rest were Azerbaijanis. At the time, we were told that the law required the secretary to be Azerbaijani. Later, Armenians from Lebanon and elsewhere were brought to Masis … in 1982–1983 so that they would make up the majority."
In the late 1980s, as a result of Armenian territorial claims to Karabakh and escalating tensions between the two republics, Azerbaijanis were permanently driven out of the territory of the Armenian SSR.
Sulduz Khalilov: "Thus, in 1988, we were all driven out… We were openly told to leave. During the last two months [September–October 1988], the village was subjected to nighttime raids. No one was specifically responsible for protecting us. The troops had either been disbanded, or something else had happened, but it went as far as armed raids."
Between 2021 and 2024, extensive fieldwork was conducted across the territory of Armenia, including in remote mountainous regions. The research was undertaken in preparation for the book The Perished Civilization and focused on identifying and documenting surviving Azerbaijani heritage sites. During the fieldwork, an Azerbaijani cemetery containing several dozen damaged tombstones was discovered in Abilkend.

title: ‘Identity is who we are’: Nhlanhla Kunene on his Zulu roots, Heritage Day and preserving culture in the modern age
content:
As South Africa celebrates Heritage Day, actor Nhlanhla Kunene reflects on identity and the importance of young people understanding their roots.
For actor Nhlanhla Kunene, Heritage Day reminds South Africans who they are, where they come from and the generations that came before them.
Heritage Day is celebrated annually in South Africa on 24 September to recognise and celebrate the country’s diverse cultures, traditions and history.
Kunene, who currently plays Mxolisi on Kwa’Baba and previously appeared on Skeem Saam, spoke to The Citizen about his Zulu identity, the role of entertainment in preserving culture and why young people should take the time to understand their roots.
“Culture, identity and heritage are who we are, so it’s very important to celebrate them,” Kunene said.
He said the demands of modern life can sometimes cause people to lose sight of their roots.
“Because of our busy schedules, we can sometimes forget where we come from and where we gain our strength and power. Heritage Month helps to solidify that reminder.”
‘It comes from home’
Kunene said his connection to his Zulu heritage was shaped by his upbringing, which included lessons about what it meant to be Zulu and how to carry himself.
“It comes from home. I am Zulu and I was raised speaking isiZulu, so culture and identity have always been part of how I was brought up,” he said.
“We were taught that when you walk, you are carrying the lineages and generations of people who came before you.
“That is something that has stayed with me. It reminds me that identity is not just about how people describe you; it is connected to where you come from and how you were raised,” he said.
Kunene added that understanding one’s identity also requires an understanding of family and lineage.
“Knowing who you are goes deeper into understanding your family, your relatives and your lineage. For example, knowing your family connections and understanding who you are related to can shape the way you live and the choices you make.”
The role of entertainment in preserving culture
Kunene believes popular culture and entertainment can also play a role in keeping African heritage visible, particularly among young people who consume content on social media.
“Popular culture and entertainment can play a big role because young people are constantly consuming content, particularly on social media,” he said.
He said cultural representation should remain part of the content being produced.
“There is often a focus on flashy lifestyles, and sometimes content can feel like it is speaking from other people’s experiences or becoming too Westernised. I think there should always be a dash of culture in the content we create.”
Language, he said, is another area where entertainment can make a difference.
“We have children growing up who don’t fully understand or speak their home languages, whether they are growing up in townships or suburbs.”
“Social media is such a big part of young people’s lives, so incorporating culture into the content they consume can help remind them where they come from.”
‘Identity and respect go hand in hand’
Kunene said he would like to see more young South Africans take the time to learn about their backgrounds and the generations that came before them.
“I think our generation needs to understand who they are, where they come from and what kind of people their forefathers were,” he said.
He also believes identity is connected to respect and values passed down through generations.
“Identity and respect go hand in hand. There are certain core principles that come from our lineages, and because life is moving so fast, people can sometimes forget those principles.”
He said young people should make an effort to understand and appreciate those aspects of their heritage.
“I feel our generation needs to take the time to understand and appreciate those things.”

title: Gather 'Round, Willie Birch Is Speaking
content:
Gather 'Round, Willie Birch Is Speaking
Across five decades of work, he always asked: What's my neighborhood, and what does it need?
LOS ANGELES — Imagine sitting next to your favorite uncle. Or rather, you’re a child perched on his lap, enraptured by the tales he tells of things he’s seen and places he’s been. He draws you in with his eloquence, the vividness with which he can animate and transfer the world he’s explored into your own mind. You can taste, hear, and feel everything he’s sharing with you, right where you are. Willie Birch: Stories To Tell is an exhibition that plants every viewer in that position: safely ensconced in the sphere of sharing. At the California African American Museum, this career retrospective of Birch — his first ever — spans over five decades of work across multiple mediums and cities.
Weaving chronologically through Birch’s life and art, this exhibition gives one the sense that he has a keen interest in people — at large, but especially Black people. There is an affinity for observing community practices, ways individuals navigate the world, and how past actions influence and inform present activities.
The exhibition begins in the 1970s, a decade when Birch seemed amused by patterns of behavior. His work from this period comments on and codifies how people move within Black traditions and histories. There is “Voodoo Series #1” (1978–79), a mixed-media work based in Xerox collage that marries symbols of ancient spiritual and medicinal practices with then-burgeoning household technology. Or “Passages” (1982), a literal rumination on movement across oceans with carved, brown wooden bodies on a painted water-like surface. The figures are arranged like a second-line parade from Birch’s hometown of New Orleans, their faces either appearing serene or portending great danger. After moving to New York City in 1975, Birch created “New York City Jazz Series” (1978) — a gridded painting of invented symbols, pictograms, and hieroglyphs — to mimic jazz musical notation and codify the goings-on of his new environment.
New York grows more prominent as the exhibition moves into the second major era of Birch’s work, when he began introducing paper-mâché to his technique. Graphite, charcoal, and acrylic paint form large-scale New York scenes like short stories, while paper-mâché frames extend the core ideas of these works. Three-dimensional touches and debossed words give context to Birch’s thinking at the time. Works like “Keeping Up with the Iran-Contra Hearings” (1987) and “Birthday Celebration for Nelson Mandela” (1988) reflect the concerns of New York City's Black community with its leading figures while situating those concerns within the broader national and political issues shaping life in the city.
The wall-hanging pieces give way to a new era in Birch’s work: life-size figures. Variously hued Black bodies animate the exhibition space, posed as if telling their own stories. From smaller, sconce-sized sculptures like “For Alex Haley” (1993) to figures that could fill a room, each lifelike presentation represents a layered aspect of Black existence. “Memories of the ‘60s” (1992) is a sprawling, intricate quilt of important events from the Civil Rights Movement. Centered on the words of Malcolm X and Martin Luther King Jr., the quilt rests across the knees of a woman with grayed locs sewing in the final seams; a gold Gye Nyame, an Adinkra symbol that gives praise to God, hangs around her neck. It’s an arresting piece, not only for its gargantuan size but for the simultaneous serenity and gravity it elicits. It also ushers viewers into a larger gallery of Birch’s more recent work.

title: Zuenir Ventura, Vigário Geral e a cidade que ainda precisa se encontrar
content:
Conheci Zuenir Ventura em 1993, em Vigário Geral. A comunidade ainda vivia o luto pela chacina que assassinara 21 moradores. Naquele domingo, estávamos ali com o Grupo Cultural AfroReggae para realizar uma atividade que durou o dia inteiro. Havia crianças, música e o esforço de construir, junto com os moradores, um espaço de convivência em meio à dor. Era o AfroReggae em seus primórdios, e eu fazia parte daquela organização.
Eu também integrava o Centro de Articulação das Populações Marginalizadas, o CEAP, onde atuava na articulação da juventude negra. Estavam conosco o saudoso Jorge Damião, outro diretor do CEAP, José Júnior, Teco Rastafari, Mônica, Arcélio Farias, Marcelo Yuka e tantos outros companheiros daquela caminhada. José Júnior e Teco Rastafari estavam entre os criadores do AfroReggae e seguem ligados à sua direção. Marcelo Yuka, também saudoso, seria conhecido como um dos criadores e fundadores da banda O Rappa. Naquele tempo, eu era o Big Richard, um jovem do hip-hop que encontrava na cultura uma forma de organização e luta. Zuenir também estava lá. Foi assim, dividindo um dia de trabalho em Vigário Geral, que nossas histórias se cruzaram.
Ao final da atividade, o comando local da Polícia Militar decidiu interromper o evento. Até então, tudo transcorria de forma tranquila. A polícia entrou na comunidade e nos tratou como suspeitos, como se a presença de jovens negros organizando cultura e convivendo com os moradores bastasse para nos associar ao crime. Houve tiros, repressão e medo. Saímos dali com a ajuda de moradores que, mesmo expostos à violência, nos protegeram.
Guardo uma lembrança muito nítida daquele contraste. Durante o dia, tínhamos visto o que uma comunidade era capaz de fazer por suas crianças e por sua própria vida coletiva. Ao anoitecer, vimos a facilidade com que uma ação cultural podia ser tratada como ameaça. Para nós, jovens negros, aquela abordagem tinha um significado conhecido: a suspeita chegava antes de qualquer pergunta.
Escrevi sobre o episódio no AfroReggae Notícias, jornal publicado pelo grupo. A imprensa carioca também registrou o ocorrido. Mais tarde, Zuenir o retratou em Cidade partida, livro que considero um clássico. Nas páginas da obra, ele registrou também minha atuação na juventude negra e no hip-hop naquele período. Ver aquela experiência narrada por alguém que estivera conosco tinha um peso especial. Zuenir conhecia a cena, as pessoas e o trabalho que tentávamos construir.
O título de seu livro continuou a me acompanhar. A cidade partida estava diante de nós naquele domingo: uma cidade na qual a entrada de um grupo cultural numa favela podia despertar desconfiança policial, enquanto os moradores precisavam proteger quem tinha ido até lá para estar com eles. A chacina já havia mostrado, da maneira mais cruel, o valor desigual atribuído às vidas no Rio de Janeiro. O que vivemos depois expunha outra parte dessa mesma lógica, presente até em um dia dedicado à música e às crianças.
A morte de Zuenir, em 22 de setembro, me devolve àquele encontro. Penso no repórter que foi a Vigário Geral e acompanhou de perto seus moradores. Penso também no homem com quem, desde então, desenvolvi uma relação de carinho. Sempre que nos encontrávamos, havia o reconhecimento de quem compartilhara um momento difícil e guardava dele uma memória comum.
Neste setembro, pouco antes de receber a notícia de sua partida, estive novamente no Rio de Janeiro. Era o mês do meu aniversário. Moro hoje em Salvador, cidade que também conhece a violência e as marcas profundas da desigualdade. Volto ao Rio sempre que posso, mas desta vez o retorno ao Rio Comprido, meu bairro de origem, me atingiu de maneira particular. Caminhei por lugares que fazem parte da minha história e tive a sensação de que aquela cidade que chamávamos de partida agora está fraturada, sangrando a céu aberto.
Não escrevo isso como quem se espanta com uma realidade que acaba de descobrir. Conheço o Rio, suas potências e suas feridas. Talvez tenha sido justamente por conhecê-lo que o choque tenha sido tão forte. O tempo passou, muita coisa mudou na minha vida e na vida daqueles companheiros de 1993, mas certas cenas continuam familiares demais. A distância entre a cidade que se apresenta ao mundo e aquela vivida por seus moradores segue sendo medida no direito de circular, de criar os filhos, de fazer cultura e de voltar para casa.
:: Quer receber notícias do Brasil de Fato RJ no seu WhatsApp? ::
Hoje assino Richard Santos. Sou professor da Universidade Federal do Sul da Bahia, fiz pós-doutorado, participo do comitê de acompanhamento das decisões do 9º Congresso Pan-Africano ligado à União Africana e, neste momento, exerço a função de chefe de gabinete da Secretaria de Promoção da Igualdade Racial e dos Povos e Comunidades Tradicionais da Bahia, a Sepromi. Mas o Big Richard nunca deixou de me acompanhar. Ele está presente na maneira como escuto os jovens, como compreendo a força política do hip-hop e como reconheço, em cada território, pessoas criando caminhos onde tantos só enxergam problemas.
É também por carregar essa história que continuo sentindo a cidade partida. Hoje, talvez possamos chamar de país partido a tecnologia social e política que produz essas fraturas, distribui proteção de forma desigual e ensina parte da população a conviver com a dor da outra parte. Às vésperas de mais uma eleição, essa experiência não pode ser reduzida a uma disputa de palavras. Ela diz respeito às condições concretas de vida e às decisões que tomamos sobre o futuro do Brasil.
Escrevo para agradecer a Zuenir por essa convivência e por ter ajudado a registrar uma história que pertence, antes de tudo, aos moradores de Vigário Geral. Escrevo também porque lembrar aquele domingo é lembrar o trabalho de uma geração que respondeu à violência com organização, cultura e presença. Muitos dos companheiros que estiveram ali já partiram. Sua contribuição permanece nas histórias que contamos e nas iniciativas que ajudaram a criar.
Passados mais de trinta anos, ainda precisamos perguntar quanto a cidade mudou para a juventude negra de suas periferias. Essa pergunta atravessa minha lembrança de Zuenir Ventura e me acompanhou na recente volta ao Rio Comprido. Enquanto houver famílias obrigadas a temer a violência policial e jovens cuja participação cultural seja recebida com suspeita, Vigário Geral continuará nos pedindo atenção.
Despeço-me de Zuenir com tristeza e afeto. Foi em Vigário Geral que o conheci. É de lá que hoje me vem a lembrança mais forte dele: presente, atento, compartilhando conosco um dia que não terminou quando saímos da comunidade. Ao recordar aquele domingo, lembro também o compromisso que assumimos ali. O Big Richard de 1993 e o Richard Santos de hoje seguem fazendo a mesma pergunta: que cidade, e que país, estamos dispostos a construir juntos?
*Richard Santos é escritor, pesquisador, docente e extensionista da Universidade Federal do Sul da Bahia (UFSB), onde atua como professor nos Programas de Pós-graduação em Ensino e Relações Étnico-Raciais e em Estado e Sociedade. Possui Pós-doutorado em Cultura e Sociedade pela Universidade Federal da Bahia (UFBA), Doutorado em Ciências Sociais pela Universidade de Brasília (UnB) e Mestrado em Comunicação pela Universidade Católica de Brasília. Coordena o Grupo de Pesquisa Pensamento Negro Contemporâneo. Diretor Regional Nordeste da Sociedade Brasileira de Estudos Interdisciplinares da Comunicação (Intercom). Autor do livro “Maioria Minorizada: um dispositivo de racialidade”.
**Este é um artigo de opinião e não necessariamente representa a linha editorial do Brasil do Fato.

title: Circuito POCAR chega a Arraial d’Ajuda celebrando memórias indígenas e quilombolas da Bahia e do Espírito Santo
content:
Nos dias 25 e 26 de setembro, Arraial d’Ajuda, distrito de Porto Seguro, recebe o Circuito POCAR, com espetáculos teatrais, shows e apresentações ligadas à memória, à ancestralidade indígena e quilombola, e às culturas populares. O evento de origem capixaba é promovido pelo Instituto Cultural Tambor de Raiz, tem entrada gratuita e será realizado no adro da Igreja de Nossa Senhora d’Ajuda.
Criado em Conceição da Barra, no Espírito Santo, o Circuito POCAR nasceu do POCAR Festival de Cultura, que tem como objetivo levar a outros territórios a proposta artística e formativa desenvolvida pelo Instituto Cultural Tambor de Raiz. A edição em Arraial d’Ajuda marca a chegada da iniciativa à Bahia e promove o encontro entre produções capixabas, artistas locais e diferentes manifestações culturais brasileiras.
Didito Camillo, presidente do Instituto Cultural Tambor de Raiz, ressalta que o festival gera um grande impacto para os artistas participantes e para a instituição: “e também para o público, que vai ter uma pincelada de cultura capixaba com cultura baiana. Quem for ao Circuito POCAR vai presenciar um intercâmbio, um momento histórico”, afirma.
Camillo destaca que, apesar das cinco horas de distância entre as regiões, historicamente existem vários pontos em comum entre os territórios e povos. “A região do Sapê do Norte fez parte da capitania de Porto Seguro, e a produção de farinha de mandioca do Sapê do Norte contribuiu muito para a subsistência da região”, comenta.
A partir do encontro de artistas e saberes tradicionais do Espírito Santo e da Bahia, o Circuito apresenta uma programação cultural rica que valoriza a memória indígena e quilombola. Na sexta-feira (25), a abertura conta com o teatro do Instituto Cultural Tambor de Raiz abordando as vivências do Sapê do Norte, seguido pelo ritual e música da Reserva Pataxó Porto do Boi e show de Hemaidan e Banda. Já no sábado (26), as atividades começam com o espetáculo cômico infantil de Vitor Passarim e a apresentação da Família Aldeia Música Medicina e Ancestralidade; após a missa no Santuário, a noite é embalada pelas misturas sonoras da banda Maria Horta e finalizada com o tradicional forró pé de serra do Trio Fogumano.
Do festival ao circuito itinerante
Idealizado pelo Instituto Cultural Tambor de Raiz, o POCAR Festival de Cultura foi realizado pela primeira vez em 2013, em Conceição da Barra, para celebrar o reconhecimento do conjunto arquitetônico da Praça da Matriz como Patrimônio Histórico e Artístico do Espírito Santo. Desde então, o projeto ampliou sua atuação, fortaleceu a produção artística regional e reuniu patrimônio, manifestações populares, gastronomia, educação e diferentes linguagens artísticas.
O Circuito POCAR amplia esse trabalho para além do município de origem. Com atividades gratuitas, a iniciativa busca fomentar a produção cultural em cidades capixabas e de outros estados, favorecer o intercâmbio entre artistas e comunidades e ampliar o acesso do público à cultura.
De acordo com Didito Camillo, existe a intenção de expandir o circuito para outros locais: “queremos levar para outros territórios no sul da Bahia, quem sabe Salvador, e temos propostas de expansão para algumas cidades do Centro-Oeste. Além disso, este ano o Circuito POCAR ainda vai acontecer em Aracruz (ES) e Curitiba (PR)”, conclui.

title: In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
url: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019060/In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
content:
In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
SHANGHAI – At the Sept. 19 Shanghai premiere of her feature debut, “Shanghai Daughter,” Shen Zhongmin carried a rubber seed from the forests of the Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture, nearly 3,000 kilometers away in southwestern China’s Yunnan province, where her late father had worked.
“The seed fell from the canopy and struck me as I retraced his life there,” Shen, 41, tells Sixth Tone.
Her father was among the millions of urban Chinese youths “sent down” to work in rural areas under the Down to the Countryside Movement, a campaign that ran from the mid-1950s through the late 1970s. He spent a decade on a state-run rubber farm near China’s border with Myanmar but rarely spoke to his daughter about those years.
Shen, who works professionally as Agnis Shen, first traveled to Xishuangbanna in 2011, the year after her father died. A former culture editor at the Shanghai-based magazine The Bund and the author of “The Traveler’s Desire,” a collection of short fiction. She returned to the region repeatedly, retracing her father’s life and meeting people from his generation.
Nearly a decade after her first trip, those encounters and widespread coverage of a herd of wild Asian elephants wandering north from Xishuangbanna helped inspire the idea for a film. The herd’s journey drew attention to the rubber plantations that had transformed parts of the region’s rainforest habitat.
Blending fiction with documentary methods, “Shanghai Daughter” follows Ming, a fictional Shanghai woman played by Liang Cuishan, as she seeks out her father’s former acquaintances in Xishuangbanna.
She encounters workers’ dormitories facing demolition and a landscape where mining and modern agriculture are replacing former rubber plantations. She also meets rubber tappers, village doctors, ethnic Dai villagers, and ecological researchers, all of whom appear as themselves and recount their own experiences.
“The film asks how we deal with memory,” Shen says. “When you want to understand something from the past but cannot find reliable firsthand records, how do you search for the answers?”
“Shanghai Daughter” had its world premiere in the Panorama section of the Berlin International Film Festival in February and was later selected for the Hong Kong International Film Festival and the Malaysia International Film Festival.
Seven months later, the film’s Shanghai premiere drew at least a dozen former sent-down youths from the city, all now in their 70s. They traveled about an hour by subway to attend.
At the theater, they shared old photographs from their years in Xishuangbanna, including images taken with Shen’s father, Shen Wanxiong, and posed for a group photo with the director.
Among them was Shen Weilong, 73, a former rubber tapper who had worked alongside Shen Wanxiong and describes him as his best friend. Looking at one of the photographs, he jokes, “This one doesn’t show just how handsome he was. If you want to know what he looked like, just look at his daughter.”
As he speaks about his generation, tears well in his eyes. “Our generation is rarely talked about, and now our time is running out,” he says.
Sixth Tone spoke with Shen Zhongmin the following day as she continued a multi-city promotional tour. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.
Sixth Tone: Not a single scene in “Shanghai Daughter” was shot in Shanghai. Why did you choose the title, and what does it mean to you?
Shen: “Shanghai daughters” was originally a local term. Villagers near the farms used it for daughters left behind by sent-down youths. Over time, the label seemed to replace each woman’s real name.
Because of my father’s history, I am also, in a sense, a “Shanghai daughter,” and so I went there too. In Xishuangbanna, the phrase took on a double meaning for me. It suggested a kind of twin existence, like looking in a mirror. We seemed to have completely different yet intersecting destinies, one born in Shanghai and the other 3,000 kilometers away in Xishuangbanna.
To me, “daughter” carries something different from either “woman” or “boy.” One of the first Dai expressions my father taught me was “long yin,” meaning “girl.” The image of a girl carries a particular gentleness that can help heal or ease the deep wounds and heaviness behind this subject. The emotional connection extends beyond father and daughter to one girl and another, and one daughter and another.
I did not want to remain trapped within a particular historical wound or view that period only through criticism. I hoped to create something relevant to the present and oriented toward the future, an expression of repair, renewed empathy, and hope.
Sixth Tone: By telling the story from a daughter’s perspective, the film approaches the sent-down youth movement through one family. How does that perspective differ from other portrayals of the movement?
Shen: This is a deeply personal and highly artistic undertaking. It emphasizes experiencing and observing our surroundings and sensory world anew.
While writing the screenplay, I did extensive research. I gathered oral histories, consulted historical archives, and reconnected with researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences who study rainforest restoration. But I wanted to hold back those “concrete” materials for as long as possible and put perception first. Thoughts and opinions can easily create divisions, and once expressed, they have their limits. Perception, however, can be shared and remains more open.
Later, an academically minded journalist asked whether this might be related to ecofeminism. I thought the observation was perceptive. It points toward a perspective that moves beyond anthropocentrism and rejects a structure in which “I am the center, and everyone else is the other.”
Sixth Tone: Rubber trees, dragon fruit, and other elements of the landscape recur throughout the film. How did you use them to connect personal memory with the region’s history?
Shen: During my fieldwork in Xishuangbanna, I often walked around whenever I had time. I gradually came to see the landscape itself as a theater. All the legends and stories I had heard, with their intense dramatic and emotional tension, lay silently buried in a small hill in the village.
Generations have cultivated different crops there, from rice and corn to bananas and, more recently, dragon fruit. A small patch of primary forest protected by the Dai people remains on the hillside. Beneath the present landscape lie my father’s old dormitory and the former rubber plantation.
People disappear faster than memories, but stories spanning more than half a century survive in the land’s subtle traces. When you look at the plants and the land and listen to their voices, it feels as if they are telling you stories, though not in a language humans can hear.
I brought the rubber seed to the screening because, to me, it represents a transformation of cause and effect. More than half a century ago, people had little choice but to clear primary rainforest and plant rubber trees to meet the needs of national development. We now understand that this harmed local biodiversity.
A Chinese Academy of Sciences team is rehabilitating degraded rubber groves. Its goal is not to return them to primary rainforest, which would be scientifically unsound, but to rebalance relationships among species. The researchers are restoring poor-quality groves left by haphazard planting and tapping and introducing species that can bridge rubber plantations and native tropical rainforest. By giving the rubber trees a range of “good neighbors,” they can gradually restore the ecosystem’s layers.
To me, they are taking the “effect” of an earlier decision and planting within it a new, positive “cause,” one that may bear better fruit in the future. The relationship between seed and fruit becomes a metaphor for the transformation of cause and effect. I find that deeply inspiring.
Making the film also took me to Malaysia, where I saw some of the country’s earliest rubber trees. Without that initial transplantation, rubber would not have been planted on such a large scale in Xishuangbanna, and many of these stories would not exist.
Sixth Tone: Why did you blend fiction and documentary methods rather than make a conventional documentary centered on your own search?
Shen: I have always felt that the boundary between reality and fiction is unclear, much like the line between dreams and waking life. Historical narratives also have a dreamlike quality for me, something I have explored in my fiction.
If I had relied on documentary methods alone to examine the sent-down youth movement or my relationship with my father, the film would have felt too narrow.
I drew on my own experience to present subjects I have long cared about in a more contemporary, open form. If I had appeared as myself and made a pure documentary, the film would have become too narrow, confined by the standards of historical fact and leaving viewers less room to project themselves into it and experience it openly.
Sixth Tone: How did you approach your father’s past and his former co-workers while making the film? How did they respond after the premiere?
Shen: My father rarely spoke about the decade he spent in Xishuangbanna. People of his generation generally do not talk about those experiences.
You could sense a deep wound behind the way an older audience member spoke yesterday. At times, his questions seemed to judge other people, but they ultimately revealed his own views and emotions.
I didn’t even know my father had tapped rubber. He had never told me what work he did there. Only when I first walked into the plantation did I understand that these were rubber trees and that his generation had planted and tapped them.
At first, I avoided contacting my father’s former co-workers. I knew they would be eager to help and provide a great deal of firsthand material. But the film began with the particular relationship between my father and me. He had told me very little and died before I could learn more, so I went there to search for and reconstruct that missing part of his life.
I also did not want to disturb them for what was, after all, a small personal project. Revisiting those experiences can be extremely painful, especially for some of them.
Since yesterday’s premiere, I have spent all morning replying to their messages. Today, they are gathering for a reunion lunch to discuss the film.
One of my father’s former co-workers wrote: “Thank you to the screenwriter, creative team, and director for bringing a fitting close to our 50 years as sent-down youths.”
Editor: Apurva.
(Header image: A still from “Shanghai Daughter.” Courtesy of Shen)
